Preface




     Writing a grammar is a profoundly humbling experience. Languages are almost unbe-
lievably complex and represent the richest traditions that we as human beings possess. What
remotely compares with them, whether we are considering the massively intricate and fluid
physical gestures involved in the articulation of sounds, or the systems behind the thousands
of possibilities of distinct expression in the verb system of a language such as Nishnaabem-
win? A language is a natural object with a beauty and a capacity to inspire awe on the order
of Niagara Falls or Lake Superior, if we take the time to appreciate it. Writing a reference
grammar provides the enjoyment of thousands of hours of careful scrutiny, though at the
same time one realizes acutely the truth of Michael Krauss's statement that a hundred lin-
guists working for a hundred years could never get to the bottom of a single language. Nish-
naabemwin is a language exceedingly rich in structure, inviting many levels of analysis—it
is an inexhaustible source of pleasure and challenge for its students.
     This grammar is designed to be useful to a variety of readers, including researchers,
Nishnaabemwin teachers, and any diligent student of the language. At the back of the gram-
mar can be found an extensive index, and a glossary of almost all of the grammatical termi-
nology used throughout. Crucially, the index also lists all finals introduced in Chapters 9
through 11, which are not individually identified in the table of contents, under the heading
 'finals.' Something in the vicinity of 5,000 items of vocabulary are organized into coherent
structural and notional systems. The table of contents provides a detailed map of the gram-
mar as well. There are a couple of thousand example sentences, and each is provided with a
complete analysis of the grammatical properties of every word. This wealth of material by
no means serves to exhaust the topics addressed. In fact, the very extensiveness of the gram-
mar underscores how much we have to learn before we even begin to fathom the real intri-
cacies and richness of the language. This is the barest beginning, one that any fluent speaker
could easily double or triple in size with the least bit of reflection.
     The overall structure of the book is as follows: the first chapter introduces the language,
discusses dialect variation, the Algonquian language family, Anishinaabemowin dialects,
and sub-dialects within Nishnaabemwin. There is also a brief discussion of the kinds of
information that speakers of a language employ in speaking, and therefore, must be
accounted for in a grammatical description. The second chapter addresses the sound pat-
terns and writing system of the language. The third chapter introduces the parts of speech,
and the grammatical categories associated with each. Chapters 4 through 8 treat the inflec-
XXX11



tion of the primary lexical word classes, nouns, animate intransitive verbs, inanimate intran-
sitive verbs, transitive animate verbs, and transitive inanimate verbs. Chapters 9 through 11
treat the derivational morphology of the language, focussing first on intransitive verbs, then
transitive, then nouns and adverbs. Chapters 12 through 18 treat various aspects of lexicon
and syntax, including chapters addressing the structure and function of nominals, predi-
cates, expressions of location and manner, time and certainty, and quantity and degree. The
final chapter provides a general discussion of syntactic issues, as well as specific topics such
as the use of the ubiquitous discourse element mil, and an account of the ways that ques-
tions and commands are formed.
    SENTENCE EXAMPLES. Example sentences for the most part have the following format:

   (1)   Zhashkoonyan gye zhaangweshwan wnisaawaan daawewaad.
         'They kill muskrats and mink and sell them.' (AMIS.7)

          Zhashkoonyan no. 3obv 'muskrat(s)'; gye av 'and'; zhaangweshwan na 3obv 'mink';
          wnisaawaan vta ind 3pProx»3obv 'ANpl kill ANobv'; daawewaad vaio conj SpProx
          '(CONJ) ANpl sell (Y).'


      Each example sentence is introduced with a specific reference number, and below the
sentence, there appears a free English translation. At the end of the free translation, there is
usually a reference code, here (AM15.7) providing the source of the example. These codes
 are discussed at length in Section 1.5.1 (p. 21), in Chapter 1. Below the free translation is a
box containing a word-by-word analysis of each word in bold face, followed by an italicized
annotation of its grammatical properties, followed by a word-level gloss. For the most part I
have omitted from this glossing the two pragmatic particles go and sa, simply to save space,
 and because their usage is not reducible to succinct glossing. Overall, the glosses introduce
many useful innovations in the characterization of Algonquian meanings. For example,
rather than resorting to the use of gender-specific English pronouns such as 'he,' 'she,' and
 'it,' verbal arguments are indexed with codes such as ANsg, ANobv, and IN. Verbs that are
inflected for the conjunct inflectional order have a gloss prefaced with (CONJ), and those
that show changed conjunct, with (CCNJ). This is to avoid over-translation, since the con-
junct usually simply signals subordination, and clauses showing it manifest a variety of
semantic relations with respect to the superordinate clause, including relations coded in
English by means of conjunctions such as 'as,' 'when,' 'because,' 'in order to,' and 'if.'
      Each boldfaced word is followed by a part of speech label, agreeing with the notational
system used in Rhodes 1985. For verbs, this is followed by a specification of the inflectional
order it carries, whether independent (ind), conjunct (conj) or imperative (imp). If a con-
junct verb shows initial change it is indicated with ic. Participles are indicated with the code
part, and inflectional negatives with neg. Reduplication of the stem is indicated with the
code redup, and the iterative with iter. The three marked inflectional modes of the indepen-
dent and conjunct order are indicated with the codes pret for preterit, dub for dubitative, and
                                                                                         xxxm


pdub for preterit dubitative. All other verbs are indicative mode, which is unmarked in Nish-
naabemwin. Following this is a representation of the verb's argument structure, indicated as
directional action in the case of transitive verbs, such as 3pProx»3obv, which specifies an
animate proximate third person plural actor acting on an animate obviative goal. Animate
third persons are indicated with a code 3, and inanimates with a code 0, in keeping with
conventional Ojibweist practice. In cases where number is inflectionally neutralized, no
number specification is provided, e.g., conjunct inanimate intransitive verbs have subjects
labeled 0, since the simple conjunct does not distinguish singular and plural. First person
plural inclusive is signalled with 27, and exclusive, with Ip. Readily interpretable codes
include Is, 2s, SsProx, Os, Oobv, 2p, 3p, and Op. In the English glosses, as mentioned above,
third persons are identified by straightforward codes specifying grammatical properties,
such as ANsg, ANobv, ANpl, INsg, INpl, and INobv. The inflectionally unmarked second-
ary object of ditransitives and optional object animate intransitive verbs (vaio) are often
indicated with the code (Y). The English glosses of obviatives are cast ambiguously as to
number, as in 'muskrat(s),' above. In cases where English is ambiguous, as in 'mink,'
above, no additional specification is provided, though one can readily inspect the argument
specification to determine the precise inflectional configuration. All abbreviations used in
glosses are identified in the table of abbreviations.
    Linguistic researchers may be disappointed to see that morpheme-level segmentations of
examples are rarely provided. At a conference held in Thunder Bay, Ontario, in 1996, a
steering committee of Nishnaabemwin speakers explicitly requested that such details not be
included, as it was felt that they interfered with the flow of the presentation, and contributed
to what is sometimes called the "intellectual mining" of aboriginal languages and cultures.
To accommodate these concerns, I initially provided the word-level annotations in an
appendix, but under review by the press, intercalation of the annotations into the text was
made a requirement for publication, so I had no choice but to comply. Upon reflection, it
seems to me that there are many good reasons for working the annotations into the text. For
one, many of my readers will be semi-speakers of Nishnaabemwin, who will benefit from
the help the annotations provide; secondly, Nishnaabemwin varies dialectally, and the
word-level glosses will allow fluent readers to more readily accommodate dialect differ-
ences; lastly, of course, the annotations make the language more accessible to those lacking
prior exposure. One reviewer pointed out that this grammar is actually a compound work,
consisting of an introduction to linguistics as well as a grammar. This I have done, again, to
accommodate my intended primary audience, those interested in teaching the language,
who typically lack extensive linguistic training.
    This work would not have been possible without the assistance of many individuals. I am
particularly appreciative of the insights into Algonquian provided by Mary Ann Corbiere,
Amy Dahlstrom, Peter Denny, Ives Goddard, Ann Grafstein, Bill Jancewicz, Jonathan
Kaye, Rose Nadjiwon, Thecla Neganegijig, John Nichols, Pat Ningewance, John O'Meara,
Glyne Piggott, Richard Rhodes, Reta Sands, Roger Spielmann, Isadore Toulouse, Helen
Wassegijig, the late Lena White, and Shirley Williams. Few things have been more reward-
ing to me than the breezy summer days I have spent in the company of so many speakers of
XXXIV



Nishnaabemwin at the Native Language Instructors' Program at Lakehead University,
Thunder Bay, Ontario. I am thankful to the Walpole Island Heritage Centre, for its patience
in waiting so long for this manuscript, and to the community of Walpole Island for the lan-
guage help that many people have provided. I am grateful to John Stanley for his assistance
in procuring funds to undertake this project. Thanks to Conrad Treff and John Taylor for

Introduction to Nishnaabemwin




1.1 Introduction

    This grammar presents a linguistic study of an Algonquian language spoken in southern
Ontario along the shores of Lake Huron and points to the east roughly as far as the Ottawa
River. The language is here identified as NISHNAABEMWIN, because that is the term that its
speakers, the NISHNAABEG (singular, NISHNAABE), typically use to identify their language.
The varieties of language represented by this grammar are called by many names in
English, including ODAWA, OTTAWA, CfflPPEWA, OJIBWAY, or even simply "Indian," espe-
cially by older Nishnaabe people. As with all languages spoken over broad geographical
areas, speakers of Nishnaabemwin show variation in all aspects of their language use,
including VOCABULARY, PRONUNCIATION and GRAMMATICAL PATTERNS. This variation cre-
ates a fabric of loosely-defined local DIALECTS, that taken together, fit into an even broader
pattern of languages which are commonly collectively identified as OJIBWE (also spelled
Ojibway and Ojibwa), or ANISHINAABEMOWIN, though neither term is entirely satisfactory.
Anishinaabemowin is spoken over a vast region of central Canada and in U.S. border states
from Michigan to Montana. Of the three hundred or more languages that were spoken in
North America at the time of contact with Europeans, the Anishinaabemowin GROUP is one
of the few that is still spoken by large numbers of speakers, and one of the few that has a
chance of lasting more than a couple of generations into the future. Many northern Anishi-
naabemowin dialects are still being learned as first languages by children, but Nishnaabem-
win is often not learned as a first language anymore, though, of course, children do continue
to learn the language in homes where their parents and grandparents speak it to them regu-
larly. The language is also now being taught to children as a SECOND LANGUAGE in primary
and secondary schools in many reserve communities, as well as in some urban school dis-
tricts. This grammar is designed in part to serve as a resource and reference for teachers
engaged in the promotion and preservation of their language. A map showing most commu-
nities for which the grammar will be pertinent is provided on the following page.

    VARIATION IN NlSHNAABEMWIN. As an example of the variation in vocabulary that
exists among speakers of Nishnaabemwin, the words that translate into English as 'this' are
maaba (anim.) and maanda (inan.) for some speakers, and aw (anim.) and ow (inan.) for
others. Sometimes the distribution of variable vocabulary such as this can be described in
terms of COMMUNITY LANGUAGE USAGE patterns, such that maaba and maanda can be said
to be used in the communities of Walpole Island and Wikwemikong (Manitoulin Island),
while aw and ow are used at Curve Lake and Rama. But there are also communities where
both sets of words are used, and many individual speakers use both sets of terms, or even
vary in the use of individual terms. Variation of this sort is part and parcel of any spoken
language, and no grammar can hope to capture the grammatical patterns of every speaker—
rather some compromise must be reached which allows for an acceptable job of represent-
ing those of a majority of speakers, which can serve as a guide to the language's most
important grammatical features. I will discuss the nature of dialect variation in more detail
below, but at this point want to emphasize that this grammar presents only a few of the
many ways of speaking varieties of a language called Nishnaabemwin, and makes no claim
to be the only way, especially, to be the correct way of speaking. Ultimately the materials of
this grammar are based on the speech of a only a handful of speakers. If Nishnaabemwin-
speaking readers find that their own speech departs from what is presented here, they may
still find the grammar useful as a structural guide by which to document their own personal
and community language patterns. The GRAMMATICAL CATEGORIES presented will be found
almost everywhere among Nishnaabemwin speakers, even though the exact expression of
these categories may vary. For example, all speakers and all communities will have sets of
DEMONSTRATIVE PRONOUNS meaning 'this' and 'that,' and 'these' and 'those,' indexed for
the same grammatical features of GENDER, NUMBER, and OBVIATION, but the actual forms
filling each grammatical slot in the system may vary.

1.1.1 Nishnaabemwin and Syncope

   In the last seventy-five years, certain varieties of Anishinaabemowin found along the
northern and eastern shores of Lake Huron, extending east into southwestern Ontario, have
undergone a major sound change that both unites these dialects and distinguishes them from
other dialects to which each was historically more closely related. The nature of this change
can be seen by comparing a few words from Anishinaabemowin spoken in northern Ontario
and Minnesota with the same words as they are pronounced along the shores of Georgian
Bay (GB) and Lake Huron (southwestern Ontario).

                                    Northern Ontario         GB/Lake Huron
           mosquito                 zagime                   zgime
           shoe                     makizin                  mkizin
           pipe (for smoking)       opwaagan                 pwaagan
           man                      inini                    nini
4 • 1.1.1 Nishnaabemwin and Syncope



    In each case the Northern word has VOWELS not found in the corresponding GB/Lake
Huron word. These vowels are not pronounced in the latter dialect because of a prominent
rule of vowel SYNCOPE, which deletes vowels that are not STRESSED. De-emphasizing
UNSTRESSED vowels is a very common process in the languages of the world, and the rule in
Lake Huron speech is quite regular, so that, often, given a Northern Anishinaabemowin pro-
nunciation, an approximation of the word's pronunciation in southwestern Ontario speech
can be determined by applying a patterned rule of vowel stressing, with subsequent deletion
of unstressed vowels, This rule is quite regular: notice that in all four of the example words
above, it is the first vowel of the Northern pronunciation that is not pronounced in the
Southwestern (see the chart below, which shows this clearly). The words are otherwise the
same. Notice, too, how neither the second vowel nor the last vowel of the Northern word is
absent from the Southwestern pronunciation. The point here is that the vowel-deletion rule
is regular and predictable, not haphazard. It represents a productive pronunciation change
that has taken place in the speech of Southwestern Ontario Nishnaabeg. We will look at this
rule in considerable detail in the next chapter, because it has had far-reaching effects on the
grammar of the language. Interestingly, because of this rule, the name of the language
shows the same kind of pronunciation effects that other words in southwestern Ontario do:

                     Anishinaabemowin                    Nishnaabemwin

                 Southern    z                  g            i   m           e

                  Northern m         a          k        i       z          i       n

                  Southern   m                  k        i       z          i        n

                  Northern o           pw       aa       g           a     n
                  Southern             pw       aa       g           a     n

                 man         Northern inini, Southern nini

                  Northern   i           n       i       n           i

                  Southern               n       i       n           i

    SCOPE OF THE GRAMMAR. In sum, this grammar is designed to be a resource for speak-
ers of vowel syncopating dialects of Anishinaabemowin, representing varieties here collec-
tively identified as Nishnaabemwin. The main speech varieties represented are those of
Walpole Island, Parry Island, Cape Croker, and Manitoulin Island, though other areas are
represented when data are available. Speakers of Nishnaabemwin come from many linguis-
tic and cultural backgrounds, including Chippewa, Ottawa/Odawa, and Potawatomi.
Chippewa and Odawa are recognized as dialects of Anishinaabemowin (Ojibwe), while
Potawatomi is usually considered to be a separate language, though Potawatomi and south-
ern varieties of Anishinaabemowin are quite similar and there are long traditions of contact
and cooperation between the Potawatomi and various groups of Anishinaabe people.
    As an introduction to the study of Nishnaabemwin, and language in general, I will first
discuss the notions of LANGUAGE and DIALECT, as they are particularly important in under-
standing the variation that obtains among speakers of Nishnaabemwin. I will then introduce
the ALGONQUIAN language family, of which Anishinaabemowin (Ojibwe) is a member, and
then the various recognized dialects of Anishinaabemowin.

1.2 Language, Dialect, Idiolect, and Variety

    Each of us learns one or more languages as a child, which we use in communicating with
those around us, at first our immediate family and others within our community. As we
grow, we come in contact with people from other communities, and in some cases their
speech may be similar enough to ours that we can understand each other and communicate
with ease; in other cases, even though we may share many words and grammatical patterns,
we cannot easily converse because of differences in speech forms. In the first case, in which
there is mutual understanding, we readily agree that we are speaking the "same" language,
even though there may be differences between the two forms of speech. In the other case,
while we can detect similarities, there are nonetheless too many differences to allow fluid
communication, and we may say that the other person speaks a "different" language from
us, even though there may be some undeniable similarities between the two speech forms,
and even though the different forms of language may be referred to with the same English
name, such as "Ojibwe." If the situation were always clear-cut like this, we wouldn't have
too much of a problem in determining whether two people spoke the same or different lan-
guages— if they clearly understood each other we could say they spoke the same language,
and if they didn't, we could say that they spoke different languages. However, when we
examine the kind of variation found from community to community in the aboriginal lan-
guages of North America, we discover that there are rarely clear-cut distinctions between
one language and another, but rather, slowly accumulating differences in speech forms as
the distances between communities grow. And because of this it becomes very difficult to
say then when two people speak the "same" language, or when they speak "different" lan-
guages. Often there is a CHAINING effect that is created by communities showing overlap in
language forms with nearby communities. As a somewhat simplified example, consider the
words (VOCABULARY) from the following three hypothetical Anishinaabe communities:
6 • 1.2 Language, Dialect, Idiolect, and Variety

'house'          waakaahigan                 waakaaygan             wiigwaam
'bead'           miigis                      mandoominens           mnidoomnens
'old man'        gichi-ahaa                  akiyenzi               kiwenziinh

   Here we see that all three of these communities have the same words for 'dives' and
'woman,' though each community pronounces the word for 'woman' slightly differently.
There is also small variation in the pronunciation of many of the other words. Communities

                      Community A                  Community B         Community C

                                                  1.2 Language, Dialect, Idiolect, and Variety • 7



                     Community A               Community B                Community C
'bead'               miigis                   mandoominens               mnidoomnens
'old man'            gichi-ahaa               akiyenzi                   kiwenziinh

'house'              waakaahigan              waakaaygan                 wiigwaam

    Communities A and C have only two words in common with each other, but both are
closer to Community B, with which they each share four related forms. Community B is
somewhat "central" here, in that it is the community with the highest number of forms
shared with other communities. But consider for a moment what it means to say that speak-
ers of Communities A, B, and C all speak the same language. Two of the communities are
quite different from each other, sharing just two forms in six items of vocabulary. Yet in an
important way the three communities are linked by a common thread of overlapping vocab-
ulary. Linguists typically deal with this problem by referring to the whole complex system
that includes Communities A, B, and C as a single language, and each of the forms of
speech represented by the given communities as being DIALECTS, or local VARIANTS, of
LANGUAGE X. But the term "dialect" shows the same problems that "language" does, in that
even within communities there is often considerable variation, particularly in aboriginal
communities, because people of different regional, linguistic, tribal, and cultural traditions
often came together by either choice or circumstance. We could appeal to another term,
SUB-DIALECT, which would specify an identifiable sub-group of a given dialect, but if we
were meticulous in our documentation of differences, we might end up assigning every
speaker in a given community to a separate sub-dialect. The effect of all of this is that even
when reference is made to a particular dialect of a given language, it must be understood
that such a dialect is not necessarily uniform, the same for every speaker, but almost always
shows considerable internal variation, sometimes to the point of making its identification as
a recognizable dialect as much a social or political consideration as a linguistic one.
    It is not only vocabulary that shows variation between speakers and communities.
Another prominent area of grammar where variation is found is in the pronunciation of
words, parts of words, and phrases. Speakers are often consciously aware of these differ-
ences of "accent," as can be seen from the following anecdote that was told by Andrew
Medler, who was born in Michigan but moved to Walpole Island when he was young.

    When Andrew Medler first came to live on Walpole Island, a small difference in pronun-
ciation between his speech and that of the people living there was noticed, and was a source
of friendly joking with him. The difference was minor, involving the pronunciation of a
VERBAL SUFFIX, whether -yaan, with a final /n/ sound, or-yaanh, with a NASALIZED VOWEL
at the end. Later in this chapter I will review some of the main differences that exist among
speakers of Nishnaabemwin, but for now, it is enough to realize that virtually any aspect of
language can show variation, including pronunciation, vocabulary, word structure, and sen-
tence patterns, and that speakers are often acutely aware of minor differences.
    There are many technical terms to identify various forms of speech, such as IDIOLECT,
DIALECT, LANGUAGE, SOCIOLECT, LANGUAGE FAMILY, and VARIETY. Each of these terms is
useful in talking about Nishnaabemwin. An IDIOLECT refers to the speech of a particular
individual, distinct from that of all other individuals. Every speaker of every language has
his or her own particular way of talking, including distinctive pronunciations, vocabulary
and preferred sentence patterns. The term DIALECT is used to refer to forms of language that
are shared by a significant number of speakers, usually delimited geographically. For exam-
ple, we can refer to the Odawa dialect, or the Chippewa dialect, or the Algonquin dialect of
Anishinaabemowin (Ojibwe), recognizing that while certain features shared by speakers
                                                  1.2 Language, Dialect, Idiolect, and Variety • 9



unite them, other features of language may vary within the dialect. In popular usage, the
term DIALECT sometimes has a connotation of being sub-standard or unusual, but in this
work it is never used with such evaluative judgements.
    Another aspect of dialects is that they typically have a FOCAL REGION, which shows a
majority of the features that define the dialect and distinguish it from others dialects, and
outlying regions, which show fewer of these defining, diagnostic features. Yet speakers of
both central and peripheral dialect regions may use the same term to identify their dialect
and language, and may even share attitudes about which pronunciations, vocabulary, and
grammatical patterns are preferred, even if they do not share identical behaviours with
respect to the use of such features.
    The figure below illustrates another common way of representing language variation.
Here there are nine hypothetical communities (identified with the symbol «J» and a sub-
scripted number) and four speech innovations (language features), labeled A, B, C, D, radi-
ating out from different initial locations to encompass adjacent areas, with each innovation's
range indicated by a circle. So, for example, innovation A applies only to communities 3
and 4, while innovation D applies to all communities. Community 4 shows all four innova-
tions, community 3 has three innovations, and so on. Viewed from above, the patterns of
innovation are rather like overlapping ripples produced by tossing pebbles into a tranquil
pond. In just this way innovations accumulate to produce dialects. Of course, the dialect
picture is compounded by the fact that speakers move between communities, distributing
innovations in ways that are not contiguous in the manner of ripples in water.



                                                         A community (9 total)
                                                         A set of linguistic innovations
                                                         showing variable manifestation
                                                         across communities, including
                                                         such things as pronunciation,
                                                         vocabulary, inflection or
                                                         sentence structure. Innovative
                                                         features move out in waves
                                                         from their points of origin,
                                                         usually along established social

                   WAVE MODEL OF LANGUAGE CHANGE AND RELATIONSHIP
10 • 1.2 Language, Dialect, Idiolect, and Variety


   LANGUAGE. The term LANGUAGE is more inclusive than dialect, and generally refers to
any forms of speech that are mutually intelligible, though this criterion is obviously very
inexact. Mutually intelligibility simply means that speakers are able to understand each
other. So, for example, it is often observed that speakers of Chippewa and Odawa can
understand each other, and thus speak the same language, even though they speak different
dialects.
   LANGUAGE FAMILY. Another important concept is that of the LANGUAGE FAMILY, which
is made up of languages having a common linguistic ancestry. So, for example, Ojibwe
belongs to the ALGONQUIAN language family, which includes Potawatomi, Menomini, Del-
aware, and Cree, among many others.
   We can schematically represent the various relationships we have been discussing with
the following diagram:

                                            Language Family


                   Language A                 Language B           Language C

           Dialect AI Dialect A2 Dialect BI Dialect 62         Dialect Cj Dialect C2

    Idiolect Aia     Idiolect Alb

               TREE MODEL OF LANGUAGE, DIALECT, AND IDIOLECT RELATIONSHIPS

    This branching, tree-like diagram, as opposed to the wave-model on the previous page,
indicates that a language family consists of a number of discrete languages, and that each
language consists of a number of dialects, and each dialect is made up of speakers with their
own unique way of talking, their IDIOLECTS. In this diagram, everything is very neat: the
language family consists of clearly identifiable, isolatable, distinct languages, and each lan-
guage consists of clearly identifiable, distinct dialects, which are made up of speakers who
differ in only minor ways. In actuality, though, the relationships between idiolects, dialects,
and languages are often far less clear-cut than this diagram suggests, simply because forms
of language often grade into one another, as we saw with the wave-like patterns illustrated
on the previous page.
    LANGUAGE VARIETY. Another commonly used term in describing language variation is
that of VARIETY, which specifies any distinguishable form of a language. This could refer to
the speech patterns of a region, a community, or some sub-grouping within a community. It
is a neutral term with respect to the notions of dialect, sub-dialect, and language.
    SociOLECTS. SOCIOLECTS are forms of speech shared by speakers who have some com-
mon social trait, such as being in the same age group, or being of the same gender, male or
female. In Nishnaabemwin, because of differences in the opportunity to learn the language
due to factors such as residential schools, differences in the speech of different age groups
                                                 1.2 Language, Dialect, Idiolect, and Variety • 11



can be quite pronounced. Typically in Nishnaabemwin, language proficiency is AGE-STRAT-
IFIED, such that older speakers tend to be more fluent than younger. In other cases, occupa-
tional specialty may produce language differences, so that, for example, teachers may
develop special terms for objects used in school, or farmers may have terms relating to agri-
culture. Specialists in any area usually have enriched vocabularies in the areas of their spe-
cialty, whether it be traditional herbal medicine or modern baseball.
    As an example of a gender difference in speech, Rhodes 1985 lists the term koojiish,
'louse' with the designation woman's word, meaning that it is a term mostly used by
women, and not by men. Other gender-based vocabulary differences can be seen in the
richly articulated traditional kinship system of Nishnaabemwin, where, for example, a
woman refers to her brother-in-law as niinim, while a man uses the term niitaa; a man refers
to his sister-in-law as niinim, but a woman uses ndaangwenh. Gender differences work at
many different levels of language, including vocabulary, patterns of conversational interac-
tion, preferred topics, and the appropriateness of particular vocabulary and grammatical
constructions in different social settings. These patterns vary from language to language,
and even community to community, and are an important part of general language compe-
tence. For example, English has different, contrasting sets of vocabulary for dealing with
bodily functions and related parts of the body, on an order not found in Nishnaabemwin,
because attitudes towards such processes were historically different, and cultural differ-
ences are reflected in language. Furthermore, rigid social rules of appropriate usage exist in
English for when each of these terms may be used, indexed by many social factors, such as
gender, age, and social situation, and these rules are quite different from the usage patterns
of Nishnaabemwin. Speakers of Nishnaabemwin vary in their attitudes as well. Rhodes
 1985 indexes several items of vocabulary with the USAGE CATEGORY crude, such as
miiziiwgamig 'toilet, outhouse' (M), and miiziiwaagan, 'privy.' Less socially marked than
these terms is zaaghamoogmig, 'outhouse' (M), which literally means, 'going out building.'
The verb form zaagham, 'go out,' is used euphemistically in Nishnaabemwin in a way sim-
ilar to English 'go to the bathroom.' There are no doubt social rules associated with the use
of such terms. Other vocabulary in Nishnaabemwin is rather obviously euphemistic, too,
such as the Walpole Island expression gojiing wiisni, 'she eats outdoors,' in reference to
menstruation, or Manitoulin aanji-giisiwe, lit. 'she changes months,' with the same mean-
ing. A few other words are categorized in the dictionary as socially sensitive, such as bnesi,
'thunderbird; eagle' (M), and mshi-, a PRENOUN found in the names of many mythological
beings, such as Mshibzhii, 'the Great Lynx,' and Mshi-gnebig, 'great serpent.' These are
terms that should be used with appropriate caution and respect.
    In other cases, differences may involve attitudes towards quite specific features of gram-
mar, such as the appropriateness of a particular prefix or pronunciation. Many speakers, for
example, vary in their attitudes towards vowel syncope and the use of person(al) prefixes
such as ndoo-, ndi-, and nda- with different words.
    PRESCRIPTION AND DESCRIPTION. Related to social variation in language and the writing
of grammars are the notions of description and prescription. A DESCRIPTIVE GRAMMAR is
one that describes what people actually say, while a PRESCRIPTIVE GRAMMAR is one that
12 • 1.3 The Algonquian Language Family


seeks to dictate particular ways of speaking. For example, a descriptive grammar might
point out that some speakers of Nishnaabemwin use the FIRST PERSON PREFIX ndoo- with
verbs such as niimi, 'dance,' and boodwe, 'make a fire,' whereas a prescriptive grammar
might insist that because these words traditionally had long vowels in their first syllables,
the appropriate form of the prefix is «n». I mention this issue because it actually came up in
readers' comments on the grammar, when one reader suggested that certain forms with
ndoo- were incorrect. Another said that its usage with certain verb stems was a sign of a lack
of fluency. This is a particularly thorny issue in Nishnaabemwin, where some patterns of
usage probably do represent less fluency than others do. But it is not my purpose here to
prescribe ways of speaking the language.

1.3 The Algonquian Language Family

    Anishinaabemowin belongs to the Algonquian language family, which at the time of
European contact was spoken widely over the eastern North American continent. The delin-
eation of the Algonquian language family and the RECONSTRUCTION of the PARENT LAN-
GUAGE from which the modern languages have descended is mostly due to the work of
Leonard Bloomfield (1925, 1946). On the basis of comparison of four central Algonquian
languages, Fox, Cree, Ojibwe and Menominee, Bloomfield was able to reconstruct the PHO-
NO.LOGICAL INVENTORY (set of distinctive sounds) of Proto-Algonquian to a surprising
degree of detail, and also many aspects of its rich word structure (morphology), even though
there existed no ancient documents for Algonquian such as aided scholars in reconstructing
the hypothesized parent language of many European languages, Proto-Indo-European. The
reconstruction of Proto-Algonquian was done by a careful comparison of SOUND CORRE-
SPONDENCES in COGNATE vocabulary in the daughter languages, such as is illustrated by the
sample of words on the following page from seven Algonquian languages. Cognates are
related words in daughter languages that have developed from the same source word in the
mother language.
    Since the relationship between a word's form (pronunciation) and its meaning is essen-
tially an arbitrary one, when words having similar meanings sound similar in different lan-
guages, one possible explanation is genetic relationship, that is, that the languages have
come from a common parent language, and have as a result inherited common vocabulary
and grammar. Compare the Algonquian words for 'bear,' in the table on the following page,
with those of some Germanic languages: English, bear, Swedish, bjorn; Danish, Bj0rn;
Dutch, beer, German, Bar. These words share obvious similarities. An examination of the
words in some Romance languages yields different results: French, I'ours; Spanish, el oso;
Portuguese, o urso; Italian, Vorso. In each case the relationship between the word and the
thing is arbitrary, that is, there is nothing about bears that suggests that bear or urso or
mkwa is somehow a more natural or appropriate set of sounds to use to identify this animal
than any of the other languages' sounds. So when groups of languages show extensive,
structured similarity between their vocabularies, one possibility is that they have all inher-
ited their vocabularies from a common "mother" language.

    Genetically related languages not only share common vocabulary (cognates), but also
show patterned relationships between the sounds of this vocabulary. Note, for example, in
the Algonquian data above, that where Plains Cree has sk as its reflex of the Proto-Algon-
quian consonant cluster, *0k, Delaware has xk and Ojibwe kk (spelled «k» in contemporary
practical orthography), in both the words for 'beaver' and 'bear.' The sound changes that
languages undergo over time are often consistent and regular. Based on comparisons of this
sort between languages such as Cree, Ojibwe and Fox, the sound system and vocabulary of
their common parent language, Proto-Algonquian, was pieced together. Note the recon-
structed Proto-Algonquian forms in the table above, given at the bottom of the table, and
marked with an asterisk (*), for example, *pelee\va is the Proto-Algonquian word for a
large game bird. The asterisk preceding the word is to identify it as a hypothetical form, that
is, one postulated to have existed on the basis of comparative research, rather than a word
that has actually been attested in spoken or written form.

   It is customary to divide the non-Eastern languages into two subgroups, a PLAINS group,
consisting of Arapaho, Blackfoot, and Cheyenne, and a CENTRAL group, consisting of all
the other languages. These designations do not, however, represent GENETIC (familial) sub-
groupings, but are rather for convenience in referring to the languages in a given geographi-
cal area. For example, some analysts feel that Cheyenne, a "Plains" language, is more
closely related genetically to the other Central Algonquian languages than is Cree. The
amount of contact, BiLiNGUALiSM, and INDEPENDENT PARALLEL DEVELOPMENTS of Proto-
Algonquian reflexes in the Central languages has obscured the genetic relationships that
existed between them.

    The general pattern of Anishinaabemowin dialects is relatively clear, and can be summa-
rized with the map below. Some dialects are rather clearly defined, and have quite distinc-
tive features by which affiliations can be identified. This includes especially the dialects of
Algonquin, Nipissing Algonquin, Odawa and Severn Ojibwe (Oji-Cree). On the north shore
of Lake Superior, we find northern elements occurring in the eastern communities (e.g., Pic

                           MAP OF ANISHINAABEMOWIN DIALECTS

   A few general observations on Anishinaabemowin dialects follow.

• ALGONQUIN as a group is popularly distinguished from Ojibwe as if it were a sepa-
  rate language. It is only linguists that recognize it as a variety of Ojibwe, though they
  do so on the basis of very sound linguistic evidence. The Algonquins have been
  located in the Ottawa Valley along the present day Quebec-Ontario border, in a large
  area centered around Lake Abitibi (also on the Quebec-Ontario border), and along the
  St. Lawrence, since the earliest periods of European contact. There are two quite dis-
  tinct varieties of Anishinaabemowin popularly identified as Algonquin, a northern
  and a southern. The southern I refer to as NIPISSING ALGONQUIN, below.

• CHIPPEWA. The name Chippewa is ultimately derived from another European render-
  ing of the word Ojibwe, though its pronunciation is now based on its English spell-
  ing. This term is sometimes used to designate Nishnaabeg in southwesterly Ontario
  whose ancestors moved into Canada from the U.S. in historical times, many of whom
  have maintained their Chippewa cultural identity. EASTERN OJIBWA is sometimes
  used, particularly by linguists (e.g., Rhodes 1985), to designate the modern reflexes
  of Chippewa in Ontario, which have undergone innovations that distinguish them
  from American varieties. The dialect of Anishinaabemowin spoken in the United
  States is often designated SOUTHWESTERN OJIBWA (e.g., Rhodes and Todd 1981),
  though speakers tend to use Ojibwe or Anishinaabemowin.
16 • 1.4 An Overview of Anishinaabemowin Dialects


• NIPISSING ALGONQUIN. The Nipissings have long been associated with Lake Nipiss-
  ing, which is north of Lake Huron and connected to the drainage of the Ottawa River.
  The identification of a modern descendant of the Nipissing dialect is uncertain. Val-
  entine 1994 refers to the variety of Anishinaabemowin spoken at Maniwaki, Quebec
  and Golden Lake, Ontario as Nipissing. Day and Trigger (1978) state that the Ojibwe
  dialect in Cuoq (1891-92) is Nipissing, though its title is Grammaire de le Langue
  Algonquine. Cuoq's data is fairly close to materials published by the River Desert
  (Maniwaki, Quebec) band. Although these speakers identify themselves and their
  language as Algonquin, the language is markedly different from the Algonquin found
  to the north, and has many features that distinguish it from all other dialects. It shares
  many features with both northern and southern Anishinaabemowin dialects, suggest-
  ing that it may indeed represent a historically distinct dialect in the area, possibly
  Nipissing, which would have been located between the two primary dialect groupings
  of Anishinaabemowin. A problem with the use of Nipissing to identify this dialect is
  that there is another distinct dialect spoken around North Bay, Ontario, along Lake
  Nipissing, which also might reflect the historical Nipissing dialect. Furthermore,
  speakers of this variety of Anishinaabemowin refer to their own language in English
  as Algonquin. So I refer to it as Nipissing Algonquin.

• ODAWA, sometimes referred to as OTTAWA in parts of the United States, is spoken on
  the shores of Lake Huron and in Michigan. Many speakers of Odawa in Ontario iden-
  tify their dialect as Ojibwe, or in some cases, Chippewa. Most modern varieties show'
  some admixture of Chippewa, or Potawatomi, the closest linguistic relative of Anish-
  inaabemowin. Many Potawatomi fled to Canada in the nineteenth century, often set-
  tling in Odawa areas. According to popular lore, this word is related to the word,
  adaawe, 'sell, trade,' in recognition of the prominence of the Ottawa in the develop-
  ment of the fur trade, but the actual source of the name is obscure. The word is very
  old, predating contact with Europeans.

• OJI-CREE (ANIHSHININIIMOWIN, SEVERN OJIBWE). There is a variety of Anishinaabe-
  mowin spoken in northwestern Ontario that is commonly identified in English by its
  own speakers as Cree, a sister language of Anishinaabemowin found in the Hudson
  Bay lowlands adjacent to this dialect area. OJI-CREE is also used popularly to desig-
  nate this dialect, because of its allegedly being a mixture of Ojibwe and Cree. Within
  the language, a unique term ANIHSHININIIMOWIN is often used in place of Anishinaa-
  bemowin, though the latter is not uncommon either. This variety is sometimes
  referred to as SEVERN (RIVER) OJIBWE by linguists, in reference to one of the river
  systems defining its geographical locus. The Severn River flows north into Hudson
  Bay along with its sister the Winisk, and the two sub-dialects of Severn Ojibwe
  reflect the locations of communities on these river systems.
                                                       1.4.1 Dialects within Nishnaabemwin • 17



• SAULTEAUX, or PLAINS OJIBWA, is used popularly to identify closely-related variet-
  ies of Anishinaabemowin spoken in the Border Lakes area of northwestern Ontario,
  and in Manitoba, Saskatchewan, and Alberta. The term Saulteaux arose from a
  French translation of the Anishinaabemowin word bawitigong, 'at the rapids,' by
  which the Anishinaabeg referred to a stretch of the St. Mary's River near present day
  Sault Ste. Marie, Ontario. This river connects Lakes Huron and Superior, and histori-
  cally was a popular gathering spot for Anishinaabeg because of the abundance offish,
  especially whitefish, during the seasonal runs. The Saulteaux are said to have moved
  west in concert with French traders, a theory borne out by many similarities between
  Saulteaux and southern Anishinaabemowin dialects to the east. Some Saulteaux bor-
  rowed vocabulary is clearly from French, such the common designation for a white
  man, Mooniyaans, which is an adaptation of the French term for someone from Mon-
  treal. Western Saulteaux is not so much a distinct sub-dialect, as an area showing
  many kinds of differences in comparison with the more uniform dialect to the east.

« NORTHERN (NORTHWESTERN) OJIBWE. While many regional varieties of Anishinaa-
  bemowin have distinct names, such as those outlined above, there is a large area north
  of Lake Superior and in northwestern Ontario for which the general term Ojibwe is
  used. This includes the dialect which I have designated as Northern Ojibwe.

   As I have already noted, most dialects of Anishinaabemowin show gradual transition
from one region to another, though there are some areas of relative focus. The dialects of
Algonquin, Nipissing Algonquin, Odawa, and Oji-Cree show the greatest divergence from
the other dialects. All dialects show considerable internal variation. Nishnaabemwin is a
recent development of several distinct varieties of Ojibwe that were spoken on the shores of
Lake Huron and Georgian Bay, and inland points to the east. Historically, speakers of Nish-
naabemwin are descended from groups identified in English as Chippewas, Ottawas,
Odawa, Potawatomi, and perhaps other indigenous peoples. Linguistic heritage can easily
be confused with personal and family history, and linguistic features can be asserted to be
Potawatomi, Chippewa, or Odawa on the basis of the cultural heritage of a given speaker.
All of this contributes to a very complex contemporary situation, both in terms of linguistic
variation in Nishnaabemwin and in attitudes towards that variation.

1.4.1 Dialects within Nishnaabemwin

   In the most general terms, there exist two distinct sub-dialects within Nishnaabemwin,
Odawa (or Ottawa), spoken in Michigan and along the shores of Lake Huron, and Eastern
Ojibwe, spoken in the area to the east, and including especially the communities of Rama
and Curve Lake. The Odawa dialect shows considerable divergence from other varieties of
Anishinaabemowin, while Eastern Ojibwe is only minorly different from other southern
dialects spoken in the United States and border regions, though the feature of vowel syn-
cope has made it more distinct in the last century. In this section I will lay out a few of the

more prominent differences between the two dialects of Odawa and Eastern Ojibwe.

do not. The following table shows some of the contrasts between the two dialects.

1.5 Source Materials

   A variety of materials has aided me in the preparation of this grammar. These include
dictionaries, text collections, and example sentences which were elicited specifically for the
purposes of this research. In the following sections I discuss my different sources, address-
ing their form, content, and their strengths and weaknesses for the purposes of grammatical
documentation.
20 • 1.5 Source Materials


    DICTIONARIES. A primary source for our work is the invaluable dictionary of Ottawa,
Chippewa, and Eastern Ojibwa compiled by Richard Rhodes (Rhodes 1985). This dictio-
nary is extensive in its vocabulary, insightful in its glosses, contains many example sen-
tences, and carefully documents the dialect affiliations of all vocabulary. I have also adopted
Rhodes' conventions for labelling the dialect and community affiliations of vocabulary, and
discuss these in detail below.
    Another source of vocabulary is the dictionary edited by Glyne Piggott and Ann Graf-
stein (published 1983), which contains Nishnaabemwin vocabulary based primarily on
research carried out on Manitoulin Island. The orthography used in this dictionary is quite
idiosyncratic, involving such things as the use of «$» to represent the sound spelled «zh» in
Rhodes 1985, and a trailing colon (:) to identify long vowels, resulting in spellings such as
«ni:$w» for the word spelled niizh, 'two,' in Rhodes 1985. The chief value of Piggott and
Grafstein 1983 is that it contains a list of all vocabulary alphabetized from the end of the
word to the beginning, which groups together words that share endings, a feature which
proved very helpful in carrying out the lexical research that lies behind the presentation and
analysis of Nishnaabemwin word-structure found in Chapters 9 through 11. Since Rhodes
1985 used this work as a'source, I checked most forms against Rhodes, recognizing the lat-
ter to represent the more thorough and meticulous documentation.
    TEXTUAL MATERIALS. This grammar contains extensive sentence examples from vari-
ous published and unpublished text collections. The source of each sentence is identified
with a two-letter speaker code (explained elsewhere), and where extensive text collections
exist, a text number and sentence number, following the English free (loose) translation, as
in the following example:

   (6)   Gbe-dbik gii-bmibzo aw mshkode-daabaan gye go gbe-giizhig, miinwaa go gbe-
         dbik.
         'The train went all night and all day and all the next night.' (AM8.10)

          Gbe-dbik av 'all night'; gii-bmibzo vai indBsProx 'ANsg ran along'; aw/?r SsProx
          'that'; mshkode-daabaan na SsProx 'train' (lit. 'prairie vehicle'); gye av 'and'; gbe-
          giizhig av 'all day'; miinwaa av 'and (again)'; gbe-dbik av 'all night.'

   Here the abbreviation AM indicates that the source is Andrew Medler, who worked with
Leonard Bloomfield in the 1930's. The code 8.10 identifies this example as representing the
tenth sentence in the eighth text (of 38 total) published in Bloomfield 1958, a grammar of
Medler's Nishnaabemwin. There are also just under 900 numbered isolated-sentence exam-
ples in Bloomfield 1958, which I have collectively labeled AM39 in the sentence references
for this grammar. This text collection has recently been republished under the title of
Weshki-Bmaadzijig Ji-Noondmowaad (Valentine, ed. [1998]), and should be considered a
textual supplement to this grammar. The introduction to that work provides an extensive
outline of the basic categories of Nishnaabemwin grammar, and contains a complete con-
cordance of all verb forms, organized according to verbal INFLECTIONAL categories.

    Each example sentence includes a word-by-word analysis, providing both grammatical
information and English word-level glosses. Conventions used in the word-by-word analy-
sis are explained in the preface (see p. 32ff.).
    Another significant source of textual materials is a collection of eighteen stories told by
Alice King, of Parry Sound, in the 1970's, and written down by the linguist Jean Rogers.
Some of these are published in Nichols 1988. The Odawa Language Project, a linguistic
research program carried out approximately thirty years ago on Manitoulin Island, recorded
several Odawa speakers, including Sam Osawamick, a gifted storyteller, and I have used
these texts as well. These are published in Kaye, Piggott and Tokaichi 1971 and Piggott and
Kaye 1973, the two Odawa language reports.
    One potential problem that arises when using sources that date back to the thirties and
seventies is that they may represent somewhat dated forms of speech. For example, it is very
obvious that many speakers now use extensively the extended PERSONAL PREFIXES ndoo-,
FIRST PERSON, and gdoo-, SECOND PERSON, as in ndoo-ngam, 'I am singing,' whereas his-
torically the form was nnagam. These forms are not common in the three primary text
sources cited above, which means that they may sometimes not be entirely representative of
contemporary speech. This issue is complicated by the fact that there really is no well-
defined standard with respect to the use the extended prefixes, though there are certainly
broadly identifiable patterns of usage, which I discuss in detail in the next chapter. I am
quite confident that the examples are not far from contemporary fluid usage.
    I also found a rich source of textual materials in the language booklets prepared by stu-
dents of the Native Language Instructors' Program, held each summer in Thunder Bay,
Ontario (e.g. Valentine and White, eds., 1987). These represent more contemporary patterns
of speech, and evidence much variation in certain linguistic features, particularly the use of
person prefixes.
    SENTENTIAL EXAMPLES. I also compiled large amounts of material addressing particular
points of Nishnaabemwin grammar, mostly in the form of translations of English sentences.
Most of these are due to the courtesy and patience of colleagues Mary Ann Corbiere, of
Wikwemikong, and Reta Sands, of Walpole Island.

1.6 Introduction to the Study of Grammar

   Children around the world learn one or more languages as a normal part of growing up,
seemingly with little conscious effort. What is it that a child learns in the process of becom-
ing a fluent speaker of a language? One part of learning a language is acquiring a vocabu-
lary, learning literally thousands of words which carve the world up into the conceptual
categories that are unique to each language. Language has been described as a coding sys-
tem which relates sounds to meanings. For example, to talk about the meaning 'man,' an
English-speaking child must learn to pronounce an m sound followed by an a sound fol-
24 • 1.6 Introduction to the Study of Grammar


lowed by an n sound, and the child must associate this sequence of sounds with the appro-
priate meaning. A child learning Nishnaabemwin, to express a similar meaning, must learn
to pronounce an n sound followed by an i followed by an n followed by an i, nini. This pro-
cess of memorization must be repeated for every single word in the language, until the child
has acquired a full working vocabulary of many thousands of words. The record of such
knowledge is in part what is found in a dictionary, which would ideally contain a list of all
of the words in a language, including their pronunciations and their meanings, though, in
practice, no dictionary is complete.
    It is not just the pronunciations and meanings of words that children must learn. An
English-speaking child must also learn, for example, that there is a PLURAL form for man,
used to make reference to more than one man, and that it is men. A Nishnaabe child must
learn that to refer to more than one nini, the plural is ninwag. English-speaking children
must learn that to refer to more than one boat, they must add an s to the end of the word,
making boats. Nishnaabemwin-speaking children must learn that to express the idea of a
boat, they must sayjiimaan, and to express the plural, the sounds an are added to the end of
the word, giving jiimaanan. In another language, Slave, a Na-Dene language spoken in
western Canada, the plural is made by adding -ke to the end of a word: dene means 'person,'
and deneke, 'people' (Rice 1989:247). Each of these languages, Slave, English, and Nish-
naabemwin has its own ways of modifying singular words to make plurals, and children
must learn the appropriate system for the language they speak. In the case of the Nishnaabe
child, we see that there are two forms of the plural, an and ag. The existence of two distinct
plurals is not an accident, but related to a core feature of Nishnaabemwin grammar, namely,
the classification of nouns as either ANIMATE, in which case their plurals end with g (often
spelled «k»), or INANIMATE, in which case their plurals end with n. In English, animacy is
not a factor in the formation of plurals, so, for example, the plural of boy, something ani-
mate, and the plural of house, something inanimate, are made in very similar ways, by add-
ing s, giving boys and houses. In Nishnaabemwin, however, the plurals of these two words
are different, because wiigwaam, 'house' is grammatically inanimate, and gwiiwzens, 'boy'
is grammatically animate, giving the plurals wiigwaaman and gwiizensag, respectively.
Learning a language thus involves learning language-specific grammatical properties and
patterns of words, such as their ANIMACY in Nishnaabemwin, and how plurals are made.
    Another kind of knowledge speakers must have is how words are put together to form
sentences. Consider, for example, how children might make the simple observation that they
see something. In English, one can say:

   I see the boat.   I   I see the man.

    In both of these sentences, there is a PRONOUN /, a VERB see, an ARTICLE the, and a
NOUN, either man or boat. The only difference between the two sentences is the final word.
However, if we consider the equivalent Nishnaabemwin sentences, we find significant dif-
ferences:
                                                   1.6 Introduction to the Study of Grammar • 25



   Nwaabndaanjiimaan. 'I see the boat.' I Nwaabmaa nini.'I see the man.'

    Here we have only two words, a verb of seeing, and then a noun. There is no pronoun
such as in English. Yet it is clear in the Nishnaabemwin sentences that the SUBJECT of the
act of seeing is T. How is this? Simplifying somewhat, the answer is that the doer of the
action, the one seeing, is indicated on the verb, by means of a PREFIX, an element attached
to the front of the verb. In this case the prefix is «-. Because this element signals the mean-
ing T, there is no need for a separate pronoun to indicate the one seeing. Also, the verbs are
not quite the same in the two Nishnaabemwin sentences, being nwaabndaan in the first sen-
tence and nwaabmaa in the second. The reason for this is that the first verb is used when
making reference to seeing something referred to by a word that is grammatically inani-
mate, such asjiimaan, 'boat,' while the second verb is used when making reference to see-
ing something that is referred to by a word that is grammatically animate, such as nini,
 'man.' Thus, these two Nishnaabemwin sentences have slightly different verbs, depending
on whether the word for what is seen is animate or inanimate. A child learning Nishnaabem-
win must learn these things in order to speak the language correctly.
    Consider next the order of the words in the two sets of sentences. The English sentences
do not allow much variation in the word order:

   *I the man see. I *The I see man. I The man I see.

   Here I place an asterisk (*) before sentences that are not likely to be heard in English
because they violate basic grammatical principles of the language. Each of these sentences
seems odd in English, with the preferred ordering of words clearly that of / see the man. In
Nishnaabemwin, however, the word order is much freer. One can readily say both of these
sentences, with either ordering of words:

   Nwaabmaa nini. I Nini nwaabmaa.

    In summary, we see that learning a language involves many different kinds of knowl-
edge. For one, we must learn the pronunciation of words, and their meanings. We must also
learn the grammatical properties of words, such as whether they are of animate or inanimate
gender, and how to form their plurals. We have also seen that we must learn how words are
arranged to form sentences, and while the word order of Nishnaabemwin is much freer than
that of English, we will see that there are often preferred or obligatory orderings of words in
Nishnaabemwin as well.
    The rules of language pertaining to pronunciation and the behaviour of sounds are called
PHONOLOGICAL RULES, and the study of the sound system of a language is called PHONOL-
OGY. The study of the patterns of word structure and the grammatical properties of words is
called MORPHOLOGY. The rules for putting together words to form phrases and sentences are
called SYNTACTIC RULES, and the study of this area of a language is called SYNTAX. The
study of meaning in a language comes under the heading of SEMANTICS. All of these areas
26 • 1.7 Additional Reading


of study point to different kinds of knowledge that fluent speakers have of their language,
and which together constitute what contemporary linguists call the GRAMMAR of a lan-
guage. The term GRAMMAR is of course also used to refer to a monograph which seeks to
outline this knowledge on paper/This study is such a document for the language Nishnaabe-
mwin, and has been produced in order to document the language, and to help teachers of the
language understand aspects of its grammar, and to help them in the development of curric-
ula by pointing to areas of the language requiring treatment in a structured program of sec-
ond language instruction. While I wish to treat as thoroughly as possible the grammar of
Nishnaabemwin, and so must go into considerable detail, at the same time I wish this work,
as much as possible, to be accessible to non-linguists, and so take precautions to explain lin-
guistic terminology as it arises. Every word appearing in SMALL CAPITALS is defined in the
glossary at the back of the book.
    It is also very important to realize that knowledge of the formal grammatical patterns of
a language accounts for only part of what a fluent speaker knows. Fluent speakers also know
how to use language appropriately in particular social situations. This knowledge takes
many forms, including such things as how to greet people, how to take one's leave, what
constitutes appropriate topics of conversation with people of all ages, what tone to use in
different social contexts, what vocabulary, when joking is appropriate, when one should be
silent, and so on. For most speakers of the language, these aspects of language use are much
more salient than the formal patterns of grammar, such as how to inflect an animate intransi-
tive verb in a subordinate clause. Scholars sometimes make a distinction between GRAM-
MATICAL COMPETENCE, knowledge of formal structures and patterns of language, and
COMMUNICATIVE COMPETENCE, knowledge of how language is used socially. This grammar
concerns itself with grammatical competence, and has almost nothing to say about commu-
nicative competence. This is not because I feel that grammatical competence is more impor-
tant than communicative competence, but only because I believe that a rigorous outline of
grammatical forms must precede an account of how such resources are used communica-
tively, and because time and space limit what I can address in a single monograph. Some
issues pertaining to Odawa communicative competence are addressed in Spielmann 1998,
and in northern Ojibwe, in L. Valentine 1995.

1.7 Additional Reading

   For an extensive overview of Anishinaabemowin dialects, see Valentine 1994. For an
overview of the history of various Nishnaabemwin groups, including the Odawa, Chippewa,
and Potawatomi, many articles in Volume 15 of the Handbook of North American Indians
(published in 1978, with Bruce Trigger as general editor of the volume) can be consulted,
including Goddard on Central Algonquian languages, Feest and Feest on Odawa (called
Ottawa in the handbook), and Clifton on Potawatomi. An invaluable general source for
materials are the various proceedings volumes of the annual Algonquian Conference, which
have enjoyed the editorial direction of several Algonquianists, including William Cowan,
David Pentland, and most recently, Arden Ogg. As to history, a community-based research
                                                                   1.7 Additional Reading • 27


project at Walpole Island resulted in the publication in 1987 of Minishenhying Anishnaabe-
aki, Walpole Island: The Soul of Indian Territory. This volume provides a detailed history of
Walpole Island, going back to prehistoric times. Also of note is Schmalz 1991, a history of
the area. Theresa Smith has written an interesting book examining traditional religious
beliefs and practices on Manitoulin (Smith 1995). For an introduction to linguistics,
O'Grady and Archibald 2000 is a good choice for those living in Canada, though some of its
treatments, particularly those on phonology and syntax, are quite advanced for beginners.
    As to specific grammatical materials for the varieties of Anishinaabemowin documented
in this work, there is a long and excellent tradition. Baraga's grammar, published in 1850, is
still useful, as is his dictionary (Baraga 1878). Andrew Blackbird's brief grammar of his
native Ottawa, contained within Blackbird 1887, offers another early approach to Anishi-
naabemowin grammar. In more recent years Bloomfield 1958, published posthumously
after the author's death in 1949, provides a look at Odawa through the eyes of one of the last
century's most gifted linguists. The texts in that work have been reprinted in Valentine, ed.
1998, which contains word-by-word grammatical analysis as well as a concordance of every
verbal inflectional form. Bloomfield 1962 provides a similar, and even more detailed,
account of Menominee grammar. For more recent approaches, see Rhodes 1976a, a theoret-
ical account of Odawa using the approach of relational grammar.
