Phonology and Orthography




2.1 Introduction

    In this chapter I examine the PHONOLOGY, or sound system, of Nishnaabemwin, includ-
ing a look at the distinctive sounds of the language, at how these sounds pattern and interact,
and the ways that they are customarily represented in written form. Phonological behaviour
is also treated in several other chapters, for which the index can be consulted.
    I have chosen to follow the rather conservative spelling norms of Richard Rhodes' dic-
tionary of Eastern Ojibwe-Chippewa-Ottawa (Rhodes 1985), as they are particularly useful
for explaining and illustrating the grammatical system of Nishnaabemwin. These spelling
norms are conservative in the sense that they tend to reflect the pronunciation of Minnesota
Ojibwe more than that of phonologically more innovative dialects to the east, such as Nish-
naabemwin. Many Nishnaabe writers and teachers depart in various ways from this system,
in order to more directly represent their own regional and local pronunciation, usually on
the basis of assumed phonetic correspondences to conventional English spellings. In this
chapter I will lay out many of the principles at work in such local variation, and explain how
they relate to broader patterns of speech across Nishnaabemwin dialects and the Anishinaa-
bemowin group in general.
    Many of the concepts presented here will be new to readers lacking linguistic training,
but some familiarity with them is necessary, in order to better understand the behaviour of
sounds in Nishnaabemwin. For example, speakers of the language often pronounce b, d and
g at the ends of words as if they were p, t, and k, respectively. This behaviour makes perfect
sense once one has a proper understanding of the systematic relationships that exist between
different groups of consonants. An understanding of the properties and patternings of
sounds should also help in the teaching of the language, especially to adults, who often want
logical explanations for the linguistic patterns they encounter. While many unfamiliar terms
are introduced in this chapter, all SMALL CAPITAL terms are defined in the glossary as well
as when they are introduced in the text.
                                             2.2 PRACTICAL AND PHONETIC ORTHOGRAPHIES • 29


    I begin with a discussion of the representation of the sounds of the language, in terms of
their distinctive values, their phonetic variants, and their representation in writing. Crucial
to this presentation are the concepts of PHONEMES and PHONES. Next we examine the human
VOCAL TRACT and how speech sounds are made, then look at the vowels and consonants of
Nishnaabemwin. We then take up the STRESS patterns of the language, that is, the rules for
emphasizing and de-emphasizing particular SYLLABLES in words. One particularly impor-
tant aspect of the stress rules is that many short vowels are weakened or deleted from pro-
nunciation, by the rule of SYNCOPE. Syncope in turn gives rise to many adjustments in the
consonants it juxtaposes, which I discuss in detail as well.

2.2 Practical and Phonetic Orthographies

    In linguistic studies, sounds are typically represented using a phonetic alphabet,
designed specifically to provide a unique symbol for each distinctive sound found in lan-
guage. The phonetic alphabet most widely used is that of the INTERNATIONAL PHONETIC
ASSOCIATION ALPHABET, usually abbreviated IPA. The IPA uses many symbols not found
in the regular English alphabet, nor in the Nishnaabemwin alphabet. For example the 'ng'
sound at the end of the English word sing and the Nishnaabemwin word dgoshing, 'when
ANsg arrives' is represented in the IPA with the symbol, [rj]. In this work I use special IPA
symbols only when they are absolutely required in order to make a point clear. Otherwise, I
use the practical orthography used among the languages of the Anishinaabemowin group,
the so-called double vowel orthography, so named because of its use of double letters to
represent the long vowels /i:/, /a:/, and /o:/. This orthography is also sometimes called the
Fiero system, after Charles Fiero, a linguist who devised it in the 1950's in order to repre-
sent the speech of Minnesota varieties of Ojibwe. It is now widely used throughout the
United States and Ontario.

2.2.1 Letters, Phones, and Phonemes

    In common with all spoken languages, Nishnaabemwin has a limited number of DIS-
TINCTIVE SOUNDS which are put together in different combinations to form larger units,
morphemes and words. The fundamental, distinctive sounds of a language are called PHO-
NEMES. Many of the symbols (characters, letters) used to represent phonemes in writing are
drawn from the Roman alphabet, which can be confusing, since it may not always be clear
whether one is talking about a specific phoneme, or a letter of the alphabet. To get around
such problems phonemes are usually indicated in writing by placing them within slashes,
for example, /b/ and Id are two of the phonemes of Nishnaabemwin. To represent phonemes
in writing, letters are used, placed within slashes, but it must be understood that phonemes
are units of sound, not units of writing. To refer specifically to letters in this work, I use
angle brackets, for example, «b» and «e». Sounds must be distinguished from letters
because often a single letter represents several distinct sounds in popular writing systems, or
conversely, a single sound may be represented by several letters. This is obvious to anyone
30 • 2.2.1 LETTERS, PHONES, AND PHONEMES


 who has learned to write English, but it is also true to a lesser extent of Nishnaabemwin.
     Decisions of how to represent a language in writing are based on many factors, involving
 such things as technical accuracy, simplicity, and pedagogy. By comparing and contrasting
 vocabulary, the most significant and patterned relationships between sounds in a language
 can be determined, and this knowledge can be used to devise a system of spelling that opti-
 mally expresses such relationships. Linguistically based writing systems usually stick to the
 principle that each distinctive sound, each phoneme, should have its own distinctive spell-
 ing. For example, linguistic analysis shows that there are two distinctive sounds in Nishnaa-
 bemwin, /g/ and /k/, as in the words dgonan, 'mix it in!' and dkonan, 'hold it!' The /g/
 sound also occurs in the word for 'fox,' waagosh, where it is between the vowels /aa/ and
 Id. However, in the form of the word for a small or immature fox, waagshens, the /g/ is not
 between vowels, and may sound like a [k], that is, the word may sound as if it might be
 spelled waakshens. Based on an analysis of the sound patterns of the language, however, it
.becomes clear that even though a k is heard in this context, it is different from the /k/ sound
 occurring in a word such as mik, 'beaver,' because the 7k/ in mik is always pronounced as a
 [k], even when it is between vowels, as in mikoons, 'young beaver.' So a linguistic approach
 suggests that the word for a small fox can be spelled waagshens, to capture the fact that the
 sound in question is basically a /g/ that has had its pronunciation altered because of its adja-
 cency to the consonant /sh/ (IPA ///), as opposed to the /k/ of mikoons, which has different
 properties. A further distinction is made linguistically between the basic, structural sound
 elements of a language, its PHONEMES, and their varying actual pronunciations, called
 PHONES. The same phoneme in a language may be pronounced with several different
 phones. To distinguish them from phonemes, which are often written with the same sym-
 bols, phones are placed within SQUARE BRACKETS, e.g., phones [k] and [g], as opposed to
 phonemes /k/ and /g/. Thus, we can observe of Nishnaabemwin that the phoneme /g/ is
 sometimes pronounced as [g] and sometimes as [k], depending on what sounds are around it
 and its position in the word. Between vowels it is pronounced as [g], but next to certain con-
 sonants and at the end of a word, it is pronounced as [k]. The choice of which phone is used
 to pronounce the phoneme /g/ is based on predictable distributional criteria. The phoneme
 /k/, however, is always pronounced as [k], never as [g]. Linguistic analysis of a vast number
 of languages suggests that a good principle for developing a writing system is that each
 phoneme should have a single spelling, and be consistently spelled the same way regardless
 of whatever phone is used to pronounce it in a particular context. So, for example, the pho-
 neme /g/ should be spelled as /g/ even in waagshens, where it has the sound [k]. Spelling
 systems strive to represent each phoneme with a distinct symbol, and to use that symbol
 regardless of what phones realize the phoneme in a given context.
     In sum, the following conventions are used to represent phonemes, phones, and letters.
 Concept     Description                                            Identification    Ex.
 Phonemes    distinctive units of sound                             slashes           /g/, /k/
 Phones      distinguishable pronunciations of a given phoneme      square brackets   [g], [k]
 Letters     written representations                                angle brackets    «g», «k»
                                                    2.2.1 LETTERS, PHONES, AND PHONEMES • 31


    A phonemic approach to spelling can present problems for second language learners,
however, because, lacking the knowledge that native speakers unconsciously have of their
language, the learner literate and fluent in English is likely to pronounce the /g/ in
waagshens as a [g] sound, and not as a [k]. The problem is made more severe by the fact
that most students of contemporary Nishnaabemwin are already literate in English, and
assume English letter-to-pronunciation values when reading Nishnaabemwin. Another
problem with a phonemic approach is that bilingual native-speaking Nishnaabe teachers
seeking to produce curriculum materials cannot simply listen to their own pronunciation of
a word, and spell it as they hear it, based on their English-based orthographic sensibilities,
because some [k] sounds that they hear should be spelled with a «g», as in waagshens,
'young fox,' and some with a «k», as in mikoons, 'young beaver.' Many linguistic concepts
have to be understood in order to spell with the phonemic approach, and many local lan-
guage teachers lack training in such principles, as do local elders, who, as authorities on
other matters of language use, may disdain spelling conventions that do not match their
intuitions based on English literacy. Most writers resort to some degree of phonetic tran-
scription in their representation of Nishnaabemwin, based on sound-to-letter correspon-
dences with English.
    If the issues involved in spelling were only those of local practice, solutions might be a
bit more straightforward. The problem is that pronunciations can vary considerably from
community to community. For example, one speaker may pronounce waagshens with a [k]
sound, but a speaker in another community may pronounce it with a [g]. Unless the word is
then spelled differently in each community, its spelling will not reflect local pronunciation.
This really only becomes important when materials are developed for use by a large number
of communities, embracing many different local pronunciations, for example, widely-used
language lessons, dictionaries, and grammars. A dictionary that sought to spell each word to
show all of the local pronunciations would become more complex, larger, and consequently,
more expensive and more difficult to use. In works to be used over wide areas showing lots
of local variation in pronunciation, some kind of standardized spelling system is usually
developed. Very often, in languages around the world, some socially prestigious dialect is
chosen to represent the standard, since that dialect is likely to reflect the speech of politi-
cally, economically, and educationally prominent members of society. The standard then
gets promoted by use in educational institutions that train local teachers, and certification of
teachers may involve tests showing proficiency in the standard. While such an approach
may seem unfair to local interests, it has much to commend it. For one, once the standard is
learned, it is easy to produce and use new materials that are consistent with earlier materi-
als. Materials can be used in all communities that have teachers trained in the standard, and
children advancing from grade to grade will find the same spelling system in use as they
move from teacher to teacher and from textbook to textbook. The standard also becomes an
emblem of identity for a group of people, uniting them and facilitating the sharing of infor-
mation between local communities and centralized institutions. Writers from very different
communities can share their work with each other, and such work can become the basis of a
national literature. Standardization is very often central to the development of nationhood.
32 • 2.3 THE VOCAL TRACT


The cost of standardization is that some control must be sacrificed at the local level, and
educational centres must be established. Local sovereignty must yield to national sover-
eignty.

2.3 The Vocal Tract

    To understand the dynamics of speech, it helps to know something of the structure and
function of the human VOCAL TRACT. In the broadest sense, the vocal tract consists of the
following components:

•   the lungs
•   the trachea (or windpipe)
•   the larynx (or voice box), containing the vocal cords
•   the oral (mouth) cavity and its surfaces, the tongue, and lips
•   the nasal (nose) cavity

    To produce speech, air is expelled from the lungs by controlled exhalation, through the
TRACHEA (windpipe), and into the LARYNX. In the larynx there are special structures called
VOCAL FOLDS or VOCAL CORDS, that can be drawn together or moved apart to produce dif-
ferent vocal effects. If the vocal cords are drawn closely together, they will vibrate when air
from the lungs passes between them, and produce an audible rhythmic buzzing called VOIC-
ING. Sounds produced with the vocal cords vibrating are said to be VOICED. Voicing is what
gives speech its resonance and sound volume. If the vocal cords are sufficiently far apart,
however, they will not vibrate. A sound made with the vocal cords apart is said to be VOICE-
LESS. The distinction between voiced and voiceless sounds can easily be heard by holding
the /z/ of the word 'zip' and then comparing it to the /s/ of the word 'sip'. The resonance
that is heard in the [z] of 'zip' is produced by vocal cord vibration (voicing). The [s] of 'sip',
on the other hand, lacks vocal cord vibration, and so is voiceless. Notice too that the source
of the resonance in the [z] of 'zip' is clearly in the throat, whereas the source of the hissing
sound of the [s] of 'sip' is restricted to the mouth, where the tip of the tongue is in close
proximity to the area behind the upper teeth. Since [s] lacks voicing, all of its sound volume
comes from this one source; [z], on the other hand, has sound volume associated with both
vocal cord vibration and the area behind the upper teeth where it is made. In fact, the only
difference between [z] and [s] is that the former is voiced and the latter is voiceless.
    The opening between the vocal cords is called the GLOTTIS. Sounds made in the vicinity
of the vocal cords are thus called GLOTTAL sounds. In normal resting position, the vocal
cords are apart so that unimpeded breathing can take place.
    Once past the larynx, the airflow is shaped in various ways in the throat and ORAL CAV-
ITY (mouth) to produce the different distinctive sounds of the language. In some cases, the
air is completely blocked off for a very brief time somewhere in the oral cavity. For exam-
ple, in making a /b/ sound, as in doodooshaaboo, 'milk,' the lips are brought together, creat-
ing a complete closure of the vocal tract at the lips. In the case of the sound /aa/, however,
                                                                      2.3 THE VOCAL TRACT • 33


there is no obstruction of the vocal tract, but the jaw is opened and the body of the tongue is
lowered and drawn back. In the case of /aa/, rather than the vocal tract being obstructed, as
it is with /b/ or /z/, it is shaped in a particular way. This fundamental difference in the way
these sounds are made distinguishes the two primary classes of sounds in all spoken human
languages: CONSONANTS, which typically involve constriction or blockage of the air as it
passes out of the mouth; and VOWELS, which involve the positioning of the tongue at differ-
ent locations in the mouth. Vowels are almost always voiced too, that is, involve vibration of
the vocal cords, whereas many consonants come in pairs in which one member is voiced
and the other is voiceless, as we saw with /z/ and /s/.




                                       THE VOCAL TRACT

    In order to produce NASAL sounds, such as /n/ and /m/, the SOFT PALATE (also called the
VELUM) is lowered, and air enters and passes through the NASAL CAVITY. If the soft palate is
raised, it closes off the opening to the nasal cavity, preventing the entry of air, and the sound
is said to be ORAL as opposed to nasal. When the soft palate is lowered while a consonant is
produced, a NASAL CONSONANT results; when the soft palate is lowered while a vowel is
produced, a NASALIZED VOWEL results. Nishnaabemwin has both kinds of nasal sounds.

2.4.1 The Classification of Vowels I: Vowel Quality

    Vowels group into classes on the basis of their shared properties. Vowels sharing proper-
ties behave in phonetically similar ways. Vowels are classified according to their QUALITY
and their QUANTITY. Vowel quality has to do with where in the mouth the vowel is articu-
lated, and whether the lips are ROUNDED as part of the pronunciation of the vowel; vowel
quantity concerns how long the pronunciation of a vowel is sustained and how forceful the
pronunciation is. Nishnaabemwin makes a crucial phonological distinction between long
vowels and short vowels.
    Vowel quality involves three distinct properties:

• VOWEL HEIGHT: how close the body of the tongue is to the roof of the mouth when
  the vowel is made.
• VOWEL BACKNESS: how far back in the mouth the body of the tongue is when the
  vowel is made.
• LIP ROUNDING: whether or not the lips are rounded when the vowel is made.

    Vowels are produced by placing the body of the tongue in various positions in the mouth.
The height of the tongue may be raised or lowered, and the tongue may be moved forward
or backward from its rest position. These two parameters of variation in the pronunciation
of the vowels define a region in the mouth, into which the different vowels can be mapped,
as in the chart on the following page. The chart defines a region in which each vowel is pro-
nounced. The space is divided into nine sub-areas, defined by dotted lines. Above the vowel
space there is an arcing line that shows very roughly the position of the roof of the mouth,
and positioned between the vowel space rectangle and the roof of the mouth are the two
consonant sounds, /y/ (IPA /j/) in the front area, and /w/ in the back area. Each vowel in the
figure has an oval associated with it, roughly describing the range of variation in its height
and backness when pronounced in different contexts by different speakers. No vowel is
                                    2.4.1 THE CLASSIFICATION OF VOWELS I: VOWEL QUALITY • 37


always pronounced in a single, precise location within the vowel space; rather, each has a
region in which it is articulated, resulting in variable pronunciations for the same vowel.




                                   Front     Central        Back
                                        VOWEL BACKNESS
                         ROUGH POSITIONS OF NISHNAABEMWIN VOWELS

Note too that some of the vowel regions overlap, particularly those of l\l and /e/, and lot and
/a/. These overlaps occur because the higher vowels, lit and lot, both lower at the end of a
word or phrase, and so move into the region of the lower vowels /e/ and /a/, respectively.
The vowel Id also lowers in the same context, sounding rather like a long version of the
vowel associated with the letter «a» in English sat. The vowel /oo/ also has higher and lower
variants, with the higher variant sounding something like the sound associated with the
vowel of English boot, and the lower sounding something like the sound associated with the
vowel of English boat. But variation in the height of/oo/ is not like that of/i/, /a/, and Id, in
that it is often not a matter of the vowel's position in a word. Rather, individual speakers
vary, and there is variation within the speech of individuals.

    In its rest position, the body of the tongue is essentially in the mid-central region of the
vowel space, showing neither raising nor lowering, fronting or backing. There is a special
symbol in this position in the chart above, the symbol <o» (an upside-down e), called
SCHWA, which represents a minimal vowel, one produced with a minimum of articulatory
effort. This vowel can be heard as the first syllable of the English words about and allow. It
commonly occurs in languages that de-emphasize (or REDUCE) vowels in certain positions
within words, as English and Nishnaabemwin both do, and schwa is a common pronuncia-
tion of many vowels in both languages. In Nishnaabemwin, it occurs as a reduced form of
each of the short vowels, /i/, /a/ and /o/, in the speech of some speakers, a fact which is indi-
cated on the chart by the dotted lines running from each short vowel to schwa. I will have
more to say about schwa when I discuss stress in Section (6.1), below.
38 • 2.4.1 THE CLASSIFICATION OF VOWELS I: VOWEL QUALITY


    The vowel rectangle shown in the vowel chart above has two dimensions, one of HEIGHT
and one of relative BACKNESS. Another important parameter is the presence or absence of
lip-rounding.
    VOWEL HEIGHT. There are three sub-classifications of VOWEL HEIGHT: HIGH, MID and
LOW. Vowel height relates to how close the body of the tongue is to the roof of the mouth in
the pronunciation of a given vowel. To make high vowels, the body of the tongue is rela-
tively high, closer to the roof of the mouth, and to make low vowels the tongue body is rela-
tively low, farther from the roof of the mouth, and the jaw is often lowered to accentuate the
lowness of the vowel. Mid vowels are produced with the tongue body in-between the posi-
tions assumed for high and low vowels.
    VOWEL BACKNESS. Vowels are also classified on the basis of their relative BACKNESS,
again with three degrees, FRONT, CENTRAL, and BACK. Front vowels involve advancement
of the tongue body from its rest position, and back vowels involve retraction of the tongue
body from its rest position. Central vowels involve neither advancement nor retraction of
the tongue body.
    VOWEL ROUNDING. The last parameter by which vowels are classified concerns whether
or not the lips are rounded in their production. Only the vowels /oo/ and /o/ are inherently
rounded in Nishnaabemwin, though, as we will see, certain vowels can become rounded
under the influence of neighbouring sounds which are rounded. The vowel /aa/ is often pro-
nounced with lip rounding by many speakers.
    THE CLASSIFICATION OF VOWELS. Based on these three properties of height, backness
and rounding, we can classify the vowels of Nishnaabemwin as follows:

                          iii        high front unrounded
                          e          mid front unrounded
                          oo o       high/mid back rounded
                          aaa        low/mid back unrounded

    Based on this classification we can see that certain vowels share properties: for example,
the vowels /ii/, /i/, /oo/, and /o/ share the property of being high; the vowels /e/, /aa/, and /a/
share the property of being non-high (in other words, mid or low). The vowels /oo/ and /o/
share the property of being rounded, and the vowels /ii/, /i/, /e/, /aa/ and /a/ share the prop-
erty of being unrounded.
    THE RELATIONSHIP OF GLIDES TO VOWELS. The consonants /y/ (IPA /j/) and /w/ are
associated with particular regions of the vowel space, and therefore, have closer associa-
tions with particular vowels. The glide /y/ is closely associated with the vowel region high-
front (the palatal area), and thus with the vowels /ii/ and /i/; the glide /w/ is closely associ-
ated with the vowel region high-back (the velar area) and thus with the vowels /oo/ and /o/.
The glide /w/ also shares with /oo/ and /o/ the property of being rounded, since lip rounding
is involved in its production. These shared features of the glides /y/ and /w/ with particular
vowels have important consequences in the patterning of sounds in Nishnaabemwin. The
                                  2.4.2 THE CLASSIFICATION OF VOWELS II: VOWEL QUANTITY • 39


following chart summarizes the relationships between vowels and glides.

                       Vowel and Glide Correspondences
                                       Vowel           Glide
                       Palatal         /i/, /ii/       /y/
                       Velar           /o/, /oo/       /w/

2.4.2 The Classification of Vowels II: Vowel Quantity

     Nishnaabemwin also has two very different subclasses of vowels based on their QUAN-
TITY, or length, traditionally called short vowels and long vowels. The short vowels are /a/,
/i/, and /o/; the long vowels are /ii/, /e/, /aa/, and /oo/. Short vowels are written with a single
letter, and long vowels with a double letter, except in the case of /e/, which has no short
counterpart, and so can be written with a single letter even though it is long. Short and long
vowels contrast in their pronunciation, in that long vowels usually sound longer than short
vowels, and typically involve greater muscular tension and more extreme movement of the
tongue from the rest position in the middle of the vowel region.
     Long and short vowels often behave very differently in the ways they pattern in the lan-
guage. For example, short vowels are sometimes deleted from speech, as in the following
contrasts:

    nbaap           'I laugh'               njaachaam              'I sneeze'
    gbaap           'you laugh'             gjaachaam              'you sneeze'
    baapi           'ANsg laughs'           jaachaamo              'ANsg sneezes'

   Here it can be seen that in THIRD PERSON 'ANsg' forms, there is a final vowel that is not
present in the FIRST PERSON, T forms, and the SECOND PERSON 'you' forms. The vowels in
question are short /i/ in the case of baapi and short /o/ in the case of jaachaamo. The word
meaning 'I laugh,' nbaap, lacks the short /i/ that appears on baapi 'ANsg laughs'; the word
meaning 'I sneeze' njaachaam, lacks the short /o/ that appears on jaachaamo 'ANsg
sneezes'. When we examine verbs that end in long vowels, however, we find a different pat-
tern:

    ngoogii          Tdive'                  nmaajiibtoo            'I run away'
    ggoogii          'you dive'              gmaajiibtoo            'you run away'
    googii           'ANsg dives'            maajiibtoo             'ANsg runs away

   Here the final vowel, /ii/ or /oo/, is present in the forms for all three persons. The final
vowels in this set differ from the previous only in their length. Short vowels are sometimes
deleted from pronunciation, but long vowels almost never are. Long vowels are stronger
40 • 2.4.3 NASALIZED VOWELS


than short vowels, and so are more resistant to processes which might delete them. Since Id
is a long vowel, we don't expect it to be deleted in these contexts, either, and indeed it isn't,
as can be seen from the following examples:

    nboodwe        'I make fire'           nwiindmaage               'I tell, give a report'
    gboodwe        'you make fire'         gwiindmaage               'you tell, give a report'
    boodwe         'ANsg makes fire'       wiindmaage                'ANsg tells, gives a report'

   It is on the basis of behaviour such as this that we can say with confidence that Id is a
long vowel— it patterns with the other long vowels in that it isn't deleted as short vowels
are.
   Another important difference between short and long vowels is their behaviour with
respect to rules of stress. Stress is treated in detail in Section (6.1), beginning on p. 51.

2.4.3 Nasalized Vowels

   Some vowels in Nishnaabemwin are NASALIZED, or NASAL, which means that air passes
out through the nose as well as the mouth in their articulation, by lowering the soft palate in
their pronunciation. Nasalized vowels occur at the end of some words, where they are indi-
cated in written form by the letters «nh» following them, as in the examples in the table
below. Note that the letters «nh» used to spell these words are not pronounced as separate
sounds, but simply indicate that the vowel preceding them has a nasal pronunciation.

                     iinh       kiwenziinh 'old man'

                     aanh       bnajaanh 'nestling'
                     oonh       boodoonh 'polliwog, tadpole'
                                zhashkoonh 'muskrat'

not pronounced as a separate phone, but is realized (pronounced) as nasalization on the pre-
ceding vowel, as in the following examples:

                              z akiwenziinh        'old man'

2.5.1 The Classification of Consonants

   Consonants are classified on the basis of three aspects of their pronunciation:

1. PLACE OF ARTICULATION. Where in the vocal tract the consonant is made.

2. MANNER OF ARTICULATION. How the consonant is made.

3. THE STATE OF THE GLOTTIS. Whether or not the vocal cords vibrate in the production
    of the consonant.




                         PLACES OF ARTICULATION OF NISHNAABEMWIN CONSONANTS
                                                           2.5.1.1 PLACE OF ARTICULATION • 45


2.5.1.1 Place of Articulation

    Human languages share a small number of places in the vocal tract where consonant
sounds are produced. The figure on the preceding page illustrates the main anatomical struc-
tures of the vocal tract, including the lips, teeth, ALVEOLAR RIDGE, HARD and SOFT PAL-
ATES, tongue, and VOCAL CORDS. It also shows the places in the vocal tract where
Nishnaabemwin consonants are made, along with the consonants made at each location.
The numbers in the figure are used in the following discussion to identify individual places
of articulation.
    CD LABIAL. Labial sounds involve the lips. Labial consonants in Nishnaabemwin include
/b/, /p/, /m/, and /w/. All the labial sounds of Nishnaabemwin are BILABIAL, that is, both the
upper and lower lip are used in their articulation, [baapi 'ANsg laughs'; pin 'potato'; maang
'loon'; waawan 'egg']
    © DENTAL/ALVEOLAR. DENTAL consonants are produced by putting the tongue tip
behind the upper teeth. ALVEOLAR consonants are produced by putting the tongue tip on the
bony ridge behind the upper teeth, called the ALVEOLAR RIDGE. Dental/Alveolar consonants
in Nishnaabemwin are /d/, /t/, /z/, /s/, and /n/. There is variation among speakers as to
whether these sounds are dental or alveolar, [biidoon 'bring IN!', geget 'of course', nzid
'my foot', sin 'stone', aandeg 'crow']
    <D ALVEOPALATAL. Alveopalatal consonants are made by placing the blade or tip portion
of the tongue against the vertical portion of the hard palate behind the alveolar ridge. Alveo-
palatal consonants in Nishnaabemwin include /zh/, /sh/, /j/ and /ch/ (IPA /3/, ///, /d3/, and
/tJ7). [giizhiitaa 'ANsg finishes'; zhaashaa 'IN is slippery'; maajaa 'ANsg takes off,
leaves'; miigwech 'thank you']
    © PALATAL. Palatal consonants are made by placing the front of the tongue near the
HARD PALATE. The only palatal consonant in Nishnaabemwin is the GLIDE lyl (IPA /j/).
[yekzi 'ANsg is tired'; nday 'my dog']
    © VELAR. Velar consonants are made by placing the back of the tongue against the SOFT
PALATE, or near it, in the case of glides. Velar consonants in Nishnaabemwin include /g/, /k/,
and the GLIDE /w/. [gaag 'porcupine'; kik 'kettle, pail'; waawan 'egg']
    © GLOTTAL. Glottal consonants are made at the glottis, that is, in the throat at the vocal
cords, since the glottis is the opening between the vocal cords. The primary glottal conso-
nant in Nishnaabemwin is /?/ «h», GLOTTAL STOP [ndeh 'my heart'; mzinhigan 'book'].
However, in a few expressive and orientational adverbs such as haaw, 'okay,' hawn, 'fire!,'
and ehenh, 'yes,' the glottal consonant is pronounced as [h]. Both sounds are spelled with
«h», though writers often omit representation of/?/, because it is often not pronounced.

2.5.1.2 Manner of Articulation

   There is only a small number of distinct ways in which consonant sounds are made in
Nishnaabemwin, outlined as follows.
   STOPS. Stops are made by completely obstructing the flow of air in the vocal tract at
46 • 2.5.1.2 MANNER OF ARTICULATION


some point. For example, a BILABIAL STOP is made by completely obstructing the air at the
lips, that is, by closing the lips together. The bilabial stops in Nishnaabemwin are /b/ and
/p/. [baapi 'ANsg laughs';pabwin 'cushion, chair'].
     DENTAL/ALVEOLAR STOPS are made by completely stopping the flow of air in the den-
tal/alveolar area. Dental/Alveolar stops in Nishnaabemwin include /d/ and /t/. [wdoon
 'ANsg's mouth'; toon 'put IN (there)! place IN (there)!'].
     VELAR STOPS are made by completely obstructing the flow of air by placing the back of
the tongue against the SOFT PALATE. Velar stops in Nishnaabemwin are /g/ and /k/. [gaag
 'porcupine'; wkaad 'ANsg's leg'; gookoosh 'pig']
     A GLOTTAL STOP is made by drawing the vocal cords tightly together, closing off the
GLOTTIS (the opening between the vocal cords), and momentarily stopping the air from
passing through. In Nishnaabemwin, glottal stop is a distinctive sound on a par with other
 consonants, and is symbolized by «h» in normally cited forms (IPA /?/), which means that
 the value of the letter is different from that of English, [ndeh 'my heart'; mhiingan 'wolf']
     In sum, the stops of Nishnaabemwin are /b/, /p/, /d/, /t/, /g/, /k/ and /?/. The sounds /b/,
/p/, /d/, /t/, /g/ and /k/ taken together are called ORAL STOPS, since they all involve obstruc-
 tion in the oral cavity, in contrast to the GLOTTAL STOP, /?/, in which obstruction occurs in
 the throat, in the glottal area.
     FRICATIVES. Fricatives are made by channeling air through a narrow space somewhere
 in the vocal tract, creating turbulence, or friction, but never stopping the outward flow of air
 altogether. Fricatives are consonant sounds that appear to "leak," as opposed to stops, which
 have no leakage. Nishnaabemwin has four fricatives. The DENTAL/ALVEOLAR FRICATIVES
 are /z/ and /s/, made by putting the tongue tip up against the dental or alveolar area, creating
 a constriction, but still allowing air to pass through. The ALVEOPALATAL FRICATIVES are
/zh/ and /sh/, made by placing the front of the tongue in the alveopalatal area, but allowing
turbulent air to move through a narrow opening, [zaad 'poplar'; saad '(that) ANsg put
ANobv there'; wzhigon 'its fin (of a fish)'; shigan 'bass (kind of fish)'].
     AFFRICATES. Affricates are complex sounds, consisting of a stop component followed by
a fricative component, but the two components are articulated so quickly together that they
form a unit and pattern in the language as a unit. The only affricates in Nishnaabemwin, /j/
and /ch/, are made in the ALVEOPALATAL area, /j/ is made up of the components /d+zh/, and
/ch/, /t+sh/. [maajaa 'ANsg takes off;jaachaamo 'ANsg sneezes'].
     NASALS. Nasal consonants are made with complete closure somewhere in the oral cav-
ity, but with the soft palate down, so that air is free to pass into the nasal cavity and out
through the nose. The nasal phonemes of Nishnaabemwin are /n/ and /m/, the former den-
tal/alveolar and the latter bilabial. The phoneme /n/ has two distinct pronunciations, one of
which is dental/alveolar, and the other of which is velar. A velar nasal is the sound of the
final element of the English word 'sing', and is typically represented in phonetic transcrip-
tion as /rj/, which is called ENG. This sound is made by placing the back of the tongue
against the soft palate (see the illustration of the vocal tract on page 33), creating a velar
stop in the oral cavity, but at the same time lowering the soft palate so that air can escape
through the nasal passage. The phoneme /n/ has a velar pronunciation before the sounds /g/
                                       2.5.1.3 STATE OF THE GLOTTIS: VOICED AND VOICELESS • 47


or /k/, which are themselves velar, as in maang, 'loon', and nkaad 'my leg.' Nasal conso-
nants are also often called simply NASALS, [niimi 'ANsg dances'; nmiinaa 'I give it to
ANsg'; dgoshing, '(that) ANsg arrives'].
    GLIDES. GLIDES show similarities with both vowels and consonants. Glides are made by
placing the tongue in some region of the vocal tract, and producing very little constriction,
but more constriction than a vowel has. Because they are so similar to vowels, glides are
also sometimes called SEMI-VOWELS. There are two glides in Nishnaabemwin, /y/ and /w/,
the former made in the palatal area, and is thus called a PALATAL GLIDE, and the latter made
in the velar area, but also involving the lips, so is both labial and velar, and as a result is usu-
ally called a LABIOVELAR GLIDE or a VELAR GLIDE, [wiiyaas 'meat'; yaa 'ANsg is there';
aawi 'ANsg is an X, e.g., Nishnaabe aawi 'ANsg is an Indian'].

2.5.1.3 State of the Glottis: Voiced and Voiceless

    Recall that the GLOTTIS is the opening between the vocal cords. When the vocal cords
are drawn together and air is forced between them, they vibrate and produce VOICING. When
the vocal cords are apart, they do not vibrate, and so there is no voicing. Many consonants
group into pairs based on whether or not the vocal cords vibrate when each is made. For
example, /b/ and /p/ are both labial, that is, they have the same place of articulation; /b/ and
/p/ are both stops, and thus have the same manner of articulation as well. But /b/ and /p/ dif-
fer from one another in part because /b/ is made with the vocal cords drawn together and
vibrating, and /p/ is made with the vocal cords drawn apart. So /b/ is VOICED and /p/ is
VOICELESS. In fact, except for GLOTTAL STOP, all of the STOPS, FRICATIVES, and AFFRICATES
occur in such pairs in Nishnaabemwin, with one voiced member and one voiceless member,
as follows:

     Place                Manner        Voiced Voiceless IPA Voiced           IPA Voiceless
     Labial               Stop            /b/     /p/         /b/                  /p/
     Dental/Alveolar      Stop            /d/     /t/         /d/                  /t/
     Dental/Alveolar      Fricative       Izl     /s/         IzJ                  /s/
     Alveopalatal         Fricative      /zh/    /sh/         /3/                   ///
     Alveopalatal         Affricate       /j/    /ch/        /ds/                   /tj/
     Velar                Stop            /g/     /k/         /9/                   /k/

   Because the production of stops, fricatives, and affricates all have a significant degree of
obstruction somewhere in the vocal tract, they are called OBSTRUENTS (related to the word
'obstruct'). Each of the obstruents of Nishnaabemwin is paired with a partner of opposite
VOICING. This has, very important implications for certain aspects of pronunciation. Recall
that in the normal resting state, to facilitate breathing, there is no voicing, since the vocal
cords are too far apart to vibrate. Recall too that the main difference between a /b/ and a /p/
48 • 2.5.1.4 FORTIS AND LENIS CONSONANT PAIRS


is that in the case of the /b/, the vocal cords are drawn together and are vibrating, whereas in
the case of the /p/, the vocal cords are apart, so that they do not vibrate. If, in a pronouncing
a /b/, the vocal cords are far enough apart to fail to vibrate, instead of producing a [b] sound,
a [p] sound will be produced. The same is true with /d/, /g/, /z/, /3/ «zh» and /d$/ «j» with
respect to [t], [k], [s], [J] «sh» and [tj] «ch». This process, whereby the vibration of the
vocal cords is absent in a sound which normally has vocal cord vibration, is called DEVOIC-
ING. A devoiced /b/ sounds like a /p/; a devoiced /3/ «zh» sounds like a /J7 «sh», etc. We will
see below that devoicing is very common in certain positions in Nishnaabemwin words, giv-
ing rise to variable pronunciations of many phonemes. The representation of consonant
voicing is the source of many of the differences in spelling between different writers of
Nishnaabemwin.
    Another feature related to voicing is ASPIRATION. If you place your palm up to your
mouth and say very carefully the English words 'bit' and 'pit', you will notice that in the
latter word, associated with the /p/, there is a puff of air following it that is not present when
the /b/ is articulated. This puff of air is called aspiration. Aspiration is signalled in phonetic
transcription with a small raised h, as in [ph]it, English pit. Nishnaabemwin voiceless stop
consonants (/p/, /t/, /k/) very often have aspiration associated with them, usually following
the articulation of the consonant, but occasionally preceding it.

2.5.1.4 Fortis and Lenis Consonant Pairs

      Another way that voiceless stops, fricatives and affricates differ from voiced ones is that
 the voiceless are phonetically stronger, and in most situations where a voiced and a voice-
 less obstruent come together, the voiceless one usually dominates in some way. Actually, I
 simplified things a little above in saying that the only difference between /b/ and /p/, /d/ and
 /t/, etc., is one of voicing, because in Nishnaabemwin these sound pairs differ in ways other
 than just their voicing. The voiceless member of the pair is not only voiceless, but is pro-
 nounced for a longer time than the voiced member, and with greater muscular intensity. The
 voiceless member of the pair is sometimes said to be FORTIS, or HARD, and the voiced,
LENIS, or SOFT. It is also useful to know that the fortis consonants historically come from
combinations, or clusters, of two consonants. Some analysts of Nishnaabemwin have used
the convention of writing fortis consonants with doublings of the letters they use for lenis
consonants (called LENES), for example, makkwa, 'bear' but kaak, 'porcupine', which in the
system used here would be spelled makwa and gaag. The system of double letters has the
advantage of showing more clearly the relationships between sounds. A fortis consonant
often does behave as if it were a doubled lenis consonant. One way to see this clearly is to
compare the speech of Nishnaabemwin with speakers of other Ojibwe dialects, for example,
the Ojibwe of Minnesota. In Minnesota Ojibwe, to say 'you will dive', one says giga-
googii, with four lenis consonants, all /g/'s. In Nishnaabemwin, the l\l between the first two
/g/'s is not pronounced, creating a sequence of two /g/'s, gga-googii. But many speakers of
Nishnaabemwin hear this combination of two lenis consonants as a fortis consonant, and
spell this word, ka-googii. So, to many speakers' ears, doubled (GEMINATE) lenis conso-
                                                               2.5.2 Summary of Consonants • 49



nants [gg] sound like a single fortis consonant [k].
    Another argument for saying that fortis consonants represent geminate lenes comes from
the behaviour of certain inflectional suffixes. For example, when the conjunct order third
person inanimate suffix, /-g/ is added to a verb stem ending in /d/, a /k/ is produced. Thus,
the CONJUNCT form of aabdad, 'INsg is useful' vn, is aabdak, from an UNDERLYING FORM
of /aabdad+g/. Note also that the third person animate conjunct order suffix /-d/ attaches
directly to the preterit mode suffix /-bany/, to produce /p/, the fortis equivalent of /b/. For
example, compare the verb forms niimid, '(when/that/if) ANsg dances' and niimpan,
'(that/when) ANsg had danced,' which has the underlying representation /niimi+d+bany/.
    The following diagram illustrates the nature of the relationship the between consonants
We have been discussing. Under certain conditions, when two lenis consonants are juxta-
posed across a suffix boundary (symbolized with + sign), a fortis consonant corresponding
to the second consonant results. If we analyze fortis consonants as doubled lenis conso-
nants, then the effect observed here can be explained as the spreading of the second conso-
nant's phonetic values to the first consonant, creating a doubled consonant, which is
naturally fortis (geminate).




    One last bit of support for a geminate analysis of fortis consonants concerns the behav-
iour of fortis consonants when attached to a stem that ends in a nasal, for example suffix
/-sii/, 'negative' or /-ke(n)/, 'prohibitive.' In such cases, the initial fortis consonant of the
suffix is always lenited, e.g., gego boodweke(n), 'don't make a fire!,' versus gego zhish-
nge(n), 'don't lie that way.'

2.5.2 Summary of Consonants

   The chart on the following page lays out the consonants of Nishnaabemwin in a system
that shows the different classes of sounds organized on the basis of place of articulation,
manner of articulation, and the state of glottis. Notice that /w/ is listed below under both the
velar place and the labial, because it is a complex sound involving the positioning of the
tongue body in the back of the mouth (the velar area), as well as lip rounding. IPA forms of
consonants are given in parentheses, when they differ from our standard orthography.

2.6 Syllables and Stress

   The sounds in a word organize into groupings called SYLLABLES. The two basic classes
of sounds, consonants and vowels, differ in the roles they have in syllables. Vowels occupy
the heart, or NUCLEUS, of a syllable, and consonants usually occupy the margins or "edges"
of syllables. For example, the word goon, 'snow' consists of a single syllable, with the
50 • 2.6 SYLLABLES AND STRESS

vowel /oo/ in its nucleus, preceded and followed by the consonants /g/ and /n/, respectively.
Many words have more than one syllable, and speakers of a language do not usually have
much trouble determining how many syllables there are in a word, and how the sounds
within the word group into syllables. For example, the wordjnmaan, 'boat,' consists of two
syllables, /jii/ and /maan/:
                                     Syllable     Syllable


   Many languages have systems of STRESS, whereby some syllables in a word are given
more prominence than others. For example, consider the two English words, both spelled
«content», as used in the following sentences.

   (a)   Tebo was content to sit watching the ducks.
   (b)   I think that Tebo's play is clever, but it lacks content.
                                                                             2.6.1 STRESS AND SYNCOPE • 51


    Although the two italicized words are spelled the same, they are pronounced differently.
The difference in pronunciation is due to different syllables receiving primary emphasis in
the two words. In sentence (a), the second vowel of content is pronounced with the greater
force, that is, it is both louder and of higher pitch than the other vowel in the word. In sen-
tence (b), though, it is the first vowel which has more emphasis. Vowels that are spoken with
such emphasis are said to be STRESSED, and vowels pronounced with little or no emphasis
are said to be UNSTRESSED. Different languages have different patterns of stress, which
determine how much emphasis each of the syllables in a word receives. Now consider the
following two sentences:

   This is a nice photograph.          I     I like photography.

    In the word photograph, the vowel in the middle of the word is unstressed and sounds
like 'uh' when spoken at normal speed. Such a vowel is said to be REDUCED, or de-empha-
sized. However, in the word photography, this same vowel does not sound like 'uh', because
now it is stressed. So there are really two aspects to stress systems: emphasizing stressed
syllables, and de-emphasizing unstressed syllables. Recall that the reduced vowel that
sounds like 'uh' is called SCHWA. De-emphasizing vowels in English involves reducing
them to schwa. Recall that schwa is a kind of minimal vowel lacking the distinctiveness of
unreduced vowels such as /i/, /a/, and /o/. Like English, Nishnaabemwin has intricate pat-
terns of stressing and de-stressing that apply to the syllables of its words. However, in Nish-
naabemwin, de-emphasized vowels may not only be reduced, but in many cases, are deleted
as part of the process of de-emphasis. Consider the following words:

   waagosh            'fox'                 waagshag               'foxes'

   Notice that there is an /o/ in waagosh which appears between the consonants /g/ and /sh/.
This vowel is not present in waagshag because it has been deleted due to its being
unstressed. The differing vowel compositions of these two words is due to different sylla-
bles receiving stress. The stressing of vowels in Nishnaabemwin is systematic, subject to
the interaction of several simple principles. These are described in detail in the next section.

2.6.1 Stress and Syncope

   Many Algonquian languages share similar rules of stress patterning. The stress patterns
that are presented in this section show similarities with those found in Delaware, Pota-
watomi, and Menominee, all sister languages of Nishnaabemwin.
   We have already seen that the consonants and vowels of words are organized into sylla-
bles. Syllables are also organized into larger groupings called METRICAL FEET. By "metri-
cal" I mean having to do with rhythmic patterns of pronunciation. In Nishnaabemwin a

1. Some people say foe-toe-graph when their attention is on their pronunciation.
52 • 2.6.1 STRESS AND SYNCOPE


metrical foot is a grouping of two syllables together, in which the first syllable of the foot is
weaker, and the second syllable is stronger. This pattern can be represented as follows.

                                            Foot

                                Syllabnle          Syllable
                                weakef             streonger

    The system here is quite simple: a standard foot consists of two syllables, the first of
which is the weaker member and the second the stronger. To see how this system works, we
will use a few words as they are pronounced in Minnesota Ojibwe, closely related to Nish-
naabemwin, and show how the stress rules relate the pronunciations of Nishnaabemwin and
Ojibwe. Consider the word gidagoshin, meaning 'you arrive' in Minnesota Ojibwe. If we
organize the syllables of this word in patterns of feet with weak and strong components, we
arrive at the following specification:




    This word consists of four syllables organized into two metrical feet. When we compare
this Minnesota Ojibwe word to its Nishnaabemwin counterpart, we make an interesting dis-
covery. The Nishnaabemwin pronunciation (and spelling) is often gdagshin, which lacks
some of the vowels of the Minnesota Ojibwe. If we examine the two pronunciations, we
find that the missing vowels in Nishnaabemwin are exactly those which happen to fall in
weak metrical positions.




   So the Nishnaabemwin word is actually identical to the Minnesota Ojibwe, the only dif-
ference between the two words being that in Nishnaabemwin metrically weak vowels are
de-emphasized to the point of deletion, while in Minnesota Ojibwe they are not.
                                                                2.6.1 STRESS AND SYNCOPE • 53


    One principle of Nishnaabemwin stress that I haven't explicitly mentioned is that footing
starts from the beginning of the word, and proceeds towards the end. In some other lan-
guages of the world, the system works in the opposite direction.
    Another rule of Nishnaabemwin stress is that the final vowel of a word must always be
strong (stressed), even if it falls in a position that would otherwise make it weak. To see how
this works, we will examine another Minnesota Ojibwe form, and compare it to Nishnaabe-
mwin, in this case the word dagoshin, 'ANsg arrives,' which is pronounced and spelled
dgoshin in Nishnaabemwin.




    Nishnaabemwin

   Minnesota Ojibwe

    Here, even though the last vowel naturally falls in a WEAK position counting from the
beginning of the word, it is strong because of the overriding principle that the last vowel of
a word is strong. So there is only one weak vowel in this word, the first one, which is
deleted in Nishnaabemwin, according to the rule that de-emphasizes weak vowels.
    Another aspect of Nishnaabemwin metrical footing is that long vowels can never occupy
weak metrical positions. What this means is that long vowels always receive some stress,
that is, they are never de-emphasized to the degree that short vowels can be. If a long vowel
falls in what would be a weak position, it is treated as if it were the strong component of a
foot consisting of only the syllable containing the long vowel. This can be made clear with
an example, esbanag, 'raccoons,' which in Minnesota Ojibwe is pronounced and spelled
esibanag.




   Nishnaabemwin

   Minnesota Ojibwe

    In this word, the first vowel cannot be weak, because it is long. So we create a DEFEC-
TIVE FOOT, consisting of a single syllable having a long vowel, instead of the normal foot
structure of two syllables. We then proceed on through the word, trying to build weak-
strong feet. The next vowel in the word is the short vowel HI, which can occupy the weak
position in a foot. The next vowel, short /a/, serves as the strong partner of HI. The last
54 • 2.6.1 STRESS AND SYNCOPE


vowel, even though short, cannot be weak because of the rule that requires that the last
vowel of a word always be strong. And once again we see that the only difference between
the Minnesota Ojibwe form and Nishnaabemwin is that the Nishnaabemwin pronunciation
(and spelling) shows deletion of the metrically weak vowel /i/.
   I have now introduced all of the basic rules pertaining to stress in Nishnaabemwin. They
are summarized as follows.

    METRICAL STRESS RULE(S)

    A. A metrical foot consists of a pairing of a weak and a strong syllable, with
       the following restrictions:

       Al Only short vowels can be weak; long vowels are always strong.

       A2 The last vowel in a word is always strong (or alternatively, is exempt from
          the stress rules).

    B. Build weak-strong metrical feet starting from the beginning of the word.

    C. Once footing is completed, de-emphasize metrically weak vowels by reducing
       them to schwa or deleting them, and give stress to metrically strong vowels.

    The systematic deletion of metrically weak vowels is called VOWEL SYNCOPE, or simply
SYNCOPE for short. A vowel that has been deleted by syncope is said to have been SYNCO-
PATED. Note that it is older speakers who tend to have reduced vowels in metrically weak
positions, while younger speakers typically delete weak vowels entirely. Vowel syncope is
pervasive in Nishnaabemwin, and serves as one of the defining features of the language
group, as we saw in the last chapter. We will see too that the effects of syncope extend far
beyond the simple deletion of weak vowels. In Section 5 we will examine some of the
effects on consonants that end up adjacent to each other when a weak vowel between them
is deleted.
    Another important point is that various kinds of reanalysis are presently taking place, in
reaction to the vast amount of variation introduced by syncope. For example, Rhodes
1985:113 records the word diyaawi, 'be an ass.' This word seems to have a dependent noun
as initial, /-diy-aa-/, 'rump,' which we might expect to have a third person or indefinite pos-
sessor prefix, /o/ or /i/, which is deleted by syncope. However, Rhodes also lists the first per-
son singular present tense form as ndiyaaw, 'I am an ass.' Note that in both forms, the /i/ of
/diy/ is pronounced. The rule of syncope predicts no such continuity, and thus seems to be
ignored in the third person form. If there were an initial short vowel in the basic stem, it
should surface in the first singular form because its person prefix shifts the stress onto it, but
no such vowel is present. We see a similar phenomenon with the forms Rhodes provides for
kik, 'kettle, pot,' which include ndakik, 'my kettle,' which we predict by syncope, but also
                                                           2.6.2 MAIN STRESS IN A WORD • 55


nkikom, 'my kettle,' in which the historical initial vowel /a/, does not show up in alterna-
tions. A speaker using the latter form has evidently reanalyzed this word to have a stem
lacking this initial vowel.

2.6.2 Main Stress in a Word

    Since metrically weak vowels are typically deleted in Nishnaabemwin, only metrically
strong vowels usually get pronounced, and as we have seen, these always have some stress.
However, typically one syllable in a word receives more stress than the other syllables, and
is said to bear the MAIN (OR PRIMARY) STRESS of the word, while the other syllables bear
SECONDARY stresses. The basic rule for determining the main stress of a Nishnaabemwin
word is quite simple, given below.

       MAIN STRESS RULE

       Give main stress to the strong syllable in the third foot counting back from the
       end of the word.

    Since all weak (unstressed) vowels are omitted in the standard writing system, even if
they are schwas, the rule basically allows one to count three vowels in from the end of a
spelled word in order to determine the main stress in a Nishnaabemwin word. To illustrate
this rule, we will examine a couple of words, by comparing their pronunciation in Nishnaa-
bemwin with Minnesota Ojibwe. Recall the word for 'raccoons,' esbanag, which had the
following representation when we examined its stress pattern:




   Nishnaabemwin

   Minnesota Ojibwe

    Now, if we count to the third foot from the end of the word, and give main stress to its
strong syllable, we arrive at the vowel /e/, the first vowel in the word.
    As another example, consider the Nishnaabemwin word nwaabmigonaa(n), 'ANsg sees
us(excl.)':
56 • 2.6.2 MAIN STRESS IN A WORD




Nishnaabemwin

Minn.Ojibwe

    Again, we find that the strong syllable in the third foot from the end of the word, the syl-
lable /waab/, receives the main stress.
    If a word has less than three feet, then main stress is given to the one farther from the end
of the word, in other words, to the strong syllable in the first foot in the word, as in the fol-
lowing examples, mkiznan 'shoes', which contains two feet, and goon 'snow', which con-
tains one. Notice that in the case of mkiznan 'shoes', vowels in weak syllables are deleted.




    Nishnaabemwin

   Minnesota Ojibwe




   Nishnaabemwin

   Minnesota Ojibwe

    To summarize the stress rules of Nishnaabemwin: iambic (weak-strong) feet are built
from the beginning of the word to the end; only short vowels can fill weak positions, and the
last vowel of a word is always strong. All weak vowels are deleted, or reduced to schwa, and
all strong vowels receive stress. Main (primary) stress for a word is given to the strong syl-
                                                 2.6.3 THE FORM OF NISHNAABEMWIN WORDS • 57


lable in the third (antepenultimate) foot from the end of the word in words of three or more
feet, and to the strong syllable in the first foot of words of two feet of less.
    The main stress rule posited here is taken from an article by Jonathan Kaye (Kaye 1973).
Kaye also notes that there is one small group of exceptions to the rule discussed in this sec-
tion, a set of words all of which consist of two syllables containing short vowels, e.g.,
gonda, 'these (an.),' nongo, 'now,' nonda, 'these (in.),' bangii, 'a little, few,' and zhanda,
'here.' For the speakers with whom Kaye worked at Wikwemikong, these words did not
syncopate the first short vowel, and furthermore, it received the main stress of the word. All
of these words have a similar phonological structure, consisting of two syllables both con-
taining short vowels, with the first syllable closed by a nasal, and the second syllable begin-
ning with a stop consonant. Kaye suggests that an additional rule is needed to stress the first
short vowel in such words. These words also appear to violate the rule of syncope. Many
speakers, however, apply syncope to bangii, producing bngii. Furthermore, in Angeline
Williams' Ottawa (Bloomfield/Nichols, eds. 1991), which did not show syncope, the form
corresponding to gonda is agonda, and to nonda, anonda. If these were the underlying
forms in contemporary Odawa, they would be regular in their stress behaviour. But there are
no doubt many idiosyncrasies in the workings of stress in Nishnaabemwin, as it is a system
that is presently in considerable flux.

2.6.3 The Form of Nishnaabemwin Words

   In the discussion in the previous section, I resorted to using word forms from another,
closely related, language in the Anishinaabemowin (Ojibwe) group, Minnesota Ojibwe, in
order to determine the basic word forms to which the Nishnaabemwin stress rules applied.
For example, to determine the basic form of the word for 'shoes', I listed the Ojibwe form
makizinan, even though what Nishnaabemwin speakers actually say is mkiznan. If we com-
pare the two forms, we see the following relationships (with the segments numbered for
easier reference):




   A question arises concerning what support there is that Nishnaabemwin speakers know
that /a/2 and /i/g are in this word, in order for the stress rules to work, since they are not pro-
nounced. The answer lies in an examination at other forms of the word. Consider, for exam-
ple, the singular form for shoe, which is mkizin in Nishnaabemwin and makizin in
Minnesota Ojibwe.
58 • 2.6.3 THE FORM OF NISHNAABEMWIN WORDS



Nishnaabemwin

Minnesota Ojibwe

   Here /i/g shows up in the Nishnaabemwin word as well as the Ojibwe, because it is no
longer in a metrically weak position, since it is now the last vowel in the word. So based on
the singular, we can say that Nishnaabemwin speakers know that this word has an /i/6 which
gets deleted in the plural. What about /a/2? Here, we must look at another form of this word,
the one that means 'my shoe,' which in Nishnaabemwin is nmakzin (or nmakzinim) and in
Minnesota Ojibwe is nimakizin.


Nishnaabemwin

Minnesota Ojibwe

    So, here we see /a/2 showing up in Nishnaabemwin, because the addition of the prefix
meaning 'my,' /ni-/, causes the first vowel of the basic word to appear in the second syllable
of the new word, where it will be strong, and thus not be deleted. Now, if we put together
the Nishnaabemwin words for 'shoe' and 'my shoe' that we have seen, we arrive at an inter-
esting conclusion:

 'shoe'

 'my shoe'


    By "adding up" the phonemes that are pronounced in each of these words, we can say
that the basic word for 'shoe' in Nishnaabemwin consists of the seven phonemes /makizin/,
but that because of the rule of syncope, all seven phonemes never show up together in the
same word form. And notice too, that the basic word for shoe that we postulate for Nishnaa-
bemwin is the same as the Minnesota Ojibwe word, makizin. This means, though, that to
determine the basic form of a Nishnaabemwin word, a language learner must hear a variety
of forms with different elements attached to the beginning and end of the basic word, so that
the short vowels will have opportunity to be in metrically strong positions and thereby avoid
deletion.
                                 2.6.4 PREFIXES, SUFFIXES, STEMS, PRENOUNS AND PREVERBS • 59


   If we consult Rhodes 1985, we find the following entry for mkizin 'shoe'

          mkizin ni boot, shoe, moccasin; pi mkiznan; pos nmakzin; pos pi
          nmakzinan

    Rhodes provides the POSSESSIVE form nmakzin 'my shoe' so that the user of the dictio-
nary can see the form of the word with a PREFIX attached to the beginning of the word, in
this case the first person marker, meaning 'my,' spelled «n». Providing a form of the word
with a prefix attached is especially important when the unprefixed word has a short vowel in
its first syllable, since when there is no prefix present the vowel will occupy a metrically
weak position and be deleted (syncopated), but will remain when a prefix containing a sin-
gle short vowel is present, since it will then be shifted to a metrically strong position. It is
important to realize, though, that many speakers now use person prefix forms such as ndoo-,
'my,' which prevents the basic noun stem from alternating its vowels, suggesting that for
them the word has been reanalyzed to lack the /a/ it had historically.
    In this section we have seen arguments for saying that the "basic" forms of Nishnaabem-
win words are similar those of its sister language, Minnesota Ojibwe. Whereas all of the
short vowels are present in the different forms of Minnesota Ojibwe words, the patterns of
alternations in Nishnaabemwin words with and without prefixes show the same vowels to be
present in the representations of these words in the minds of at least some Nishnaabemwin
speakers. In the next section we will examine some adjustments that contemporary speakers
have made in the face of the immense amount of alternation in word forms introduced into
the language by the application of the syncope rule.

2.6.4 Prefixes, Suffixes, Stems, Prenouns and Preverbs

    In discussing the phonological and morphological properties of words, we must distin-
guish between different ways in which the concept "word" applies to grammatical descrip-
tion. For example, the words gjiimaan(im) 'your boat' and njiimaan(im) 'my boat' can both
be said to consist of the "basic" word /jiimaan/ along with additional elements, AFFIXES,
which may be PREFIXES or SUFFIXES. Many affixes can occur in a single word, for example,
gjiimaan(mi)naa(n) 'our (excl.) boat' has a prefix spelled «g» and a suffix spelled «naa(n)».
An additional suffix can also be added to form gjiimaan(mi)naanin 'our boats.' Since
gjiimaan(mi)naa(n) is not a basic word, we need another term to refer to it when discussing
the attachment of additional affixes. The term that is most commonly used in linguistics to
refer to the element to which affixes are attached is BASE. So jiimaan is the base to which
/g(i)-/ is attached, and gjiimaan(mi)naa(n) is the base to which the inanimate plural suffix
/-in/ (or /-an/) is attached.
    There are far more suffixes than prefixes in Nishnaabemwin. In fact, the only true pre-
fixes are the person prefixes for first, second and third person. Suffixes on the other hand
add a variety of meanings, including plurality on nouns and verbs, negation, doubtfulness,
and many others. All of these categories are discussed in the chapters which follow.
60 • 2.6.4 PREFIXES, SUFFIXES, STEMS, PRENOUNS AND PREVERBS

    Another important distinction is that between WORD FORMS and STEMS (also called
WORD-STEMS or LEXEMES). A stem is a word minus any of its inflectional elements, along
with the "undoing" of any phonological processes, such as deletions and INITIAL CHANGE
(discussed in Chapter 3, p. 155). Inflectional elements include such things as person prefixes
and the various grammatical endings found on nouns and verbs. The stem provides the basic
meaning of the word, and the word form consists of the basic meaning component along
with whatever prefixes and suffixes are present, and any PREVERBS. So, for example, in the
case of the word gii-bmosewag, 'they (anim.) were walking along,' the inflectional material
is the ending /-wag/ and the preverb gii-, 'past tense'; in the case of the word nbimse, T am
walking along,' the inflectional material is the prefix spelled «n». This suggests that the
stem in the first word is bmose and in the second bimse. Yet clearly we have the same basic
meaning in both cases, indeed the same word stem. The difference in the two forms is due to
the variable deletion of short vowels created by syncope. The basic word stem is thus deter-
mined not only by removing all inflectional affixes, but by systematically restoring all
deleted short vowels, and putting the restored form within slashes, as in /bimose/.
    The last kind of word we will consider here is that of the MORPHOSYNTACTIC WORD,
which distinguishes identical word forms having different grammatical properties, as in the
case of, for example, mtigoon, which is the PLURAL form of the inanimate noun mtig,
'stick,' and the OBVIATIVE form of the animate noun mtig, 'tree.' This single word-form thus
represents two distinct morphosyntactic words. The same is of course true of the form mtig,
which represents both an inanimate and an animate singular noun. These forms also repre-
sent different lexemes.
    PREVERBS AND PRENOUNS. Many elements can be attached to the front of nouns and
verbs, and in this way resemble prefixes, but their relative PHONOLOGICAL autonomy, most
notably with respect to STRESS RULES and EPENTHETIC processes, distinguishes them from
person prefixes. Consider, for example, the following words:

   bi-ngamon!      'Come and sing!'     I o-ngamon! 'Go and sing!'

    Both examples ofngamo 'ANsg sings' have a suffix attached, /-n/, which makes the verb
into an IMPERATIVE form, that is, one expressing a positive command, to a single individual.
But both words also have elements attached to the front of them, in the one case hi-, 'come
and...' and in the other case <?-, 'go and...'. These DIRECTIONAL elements are different from
person prefixes, though, in that they are treated as separate words when applying the metri-
cal stress rules. Both of these elements, in all dialects of Ojibwe, consist of a single syllable
containing a single short vowel. Since the metrical stress rule creates weak-strong pairings
of syllables into feet, if these elements were attached directly to their stems as prefixes, we
would predict the form *bnagmon for the meaning 'come and sing!' This can be seen
clearly with the following diagram of predicted metrical structure:
                                  2.6.4 PREFIXES, SUFFIXES, STEMS, PRENOUNS AND PREVERBS «61

Minnesota Ojibwe

    The Minnesota Ojibwe form is included here once again, to provide evidence for what
the underlying short vowels of this word are. The point here, though, is that the vowel of bi-
is not deleted, because it is treated as a separate unit for the stress rules, and being a separate
unit, it too defines a domain in which the vowel in its last syllable is always strong. As far as
the stress rules are concerned, hi- acts as if it were a separate word.
    Elements that attach to the front of a verb such as hi- are called PREVERBS. Similar ele-
ments attached to nouns are correspondingly called PRENOUNS. In standard written form,
preverbs and prenouns are always separated from the stems they are attached to, and from
each other, by means of hyphens. Nishnaabemwin has a great number of preverbs and pre-
nouns. For example, the following sentence contains the preverbs e-, 'when,' shki-, 'first,'
and gii-, past tense, as well as the prenoun gchi- 'great, big.'

2.6.4.1 Person Prefix Forms and Extended Forms with doo-, di- or da-

   Consider the following words for 'smoking pipe' in Nishnaabemwin and Minnesota
Ojibwe, the singular (simple) form first, and then the possessed form:




Nishnaabemwin

Minnesota Ojibwe
                 2.6.4.1 PERSON PREFIX FORMS AND EXTENDED FORMS WITH DOO-, DI- OR DA- • 63




Nishnaabemwin

Minnesota Ojibwe

   The simple noun form is pronounced as pwaagan, because syncope deletes the initial
vowel, /o/, which is in a weak position. However, when the POSSESSIVE PREFIX meaning
'my' is added, two changes in the word form occur: first, an extended form of the first per-
son prefix, /nid-/, with a final /d/, is added, and secondly, the initial short /o/ of the stem
lengthens after this prefix to /oo/. This lengthening of/o/ to /oo/ is found in all varieties of
Ojibwe, it has nothing to do with stress in the contemporary language. Now, some speakers
hear these two forms, pwaagan and ndoopwaagan, and make an interesting inference:

if...       'pipe' =                              p      w         aa    g       a        n
and...      'my pipe' =      n     d       oo     p      w         aa    g       a        n
then...     'my'=            n     d       00


   Faced with the kind of variation that the syncope rule presents, many speakers have
come to assume that the singular, /pwaagan/, is the basic form of the word for 'pipe', and
that the prefix meaning 'my' is /ndoo-/. They have then begun to use this form elsewhere as
the basic prefix meaning 'my' and attach it to words such as mkizin, 'shoe', producing
ndoo-mkizin 'my shoe'. The historical prefixes for first, second and third person possessors
were as follows:

                                       Before a Consonant Before a Vowel
                   First Person        ni(n)              ni(n)d
                   Second Person       gi                 gid
                   Third Person        o                      od

    Since these elements are prefixes, they are attached to the front of the word. Since they
all consist of a single syllable containing a short vowel, they will all always occupy a weak
metrical position in a foot in Nishnaabemwin, regardless of the constitution of the stem they
are attached to. If they are attached to a stem that contains a short vowel in its first syllable,
however, that syllable will move from a weak metrical position in the first foot to a strong
one, since the prefix will now be occupying the weak metrical position. For example, con-
sider mkizin, 'shoe'.
64 • 2.6.4.1 PERSON PREFIX FORMS AND EXTENDED FORMS WITH DOO-, DI- OR DA-



'shoe'



 'my shoe'
    Adding the prefix meaning 'my' sets up a ripple of effects in the word— the first vowel
of the basic word moves into a metrically strong position, and the second vowel moves into
a metrically weak position, resulting in a very different appearance to the word meaning
'shoe', mkizin, and the word meaning 'my shoe' nmakzin. Now let's examine some forms
involving a third person possessor, 'ANsg's...', compared to the basic form of the noun.

(a)      'shoe'                m           k       i       z       i       n
         'ANsg's...'     (o)   m    a      k       _       z       i       n
(b)      'mitten'              m          j        i       k       aa      w       a    n
         'ANsg's...'     (o)   m    i     j                k       aa      w       a    n
(c)      'boat'                j    ii    m        aa      n
         'ANsg's...'     (o)   j    ii    m        aa      n

    What is striking about these forms is that possession by a third person possessor is
shown only by the alternation of vowels inside the basic word, since the third person pos-
sessor prefix is a short vowel /o/, which is always deleted because, being first in the word, it
is always in a metrically weak position. We see this in the third person possessed forms of
(a) mkizin, 'shoe' and (b) mjikaawan 'mitten', which are makzin and mijkaawan, respec-
tively. In the case of (c) jiimaan, there is no difference between the simple noun and the
third person possessed form.
    These are not the only kinds of variation found in the third person possessed forms. Con-
sider the simple and possessed forms of the following words, which includes the words
we've already seen:

                                           Simple           ANsg's...
                   (a)         shoe        mkizin           makzin
                   (b)         mitten      mjikaawan        mijkaawnan
                   (c)         boat        jiimaan          jiimaan
                   (d)         paddle      bwi              dabwi
                   (e)         pipe        pwaagan          doopwaagnan
                   (f)         snowshoe    aagam            daagman
                   (g)         spoon       emkwaan          demkwaan
                   2.6.4.1 PERSON PREFIX FORMS AND EXTENDED FORMS WITH DOO-, DI- OR DA- • 65


     A child learning the language, trying to figure out how the third person possessed form
 relates to the simple form would have considerable difficulty, because of the variation in
 forms that arises from the simple rule of vowel syncope. The word for 'shoe' appears to
-insert one vowel and delete another; the word for 'mitten' appears to flip the second and
 third sounds of the word; the word for 'boat' shows no change at all; the word for 'paddle'
 appears to add a prefix /da-/; the word for 'pipe' appears to add a prefix /doo-/; the words for
 'snowshoe' and 'spoon' appear to add a prefix /d-/. And because the person prefixes are also
 used with verbs, the variation is not limited to the possessive forms of nouns, but extends to
 other parts of speech as well.
     One way that speakers of Nishnaabemwin have dealt with the massive amount of word-
 form alternation that has arisen through syncope is to REANALYZE the person prefixes, based
 on the following forms that existed historically:

             Modern Singular       Old Form ANsg's...          Reanalyzed Form ANsg's.
 (a)   pipe pwaagan                odoopwaaganan               doo-pwaagnan
 (b)   doll  damnowaagan           odaminowaagan(an)           doo-damnowaagan(an)
 (c)   seat  pabwin                odapabiwin                  da-pabwin
 (d)   work nokiiwin               odanokiiwin                 da-nokiiwin
 (e)   word kidwin                 odikidowin                  di-kidwin
 (f)   match shkodens              odishkodens                 di-shkodens

   Younger speakers have evidently taken the singular form to be the basic form, and have
reanalyzed the old stem-initial vowels as part of the person prefixes. They then use these
new prefix forms with other words, to great effect.

                      Modern Singular      Unreanalyzed Form          Reanalyzed Form
                      Form                 ANsg's...                  ANsg's...
 (a)       shoe       mkizin               makzin                     doo-mkizin

                     Form                ANsg's...                  ANsg's...
