                                                                    di-shkodens

    What the reanalysis does is make the basic stem of the word more constant, even when
prefixes are added. While the unreanalyzed possessive forms above show all sorts of varia-
tion between the simple and possessed word, this variation is simply eliminated by using the
reanalyzed prefixes. There are three forms of this prefix, di-, da-, and doo-, as shown above.
This is true of all three persons: first person, ndi-, nda-, and ndoo-; second person, gdi-,
gda-, gdoo-. The third person prefix must have a short /o/ in the forms /di-/ and /da-/, which
creates a metrical foot with the structure weak-strong, and the /o/ is then deleted.




   The extent to which these reanalyzed (extended) prefixes are used is unknown at present,
though they are certainly common. In discussing the application of the 'prefix doo-' to
verbs, Corbiere 1994:21 writes, 'You can never go wrong with it when you have a verb in
present tense', and suggests it as a particularly safe strategy for new language learners,
though not reflecting the usage of fluent speakers. Rhodes 1985 implicitly analyzes the per-
son marking system as using the extended form only before verbs that historically had short
vowels in their initial syllables, in other words, exactly in those places where its use would
be effective in reducing alternations of the basic word form. Furthermore, throughout the
dictionary (Rhodes 1985), only the variant /ndi-/ is listed for those verbs that contain the
RELATIVE ROOT AN/, /izh/, as in ndi-kid, 'I say something' (historically from /ikido/), and
ndi-nenmaa 'I think such of ANsg' (historically from /nid-inenim-aa/), but Rhodes suggests
that any of the extended forms may occur with words that do not begin with this root, for
example, the entry for ngamod 'sings' lists the present tense forms as nda-ngam, and nna-
gam (historically from /nagamo/), where nda-ngam is shorthand for nda-ngam, ndi-ngam,
and ndoo-ngam. However, for all stems having initial syllables containing long vowels
Rhodes does not list the extended prefix as an option, for example, the entry for niimid
                                              2.6.4.2 EXAMPLES OF PERSONAL PREFIX USAGE • 67


'dances' lists only nniim as the first person singular, present tense form. Corbiere's (1994)
examples representing Manitoulin Island Nishnaabemwin agree with Rhodes, in that she
consistently uses the extended first person form /ndoo-/ before stems that historically con-
tained short vowels in their initial syllables, such as in ndoo-ngam (from historical nagamod
'sings'), ndoo-damin (from historical odaminod 'plays'), and ndoo-skooniw (from historical
iskooniwid 'ANsg attends school, studies'). Beside these verbs with the extended prefix she
lists verbs with simple prefixes, all of which historically have long vowels in the first sylla-
ble of their stems: nniim (from historical niimi 'dances'), nwiisin (from historical wiisini
'eats'), ndaakoz (from historical aakozi 'be ill'), njiibaakwe (from historical jiibaakwe
'cooks'), ndebsinii (from historical debisinii 'eats enough, eats sufficiently'), and nmaajaa
(from historical maajaa 'leaves'). Note, though, that Corbiere does not list the simple prefix
historical forms of verbs with short vowels in their initial syllables, such as nnagam 'I sing',
ndoodmin 'I play', and ndiskooniw 'I attend school, study.'
    We thus have three possible patterns of use of the extended prefixes by various speakers
of Nishnaabemwin, varying in their conservatism:

• Speakers who do not use the extended prefixes, or use them very little.
• Speakers who use the extended prefixes only before stems that historically had a
  SHORT VOWEL in their first SYLLABLE.
• Speakers who use the extended prefixes even with stems that historically had LONG
  VOWELS in their first syllables.

   Many speakers use extended prefixes with words borrowed from English, such as ndoo-
contractual allowance, 'my contractual allowance', suggesting that they have become the
default form of the prefixes.
   Note that the extended prefixes are attached with hyphens, thus being treated as preverbs
and prenouns.

2.7 Clitics

    There is a small, very important class of emphatic word-like elements in Nishnaabem-
win called PARTICLES. These include such words as sa, go, wii, and dash. Particles often
become CLITICS, meaning that they rather freely lose their own word stress and attach them-
selves to an adjacent word, in Nishnaabemwin, almost always the preceding word. Clitics
that attach to preceding words are called ENCLITICS. Nishnaabemwin enclitics usually attach
to the first word in a CLAUSE, which is often an ADVERBIAL word itself, such as mii, 'it's, so,
and.' In some cases clitic particles fuse to a given word, and become a basic part of the
word, such as the fusion that has taken place in the word wenesh, 'who,' from wenen dash,
in sentence (6), above. Often more than one particle occurs in this position, bunched
together after the first word of the clause. Clitics often lose segments when they fuse to their
hosts, as when dash reduces to «sh». Some spellers recognize the presence of an enclitic by
separating it from its host with a hyphen, as in mii-sh. Other writers don't bother with this
convention.
    As a word class, particles (most of which are regularly clitics) are discussed in greater
detail in Chapter 3. The following sentence illustrates a typical usage of particles.
                                                              2.8 PHONOLOGICAL PROCESSES • 73


   (6) Kina go gii-mnognini pii gaa-bskaabiid, mii-sh go naa aazhgo iw zgaknamwaad iw
       gaa-ntaawgitoowaad.
        'Everything was growing well when he got back, and already they were harvest-
        ing what they had grown.' (AK10.19)
         Kina av 'everything'; gii-mnognini vii indOobv 'INobv was growing well'; pii av 'when';

2.8 Phonological Processes

    Sounds group into classes on the basis of shared properties and shared behaviour. The
term NATURAL CLASS is used to identify a group of sounds which exclusively share proper-
ties or behaviours in a given language. For example, /b/, /p/, and /m/ are a natural class in
Nishnaabemwin, because they have in common that they all involve bilabial articulation;
/m/ and /n/ are a natural class, because they are both nasals; /b/, /d/ and /g/ are a natural
class, because they represent the class of voiced stops in the language.
    Typically, sounds undergo adjustments of various sorts when they are used in speech.
These adjustments have to do with the position in the word in which the sound appears, and
the constitution of neighbouring sounds. In this section we will look at some of the common
adjustments that sounds make in Nishnaabemwin speech. Once again, the discussion is
organized around the two major classes of sounds, consonants and vowels.

2.8.1 Consonant Processes

  In this section we will examine common processes that apply to consonants, including
NASAL ASSIMILATION, final DEVOICING of obstruent consonants, the effects of ROUNDED
VOWELS on neighbouring consonants, PALATALIZATION, and the deletion of GLIDES.

2.8.1.1 Nasal Assimilation and Nasal Syllabification

   ASSIMILATION is a process whereby neighbouring sounds become more alike in some
aspect of their pronunciation. For example, if an /n/ sounds like [m] next to a /b/, assimila-
tion has taken place, because [m] is made with the lips just as [b] is, unlike [n]. In rapid
speech, assimilation of adjacent sounds is very common in all languages. The most com-
mon type of assimilation is NASAL ASSIMILATION, in which a nasal consonant takes on the
PLACE OF ARTICULATION of a neighbouring sound, usually a voiced stop. For example, one
form of the first person prefix in Nishnaabemwin is [n], as in the following:
74 • 2.8.1.2 FINAL (OBSTRUENT) CONSONANT DEVOICING


         ndagshin           'I am arriving'    ndaashkboojge      'I do ripsawing'

   However, under some circumstances, namely before a /b/, the first person prefix may be
pronounced [m] by some speakers, as in the following examples.

                           Written       Phonetic      Meaning
                           nbiidoon      [m]biidoon    'I bring it'
                           nbaap         [m]baap       'I laugh'

   The small mark under the /m/ in these cases indicates that these nasals are SYLLABIC,
that is, that they constitute a simple, reduced syllable unto themselves. Nasals can some-
times represent all that remains of a syllable that has had its vowel deleted. Note that even
though the first person prefix can be pronounced as [m] before a /b/, it is standardly spelled
with an «n», as in the forms in the leftmost column above. Such a spelling gives more
importance to its underlying form than its actually pronounced form.
   Before the velar stops /g/ and /k/, /n/ has a velar pronunciation, like the last sound in the
English word 'sing', which is represented in phonetic transcription with the symbol [rj], as
we saw earlier in section (5.1.2). These forms, too, are written with an «n».

                          Written         Phonetic       Meaning
                          ngoogii         [rjlgoogii     'I dive'
                          ngiigoonyke     [rj]giigoonyke 'I fish'

   A DENTAL/ALVEOLAR nasal assimilates its place to that of a following /g/ at the end of a
word, and the /g/ is then deleted, leaving only the [rj] to evidence the presence of/g/, though
the word is spelled with a final «ng». Compare the following pronunciations.

                    Written      Phonetic      Meaning
                    dgoshin      dgoshifn]     'ANsg arrives'
                    dgoshing     dgoshi[rj]    'when ANsg arrives'

    Writers of Nishnaabemwin sometimes represent nwaabndaan, 'I see INsg,' as
«nwaamdaan», suggesting that the /n/ following /b/ has assimilated its labial place, after
which the /b/ deletes. In speech, there is often a very weak [b] and the nasal perhaps doubly
articulated at both the alveolar ridge and the lips.

2.8.1.2 Final (Obstruent) Consonant Devoicing

  Silence, of course, has no vocal cord vibration (voicing). When a sound at the end of a
word loses its voicing, as commonly happens in many languages of the world, it is reason-
                                            2.8.1.2 FINAL (OBSTRUENT) CONSONANT DEVOICING • 75


able to say that a type of assimilation has taken place, in that vocal cord vibration has been
turned off in anticipation of the following silence. In Nishnaabemwin it is common for
voiced consonants (stops, fricatives and affricates) to become voiceless at the end of a word.
This means that the following correspondences occur:

                      /b/     sounds like        /p/     at the end of a word
                      /d/     sounds like        /t/     at the end of a word
                      /g/     sounds like        /k/     at the end of a word
                      /z/     sounds like        /s/     at the end of a word
                      /zh/    sounds like        /sh/    at the end of a word
                      /)/     sounds like        /ch/    at the end of a word

   Writers of Nishnaabemwin often write words with final voiced consonant sounds as if
they were their voiceless equivalents. Many words have sounds of this sort that sometimes
occur at the end of the word and sometimes do not, as in the following examples:

b       nnamdab              'I am sitting'             nmadbi         'ANsg is sitting'
d       nmidid               'I am big'                 mdido          'ANsg is big'
g       gnebig               'snake'                    gnebgoog       'snakes'
z       ndizhnikaaz          'lam named...'             zhinkaazo      'ANsg is named...'
zh      miizh                'give it to ANsg'          miizhid        'if I give it to ANsg'
j       ngiikaj              'I am cold'                giikji         'ANsg is cold'

    The lenis consonants often sound differently, then, depending on whether they are at the
end of the word or not. At the end of the word, they sound voiceless. When not word-final,
they sound voiced. The word meaning T am sitting,' nnamdab, for example, sounds as if it
ends in a voiceless [p]; nmindid, 'I am big,' sounds as if it ends in a voiceless [t], and so on.
However, when not at the end of the word, each of the sounds in these words sounds voiced,
as [b] and [d], respectively. Fords consonants sound consistently voiceless, however,
whether they are at the end of a word or not. For example, the /p/ in baapi, 'ANsg laughs'
sounds voiceless whether it is final or not, as does the /k/ in mik, 'beaver':

             p        nbaap         'I laugh'           baapi       'ANsg laughs'
             k        mik           'beaver'            mikog       'beavers'

    There are two approaches to the spelling of lenis consonants at the end of a word. In the
Rhodes dictionary, and in this work, consonants that alternate between voiced pronunciation
inside a word and voiceless pronunciation at the end are considered to be fundamentally
lenis, to be in a contrastive phonemic relationship with their fortis counterparts, and are
always spelled with letters representing voiced sounds, «b», «d», «g», «z», «zh», or «j».
76 • 2.8.1.3 SYNCOPE AND THE JUXTAPOSITION OF IDENTICAL CONSONANTS


The disadvantage of this approach is that a word is not always spelled exactly as it sounds,
since no word is pronounced with a voiced obstruent in final position. The only way to con-
sistently spell words that appear to end in voiceless consonants then is to learn the spelling
of the consonant based on how it sounds inside of a word.
    The alternative approach, taken by many writers, is to spell final consonants according to
their phonetic values, so that a lenis consonant phoneme will be spelled differently, depend-
ing on whether or not it is final. The principal advantage of this approach is that it allows
language learners to more readily approximate the proper pronunciation on the basis of the
way the word is spelled. However, it has the disadvantage that students may not recognize
that they are dealing with the same word when it is spelled in multiple ways, or may not
themselves understand the relationship between the variable spelling and pronunciation.
    THE SPELLING OF FINAL CONSONANTS THAT Do NOT ALTERNATE. In the discussion
above, I have emphasized the fact that lenis obstruents show variable pronunciation, being
pronounced with voicing inside a word, but lacking it when independent phonological pro-
cesses result in the segment being in word-final position, always those involving the loss of
a final short vowel. In these cases, there is language-internal phonological justification for
consistently spelling the consonant with a symbol representing voicing, since that is its fun-
damental phonemic value, and this value can readily be determined by examining its behav-
iour inside of a word. In some cases, however, certain consonants that never occur inside a
word are consistently spelled with a voiced symbol, in this case, not on the basis of lan-
guage-internal factors, but to promote cross-dialect consistency with other varieties of
Anishinaabemowin. The most significant morpheme in this regard is the animate plural suf-
fix, here spelled «ag», as in waagshag, 'foxes.' For many Nishnaabemwin speakers, the
final consonant of this suffix is consistently pronounced [k], since the plural suffix always
occurs in word-final position. Many adverbs, too, show a final /j/ in other dialects, but are
pronounced with a [ch] by many Nishnaabemwin speakers. These segments do not show the
alternations that support their analysis as lenis consonants, since they never occur anywhere
except in word-final position, and therefore are always pronounced as fortis (voiceless) con-
sonants. Rhodes (1985) elects to spell these words according to their phonemic values in
other dialects of Anishinaabemowin. Examples of such words are memkaaj, 'necessarily,'
ndawaaj, 'after all, necessarily,' megwaaj, 'about, approximately, now' (Od), shkwaaj, 'for
nothing' (M), giimooj, 'secretly, on the sly,' naagaj, 'later,' and nwanj, 'more.' These words
can be contrasted with adverbs spelled with final «ch», such as miigwech, 'thank you,' and
gmaapiich, 'later on, afterwards, finally.'

2.8.1.3 Syncope and the Juxtaposition of Identical Consonants

   In some cases, two consonants may come together, usually because of the deletion of an
intervening short vowel by syncope. Various adjustments are made to the consonants in
such circumstances, and I will discuss a few of the more common ones here. To begin, con-
sider the following word, the underlying form of which is based on the Minnesota Ojibwe
equivalent, babaamose, 'ANsg walks around.'
                       2.8.1.3 SYNCOPE AND THE JUXTAPOSITION OF IDENTICAL CONSONANTS • 77




       Underlying Form


       Syncope


       Pronunciation

    Syncope will apply in Nishnaabemwin, deleting the weak vowels /a/ and Id. When /a/ is
deleted the result is that two /b/'s become adjacent at the beginning of the word. These two
/b/'s in succession sound like [p] for many Nishnaabemwin speakers, and this word is
sometimes spelled «paamse». For some speakers, though, when two identical consonants
come together, they are simplified to a single consonant, so that the combination, /bb/, for
example, will produce a single [b] in pronunciation, and in spelling, so that, for example,
the preverb bbaa- is spelled «baa-». In this work, I will spell this word bbaamse, in keeping
with the practice of Rhodes 1985, which tends to spell the consonants of words on the basis
of their historical forms.
    The same process applies to the other lenis stop consonants, /d/ and /g/, as well. For
example, the Minnesota Ojibwe word for 'you are diving' is gigoogii. This word is subject
to syncope in Nishnaabemwin, which deletes the l\l between the two /g/'s, creating a
sequence of two lenis consonants which sound like fords /k/ to many speakers.

                 Pronunciation

    The future preverb is in some cases /ga-/, as in nga-niim 'I'll dance.' But when the sec-

the vowel between the two /g/'s is deleted. Speakers vary in their pronunciation of this
sequence. Some pronounce the two successive soft consonants /g/ + /g/ as their hard coun-
terpart, /k/, with an associated spelling of ka-niim. In other cases, speakers simplify the two
78 • 2.8.1.4 SYNCOPE AND THE JUXTAPOSITION OF NON-IDENTICAL CONSONANTS

/g/'s in succession and just pronounce one, which sounds like its common spelling, ga-niim.
Based on these variations, there are three possible spellings for this word:

                  gga-nnm            ka-niim            ga-nnm

   In this grammar I will use the first spelling, the most conservative, since this is the one
that is most neutral with respect to dialects, and it is the one that shows most clearly the
grammatical components of the word. There is a continual dilemma in the spelling of Nish-
naabemwin, the trade-off between grammatical and phonetic transparency.

2.8.1.5 Loss of Segments and Structural /w/

   We have seen that in Nishnaabemwin when two similar or identical sounds are next to
each other, they may sound like a single segment, or at least enough like a single segment
that writers will use a single symbol to represent them. As a result, important grammatical
features can become obscured. To illustrate, consider the following examples:

         nniim     'I am dancing'
         gniim     'you (sg.) are dancing'
         niimi     'ANsg is dancing'

    In Nishnaabemwin, the SECOND PERSON PREFIX begins with a /g/, and the first person
prefix, an /n/. However, when a verb begins with /n/, as in the case of the verb /niimi/, the /n/
of the first person is situated right next to the /n/ of the verb stem. So spellers sometimes
simplify the two /n/'s in a row and spell the word with a single «n». However, doing so
obscures the presence of the marker /n/ that signals first person. Consider also the following
words.

         nnik      'my arm'           gnik      'your arm'        nik       'ANsg's arm'

    Here, the only difference between the words for 'my arm' and 'ANsg's arm' is the pres-
ence of an /n/ on the front of the former. Without the /n/ signalling first person, the words
are identical, and so can easily be confused.
    Because the /o/ of the third person prefix is so structurally important, some writers of
Nishnaabemwin include it even when it is not pronounced, but represent it with a «w»
instead of an «o», as in the following examples:

         wnik      'ANsg's arm'                wmookmaan           'ANsg's knife'

   The /w/ used in this way is sometimes called STRUCTURAL-w, referring to its function in
elucidating grammatical structure. Structural-w may also be used with basic words that
                              2.8.1.6 EFFECTS OF VOWEL ROUNDING ON ADJACENT SEGMENTS • 83


begin with a /w/, though there its appearance is a little less aesthetically satisfying:

         wwaabmaan           'ANsg sees ANobv'           wwaagaakwad(om) 'ANsg's axe'

    The representation of the person prefixes as «n» in nnik, 'my arm', «g» in ggoogii, 'you
dive,' and «w» in wnik, 'ANsg's arm' gives ORTHOGRAPHIC substance to crucial grammati-
cal elements. We can also see how fundamental an understanding of the rich grammatical
structure of Nishnaabemwin words is to spelling them in ways that are helpful to language
learners. At the same time that we recognize the importance of representing these structural
elements in the spelling of words, we also recognize the need to teach pronunciation as
somewhat independent of spelling. Spelling in a way that is very close to pronunciation will
often obscure important grammatical relationships and may be extremely confusing to lan-
guage learners. At the same time, learners need to be aware of the differences between writ-
ing and pronunciation in the language.

2.8.1.6 Effects of Vowel Rounding on Adjacent Segments

    The rounded vowels in Nishnaabemwin are /o/ and /oo/. Closely related to the rounded
vowels is the glide /w/, which also involves lip-rounding in its production. Many varieties of
Anishinaabemowin, including Nishnaabemwin, show alternations between the sounds /wa/
and /o/ after a /g/ or a /k/. For example, a very common EMPHATIC particle is pronounced
and spelled gwa by some speakers, and go by others. Some speakers pronounce the word
for 'axe' as waagaakwad, and others waagaakod. The reason for this variation is that some
speakers COALESCE the sounds /w/ and /a/ together to form /o/. Recall that /w/ is like /o/ in
having lip-rounding. When /w/ and /a/ combine, they produce a hybrid sound that has prop-
erties of both sounds, the lip rounding and height of/w/ and the vocality and backness of/a/.
    The consonant /w/ may also cause an immediately preceding /a/ or l\l to be pronounced
as [o], as in the word ntawag, 'my ear,' which is often pronounced nt[o]wag. Also, after a
/w/, the vowel /aa/ is pronounced with considerable rounding of the lips, somewhat like the
vowel in the English word law, as in gshkigwaaso, 'ANsg sews' and waawaashkesh, 'deer.'
If the /waa/ sequence follows a consonant, the /w/ is often not pronounced separately, but
rather, appears to coalesce with the vowel, in a manner similar to that of /w/ + /a/, but in this
case with a long vowel, /aa/.
    The vowels /oo/ and /o/ also cause lip rounding of consonants that precede them, espe-
cially /g/ and /k/ when they are in the same syllable as the /oo/ and /o/. What is especially
interesting about this behaviour is that an /o/ can cause such lip-rounding, and then be
deleted by SYNCOPE, leaving as the main sign of its presence the lip-rounding of the preced-
ing consonant. An example will clarify, the word for 'knife,' mookmaan. In this word the /k/
is pronounced with lip-rounding, which is caused by a following /o/ that is itself never pro-
nounced, because it is always deleted by the rule of syncope.

   In Rhodes 1985, /k/'s and /g/'s that have this lip-rounding due to their preceding an /o/
which has been deleted or lost by syncope, are spelled with a small dot under the letter, for
example:

         mookmaan           'knife'            gjitood       'test s.t, try s.t.'

    Such words are not spelled this way in normal writing, however, only in the dictionary.
The use of the dot assists language learners in the pronunciation of these words. Many
speakers today have lip-rounding as the only reflex of the historical short /o/, in other words,
they no longer have /o/ in these words at all, only the remnant of it, lip-rounding on the /k/
or /g/ sound. Notice that because these lip-rounded /g/'s and /k/'s are associated with the
absence of /o/, they always occur before consonants, because the /o/ that formerly separated
the /g/ or /k/ and the following consonant has been lost.
    It is not just /k/'s and /g/'s that precede /o/ that show lip-rounding— those that precede
/oo/ show the same effect. For example, the word for '(long-eared) owl' would be written
«gookookhoo» if all of the /g/'s and /k/'s showing lip-rounding were spelled to show their
rounding. However, since /oo/ is never deleted by syncope, it is always pronounced, and
there is never any confusion about the /g/'s and /k/'s that precede it; it is always clear that
                                     2.8.1.7 THE USE OF APOSTROPHE WITH «N», «z», AND «s» • 85


they show lip-rounding. A dot is put under just those /g/'s and /k/'s whose lip-rounding can-
not be predicted from the normal spelling of the word. This circumstance always arises
when the source of the lip-rounding, a short /o/, is deleted by syncope.
    UNROUNDING OF /o/. An /o/ often loses its rounding at the end of a word, after a conso-
nant other than /g/ or /k/. The words written as kido, 'ANsg says' and zhinkaazo, 'ANsg is
named' sound as if they end in /a/, which is usually pronounced something like the vowel of
English cut. This change makes phonetic sense when we recall that the other short vowel in
the back region is /a/, and that one of the chief differences between /o/ and /a/ is that the
former is rounded and the latter unrounded. This change also reflects a common tendency
for vowels to lower at the end of a word in Nishnaabemwin.

2.8.1.7 The Use of Apostrophe with «n», «z», and «s»

    Recall that an /n/ before /z/, /s/, /zh/ (IPA /3/), /sh/ (IPA ///) and /y/ (IPA /j/) is phoneti-
cally realized as nasalization of a preceding vowel, and not with the full pronunciation of
/n/. An example is binoojiinyag, 'children.' In some cases, however, an /n/ can be juxta-
posed with one of these consonants due to the loss of an intervening vowel by syncope. In
such cases the /n/ is more fully pronounced. For example, the word for 'your (single) hair'
in Nishnaabemwin is giin'zis. The /n/ and /z/ are in different syllables, and the /n/ is fully
pronounced, not realized merely by the nasalization of the preceding vowel. Rhodes 1985
follows a convention of using an apostrophe (') to show the point where the vowel has been
deleted, as indicated above. This use of apostrophe is rather similar to its usage in English in
such words as don't and can't, where it also indicates that sounds have been deleted. Other
Nishnaabemwin examples are miin 'shin 'give it to me,' zhoon 'yaa, 'money,' and biiskon 'ye
'ANsg is dressing.'
    As discussed on page 46, the sound /n/ directly before a /g/ has a pronunciation like the
final nasal sound at the end of the English word sing, as in the word for 'loon,' maang (a
velar nasal, represented by the phonetic symbol [rj]). Sometimes, however, a regular /n/
(dental/alveolar) and a /g/ are juxtaposed due to a weak vowel being lost between them. In
such cases, the /n/ retains its normal (dental/alveolar) pronunciation, even though it is adja-
cent to a /g/. Some examples are san'goo, 'black squirrel,' en'goons 'ant,' and shkon'gan,
 'reservation.' Because historically, prior to syncope, there were no sequences of /nk/ in
Ojibwe, all contemporary juxtapositionings represent/n/ and /k/, and never [rjk], so there is
no ambiguity in the interpretation of this sequence. But some writers use apostrophe
between «n» and «k», as in aan'koopzo, 'be tied together' (VAI), and /n/ before /k/ is some-
times pronounced as [rj].
    Another place where syncope can cause ambiguities in spelling is when a short vowel is
deleted between an /s/ or /z/ and an 111 (spelled «h»). Some examples are baas 'han, 'break it
apart!' and bniz'haad, 'cause s.o. to miss an event.' Here again an apostrophe can be used
where there is a need for explicitness. There are not many words where such juxtaposition-
ings of /z/, /s/ and /?/ arise, but without the apostrophe, these sequences of «sh» and «zh»
could be mistaken for /sh/ (IPA ///) and /zh/ (IPA /3/), respectively.
86 • 2.8.1.8 PALATALIZATION

2.8.1.8 Palatalization

    PALATALIZATION refers to a phonological process which results in consonant pronuncia-
tions that are in the palatal or alveopalatal area, that is, in the vicinity of the sounds /ii/, /i/,
and /y/. It is thus primarily an assimilation of place of articulation, in which, typically, an
alveolar consonant adjusts its place to be more palatal, under the influence of a following
palatal (high front) vowel or glide.
    PALATALIZATION OF /d/ AND /t/ TO /j/ AND /ch/. The dental/alveolar stops /d/ and lil pal-
atalize to corresponding alveopalatal affricates, /j/ (IPA /d3/) and /ch/ (IPA /tJ7), respec-
tively. As an example, in the first two forms below, the root meaning 'come' has the form
/biid/, while in the last two its form is /biij/. In both cases, the high front vowel /i/ condition-
ing the palatalization of/d/ to /j/ has been subsequently deleted by syncope.

           Spelled Form        Underlying Form        Gloss                     PoS
           biidaadge           /biid+aadage/          'come swimming'           VAI
           biidaagmose         /biid+aagimose/        'come snowshoeing'        VAI
           biijbizo            /biid+i+bizo/          'come driving'            VAI
           biijbatoo           /biid+i+batoo/         'come running'            VAI

   The same alternation occurs with /t/ and /ch/, as in the following examples.

        Spelled Form       Underlying Form       Gloss                            PoS
        piitaa             /apiit+aa/            'have height to such extent'     VII
        piitaapi           /apiit+aapi/          'laugh to such extent'           VAI
        piichgi            /apiit+i+gi/          'grow to such extent'            VAI
        piichgidaazo       /apiit+i+gidaazo/     'be angry to such extent'        VAI

    ALTERNATION BETWEEN /n/ AND /zh/. A few MORPHEMES, some very common, show an
alternation in their final segment between /n/ and /zh/ (IPA /3/), in which /zh/ occurs in pal-
atalizing environments. This alternation reflects a very ancient one, in which Proto-Algon-
quian *0 palatalized to *J. Over time, *0 merged with *1, which then merged with *n,
producing the contemporary alternation between modern /n/ derived from *0 and *J. The
following chart lays out the historical developments.

those that have their source in Proto-Algonquian */9/ that show an alternation with /zh/. The
most significant effect of this ancient process is that some morphemes show an alternation
between /n/ and /3/ «zh» in their final segment, as in the form zhinkaazo, 'be so named' VAI

            dso-              /daS-w+i/             'every time'               PV
            dshi              /daS+i/               'be a certain amount'      VAI
            dshing            /daS+ing/             'so many times'            AV       ,

    PALATALIZATION BY /y/ (IPA /j/). A /y/ following /d/, /t/ or /N/ also causes palataliza-
tion. For example, a VERBAL FINAL meaning 'go, move' has the form /-yaa/, which, when
attached to roots ending in /d/ or /t/, causes palatalization. This final probably occurs in the
common verb maajaa, 'leave, take off' VAI, which has an underlying structure /maad+yaa/,
containing the INCEPTIVE root, /maad/, 'start, begin.' The final /-yaa/ also occurs in zhaa,
 'go' VAI, where it combines with the relative root /iN/, /iN+yaa/, and again results in pala-
talization of the last consonant of the root, in this case, /N/. After it has caused palataliza-
tion, /y/ in these sequences is deleted.
    PA *e AND PALATALIZATION IN NISHNAABEMWIN. The vowel system of Nishnaabem-
win has four long vowels (/aa/, /ii/, /oo/, /e/) and three short vowels (/a/, /i/, /o/), and there is
no short /e/ corresponding to the long /e/ (which we would probably write as «ee» if there
were such a contrast). Proto-Algonquian (PA), the ancient parent language of Nishnaabem-
win, evidently did have a short /e/, but in Ojibwe, this segment has merged with /i/. So there
now exist in Nishnaabemwin some /i/'s that come from PA short *i and some that come
from PA short *e. This fact is significant with respect to palatalization, because it is usually
those /i/'s that come from PA *i that cause a following segment to palatalize. This makes
sense, since, as we have seen, palatalization is an assimilation of place of articulation to
more palatal location, and it is only /i/, /ii/ and /y/ that are palatal in Nishnaabemwin. The
vowel Id is not palatal.
    The fact that /i/'s from PA *e do not cause palatalization means that the Nishnaabemwin
rule of palatalization appears to have many exceptions. For example, the verbs nitaagod,
'sound a certain way' VII (Od) /iNitaagod/, and nitaagzi, 'sound a certain way; say s.t.' VAI
/iNitaagozi/, both contain the relative root /iN/, but here we do not find the expected palatal
form /zh/ of the last segment of /iN/. This is because the /i/ in this word comes from PA *e.

2.8.1.9 Glide Deletion

    It is very common for the glides /w/ and /y/ (IPA /j/) to be deleted between vowels. This
is especially common when /w/ is flanked by /aa/, as it is in many TRANSITIVE VERB INFLEC-
TIONS involving second and third person plurals, for example, gwaabmaawaa, 'you (pi.) see
them (anim.).' In such cases, /w/ is often pronounced only very lightly, if at all. Nishnaabe-
mwin writers sometimes write a «y» at the point of /w/ deletion, especially if it is preceded
by /ii/, e.g., «giiyenh», 'so it seems,' from giiwenh. The «y» in these cases probably repre-
sents the transition between vowels, as the tongue moves between their relative positions.
    A few words show variation as to the presence of/y/ or /w/, e.g., giiwse, 'hunt' VAI ver-
sus giiyse in Odawa. The word for 'boy,' is variously written as giizens, giiwzens, and
                                              2.8.1.10 DELETION OF 111 «H» (GLOTTAL STOP) • 89


gwiiwzens, reflecting variant pronunciations based on the presence or absence of one or
both instances of /w/ in this word.

2.8.1.10 Deletion of /?/ «h» (Glottal Stop)

   As mentioned previously, it is very common for /?/ (glottal stop, spelled «h») to be
weakened to the point of deletion, and thus not pronounced or written, when it occurs adja-
cent to a consonant, either historically or due to syncope. For example, historical
/dewehigan/, 'drum' is often spelled «dewegan», and /ipahiwe/, 'run from something along
a certain route' VAI, is spelled as «pawe». Another process undoubtedly related to this phe-
nomenon is the general loss of /h/ (IPA /?/) in VTA INSTRUMENTAL FINAL /-ahw/, in words
such as dbaw, 'pay for something (animate), which can be compared to stem /dibahw/ in
other dialects. Nishnaabemwin retains the /w/ in the simple IMPERATIVE form, dbaw,
whereas the equivalent Minnesota Ojibwe form is dbah (Nichols and Nyholm 1995:44),
showing loss of final /w/. Another example is Nishnaabemwin zkaw, 'ignite s.t. (anim.),'
versus Minnesota Ojibwe zakah, both historically from stem /zakahw/.

2.8.2 Processes Related to Vowels

   We have already examined several processes relating to vowels, most notably the rule of
syncope, which deletes unstressed short vowels. Another common process deletes final
short vowels (and glides) in certain contexts. This rule is discussed in more detail in Chapter
5, since it is especially pertinent to the pronunciation of ANIMATE INTRANSITIVE (VAI)
VERBS.


2.8.2.1 Variation Between /a/, I'll and /o/

    Many words show variation in their short vowels, creating variant spellings. For exam-
ple, the word 'work' (VAI) is variously nokii and nakii; the word for 'snowshoe' is variously
aagim and aagam; the word for 'my wife, my woman' is variously ndakwem and ndikwem;
the word for 'my husband, my man' ndanniim and ndinniim. Some occurrences of/a/repre-
sent a well-known feature of Ottawa/Odawa, which frequently has /a/ where other dialects
have l\l, as in the words for man and woman, cited above.
    There is also a very common tendency in contemporary Nishnaabemwin, perhaps even a
norm, to pronounce historical /o/ as [A] (the vowel of English cut) after a consonant other
than /k/ or /g/, and spell it with «a», as in «nakaaza», 'use Y' VAIO, from /anokaazo/, which
shows both historical /o/'s spelled with «a».

2.9 Borrowed Vocabulary

   Nishnaabemwin speakers, being bilingual, frequently borrow from English, often inte-
grating English elements into Nishnaabemwin words, such as in callwihaad, 'call AN on
90* 2.10 INFLECTION


the telephone' (Od), and telephonewihaad, 'call AN on the telephone.' In such cases, it is
customary to retain English spellings, as in these examples.
   In the cases of words that have been adapted to Nishnaabemwin phonological patterns,
spelling tends to follow Nishnaabemwin norms. For example, many names borrowed from
English which begin with a voiced stop or affricate (/b/, /d/, /g/, /j/ (IPA /d3/)) show an
EXCRESCENT NASAL initially, which is customarily written in the Nishnaabemwin form,
though without capitalization, as in mbingo, 'bingo,' mBil, 'Bill' (CL), nDeben, 'David'
(W), and nDebid, 'David' (W).

2.10 Inflection

    Many of the grammatical categories of Nishnaabemwin are marked on words by means
of INFLECTION. Inflection refers to the variation that occurs in the shape of words— verbs,
nouns, and pronouns in Nishnaabemwin, in order to express grammatically relevant infor-
mation, such as a verb's ACTORS and GOALS, its status as positive or negative, and its TENSE,
along with many other properties. In Nishnaabemwin, inflection is accomplished primarily
by means of AFFIXATION', PREFIXATION and SUFFIXATION. The following words, for exam-
ple, represent a tiny sample of the various inflectional possibilities of the basic transitive
animate (vta) verb stem /waabam/, 'see AN':

    waabmad                   nwaabmaa                  gwii-waabmaasii          waabmagwaa
    gwaabmaaban               bi-waabmishin             gwaabmin                 gaa-waabmaad1

   Nouns too can have inflectional affixes, indicating such things as PLURALITY, OBVIA-
TION, status as a LOCATION, and the grammatical features of their POSSESSORS. For example,
ngwis, ngwisan, ngwisag, ggwiswaan, ggwiswaag, and gwisan (or wgwisan) represent but a
few of the different inflectional possibilities for the DEPENDENT NOUN STEM /gwis/, 'son.'2
    Some languages use inflection very sparingly. Most verbs in English, for example, have
only a few inflectional forms, as exemplified by take, takes, taking, took, and taken. ACTORS
(SUBJECTS) and GOALS (DIRECT OBJECTS) in English grammar are generally expressed by
means of separate words, PRONOUNS. In Nishnaabemwin, however, verb inflection is
exceedingly rich. Some verbs have hundreds and even thousands of distinct inflectional
forms. Nouns, too, show many more inflectional forms than their English equivalents. The
study of inflection is thus much more central to Nishnaabemwin grammar than it is to
English. Without a working knowledge of inflection and the categories it realizes, the lan-
guage can neither be spoken nor understood, and any dictionary will be of minimal use to
the student as well, since words are listed in dictionaries on the basis of particular inflec-

1 .waabmad: 'that you see ANsg,' nwaabmaa: 'I see ANsg'; gwii-waabmaasii: 'you (sg.) will not see ANsg';
waabmagwaa, 'that I see ANpl'; gwaabmaaban, 'you (sg.) had seen ANsg'; bi-waabmishin, 'come and see me';
gwaabmin, 'I see you (sg.)'; gaa-waabmaad: 'that ANsg had seen ANobv.'
2. ngwis: 'my son,; ngwisan: 'my son (obviative)'; ngwisag, 'my sons'; ggwiswaan, 'your (pi.) son/s (obviative)';
ggwiswaag, 'your (pi.) sons'; ogwisan, 'ANsg's son(s) (obviative).'
                                                                            2.10 INFLECTION* 91


tional forms, called CITATION forms, and to use the dictionary the student must be able to
determine the citation form from whatever inflected form is encountered in speech or writ-
ing, and conversely, to speak or write the language, be able to produce an inflectionally
appropriate form on the basis of the citation form. For example, if we look up 'see' in the
dictionary, one of many words that we find is waabmaad, 'see AN.' But to say, 'you (sg.)
see ANsg' the appropriate form is gwaabmaa, and to say 'ANsg sees you,' the appropriate
form is gwaabmig, neither of which is listed in any existing Nishnaabemwin dictionary.
There is simply no practical way that a printed dictionary can list all of the vast number of
inflected forms that exist for each verb in the language. Without a knowledge of inflection, a
dictionary reader may not even realize that the citation form such as waabmaad does not
itself actually mean, 'see s.t. (an.),' as it is glossed, but rather means something akin to
 '.. .that/if/when ANsg sees ANobv,' in other words, that it is the plain CONJUNCT form spe-
cifically indicating a third person PROXIMATE acting on an OBVIATIVE. To use the informa-
tion provided in the dictionary, the student must recognize that the ending /-aad/ in
waabmaad is not a part of the basic word stem, and that it must be removed to produce other
actor-goal combinations; and when encountering a word such as gwaabmig, the student
must know that the initial /g/ is an inflectional prefix, which will not be part of the citation
form listed in the dictionary. Otherwise, the student will search in vain for this word in the
dictionary by seeking under listings beginning with «g». Without knowledge of inflection,
students will be very obviously limited in their capacity to produce and understand novel
utterances. And without some knowledge of the system underlying Nishnaabemwin inflec-
tion, it is less unlikely that an adult student will be able to master the vast number of differ-
ent verb forms, even to recognize them, much less use them. For fluent speakers who
learned the language in childhood, all of this knowledge is unconscious, and the whole sys-
tem can be taken for granted, but this is not an option for those learning Nishnaabemwin as
a second language. How much knowledge of inflection the student must explicitly com-
mand is, of course, a matter of one's pedagogical theory and practice, and will vary signifi-
cantly depending on the age level of the student and the goals of instruction. The instructor
must, however, have a good knowledge of the range of inflectional possibilities the language
presents if she is to be effective in developing and implementing a comprehensive curricu-
lum that presents the language in its full richness. And pedagogical methods must take into
account the centrality of inflection to so much of the language.
      In Chapters 3 through 8,1 lay out the inflectional systems of nouns, pronouns and verbs
in their full complexity, both as a record of the language and as an resource for those seek-
ing to develop comprehensive programs of language instruction. Two kinds of information
will be presented, actual inflectional forms, usually in the form of PARADIGMS, and linguis-
tic discussion addressing the characterization of the forms and their relationships to one
another, in other words, the structural system underlying the language's inflectional
resources.
92 • 2.11 MORPHEMES, UNDERLYING FORMS, AND PHONOLOGICAL DERIVATIONS


2.11 Morphemes, Underlying Forms, and Phonological Derivations

    In thinking about the relationships of morphemes to pronunciations, it is often useful to
try to motivate a single basic form for each morpheme, usually specified as a string of pho-
nemes, which is then combined with other morphemes to produce words. For example, the
word nwiisin, 'I eat,' can be considered to have the basic forms /ni-/, 'first person,' and
/wiisini/, 'eat' VAI, producing /ni+wiisini/. Note that the plus symbol (+) is used to mark
MORPHEME boundaries. This basic form of the word, with all morphemes specified, is then
subjected to the PHONOLOGICAL RULES of the language, applied in an ordered fashion, to
produce the spoken form. The "basic form" of the word in which all of its morphemes are
listed in their basic forms as strings of PHONEMES, and prior to the application of any phono-
logical rules, is called its UNDERLYING FORM. The process of successively applying phono-
logical rules to the underlying form to produce the pronounced form is called the
PHONOLOGICAL DERIVATION of the word. The following chart illustrates a simple example
of a phonological derivation.

                     Underlying Form                         /ni+wiisini/
                     Rule: Final Short- Vowel Deletion       /ni+wiisin_/
                     Rule: Syncope                           /n_+wiisin/
                     Pronounced Form                         nwiisin

    Occasionally, it is not possible to determine the exact underlying form of a given mor-
pheme. For example, the underlying form of the FIRST PERSON PREFIX cannot strictly be
said to be /ni/ in Nishnaabemwin, because its vowel is never pronounced, always being
deleted by syncope. All that is known of the vowel is that it is short, since it is subject to
deletion. In this case, the proper specification of the morpheme can only be /nV/, where IVI
stands for some unspecified short vowel. Inspection of non-syncopating dialects shows that
this vowel was historically /i/.
    The morphological structure of a Nishnaabemwin word consists of a basic STEM to
which additional elements may be attached. The stem is the core component of the word,
and may consist of a single morpheme, or, more commonly, may be morphologically com-
plex, consisting of several morphemes. These morphemes appear in structurally specifiable
positions traditionally called the INITIAL, MEDIAL, and FINAL positions. The following
words illustrate these categories.

               Word Stem      Gloss                Initial       Medial Final
              mnwenim          'like AN'           /minw/                   /enim/
              gaagiijnike      'have a sore arm'   /gaagiij/     /nik/      Id
              jiimaan          'boat'              /jiimaan/
                   2.11 MORPHEMES, UNDERLYING FORMS, AND PHONOLOGICAL DERIVATIONS • 93


   All words have initials, but only some have medials and finals. Each of these elements
may themselves be complex as well. These categories are all discussed in depth in chapters
9 through 11. The combination of a word's initial, medial and final constitute its stem. To
the stem may be added prefixes and suffixes which signal various kinds of grammatical
information. Suffixes greatly outnumber prefixes in Nishnaabemwin. The only indisputable
prefixes in the language are the PERSON PREFIXES, which occur in identical form with POS-
SESSED NOUNS, with some verb inflections of the INDEPENDENT ORDER, and arguably with
PERSONAL PRONOUNS. Person prefixes are never preceded by any other element within the
word, so when present, always constitute the first morpheme in the word, and indeed, can
serve to delimit the word's boundary. While there can be only one personal prefix associated
with a verb, it is not uncommon to find more than one PREVERB. There is no logical limit to
the number of preverbs that a given verb can have, though in actual usage, words with more
than two or three preverbs are not common. PRENOUNS typically have meanings equivalent
to English attributive ADJECTIVES, and other than the prenoun gchi-, 'big, great,' are much
less common than preverbs. They follow the same ordering conventions as preverbs,
though.
   We can capture these constraints on the ordering of morphological elements within the
word with the following simple template:

          (personal prefix)0_i + (preverb)0_n+ word stem              + (Suffix)0_n
                                 (prenoun)0_n+ [initial-medial-final]

    Items in parentheses are "optional," that is, are present in some inflectional forms but
absent in others. The number subscripted to the right of a given parenthetic element indi-
cates the number of possible iterations within that category. Thus, while there may be at
most one personal prefix, there is no structural limit to the number of preverbs or prenouns
that may occur, and the number of potential suffixes is likewise large. I have used sub-
scripted «n» in the table to indicate a large, unspecified number. In part the number of suffix
positions argued to exist in Nishnaabemwin depends on the abstractness of one's analysis of
the suffix system. Nichols 1980:158, for example, lists 14 suffix position classes for Minne-
sota Ojibwe verbs, though these do not all occur in the same word form since some are
mutually exclusive. I have listed '0-n+' in the template above, simply to indicate that many
suffixes can occur, though there are usually no more than a few in any given verb. Often the
group of suffixes occurring with a word are treated as a unit and the entire unit is called an
ENDING. So, for example, in nwaabmaanaanig, 'we (excl.) see ANpl,' the ending is
/-aanaanig/, which consists of several distinct morphemes.
    The stem of a word along with its inflectional morphemes can also be expressed by
means of a linear table of elements laid out in STRUCTURAL-POSITIONAL SLOTS, as in the
following examples (note: many morpheme forms listed here are revised in later chapters.)
94 • 2.11.1 ALLOMORPHY, AND THE MEANINGS OF MORPHEMES


              n+ gii+ waabam +aa +naan +ig 'we (excl.) see ANpl)'
              n+ gii+ waabam +ig +naan +ig 'ANpl see us (excl.)
              g+ ga+ waabam +aa +waa +g 'you (pi.) will see ANpl'
              n+        gwis           +naan +ig 'our (excl.) sons'
              n+        gwis           +naan +in 'our (excl.) son(s) (obv.)'
              g+       daanis          +waa +g 'your (pi.) daughters'
              g+       jiimaan         +waa +n 'your (pi.) boats'

    By aligning a large number of forms in this simple structural fashion, we can determine
the relative ordering of elements, and also ascertain which elements fill the same structural
positions, which reveals the range of possibilities within a given slot, and thus identifies the
grammatical options of the language for the category. In the forms listed above, for exam-
ple, we can see that there are two elements -aa and -ig occurring in transitive animate verbs
(VTA), evidently occurring in the same structural position, suggesting the possibility that
they stand in some kind of functional opposition to each other, and that their meanings are
related to one another, which is indeed the case. We can also see that affixal elements shared
by nouns and verbs show the same relative ordering within each part of speech— e.g., per-
sonal prefixes occur first in a word whether the word is a noun or a verb, and suffixes indi-
cating third person plural and obviative appear to come after suffixes indicating plurality of
a first or second person in both possessed nouns and verbs.

2.11.1 Allomorphy, and the Meanings of Morphemes

    Another discovery that we make in laying out words so as to show their structures is that
a given morpheme often has more than one 'spelling,' or phonological shape. The different
forms that a morpheme may take in different morphological contexts, that is, when com-
bined with different morphemes, are called the ALLOMORPHS of the morpheme. For exam-
ple, the plural suffix on animate nouns may be said to have several allomorphs, including
/-iig/ in sabiig, 'nets,' /-oog/ in kikoog, 'kettles,' and /-ig/ in nmishiimnaanig, 'our apples,'
among many others. Such an interpretation begs an important question, however, namely
that of how we determine the boundaries of morphemes when they are in combination with
other morphemes. In some cases morpheme boundaries within a word are readily and
uncontroversially specifiable, as with English book+mark+s. In other cases segmentation is
less straightforward, and may depend on the relative abstractness of one's analysis of the
overall morphological system of the language. 'Abstractness of an analysis' has to do in part
with how different the hypothesized underlying form of the stem and the affixes are from
what is actually pronounced. So, for example, in the case of the plural form kikoog, 'kettles,
pots,' at first glance there appears to be a plural suffix /-oog/ which has been attached to a
stem form /kik/. Many linguistic analyses of Ojibwe, however, have interpreted this word to
consist of a basic stem that ends in /w/, /akikw/, to which the regular animate plural suffix
                                   2.11.1 ALLOMORPHY, AND THE MEANINGS OF MORPHEMES • 95


/-ag/ is added. A MORPHOPHONOLOGICAL RULE of COALESCENCE then applies, which unites
the final /w/ of the stem with the /a/ of the suffix to produce /oo/, and the pronounced form
kikoog. This is the nature of abstract analyses, as mentioned above— a basic form is
hypothesized to exist, which undergoes an ordered series of transformative phonological or
morphological rules, ultimately producing a "surface," attested form. An analysis is more
valued linguistically to the extent that the forms and rules it hypothesizes are natural (found
widely across languages) and general (at work at many places in the language being investi-
gated). A morphophonological rule is a phonological rule whose operation is restricted to
particular morphologically defined contexts, in other words, applies to a particular mor-
pheme or class of morphemes in the presence of other morphemes.
    As mentioned earlier, conventional linguistic analyses of the morphological structures of
language usually strive to represent each morpheme with a single, specific phonological
shape (i.e., spelling, string of phonemes), whenever possible, and to order the morphemes in
a word in a specific linear sequence, rather like beads on a string. The analysis of one part of
the system invariably has implications for other parts. For example, the analysis of kikoog,
 'kettles' as deriving from /akikw+ag/, presented above, also requires that the simple singu-
lar form of the word for 'kettle, pot,' kik, have been subjected to a phonological rule that
deleted the final /w/ of its basic form /akikw/, a rule which, in more general terms, deletes
word-final post-consonantal glides, that is, deletes /w/ and lyl at the end of a word when
they are preceded by a consonant, as in the case of/kikw/. The benefit of such an analysis is
that it accounts for the apparent allomorphy of different stems and suffixes on the basis of
general principles at work in many different places in the grammar, and thus captures gener-
alizations about the language. One of the most intriguing questions in the contemporary
study of human language is how children are able to learn so much language so consistently
in such a short time, and contemporary theories suggest that one reason is that beneath the
great apparent diversity of surface (actually pronounced) forms of language there are sim-
pler systems governed by simple and general universal structures and principles. For exam-
ple, as we have already seen, under a more abstract analysis, the animate plural suffix can be
motivated to consistently be /-ag/, which it clearly is in words such as waagshag, 'foxes,'
and zhiishiibag, 'ducks.' An abstract analysis might try to motivate this as the only basic
form of this suffix, and seek to explain the apparent variations in actually pronounced forms
on the basis of the interaction of the suffix with stems having different phonological shapes,
particularly with regard to the phonemic makeup of their final syllables. The drawback of
such an analysis is its relative abstractness, in that neither /akikw/ nor /akikw+ag/ is ever
actually pronounced as such, and all evidence of the basic forms is thus indirect. This
doesn't necessarily mean that such analyses are wrong, but it does make their value as
teaching tools questionable. There is often little doubt that they express something "real"
about the language, though.
    An alternative, more superficial and pragmatic approach to the language's morphology
simply examines the nature of actually pronounced forms, and seeks to make as straightfor-
ward a segmentation into components as is possible. So, for example, we might consider
kikoog as consisting of a basic form /kik/, corresponding to the actual pronunciation of the
96 • 2.11.1 ALLOMORPHY, AND THE MEANINGS OF MORPHEMES

singular form, to which an animate plural suffix of the form /-oog/ has been attached. This
allomorph of the animate plural also shows up on words such as gnebig, 'snake' (plural
gnebgoog), and mtig, 'tree,' (plural mtigoog). These three words also have similar DIMINU-
TIVE forms, kikoons, gnebgoons, and mtigoons, respectively. A structural linguistic analysis
would argue that the basic stems of each of these words ends in /w/, i.e., /kikw/, /gnebigw/,
and /mtigw/,1 and that the final /w/ coalesces with the /a/ vowel of the plural suffix and Id
vowel of the diminutive suffix to produce /oo/ in actual pronunciation. Many other aspects
of the behaviour of these words become systematic if one hypothesizes a basic stem form
ending in /w/. For example, the word for 'be a snake, become a snake,' is gnebgowi, while
that for 'be a man, become a man' is niniiwi. The /o/ that appears in gnebgowi can be
explained on the basis of the stem-final /w/ found in the abstract form. Otherwise, it just
seems to be an accident that both the plural and the "be a..." forms both have an /o/ in them,
but that neither form with nini does.
    In the interests of straightforward pedagogy, however, I will usually take a somewhat
less abstract tack in the chapters which follow, at least in terms of my ultimate presentation
of forms, if not in my analyses, and identify, for example, simple classes of nouns which
share superficial inflectional traits. So, for example, the three words discussed here, kik,
gnebig, and mtig, will all be grouped together into the same noun class on the basis of their
plural and diminutive forms, and this class will be distinguished from another noun class
containing words such as sab, 'net,' pin, 'potato,' and mtigmizh, 'pin oak,' which have their
respective plurals in sabiig, piniig, and mtigmizhiig, and their diminutives in sabiins, pini-
ins, and mtigmizhiins. The process of determining such classes is a fairly straightforward
one, proceeding by the examination of the nouns of the language and grouping them into
classes on the basis of similarities of inflectional behaviour. The goal is to arrive at an
exhaustive account of the workings of all the nouns in the language, cast in terms as
straightforward and simple as the data permit, in other words, with as few distinct classes as
required, but without appealing to excessive abstractness. It is important to realize, however,
that membership in the different classes I posit can almost always be explained on the basis
of shared abstract phonological stem shapes. And while the notion of abstract shapes may at
first seem an impediment to straightforward teaching, once one gains a working knowledge
of a few principles and rules, much of Nishnaabemwin inflection becomes quite straightfor-
ward, though puzzles will always remain.
    Turning from noun to verbal inflection, related analytic problems of determining
straightforward meanings of grammatical morphemes arise. As we have seen, for example,
words such as ngikenmaa, 'I know ANsg,' ggikenmaa, 'you know ANsg,' and wgikenmaan,
 'ANsg (prox.) knows ANobv' all contain an element /-aa/ which we can isolate on the basis
of comparison with other forms such as ngikenmig, 'ANsg knows me,' ggikenmig, 'ANsg
knows you,' and wgikenmigoon, 'ANobv knows ANsg (prox.).' In these words, a morpheme
/-ig/ (actually, often analyzed more abstractly as /-igw/) appears to occur in the same struc-

1 .Actually, based on patterns of short vowel alternations, the basic forms of these words would be hypothesized to
be /akikw/, /ginebigw/, and /mitigw/.
                                              2.11.2 DICTIONARY ENTRIES AND INFLECTION • 97


tural position that /-aa/ does in the former set of words. But even the most fluent speaker of
the language is unlikely to be able to articulate the meaning of /-aa/, without considerable
thought, because speakers have internalized its use without giving any conscious attention
to its meaning, which is purely grammatical. Speakers of a language are rarely conscious of
the grammatical properties of their utterances, though they consistently use grammatical
forms appropriately, and careful linguistic analysis often reveals that the underlying gram-
matical system is structured, elegant and simple. For example, the morphemes /-aa/ and
/-ig/, discussed above can be readily explained on the basis of a GRAMMATICAL HIERARCHY
of actors and goals found in all Algonquian languages. I will discuss this hierarchy in Chap-
ter 8. But it is only through a careful study of the entire grammatical system of actor and
goal marking on transitive animate verbs (VTA) that one arrives at a satisfactory sense of
their systematic functions in the various verb forms in which they occur. Once again there
are two possibilities of presentation, which differ in being ANALYTIC or SYNTHETIC in orien-
tation. An analytic approach seeks to exhaustively analyze word forms into all of their com-
ponent morphemes, with each morpheme having a constant, if sometimes abstract, shape.
Morphological analysis of this sort requires a very good knowledge of grammatical princi-
ples and the grammatical functions of individual morphemes within morphologically com-
plex words, and the task is particularly daunting for languages as richly endowed
morphologically as Nishnaabemwin is. By contrast, a synthetic approach lays out all of the
relevant word forms in some structurally suggestive ordering, leaving the nature of the sys-
tem implicit, and does not necessarily draw the learner's conscious attention to the identity
or function of individual morphemes. Both approaches have value, and both are used in this
grammar.

2.11.2 Dictionary Entries and Inflection

   To be maximally useful, the dictionary must provide a means of deriving all of the many
hundreds of inflectional forms of a verb from the information provided in its entry. For
example, it would not do to simply list the verb forms ndaandkwenaa, 'I put ANsg's head in
a different position,' and nmiinaa, 'I give (something) to ANsg,' because of the variation
that occurs in the stem shape of one of them, but not the other, as can be seen from the fol-
lowing table:

 1 miinaad   'that ANsg gives Y to    aandkwenaad    'that ANsg moves ANobv's head
            ANobv'                                   over'
2 nmiinig   'ANsg gives Y to me'      ndaandkwenig   'ANsg moves my head over'
3 nmiin'goo 'I am given Y'            ndaandkwen'goo 'my head is moved over'
4 mii zh    ' give Y to AN!'          aandkwen       'move AN's head over!'
5 gmiizh    'I give Y to you'         gdaandkwen     'I move your head over'
6 miizhiyan 'that I give Y to you'    aandkwen'yan   'that I move your head over'
98 • 2.12 DERIVATIONAL AND INFLECTIONAL MORPHOLOGY

    In all cases, the final consonant of the stem /aandkwen/ remains /n/, while in the case of
/miiN/, the final consonant is sometimes /n/, as in the first three examples, and sometimes
/zh/ (IPA /3/), as in the final three. Part of the (unconscious) knowledge a speaker of Nish-
naabemwin has of the word meaning 'give Y to AN' is that it is of the class of transitive ani-
mate verbs having a stem varying in just this way. In the case of the word meaning 'move
AN's head over,' a speaker knows that it belongs to the group of transitive animate verbs
which have stems that always ends in /n/, regardless of how they are inflected. To aid the
language learner, at the very least the dictionary must distinguish these two types of transi-
tive animate verbs. One way of doing this is to provide a relevant inflectional form in each
entry's listing that shows whether or not the stem-final consonant is ever /zh/, for example,
the imperative forms listed in the fourth line of the table above might be used. Rhodes 1985
does exactly this. The headword corresponds to the entry in the first row of the table above,
miinaad and aandkwenmaad, respectively, and additional forms are provided in the entry to
reveal various aspects of the verb's behaviour when inflected. The following is Rhodes'
entry for miinaad:

                 miinaad vta give something to s.o.; pres nmiinaa; imp
                 miizh, miinizh; cc e-miinaad, maanaad

    The IMPERATIVE form, labeled imp, is given to show that the last consonant of this stem
varies between /n/ and /zh/ (see discussion on page 86 above, for details of why). There are
many different imperative inflections in Nishnaabemwin, and this one specifically refers to
a command given to a single (second-person) actor to be carried out on a singular or plural
goal, in other words, the listed form specifically means '(you sg.) give Y to AN!' The two
forms listed for this inflection represent dialect variation, and they are ordered to reflect
their relative commonness: the form miizh is more commonly heard than miinizh. The sin-
gle imperative form listed, however, is not the only inflectional form that shows a stem form
in /zh/ for verbs such as miinaad, there are many others such as miizhid, 'that ANsg gave Y
to me,' and miizhyan, 'that you (sg.) gave Y to me.' I have indicated all such inflectional
configurations in the transitive animate paradigms listed in Chapter 8.

2.12 Derivational and Inflectional Morphology

    The study of morphology has traditionally been divided into two sub-areas, DERIVA-
TIONAL MORPHOLOGY and INFLECTIONAL MORPHOLOGY. Derivational morphology is con-
cerned with the structure of a language's vocabulary, also known as its LEXICON or
WORDSTOCK, in terms of how words and their parts relate to one another in their structures
and functions, and in terms of how new words are formed from existing ones or from com-
ponent parts of words. The derivational morphology of Nishnaabemwin vocabulary, for
example, would seek to account for the structure and relationships that exist between each
HEADWORD in the Rhodes dictionary, minus its inflections, but not concern itself with the
inflectional forms listed within each entry. For example, derivational morphology would
                                      2.12 DERIVATIONAL AND INFLECTIONAL MORPHOLOGY • 99


account for the relationships that exist between the words daashkboodood, 'split IN sawing
it' VTI, daashkboonaad, 'split AN sawing it' VTA, and daashkboojged, 'do sawing' VAI.
Inflectional morphology as it pertains to Nishnaabemwin addresses the prefixes and suffixes
that are relevant to GRAMMATICAL RELATIONS obtaining between words, or those which
represent properties of larger grammatical structures, such as the TENSE of a clause or the
status of a verb as belonging to a MAIN or SUBORDINATE CLAUSE. One especially important
area of inflectional morphology in Nishnaabemwin is the study of the morphological rela-
tionships between a verb and the pronouns and nouns which realize its SEMANTIC ROLES of
ACTORS and GOALS.
    The distinction between inflection and derivation is sometimes controversial in linguis-
tics, because there are some morphological categories that can be analyzed in either way in
a particular language, and which vary in their classification as inflectional or derivational in
different languages. Basically, we can say that a morpheme is derivational if its presence in
a word is a matter of the word's basic stem shape, and inflectional if it has to do with the
role a word is playing in a particular grammatical context. Inflectional categories often indi-
cate AGREEMENT between two major WORD CLASSES within a clause. For example, the ANI-
MATE PLURAL SUFFIX shows agreement between a verb and an associated noun, as in
wiisniwag ninwag, 'the men are eating,' where the plural morpheme /-ag/ appears on both
the verb wiisni and the noun nini. This agreement is a hallmark property of an inflectional
morpheme. Consider, by contrast, the DIMINUTIVE suffix, which appears on the word nini-
ins, 'little man.' This morpheme does not produce agreement on an associated verb, as we
can see with wiisniwag niniinsag, 'the little men are eating.' The verb is identical in form
whether the noun associated with it is diminutive or not. On the basis of agreement, the
diminutive is a derivational category, changing the stem nini into another word, niniins.
    Morphemes also vary is in their relative productivity, that is, the relative freedom with
which they can be attached to LEXEMES of the appropriate LEXICAL CATEGORY and subcate-
gory. For example, the diminutive suffix is attached to words belonging to the lexical cate-
gory of nouns, and can be attached to almost any noun in Nishnaabemwin, and so is
extremely productive. Another function of productivity is the extent to which the meaning
of the derived form is predictable from the meanings of its component parts. For example,
for the most part diminutives have very predictable meanings, referring either to small or
immature members of the class identified by the non-diminutive stems, for example, waag-
shens, 'fox kit,' orjiimaanens, 'small boat.' On the basis of the predictability of meaning
and the freedom with which it attaches to nouns, the diminutive aligns more with inflec-
tional categories than derivational, because inflections, too, tend to be very productive. One
important consequence of the productivity of the diminutive is that there is no need to list
diminutive forms such as jiimaanens in the dictionary since their meanings are predictable
from the basic stem forms from which they are derived. The only diminutives which must
be listed are those which have either an unpredictable form or an unpredictable meaning, for
example, mikoons, 'beaver kit,' derived from mik, 'beaver,' has a diminutive with /oo/, and
sabiins, 'small net,' derived from sab, 'net,' has a diminutive with /ii/.
100 • 2.13 ADDITIONAL READING


    The discussion of a morpheme's productivity is also important from the point of view of
teaching the language. Particular emphasis should be placed on those morphemes, whether
inflectional or derivational, that are most productive, that is, tend to be more common in
speech. This also entails to some extent identifying morphemes when teaching, or at least
devising lessons that implicitly take stock of the relative productivity of forms, which
means that the teacher must have a reasonably good knowledge of the form and meaning of
such morphemes, and of the grammatical systems underlying their usage. I cannot overstate
how much more central morphological knowledge is to Nishnaabemwin than it is to
English. For example, the inflection of the TRANSITIVE ANIMATE VERB in the INDEPENDENT
ORDER can be readily understood if one identifies a couple of dozen morphemes and the
principles that govern their selection. And there are hundreds, even thousands, of distinct
forms. The alternative is to simply have the student learn each form as if it were indepen-
dent of the others in its workings.
    Morphemes can be treated in two distinct ways, either in terms of their form (STRUC-
TURE) or their FUNCTION. Form has to do with the PHONOLOGICAL properties of morphemes,
issues that we have looked at in this chapter, that is, their PHONEMIC constituency (or spell-
ing), and how these phonemes behave when the morpheme combines with other morphemes
to form words. Function has to do with the meaning of morphemes and their combinations,
ultimately determined on the basis of usage, and by examining the contrasts a given mor-
pheme shows with other morphemes in the same structural position. In this chapter I have
concentrated on form, and left discussion of functions to later chapters.

2.13 Additional Reading

   There are many materials which address the nature of Nishnaabemwin sounds and their
representation in morphemes. A good place to start is the introduction to the Rhodes (1985)
dictionary, which discusses each letter used in the dictionary and its relationship to pronun-
ciation. Piggott 1980 addresses many aspects of phonology in a very technical, theoretical
manner, but is invaluable for anyone earnestly desiring a thorough, linguistically-based
account of the general sound patterns of the language. Many articles in the two Odawa Lan-
guage Reports (Kaye, et al. 1971, Piggott and Kaye 1973) discuss aspects of Nishnaabem-
win phonology and morphology in theoretically interesting and insightful ways. Valentine
1994 contains a chapter on general Anishinaabemowin phonology, which relates some of
the distinctive features of Nishnaabemwin to wider dialect relations.
