Parts of Speech




3.1 Introduction

    The parts of speech in Nishnaabemwin are NOUNS, PRONOUNS, VERBS, ADVERBS, NUM-
BERS, PARTICLES, PRENOUNS and PREVERBS. In this chapter I will discuss each of these cat-
egories in turn, and provide examples of each. As an introduction to Nishnaabemwin parts
of speech, consider the following simple sentence.

    (1)   Maaba gwiiwzens gii-waannose. I This boy walked in a circle.' (RV)

          Maabapr SsProx 'this'; gwiiwzens na SsProx 'boy'; gii-waannose vai ind3sProx
          'ANsg walked in a circle.'

     This sentence contains three words, maaba, 'this one,' gwiiwzens, 'boy,' and gii-
waannose, 'ANsg walked in a circle.' Speakers know far more than how many words there
are in this sentence and their individual meanings, though. They also have unconscious
knowledge of the word class, or part of speech, to which each word belongs. For example,
they know that there are two distinct classes of words in their language, conventionally
labeled nouns and verbs, and they know that gwiiwzens belongs to the class of nouns and
waannose to that of verbs. Consider the latter word, for example. In the sentence above, it
has a leading element gii-, which indicates PAST TENSE, that is, indicates that the action
referred to occurred sometime prior to the moment the sentence was spoken. Speakers know
that to make the same statement about the boy's walking in a circle in present time, they
say:

    (2)   Maaba gwiiwzens waannose. I 'This boy is walking in a circle.' (RV)

          Maaba pr SsProx 'this'; gwiiwzens na SsProx 'boy'; waannose vai indSsProx 'ANsg is
          walking in a circle.'
102 • 3.1 Introduction


   Speakers also know that to make the same statement into a prediction about the boy's
walking in a circle in the future, they can add preverb wii-, 'volitional future,' to the verb
and say the following:

    (3)     Maaba gwiiwzens wii-waannose. I This boy will walk in a circle.' (RV)

             Maabapr SsProx 'this'; gwiiwzens na SsProx 'boy'; wii-waannose vai ind SsProx
             ' ANsg will walk in a circle.'


    The reason we can say with confidence that speakers know that waannose is a verb,
without their ever having studied the "grammar" of Nishnaabemwin, is that they will only
attach these tense elements specifying the time of the action onto verbs. Speakers do not say
such things as the following:1

    (4)     *Gii-maaba gwiiwzens waannose.

             *Gii-maabapr SsProx 'this' (with past tense); gwiiwzens na SsProx 'boy'; waannose
             vai ind SsProx 'ANsg walks in a circle.'


    (5)     *Maaba gii-gwiiwzens waannose.

             *Maabapr SsProx 'this'; gii-gwiiwzens na SsProx 'boy' (with past tense); waannose
             vai ind SsProx 'ANsg walks in a circle.'

    The reason for this is that the words maaba and gwiiwzens are not verbs, and so cannot
have a tense element attached to them. The point is that speakers know from experience that
different classes of words function differently in the language, and employ this knowledge
in both creating and interpreting utterances. These differences have to do with many aspects
of grammatical behaviour, one of which we have seen here, that different classes of words
have different elements, such as tense, associated with them. In this chapter we examine the
classes of words in Nishnaabemwin in detail, and attempt to lay them out in a way that
accurately reflects the workings of the language. Perhaps a bit surprisingly, when we
endeavour to formulate all of the things speakers must know in order to speak the language
fluently, we find that a bewildering amount of information must be accounted for. This is an
important discovery, because it reinforces the basic truth that the best way to learn a lan-
guage is by hearing it and speaking it as a child. Many linguists believe that children are
endowed with special abilities in the area of language learning, that there is in fact a biolog-
ical program coded into us as children that allows us to learn languages with very little con-
scious effort. This certainly seems true, since all of the vast complexity of Nishnaabemwin

1.1 put an asterisk (*) in front of sentences that are not grammatical, that is, would never be said by a speaker, since
they violate grammatical principles of the language.
                                            3.2 Guidelines for Determining Parts of Speech • 103



which I will lay out in this grammar, and much, much more, is acquired by any child who is
given adequate exposure to the language and has adequate opportunity to speak it. Parts of
speech are also summarized in Chapter 18.2, Nishnaabemwin Parts of Speech, beginning on
page 921.

3.2 Guidelines for Determining Parts of Speech

    Languages show variation in their inventories of parts of speech, though all languages
show considerable overlap in the categories they manifest. The determination of the parts of
speech for a given language is based on a consideration of several factors, including SEMAN-
TIC, MORPHOLOGICAL, and SYNTACTIC criteria. Semantic properties are those related to
meaning. For example, nouns are often said to denote objects, or concepts that tend to be
"time-stable," meaning that their identifiable form and substance tends to remain relatively
static over time; verbs are said to denote states, processes, events, and actions associated
with and applying to entities identified by nouns and pronouns; and adverbs often denote
notions of time, location, and manner, among others/The problem with semantic definitions
is that classes of words often show gradation in their meanings, blending into one another,
so that, for example, alongside adverbs referring to time such as noongwa, 'now, today' and
ggizheb, 'early in the morning,' there are verbs referring to time-related concepts in Nish-
naabemwin, such as giizhgad, 'be day' VII and dbikad, 'be night' VII. Nouns can be freely
derived from verbs in Nishnaabemwin, so, for example, there are nouns that represent
events, such as niimwin, 'dance' Nl and ggwejkandiwin, 'race,' (M) Nl, which are derived
from their corresponding animate intransitive (VAI) verbs, niimi, 'dance,' and
ggwejkandiwag, 'ANpl race against each other.'
    DERIVATIONAL MORPHOLOGY. One type of morphological evidence which can be used
to identify parts of speech pertains to the components of words that are either specifically
related to a particular class or sub-class of words, or which derive one class of words from
another. As an example of the former type, all words that end with the derivational compo-
nent /-shin/ are animate intransitive (VAI) verbs, and many have corresponding inanimate
intransitive verbs that end in /-sin/, for example, bngishin, 'fall down' VAI and bngisin, 'fall
down' VII. Furthermore, related to these intransitive verbs are corresponding causative tran-
sitive verbs, bngishim, 'drop s.t. (anim.)' VTA and bngisdoon, 'drop s.t. (inan.)' VTI, the
former with characteristic transitive animate FINAL /-shim/ and the latter with characteristic
transitive inanimate final complex, /-sid-oo/. The association of specific derivational final
components with specific sub-classes of verbs is so strong in Nishnaabemwin that it is only
somewhat exceptional verbs that cannot be typed in this way. Even the exceptions, that is,
those that do not have obvious class-defining finals, can be classed by their exceptionality,
as most are VAI verbs.
104 • 3.2 Guidelines for Determining Parts of Speech


    Another means of classifying words by derivational morphology is by virtue of suffixes
that derive words of one part of speech class or sub-class from another. For example, the
suffix /-win/ can be added to almost any animate intransitive verb (VAl) to form a noun, as in
ngamwin, 'song' Nl, from ngamo, 'sing' VAl and niimwin, 'dance' Nl, from niimi, 'dance'
VAl. Such a classificatory tool is particularly powerful in Nishnaabemwin because it allows
for the identification of both the stem that the suffix is added to, and the resulting word. So,
for example, the word dnakiiwin, 'town, residence, village,' can be readily identified as a
noun, derived from VAldnakii, 'live in a certain place' (Od). The strong derivational class-
typing of words in Nishnaabemwin results in complex words with very specific derivational
pedigrees. For example, the suffix /-ige/ can be added to a transitive inanimate verb (VTI) to
produce an animate intransitive verb (VAI) with a focus on AGENTIVE activity. So, for exam-
ple, from the VTI verb giishkboodoon, 'saw s.t. (inan.) off cleanly,' can be derived the VAl
form giishkboojge, 'do cutting with a saw, do sawing,' which focuses on the activity of saw-
ing by someone. The word giishkboodoon is readily identified by its transitive inanimate
final /-bood/, meaning 'apply sawing action to s.t. (in.).' The suffix /-ige/ is added to the
stem /giishkbood-/, producing an animate intransitive verb, which can then serve as a stem
for the addition of the nominalizing suffix /-n/, to produce the noun, giishkboojgan, 'saw'
Nl. Here, too, we can see how knowledge of sound patterns can help us in understanding
word relationships— the HI of the suffix /-ige/ causes the /d/ of /-bood/ to PALATALIZE to l]l
(IPA /d3/), a very common process in many languages, including Nishnaabemwin.
    INFLECTIONAL MORPHOLOGY. Another powerful morphological means of determining
word class and sub-class in Nishnaabemwin is that of INFLECTIONAL MORPHOLOGY. Inflec-
tional morphology has to do with those morphological operations, most commonly AFFIX-
ATION, that are applied to word stems in order to indicate various kinds of grammatical
information, such as the subjects and objects of verbs, their tense, the presence of negation,
and for nouns, their possessor(s) and whether they are singular or plural. For example, most
nouns can be made plural by the addition of a suffix, a property which they could be said to
share with verbs. However, in contexts of negation, verbs show negative marking but nouns
do not. So, for example, if we take a sentence such as Gaawiin gii-wiisnisiiwag ninwag, 'the
men did not eat,' it is easy to determine that wiisni is a verb by virtue of its showing the
NEGATIVE SUFFIX /-sii/. This suffix cannot be applied to the words gaawiin, 'not' and nini,
'man' to produce *gaawiinsii or *ninwsiiwag respectively, since the first is an adverb and
the second a noun, and negative suffixes are only added to verbs. We can also easily distin-
guish nouns from adverbs on the basis of inflection, in that most nouns can be pluralized,
but adverbs cannot, so the form *gaawiinag, a pluralized form of gaawiin, 'no, not,' does
not exist.
    There are many, many derivational and inflectional morphological properties associated
with nouns, pronouns and verbs in Nishnaabemwin. While it may seem something of an idle
exercise to use these properties as tests of word class and sub-class, the "tests" themselves
point to an extremely important fact, namely that speakers command the vast derivational
and inflectional systems of the language, and that the language cannot be spoken without
such knowledge. Every test I present here points to a grammatical fact of Nishnaabemwin,
                                                                               3.3 Nouns • 105



something that must be controlled in order to speak, though, of course, for most speakers all
of this knowledge is completely unconscious. Knowledge of the parts of speech in the lan-
guage is important, since each part of speech has its own elaborate grammatical properties
and complex behaviour.
    SYNTACTIC TESTS OF WORD CLASS. The last type of test that I will mention is that of
SYNTACTIC behaviour, that is, the ways in which classes of words interact with each other,
and what groupings of words of different classes occur in the phrases and sentences of the
language. For example, a verb in Nishnaabemwin typically has a SUBJECT associated with
it, which can be a noun phrase or a pronoun. Thus, in the simple sentence, wiisniwag
ninwag, 'the men are eating,' the verb wiisniwag, 'they are eating,' has a noun subject asso-
ciated with it, ninwag, 'men.' Transitive verbs may have two or more noun phrases associ-
ated with them, as in Giw kwewag wgii-gnawenmaawaan niw binoojiinyan, 'those women
were watching those children,' which has a subject noun phrase giw kwewag, 'those
women,' and an object noun phrase, niw binoojiinyan, 'that child/those children' (number is
indeterminate because the form in OBVIATIVE). This example illustrates another aspect of
Nishnaabemwin syntax, namely that nouns may have DEMONSTRATIVE PRONOUNS associ-
ated with them, which must agree with their associated nouns in gender (animate or inani-
mate), number (singular or plural), and obviation (proximate or obviative). Thus, for
example, to say 'those men are eating,' one says wiisniwag giw ninwag, with demonstrative
pronoun giw, 'those,' which is ANIMATE PROXIMATE PLURAL. Use of other demonstrative
pronouns, such as niw, 'those (man.),' with ninwag is not grammatical in Nishnaabemwin.
Agreement always specifies relationships between syntactic entities.

3.3 Nouns

    The classic definition of nouns which students of English learn is semantic, based on the
things that nouns refer to— nouns are said to represent "persons, places, and things." Nouns
essentially give names to, or identify, objects in the culturally-constructed world of the
speakers of a language. Nouns typically represent words for living things such as persons,
spirits, animals, fish, birds, insects, trees, plants, and for non-living things such as tools,
household items, other objects of manufacture, and objects in the natural world. All of the
words listed in the table below are nouns.

                             Some Sample Nishnaabemwin Nouns
kwe           'woman'           gaazhgens       'cat'           jiibay          'ghost, soul'
nini          'man'             bneshiinh       'bird'          mnidoo          'spirit'
mdimooyenh 'old woman'          mgizi           'eagle'         jiibay          'ghost,, soul'
kiwenziinh    'old man'         mnidoons        '(flying) insect' pakweyashk    'cattail'
gwiiwzens     'boy'             tree            'mtig'          bkitehgan       'hammer'
kwezens       'girl'            ninaatig        'maple tree'    mookmaan        'knife'
mkwa          'bear'            miishkoons      'grass'         doopwin         'table'
106 • 3.3.1 Dependent and Independent Nouns


    CONCRETE AND ABSTRACT NOUNS. Nouns such as those listed in the table above are
called CONCRETE NOUNS, because they refer to physical objects, that is, to things that have
physical substance, take up space, and can be touched, or are treated culturally like things
that have these properties. The American Heritage Dictionary's definition of concrete
expresses some of the properties of the referents of concrete nouns: 'Of or relating to an
actual, specific thing or instance, particular; existing in reality or in real experience, percep-
tible by the senses; real; of or relating to a material thing or group of things as opposed to an
abstraction; formed by the coalescence of separate particles or parts into one mass; solid.'
Concrete nouns are contrasted with ABSTRACT NOUNS, which refer to concepts that are less
objective and which usually do not have physical existence. For example, the words kidwin,
 'word, utterance' zaaghiwewin, 'love,' dkajwin, 'flu,' and zoongdehewin, 'courage,' are all
nouns, but are different from concrete nouns, in that these do not refer to discrete physical
objects, to substances, or to things that can literally be seen, touched, or separated as objects
in the world. Nouns of this sort which name states, conditions and acts are called ABSTRACT
NOUNS. Abstract nouns in Nishnaabemwin often have a characteristic ending, -win, which is
commonly added to verbs to DERIVE nouns referring to a concept associated with the verb,
though not all nouns having this ending are abstract. The meaning relationship between the
verb to which -win is added and the noun that results is not always predictable, as can be
seen from the DERIVED NOMINAL (noun) form of the verb, giigdo, 'talk, speak' (VAI), which
is giigdowin. At Curve Lake this word is used to convey such diverse meanings as 'sen-
tence,' 'conversation,' 'telephone,' and 'microphone,' that is, various 'units' of speaking, or
instruments associated with speaking. In the meanings 'telephone' and 'microphone,'
giigdowin is a concrete noun, since these are physical objects; in the meanings 'sentence'
and 'conversation,' giigdowin is an abstract noun, since these concepts do not refer to
objects having physical substance.

3.3.1 Dependent and Independent Nouns

   BODY PART TERMS. Another identifiable group of nouns in Nishnaabemwin are those
referring to the parts of the body, as in the following examples:

                                     nnik      'my arm'
                                     nkaad     'my leg'
                                     nninj     'my hand'
                                     nzid      'my foot'

   All of these words are usually specified for a POSSESSOR, that is, someone or something
(an animal, bird, insect, etc.) of whose body the item in question is a part. Nouns that nor-
mally require a possessor are said to be DEPENDENT, and are usually INHERENTLY POS-
SESSED, meaning that they are by nature associated with a particular possessor, and cannot
readily be exchanged with others, that is, their ownership doesn't normally change. A pos-
                                                   3.3.1 Dependent and Independent Nouns • 107



session that can change ownership is said to be an ALIENABLE POSSESSION, and another
common way of describing inherently possessed objects is to say that they are INALIENABLY
POSSESSED. Cars, books, shoes— things of this sort can easily change owners, and so, are
alienably possessed, but body parts typically do not change possession, though, of course,
"normal" situations can be suspended, such as when one receives an organ transplant, or
hunters refer possessively to the body parts of their game. In Nishnaabemwin an important
distinction is usually made between DEPENDENT NOUNS, which are generally inherently
possessed, and INDEPENDENT NOUNS, which are not.
    Most body part terms in Nishnaabemwin are dependent nouns. Notice that all of the
nouns listed above begin with a prefix spelled «n», which indicates that the possessor is
FIRST PERSON, for example, nkaad, 'my leg,' and nnik, 'my arm.' Because dependent nouns
generally require a possessor, they are listed in the dictionary with the prefix n, meaning
'my,' but the prefix is ignored in the alphabetical listing of words. So, for example, nkaad is
listed under «k» in the dictionary. The prefix is not in boldface in the dictionary, either,
whereas the rest of the word is, as in, for example, nkaad, 'my leg.' Dependent nouns can
present problems for language learners, because in order to look up a word, the dictionary
user must know whether or not the word has a prefix, and if so, roughly what the prefix is.
So, for example, when encountering the word gkaad, 'your (sg.) leg,' the student must rec-
ognize that it has a prefix, and that the word will not be listed under «g», since that portion
of the word represents the prefix, meaning 'your.' In this regard, Nishnaabemwin is very
different from English, where concepts such as these are usually represented by separate
words, 'your,' and 'leg.' Conventional dictionary organizations present many problems for
language learners in Nishnaabemwin because of the rich system of inflectional prefixes and
suffixes in the language. Furthermore, it is obvious that in order to use dependent nouns cor-
rectly, students must have an understanding of possession inflection (See 196).
    Page 109 lists many of the body part terms cited in the Rhodes dictionary. Note that
while the great majority of such vocabulary requires a possessor, and are thus dependent
nouns, not all terms do, such as miishaaboojiinaagan, 'eyelash,' and miishgondaagan,
'beard hair.' Somewhat surprisingly, the words for female breast, doodoosh, and bone, kan
(or kanenh), are also listed in Rhodes as not requiring a possessor, though they do in other
varieties of Anishinaabemowin. A few terms for bodily substances are dependent nouns as
well, such as nminiingwaagan, 'my sand [in eyes], my sleep [in eyes].' Terms which do not
have a designated dialect affiliation are general Nishnaabemwin.
    KINSHIP TERMS. Another significant subclass of dependent nouns is those referring to
various family and social relationships, vocabulary that is commonly called KINSHIP TERMI-
NOLOGY. Here are some examples.

                                    Some Kinship Terms
           ngashi, nmamaam          'my mother' ndaan(is)            'my daughter'
           nhoos, noos, ndedem      'my father'  ngwis               'my son'
108 • 3.3.1 Dependent and Independent Nouns


    These nouns too carry a prefix that identifies a FIRST PERSON 'POSSESSOR,' or subject of
the relationship, «n», translated into English as 'my.' And again, although these words are
listed in the dictionary with the prefix spelled «n», they are alphabetized according to the
basic word without the prefix, so, for example, ngashi, 'my mother,' is listed under «g».
    Historically, the Anishinaabe kinship system fundamentally distinguished between PAR-
ALLEL and CROSS-relations of aunts, uncles, and cousins. A parallel cousin is the child of
one's mother's sisters or father's brothers; a cross-cousin is the converse, the child of one's
mother's brothers or father's sisters. Much of the rich traditional Nishnaabe kinship vocabu-
lary is included in the Rhodes dictionary, and tables of various kinship terms extracted from
the dictionary are included below and on the following pages. I have divided the terms into
four subsets, strictly for convenience of presentation— there is no semantic or cultural rea-
son for doing so. Today there are two systems of kinship terminology, the traditional,
'older' system, and a newer system, more akin to the European system. These are identified
with the labels OLD SYSTEM and NEW SYSTEM in the dictionary, and those designations have
been retained in the charts which follow. The codes in the final column refer to dialect
restrictions.

    OTHER DEPENDENT NOUNS. In addition to BODY PART TERMS and KINSHIP vocabulary,
there is a very small set of additional words which are also grammatically dependent, mean-
ing that they typically occur with specification of a possessor. Traditionally the few words in
this class consisted mostly of articles of clothing or other objects of close personal posses-
sion, but exactly which items are to be treated as dependent seems to be rather unpredictable
and variable— there is no way to tell strictly from any property of the item, and there is
variation across dialects. Rhodes (1985) lists ndahiim, 'my possession,' nnagway, 'my
sleeve' (Od), ndaas, 'my legging, sock, stocking,' ndazhgan, 'my sock (archaic),' and
ndiknaagan, 'my cradleboard' (W), among others. Perhaps reflecting a humourous use of
the concept of inalienable possession, the words nmaznagan, 'my (financial) bill,' and
ndindwin, 'my fault' (M, CL) are also among those listed by Rhodes as requiring a pos-
sessor.

   INDEPENDENT NOUNS. Nouns that do not require possessors are termed INDEPENDENT.
Jiimaan, 'boat,' and nini, 'man,' are independent nouns, and are not listed in the dictionary
with a personal prefix designating a possessor. Most nouns are independent. It is possible,
of course, even common, for independent nouns to have possessors, such as njiimaan, 'my
boat' (also njiimaanim) or gjiimaan, 'your (sg.) boat' (also gjiimaanim), but they are not
generally required to do so. Independent nouns typically refer to objects and entities that
can relatively easily change possession, or which are not normally possessed.
   For some speakers, certain nouns that were historically dependent can now be used in a
fashion after English that makes them more independent. For example, the following sen-
tence introduces a grandfather in a written story, without any possessive prefix to indicate
relationship. The word for grandfather, mishoomis, does not show the effects of VOWEL
SYNCOPE, either.

   (7)   Mtiggamgoonsing gii-daa mishoomis. Ngoding giizhgak ooshenyan wgii-
         gnoonaan wmishoomsiman biiwaabkoonsing.

          'A grandfather dwelt in a cabin. One day his granddaughter called her grandfa-
         ther on the phone.' (GS/EO)

          Mtiggamgoonsing ni 0 loc 'in a little log cabin'; gii-daa vai ind3sProx 'ANsg lived
          there'; mishoomis na(d) 3sProx 'a grandfather.' Ngoding av 'one time'; giizhgak vii
          conj 0 '(CONJ) is day'; ooshenyan na 3sProx(3obv) 'ANsg's grandchild'; wgii-gnoon-
          aan vta ind 3sProx»3obv 'ANsg spoke to ANobv'; wmishoomsiman nad 3sProx(3obv)
          'ANsg's grandfather'; biiwaabkoonsing ni 0 loc 'on the telephone.'


    Another example uses the dependent noun for mother, gashi, as a free form, which
again, reflects a stem form that would otherwise only occur with a personal prefix, since the
first vowel of the stem /a/ (stem /-gashiw/) is not SYNCOPATED.

3.3.2 Grammatical Gender: Animate and Inanimate Nouns

    Another extremely important sub-grouping of Nishnaabemwin nouns is according to
kind, or to use the more general linguistic term, GRAMMATICAL GENDER. There are two
basic subclassifications, or genders, of nouns in Nishnaabemwin, ANIMATE and INANIMATE.
For the most part, nouns belong to one or the other category on the basis of the inherent
properties of the things they refer to, though one must keep in mind that there is a strong
cultural component in the identification and characterization of objects known or believed
to exist in the world. As a very rough guide, animate nouns typically refer to living things,
such as people, animals, spiritual beings, fish, birds, trees, and many plants. Inanimate
nouns typically refer to non-living things, such as chairs, tables, boats, and books, but
include certain plants as well. The following nouns are organized according to their ani-
macy.

                 Some Animate Nouns                     Some Inanimate Nouns
            nini       'man'                       bkitehgan 'hammer'
            mnidoo     'spirit, manitou'           doopwin     'table'
            gaazhgens 'cat, kitten'                mtigoons 'stick'
            aamoo      'bee'                       kidwin      'word'
            mtig       'tree'                      naagan      'dish'

   There is also a substantial group of nouns that refer to things that are not usually consid-
ered to be 'living,' but which are grammatically animate, meaning that they are treated in
the language as animate nouns. For example, the words sab, 'net', kik, 'kettle, ashcan, pot,'
                                   3.3.2 Grammatical Gender: Animate and Inanimate Nouns • 115


and aagam (or aagim), 'snowshoe,' are all grammatically animate. In some cases, objects
belonging to similar notional classes show variation in their grammatical gender. For exam-
ple, mskomin, 'raspberry,' and zhaaboomin, 'gooseberry' are animate, while dehmin (also
deymiri), 'strawberry' and miin, 'blueberry' are both inanimate. In all dialects of Nishnaabe-
mwin, mnoomin, 'rice' is inanimate, but mdaamin, 'corn' is animate.
    There are a few words that occur with variable animacy, but have different, though usu-
ally related, meanings according to their gender. For example, mtig as an inanimate noun
means 'stick,' and as an animate noun, 'tree'; on Manitoulin Island, bwi as an inanimate
noun means 'paddle', and as an animate, 'propeller,' and the DIMINUTIVE of the animate
form, bwiins, means 'fan.' On Manitoulin Island, as well, zhibiihganaatig as an inanimate
noun means 'pencil' and as an animate, 'pen.' In some communities mkizin when inanimate
is a shoe, but when animate, a tire. On Walpole Island, inanimate biiway refers to fur, or the
hair of fur, but animate biiway refers to fur, wool, or yarn.
    The word ndahiim, 'my possession,' varies in its animacy depending on the animacy of
what is being referred to. If it is referring to grammatically animate things, it is animate; if it
is referring to grammatically inanimate things, it is inanimate.
    There are many simple grammatical tests for determining the animacy, or gender, of a
noun. For one, the plurals of nouns show structured variation, in that animate nouns have
plurals ending in «g» (or «k», depending on how one spells), and inanimates have plurals
ending in «n». The following examples illustrate this:

                     Plural Forms of Animate and Inanimate Nouns
           Singular    Meaning         Plural         Final Letter           Gender
                                                       of Plural
           nini        'man'           ninwag              g                 Animate
           mnidoo      'spirit being'  mnidoog             g                 Animate
           gaazhgens   'cat, kitten'   gaazhgensag         g                 Animate
           mtig        'tree'          mtigoog             g                 Animate
           bkitehgan   'hammer'        bkitehganan         n                 Inanimate
           doopwin     'table'         doopwinan           n                 Inanimate
           mtigoons    'stick, twig'   mtigoonsan          n                 Inanimate
           kidwin      'word'          kidwinan            n                 Inanimate
           naagan      'dish'          naagnan             n                 Inanimate

   Another grammatical test of a word's animacy is whether the TRANSITIVE verb
nwaabmaa, 'I see (animate)' (VTA) or nwaabndaan, T see (inanimate)' (VTI) is used when
making reference to seeing the object in question, for example, nini nwaabmaa, 'I see the
man,' (animate), butjiimaan nwaabndaan, 'I see the boat' (inanimate). The same sort of test
can be used with the INTRANSITIVE verbs meaning 'be big,' mdido (VAl) for animates and
mchaa(mgad) (VII) for inanimates.
116* 3.3.2 Grammatical Gender: Animate and Inanimate Nouns


  Another grammatical test of animacy is to determine which (DEMONSTRATIVE) PRO-
NOUN meaning 'this' is used with the noun in question, whether maaba (or aw), for ani-
mates, or maanda (or ow), for inanimates. We can summarize these tests as follows:

                    Various Tests for Noun Gender in Nishnaabemwin
                          Test 1        Test 2         Test3                Test 4
Gender       Example      Plural Test 'See' Test        'Be Big' Test       Pronoun Test
Animate      nini         ninwag        nwaabmaa       mdido                maaba/aw
Inanimate    jiimaan      jiimaanan     nwaabndaan     mchaa(mgad)          maanda/ow

    DIALECT VARIATION IN GENDER ASSIGNMENT. Many words show variable gender in
different communities. For example, daabaan 'car, wagon' is animate for speakers at Wai-
pole and on Manitoulin Island, but is inanimate for those at Curve Lake. The word
dewehgan, 'drum' is also inanimate at Curve Lake, but animate at Walpole and on Manitou-
lin. In some cases, there are small families of words that tend to be grammatically animate
across Nishnaabe communities. For example, words referring to heavenly bodies such as
the sun, giizis, the moon, dbik-giizis, and the stars, nangoonsag, are all animate in all com-
munities. Words referring to processed lumber and wooden objects are often animate, such
as bzagaak (or nbagsag), 'board, plank,' bmidsaa, 'canoe thwart,' andjiibyaatig, 'cross,
crucifix.' The names of cards are animate, such as bezhgoobiihgaan, 'ace,' niizhoobiihgan,
 'deuce,' and zhmaagni-gimaa, 'jack.' In many communities, words for grains and grain
products are often animate, though here there is variation. Bkwezhgan, 'bread,' skaan, 'bis-
cuit,' and mdaamin, 'corn,' are all animate at Curve Lake. Bkwezhgan is inanimate at Wal-
pole and on Manitoulin Island, however, though one word for a wedding cake at Walpole,
waab-gookookhoo, literally 'white owl,' is animate, as is biitoojiishkwegnigan, 'pie.' Terms
for tobacco and related paraphernalia are usually animate, for example, semaa, 'tobacco,'
semaans 'cigarette' (CL), and pwaagan, 'pipe,' are all animate. Tobacco has religious sig-
nificance in Nishnaabe culture, and the observation has been made that items of traditional
religious significance are often animate, as we saw with the word for 'drum,' dewehgan, at
least in some communities. This may also be the reason that celestial objects are animate,
because in traditional mythology they were associated with living beings. The word for the
group of stars in Orion's belt, for example, Aadwahamoog, is animate plural, and literally
means, 'they travel together in a boat,' evidently in reference to a story connected with this
constellation.
    Although there is variation among the languages and dialects of the Anishinaabemowin
(Ojibwe) group as to which nouns are grammatically animate, there is substantial agree-
ment for many words. The table on the following page presents a set of words for which
Nishnaabemwin agrees with most of its sister dialects in animacy (gender) assignment.
Nishnaabemwin can be distinguished from other varieties of Ojibwe, however, on the basis
of a small but consistent set of words that it does not treat as animate. In most Ojibwe dia-
lects, for example, all terms for money are animate, but in Nishnaabemwin they are consis-
                                           3.3.2 Grammatical Gender: Animate and Inanimate Nouns • 117


tently inanimate, including zhoon'yaa, 'money,' ihoomaankenh, 'penny,' bezhigwaabik,
'one dollar,' and niizhwaabik, 'two dollars.' Even the archaic word shining, 'bit, twelve and

word for 'small change,' zhoomaankensag, is animate, as we can see from its plural ending.

    GENDER SHIFT. Another noteworthy aspect of gender is the traditional phenomenon of
GENDER SHIFT, in which an object that is "normally" grammatically inanimate becomes ani-
mate due to its assuming animate properties, such as the ability to speak or exert spiritual
power. A good example of this is found in Andrew Medler's story of the mirror being
(Bloomfield 1958:213-216), in which a young man during a fast receives a blessing from a
mirror, which later provides him with protection in battle. When the mirror visits the young
man during his vision fast and offers its protection, it is initially referred to with grammati-
cally inanimate words, but then, when it confers its blessing, it becomes animate; later,
when it protects him in battle, it is once again inanimate. The following sentences from Mr.
Medler's story illustrate the difference.

   (10) Baamaa dash ngoding dbikak gii-bi-yaamgadni iw waawaabmowin.

         'Finally then one night there came that mirror.' (AM31.8)

          Baamaa av 'later'; dash av 'then'; ngoding av 'one time'; dbikak vii conj 0 '(CONJ)
          IN be night'; gii-bi-yaamgadni vii ind Oobv 'INobv came'; iw pr Os 'that'; waawaab-
          mowin ni Os 'mirror.'


   Here, the word for mirror, waawaabmowin, is clearly inanimate, as can be seen from the
inanimate pronoun iw, 'that' which occurs with it, and the use of an inanimate subject verb
(vii), bi-yaamgad, 'come (there).' Later in this story, when the mirror comes to bless the
young man, it is animate, as can be seen from its occurrence with the animate pronoun aw,
'that', and the animate subject verb (VAI), bi-yaa, 'come (there)':
                                   3.3.2 Grammatical Gender: Animate and Inanimate Nouns • 119


   (11) Miinwaa dash e-aazhoo-dbikak gii-bi-yaa aw waawaabmowin.
         'The next night that (anim.) mirror being came again.' (AM31.14)

          Miinwaa av 'and'; dash av 'then'; e-aazhoo-dbikak vii ic conj 0 '(CCNJ) when IN be
          next night'; gii-bi-yaa vai indSsProx 'ANsg came'; awpr SsProx 'that'; waawaab-
          mowin no. 3sProx 'mirror.'


   Note too that Bloomfield has now translated the word waawaabmowin as 'Mirror
Being,' though the only difference in the Nishnaabemwin between this sentence and the
preceding example is the shift in grammatical gender.
    Gender shift almost always involves the shift of something that is grammatically inani-
mate to the status of grammatically animate. The opposite case, where grammatically ani-
mate objects become inanimate, does not seem to occur, or at least is very uncommon. It is
also very important, in the light of phenomena such as gender shift, to recognize the fluidity
of grammatical categories. Cecil King (1997:116-17), for example, feels very strongly that
the terms animate and inanimate for the two classes of nouns in Nishnaabemwin are mis-
leading and restricting, and too dependent on English criteria. He writes:

         My language is an Algonquin language, I am told, and it is structured by
         describing things as animate or inanimate, so I am told. English defini-
         tions of the terms "animate" and "inanimate" lead people to think of
         things being alive or not alive. Is this how our language is structured? I
         think not. In Odawa all so-called inanimate things could not be said to be
         dead. Does animate then mean having or possessing a soul? Is this a suffi-
         cient explanation? I think not. Is the animate-inanimate dichotomy help-
         ful in describing the structure of my language? I think that it is limiting, if
         not wrong outright. For in Odawa anything at some time can be animate.
         The state of inanimateness is not the denial or negation of animateness as
         death is the negation of the state of aliveness. Nor can something have a
         soul and then not have a soul and then acquire a soul again. In Odawa the
         concept of animateness is limitless. It can be altered by the mood of the
         moment, the mood of the speaker, the context, the use, the circumstances,
         the very cosmos or our totality. English terms imprison our understanding
         of our own linguistic concepts.

    These points on grammatical animacy are useful. Most concepts in grammar are rela-
tively fluid, and in Nishnaabemwin the category labeled animacy seems to be particularly
so. There is no doubt, though, that from a grammatical point of view, there are two catego-
ries of nouns in Nishnaabemwin, and that the distinction between these categories is abso-
lutely fundamental to the workings of the language, whatever we choose to call them. All
nouns are identified in the dictionary as to the grammatical feature that linguists commonly
120 • 3.3.2 Grammatical Gender: Animate and Inanimate Nouns


refer to as animacy. Animate nouns are labeled na and inanimate nouns, ni. Dependent
nouns show variable animacy as well. All terms of kinship relation are of course animate,
since they refer to relations among living beings. Terms for body parts are most often inani-
mate, but there is a small class that is animate in at least some communities. For example,
ngidig, 'my knee,' nshkanzh, 'my (finger)nail,' and nzhaghay, 'my skin,' are all animate for
most Nishnaabemwin speakers. In the dictionary, dependent nouns are only distinguished
from independent nouns on the basis of the former having a personal prefix, n, 'my' in their
listings, as in ngidig, 'my knee.'
     GENDER AND PROPER NAMES. Another aspect of gender to bear in mind is that while
words such as mookmaan, 'knife' and aankod, 'cloud' are usually inanimate when referring
to knives and clouds, they are animate when used as the names or designations of living
beings such as people. For example, Gchi-mookmaan, which literally means something like
'big knife,' is the common designation for an American, and when used with this meaning
and reference, it is animate. However, gchi-mookmaan can also be used to designate a large
knife such as a cleaver, in which case it is inanimate. In many communities the word
miishgondaagan means 'beard hair,' if inanimate, but 'person with a beard,' if animate.
Another example is the name Biidaankod, 'Cloud Approaches,' which also occurs as a verb
meaning 'clouds are approaching.' When used as a name of a person, though, this word is
an animate noun.

                           Some Nishnaabemwin First Names
                Bebaamaash            'Blowing- Around'
                Biidwewdam            'Come-Hither-Talking'

                Dkamse                'He- Walks- Across' (Tecumseh)
                Naadgiizhgokwe        'Day-Fetching-Woman'
                Naawkwegiizhgokwe     'Noonday- Woman'
                Wezhgonid              'Fishtail'

    Some names of places are inanimate nouns. For example, the Nishnaabe name for the
community which in English is called Petoskey, Michigan, is Biidaasge. As a name, the
word is an inanimate noun, though biidaasge is otherwise a verb (VAI) taking an animate
subject (giizis, the sun, NA), and meaning 'shine in this direction, [the sun] breaks through.'
Since the Nishnaabe names of people and places are often based on some salient attribute of
the person or place, and since attributes are commonly expressed in Nishnaabemwin by
verbs, names derived from verbs are very common. Another point to make is that because of
potential problems of ambiguity, it is probably best to capitalize names in writing, as an aid
to the reader, especially for readers who many not be completely fluent in the language.

3.3.3 Pronouns

    Another important class of words in any language is its PRONOUNS. There are many dis-
tinct kinds of pronouns in Nishnaabemwin. Pronouns are traditionally described as words
which stand in place of nouns, but this is a less useful definition for languages such as Nish-
naabemwin than it is for English. English, for example, uses PERSONAL PRONOUNS exten-
sively, to indicate who and what is involved in verbal events and actions, such as in the
following sentence. In Nishnaabemwin, no pronouns need be used.

                  / saw a moose when / was hunting. / shot (at) it.

   (12) Mooz ngii-waabmaa giiwseyaan. Mii dash gii-baashkzog. (RV)

          Mooz na 3sProx 'moose'; ngii-waabmaa vta ind ls»3sProx 'I saw ANsg'; giiwseyaan
          vai conj Is '(CONJ) when I was hunting.' Mii av 'so'; dash av 'then'; gii-baashkzog
          vta conj ls»3sProx '(CONJ) I shot ANsg.'


    Nishnaabemwin often expresses the equivalent concepts by means of prefixes and suf-
fixes on nouns and verbs. There are pronouns corresponding to the English personal pro-
nouns, but they are used differently, often for EMPHASIS or CONTRAST, or in contexts in
which there is no verb in the sentence. I discuss many of these differences in Chapter 12. In
this section, though, I simply introduce the different kinds of pronouns that occur in the lan-
guage, though the reader should be aware that there is much dialect variation in the forms of
many pronouns, and that I have undoubtedly missed some regional forms.
    Rhodes 1985 does not use a special code for pronouns in the dictionary. Rather, because
they often substitute for nouns, they are treated as independent nouns, and use the appropri-
ate codes for their gender. So, for example, the personal pronoun niin (or nii), T, me,' is
labeled NA, and the demonstrative pronoun wi, 'that (inan.)' is labeled NI.
122 • 3.3.3.1 Personal Pronouns


3.3.3.1 Personal Pronouns

    PERSONAL PRONOUNS identify people and things on the basis of their relationship to the
discourse in which they are referred to, in other words, on the basis of their CONVERSA-
TIONAL ROLE. For example, the pronoun nil (or mm), T is used by anyone who takes the
role of speaker in a discourse (grammatically, called FIRST PERSON); the pronoun gii (or
giiri), 'you (sg.)' is used to refer to anyone who is being spoken to in a discourse (grammat-
ically, called SECOND PERSON); the pronoun wii (or wiiri), 'she, he, it (anim.)' is used to refer
to anyone who is referred to in the discourse but is not directly involved in it at the moment
of speaking (grammatically, called THIRD PERSON). Each person category can be SINGULAR
or PLURAL in NUMBER. The personal pronouns of Nishnaabemwin are listed in the following
chart. The numbers in the left column are codes customarily used to identify the different
categories of the personal pronouns when they are realized as prefixes and suffixes on verbs,
that is, these codes represent a shorthand way of referring to the grammatical categories of
person and number which each pronoun realizes.

                                     Personal Pronouns
 Code     Short       Long         Meaning                  Grammatical Categories
 Is       nii         niin         T                        First Person Singular
 2s       gii         giin         'you'                    Second Person Singular
 3s       wii         wiin         'he, she, it (anim.)'    Third Person Singular
 IP       niinwi      niinwin      'we (but not you)'       First Person Plural Exclusive
 21       giinwi      giinwin      'we (including you)'     First Person Plural Inclusive
 2p       giinwaa                  'you'                    Second Person Plural
 3p                 wiinwaa        'they'                   Third Person Plural

    INCLUSIVE AND EXCLUSIVE. First person plural in Nishnaabemwin makes a distinction
between INCLUSIVE and EXCLUSIVE. FIRST PERSON PLURAL INCLUSIVE includes the person
or persons addressed, so carries a meaning something like English 'we, you and I (and per-
haps others).' FIRST PERSON PLURAL EXCLUSIVE excludes the person or persons addressed,
and conveys the meaning, 'we, that is, I and others, but not you.' The numeric abbreviation
for first person plural inclusive, 21, explicitly recognizes that the second person is included,
as opposed to Ip, used for the exclusive, in which no reference to second person is made.
The presence or absence of second person is extremely important to many aspects of the
workings of Nishnaabemwin, so these codes explicitly index whether or not second persons
are involved. Grammatically, first person plural exclusive is strictly first person, and not
grammatically third person, while first plural inclusive is grammatically both first person
and second person.
    Two distinct forms are given for most of the personal pronouns listed, in columns
labeled short and long. These two sets of personal pronouns reflect dialect differences, with
                                                      3.3.3.2 Personal Pronouns of Precedence • 123



some speakers using the shorter forms and some the longer. There is no grammatical differ-
ence between them. Other variants probably exist as well. The usage of personal pronouns
is exemplified in detail in Chapter 12.

3.3.3.3 Demonstrative Pronouns

    Demonstrative pronouns specify concepts equivalent to English 'this (one)' and 'that
(one),' that is, they specify persons and objects on the basis of their proximity to the place of
speaking, or to the location of the speaker, or to some other point that the speaker chooses to
make the point of reference. Demonstrative pronouns index the nominal categories of GEN-
DER, NUMBER, and DEVIATION. I discuss the use of demonstratives in greater detail in Chap-
ter 12, but for now, provide tables of their forms.

    The terms PROXIMAL and DISTAL are used to label the two demonstrative categories rep-
resenting the degree of proximity (closeness) to the reference point (often, the speaker's
location), with the "nearer" set labeled proximal (not to be confused with the term PROXI-
MATE, which is contrasted with OBVIATIVE), and the farther set labeled distal. Note also that
within each of these categories two sets of demonstrative pronouns are indicated in the
tables, labeled Set 1 and Set 2. These two sets reflect dialect variation in Nishnaabemwin,
with those labeled Set 1 strongly historically associated with Manitoulin Island Odawa, and
those of Set 2, with other locales. For example, both Gregor McGregor, who was from Birch
Island, on the north shore of Lake Huron, and Angeline Williams, who was from Sugar
Island, near Sault Ste. Marie, used a 'aw (or aw) and / 'iw (or iw), but not wa or wi. The same
is true of Nora Soney, from Walpole Island. The texts of Sam Osawamick and Francis Fox,
both from Manitoulin Island, however, have only wa and wi forms. In some areas speakers
vary in the usage of these sets, and some communities and speakers use mixed sets of
demonstratives, reflecting the historical constituency of the communities as both Odawa and
Chippewa. I will use both of these sets without comment, based on the forms provided by
speakers.

3.3.3.4 Indefinite Pronouns

    INDEFINITE PRONOUNS are used when the identity of what is being mentioned is either
unknown or not important, or is of a general nature, and correspond to the English words
'someone, anyone,' and 'something, anything.' The inanimate indefinite pronoun is gegoo
(or gegoon in some communities), and the animate is waya (or gwaya) or wiya. The animate
pronoun can also be inflected for the nominal feature of OBVIATION by some speakers, pro-
ducing, for example, wayan (or wiyan). Inflection for PLURALITY is evidently not common.

3.3.4 Dubitative Pronouns

   DUBITATIVE PRONOUNS are used to express the concepts 'what(ever) might (that be)...'
and 'who(ever) might (that be)...'. They are rather similar to the English expressions 'what-
ever' and 'whoever,' and like these English expressions, tend to occur in association with
DUBITATIVE elements indicating uncertainty, and verbs associated with them are often
INFLECTED with the DUBITATIVE MODE. The Nishnaabemwin dubitative pronouns are ani-
mate, wegwen (also wegwenh, wegwendig) and inanimate, wegdagwen (also wegdogwen,
wegwen, wegwenh, wegwendig). For many speakers, wegwen(h) has become the general
form of the dubitative pronoun, both animate and inanimate. Some examples of dubitative
pronouns:

   (18)   Ngii-miinig dash aw maa nembaaswid carpenter shop gii-zhid, Wa-waabndan
          wegdagwen nendwendaagdogwen.
          The instructor in the carpenter shop gave it to me, saying, "Go see whatever
          might be wanted.'" (AM8.28)

          Ngii-miinig vta ind ls»3sProx 'ANsg gave Y to me'; dash av 'then'; awpr SsProx 'that';
          maa av 'there'; nembaaswid vai ic conj part 3sProx '(CCNJ) who (ANsg) instructed';

3.4 Verbs

   VERBS specify actions, states, and events, in relation to beings and things in the world or
the imagination. The table below provides a few examples of Nishnaabemwin verbs.
130 • 3.4.1 Transitivity and Animacy


                          Some Sample Nishnaabemwin Verbs
            bgambiisaa            'the rain comes here' VII
            Gchi-namhe-giizhgad   'it is Easter' vil
            gichii                'ANsg takes footwear off VAI
            gminpwaa              'you like the taste of it (anim.)' VTA
            gnwabiigzi            'be long' (of stringlike objects) VAI
            gnwaakzi              'be long' (of wooden objects) VAI
            gnwegad               'be long' (of cloth) VII
            gokzigaade            'be stuck on' vii
            naagne                'go such direction through the snow' VAI
            ngodooshkne           'be a container full' VII
            shkwaa-naagshi-wiisni 'eat dinner' VAI

   Many concepts which are expressed by nominals in English find expression as verbs in
Nishnaabemwin. The seasons of the year, the days of the week, the time of day, weather
expressions, geographical features, and number expressions are all commonly expressed
with verbs. Nishnaabemwin verbs are typically structurally complex as well, encoding
many components of meaning in richly articulated word structures. These structures are
examined in detail in Chapters 9 and 10. In the following sections, we will examine some of
the more important grammatical categories relevant to understanding the classification of
Nishnaabemwin verbs.

3.4.1 Transitivity and Animacy

   Consider the following sentence.

   (25)   Wnaadmawaan nini gwiiwzensan. I 'The man helps the boy.' (RV)
          Wnaadmawaan vta ind3sProx»3obv 'ANsg helps ANobv'; nini na SsProx 'man'; gwiiw-
          zensan na 3obv 'boy/s.'

    The verb naadmaw 'help AN' has two SEMANTIC ROLES associated with it, that of the
helper, in this case filled by nini, 'man,' and that of the one helped, in this cased filled by
gwiiwzensan, 'boy.' Even if we make the roles plural, there are still only two, as in
Wnaadmawaawaan ninwag gwiizensan, 'The men are helping the boys.' In this case both
roles are filled by more than one person, but there are still only two identifiable roles, that of
helper(s) and that of helped. Compare this to a verb such as niimi, 'dance,' as in Niimi
gwiiwzens, 'The boy is dancing.' Here there is only a single role, that of the dancer. Verbs
that have two (or sometimes, more) specific roles associated with them, and in which the
filler(s) of one role act(s) upon the filler(s) of the other role, are said to be TRANSITIVE,
                                                             3.4.1 Transitivity and Animacy • 131



while verbs with only a single role are said to be INTRANSITIVE. In English, most verbs can
function both transitively and intransitively, depending on how they are used in a given sen-
tential context, but this is not usually the case in Nishnaabemwin. Consider, for example,
the following sentences:

   (26) Mshiimnan wdamwaan gwiiwzens. I 'The boy is eating an apple.' (RV)
        apple.AN eat      boy

   (27) Wiiyaas     wmiijin gwiiwzens.         I The boy is eating meat.' (RV)
        meat.IN     eat     boy

   (28) Wiisni gwiiwzens.                      I The boy is eating.' (RV)
        eat    boy

    The English sentences all appear to use the same verb, eat. In (26) and (27) the verb has
two roles, one, the eater, gwiiwzens, 'boy,' and two, that which is eaten, either mshiimnan,
'apple' (anim.) (in (26)) or wiiyaas, 'meat' (inan.) (in (27)). In (28), however, there is only
one role, that of an eater. Since the first two verbs have two roles associated with them, and
transferred action, they are transitive; the last verb has only one role associated with it, and
is thus intransitive. In English, the same verb is used in all three sentences, but in Nishnaa-
bemwin there is a different verb in each case. The transitive verbs maw and miijin differ in
that the role of what is eaten is filled in the case of maw by a grammatically animate noun,
and in the case of miijin, by an inanimate noun. However, when there is only one role, that
of eater, the verb is wiisni. We thus find three different verbs in Nishnaabemwin, clearly
indicating transitivity and even whether what is eaten is animate or inanimate. In English,
there is a single verb, eat, which may be used either transitively or intransitively.
    Choosing an intransitive verb other than wiisni, we see that there are often two distinct
intransitive verbs in Nishnaabemwin associated with a given concept as well, as in:

   Mdido gwiiwzens.                            'The boy is big.' (RV)

   Mchaa (or mchaamgad) jiimaan.               'The boat is big.' (RV)

    Each of these verbs has only one role associated with it, whatever has the property of
being big. In the first sentence that role is filled by gwiiwzens, 'boy,' which is animate. In
the second sentence the role is filled by jiimaan, 'boat,' which is inanimate. In each case, we
must use a different verb in Nishnaabemwin, sensitive to whether what is being described as
big is grammatically animate or inanimate. Notice that, again, English uses the same word
in both cases. This is a huge difference between the two languages.
    In TRANSITIVE verbs, it is the role of the object (goal) of the action that determines which
verb is used. Transitive verbs have two roles, one of which tends to be more active than the
other, more clearly an initiator of the action of the verb in some way, and one of which is
132 • 3.4.1 Transitivity and Animacy


usually more passive in the action, more clearly the receiver of the action. The more active
role is identified in Algonquian grammatical tradition as the ACTOR, and the more passive
role the GOAL of the action. It is the role of the recipient of the action (the goal or object)
that is crucial in choosing the appropriate transitive verb in Nishnaabemwin: maw is used
when the recipient of the verbal action is animate, and miijin when the recipient is inani-
mate.
   Based on the number of roles that a verb has and the grammatical gender of these roles,
four main classes of verbs in Nishnaabemwin can be established, outlined as follows:

                        Animate                             Inanimate
         One Role       Animate Intransitive (VAI)       Inanimate Intransitive (vn)
         Two Roles      Transitive Animate (VTA)         Transitive Inanimate (VTI)

    Note the abbreviations used with each subclass of verbs, VAI, VII, VTA, and VTI. The first
letter of the abbreviation, V, specifies the major part of speech of the word, that of a verb.
The next letter, if the verb is intransitive, specifies whether the single role is animate (VAI)
or inanimate (vil), and the last letter identifies the verb as intransitive. If the verb is transi-
tive, the second letter specifies it as such, and the third letter specifies whether the recipient
of the action is animate (making the verb a VTA) or inanimate (making the verb a VTI). In
designing this coding system, Leonard Bloomfield created these abbreviations in part on the
basis of the English ordering of subjects, verbs, and objects. The reason that the A and I are
last in the transitive verb codes (VTA and VTI) is to underscore the fact that it is the object,
the recipient of the action, that determines the subclass of the verb as VTA or VTI. In the case
of intransitive verbs, though, there is only a subject, which, in English, precedes the verbs,
as in The apple is big. So, schematically, we arrive at the relations outlined in the following
table.

          SUBJECT        VERB            OBJECT
          Animate        Intransitive
          A              I                            Animate Intransitive (VAI)
          Inanimate      Intransitive
          I              I                            Inanimate Intransitive (VII)
                         Transitive      Animate
                         T               A            Transitive Animate (VTA)
                         Transitive      Inanimate
                         T               I            Transitive Inanimate (VTI)
                                                             3.4.1 Transitivity and Animacy • 133



   It is also important to recognize that in Nishnaabemwin a verb's TRANSITIVITY does not
have to do with whether there are nouns explicitly mentioned in the sentence. For example,
the following sentences might be said in Nishnaabemwin.

   (29) Gii-bkade         gwiiwzens.            I The boy was hungry.'
        ANsg. was. hungry NA.boy

   (30) Mshiimnan          wgii-mwaan.          I 'He ate an apple.'
        NA.apple.OBV       ANsg.ate.ANobv

    The verb in (30), wgii-mwaan, is transitive, even though only one of the fillers of the two
roles of the verb is explicitly mentioned with a separate noun in the sentence. While the role
of the eater is not specified with a separate noun here, it is clear from the prefix and suffix
inflections on the verb and from the conversational context who the eater is. Being transitive
animate is a property of the verb itself, not the context in which it occurs, that is, is not a
matter of whether the two roles of the verb are explicitly identified by nouns in the sentence
or not. This is rather different from English, where one can say, The boy ate, in which case
the verb is intransitive, or The boy ate an apple, in which case the verb is transitive. In
English, whether a verb is transitive or intransitive is partly determined by what nominals
occur with it in a sentence, but this is not so in Nishnaabemwin. In Nishnaabemwin, one
need only inspect a verb to determine whether it is transitive or not, and even to determine if
it is transitive animate or transitive inanimate. In Nishnaabemwin, transitivity is based on
properties of the verb itself, including its derivational structure and the inflectional configu-
ration that is used with it. Of course, the choice of what nouns can occur with a given verb
are also based on the properties of the verb, for example, one cannot say, *Mshiimnan wgii-
miijin gwiiwzens, 'The boy ate (inanimate) the apple,' because the verb miijin is transitive
inanimate (VTI), and requires that the recipient of the action be grammatically inanimate,
but mshiimin, 'apple' is grammatically animate. The sentence is thus not grammatical.
    The status of VTI verbs as transitive has been rather controversial, owing to the behaviour
of their THEME SIGNS, which are invariant, and are selected for a particular verb rather in the
way that FINALS are. An excellent critique of the issues can be found in O'Meara 1990. For
additional discussion of transitivity see Chapter 5.2, Different Ways of Assessing Transitiv-
ity, beginning on page 214.
    PAIRED TRANSITIVES AND PAIRED INTRANSITIVES. The effect of the interaction of tran-
sitivity and animacy creates four subclasses of verbs, as we have seen. And fundamentally,
in Nishnaabemwin, for all concepts that can be applied equally well to animates and inani-
mates, there are two somewhat different verbs depending on whether the object being dis-
cussed is grammatically animate or inanimate. In other words, most of the time that a verbal
concept is introduced as vocabulary for a language learner, both the animate and inanimate
forms should be provided. The following chart illustrates animate and inanimate intransitive
verbs:
134 • 3.4.1 Transitivity and Animacy




                         Some Animate and Inanimate Intransitive Verbs
       Concept          Animate Intransitive Subject  Inanimate Intransitive Subject
      'be big'         mdido                         mchaa(mgad)
      'be small'       gaachiinyi, gaashiinyi        gaachin
      'be clean'       biin'zi                       biinad

    The concept 'be clean,' for example, is expressed in Nishnaabemwin by two somewhat
different verbs, bun 'zi, when cleanliness applies to an animate, and biinad, when it applies
to an inanimate; the concept of 'being small' is expressed by two somewhat different verbs,
depending on whether what is small is grammatically animate or inanimate. The only cases
where there is not a pairing of animate and inanimate intransitive verbs are those in which a
concept cannot be logically applied to a given gender-class, such as ndaadii, 'be born in a
certain place,' which usually only applies to animates, since only animate things can cus-
tomarily be born, so there is only an ANIMATE INTRANSITIVE (VAI) verb in this case. By con-
trast, there are no animate intransitive verbs corresponding to the INANIMATE INTRANSITIVE
(VII) VERBS zhitgweyaa, 'be a river running in a certain direction' and nkwetgweyaa, 'the
rivers meet,' because such concepts usually simply do not apply to animates. Note, however,
that there is a paired set of intransitives, maajiigi, 'grow (of animates)' and maajiigin, 'grow
(of inanimates).' The reason for this, as the reader will recall, is that some plants are gram-
matically inanimate, and plants grow, indeed are alive, so there is a need for a verb of grow-
ing that applies to grammatically inanimate things. And, of course, not all grammatically
animate words represent things that grow, as we have seen, so for, example, maajiigi would
probably never be said of kik, 'kettle' or shkode-daabaan, 'train.' But we must remember
too that languages are infinitely resourceful, and they are capable of expressing all sorts of
things that don't exist in the "real" world. Resourceful speakers will always find a way to
express whatever their imagination inspires them to present to the world, so we must be
very careful in saying what a language can and cannot do. Languages can express almost
anything we can imagine, and sometimes the rules are bent a little to accommodate the
vision.
    Just as many intransitive verbs come in pairs, so too do transitives. The following table
provides a few examples.

                         Some Animate and Inanimate Transitive Verbs
                         Animate Object              Inanimate Object
        'see x'          waabmaad                    waabndang
        'eat x'          mwaad                       miijid
        'cook x'         mnzwaad                     mnozang
        'shoot at x'     baashkzwaad                 baashkzang
                                                             3.4.1 Transitivity and Animacy • 135



    Once again, it should be clear that to know a verbal concept in Nishnaabemwin, for a
large portion of transitive verb vocabulary, one must know both the transitive animate (VTA)
and the transitive inanimate (VTI) forms. Usually, as can seen from the list above, the rela-
tionship between the paired verbs is very structured, but occasionally, it is not.
    GLOSSING VERBS IN THE DICTIONARY. A great problem arises in artfully translating
concepts involving animacy from Nishnaabemwin into English. This is because English has
three distinct pronouns for its three genders, masculine ('he'), feminine ('she'), and neuter
('it'), and distinct subject and object forms for the masculine and feminine. But animate
nouns in Nishnaabemwin can include: kettles, pipes, wolves, walleye and whippoorwills,
which are referred to in English with the pronoun 'it'; female humans, which are referred to
in English with the pronoun 'she'; and male humans, which are referred to in English with
the pronoun 'he.' So if we wanted to give an accurate translation of the meaning of the ani-
mate intransitive verb mdido, we would have to provide something like 'he, she, or it
(including animals, fish, birds, spirits, and other grammatically animate vocabulary in Nish-
naabemwin) is big.' We might be able to shorten this to 'he, she, it (anim.) is big,' but that is
still rather awkward. Anyone who makes a dictionary of Nishnaabemwin must deal with
this problem, and different compilers have taken different approaches. If we examine
Rhodes 1985, we find that the gloss for animate intransitive mdido cleverly avoids the issue
altogether, and is simply given as 'be big, be large,' without any reference to a subject. The
gloss for the inanimate intransitive verb mchaa is equally simple, 'be big.' The only way to
know that mdido applies to animates and mchaa to inanimates is by the inspecting the part
of speech designation, which is given as vai for animate intransitives and vii for inanimate
intransitives. This means that students learning Nishnaabemwin cannot use the dictionary
properly unless they understand the relationship of the grammatical code to the kinds of
subjects (roles) that are associated with each of these kinds of verb.
    Turning to transitive verbs, we find that the dictionary uses a somewhat different strat-
egy. Looking up waabmaad and waabndang, we find the glosses 'see s.t. (an.)' for the
former and just 'see s.t.' for the latter. The abbreviation s.t. does not stand as a short form of
the word 'something,' though, as we might initially assume. Rather, it represents 'anything
referred to by a word that is grammatically inanimate' and s.t. (an.) stands for 'anything
referred to by a word that is grammatically animate.' Rhodes also uses the abbreviation s.o.
in the glosses of words that usually have human recipients, such as miinaad, VTA, which is
glossed 'give something to s.o.' Note, too, here, the use of the fully spelled out word,
something, which refers to an object that is involved in the meaning of the verb, but is not
inflectionally indexed on it, since it is almost always the case that only two roles are inflec-
tionally marked on the verb, and in this case it is the giver and the receiver that are marked,
and not the object given. Again, students must be aware of these conventions in order to
make use of the information provided by the dictionary.
136 • 3.4.2 Animate Intransitive Verbs with Objects (VAIO Verbs)


3.4.2 Animate Intransitive Verbs with Objects (VAIO Verbs)

    In Chapters 9 and 10,1 show that verbs generally have specific morphological structure
that identifies them as belonging to a verbal subclass, either VAI, VII, VTI, or VTA. I have
made the point that transitive verbs are those which have (at least) two semantic roles asso-
ciated with them, and intransitives, those with one role. However, there are verbs which are
animate intransitive in terms of their basic (derivational) word structure, but which some-
times occur with a second role associated with them. The linguist Edward Sapir once
observed that "all grammars leak," and this is a place where Nishnaabemwin leaks, though
the leakage occurs to some extent in all varieties of Anishinaabemowin. These verbs are dif-
ferent from VTA or VTI transitive verbs, in that their recipients (patients, goals, objects) can
be either animate or inanimate, whereas with regular transitive verbs, the verb takes either
an animate goal or an inanimate goal, but not both. They are different too from VTA verbs in
that their goals can only be third person, whereas in VTA verbs, goals can also be first or sec-
ond person, as in nwaabmig, 'ANsg sees me,' (with a first person goal), and gwaabmig,
'ANsg sees you' (with a second person goal). These structurally intransitive verbs that take
optional third person objects are labelled VAIO (for verb animate intransitive + object) in the
Rhodes dictionary. What is particularly striking about them is that, although they are struc-
turally intransitive verbs, they take inflectional suffixes which code the grammatical proper-
ties objects (goals) associated with them, including gender, number, and obviation. I will
have more to say about them in Chapter 5, but for now, provide a couple of examples.

   (31)   Kina dash niw wdadaawenaawaan. I 'All these things (inan.) they sell.' (AMIS.3)
          Kina av 'all'; dash av 'then'; niw/?r Op 'those'; wdadaawenaawaan vaio ind3p»0p
          'ANpl sell INpl.'

   (32) Zhashkoonyan gye zhaangweshwan wnisaawaan daawewaad.
          'They kill muskrats and mink and sell them.' (AM15.7)

          Zhashkoonyan na 3obv 'muskrat(s)'; gye av 'and'; zhaangweshwan na 3obv 'mink';
          wnisaawaan vta ind 3pProx»3obv 'ANpl kill ANobv'; daawewaad vaio conj SpProx
          '(CONJ) ANpl sell (Y).'

3.4.3 Ditransitives

    Some transitive verbs have more than two semantic roles associated with them. The most
common notional classes of such verbs are those that involve the transfer of something from
one person to another, as in miinaad, 'give something to s.o.,' and those which involve
doing something (transitive) for the benefit of another, as in zkahmawaad, 'light something
for s.o.' Traditionally such verbs are said to have a DIRECT OBJECT, the item transferred, and
an INDIRECT OBJECT, the recipient of the transfer. Verbs having two objects of this sort are
                                 3.4.4 Inverse-Only Transitive Animate Verbs (VTAI Verbs) • 137



commonly called DITRANSITIVES. All such verbs are transitive animate, and all have animate
GOALS. These verbs are treated in more detail in Chapter 13. The following table lists a few
ditransitives to illustrate.

                    dbahmawaad     pay for something for s.o.
                    mkamaad        take something away from s.o.
                    ndaknaad       cut into something in search of s.o.
                    niindaahaad    send something to s.o.
                    nsitamoohaad   explain something to s.o.
                    waabndahaad    show something to s.o.

3.4.4 Inverse-Only Transitive Animate Verbs (VTAI Verbs)

   There is a small set of transitive animate verbs (VTA) that refer to bodily states induced
by some foreign agent. The following list of some of these words, using the form of entry
and gloss found in the Rhodes dictionary, will illustrate their nature.

                     Some Transitive Animate Inverse-Only Verbs
      aakshkadeshkaagod            'give s.o. a stomach ache' (of things ingested)
      aakziishkaagod               'make s.o. sick' (of things ingested)
      dewkweshkaagod               'give s.o. a headache'
      gaasknaabaawgweshkaagod 'make s.o. thirsty'
      giiwshkwebiishkaagod         'make s.o. drunk'
      giiwshkweshkaagod            'make s.o. dizzy'
      sosnaamshkaagod              'make s.o. cough'

   These words have only third person actors, never first or second person. For example,
one can say, ngiiwshkweshkaagon, 'it's making me dizzy' (CL.R161), but not
*ggiiwshkweshkoon, 'you are making me dizzy.' These verbs are always transitive animate
(VTA), since they necessarily involve action upon objects that are persons or animals, which
are always of animate gender in Nishnaabemwin. They are indicated in the Rhodes dictio-
nary with the code VTAI, which stands for Verb Transitive Animate, Inverse (only). I discuss
the meaning of the grammatical category INVERSE and related terms in Chapter 8.

3.4.5 Participles

   There is another class of words in Nishnaabemwin that is something of a hybrid between
nouns and verbs, traditionally called PARTICIPLES in Algonquian grammatical tradition,
though they have similarities with English gerunds. A participle is a verb used as a nominal
138 • 3.5 Adverbs


expression, that is, one which is used similarly to the way a noun is customarily used, to
identify people and objects. Although they are clearly verbs, participles have properties of
both nouns and verbs, and have distinctive endings that reflect both their nominal and verbal
properties. An example of a participle found in the dictionary is weniijaanid, which Rhodes
glosses as 'mother.' This word is actually a participial form of a VERB OF POSSESSION,
wniijaani, and literally means, 'one who has a child.' The plural form is weniijaan'jig,
which shows a verbal element, -j, designating a third person animate, and a special plural
ending, -ig, resembling the plural of animate nouns. While Rhodes does not explicitly iden-
tify participles in the dictionary with any special code, they are usually recognizable from
their form. The dictionary sometimes includes the obviative form of participles, an inflec-
tion in Nishnaabemwin that is used to designate a noun, or a verb associated with a noun, as
backgrounded or otherwise grammatically secondary to another noun. I discuss participles
in more detail in chapter 12, along with associated concepts such as obviation, so will not
pursue the subject here. Obviative forms are identified in the dictionary with the abbrevia-
tion obv. The obviative of weniijaanid is weniijaannijin, and is listed as such in the dictio-
nary. Any verb can be made into a participle in Nishnaabemwin, for example, nebaajig,
'those who are sleeping,' can be made from the verb nbaa, 'ANsg sleeps.' To list every par-
ticiple form in the dictionary would result in a bewildering number of terms, since there are
potentially hundreds of participle forms for some verbs. Rhodes has chosen to list only
those participles whose meanings have become conventionalized in some way, that is,
where a given participle is widely accepted to have a specific meaning not necessarily deter-
minable from its literal meaning. For example, the word bemaabiigniged is listed in the dic-
tionary with the meaning 'baseball manager' (on Manitoulin Island). This word literally
means 'one who holds the reins,' so shows a METAPHORICAL SHIFT from one who manages
a team of horses to one who manages a team of baseball players.
    Gidaagon bembizod, a word for 'snowmobile' on Manitoulin Island, illustrates another
aspect of some dictionary entries containing participles, namely, that they can consist of a
verb along with other, associated, words, creating a phrase. This word literally means 'that
(animate) which drives along on top of the snow.' The meaning 'on top of the snow' is pro-
vided by the separate word, gidaagon.

3.5 Adverbs

    Rhodes also identifies a class of words in Nishnaabemwin as ADVERBS, identified with
the label AV. Traditionally, adverbs are defined as a class of words which modify verbs,
adjectives, and clauses, typically expressing such notions as time, location, manner, degree,
or circumstance. Such a classification can also be used with Nishnaabemwin, which has
many words fitting each of these categories. For example, time (temporal) adverbs include
bjiinaago, 'yesterday,' waabang, 'tomorrow,' megwaa, 'meanwhile,' and noongwa, 'now'.
Place (LOCATIONAL) adverbs include maa, maanpii, zhonda, and zhanda, all meaning
'here,' as well as shpiming, 'above,' aazhoogaam, 'across the lake,' and shaweyhiing,
'alongside.' Adverbs of CIRCUMSTANCE include njida, 'on purpose,' and nshike, 'alone.'
                                                                    3.5.1 Temporal Adverbs • 139



MANNER terms include aabdig, 'absolutely,' gaawaanh, 'barely,' geskana (or gshkonwaaj),
'suddenly,' and maamkaadkamig, 'amazingly.' These few examples are only representative
of large numbers of adverbs belonging to each of the classes outlined here.
    There are important differences between Nishnaabemwin and English in the expression
of concepts associated with English adverbs. Some of these ideas, as we can see from the
examples above, are expressed in Nishnaabemwin by separate adverbial words, just as they
are in English. In other cases, though, elements attached to the verb itself express the ideas
that separate English adverbs do. For example, to express the idea of 'accidentally,' a PRE-
VERBAL element bichi- can be attached to the front of the verb, as in ngii-bchi-
btaagshkawaa, 'I accidentally bumped ANsg.' (CL, RH:413). In some words, though, the
element meaning 'accidentally' is a basic (ROOT) component of the word, as in bchichged,
'do something accidentally, make a mistake,' and bchinaajged, 'shoot (at) something acci-
dentally.' These words have the same element that is found in the preverbal element bichi-,
but in their cases it functions as a root component of the word.
    In the notes which follow, I will lay out some of the more common NOTIONAL CLASSES
of adverbs, with a substantial listing of the members of each class, based on the rich corpus
of materials in the Rhodes dictionary. In this chapter my focus is on presentation and classi-
fication, rather than function, that is, how these items are used. I discuss the functions of dif-
ferent adverb classes in Chapters 15, 16, and 18.
