3.5.7 Negative Adverbs

    Negative adverbs are of two basic types, those that have some negative component in
their meaning, and those that function fundamentally in contexts of syntactic negation. The
second class typically requires that associated verbs be marked with negative inflectional
suffix, as in example (42) below, while the first class does not generally have this restriction
(as in example (43) below). The first class includes the words aana, 'in spite of, in vain,' and
eshkwaaj, 'for nothing.' The second class includes the negative words gaa and its many
combinations, as well as gego (or gegwd), which is used in NEGATIVE COMMANDS (PROHIBI-
TIONS).

3.6 Numbers

    NUMBERS show variable expression in Nishnaabemwin, in some cases occurring as sep-
arate words, in others as elements attached to the front of nouns or verbs, and in others, as
ROOT COMPONENTS of words. Rhodes identifies numbers in the dictionary with the abbrevi-
ation, nm. A couple of examples of number expressions using a free word:

   (48)   Naan'godnong niizh nde-bjibwaag ji-bwaa-kina-gnjibhiwewaad.
          'Sometimes I manage to spear two of them before they all get away.' (AM14.9)

          Naan'godnong av 'sometimes'; niizh nm 'two'; nde-bjibwaag vta ind ls»3pProx 'I am
          able to spear ANpl'; ji-bwaa-kina-gnjibhiwewaad vai conj 3p '(CONJ) before ANpl all
          escape.'

   (49) Gmaapii dash wgii-noondwaan niizh kwewan bi-debtaagzinid bi-gaagiigdonid.
          At last he heard two women who came within hearing as they talked.' (AM38.15)

          Gmaapii av 'finally'; dash av 'then'; wgii-noondwaan vta ind 3sProx»3obv ' ANsg heard
          ANobv'; niizh nm 'two'; kwewan na 3obv 'woman/women'; bi-debtaagzinid vai conj
          3obv '(CONJ) ANobv came within earshot'; bi-gaagiigdonid vai conj 3obv '(CONJ)
          ANobv were conversing.'

   Number elements can also occur as PREVERBS or PRENOUNS, just as many other adver-
bial elements do, as in the following example:

   (50)   Mizfco-dbahgaans dnizan. I 'Cook it for two hours.' (AM39.818)
          Niizho-dbahgaans ni Os '(for) two hours'; dnizan vti imp 2s»0 'cook IN.'

   VERBS OF NUMBER are also common in Nishnaabemwin, in which the number compo-
nent functions as the ROOT element of a word, as in the following examples.

   (51) Niizhnoon doopwinan. I "There are two tables.' (AM39.221)
          Niizhnoon vii ind Op 'INpl are two in number'; doopwinan ni Op 'tables.'

            have two ears from.'


3.7 Particles

   Rhodes also identifies a class of particles in Nishnaabemwin, closely related to numbers
and adverbs. Of particles, Rhodes says, "all forms which do not readily fit in one of the
other classes are treated as particles" (p xv). Particles are identified in the dictionary with
the abbreviation PT. The distinction between particles and adverbs is not made in other dic-
tionaries of varieties of Anishinaabemowin (e.g. Nichols and Nyholm 1995), and all such
words are called particles.
    INTERJECTIONAL AND EXHORTATIVE TERMS. Particles include the rich sets of interjec-
tional and exhortative words of Nishnaabemwin. INTERJECTIONS are simple expressions of
one or two adverbial words that serve to express emotional and evaluative attitudes. EXHOR-
TATIVES serve to enjoin others to undertake some activity. Other kinds of meaning are con-
veyed by interjections as well, such as basic greetings. Interjections are unique in
Nishnaabemwin in sometimes having the sound [h] (IPA [h]). The table below lists some of
the interjectional vocabulary of Nishnaabemwin.

    EMPHATIC PARTICLES. EMPHATIC PARTICLES add various kinds of emphasis to state-
ments or components of statements. They are extremely common in running conversation
and narrative. For example, in Sam Osawamick's telling of six stories, comprising approxi-
mately 450 sentences, the emphatic particle sa occurs 150 times. Particles are often phono-
logical CLITICS (see §2.7 (page 72)). Nishnaabemwin enclitics usually attach to the first
word in a CLAUSE, which is often an adverbial word itself, such as mil, 'it's, so, and.' Often
more than one particle occurs, bunched together after the first word of the clause. Pat
Ningewance, a northern Ojibwe speaker, has pointed out how important the proper use of
these particles is to speaking the language fluently, and describes the particles as being akin
to salt, sprinkled through the language to give it spice and flavour.
    The following is a list of some of the more common emphatics of Nishnaabemwin, with
the insightful glosses listed in the Rhodes (1985) dictionary, followed by a few examples in
sentential contexts. Emphasis is treated in Chapters 12 and 18.

          maa       emphatic expressing cooperation or a request for cooperation
          naa       emphatic marking evaluative information
          sa        emphatic of novelty
          sha       emphatic of contradiction
          wii       emphatic expressing unexpectedness

    THE SEQUENCING PARTICLE/ADVERB DASH. The adverbial element dash, 'so, then,' is
extremely common in Nishnaabemwin, one of the most common words in the language. It
is especially prone to ENCLITICIZATION with a preceding word, and many conventional
terms, such as aanii-sh, 'how,' wegne-sh, 'what,' and mii-sh, 'and then...' have it so com-
monly that it has arguably become an integral part of the word it is associated with. It is
especially common for dash to attach to interrogative (question) words that begin a sen-
tence. The particle go commonly attaches to adverbial words, such as aazhi, 'already.' Sev-
eral examples of dash occur in example sentence (58), below. The element dash is rather like
English 'so,' or 'then,' in running narrative, that is, it serves to pace and delimit sequential
narration. It also occurs in contrastive constructions with the adverb wii(n), similar to
English expressions such as 'on the one hand... and on the other hand...'. The many func-
tions of particles could fill a grammar of themselves, and I recognize that my treatment in
this grammar is quite incomplete.
    THE PREDICATIVE ELEMENT Mil. The adverb/particle mil is as common as it is impor-
tant to the workings of Nishnaabemwin discourse, functioning both as a DISCOURSE
SEQUENCING device and, in construction with RELATIVE CLAUSES and related constructions,
as a FOCUSER. Rhodes (1985:231) glosses it with the meanings 'that is what...' and 'that's it
(with nouns),' which represent its most common meanings. I examine the use of this this
particle in Chapter 18, but here provide a couple of examples of its usage. In the first, mii
serves as a discourse sequencer; in the second example, it provides very explicit focus.

3.8 Prenouns, Preverbs, and Pre-Adverbs

    PRENOUNS and PREVERBS are elements that attach to the front of nouns and verbs,
respectively. Much less common are PRE-AD VERBS. The PHONOLOGICAL behaviour of these
elements is noteworthy, in their clearly being PREFIXES in some aspects of their behaviour,
though each preverb, prenoun, or pre-adverb acts as a separate 'word' with respect to the
VOWEL DELETION RULE of SYNCOPE, in that their final vowels are never deleted, that is, act
as if they were the last vowel in a word.

3.8.1 Prenouns

    PRENOUNS specify several kinds of relations, including location, number, colour, and
various other qualities. They are not common, occurring most frequently in expressions of
quantification, such as ngo-bboon, 'one year,' and nso-naagaans 'three cupfuls.' The lists
below illustrate some of the more common notional classes of prenouns.
    PRENOUN AND ROOT FORMS. Many of the classes of prenouns discussed below have
corresponding ROOT forms, occurring as INITIAL (ROOT) components of basic noun (and
verb) STEMS. For example, the prenoun msko-, 'red,' has a corresponding root form,
/miskw/, which occurs in words such as mskodiismin, 'bean' NA, and mskomin, 'raspberry'
NA. The morphological structure of nouns is treated in Chapter 11. See also 9.10.1, Attribu-
tive (Descriptive) Expressions, beginning on page 342, for details of the use of such descrip-
tive roots with intransitive verbs.

3.8.2 Preverbs

    PREVERBS are extremely common in Nishnaabemwin, and are used to signal many dif-
ferent kinds of meanings, including the time of the action (tense), desire, obligation, possi-
bility, the beginning and ending of an action or event, and relations between verbs and other
elements in the sentence that translate with such diverse expressions as 'there', 'from,' 'so,'
 'so many,' 'to such an extent,' and 'in that place.' In this section I will introduce the major
categories of preverbs in Nishnaabemwin. Based on a consideration of meaning and posi-
tional distribution, the classes of preverbs include those of TENSE and MOOD, DIRECTION
(LOCATION), RELATION, ASPECT, MANNER, QUALITY, and QUANTITY.
    PREVERB AND ROOT FORMS. Many of the classes of preverbs discussed below have cor-
responding root forms, occurring as initial (root) components of basic verb stems. For
example, the directional preverb bmi-, 'along,' has a corresponding root form, /him/. The
following examples illustrate the contrast, with a preverb in example (61), and correspond-
ing root in (62). The morphological structure of verbs is treated in Chapters 9 and 10.
                                                                               3.8.2 Preverbs • 155


   (61)   Mii-sh gii-zhi-bbaabtood maa nsawhigning mdaaching, gii-£/m-ngamo gn-bmi-
          dkonang iw biiwaabik gechi-giinaag.
          Then he ran around the tipi ten times, he was going along singing and carrying
          along a very sharp metal spear point.' (AK11.12)

           Mii-sh av 'and then'; gii-zhi-bbaabtood vai conj SsProx '(CONJ) ANsg ran around

    INITIAL CHANGE. Before introducing the various subclasses of preverbs, it is necessary
to describe a MORPHOLOGICAL PROCESS called INITIAL CHANGE, which occurs only with the
CONJUNCT ORDER of inflection, and affects the first vowel in a verbal complex consisting of
a verb and any associated preverbs. Initial change is used in a variety of grammatical con-
texts, such as the formation of PARTICIPLES and ITERATIVE forms, and in constructions hav-
ing relative roots or relative preverbs, such as most content questions. Each of the seven
vowels of Nishnaabemwin has a characteristic CHANGED FORM, as illustrated by the follow-
ing table.

                                          Initial Change
                                   Unchanged         Changed
                                         i                 e
                                         a                 e
                                         o              (w)e
                                        ii                aa
                                        aa               yaa
                                         e               ye
                                        oo              waa

   Initial change always results in a syllable with a long vowel. If we consider the process
of short vowel syncope (weak vowel deletion), discussed in Chapter 2 (esp. p. 54ff.), we
recognize that the first short vowel of a word is always deleted because it is in a metrically
156* 3.8.2 Preverbs


weak position. The process of initial change, however, strengthens this vowel by making it
long, so that it is not subject to deletion. For this reason, some processes of initial change
may appear more irregular than they really are, especially to language learners. Consider the
following preverbs, for example, in their contemporary and historical plain (unchanged) and
changed forms.

                             Contemporary              Historical
                         Plain     Changed       Plain       Changed
                         nji-      (w)enji-      onji-       wenji-
                         piichi-   epiichi-      apiichi-    epiichi-
                         zhi-      ezhi-         izhi-       ezhi-
                         bbaa-     bebaa-        babaa-      bebaa-
                         bmi-      bemi-         bimi-       bemi-

    Upon inspection, it appears that the changed forms are made by prefixing /we/ or Id in
the case of nji-, and /e/ in the cases ofpiichi- and zhi-. For bbaa- and bmi-, however, a vowel
/e/ appears to be inserted after the initial consonant. But inspection of the historical forms,
provided in the right two columns of the table, suggests that initial change may be applying
to these preverbs before they undergo vowel syncope, making the first short vowel in the
word long, and therefore not subject to deletion by syncope.
    Words with /w/, either initially with /aa/, or which traditionally had /w/ due to the change
of /o/ to /we/, sometimes lose their /w/ in the process of initial change. For example, the
changed form of waabi, 'be able to see,' vai,.is for some speakers, yaabid, 'one who sees,'
and the changed form of shki-, 'first, new' (from /oshki-/) is often eshki-, though here it is
possible to analyze this sequence as e-shki- (see discussion below), in which case the initial
/o/ of/oshki-/ is lost by syncope.
    Aside from problems related to vowel syncope, there are some ancient and widespread
idiosyncrasies in the workings of initial change. For example, several preverbs and words
that begin with /d/ have initial changed forms with a prefixed /en/, as in dzhi-, 'there, in that
place' and dso-, 'so many,' which have changed forms endzhi- and endso-, respectively. The
verb daa, 'live there,' has an initial changed form endaad, which has a somewhat special-
ized meaning, 'where s/he lives.' The changed form of the preverb aano-, 'try in vain to...'
is aano-, for some speakers, in other words, the changed form is unchanged. The changed
form of the preverb da- 'FUTURE TENSE' is ge-. Because so many verbs and preverbs have
rather irregular initial change forms, Rhodes elected to list initial change forms in the dictio-
nary, preceded by the code cc, for CHANGED CONJUNCT. For example, Rhodes lists the
changed forms of nbaa, 'sleep,' as e-nbaad and nebaad.
    PREVERB E-. In order to stabilize the form of preverbs and verb stems between their
changed and unchanged forms, many contemporary speakers of Nishnaabemwin attach a
preverbal element e- in place of initial change. This preverb itself probably derives from the
                                                                             3.8.2Preverbs»157


changed form of a preverb a-, which Rhodes glosses with the meaning 'where,' and notes
that it normally only occurs with the conjunct order of verbal inflection. By attaching this
preverb to the front of the word, any preverb that would normally otherwise contain the first
vowel in the word no longer does so, and, as such, does not have to show any alternation in
its form. This strategy is also used with initial change in verb roots, as well, especially those
that historically had a short vowel in their first syllable. This phenomenon gives rise to some
interesting alternations between forms that use preverb e- and those that change a short
vowel in the initial syllable. For example, there are two forms of the expression meaning,
'the one who does (something),' ezhchiged and e-zhichged, depending on the strategy used
to represent initial change. The following charts show how the application of vowel syncope
gives rise to the variant forms.

                             ezhchiged, With changed root Vowel




          Syncope

                            ezhchiged, With preverb e-attached




    Syncope

    Rhodes 1996:4 notes that e- tends to be used much less with participles than with other
construction-types calling for initial change, e.g., waasnid, 'the one who ate,' is greatly pre-
ferred to e-wiisnid, with the former showing initial change of the first vowel of the verb
stem, /wiisini/, 'eat' VAI.
    VERBAL ORDER. Another concept that must be introduced at this point is that of VERBAL
ORDER. In this usage an order designates a unified inflectional system for indicating subjects
and objects on verbs by means of prefixes and suffixes. Nishnaabemwin has three such ver-
bal orders, called the INDEPENDENT, CONJUNCT, and IMPERATIVE. The following table
shows some inflectional forms for the animate intransitive (VAI) verb jiibaakwe, 'ANsg
cooks,' using the three different orders:
158 • 3.8.2 Preverbs


                                                 Verbal Order
                              Independent       Conjunct       Imperative
               T              njiibaakwe        jiibaakweyaanh (no form)
               'you' (sg.)    gjiibaakwe        jiibaakweyin   jiibaakwen
               'ANsg'         jiibaakwe         jiibaakwed     (no form)

    Each of these forms consists of the basic word (LEXEME) jiibaakwe, along with prefixes
or suffixes which specify who is cooking. In the independent order column, we see that to
say 'I am cooking,' an «n» is prefixed to the verb; to say 'you (sg.) are cooking,' a «g» is
prefixed; to say 'ANsg is cooking,' nothing is apparently added. In the case of the conjunct
order, though, the system for marking the subject is quite different, and suffixes are used to
indicate person: -yaanh for T (or -yaan), -yin (or -yan) for 'you,' and -d for 's/he.' In the
imperative order, used to express commands and prohibitions, there is yet another way of
marking person, this time by adding a suffix, -n for second person singular. Note that there
are no first person or third person command forms because commands in Nishnaabemwin
can only be issued to second persons (you can only give a direct command to someone that
you're directly addressing).
    There are thus three distinct systems of prefixes and suffixes for indicating subjects and
objects in Nishnaabemwin. The imperative order, as already noted, is used in direct com-
mands. The use of the independent and conjunct orders is more difficult to define. Tradition-
ally, it has been said that the independent order is used to mark subjects and objects on the
main (or independent) verb in a sentence, and the conjunct with subordinated, or dependent,
verbs. The conjunct is also used when asking substantive questions, that is, those that ask
for information such as who, what, when, where, how, or why. But there are some cases
where usage of independent and conjunct overlap. I discuss the usage of verbal orders in
more detail in Chapter 16.
    Initial change only occurs with verbs inflected for the conjunct order, and then, only
under certain circumstances. Conjunct order inflection without initial change is often called
PLAIN CONJUNCT, and conjunct order with initial change, CHANGED CONJUNCT. Some pre-
verbs and particles have the restriction that the verb associated with them is required to be in
either the plain or the changed conjunct, or have meanings that vary depending on which
they occur with. For example, the conjunctive adverb giishpin, 'if,' only occurs with the
plain conjunct; the interrogative adverb aanii pii, 'where,' with the plain conjunct means
'where [at]?' and with the changed conjunct means 'where [to]?'
    In the discussion of preverbs which follows, I will have occasion to make use of the con-
cepts of verbal order and initial change. A few tense preverbs have different forms in the
independent and conjunct orders, and a few preverbs, as already mentioned, have irregular
initial changed forms.
                                                           3.8.2.1 Tense and Modal Preverbs • 159



3.8.2.1 Tense and Modal Preverbs

    Although I address TENSE in more detail in chapter 16,1 will illustrate some common
tense preverbs here in order to clarify what they are. Tense preverbs specify the time of the
action or state expressed by the verb. MODAL preverbs express desire, obligation, or possi-
bility. The preverb wii- is used to express both futurity and desire, and varies considerably in
its usage across dialects. The following chart lists the tense and modal preverbs of Nishnaa-
bemwin, in their independent order, plain conjunct, and changed conjunct forms.


                                 Tense and Modal Preverbs
            Ind.     Plain Conj.   Changed Conj.      Meaning
            gii-     gii-          gaa-, e-gii        past tense
            da-      ji-           ge-                future tense
            ga-      ji-           ge-                future tense
            wii-     wii-          waa-, e-wii-       future tense, want to. . .
            daa-     da-, ji-      ge- + dub.         modal
            gii-     gn-           —                  modal

   Note that the form of the plain and changed conjuncts is quite irregular for the modal and

are extremely common, and extensive discussion can be found in Chapter 16.

          Aapji av 'really'; gii-zegzi vai indSsProx 'ANsg was frightened'; awpr SsProx 'that';
          ngashi nad ls(3sProx) 'my mother'; wnji av 'from'; iwpr Os 'that'; gii-bzhineyaan vai
          conj Is '(CONJ) I had a close call'; da-gii-daapneyaambaan vai conjpret Is '(CONJ) I

3.8.2.2 Relative Preverbs

    There are six RELATIVE PREVERBS that function to relate the verbal event to various asso-
ciated circumstances, such as way in which it takes place, where it takes place, the reason it
takes place, how long since it's taken place, how many times, and how often. These ele-
ments are discussed in greater detail in Chapters 15, 16, and 17, but are introduced here.
Relative preverbs very often induce initial change when they occur with verbs inflected for
the conjunct order. All relative elements also occur as root forms, or basic structural compo-
nents, of verbs as well, in which case they are called RELATIVE ROOTS. Some relatives may
also be used as free words, especially /onji/, 'from, source, about.'

    (i)zhi-         ezhi-, e-zhi-           'like a certain thing; towards a certain place;
                                            in a certain direction; in a certain way'
    (o)nji-         e-nji-, enji-, wenji- 'from a certain direction, for a certain reason'
    d(a)zhi-        endzhi-, en'zhi-        'at a certain place; there'
    d(a)so-         endso-, en'so-          'so many times, every time'

3.8.2.5 Negative Preverbs

    Two preverbs carry a negative meaning, though verbs associated with one (aano-) does
not carry negative inflectional marking, and with the other (bwaa-) only optionally does, nor
does a negative particle occur in clauses containing them, as is typical of standard negation
in the independent order, but not the conjunct. The negative preverb aano- signals a failed
attempt at something, translating roughly into English as 'try in vain to...' The negative pre-
verb bwaa- is used only with the conjunct order, and conveys meanings such as 'not,' 'lest'
(i.e., 'for fear that...'), and 'so that not.' Negatives are discussed in detail in Chapter 16.

                                        Negative Preverbs
           Unchanged         Changed           Meaning
           aano-             e-aano-, yaano- 'try in vain to.
           bwaa-             e-bwaa-            'so that not..., lest' (conjunct only)

          Gesge av 'although'; wdaano-gnahmawaan vta ind 3sProx»3obv 'ANsg tries in vain to
          warn ANobv'; wiijkiwenyan nad 3sProx(3obv) 'ANSG's friend (ANobv)'; wii-bwaa-

not uncommon.

3.8.2.9 Subordinating Preverbs

   There are a few preverbs that are used as SUBORDINATORS, though all of these arguably
have other functions as well, particularly that of signalling tense relations. A subordinator is
a preverb that serves to subordinate one verb to another verb or a predicative particle, such
as mii. Such preverbs only occur with the conjunct order.
                                                              3.8.2.9 Subordinating Preverbs • 167



                                Some Subordinating Preverbs
                    a-      'where'

                    ji-     'to..., would, will'

    The preverb e- is evidently the changed form of a- (see discussion on page 156 regarding
its use as vehicle of initial change). The preverb gaa- is most often the initial changed form

(unchanged) conjunct of ga-/da-. It also appears related to daa-, the modal preverb.

3.8.2.10 The Relative Order of Preverbs

    We have seen a rich variety of preverbs that occur with verbs, including those of tense,
mode, relation, direction, aspect, negation, manner, degree, evaluation, enumeration, and
subordination. Given such an array, an obvious question arises as to what ordering relations
exist among classes of preverbs. Since the classes of preverbs outlined here have quite dif-
ferent functions, it should not surprise us that members of different classes can co-occur, as
we find in the following examples:

   (84) Kina dash gegoo zhi-wzhiitaawag gonda Fair Company ge-zhi-mno-yaawaad waa-
        bi-zhaajig.
         'The Fair Company are doing everything possible for the convenience of those
         who come.' (AM 16.5)

          Kina av 'every'; dash av 'then'; gegoopr indefO 'thing'; zhi-wzhiitaawag vai ind
          3pProx 'ANpl are thus preparing'; gondaprna SpProx 'these'; ge-zhi-mno-yaawaad vai
          ic conj SpProx '(CCNJ) ANpl will be contented'; waa-bi-zhaajig vai ic conjpart 3pProx
          '(CCNJ) who (ANpl) will come here.'


   (85) Mii dash ekdod, "Jibwaa niizhgon'gak wii-bi-gchi-mmkiikaa.
         This was what he said: "Before two days have passed there will be a big thunder-
         storm." (AM 10.16)

          Mii av 'and'; dash av 'then'; ekdod vai ic conj SsProx '(CCNJ) what ANsg said'; Jibwaa
          av 'before'; niizhgon'gak vii conj 0 '(CONJ) be two days'; wii-bi-gchi-nimkiikaa vii ind
          Os 'there will be a great thunderstorm.'


   Examination of a large number of texts shows that strings of three or more preverbs are
not common. Most commonly, a tense preverb occurs with either a directional or relational
preverb. The order of preverb classes is outlined in the following table.

                                      Preverb Order
           Subordinator     Tense Directional Relational Aspectual Manner
                            Mode                                   Quality
                                                                   Number
           (1)              (2)   (3)         (4)        (5)       (6)

   The first four categories are different from the last two in that there are limited, well
defined sets of elements in them, while the classes of aspect, manner and quality are more
open, admitting new members relatively easily. There is also an overlap of meaning among
                                                 3.8.2.11 The Relative Frequency of Preverbs • 169



adjacent slots of the first four classes, in that members of categories to the right often take
on meanings that are related to the category to the immediate left. For example, tense cate-
gories sometimes have a subordinating function as well as their primary role of signalling
tense. We have seen too how some of the directional preverbs have taken on secondary tense
meanings, and two of the relational preverbs, zhi- and wnji-, at least, signal directional
notions as well as their purely relational ideas.

3.8.2.11 The Relative Frequency of Preverbs

   To determine the relative frequency of the classes of preverbs in narrative discourse, I
tabulated their occurrence in the eighteen narratives told by Alice King of Parry Island, and
present the results in the table below. These tabulations show that over 75 percent of the pre-
verbs occurring in these texts are tense/modal prefixes. The next largest group is that of
directionals, constituting approximately 11 percent of the occurrences of preverbs in Mrs.
King's stories, followed by relative preverbs with 6 percent. Interestingly, these frequency
counts also generally reflect the linear ordering sequence of preverbs within the verb, in that
the further to the left a class of preverbs is relative to the verb stem, the more frequently its
members occur in narrative.

            Preverb Frequencies in Stories of Alice King of Parry Island
            Count Preverb          Class               Meaning
            450      gii-          tense              past tense
            73       ji-           tense/modal         future tense; modal
            50       ga-/da-       tense               future tense
            37       wii-          tense               future tense, 'want'
            29       bi-           directional         'hither'
            24       zhi-          relative            'thus'
            21       ni-           directional         'in time, away'
            18       wi-           directional         'go and...'
            17       bbaa-         directional         'around'
            14       gchi-         degree              'very, greatly'
            10       wnji-         relative            'source'
            9        bmi-          directional         'going along'
            9        dzhi-         relative            'there'
            6        daa-          modal               modal
            6        dso-          relative            'so many'
            5        anda-         aspectual           'seek to'
            4         shkwaa-        aspectual            'after'

            3          a-               subordinative         'when, which, where'
            3          jibwaa-          aspectual             'before'

    There were two tokens of da-, 'modal,' de-, 'sufficient,' gii-, 'modal,' kawe-, 'first,'
mdwe-, 'audibly, out of sight,' mji-, 'evil, bad,' niizho-, 'two,' ntaa-, 'be good at, habitually,'
piichi-, 'in process,' and shki-, 'new.' Several preverbs occurred only once, as well.

          '(CONJ) ANsg ran out crawling'; awpr SsProx 'that'; Nenbozh no. SsProx 'Nenabush.'


   (87) Gchi-gzheb nga-maajaa ji-wi-daaweyaan giw mskomnag miinwaa ji-yaamoonaan

Noun Inflection




4.1 Introduction

    The grammatical categories relevant to the inflection of nouns are GENDER, NUMBER and
DEVIATION. All nouns are third person, except perhaps VOCATIVES (discussed below).
Nouns may be of animate or inanimate gender, and may be singular or plural in number.
Animate nouns can be marked as OBVIATIVE; otherwise they are PROXIMATE. Inanimate
nouns are not inflected for obviation, but verbs associated with them can optionally show
obviative inflection.
    In addition, nouns can be inflected with a LOCATIVE suffix, which is primarily used when
the noun expresses a location, but also marks the objects of RELATIVE ROOTS and RELATIVE
PREVERBS. Nouns can also be inflected to indicate the person, number, and optionally, obvi-
ation of POSSESSORS. Many possessed nouns have a distinct suffix that is said to derive a
POSSESSED THEME, to which possessive inflections are then added.
    Almost all nouns have DIMINUTIVE forms as well, formed by suffixation to a non-dimin-
utive stem. In addition, there are nominal endings which indicate CONTEMPTIVE and PEJO-
RATIVE attitudes on the part of the speaker.
    Some nouns have distinct VOCATIVE forms, used in direct address. The plural vocative
form uses a suffix found with verb inflected for the DUBITATIVE mode of the independent
order. Nouns may also carry a PRETERIT suffix, related to the PRETERIT VERBAL MODE,
which is optionally used when referring to the deceased, particularly kin relations, and with
reference to social roles and possessions that are no longer in effect. A PRETERIT DUBITA-
TIVE suffix also occurred on nouns traditionally, optionally used when making reference to
persons and things in the past which are known only by inference or report.
    Given that a noun can be marked to show so many different kinds of information, such as
gender, number, obviation, location, possession, and so on, questions arise as to the nature
and variation of the expression of these categories, and as to what system there is in their
collective expression. My goal is to provide a reasonably simple conceptual system, in order
to aid language teachers and learners. So the questions are fundamentally these— what
                                                               4.2 Noun Inflection Stem Classes • 173



kinds of grammatical information are associated with nouns, how is such information coded
on the noun, what variation occurs in the coding, and what structures and rules can be deter-
mined to underlie the coding system? For example, we can observe that the plural of sab,
'net,' is sabiig; the plural ofwaagosh, 'fox,' is waagshag, and the plural of kik, 'kettle,' is
kikoog. Simple inspection shows that in each case, the plural appears to have a suffix ending
in /g/, but that the vowel associated with this suffix varies between /ii/ (in sabiig), /a/ (in
waagshag), and /oo/ (in kikoog}. Given that the plural suffix has these different forms, how
do we know which suffix form a given noun will have? For example, why is the plural of
kik, kikoog, and not *kikiigr! When we examine the respective diminutive forms of these
nouns, we find them to be sabiins, waagshens, and kikoons. Again, just as with the plural,
the diminutive appears to be formed by adding a suffix to the basic noun, but there is varia-
tion in the form of this suffix. We notice, however, that sab has /ii/ in both its plural and its
diminutive forms, and kik has /oo/ in the same forms. This suggests that the relationship
between the form of these inflectional suffixes is subject to some sort of principle, and is not
random. With careful study of the language, we may be able to aid the student with rules of
the following sort: if the plural suffix is /-iig/, then the diminutive suffix will be /-iins/; if the
plural suffix is /-oog/, then the diminutive will be /-oons/. The student is thus freed from
having to memorize two distinct facts about every single word showing this kind of varia-
tion. By providing principles of this sort, we lessen the task of the learner. As with every
aspect of language, though, we will almost always find a few exceptions to any rule that we
might try to devise.

   Nishnaabemwin nouns can be marked to show the following kinds of information.

                                             • Diminutive

                                             • Pejorative
                                             • Possessor
                                             • Obviative Possessor
                                             • Locative
                                             • Vocative
                                             • Preterit
                                             • Preterit Dubitative


1. My analysis is heavily indebted to Nichols 1980.
174 • 4.2 Noun Inflection Stem Classes


    The first rule of noun inflection is that there is often no way to tell simply by inspecting
the simple proximate singular form of a noun, what its plural, obviative, diminutive, and
other forms will be. For example, there is no way that one can know simply from the singu-
lars ofjiimaan, 'boat,' and waawan, 'egg,' that their plurals are jiimaanan and waawanoon,
respectively; and there is no way to know from the singulars of nini, 'man' and mooz,
'moose,' that their plurals are ninwag and moozoog, respectively. However, the overall
amount of variation in the noun plural suffix is rather restricted, with only a limited number
of suffix forms occurring, most prominently «ag», «yag», «wag», «iig», «og», «oog» and
«g» for animate nouns, and «an», «yan», «wan», «iin», «oon» and «n» for inanimate nouns.
Examination of large numbers of nouns shows that most can be grouped into seven major
classes on the basis of their behaviour with respect to the different inflectional categories
introduced above. In the following table, I give both a technical and non-technical designa-
tion for each of these classes. The technical designation is based on MORPHOPHONOLOGICAL
patterns, that is, relatively ABSTRACT STEM SHAPES of the nouns, and the non-technical des-
ignation, on a representative member of the class.

                                         Noun Stem Classes
 nm. Technical Designation                 Non-Technical     Examples
 I   Consonant-Final Stems                 Waagosh Class     NA waagosh 'fox'
                                                             Nljiimaan 'boat'
 II     Long Vowel-Final Stems             Mnidoo Class      NA mnidoo 'spirit'
                                                             Nl zenbaa 'ribbon' (M)
 III    Post- Vocalic W-Stems              Nini Class        NA nini 'man'
                                                             Nl ziibi 'river'
 F/a Post-Consonantal W-Stems              Kik Class         NA kik 'kettle'
     Long Vowel Plural                                       Nl mkak 'box'
 IVb Post Consonantal W-Stems              Zhgaag Class      NA zhgaag 'skunk'
     Short Vowel Plural                                      (no inanimates)
 V   Post-Consonantal Y-Stems              Sab Class         NA sab 'net'
                                                             Nl bwi 'paddle'
 VI     Augment Stems                      Nzid Class        NA nzhaghay 'my skin'
                                                             Nl nzid 'my foot'
 VII    Participles                        Bemaadzid Class   NA bemaadzid 'person'
                                                             Nl ezaawaabgoniig 'mustard
                                                                plant'

   My goal in presenting this table is to provide a means of specifying the inflectional
behaviour of as many nouns as possible, by categorizing each as belonging to a particular
class, and by laying out the behaviour of each class of nouns for all inflectional categories.
For example, we could say of the noun mkizin, 'shoe,' that it belongs to Class I, or alterna-
                                                           4.2 Noun Inflection Stem Classes • 175


lively, that it is inflected in the same way thatjiimaan, 'boat,' is, for plurality, locative, pos-
session, and so on. By so doing, we provide the student with a simple means of quickly and
easily assessing a given noun's behaviour for all inflectional categories. It is important to
always remember, though, that there is much local variation, and that a given word may
behave somewhat differently for different speakers. I have outlined some of these differ-
ences below, but cannot possibly hope to account for all of them.
    CLASS I NOUNS (Like waagosh). Class I consists of nouns having singular forms ending
in a consonant other than /g/ or /k/, outside of a very small number of exceptions, and a plu-
ral suffix consisting of /-ag/ for animates and /-an/ for inanimates. Almost all nouns with
stems ending in /n/ belong to this class, which thus includes the majority of inanimate
nouns. All DIMINUTIVE and PEJORATIVE nouns belong to this class as well, regardless of the
class membership of their simple stems. This class is the largest and most morphologically
transparent class, in the sense that the inflected forms straightforwardly resemble the singu-
lars plus an additional, readily segmentable, "basic" suffix. It is also the class whose forms
show the least amount of dialect variation. Some representative members of this class are
waagosh, 'fox,' pwaagan, '(tobacco) pipe,' dehmin, 'strawberry,' wiigwaam, 'house,'and
mookmaan, 'knife.'
    CLASS II NOUNS (LIKE mnidoo). Class II consists of nouns having singulars ending in a
long vowel, and plurals in /g/ (animate) and /n/ (inanimate). Examples of this class include
mnidoo, 'spirit,' ginii, 'rose,' Nishnaabe, 'Indian,' and zhoon 'yaa, 'money.'Note that there
are very few inanimate nouns that end in long vowels, and of those that do, such as, ginii,
'rose,' and zenbaa, 'ribbon,' most show dialect variation in the presence of a CONTEMP-
TIVE/DIMINUTIVE suffix, that is, are giniinh and zenbaanh for many speakers, in which case
they behave as contemptives, discussed in the following section.
    CONTEMPTIVE NOUNS. Between Classes I and II are nouns that end in the suffix
/VjVjnh/, associated with the CONTEMPTIVE (discussed below), whether the contemptive
form of the noun is LEXICALIZED, that is, represents the semantically "neutral" form of the
word, or is SECONDARY, in which case it represents a form of the stem that is distinguishable
from a naturally occurring "neutral" stem in having a contemptive suffix that the neutral
stem lacks, and in having contemptive semantic force. For example, in the cases of
kiwenziinh, 'old man,' and giigoonh, 'fish,' the 'contemptive' form is the basic lexical form,
and there are no words *giigoo and *kiwenzii that they are in contrast with; however, in the
case of daabaanenh, 'car (contemptive),' the contemptive is SECONDARY, because there is a
neutral, primary word daabaan, 'car,' that lacks the contemptive ending and contrasts with
the form having the contemptive suffix. Many primary and secondary contemptive forms
behave like stems ending in long vowels (Class II) with respect to their formation of DIMIN-
UTIVES and LOCATIVES, but like Class I (simple consonant-final) stems with respect to the
formation of other categories, such as PEJORATIVES, POSSESSIVES, and PRETERITS. There is
variation in the plural suffix of both lexical and secondary contemptives, with some adding
/-ag/ (animate) or /-an/ (inanimate), just as Class 1 nouns do, e.g., kiwenziinyag, 'old men,'
and giigoonyag, 'fish (pi.).' Others add /ig/ and /in/, especially non-lexical contemptives, as
in daabaanenyig, 'cars.'
 176 • 4.2 Noun Inflection Stem Classes


     CLASS III NOUNS (LIKE mm')- Class III consists of nouns having singulars ending in a
  vowel such as /i/, /a/ or, rarely, /e/, and plurals in /wag/ for animates and /wan/ for inani-
 mates. Most nouns in this class are animate nouns having singulars ending in III. Some rep-
 resentative members are nini, 'man,' bzhiki, 'cow,' waawaashkeshi, 'deer,' zhaangweshi,
  'mink,' and kwe, 'woman.' Note that in some dialects some animate nouns that historically
 ended in HI have lost it in the singular, e.g., these dialects have waawaashkesh, 'deer,' and
 zhaangwesh, 'mink,' where more conservative dialects have waawaashkeshi, and
 zhaangweshi Regardless of whether or not the final HI is present in the singular, these
 words are almost always inflected as Class III nouns in all dialects.
     CLASS IV NOUNS (LIKE kik AND zhgaag). Class IV consists of two subclasses of nouns,
  one, labeled Class IVa, which has plural suffixes containing an /o/ or the sequence /wa/, and
 another, Class IVb, in which the plural suffix contains /oo/. Members of both subclasses
 most commonly have singulars ending in /k/ or /g/, and much less commonly, other final
 consonants, such as /d/, /n/, /z/, or /m/ for Class IVa nouns, as in waagaakod, 'axe,'
 ziisbaakod, 'sugar,' waawan, 'egg,' waabooz, 'rabbit,' and niinim, 'my sibling-in-law of the
 opposite sex.' Note too that a few nouns ending in /k/ belong to other classes, e.g., giizhik,
  'cedar,' belongs to Class I. Most nouns in class IVa are either animate nouns, or inanimate
 nouns ending in or containing the elements /-aak/ or /-aatig/, both of which mean 'wooden
 (or woodlike) object.' Nouns in Class IVa are exclusively animate, consisting mostly of the
 names of creatures, e.g., ngig, 'otter,' jiig, 'fisher,' mik, 'beaver,' gaag, 'porcupine,' zhgaag,
  'skunk,' dikmeg, 'whitefish,' aandeg, 'crow, raven,' maang, 'loon,' signaak, 'blackbird' (W,
 CL), and bbig, 'flea' (W). Examples of Class IVb include gnebig, 'snake,' mtig, 'tree, stick,'
 zhibiihganaatig, 'pencil, pen' and waagaakdaatig, 'axe handle.'
     CLASS V NOUNS (LIKE sab). Class V consists of nouns having singulars ending in /i/, or
 consonants other than /w/, /k/, or /g/, and plurals ending in /-iig/ for animates and /-iin/ for
inanimates. This is a relatively small class, consisting of many nouns with singulars ending
in /b/, l]l or /zh/, as well as most inanimate nouns ending in HI. Members include ki, 'earth,
land,' bwi, 'paddle,' sabaab, 'string, rope, cord,' sab, 'net,' mtigmizh, 'pin oak' (and all
other tree and bush names ending in -mizh), zhngob, 'evergreen,' niib, 'elm,' pin, 'potato,'
zhgaagwanzh, 'onion' (and all other plant and bush names ending in -wanzh/-winzh), nninj,
 'my hand,' nshkanzh, 'my (finger)nail,' nit, 'fish spear,' and sin, 'stone, rock.'
     CLASS VI NOUNS (LIKE nzid). Class VI consists of nouns that take a special augment
/-aa/, most commonly when inflected as LOCATIVES, e.g., nzidaang, 'on my foot,' as
opposed to nzid, 'my foot.' The augment also shows up in derivational contexts, such as in
the verb of being diyaawi, 'be an ass' (VAl), with initial /diy-aa-/, 'rump,' and in the verb of
possession zidaa, 'have a foot' (VAl), with initial /zid-aa-/, 'foot.' Inanimate nouns of this
class usually have plurals in /-an/, and the few animates, in /-ag/. BODY PART TERMS consti-
tute most of the members of the class, but a few INDEPENDENT nouns show this pattern as
well. Some inflections for Class VI are identical to those of Class I, such as the plural.
Members of Class VI include mshkimod, 'handbag,' ndeshkan, 'my horn,' nmisad (also
nmasad), 'my stomach,' and nnoogan, 'my hip.' A lengthy list of body part terms is pro-
vided on page 106.
                                                                    4.3 Gender (Animate and Inanimate) • 177



    CLASS VII NOUNS (LIKE bemaadzid). Class VII consists of PARTICIPLES, that is, verbs
used as nouns, such as ekandood, 'baseball fielder' (M) or ekwaabdang, 'baseball fielder'
(W), which are both animate, and e-zhaangseg, 'jello' (W) and endzhi-mzinaatesjigeng,
'movie theater,' (M), which are both inanimate. Because they are primarily verbal in nature,
participles lack many NOMINAL categories, such as POSSESSIVES, DIMINUTIVES, and CON-
TEMPTIVES, though they can be inflected for GENDER, NUMBER, and OBVIATION, as well as
for other strictly verbal categories lacking on other kinds of nominals, such as TENSE and
DIRECTION. The inflection of participles is treated in more detail in the appropriate sections
on verbs. Note that all participles do not share the same inflectional properties, since a given
participle will be inflected according to the pattern of its verbal subclass, whether VAI, VII,
VTA or VTI, so we could technically set up a Class VII sub-type for each sub-class of verb.
There is also variation in the extent to which forms derived from participles have become
more nominal and less verbal.

4.3 Gender (Animate and Inanimate)

    Most nouns in their isolated singular forms are not marked in any obvious way for their
GENDER, and there is no way to determine strictly from the form (pronunciation or spelling)
of a noun whether it is animate or inanimate. This is most clear with words such as mtig,
which as an animate noun means 'tree' and as an inanimate, 'stick,' and ndeshkan, which
when animate means 'my horn,' and when inanimate, 'my ice chisel.' What system there is
to Nishnaabemwin gender has more to do with meaning than form. With appropriate pre-
cautions, we can say that living things tend to be animate, and non-living, inanimate.
    There is, however, a small set of nouns where vestiges of gender-indexed marking
appear, reflecting historical relics of Proto-Algonquian word structure found in all dialects
of Anishinaabemowin. In contemporary pronunciation these words all contain a single short
vowel, which is their final segment, either /a/ (sometimes COALESCING with a preceding /w/
to form /o/), or /i/, as in the following examples:

            Class     Item                Gloss                             Final Vowel
            na        nka                 'Canada goose'                    /a/
            na        mkwa, mko           'bear'                            /a/ (or /o/ from /w/+/a/)
            ni        ki                  'earth, ground'                   I'll
            ni        bwi                 'paddle'                          l\l
            ni        mskwi               'blood'                           I'll
            ni         mshi               'piece of firewood' (M)           lil




1. Participles, of course, are marked for their gender on the basis of the class of verb they represent and the inflec-
tions that occur on them.
178 • 4.4 Number (Singular and Plural)


    These examples represent most of the few words in contemporary Nishnaabemwin that
more or less straightforwardly retain some vestigial reference to Proto-Algonquian gender
indexing, in which */a/ was associated with animate nouns and */i/ with inanimates. Of
course, it is not true that all nouns that end in I'll in modern Nishnaabemwin are inanimate,
as can be seen from words such as nini, 'man,' waawaashkeshi, 'deer,' and waawaatesi,
'firefly.' And almost no modern nouns end in short /a/, other than the couple listed here, and
the words miikna, 'road' (or miikan) and oodena, 'town' (or oodenaw), both of which are
inanimate.
    A few of the words in this set of nouns retaining the Proto-Algonquian gender indexing
are somewhat irregular in their inflectional behaviour, and show variation among speakers.
For example, nka, 'Canada goose,' has alternate plurals, either nkoog or nkag, and a LOCA-
TIVE form, nkang; mko has a locative form mkoong for some speakers, with an unaccount-
able long vowel. There is undoubtedly considerable dialect variation in these forms as well.

4.4 Number (Singular and Plural)

    Nouns may be SINGULAR or PLURAL in NUMBER. Plural nouns carry a suffix that is spe-
cific to their gender, ending in /n/ for inanimate nouns, and /g/ for animates. There is, how-
ever, variation in the surface forms of the plural suffix. In the following section we will look
at this form for each noun class. The following chart lays out the surface segmentable form
of the plural suffix for the different classes.

                                    Noun Plural Suffixes
                        I, VI    II    III         IVa            IVb V           VII
         Animate       -ag       -g    -wag        -oog           -wag -iig       -ig
                                                                  -og
         Inanimate     -an       -n      -wan         -oon        -    -iin       -in

    ACCOUNTING FOR VARIANT FORMS. It is easy to account for all forms if we assume that
the basic form of the plural is /-ag/ for animates and /-an/ for inanimates. Class II nouns end
in long vowels, so they absorb the short vowel of the suffix. This fact can be accounted for
with a rule of vowel deletion, specified as follows:




   This rule states that when two vowels are juxtaposed by the addition of an affix, the sec-
ond vowel is deleted. Usually VI is a long vowel, which explains the deletion of V2, since
preserving it would result in an illegal vowel sequence, in that only identical VV sequences
are allowed.
                                                          4.4 Number (Singular and Plural) • 179


    Class III nouns have stems that end in /w/, which is deleted when final, but not when a
plural suffix protects it. Class IVa stems end in /w/, but coalesce /w/ with the vowel of the
suffix to produce a long vowel, /oo/. Class IVb differ in that there is either no coalescence,
as in Class III, or the coalescence produces a short vowel, lol. Class V stems end in a conso-
nant plus /y/, the latter of which coalesces with the vowel of the suffix to produce li.il. These
phenomena can be captured with a set of coalescence rules:

                         Post-Consonantal Glide + /a/ Coalescence
                         la. Cw+a ->• o (optional)
                         Ib. Cw+a ->• oo
                         2. Cy+a -+ ii

    There does not appear to be any way to predict on the basis of underlying stem shape
whether sub-rule la or Ib will apply in the case of stems ending in /Cw/, so, for example,
we find kikoog, the plural of /akikw/, 'kettle, pot,' but mikog and mikwag, plurals of
/amikw/, 'beaver.' The only difference between these two forms is the presence of /k/ in
/akikw/ where /amikw/ has /m/, which does not provide any phonological motivation for the
variation in the coalescence. Nichols 1980 points out that for Mille Lacs Lake Ojibwe most
of the words with the short vowel variant (or /wa/ sequence) refer to the names of animals,
so there may be some semantic basis for the subclasses.
    The nature of these processes is quite straightforward. For example, the plural ofgnebig,
 'snake,' is gnebgoog, and this noun thus belongs to Class IVa. If we hypothesize that its
basic stem shape is /gnebigw/, we can readily explain why the final /w/ is not heard in the
singular, since it would be deleted by the rule of Short Vowel/Glide Deletion. However,
when the plural suffix is added, certain of the phonological features of /w/ merge with the
vowel /a/, resulting in a vowel that is [+high, +round], and long, which in Nishnaabemwin
means /oo/.




   A similar explanation can be offered for nouns that have their plurals in /iig/, such as
sab, 'net,' which has the plural sabiig. In this case, the stem ends with a glide /y/ that is
deleted in the singular form by the rule of Short Vowel/Glide Deletion, but which coalesces
with the suffix in the plural, as illustrated in the following diagram.
180 • 4.4 Number (Singular and Plural)


    In this case, lyl has the phonological features [+high, -back], meaning that the tongue is
moved forward and upward from its normal "rest" position. This is also how the vowel /i/ is
pronounced, and when these features of lyl are transferred to the following /a/, an /i/ is pro-
duced, which occupies the segmental slots of lyl and /a/, producing /ii/.
    Class VII nouns take allomorphic variants of the plural suffixes, /-ig/ and /-in/, respec-
tively. Here we have no phonological means of specifying allomorphic forms, so we must
simply stipulate the MORPHOLOGICAL contexts in which these allomorphs /-ig/ and /-in/ are
to be used, for our purposes here, when the form is participial.

                                  Plural Suffix Allomorphy
                                  a. /-ag/ ~ /-ig/
                                  b. /-an/ ~ /-in/

4.4.1 Inherently Plural Nouns

    Just as in English, a few nouns in Nishnaabemwin are inherently plural, that is, are basi-
cally thought of as consisting of a group of similar objects or a set of objects, and are almost
always used in the plural. Some examples are biiwekdamaagnan, '(wood) shavings' (W);
bootsan, 'boots' (from English boots, Od), and a plural participial noun,
e-baasgobjigemgakin, 'spring-tooth harrows,' a farm implement. Inherent plurals are
marked in the dictionary with the designations NAP and NIP, depending on their gender.

4.4.2 Mass Nouns

   Most nouns specify individual, countable objects, such as mm, 'man,' zhiishiib, 'duck,'
and jiimaan, 'boat.' Such nouns have both singular and plural forms, depending on whether
reference is to one or more discrete individuals, for example, bezhig nini, 'one man,' niizh
ninwag, 'two men, and so on. There are two subgroups of nouns, however^ which do not
generally occur in the plural: first, nouns referring to abstract things such as qualities, states,
and general topics, for example, bmaadziwin, 'life,' aazhdaadwin, 'mutual revenge,' and
gaawendmowin, 'jealousy'; second, nouns referring to substances, such as liquids or partic-
ulates, that are usually treated as a mass, for example, nbiish, 'water,' doodooshaaboo,
'milk,' negaw, 'sand,' ziitaagan (also zhiiwtaagan), 'salt' waasgan(g), 'pepper,' bkwezhgan,
'bread,' goon 'snow,' and mkom (also mkwam), 'ice.' Such nouns are called MASS NOUNS,
and are listed in the dictionary without plural forms, since the plurals are not normally used.
Note that some Nishnaabemwin words that correspond to English mass nouns can be used
with plurals, because they can refer to 'a piece of X,' or 'a portion of X,' such as miijim,
'food, a serving of food,' which has the plural miijman when referring to a serving. In
English, portions of mass nouns can be referred to by means of special QUANTIFIERS with
PARTITIVE constructions, such as a drop of water, a grain of salt, or a slice of bread. In Nish-
naabemwin, by contrast, merely using the plural with a mass noun implies division into
conventionalized units, such as pieces or servings. For example, the noun zhoon'yaa,
'money' (Nl or NA, varying by dialect), is listed without plural in the dictionary, because it is
a mass noun. However, this word commonly takes a plural when it has the meaning 'gold
                                               4.5 Noun Obviatives (Proximate and Obviative) • 183



coin,' that is, represents a countable unit of money. The following example uses zhoon'yaa
with both senses, and in the second, countable, sense, occurs with a plural suffix.

   (1)   Mii-sh endso-aabta-bboon mii gii-miinndwaa iw zhoon'yaa,
         endso-ngo-bboon'gak gii-miinaawag iw bagoowyaan, mii-sh go eta ngoding

         once.' (AK10.8)

   Note that some nouns ending in -win, the most common ending for ABSTRACT NOUNS,

    Only animate nouns have obviative inflectional forms. Obviation is used to distinguish
third persons in clauses, but may also be used to emphasize a particular character as a point

common usage. In this story, the character of Nenabush has been previously introduced, and
the storyteller presents the action from his perspective, by making reference to him PROXI-

to them is marked with an OBVIATIVE suffix, producing zhiishiiban.

4.5.1 Obviative Forms of Names

   Nouns representing personal names may be obviated, and some speakers appear to show
preferences for particular obviative forms. The following data from a speaker of Wik-
wemikong dialect (MC) are illustrative.
                                  Proximate       Obviative
                                  Bert            Bertan
                                  Al              Alan
                                  Roger           Rogeran
                                  Doug            Dougon
                                  Jack            Jackon
                                  Joe             Joewan
                                  Julie           Juliinyin
                                  Randy           Randiinyin
                                  Rita            Ritaayin
                                  Paula           Paulaayin

   Names that end in consonants other than /g/ or /k/ take obviative suffix /-an/; those end-
ing in /g/ or /k/ (velar consonants) take /-on/; those ending in /a/ lengthen the final vowel
and suffix /-yin/. Perhaps most interesting are forms ending in /ii/, such as Randy and Julie.
These extend the stem to make them identical to a contemptive (see discussion in next sec-
tion), and then suffix the usual obviative after the contemptive, /-in/.

4.6 Noun Contemptives and Diminutives

    Nouns can have endings that indicate their DIMINUTIVE or CONTEMPTIVE status. Diminu-
tives specify small or physically immature members of the group identified by the noun,
suchasjiimaanens, 'small boat,' mikoons, 'beaver kit,' and mkoons, 'bear cub.'Contemp-
tives reflect the speaker's attitude toward the object being referred to, and convey vaguely
negative or depreciative attitudes, such as 'just an ordinary one,' 'of no great value,' or 'any
old.' The following sentences illustrate the use of the contemptive:

   (3)   Gaa wii wi daopwaanh ndaa-zhi-dbahnziin wi.

    The use of the contemptive is extremely nuanced, and is undoubtedly indexed in natural
usage to subtle parameters of social context. For example, Rhodes 1985:205 annotates ten,
'bone' (NI) with the usage note: considered crass in some places; and the corresponding
contemptive form, kanenh, with the note: more polite than 'kan'to some. Here the contemp-
tive appears to have an attenuative force.
    The forms of the contemptive and diminutive suffixes for the various noun classes are as
follows. A superscript L is used with suffixes that lengthen a preceding short vowel.

non-final (i.e., when another suffix follows it), e.g., gaazhgenyig, 'lousy cats' (gaazhag,

zhaagnaashiinh. However, other forms such as gookoosh, 'pig,' and maantaanish, 'sheep,'
form their contemptives in -enh.

'partridge,' is listed by Rhodes as both bnenh and bnens.
    EXCEPTIONAL DIMINUTIVES. Some diminutives are exceptional, such as badnens, the
diminutive of badnis, 'button,' (W, CL), an old borrowing from English. Here, the neutral
form of the word is based on the English plural, but the diminutive is based on the English
singular. The plural and diminutive of nimosh, 'dog,' nimoog and nimoons, lack the pejora-
tive of the singular for some speakers.
    LEXICAL CONTEMPTIVES AND DIMINUTIVES. One of the most striking features of the
vocabulary of Nishnaabemwin is the frequency that Contemptive endings appear on basic
(LEXICAL) noun forms, in other words, on noun stems that never occur without the contemp-
tive suffix and which do not have salient Contemptive force, but rather seem to be more
diminutive or endearing in flavour. Examples include such common vocabulary as
binoojiinh, 'child,' kiwenziinh, 'old man,' mdimooyenh, 'old woman,' giigoonh, 'fish,'
bneshiinh, 'bird' (related to bne, 'partridge'), and wesiinh, '(small) animal.' Many KINSHIP
TERMS appear to have these contemptive/diminutive suffixes, including nmisenh, 'my elder
sister,' nsayenh, 'my older brother,' nshiimenh, 'my younger sibling,' nmishoomenh, 'my
parallel uncle,' nnooshenh, 'my parallel aunt,' nooshenh, 'my grandchild;' nzhishenh, 'my
(cross) uncle,' niinmoshenh, 'my cross-cousin of the opposite sex, my sweetheart.' Semanti-
cally, it is interesting that terms for the elderly, children, and siblings very often show LEXI-
CALIZED contemptive/diminutives.
                                                    4.6 Noun Contemptives and Diminutives • 189



     Other words occur with both contemptive and non-contemptive forms, but show pat-
 terned variation by community and sub-dialect in their listings in Rhodes 1985, such as
 aamoo (Oj), aamoonh (M) 'bee'; aanzyaan (Oj), aanzyaanh (CL) 'diaper'; dende (Od),
dendenh (CL) 'bullfrog'; ndiy (Oj), ndiyenh (Od) 'my rear end'; gwiingos (M, CL),
gwiingsenh (M) 'chipmunk';jiibik(Od),jiibkenh (W) 'root'; kakjiish (Oj), kakjiishenh(W),
 'woodchuck'; pakne (Oj),paknenh (Od) 'grasshopper'; pichi (Oj),pichiinh (W) 'robin';
 waagosh (Oj), waagshenh (W, CL) 'fox'; waasii (CL), waasiinh (Oj) 'catfish'; zg/me (Oj),
zgimenh (Od) 'mosquito.'; zhiishiib (Oj), zhiishiibenh (Od) 'general word for ducks and
 teals.' A few kin terms too vary as to whether or not they have contemptive suffixes, such as
 niidgik(oonh), 'my sister (female speaker),' and niikaan(enh), 'my brother (male speaker),'
 once again, involving terms for close kin relations.
     Though less common than the dialect variation in contemptives, the presence or absence
 of diminutives on "basic" terms too occasionally shows variation from one community to
 another, for example, the basic words gaazhag, 'cat' and mzhiwe, 'cottontail rabbit' vary
 dialectally with their diminutive forms gaazhgens and mzhiwens; nang, 'star' varies with
 the diminutive nangoons.
     While there is thus considerable cross-dialect variation in the presence or absence of
 contemptive and diminutive suffixes on neutral nouns, in other cases these suffixes are used
 within a given dialect to make lexical distinctions, that is, to name different, related objects,
 such as bbagwayaan, 'shirt' vs. bbagwayaanenh, '[thin] cloth' (Od), nmegos, 'brown trout,'
 vs. nmegshens, 'rainbow trout' (W); miin, 'blueberry, huckleberry' (inan.) vs. miinens 'haw-
 thorn berry' (anim.); mnidoo 'spirit, being with spiritual power,' vs. mnidoons, 'insect.'
 Related to the last word is mnidoosh for insect, bugs, and caterpillars, with its diminutive,
 mnidooshens, used to signify 'gnat' at (W); mshkiki, 'medicine, medicinal herb' versus
 mshkikiins, 'pill' (W, CL). The words miimii, 'pigeon, dove,' miimiinh, 'large flying insect'
 and miimiins, 'mayfly,' all show lexical specificity on Manitoulin Island. The diminutive of
 animate noun bwi, 'propeller,' bwiins, is used as the word for 'fan,' on Manitoulin Island,
 representing an obvious physical relationship, though in this case it is not size, but force or
power that dictates which term is diminutive. One word for playing card, mzinhigaans (W,
 arch.), is derived from a general word for paper, mzmhigan. The diminutive ofjiis, 'radish'
jiisens means 'carrot' at Walpole. The diminutive of bkwezhgan, 'bread, slice of bread,'
 bkwezhgaans, means 'donut, sweet roll, cookie' in general Ojibwe, but is used as a word for
 wheat at Walpole Island. Doodooshens, the diminutive of doodoosh, 'breast' means 'paci-
 fier' at Curve Lake. Goonens, the diminutive of goon, 'fallen snow, chunk of snow,' means
 'snowflake' at Walpole. Gyaashkshens, the term for a common tern, is the diminutive of the
 general word for gulls and terns, gyaashk. Mtigwaabiins, diminutive of mtigwaab, 'bow
 (archery)' means 'ice fishing pole' at Curve Lake. Consider too shkikmaan, 'lead, piece of
 lead, lead weight,' vs. shkikmaanens, 'bullet' (M); wiigwaam 'house,' vs. wiigwaamens,
 'outhouse, bathroom;' waasgonechgan, 'lamp, lantern,' (Oj) vs. \vaasgonechgaans, 'light
 bulb' (W, CL). The diminutives of nninj 'my hand,' and nzid, 'rny foot,' nninjiins and
 nzidens, respectively, are used to refer to fingers and toes.
190 • 4.7 Noun Pejoratives


   CONTEMPTIVE AND DIMINUTIVE PLURALS. The plural endings after the contemptive
often have the forms -ig and -in, for animate and inanimate, respectively, and the animate
obviative suffix is -in. The plurals of diminutives pattern as Class I nouns. The following
forms for daabaan, 'car' (NA) are illustrative.

                                       Contemptive      Diminutive
                           singular    daabaanenh
                          plural    daabaanenyig
                          obviative daabaanenyin

    The forms of the plural suffixes used after contemptives can be understood as involving
the raising of the vowel /a/ of the standard suffixes, /-ag/ and /-an/ due to assimilation to the
frontness and height of the final /y/ of the contemptive suffix, which has the basic form
/-eny/. Under normal circumstances, the /n/ nasalizes the preceding vowel, and in the singu-
lar, the final /y/ is lost by the rule of final short vowel/glide deletion. But in the plural, since
/y/ is [+high], the articulation of the suffixal /a/ moves toward it, ultimately resulting in a
high vowel articulation, as HI. The following diagram, showing the vowel quadrilateral,
illustrates the dynamics of this process.




    There are still uncertainties regarding contemptives and diminutives. The diminutive suf-
fix, for example, is virtually the only form in any Nishnaabemwin word in which a nasal
precedes a fortis (hard) consonant in the same syllable. Furthermore, while it is clear that
the vowel associated with the contemptive is long, it is not obvious that this vowel should
have the underlying form /e/, since it varies between all possible long vowels, /e/, /aa/, /ii/,
and /oo/.

referred to. The following examples illustrate some contexts in which it might be used:

                       gaag              'porcupine'     gaagosh
                       Class V
                       sin               'rock'          siniish
                       nwi               'bullet'        nwiish
                       Class VI
                       nwiibid           'my tooth'      nwiibdaash
                       nzid              'my foot'       nzidaash
                       ndooskon          'my elbow'      ndoosknish

    The variants that occur with different classes of nouns suggests that the underlying form
of the pejorative is /-ish/, which is added directly to Class I and Class III nouns, but loses its
vowel when added to Class II nouns. With Class IV nouns it shows customary coalescence
of /w+i/ to /o/, and with Class V, of /y+i/ to /ii/. Class VI nouns show variable presence of
augment/-aa-/, which, if present, absorbs the/i/ of the pejorative suffix. The straightforward
nature of the pejorative contrasts particularly with the behaviour of diminutives with Class
III nouns, where stem-final /w/ is somehow deleted. So, for example, /w/ is present in
ninwish, 'worthless man,' but absent in niniins, 'little man.'
    The pejorative is added to the inanimate dubitative pronoun wegdagwen, 'whatever it
be,' with humourous effect, producing an animate noun, wegdagwenish, 'a jerk, a nobody'
(M, CL).

4.7.1 Relative Ordering of the Diminutive/Contemptive and the Pejorative

    The diminutive suffix occurs directly after the noun stem, and before the POSSESSIVE
MARKER (POSSESSIVE THEME SUFFIX, discussed below), while the pejorative may appear
either before or after the possessive marker. Nouns can be both diminutive and pejorative, as
in the form ndakwezhenzhishim, 'my naughty little girl,' based on the noun stem kwezens,
'girl.' Pejorative nouns are often also diminutive, especially in Manitoulin usage, even for
                                                                             4.8 Noun Locatives • 193


large objects, such as zaadiinzhish, 'darn (little) poplar (tree)' (from zaad, 'poplar'),
niniinzhish, 'darn (little) man' (from ram, 'man'), and waawaashkeshiinzhish, 'darn (little)
deer,' (from waawaashkeshi, 'deer'). This usage perhaps reflects a common metaphorical
practice in which diminutive expressions are used to index a lack of esteem, as in English
expressions such as 'you little rat.' Note that the final /s/ of the Nishnaabemwin diminutive
weakens (LENITES) to /z/ when followed by the pejorative suffix, representing a common
pattern in most dialects of Ojibwe. Usually the /z/ shows PALATALIZATION as well, becom-
ing /zh/.

                            Neutral          Gloss      Pejorative
                            kwezens          'girl'     kwezhenzhish
                            gwiiwzens        'boy'      gwiiwzhenzhish

   The following examples illustrate that /z/ and /s/ which are part of the stem and not part
of a diminutive or quasi-diminutive suffix (such as the /z/ in kwezens) do not palatalize. For
example, the /s/ ofsabiins, 'little net,' does not become /zh/.

                        Neutral          Gloss            Pejorative
                        sabiins          'little net'     sabiinzhish
                        mzin'gaans       'little book'    mzin'gaanzhish
                        nzidens          'my little foot' nzidenzhish

4.8 Noun Locatives

    A LOCATIVE suffix is added to nouns when they specify a location, and also when they
are the objects of RELATIVE PREVERBS and RELATIVE ROOTS. The following examples illus-
trate.

   (8)    Giishknakdoonying bkodbi. I 'He's sitting atop the tree stump! (MC)
          Giishknakdoonying ni loc 0 'on a tree stump'; bkodbi vai indSsProx 'ANsg is sitting
          up.'

   (9)    Jiibkenying gii-bzogeshin. I 'He tripped on the root: (MC)
          Jiibkenying ni loc 0 'on root'; gii-bzogeshin vai ind BsProx 'ANsg tripped.'

   (10)   Giigoong (or giigoonying) piichi-ntaa-bgiza. I 'He can swim like a fish: (MC)

          Giigoong na loc 3 '(like) a fish'; giigoonying na loc 3 '(like) a fish'; piichi-ntaa-bgiza vai
          ind 3sProx 'ANSG is good at swimming to such extent.'
194 • 4.8 Noun Locatives


   (11)   Mhiingning zhinaagzi gday. I 'Your dog looks like a wolf.' (MC)

          Mhiingning na loc 3 '(like) a wolf; zhinaagzi vai ind 3sProx 'ANsg looks like'; gday
          nad 2s(3sProx) 'your dog.'

    Regular plural and obviative suffixes are usually not present on locative forms, so there
is standardly no additional marking on locative nouns for number or obviation. However, a
suffix indicating grammatical features of NUMBER or OBVIATION of a POSSESSOR can be
added, prior to the locative ending.

                                         Locative Endings
                 I          II            III        IV           V           VI
               -ing        -ng             L
                                        -V ng       -ong        -iing       -aang

    The superscripted L associated with the Class III suffix indicates that stem-final /w/ is
lost and the exposed final vowel lengthened, e.g., stem /aniniw/ (or /ininiw/), 'man,' has a
locative niniing. Examples for each class follow.

               Class I
               zhiishiib         'duck'        zhiishiibing
               gaazhag           'cat'         gaazhging, gaazhgong (M)
               jiimaan           'boat'        jiimaaning
               Class II
               mnidoo            'spirit'      mnidoong
               ginii             'rose'        giniing
               Class III
               nini              'man'         niniing
               kwe               'woman'       kweng
               bgiw              'gum,         bgiing

               Class IV
               kik               'kettle'      kikong, kikoong (M)

               Class V
               sin               'rock'        siniing
               nwi               'bullet'      nwiing
                                                                         4.8 Noun Locatives • 195



                Class VI
                nzid            'my foot'        nzidaang
                nnik            'my arm'         nnikaang
                mshkimod        'handbag'        mshkimdaang
                nnagway         'my sleeve'      nnagwaang
                ndengway        'my face'        ndengyaang, ndengwaang

    The basic form of the locative suffix is /-ing/, which surfaces directly when added to
Class I noun stems. Class II stems absorb the III of the suffix; Class III, as mentioned above,
lose stem-final /w/ and lengthen the vowel; Class IV show standard coalescence of /w+i/ to
/o/, and Class V, coalescence of /y+i/ to /ii/; Class VI stems show augment /-aa-/ before the
locative, which absorbs the initial lit of the suffix.
    Both LEXICAL and DERIVED CONTEMPTIVES vary in their locatives, depending on
whether or not the final NASAL COMPLEX is treated as a consonant cluster and the suffix
/-ing/ added to it, or the final nasal complex is ignored, and the STEM then treated as a class
II long vowel final stem, giving rise to such variation as giigoonying and giigoong. Locative
forms listed in Rhodes often show a preference for one or the other of these treatments, as
can be seen from the following citations:

                                                                  Locative
            bashkwaanaajiinh        'bat'                         bashkwaanaajiing
            bebaabgaanh             'pancake' (W)                 bebaabgaanying
            binoojiinh              'child'                       binoojiing
            e-zaawaanh              'melon' (W)                   ezaawaanying
            gebkadiinh              'comforter (blanket)' (W)     gebkadiinying
            giigoonh                'fish'                        giigoong
            giishknakdoonh          'tree stump'                  giishknakdoong
            jiibkenh                'root' (W)                    jiibkeng
            jikenh                  'tree stump' (W)              jikeng
            ndiyenh                 'my rearend'                  ndiyeng
            zegaabkaadenh           'market basket' (W)           zegaabkaadenying
            ziibiiwenh              'stream, creek' (W)           ziibiiwenying

   Note that in class III, the final vowel of the singular is lengthened if it is not already long,
and the derived stem is treated just as Class II 'long vowel-final' stems are (for example,
nini, 'man,' vs. niniing, 'on the man'). A couple of words of class III having a final /w/ in
the singular, such as bgiw, 'gum, pitch,' lose the /w/ and lengthen the vowel.
196 • 4.9 Noun Possession


    Class VI nouns, most of which are body part terms, take an augment, /-aa/, before the
locative suffix. For nouns that end in /-ay/, this element is either obligatorily or optionally
deleted prior to adding the augment, as in nzhagay, 'my skin,' but nzhagaang, 'on my skin,'
where it is obligatory, and ndengway, 'my face,' which Rhodes lists as having two locative
forms, ndengyaang, which retains the /-ay/ element before /-aa/ (but loses the /w/), and
ndengwaang, which lacks it. Occasionally, words show variation as to whether or not they
take the augment, as in ndenniw, 'my tongue,' which has both ndenniwaang and
ndenniwing as locative forms. The same is true ofndiniigan, 'my shoulder blade' (Od) with
locatives ndiniignaang and ndiniigning. In at least one case, variation between the presence
and absence of /aa/ augment is exploited for semantic purposes, in the locatives at CL asso-
ciated with ntawag, 'my ear,' which Rhodes records as ntawganaang, 'on my ear,' and
ntawganing, 'in my ear,' perhaps under the influence of the semantic specificity offered by
the English prepositions in comparison to the traditional locative.
    Some nouns have irregular locative forms, such as oodewin, 'town,' which has a locative
form oodenaang, identical to the regular locative form of the Class VI noun with the same
meaning, oodenaw. Rhodes lists the locatives for shkwaandem, 'door,' as both regular
shkwaandeming and irregular shkwaandeng. One motivation for the latter form is that loca-
tive nouns grade structurally and semantically into locative adverbs, which often have
reduced forms compared to equivalent locative nouns. The locative of aazhwaakwaa, 'the
back settlement on Walpole Island' is identical to the base form. The locative of msan,
'piece of firewood,' (archaic) is mshing, showing the historical alternation of /S/.

   The template shows one prefix position and four suffix positions. The prefixes indicate

The second suffix position contains a possession marker (also called a POSSESSION THEME
