4.9.1 Indefinite (Unspecified) Possessors

    Historically, as recorded in Bloomfield (1958:24), Odawa had an INDEFINITE POSSESSOR
prefix /i-/. This possessor prefix is used as a kind of structural placeholder in cases where
the possessor of a normally inalienable body part is either not known or is irrelevant, as in,
say, a drawing of a disembodied body part, or a cut of meat offered as a gift from a hunter.
Such examples certainly occur in Nishnaabemwin, as in the following sentences, but since
syncope always deletes the initial vowel, it is not possible anymore to determine the quality
of the prefix vowel.

   (12) Waabang sa nga-mnazaan maanda kaad.
          'Tomorrow I'm going to cook up this leg (of game animal).' (MC)
                                                        4.9.2 The Form of the Person Prefixes • 199



          Waabang av 'tomorrow'; nga-mnazaan vti ind ls»0s 'I will cook INsg'; maanda pr Os
          'this'; kaad nidOs 'leg.'

   (13)   Bezhig wiibid ngii-naajtoon. I 'I lost a tooth.' (MC)
          Bezhig nm 'one'; wiibid nid Os 'tooth'; ngii-naajtoon vti ind ls»0s 'I lost INsg.'


   (14)   Jaanzh mzinbiihan! I 'Draw a noser (MC)
          Jaanzh nid Os 'a nose'; mzinbiihan vti imp 2s»0 'draw IN.'


   (15) Ngii-zhibiihaan toowag. 1 'I have made a drawing of a(n) (human) ear.'
          Ngii-zhibiihaan vti ind ls»0s 'I drew INsg'; toowag nid Os 'an ear.' (AM39.376)

   This prefix seems largely restricted to occ.urrence with body part terms. In the case of
dependent kinship terms, indefinite possessor forms are expressed by verbal derivatives,
such as woosi, 'have a father,' used in participial form, weyoosijig, 'those who have a(n
unspecified) father,' i.e., a given man's children. The form niijaani, 'have a child,' can be
used in its participial form, weniijaanid (alternatively e-niijaanid), to refer to an unspecified
parent, especially a mother.

4.9.2 The Form of the Person Prefixes

    The PERSON PREFIXES show variation according to the form of the stem that they are
attached to. Prefixes attached to stems beginning with a vowel have a linking element /d/,
while those that are attached to stems beginning with consonants do not, for example,
emkwaan, 'spoon,' has as its first person possessor form, ndemkwaan, 'my spoon.'
    In Chapter 2 (p. 62 and following) I discussed at length a process which has resulted in a
new, extended set of person prefixes, such that there are now several distinct forms for each
prefix. These forms are as follows:

                           First Person        ndi-     nda-      ndoo-
                           Second Person       gdi-     gda-      gdoo-
                           Third Person        wdi-     wda-      wdoo-

    Because the extended person prefixes have the form of a complete METRICAL FOOT, and
to distinguish them from words in which the prefix extension is an integral part of the word,
they are sometimes written with a hyphen, as if they were prenouns, as in ndoo-mkizin, 'my
shoe.' They are also commonly used with borrowed words, where they are also usually sep-
arated from the stem with a hyphen as well, as in ndoo-contract, 'my contract.' Such usage
suggests that for some speakers these extended prefix forms are becoming the "default" or
200 • 4.9.2.1 Person Prefixes and Vowel-Initial Dependent Noun Stems


basic forms.

4.9.2.1 Person Prefixes and Vowel-Initial Dependent Noun Stems

    Person prefixes attached to DEPENDENT NOUNS do not insert a /d/ before long vowel-ini-
tial stems. All such stems begin with a long vowel, usually /ii/, but sometimes /oo/. Before
STEM-INITIAL /ii/, the form of the third person prefix is /w/, and before stems beginning with
/oo/, the third person prefix is absorbed completely, as it is in other dialects of Anishinaabe-
mowin. The following table provides examples of these vowel-initial dependent forms,
inflected for first, second, and third person possessors.

                            Inflection for Vowel-Initial Dependent Stems
       /ii/-Initial Stems
       'tooth'                -iibid         niibid         giibid         wiibid
       'brain'                -iindib        niindib        giindib        wiindib
       'body'                 -iiyaw         niiyaw         giiyaw         wiiyaw
       'brother'              -iijkwem       niijkiwem      giijkiwem      wiijkiweman
       'brother-in-law'       -iinim         niinim         giinim         wiinman
       'fellow...'            -iiji          niiji-         giiji-         wiiji-
       /oo/-Initial Stems
       'father'           -oos               noos           goos           oosan
       'grandmother'      -ookmis            nookmis        gookmis        ookmisan
       'grandchild'       -ooshenh           nooshenh       gooshenh       ooshenyan

    PREFIX REANALYSIS. From time to time, these vowel-initial dependent stems get REAN-
ALYZED, so that one or the other of the prefixed forms begins to serve as the basic stem
form. So, for example, some speakers say nwiibid for 'my tooth,' or nwiiji-Nishnaabe 'my
fellow Indian' (from a stem having the historical form /iiji-/), or ngookmis or nnookmis for
'my grandmother' (from historical /ookomis/) showing that any of the three person prefixes
may be absorbed into the basic stem, though perhaps absorption of the third person prefix is
a bit more common.
    Other forms with an incorporated third person prefix include niidgik, 'my sister (female
speaking),' also nwiidgik (W), niiyaw, 'my body,' also nwiiyaw (W), and niitaawis, 'my
cousin' (new system), also nwiitaawis (M).

4.9.3 Possessed Noun Theme Suffix

   Many nouns show an additional suffix in their possessed forms, having the form /-Vm/
with variable vowel, added directly after the noun stem. For example, the possessed form of
                                                       4.9.3 Possessed Noun Theme Suffix • 201



kik, 'kettle,' for some speakers is ndakkom. This complex of noun stem and possessive suf-
fix is sometimes called a POSSESSED THEME. There appears to be much variation among
speakers and dialects as to which words take this possessive suffix. I have indicated its
optional status in the tables above by putting it in parentheses, as (im). The quality of the
vowel associated with this suffix varies, depending on the class of the noun it is attached to,
according to the following specifications.


                                   Possessed Theme Suffix
                  I         II       III      IV        V           VI
                  -rm       -m       -VLm     -om       -iim        -aam

   The superscript L in the Class III suffix indicates that stem-final /w/ is deleted and the
final (short) vowel lengthened.
    Some examples of nouns with this possessive suffix follow, using first person singular
possessor forms ('my...'):

                                                 'my...'
                   bneshiinh     'bird'          nbineshiim
                   zhiishiib     'duck'          nzhiishiibim
                   kwe           'woman'         ndikwem, ndakwem
                   nini          'man'           ndinniim, ndanniim
                   bzhiki        'cow'           nbizhkiim, nbazhkiim
                   mskwi         'blood'         nmiskwiim
                   oodena        'town'          ndoodenaam
                   kik           'kettle, pot'   ndakkom
                   pin           'potato'        ndoopniim

   As mentioned already, there is considerable variation as to which noun stems take the
possessive suffix. Rhodes 1985 occasionally lists variable forms for words, such as the
words meaning 'my dad,' which may be either nbaabaa and nbaabaam, and 'my mother,'
which may be either nmamaanh or nmaamaam, varying by community. In other cases, both
forms are listed, such as for kik, 'kettle, pot,' where both ndakik and ndakkom are given. In
other cases, a single form is given, such as ndaagam, 'my snowshoe,' and ngiboosnenh, 'my
trousers' (W), which lack the possessive suffix, and nmitgom, 'my piece of wood,' which
has it. Some variation is evidently at the community level, such as njiibay, 'my corpse,' at
CL, versus njiibaam, 'my soul, spirit, ghost,' for general southern Ojibwe. In this case, the
general pattern treats this word as belonging to Class VI, while at CL, it is a regular Class I
noun. Note that both groups have a locative, jiibying, which lacks the augment of Class VI
202 • 4.9.3.1 Suppletive Possessive Themes


nouns, again treating it as a Class I noun. In general, Nishnaabemwin probably follows or
followed other varieties of Anishinaabemowin, where the suffix tends to be used less after
stems that end in /n/ or /m/. For example, Bloomfield (1958:41) noted that for Andrew
Medler (of Walpole Island) nouns that end in /n/ or /m/ tended not to take the possessor suf-
fix, and provides a list of other words which also did not take it, including kik, 'kettle,' nit,
'fish spear,' bwi, 'paddle,' semaa, 'tobacco,' gboosnenh, 'trousers,' mshkimod, 'bag,'
mtigwaab, 'bow,' and bkok, 'arrow,' as well as almost all dependent nouns. Bloomfield
notes two exceptions to this rule at Walpole Island, though, nmiignim, 'my feather' (from
noun stem miigon), and ndaknim, 'my bone' (from noun stem kan, 'bone'). Historically, the
stems most likely to take the possessive suffix are those that end in vowels, because the con-
sonant (/m/) of the possessive suffix provides a final consonant for the stem, facilitating the
attachment of other suffixes. All of these exceptional nouns appear to represent items of
great cultural antiquity, and close personal possession. A striking feature of such words in
Anishinaabemowin^ generally is how frequently they pattern together in their behaviour.
    In contemporary Nishnaabemwin the possessive theme suffix takes on especial impor-
tance as a marker of a noun having singular third person possessor, because, as we have
seen, SYNCOPE may otherwise delete all direct evidence that the noun is possessed, namely
the person prefix /o/, as injiimaan, which may mean either 'boat' or 'ANsg's boat,' because
the person prefix /o/ of the possessed form is always deleted by syncope. Elsewhere I have
suggested that such possessed forms can be spelled with STRUCTURAL-w, that is, with a «w»
in the place of the syncopated /o/, wjiimaan. This solution only works for written forms, of
course. One adjustment that contemporary speakers are making to the ambiguities caused
by syncope is to make much greater use of the possessive theme suffix, which shows the
noun to be possessed even if the person prefix is syncopated, as injiimaanim, 'ANsg's boat.'
Such usage is growing rapidly, as speakers seek to regularize a system set adrift by syncope.
    LEXICALIZED POSSESSIVE SUFFIXES. A few dependent nouns appear to have the posses-
sive suffix built into the basic word, such as nmishoomis, 'my grandfather,' and nookomis,
'my grandmother,' where in both cases there appears to be material added after the suffix. In
other dependent nouns, the suffix appears at the end, as in ngitziiuL 'my parent,' and
ndahiim, 'my possession.'

4.9.3.1 Suppletive Possessive Themes

   A very few nouns have SUPPLETIVE possessive themes, meaning that the basic noun stem
used in possessed forms is not the same as that used when the noun is used without a pos-
sessor. The most noteworthy are nday, 'my dog, my pet,' which is the possessed stem for
nimosh or nimookaajiinh (M), 'dog,' nniijaanis, 'my child,' which is for some speakers a
possessed form of bnoojiinh, 'child' (alongside ndabnoojiinh), and nnaabem, 'my hus-
band,' the possessed form of nini, 'man,' though in this case too, a non-suppletive form,
ndinniim, occurs as well. On Walpole Island, the form ndayhaam (NA) is used for 'my ani-
mal,' which literally means 'my animate possession,' whereas the independent words for
animal are wesiinh for small, usually wild, animals, and ookaan, for farm animals.
                                                                      4.9.4 Obviative Possessors • 203

4.9.5 Plural Possessor Suffixes

    There are only two distinct suffixes to indicate the plurality of the possessor, having the
following form:

                                      Plural Possessor Suffixes
                        -naan   first person plural possessor
                        -waa       non-first person plural possessor

   Vowels are added to consonant-final stems, prior to these suffixes, as follows:

                    Vowels Occurring Before Plural Possessor Suffixes
                 1              n        m            i v v                       vi
                    i           —       /i           o            ii             aa
                 1. Seem always to take possessive theme /-im/, so act like Class I forms.


   As with other suffixes, depending on the vowel configuration of the stem to which the
linking vowel is added, it may or may not actually be pronounced (and spelled). Here are
some examples showing forms with and without link vowels:

            LinkV        Stem                Possessed Form             Gloss
               i         /onaagan/           ndoonaagnmaanin            'our (excl.) dishes'
               i         /makizin/           nmakzinnaanin              'our (excl.) shoes'
               i         /makizin/           ndoo-mkizmnaanin           'our (excl.) shoes'
                o        /mitigw/            nmitgonaan                 'our (excl.) tree'
                o        /mitigw/            nmitgomnaan                'our (excl.) tree'

    Note, too, that the PLURAL and OBVIATIVE POSSESSUM suffixes have /i/ instead of /a/
after the first person plural possessor suffix, /-naan/. After the non-first person plural pos-
sessor suffix, /-waa/, the initial short vowel of the possessum suffixes is absorbed.

4.10 Noun Vocatives

   Traditionally Anishinaabemowin had special forms for direct address, called VOCA-
TIVES, and some of these survive in modern Nishnaabemwin. Vocatives seem to frequently
involve a shortening of a TERM OF REFERENCE, often by deleting the last syllable or the last
consonant. Rhodes lists several of vocatives in the dictionary, exemplified by the following:
206 • 4.11 Noun Preterits



                                          Term of Reference      Vocative Singular
         'my brother'                     niijkiwem              niijkiwenh!
         'my grandfather'                 nmishoomis             nmishoo!
         'my grandmother'                 nookmis                nookoo!
         'my grandmother' (W)             ngookmis               ngookoo !
         'my father'                      noos                   noose!
         'my grandchild'                  nooshenh               noosiz!
         'my dad' (CL)                    ndedem                 ndede!
         'my mother' (CL)                 ndoodoom               ndoodoo!
         'chick' (of chickens, turkeys)   biidiins               biidii !

    VOCATIVE PLURALS. The vocative plural form is used in contexts of formal address. It is
formed by addition of the suffix /-/dog/ (or -/dig), resembling the DUBITATIVE suffix used on
verbs in the independent order to express uncertainty, as in wiisnidig, 'perhaps ANsg's eat-
ing.' As an example of vocative plurals, Andrew Medler used the following forms in a play-
fully formal speech detailing plans for an upcoming fair to be held on Walpole Island:

   (20) Mandaagkwedog gye mandaagninwidog! I 'Ladies and Gentlemen!' (AM 11.1)
          Mandaagkwedogna voc 2p 'ladies'; gye av 'and'; mandaagninwidogna voc 2p
          'gentlemen.'


    Based on these forms, it appears that vocative plurals pattern in the same way as pejora-
tives with respect to noun classes, that is, according to the following patterns:

                     I        II     III          IV            V
                    -/dog     -dog   -w/dog       -odog         -iidog
                    -/dig     -dig   -w/dig       -odig         -iidig

varies by noun class, as follows:

4.12 Noun Preterit Dubitatives

    Historically, PRETERIT DUBITATIVE forms for nouns also existed. These forms were used,
 according to Baraga (1850:71), in 'terms denoting relationship when they speak of
 deceased persons whom they never saw' (emphasis in original). Baraga suggests that the
 formation of such forms is on the basis of the following: The invariable rule for the
formation of the traditional in this imperfect tense is, to put the syllable go before the letter
 b in the terminations of the imperfect tense. The forms Baraga cites are as follows:

                 Preterits and Preterit Dubitatives of Nouns in Baraga 1850:71

 nossiban                'my deceased      nossigoban                   'my deceased father
                         father' .                                      whom I never saw'
 kokomissinaban          'our deceased     kokomissinagoban             'our deceased
                         grandmother'                                   grandmother whom we
                                                                        never saw'
 nind                    'our deceased     nind ogimaminagoban          'our deceased chief
 ogimaminaban            chief                                          whom we never saw'

   These forms are evidently not used today, though they certainly were used in the past,
and are found in other dialects of Anishinaabemowin. I include them here in the interests of
thoroughness, and in the possibility that they are still used somewhere, or that historical
materials which use them may become available.

4.14 Participles

    Participles are verbs used in the function of nouns. They can be of any verbal subclass,
including VAI, VAIO, VII, VTA, or VTI, and show full inflection for every verbal inflectional
category except the iterative. Participles are often used in Nishnaabemwin to express nomi-
nal concepts, that is, to identify people and things on the basis of their behaviour or of some
quality they have. In many cases, participles have become lexicalized, that is, have taken on
a particular meaning, and represent the primary way of expressing a nominal concept. This
is especially true of items of technology, and of roles played by humans. Some examples:
baatewaagmiseg, 'beer' ni (plural, baatewaagmisegin), endzhi-mzinaatesjigeng, 'movie
theater' ni (plural, endzhi-mzinaatesjigengin), and debaabndang, 'plate umpire,' na (plural:
debaabndangig).

Animate Intransitive Verb Inflection




5.1 Introduction

    In this chapter we will examine the inflection of ANIMATE INTRANSITIVE (VAI) verbs.
Nishnaabemwin has a rich variety of such verbs, including verbs of action, motion, aspect,
state, quality, quantity, making, possession, and being, among many others. The following
verbs are illustrative of these different notional categories.

                      boodwe              'make (a) fire'
                      dkaji               'catch a cold'
                      biindnakse          'fall into a hollow tree'
                      oodetoo             'go to town'
                      bgonegahge          'chop a hole [in a tree]'
                      mshkikiiwniniiwi    'be a doctor'
                      nshkaadzi           'be angry'
                      webtaa              'begin'
                      giizhtaa            'finish'
                      gaachiinyi          'be small'
                      koozi               'be such a height'
                      waagaakdaatgoke     'make axehandles'
                      dkonkeshkoozo       'be caught by the arm'
                      niizhootwage        'have two ears'
                      yaa                 'be (in a place)'
                      wdabhagiiswaani     'use (Y) as a clock'
                      naabndam            'have a vision'
214 • 5.2 Different Ways of Assessing Transitivity



5.2 Different Ways of Assessing Transitivity

    In order to understand the morphological and syntactic classification of animate intransi-
tive (VAI) verbs, we must distinguish between the derivational and inflectional morphologi-
cal traits of a verb.1 Addressing derivational morphology first, we observe that most
Nishnaabemwin verb stems have a FINAL element, a basic component of the word stem,
which determines the verb's class and subclass, as suggested by the following forms.

                 Stem                  Gloss                               Final          Class
                 daadbood-oo=          'saw IN and separate it'            -bood          VTI
                 daadbooN=             'saw AN and separate it             -booN          VTA
                 mnwend-am=            'enjoy IN'                          -end-am        VTI
                 mnwenim=              'enjoy AN'                          -enim          VTA
                 bmaashi               'sail by'                           -aashi         VAI
                 bmaasin               'sail by'                           -aasin         VII
                 mnogi                 'grow well'                          -(i)gi        VAI
                 mnogin                'grow well'                          -(i)gin       VII

    Thus, one can often determine from a stem's derivational structure what sub-class of
verbs it belongs to. For example, any verb stem that has a stem ending in /bood-oo/ is tran-
sitive inanimate (VTI), and corresponds to a transitive animate (VTA) verb stem ending in
/-booN/, and a corresponding detransitive animate intransitive (VAI) ending in /-booj-ige/;
any verb that ends in /-aashi/ is an animate intransitive (VAI), and has a corresponding inan-
imate intransitive verb (vn) in /-aasin/, and so on. So one means of classifying a verb is on
the basis of its derivational structure, that is, on the basis of what final it has.
    Verbs also differ in their inflectional behaviour, in two distinct ways. First, transitive
verbs have a suffix not found on intransitive verbs, called a THEME SUFFIX. For example, the
transitive animate verb form nwaabmaag, 'I see ANpl,' has the theme suffix /-aa/, and the
transitive inanimate verb waabndmaan, 'that/if I see IN,' has the theme suffix /-am/. Theme
suffixes function to specify role relations between actors and goals, in other words, they are
                                                                       0
present when the verb has more than one semantic role to assign. The presence of a theme
suffix is thus a morphological indicator that a verb is transitive, and since there are distinct
theme suffixes for VTA and VTI verbs, we can also easily classify a verb on the basis of the
theme suffix it has.
    A second aspect of inflection concerns the form of inflectional suffixes denoting gram-
matical properties of actors and goals, such as their features of person, number, and obvia-
tion. These suffixes differ somewhat for transitive and intransitive verbs. A small sampling

                                                          5.2 Different Ways of Assessing Transitivity • 215



of such inflectional differences is illustrated in the following table.

      Form                          Class     Gloss                             Plural Actor Suffix
      nwaabmaanaanig                VTA       'we (excl.) see them (an.)'       -naan
      ndoo-nakiimin                 VAI       'we (excl.) are working'          -min
      gwaabmaawaag                  VTA       'you (pi.) see them (anim.)'      -waa
      gwaabndaanaawaan              VTI       'you (pi.) see them (inan.)'      -naawaa
      gboozim                       VAI       'you (pi.) get on board'          -m

    The suffixes marking first person plural are usually different for transitive (VTA) and
intransitive (VAI) verbs, /-naany/ for transitive and /-min/ for intransitive; the suffixes for
second person plural are also different, /-naawaa/ or /-waa/ for transitive verbs and /-m/ for
intransitive. Each subclass of verbs (VTA, VTI, VAI, VII) has specific prefix and suffix combi-
nations associated with it, so we can say, for example, that a given combination shows ani-
mate intransitive patterns, perhaps by having independent order plural suffixes /-mi(n)/ and
/-m/. Because of this, we can often easily classify verbs on the basis of their inflection.
    Several linguistic studies of Ojibwe verbs have observed that VTI verbs share many
inflectional features with VAl's, for example, conjunct inflection is almost identical for the
two types, and in the independent order, VTl's inflect very similarly to VAIO verbs, though,
of course, they cannot be inflected for animate goals. Furthermore, one can argue that VTI
theme signs are actually VAI finals, since there are occasional VAI verbs that end appear to
end in FINALS /-am/ and /-oo/, e.g., boonam, 'lay an egg,' and verbs of running, such as
bmibtoo, 'run along.' Indisputably, there is a large class of PSEUDO-INTRANSITIVES (see
below, section 5.12, Pseudo-Intransitive Verbs, beginning on page 248) verbs which end in
VTll theme /-am/, but are inflected as intransitives, even in the independent order, e.g.,
mnwendam, 'be content, be glad.' And there are derivational VAl's that can take goals, the
VAIO verbs. Observations such as these has led Glyne Piggott (see esp. Piggott 1979, 1989)
to assert that all VTl's are intransitive verbs derived from corresponding VTA's. 1 However
one is to analyze the transitivity of VTl's, it is clear that VTA'S more consistently mark goal
arguments than do VTI'S, and are thus inflectionally "more" transitive than VTI'S. And there
is obvious derivational gradation between VTI'S and VAl's. This type of behaviour makes
sense semantically, since inanimates are inherently much more likely to function as patients
(goals), and there is thus less need to explicitly index them as goals. Animates, however,
tend to fill semantic roles associated with the actor macrorole, and so their occurrence as
goals is more "marked," and linguistically, is more likely to be explicitly indexed inflection-
ally. Also, there is a general tendency across languages to downplay the details of less
important participants, such as inanimates.
    A verb may also be classified as transitive or intransitive on the basis of its syntactic
behaviour, that is, whether or not a noun (phrase) or pronoun representing a goal can appear

1. These notes are distillations of the exposition in O'Meara 1990.
216 • 5.2 Different Ways of Assessing Transitivity


with it in its clause (minimal sentence). For example, the following sentences clearly have
verbs with both actors and goals, since both are present in the clauses containing the verbs:

   (1)    Wshki-nbagsagoon wminpawaawaan giw gaagog.
          'The porcupines like to eat new lumber.' (AK1.9)

          Wshki-nbagsagoon na 3obv 'new lumber'; wminpawaawaan vta ind3pProx»3obv
          'ANpl like the taste of ANobv'; giwrpr 3pProx 'those'; gaagog na SpProx 'porcupines.'

   (2)    Wjiigdahaan iw wtigwaam aw kwe.
          "That woman is sweeping out that house.' (AM39.398)

          Wjiigdahaan vti ind3sProx»Os 'ANsg sweeps out INsg'; iwprOs 'that'; wiigwaam ni Os
          'house'; aw/?r SsProx 'that'; kwe na 3sProx 'woman.'

    In the first example, the verb wminpawaawaan, 'ANpl like the taste of ANobv,' has an
actor role filled by giw gaagog, 'those porcupines,' and a goal role filled by
wshki-nbagsagoon, 'new lumber'; in the second example, the verb Wjiigdahaan, 'ANsg
sweeps INsg out,' has an actor role filled by aw kwe, 'that woman,' and a goal role filled by
iw wiigwaam, 'that house.' In these cases, too, there is a clear alignment of the verbs' deri-
vational structures with their syntactic behaviour, since both of these verbs have transitive
finals. When we consider the following sentence, however, we find a somewhat different
alignment of morphology and syntax:

   (3)   Gii-bootaagewag giw kwewag niw mdaamnan iw wii-bkwezhgankewaad.
          'The women ground up the corn when they were going to make bread.' (AK2.4)

          Gii-bootaagewag vai indSpProx 'ANpl ground (Y)'; giwprSpProx 'those'; kwewag na
          3pProx 'women'; niwprSobv 'that/those'; mdaamnan na 3obv 'corn'; iwprOs 'that';
          wii-bkwezhgankewaad vai conj 3pProx '(CONJ) ANpl will make bread.'

    Here the verb bootaage, 'grind,' does not have a transitive final, nor does it have a theme
suffix, nor does it make any inflectional reference to a goal, and yet, syntactically, there is an
explicitly stated goal, niw mdaamnan, 'that corn (obv.),' in the sentence— the corn is rather
obviously the object that the women are grinding. So in this case, the verb is derivationally
and inflectionally intransitive, but syntactically it is transitive. Now, of some interest is the
fact that many speakers of Nishnaabemwin add inflections for the properties of goals to
verbs of this sort, which Rhodes (1985) labels as VAIO'S. For example, instead of
gii-bootaagewag, in (3) above, many Nishnaabemwin speakers would have
wgii-bootaagenaawaan as the inflected form of this verb. Rhodes (1991) distinguishes these
                                                 5.2 Different Ways of Assessing Transitivity • 217



VAIO goals from goals associated with VTA and VTI verbs on the basis of their inflectional
behaviour, designating the latter as PRIMARY OBJECTS and the goals of VAIO'S as SECOND-
ARY OBJECTS. The goals of VAIO'S pattern identically to the secondary objects of DITRANSI-
TIVE verbs, according to Rhodes.
    If we consider the second half of sentence (3), we arrive at one more way to think about
transitivity. Notice that the English translation of this sentence has two explicitly transitive
constructions linked together, first grind up the corn, and second, make bread. In the
English translation, the concept of 'bread' is expressed by a separate noun, which functions
as a direct object. In Nishnaabemwin, however, this concept is expressed by the noun for
bread, bkwezhgan, appearing inside of the verb. The verb has a vAl derivational FINAL, /-ke/,
has inflectional marking indicating that it is intransitive, and there is no separate, free-stand-
ing noun to suggest that the verb is syntactically transitive. Yet in terms of its meaning, that
is, semantically, the verb seems transitive, but appears to have its goal incorporated within
the verb itself. There are many verbs in Nishnaabemwin which show this type of alignment,
in which something like a goal appears inside the verb, but the verb is treated grammatically
as an intransitive. For example, by far the most common way to talk about the anatomy of
living things is with verbs of the following sort:

                         zaawzide             'have brown feet'
                         niizhootwage         'have two ears'
                         waawyemoowe          'have round droppings'

     These verbs are all intransitive in terms of their derivational and inflectional properties.
 They do not take explicit syntactic goals, either. But semantically, they appear somewhat
 transitive, though not quite in the same way that more prototypical transitive verbs such as
 nshi, 'kill AN' do. For example, we can paraphrase the first two verbs above in English with
 phrases such as 'be brown-footed' and 'be two-eared,' that is, with expressions that in
 English, at least, are decidedly syntactically intransitive. We cannot, however, do this with
 the last example, since *be round-droppinged does not work in English. And we can note as
 well that the English equivalents of these Nishnaabemwin concepts are also less transitive
 than other verbs in that the English verbs cannot be PASSIVIZED, as in, for example, *Brown
feet are had by this dog, or *Two ears are had by this rabbit. But the point of this discussion
 is that languages certainly have categories such as transitive and intransitive which are very
 useful in understanding their grammatical behaviour, but different kinds of tests, such as
 inflectional, derivational, syntactic, and semantic, will not always produce results that are in
 complete agreement with each other, and often we must apply many tests to tease out the
 properties of words and expressions. For this reason, care must be taken when making state-
 ments about concepts such as transitivity. See 3.4.1, Transitivity and Animacy, beginning on
page 130, for additional discussion.
218 • 5.3 VAI Subclasses


5.3 VAI Subclasses

    This brief presentation of a verb's identity and transitivity in terms of its derivational,
inflectional, syntactic and semantic traits serves as a prelude to the introduction of animate
intransitive (VAI) verbs. There are three main sub-classes of VAI verbs, based on their mor-
phological and syntactic properties:
    (1) Regular animate intransitives (VAI), representing by far the largest class, which are
derivationally and inflectionally intransitive, for example, boodwe, 'make fire,' niimi,
'dance,' and dgoshin, 'arrive.'
    (2) Optional 'object' (goal) animate intransitive verbs (VAIO), that is, those which can be
inflected for third person goals in the independent order and in participles and thus, while
intransitive in their basic stem-derivational form, nonetheless can have certain inflections
that are transitive. Examples: daawe, 'sell Y,' and aakzi, 'have a pain in Y [some part of the
body].' VAIO verbs differ from VTA and VTI verbs, however, in that they do not have theme
suffixes, and in their capacity to have goals of either gender, animate or inanimate, while
VTA and VTI verbs require goals of the specific, appropriate gender. VAIO verbs also differ
from VTA verbs in that they allow only third person goals (but note that they resemble VTI'S
in this regard).
    (3) PSEUDO-INTRANSITIVE (PS-VAI) verbs, which end with a stem element that resembles
the theme sign /-am/ of some transitive inanimate (VTI) verbs. Examples: mnwendam, 'be
glad,' and debwetam, 'believe [what one has heard].' Other than this feature of having an
element resembling a VTI theme-suffix, these verbs are inflectionally intransitive, though
some of them can take clausal complements (see Chapter 13.3, beginning on page 665).
They are chiefly like VTI in the behaviour of their terminal element, /-am/, which behaves
phonologically similarly to the VTI theme. Additional notes on these verbs can be found in
Chapter 8.2, Pseudo-Intransitive (Objectless TI) Verbs, beginning on page 309.
    The following table lays out the derivational and inflectional behaviour of the three dif-
ferent subtypes of VAI verbs.

                                                 Derivation   Inflection
                Regular VAI           VAI        VAI          intransitive
                VAI with Object       VAIO       VAI          transitive
                                                              intransitive
                Pseudo-Intransitive PS-VAI       VTI-like     intransitive

    INHERENTLY PLURAL (VAIP) VERBS. Rhodes 1985 lists a few VAI verbs, labeled VAIP,
as obligatorily plural, for example, niizhwewaan'gizwaad, 'be in two sets, be two families'
and niizhoobhidwaad, 'be a group of two running together.' All that distinguishes these
verbs is that they have meanings that are inherently plural. They do not represent a struc-
tural sub-class.
                                         5.4 Regular Animate Intransitive Verb (VAI) Inflection • 219



5.4 Regular Animate Intransitive Verb (VAI) Inflection

    The basic person, number and obviation categories for VAI verbs are coded as Is, 2s, 3s,
3', Ip, 21, 2p, 3p, and X, representing nine distinct inflectional possibilities for each VAI
category. These categories are outlined as follows.

                   Is      first person singular
                   2s      second person singular
                   3s      animate third person singular, proximate
                   3'      animate third person obviative
                   X       unspecified actor (general activity)
                   IP      first person plural exclusive
                   21      first person plural inclusive
                   2p      second person plural
                   3p      animate third person plural, proximate
                  1. Some analysts designate animate obviatives as fourth person, so 4
                  might also be used to designate them.


    Given these categories we can compute, in rough terms, the number of inflections for a
typical VAI verb. For the INDEPENDENT and CONJUNCT ORDERS, there are theoretically nine
person/number/obviation categories, four MODES (and ITERATIVES in the conjunct), two
POLARITIES, three TENSES, and two functions (VERBAL and PARTICIPIAL in the conjunct),
creating 882 inflectional combinations. For the IMPERATIVE ORDER, there are three per-
son/number combinations, and three modes, creating theoretically nine inflectional combi-
nations, making a total of roughly 890 forms for the animate intransitive verb. Of course,
the number of inflections will increase dramatically if we consider DIRECTIONAL, RELATIVE,
and MODAL PREVERBS to represent inflectional elements, and if we consider CHANGED CON-
JUNCT forms as inflectionally distinct from PLAIN CONJUNCTS.
    Although there is a great number of inflectional combinations, the prefixes and suffixes
used to signal these grammatical combinations, and the patterns of prefix and suffix struc-
turing, are quite limited. In the following sections we will examine the constituency and
structuring of the three inflectional orders.

5.4.1 VAI Independent, Conjunct, and Imperative Templates

    An examination of general patterns in the inflected forms of regular animate intransitive
verbs shows, as we expect, that there is much structure to the inflectional system. In the fol-
lowing sections, I present the basic inflectional templates of regular VAI verbs in the three
inflectional orders, independent, conjunct, and imperative.
    INDEPENDENT ORDER TEMPLATE. The following table lays out the basic template and

    There is only one prefix slot, for first and second person prefixes. Immediately after the
stem is a slot for the negative suffix, followed by a slot for either first and second person
plural suffixes, or a third person suffix, which we have designated as /-w/. Although it is a
suffix, this /-w/ functions similarly to the first and second person prefixes. An UNSPECIFIED
(GENERALIZED) ACTOR suffix /-m/ also occurs in this slot. The next slot contains suffixes for
three marked MODES, PRETERIT, DUBITATIVE and PRETERIT DUBITATIVE, here without any

sitive forms, they share a common template, and that the fillers of each template slot are
quite limited in number.
    The morphemes within a given suffix slot sometimes interact with those in the following
slot, producing variant forms, or they may show variation on the basis of the particular per-
son category that the verb is inflected for. For example, the markers for preterit and dubita-
tive are /-naabany/1 and /-naadigw/, respectively, for all first and second person singular
independent order forms, and /-aabany/ and /-aadigw/ for first and second person plural
forms; the form of the third person plurals and obviatives are /iig/ and /iin/, respectively,
after the preterit suffix /ban/, and /enag/ and /enan/ after the dubitative, /digw/, though these
suffixes may also be analyzed as redundantly specifying the dubitative by means of the ele-
ment /en/, since such an element shows up in conjunct dubitatives as well. General Anishi-
naabemowin inflection very often treats first and second persons differently from third
persons.

of that found in positive forms, /-waa-d/.

    IMPERATIVE ORDER TEMPLATE. The IMPERATIVE order has three MODES, an IMMEDI-
ATE, a DELAYED, and a PROHIBITIVE. The delayed, as its name suggests, is used with
deferred commands, such as bi-zhaakan, 'come over later!,' and thus corresponds notion-
ally to a future tense. Of the time delay associated with the delayed imperative, Mary Ann
Corbiere (p.c.) notes:

         The time delay can vary, as long as it's not immediate, maybe at least a
         day, but not necessarily. If someone calls in the morning and I have to
         dash off on an important errand, I might say, «Baamaa naagshik
         bi-gnoosh-shiikan», 'Don't call me until this evening.' Of course, it's a
         more typical usage to say, «Aasnaa aabdek bi-nbwaachwe-kan pii miin-
         waa bbaa-yaayin», 'Be sure to visit next time you're around/in town.'

   The imperative order is incompatible with past tense, and so there are no past tense
forms. The prohibitive is used to make negative commands, that is, commands to not do
something. Because commands are necessarily limited to second person actors, the number
of VAI imperative forms is much smaller than those for the independent and conjunct, but
the system is the least orderly of all, at least in its details. A basic template can be surmised,

in which a marker of mode or POLARITY follows the stem, followed by inflections which
simultaneously index both person and number, as with the conjunct. The first person plural
inclusive structures rather differently from the purely second person forms, in having a neg-
ative element /-sii/ in the prohibitive, added to the immediate form directly after the stem,
reminiscent of the negative of the independent order. The second person singular and plural
forms seem to more transparently involve a mode marker, /-ka/ for the delayed and /-ke/ for
the prohibitive, to which person/number suffixes are attached, though it is only the second
person singular that does so in a completely straightforward way.

    There are three PHONOLOGICALLY definable subtypes of regular VAI verbs, based on the

224 • 5.5.1 Long-Vowel Final VAI Verbs


5.5.1 Long-Vowel Final VAI Verbs

    VAI verbs with stems ending in long vowels are the most straightforward type in their
inflectional behaviour, and I will treat them as basic, at least for purposes of presentation.
By this I mean that paradigm charts will most often be of long-vowel final stems, and the
inflectional behaviour of the other two subclasses of regular VAI verbs will be noted only
when it differs from that of long-vowel final stems.

5.5.2 Short-Vowel Final VAI Verbs

    The final short vowel of these stems does not appear in the first and second person singu-
lar forms of the independent order, positive polarity, that is, when no suffix follows, as can
be seen from the following examples:

                             biibaagi 'shout'   wiidookaazo 'be helpful'
                      Is     nbiibaag_          nwiidookaaz_
                      2s     gbiibaag_          gwiidookaaz_
                      3s     biibaagi           wiidookaazo

    The vowel in question is deleted by a phonological rule. We have already seen one pho-
nological rule of vowel deletion, having to do with the deletion of unstressed vowels, which
we call syncope. Syncope, however, never applies to the last short vowel of a word. The
deletion of the final vowels shown in the forms above is thus not due to syncope. Rather,
this deletion reflects a much older rule than syncope, one that is found in all dialects of
Anishinaabemowin, including those which lack the rule of syncope. I will call this rule, for
now, FINAL SHORT-VOWEL AND GLIDE DELETION to distinguish it from syncope. It applies to
glides as well as short vowels. The rule can be provisionally stated in simple terms as fol-
lows.

                           Final Short-Vowel and Glide Deletion
                           Final short vowel and glides are deleted.

   Final short-vowel deletion precedes syncope, which acts upon its output.
   One question that arises is why final short vowel deletion applies in first and second per-
son singular forms, but not in the third person singular form, since all three appear to end
with a short vowel. This question can be answered straightforwardly if we adopt a some-
what abstract analysis. Consider the following forms of the verb wiisni, 'eat.'
                                                           5.5.2 Short-Vowel Final VAI Verbs • 225



                                wiisni          'ANsg eats'
                                wiisnivrag      'ANpl eat'
                                wiisniwan       'ANobv eat(s)'

    The plural form appears to have a suffix sequence /-wag/ and the obviative form a suffix
/-wan/. These suffixes look rather similar to the plural and obviative endings found on
nouns, for example, waagshag, 'foxes,' and waagshan, 'fox(es) (obv.).' If we analyze /-ag/
as an animate plural suffix and /-an/ as the animate obviative suffix, we are still left with the
/w/ of the verb suffixes to deal with. This /-w/ has been analyzed as representing a third per-
son suffix, functioning rather similarly to the first and second person prefixes, /ni-/ and /gi-/.
To this suffix are added the suffixes of the plural /-ag/, and the obviative /-an/. In the case of
the proximate singular, though, no plural or obviative suffix is added, but the third person
suffix /-w/, is present. As mentioned previously, the rule deleting final short vowels of the
first and second person singular forms applies to glides (/w/ and /y/) as well, and it thus
deletes the third person suffix when it is the last segment in the word. The diagram on the
following page illustrates the operation of this rule in a second person singular form and a
third person singular. Given these structures, it becomes clear why the short vowel is
deleted in the first and second person singular forms, but not the third person singular— in
the latter there is a suffix /-w/, which is deleted by the Vowel/Glide deletion rule, but which
protects the final short vowel from deletion; in the case of the first and second person singu-
lars, the short vowels are not protected by any suffix, and so are subject to deletion. The rea-
son that /w/ shows up in the third person plural and obviative forms is that the suffixes
which follow the /w/, /-ag/, animate plural and /-an/, animate obviative, protect it from dele-
tion, since deletion only applies to short vowels and glides that are final in a word.

   Basic Form, 'dance'                                        n     ii     m      i


   'you (sg.) dance'                                 gi+      n     ii     m      i


   Final Short Vowel/Glide Deletion                  gi       n     ii     m      _


   'ANsg dances'                                              n     ii     m      i       +w


   Final Short Vowel/Glide Deletion                           n     ii     m      i      _
226 • 5.5.3 Nasal-Final VAI Stems


    Once one recognizes the presence of a rule of final short vowel/glide deletion, many
aspects of morphology become more transparent in their workings. For example, we can use
this rule to explain the variation between the singular and plural forms of such nouns as
mm, 'man' (plural, ninwag) and kwe, 'woman,' (plural kwewag), by suggesting that the
basic stems of these words are /niniw/ and /kwew/, respectively, and that their final /w/'s are
deleted by rule in their proximate singular forms. In the plurals and obviatives, however, the
final /w/ of the noun stem is protected from deletion by the presence of a suffix.
    We can also appeal to the structures outlined above to explain the form of a nasal-final
animate intransitive stem (discussed in the next section) inflected for third person plural or
obviative, as in, dgoshnoog, 'ANpl are arriving' and dgoshnoon, 'ANobv is/are arriving.'
Why do these words have suffixes with /oo/? The answer is that the /oo/ arises from COA-
LESCENCE of the third person suffix /-w/, with the short vowels of the /-ag/ plural and /-an/
obviative suffixes, as in the following diagram:




    The glide /w/, recall, involves lip-rounding, which we indicate with a phonological fea-
ture, [+round]. Between an /n/ and the /g/ of the plural suffix or the /n/ of the obviative suf-
fix (i.e., when /w/ follows a consonant), it spreads its feature [+round] onto the adjacent
vowel, /a/, making it [+round] as well. The vowel is effectively changed from an /a/ (which
is [-round]) to an /o/ (which is [+round]). At the same time, the /w/ itself is absorbed into the
vowel, creating a vowel two segments long, /w+a/, in other words, a long vowel. So the pro-
nunciation becomes dgoshnoog, with a long vowel in the last syllable. In order to assert
such an explanation of these forms, though, we must hypothesize the existence of a /w/ after
the verb stem /dgoshin/, which is readily available if we recognize the presence of a third
person suffix, /-w/.

5.5.3 Nasal-Final VAI Stems

    Nasal-final verbs, that is, those with stems ending in /n/ and /m/, represent the only regu-
lar animate intransitive verbs that end in consonants. This group includes the
PSEUDO-INTRANSITIVES, such as minwendam, 'be glad, be content.' When suffixes are
attached, stems ending in nasals behave differently than vowel-final verbs in several distinct
ways. Some of the more important and systematic differences are outlined here.
    1. Nasal-final stems often show a LINK VOWEL, varying by dialect and individual speaker
as either /a/, /i/, or /o/, before suffixes that begin with nasal consonants. Compare boodwen,
'make a fire!' versus dgoshnin, 'arrive!,' and nboodwemin, 'we (excl.) are building a fire,'
versus ndagoshnamin, 'we (excl.) are arriving.'
    2. Vowel-initial suffixes of the conjunct order show a glide /y/ before vowel-final stems,
but not nasal-final stems. So, for example, boodweyaanh, 'if/when I build a fire,' but
                                                                5.6 Notes on Mode Suffixes • 227



dgoshnaanh, 'if/when I leave.' Often this glide consonant is only very weakly articulated in
contemporary speech.
     3. Nasal-final stems attach the negative suffix directly to the stem, with no link vowel,
and the initial /s/ of the negative suffix lenites (softens, weakens) to its voiced correspon-
dent, /z/. So, for example, while the negative of boodwe, 'ANsg builds a fire,' is boodwesii,
it is dgoshin&i for dgoshin, 'ANsg arrives.'
     4. As mentioned previously, the morphological suffix complexes /w+ag/, and /w+an/ of
the independent order, neutral mode, animate third person plural and obviative, respectively,
coalesce to /oog/ and /oon/ with nasal-final stems. Compare boodwewag, 'they are making a
fire' and boodwewan wgwisan, 'ANsg's son is making a fire,' versus dgoshnoog. 'they are
arriving' and dgoshnoon wgwisan, 'ANsg's son is arriving.'
     5. The form of the conjunct order third person suffix is /g/ when added directly to
nasal-final stems, but /d/ in all other inflections except certain conjunct negatives. Compare
boodwed, 'if/when ANsg builds a fire,' versus dgoshing, 'if/when ANsg arrives,' but
dgoshninid, 'if/when ANsg (obv.) arrives,' which has third person suffix /d/, because of the
obviative suffix intervening between the stem and the person marker.
     The cumulative effect of the differences outlined here results in nasal-final paradigms
that are different enough from vowel-final to justify the explicit listing of nasal-final stem
inflectional forms alongside vowel-final paradigms, which I have done in the paradigm
tables below.

5.6 Notes on Mode Suffixes

    The following notes address some of the morphological adjustments that occur with var-
ious MODE suffixes in all animate intransitive verb types.
    1. The nominal suffixes (plural and obviative) have the forms /-iig/ and /-iin/ directly
after the preterit, e.g., maajaabniig, 'they had left,' and maajaabniin oosan, 'ANsg's father
(obv.) had left.' These forms are often analyzed as representing a coalescence of the vowel
of the suffix with a final glide on the preterit, which is argued to have the form /-bany/. The
presence of /ii/ in the nominal suffixes is then due to a process identical to that which pro-
duces these variants in words such as sab, 'net,' (with stem /(a)saby/), which has plural
sabiig. In some dialects of Anishinaabemowin, the preterit mode forms for animate plurals
and animate obviatives are /baneg/ and /banen/, respectively, which can be analyzed vari-
ously. Such forms may also be used by some speakers of Nishnaabemwin.
    2. The preterit suffix /-bany/ attaches directly to stems ending in the third person con-
junct suffix /-d/, and the combination of/d+b/ produces a [p], spelled «p». Compare
ngamyamban, '(if/when) you (sg.) had sung,' (from VAI verb stem ngamo, 'sing') versus
ngampan, '(if/when) ANsg had sung' (/nagamo+d+bany/) and ngamwaapan, '(that) ANpl
had sung' (/nagamo+waa+d+bany/).
    3. The form of the preterit suffix /-bany/ is /-baan(h)/ after the first person singular con-
junct suffix, and the final /n/ of /-aan/ changes to /m/, for example, ngamoyaambaanh, 'if I
had sung' (/nagamo+aan+bany/)
228 • 5.7 Syncope and the Presentation of Paradigms


    4. The preterit and dubitative suffixes have extended forms with /naa/ in the first and sec-
ond person independent order inflections, for example, ndaakzinaaba(n), 'I had been sick'
(aakzi, 'be sick') versus aakziban, 'ANsg had been sick,' and ndaakzinaadig, 'I must be
sick,' versus preterit aakzidig, 'ANsg must be sick.' A corresponding extension /aa/ occurs
with first and second person plural inflections, for example, ndaakzimnaadig, 'we (excl.)
must be sick.'
   NON-THIRD PERSON INDEPENDENT PRETERIT DUBITATIVES. Many speakers do not use
the historical independent order preterit dubitative forms for non-third person subjects, but
instead use the equivalent conjunct forms in their place. I have indicated such forms in the
independent order paradigm with the parenthetic note "(shift to conjunct)".

5.7 Syncope and the Presentation of Paradigms

    The person/number/obviation codes introduced above (p. 219) and in Chapter 3 (pp.
122-123), and also listed in the table of abbreviations at the front of the grammar) are used
throughout the paradigm tables of verbs presented below. For each inflectional category, an
inflected word form is given, along with a separate specification of the prefixes and suffixes
for that form, for both vowel-final and nasal-final stems.
    SYNCOPE AND INFLECTION. Syncope presents a problem in the presentation of inflec-
tional tables, because many suffix complexes contain short vowels which are variably
present depending on the phonological composition of the stem. For example, the following
two forms are both third person singular, positive, independent order, preterit mode:

   gtimwiba 'ANsg used to be lazy'        I zegziba    'ANsg used to be afraid'

   The stem forms of the verbs are /gitimi/ and /zegizi/, respectively, both of which are
short-vowel final stems, and are inflected for identical categories above (proximate third
person singular preterit positive, independent order). The suffix complexes for the two
forms are quite different, though, /wiba/ in the first example, and /ba/ in the second. This
discrepancy is not morphological, but partly phonological, due to syncope and the effects
that follow from it. The following diagrams show the phonological derivations of these
words.
                                              5.7 Syncope and the Presentation of Paradigms • 229




    The presence or absence of HI in the pronounced forms of these two verbs is thus
explainable on the basis of syncope. An additional rule is needed, which I call Inflectional
W-Deletion. This rule deletes /w/ in the suffix complex whenever the vowel that follows it is
deleted by Syncope, leaving it in a pre-consonantal position. This rule applies only to /w/ in
third person inflections, and not to /w/'s that are a basic part of the word, as can be seen
from forms such as nboodewzi, 'ANsg is depressed, lonely' (from stem /niboodewizi/)
where /w/ is retained even though a vowel following it (/i/) has been syncopated. The rule
can be characterized as follows:

                                   Inflectional /-w/ Deletion
          The third person independent order suffix /-w/ is deleted when it is left
          adjacent to a consonant due to the syncopation of an intervening vowel.

   Given the variation that can occur in the form of suffixes due to syncope and related
rules, a practical problem arises in the specification of inflectional suffixes in paradigm
tables. My less than perfect solution is to provide a full specification of the suffixes, with all
short vowels represented, but to identify syncopating vowels with italics. All suffixal short
vowels not in final syllables will be so represented. This means that to build a pronounce-
able form from the inflectional paradigm tables, the suffix will have to be attached to the
basic form of the verb, and Syncope then applied. The alternative is to produce massive
tables of pronounced inflectional forms, which would still fail to show the basic nature of
230 • 5.8 Dialect Variation in Inflection


the underlying system. Another value of a fully specified system is that it proves handy for
students approaching oral and written materials from non-syncopating dialects of Anishi-
naabemowin, for which many written materials are available (for example, Kegg 1991 for
Minnesota Ojibwe, and Bloomfield/Nichols, eds., 1991, for the Odawa stories of Angeline
Williams).

5.8 Dialect Variation in Inflection

   Loss OF FINAL /N/ IN ODAWA. Some consonants show variable presence in inflections
because of dialect variation. A hallmark feature of the Odawa sub-dialect of Nishnaabem-
win is that it drops /n/ from a set of inflectional suffixes when they are word-final, including
/-min/ and /-naan/, both of which signal first person plural in the independent order; /-ban/,
associated with the preterit mode; /-ken/, which occurs with negative imperatives; and /-in/,
which signals the iterative. Note that the deleted /n/'s of these morphemes are present when
another suffix follows, as can be seen from the following Odawa examples:

  zegziba_       'ANsg used to be afraid'    zegzibniig        'they used to be afraid'
  nzegzimi_      'we (excl.) are afraid'     nzegzimnaaba      'we (excl.) used to be afraid'

    To avoid listing all of the relevant forms twice, once for Odawa and once for other
sub-dialects of Nishnaabemwin, I have elected to indicate these variable /n/'s in the inflec-
tional charts in italics. It must then be understood that italicized /n/ in the paradigms which
follow represents dialect variation, while italicized short vowels represent candidates for
syncope, giving rise to phonologically-induced variation in the form of suffixes shared by
all sub-dialects of Nishnaabemwin.
    INDEPENDENT DUBITATIVE /-DOG/ vs. /-DIG/. The form of the DUBITATIVE MODE suffix
in the independent order varies dialectally between /-dog/ and /-dig/, as in boodwedog,
'ANsg must be making a fire,' versus boodwedig. I have to chosen to use /-dig/ in the para-
digm tables.
    Example Paradigms. To illustrate paradigmatic patterns, in some cases I list example
paradigms of specific verbs, all of which were kindly and patiently provided by Mary Ann
Corbiere of Wikwemikong, Ontario. In such cases I do not list dialect variants, since the
forms cited are specifically those of Ms. Corbiere.

5.9 Additional Reading

  An excellent morphological analysis of the inflection of non-VTA verbs can be found in
Rogers 1975a. VTA verbs are treated in Rogers 1975b.

5.11 VAIO Verbs

    Some animate intransitive verbs can optionally take third person goals, animate or inani-
mate, and are inflected in the independent and imperative orders, and in certain participles,
to show nominal properties (gender sensitive NUMBER and DEVIATION) of their goals. These
verbs are identified as VAIO (VAI + object) verbs in Rhodes 1985.

5.12 Pseudo-Intransitive Verbs

    PSEUDO-INTRANSITIVE VAI VERBS have an element /am/, which corresponds structurally
to the /am/ THEME SUFFIX of Class I VTI verbs. However, pseudo-intransitive verbs do not
take NOMINAL GOALS, though they can have CLAUSAL COMPLEMENTS. Many of these verbs
have identical VTI equivalents, however, which are inflected for inanimate goals, for exam-
ple, corresponding to the PS-VAI verb debwetam, 'believe [what one has heard],' there is a
VTI verb debwetang, 'believe IN' The largest class of these Verbs refers to states of the
mind, or mental processes. The list below exemplifies some pseudo-intransitive verbs.
    INFLECTIONAL PROPERTIES OF PSEUDO-INTRANSITIVES. In the CONJUNCT and IMPERA-
TIVE ORDERS, pseudo-intransitives are inflected in the same way as VAI verbs. The inflec-
tional suffixes Used in the independent also align these verbs with VAi's, in that all plural
forms are intransitive (/-min/, first person, /-m(w)/, second person, and /-wag/, third person),
and there is no agreement with any goal. In the independent order, they often show two dis-
tinct inflectional patterns, depending on whether or not a LINK VOWEL, perhaps /a/ for most
contemporary speakers, is added to the stem prior to the attachment of suffixes in the posi-
tive forms. When suffixes beginning with a nasal (/n/ or /m/) are added directly to the stem,
with no link vowel, the final /m/ of the stem is deleted and the preceding /a/ is LENGTHENED,
as in ngichi-nendaami, 'we (excl.) are in good spirits' (from /nV-gichi-inendam-min/) just
as with transitive inanimate (VTI) verbs. However, if a link vowel is added, no deletion and
COMPENSATORY LENGTHENING occurs, as in ngichi-nendmami (from /nV-gichi-inen-
dam-a-min/). This pattern is the same as that of VAI verbs. Because the independent order
negative suffix complex always begins with an /s/, a link vowel is evidently not added.
    Pseudo-Intransitive verbs are not identified in any way in Rhodes 1985, being classed
simply as VAI verbs. The following is a representative list of such verbs.

Inanimate Intransitive Verb Inflection




6.1 Introduction

    Inanimate intransitive verbs (VII) are those verbs having a single semantic role, which
must be filled by a grammatically inanimate subject, or, in the case of impersonal verbs,
often do not have an overt subject associated with the verb, though the verb shows third per-
son (singular) inflection. VII verbs have only third person inflection, and thus, have no
imperative forms, since all imperatives require a second person actor. Nishnaabemwin has a
large number of impersonal verbs which indicate notions such as environmental features
and time expressions, including seasons and days of the week. VII verbs can be inflected for
all modes (indicative, preterit, dubitative, preterit dubitative), and for positive and negative
polarity, in both the independent and conjunct orders. They have participial and iterative
forms as well.
    VII verbs can be inflected to show obviation, even though the (inanimate) nouns associ-
ated with them do not, as in the following examples from Andrew Medler, from two tellings
of the same story, about a man who becomes ill while travelling in the north, and is subse-
quently cured by a sweatlodge treatment. These sentences both have an overt possessed
inanimate noun as subject of the second clause, in one case wdakjiwin, 'ANsg's cold,' and in
the other, wdaakziwin, 'ANsg's illness,' and in both the verb maajaamgad, 'leave, depart,'
occurs with these subjects, inflected in one instance in the independent order (1) and the
other in the conjunct (2), and in both cases, with obviative inflection.
252 • 6.2 Phonologically-Defined Inflectional Subclasses of VII Verbs


   (1)   Aapji dash gii-mno-bmaadzi, gye go kina gii-maajaamgadni wdakjiwin.

          'He felt very well and all his cold had gone away.' (AM 19.15)

          Aapji av 'really'; dash av 'then'; gii-mno-bmaadzi vai ind3sProx 'ANsg felt well'; gye
          av 'and'; kina av 'all'; gii-maajaamgadni vii ind Oobv 'INobvSg was gone'; wdakjiwin
          ni 3sProx(Os) 'ANSG's cold.'


   (2)   Gegzhebaawgak gii-wnishkaa, gye go mil iw gii-mno-bmaadzid,
         gii-maajaamgadnig wdaakziwin.
          'When morning came he got up, and now he felt well and his illness had gone!

          Gegzhebaawgak vii ic conj 0 '(CCNJ) when IN was morning'; gii-wnishkaa vai ind
          3sProx 'ANsg got up'; gye av 'and'; mii av 'and'; i\vpr Os 'that'; gii-mno-bmaadzid vai
          conj SsProx '(CONJ) ANsg felt well'; gii-maajaamgadnig vii conj Oobv '(CONJ) INobv
          left'; wdaakziwinni3sProx(Os) 'ANSG's illness.' (AM20.12)


   While number (singular versus plural) is neutralized in both the proximate and obviative
forms of VII verbs in the conjunct order, independent order forms and participles show dis-
tinctions of number in both the proximate and obviative.

6.2 Phonologically-Defined Inflectional Subclasses of VII Verbs

   There are three minorly different phonologically-defined inflectional subclasses of inan-
imate intransitive (VII) verbs, defined on the basis of the last segment of their stems:
   • Those with stems ending in vowels (e.g., mchaa, 'be big,' zhin'kaade, 'be so named')
   • Those with stems ending in /n/ (e.g., bngisin, 'fall down,' naangan, 'be lightweight')
   • Those with stems ending in /d/ (e.g., znagad, 'be difficult, mchaamgad, 'be big')
   Most vowel-final VII stems end in /aa/ and /e/, and none end in /oo/ and /a/. An augment,
-mgad (/-magad/) may be added to any VII verb ending in a vowel, but especially those end-
ing in long vowels, as in mchaamgad, 'be big,' which occurs alongside mchaa. This suffix is
also used to derive VII verbs from VAI verbs, as in kidoomgad, 'INsg says, means,' (VII)
from the VAI verb kido, 'say, speak.'
   The following table provides more extensive examples of each of the phonological sub-
types of vn verbs.
                         6.2 Phonologically-Defined Inflectional Subclasses of VII Verbs • 253



            Stem Type        Example           Gloss
            Vowel Stems      mchaa              'be big'
                             gpagaa             'be thick'
                             mooshkne           'be full'
                             bmise              'fly around'
                             mooshknebii        'be full of liquid'
                             zgaabii            'be a thin connection' (Od)
                             wiinaagmi          'be dirty' (of liquids)
                             biinaagmi          'be clean' (of liquids)
                             dgo                'be in a place'
            /n/ Stems        wiisgan            'be bitter'
                             naangan            'be light in weight'
                             gzigon             'be heavy in weight'
                             gaachin            'be small in size'
            /d/ Stems        aabdad             'be useful; be used'
                             biinnaagod         'look clean'
                             mnopgod            'taste good'
                             yaamgad            'be (there)'

Some features of these different phonological sub-types:

• The two stem classes ending in consonants (/n/ and /d/) usually take a link vowel
  before inflectional suffixes, often /i/, though there is some dialect variation and /a/ is
  commonly found as well. For example, znagdini, 'INobv is difficult,' gzignini,
  'INobv is heavy.'
• The /d/ stems attach the conjunct ending /g/ directly, but the combination produces
  [k], for example, zhinaagok, '(that) IN looks so,' from zhinaagod, 'IN looks a certain
  way, looks so'; zhiwebak, '(that) IN happens so,' from zhiwebad, 'IN happens so.'
• Just as with animate intransitive verbs (VAl), the /s/ of the negative suffix weakens to
  /z/ when it is attached directly to stems ending in a nasal (/n/). The d-stem class drops
  the final /d/ of the stem before the negative. For example, wiisganznoon, 'IN is not
  bitter,' from wiisgan, 'IN is bitter; znagasnoon, 'IN is not difficult,' from znagad, 'IN
  is difficult.'

6.3 Impersonal Verbs

   Some inanimate intransitive verbs are IMPERSONAL, and so typically do not have nomi-
nal subjects. These verbs express such things as seasons, times of day, geographical fea-
tures, and states of the weather. Some examples of the different notional classes of
impersonal verbs are provided in the following table.

                                    Some Impersonal Verbs
  Times and Seasons dbikad                  'be dark, be night'
                    giizhgad                'be daytime, be day'
                        waaban               'be dawn, be light out'
                        mnookmi              'be springtime'
                        niibin               'be summer'
  Weather               zoogpo               'snow'
                        gmiwan               'rain'
                        wan                  'be foggy'
                        maajbiisaa           'start drizzling'
                        nimkiikaa            'be thundering'
  Geography             zhitgweyaa           'be a river running in a certain direction'
                        shpaagnagaa          'be deep snow'
                        shpadnaa             'be a high ridge'
                        zhgakmigaa           'be a depression in the ground'
                        zhkashkwaa           'be [a condition of] damp grass'
                        zhooshkdamo          'be [a condition of] slippery road'

    Impersonal verbs often have subjects similar to the 'dummy subject' it found in English
expressions such as it's raining or it is daytime. Such constructions cannot have an explicit
subject, such as *This place is raining, nor can they be pluralized, as in *They are raining,
or be made into participles, as in *the place that is raining. All of these grammatical fea-
tures are common with Nishnaabemwin impersonal verbs as well. Impersonal verbs are
marked in the Rhodes dictionary with the code IMPERSONAL. In common with other dia-
lects, however, Nishnaabemwin impersonal verbs occasionally have subjects, though, as in
the following examples, where ziibi, 'river' Nl functions as a subject of the impersonal verb
eni-zhitgweyaanig, 'the direction where the river flowed.'

6.4 VII Paradigms

   In the charts which follow, the three subclasses of VII verbs are identified as
V(owel)-final stems, d-final steins, and n-final stems. In some cases, because both end in
consonants, d-final and n-final verb stems pattern together in their inflectional behaviour. In
other cases, since nasals and vowels are both sonorants, n-final and V-final stems pattern
together, in opposition to stems ending in the more consonantal /d/.
