Transitive Animate Verb Inflection




7.1 Introduction

    Transitive verbs have a suffix called a THEME, or theme sign, occurring directly after the
basic verb stem, and specifying properties of one or both of the two grammatical roles
indexed on the verb. In the independent order, the theme suffix works in conjunction with
the person prefixes to specify the actor and goal roles in a predication. The following forms
illustrate these two classes of affixes:

    Form                  Prefix          Stem              Theme
    gwaabmaa              /gi-/1          /waabam/          /-aa/           'you (sg.) see AN'
    gwaabmig              /gi-/           /waabam/          /-igw/1         's/he sees you (sg.)'
    gwaabmin              /gi-/           /waabam/          /-in/           'I see you (sg.)'
    gwaabam               /gi-/           /waabam/          /-i/2           'you (sg.) see me'
  1. The lit of this prefix is speculative, as it is always deleted by syncope.
  2.Subject to phonological rule deleting final short vowels and glides.


    The following sections provide notes on the workings of the system underlying the
selection of prefixes and theme signs.

7.2 The Topicality Hierarchy

   Nishnaabemwin inflection is sensitive to a relative ranking of categories of person, gen-
der, and obviation, according to the following scales, each in descending order of rank.
                  Person:            2 > 1 > X > 3
                  Gender:            Animate   > Inanimate
                  Obviation:         Proximate > Obviative
268 • 7.2 The Topicality Hierarchy


    Thus, among person categories, second person is ranked highest, then first person, then
the UNSPECIFIED ACTOR (represented with an X), then third person. Some grammarians feel
that the ranking of second persons over first is less significant than other ranking relation-
ships. In certain inflections in which both actors and goals are plural, first person plural suf-
                                                    1
fixes trump second person, e.g., waabmiyaang
                                         f\
                                                      , '(if) you (sg/pl) see us' has first person
plural suffix /-aang/, and gwaabmimin , 'you (sg./pl.) see us,' has first person plural suffix
/-min/. At the same time, the passive is used in the paradigm slot signalling first person plu-
ral acting on second person, singular and plural, e.g., the form gwaabmigoo, 'you (sg.) are
seen,' is also used to indicate 'we see you (sg.).' This usage suggests deference, signalled by
means of the agent defocusing inherent in the passive.
    Grammatical animates rank higher than inanimates, and proximates outrank obviatives.
These rankings represent common asymmetries in the grammars of the languages of the
world. They are found in one form or another in many languages, and are often called
agency hierarchies or empathy hierarchies. Generally, the more likely a given grammatical
category's referents are to serve as topics, the higher that category will be in hierarchical
ranking. Thomas Payne (Payne 1997:151) states of similar hierarchies, "the reality that this
hierarchy reflects is the fact that certain kinds of entities, namely things that move, have
power, and initiate action, are more likely to be topics of conversation than are others." In
the gender hierarchy, for example, animates outrank inanimate, which makes sense in terms
of topicality, since animates, involving humans, animals, and mythological beings, are
much more likely to be initiators of actions, and our sympathies and point of view are much
more likely to reside with them than with inanimate objects. Obviation is in part a function
of discourse perspective, that is, a storyteller chooses to view the action of the story from a
particular character's perspective, which is then proximate, and other characters are back-
grounded by being made grammatically obviative. Here again it is no surprise that proxi-
mates rank higher in topicality than obviatives.
    With regard to the person rankings, we generally make ourselves and our interlocutors
topics, and present ourselves as having agency in the world. As such, there is a universal
tendency for speech act participants, first and second person, to be cast as having more top-
icality than third person discourse participants.
    The three hierarchies outlined above can be collapsed, at least for convenience, into a
single hierarchy with the following rankings, in descending order:

                                  Nishnaabemwin Topicality Hierarchy
                                           2 1 X 3 3' 0

   I will call this conflated hierarchy the TOPICALITY HIERARCHY. It is relevant to two very
specific areas of Nishnaabemwin inflection, which I now address.

l.From /waabam-i-aang/, with: /waabam/, 'see ANsg,' /-i/1 goal theme, /-aang/, 1 plural, conjunct.
2.From /gi-waabam-i-min/ with: /gi-/ 2 prefix (independent order), /waabam/, 'see ANsg,' /-i/ 1 goal theme, /-min/,
1 plural (independent order).
                                        7.2.1 The Selection of Person Prefixes in VTA Verbs • 269



7.2.1 The Selection of Person Prefixes in VTA Verbs

    In the selection of person prefixes in the independent order and in noun possession, the
person prefix representing that of the higher ranking member of the predication or possessor
is chosen, as in the following examples of transitive animates.

       Form                Gloss                           Actor      Goal      Prefix
       gwaabam             'you (sg.) see me'                 2          1          g
       gwaabmin            'I see you (sg.)'                  1          2          g
       nwaabmaa            'I see ANsg'                       1          3          n
       nwaabmig            'ANsg sees me'                     3          1          n
       gwaabmaa            'you see ANsg'                     2          3         g
       gwaabmig            'ANsg sees you'                    3          2         g
       wwaabmaan           'ANsg sees ANobv'                  3          3'       «w»
       wwaabmigoon         'ANobv sees ANsg'                  3'         3        «w»

    Since all of these verbs are transitive animates, they grammatically index two
macro-roles, which I have identified as actor and goal. To determine which person prefix
appears, whether /ni-/ first person, /gi-/ second person, or «w» third person (from /o-/,
which is always syncopated, but which I sometimes represent with STRUCTURAL-w, «w»),
one need only determine the person categories of the actor and goal, and then choose the
category that is higher on the Topicality Hierarchy. For example, the form gwaabam, 'you
(sg.) see me,' has a second person actor and a first person goal, while the form gwaabmin, 'I
see you (sg.),' has a first person actor and a second person goal. In each case, because there
is a second person involved in the action, as either actor or goal, the prefix is «g», the
marker of second person, since second person outranks first on the agency hierarchy. The
prefix /n/ appears only when there is no second person involved in the predication, as in
nwaabmaa, 'I see ANsg,' and nwaabmig, 'ANsg sees me,' and the prefix /w/ only when
there is neither a first person nor a second person, as in wwaabmaan, 'ANsg sees ANobv.'
    Another area of grammar where the topicality hierarchy is involved is in the selection of
the prefix for first person INCLUSIVES and EXCLUSIVES, e.g., gboodwemin, 'we (incl.) make
a fire,' versus nboodwemin, 'we (excl.) make a fire.' The inclusive form, which includes a
second person, has a prefix «g», indicating second person; the exclusive form, which explic-
itly excludes a second person, has a prefix «n», indicating first person.
270 • 7.2.2 VTA Theme Suffixes


7.2.2 VTA Theme Suffixes

   There are four primary transitive animate theme suffixes (or theme signs), as outlined in
the following chart. These suffixes follow directly after the verb stem.

    Transitive Animate (VTA) Theme Suffixes

    /-aa/      DIRECT: third person involved, action is down the hierarchy
    /-igw/     INVERSE: third person involved, action is up the hierarchy
    l-il   first   person GOAL (and second person ACTOR in independent order)
    /-iN/      second person GOAL (and first person ACTOR in independent order)

   Note that there are distinct GOAL suffixes for first and second person (l-il and /-iN/), but
the goal markers involving third persons are relational, in that they do not so much identify
an explicit third person goal as much as the hierarchical relationship between the actor and
the goal, one of which must be third person. An examination of a few transitive animate
independent forms will make this clear.

         Form                   Gloss                          Actor       Goal      Theme        Prefix
         gwaabam_               'you (sg.) see me'                2          1           i          «g»
         gwaabmimin             'you (sg.) see us'                2         IP           i          «g»
         gwaabmin               'I see you (sg.)'                 1         2           iN          «g»
         gwaabminim             'I see you (pi.)'                 1         2P          iN          «g»
         nwaabmaa               'I see ANsg'                      1         3           aa          «n»
         gwaabmaa               'you see ANsg'                    2         3           aa          «g»
         wwaabmaan              'ANsg sees ANobv'                 3         3'          aa          «w»
         nwaabmig               'ANsg sees me'                    3         1          igw          «n»
         gwaabmig               'ANsg sees you'                   3         2          igw          «g»
         wwaabmigoon            'ANobv sees ANsg'                3'          3         igw          «w»
         wwaabmigon             'INsg sees ANsg'                  0          3         igw          «w»

   Each of these independent order transitive animate verbs has a theme suffix, though in
the case of gwaabam, 'you (sg.) see me,' it has been deleted by a phonological rule which
deletes final short vowels, discussed in Chapter 5 (p. 224). We can recognize the presence of
theme sign /-i/, though, even in forms such as this, because of its effects on stems ending
with /N/ or /S/, in which case these elements are realized as their PALATAL variants, as in,

1. One more transitive animate theme suffix, /-igoo/, used in passives, is discussed below. There is also a theme
sign /-i/ found in VTA imperatives with third person goals, e.g. miizhig, '(you pi-) give Y to AN' (/miiN-i-g/) which
is barely treated here. It is obviously a direct theme, and may be an allomorph of /-aa/.
                                                                 7.2.2 VTA Theme Suffixes • 271



gmiizh, 'you (sg.) give Y to me' (from stem /miiN/) and gnish, 'you (sg.) are killing me'
(from stem /niS/). The l-il theme sign is also evidenced by its presence when a following
suffix protects it from deletion, as in gwaabmimin, 'you (sg.) see us.'
    Examining the distribution of theme suffixes, we find two general principles at work.
The first principle involves a concept Algonquianists have called LOCALITY, which contrasts
first and second persons, which are said to be LOCAL to the COMMUNICATIVE CONTEXT, in
opposition to third persons, which are said to be NON-LOCAL. Thus, a participant is local if it
is directly involved in the communicative act, as either speaker (first person) or addressee
(second person). This concept is needed to account for the usage of the four theme suffixes,
in that two of them are used only when neither the actor nor the goal is third person, in other
words, when both actor and goal are local, and the other two theme suffixes are used when
either the actor or goal, or both, are third person, in other words, when there is at least one
non-local argument. Stated more succinctly, if there is a third person involved as actor or
goal, the predication is said to be non-local, otherwise it is local.

   Local Theme Suffixes           l-\l /-iN/
   Non-local Theme Suffixes       /-aa/ /-igw/

   The second principle at work is that of DIRECTION, referring to the relative ranking of the
actor and goal on the topicality hierarchy, and so, the direction of the action from actor to
goal, whether moving up the hierarchy or down it. Note too the relevance of DISJOINT REF-
ERENCE, which requires that the actor and goal be grammatically distinct, so they must
always differ in rank. The non-local theme signs differ, in that /-aa/ is used when the actor
outranks the goal, and /-igw/ when the goal outranks the actor. A few forms will clarify:

   Form                Gloss             Actor Goal Relationship                     Theme
   nwaabmaa            'I see ANsg         1    3 actor outranks goal                -aa
   gwaabmaa            'you see ANsg      2     3 actor outranks goal                -aa
   wwaabmaan           'ANsg sees ANobv    3    3' actor outranks goal               -aa
   nwaabmig            'ANsg sees me'      3    1 goal outranks actors               -ig
   gwaabmig            'ANsg sees you'     3    2   goal outranks actor              -ig
   wwaabmigoon         'ANobv sees ANsg'  3'    3 goal outranks actor                -ig
   wwaabmigon          'INsg sees ANsg'   0     3 goal outranks actor                -ig

    The theme suffix /-aa/, in which the direction of the action proceeds down the hierarchy,
is said to be DIRECT, and the theme suffix /-ig/ (underlying /-igw/), in which the action pro-
ceeds up, is said to be INVERSE, since the 'normal' direction of agency is inverted.
    The last set of transitive forms to account for are the PASSIVES, that is, those involving an
UNSPECIFIED ACTOR. The following forms are illustrative.
272 • 7.2.2 VTA Theme Suffixes


          Form                   Gloss                         Theme Sign
          nwaabmigoo             'I am seen'                   -igoo
          gwaabmigoo             'you are seen'                -igoo
          waabmaa                'ANsg is seen'                -aa
          waabmaawan             'ANobv is seen'               -aa

    In these examples, in the case of first and second person forms, a theme suffix /-igoo/
occurs, perhaps related to the NON-LOCAL INVERSE theme suffix /-igw/. For the third person
passive forms, however, the theme suffix is /-aa/, that is, the NON-LOCAL DIRECT theme suf-
fix. The fact that the theme suffix is DIRECT, indicating movement of action down the TOPI-
CALITY HIERARCHY, and involves the actor-goal combinations X » 3 and X » 3', suggests
that the UNSPECIFIED ACTOR ROLE, X, outranks 3 and 3' on the hierarchy. The fact that a
theme sign /-igoo/ occurs with first and second person goal forms, which resembles the
non-local INVERSE theme sign, /-igw/, suggests as well that first and second person outrank
the unspecified actor. It is on this basis that we can say that the hierarchy ranks categories in
the order 2 > 1 > X > 3 > 3 ' , that is, with 2 and 1 outranking X, and X, in turn, outranking 3
and 3'.
    Using the principles of the topicality hierarchy, locality, and direction, we can explain
the distribution of the five theme suffixes, as well as the person prefixes, in Nishnaabemwin
independent order verbs.

   • To determine the THEME SUFFIX in the INDEPENDENT ORDER:
       Determine the person category of the actor and goal of the predication.
       a. If both are local, use the appropriate local theme suffix of the goal...
           l-il if the goal is first person
           /-iN/ if the goal is second person
      b. If the goal is local and the actor is an unspecified agent...
           /-igoo/ is used
      c. If either the actor or goal, or both, are non-local (not first or second person), use
           one of the two non-local theme suffixes, chosen according to the following con-
           ventions:
           /-aa/ if the actor outranks the goal on the topicality hierarchy
           /-igw/ if the goal outranks the actor on the topicality hierarchy
   • To determine the PERSON PREFIX:
      a. If the actor is the unspecified agent (X) and the goal is third-person, there is no pre-
           fix
      b. Otherwise, choose the person prefix representing the higher member on the topi-
           cality hierarchy

  PASSIVES AS INTRANSITIVES. The inflection of third person passives, such as waabmaa,
'ANsg is seen,' is very similar to that of intransitive verbs, in that no person prefix occurs
                                                                   7.2.2 VTA Theme Suffixes • 273


(even in non-syncopating dialects of Ojibwe), and the endings /-wag/ and /-wan/ are used to
indicate plural and OBVIATIVE INFLECTION, respectively. Similarly, the inflectional forms of
first and second person passives resemble intransitives, too, particularly in the use of the
suffixes /-mini and /-m/ to indicate plurality, as in nwaabmigoomin, 'we (excl.) are seen,'
and gwaabmigoom, 'you (pi.) are seen.' Passive forms thus stand in between transitive
verbs, in having intransitive agreement, but also showing theme suffixes, like transitive
verbs.
    REFLEXIVES, RECIPROCALS, AND DISJOINT REFERENCE. Actors and goals in a transitive
predication must constitute disjoint groups. For example, there is no form in Nishnaabem-
win in which a second person singular (2s) acts upon a first person plural inclusive (21),
'you (sg.) see us (including you),' because the second person is included in the inclusive
goal. Similarly, there is no form for a first person singular (Is) acting on either a first person
plural inclusive or exclusive, since in both cases, the actor would be included in the goal.
When the actor and goal are identical, a REFLEXIVE form is used. Reflexives are inflection-
ally intransitive, and are derived from transitive stems by the addition of suffix (complex)
/-idizo/ (see Chapter 9, section 9.12.18, Reflexive /-idizo/, beginning on page 408 for addi-
tional details on the derivation of reflexives). If the actor and goal are distinct, but act on
each other, RECIPROCAL forms are used, which, like reflexives, are intransitive, and derived
from transitive stems. The reciprocal suffix is /-idi/ (see Chapter 9, section 9.12.19, Recipro-
cal /-idi/, beginning on page 409 for details).
    The following chart lists those person/number/obviation actor-goal combinations that
are illegal in Nishnaabemwin, that is, those which violate the requirement of disjoint refer-
ence. Actors are designated in the column on the far left, and goals in the topmost row. Dis-
allowed combinations are labeled "no," and reflexives, "rfl." Note that obviatives (3') are
grammatically distinct from both third person singular and third person plural.

                          Is     2s     3s     3'      lp     21      2p     3p
                   Is     rfl.                         no     no
                   2s            rfl.                         no      no
                   3s                   rfl.                                 no
                   3'                          rfl.

                   lp     no                           rfl. no
                   21     no     no                    no     rfl. no
                   2p            no                           no rfl.
                   3p                   no                                 rfl.
274 • 7.3 VTA Independent Order Inflectional Template


7.3 VTA Independent Order Inflectional Template

   Examination of the various inflections of the transitive animate independent order, pro-
duces the following template:

   Prefix Stem Theme                   Neg.      Pron. Plural      Mode          Nominal
   ni-1 vta    -IN 2 goal              -si(w) or -naan 1           -ban pret.    -ag 3p
   gi-2        -i 1 goal                -sii(w) -waa 2/3           -dig dub.     -an 3'
   o-3         -aa 3 direct
               -igw 3 inverse
               -igoo X actor

    There are two distinct sets of plural markers, as we find with possessed forms of nouns
as well, a pronominal set and a nominal set. The pronominal set makes a fundamental dis-
tinction between first person and non-first person. Nominal markers are only third person,
and include the category of obviation, which is only marginally present in the pronominal
system. The nominal markers are used to mark third person plural, animate and inanimate,
and obviative goals. The marking of third person plural actors shows an interesting distribu-
tional constraint— if the goal does not include a first person, either singular or plural, or a
second person singular, then /-waa/ is used to mark plurality of the third person actor; if the
goal includes a first person or is a second person singular, then the nominal markers are
used to indicate plurality of the third person actor. The system thus shows the following dis-
tribution:

                        Third Person   Suffixes with Third Person Actors

   None of the ALLOMORPHY of the nominal third person suffixes is unique to Nishnaabem-
win, as these forms are found in all dialects of Ojibwe, suggesting that they are very ancient,
and represent a common inheritance in each of the modern daughter languages of processes
at work in the shared language that preceded them, a language we might call Gete-Anishi-
naabemowin, or Proto-Ojibwe in English translation.

   Each slot may contain at most one member. The following theme signs occur in conjunct
order inflection:

             Theme Sign        Grammatical Indication
             /~i/              person goal, specified1 animate actor
             /-iN/             second person goal, specified animate actor
                /-inin/        second person or first person inclusive plural goal,
                               specified animate actor
             /-igw/            1. local goal: inanimate actor
                               2. non-local actor and goal: inverse
             /-igoo/           local goal, unspecified actor (passive)
             /-in/             non-local goal, unspecified actor (passive)
             /-aa/             non-local actor: direct
            1. As opposed to the unspecified actor of passive forms.


    First, note that in the conjunct order, the first and second person goal theme signs appear
even when there are third person (but only animate) actors, unlike in the independent, where
only non-local theme signs (direct and inverse) are used when there is a third person
involved. Third person animate actor forms with local goals use the appropriate local theme
sign. When the goal is local, the theme sign /-igw/ is used only when the actor is inanimate,
though it has its usual function of marking INVERSION when the goal is NON-LOCAL (third
person).
    The person/number suffixes are identical to those found with animate intransitive (VAI)
verbs. However, since there may be at most only one local person/number suffix, potential
problems arise when both actor and goal are local. When the goal is first or second person
singular, the theme sign alone functions to indicate the goal's grammatical properties, for
example, waabm-i-d, '(if) ANsg saw me,' and waabm-i-yan, '(if) you (sg.) see me'; when
the goal is first person plural exclusive and the actor second person (either singular or plu-
ral), there is no marking whatsoever for the second person actor, since the theme sign is first
person, and the local suffix first person plural exclusive, waabm-i-yaang, '(if) you (sg. or
pi.) see us (excl.).' In the case of first person plural actors and second person goals, either
278 • 7.4.1 Alternate VTA Conjunct Forms with Third Person Actors


singular or plural, the unspecified actor form is used, so that the forms filling the paradigm
slots for 'we see you (sg. or pi.),' literally mean, 'you (sg. or pi.) are seen,' gwaabmigoo(m).
    The third person (non-local) suffix slot is filled with the morphemes /-d/ or /-g/, 'third
person,' and /-waa/, 'third plural,' but in variable order, sometimes as /-waa-d/, and some-
times with the opposite ordering /-d-waa/ (or /-g-waa/, if the stem ends in a nasal conso-
nant). In some cases the third person marker is absent, as in the forms with first person
plural inclusive goals, waabminnang, '(if) s/he sees us (incl.),' and waabminnnangwaa, '(if)
they see us.' The third person marker, /-d/, is also not present when the goal is second per-
son plural. When both /-d/ and /-waa/ are present, their ordering is a function of the phono-
logical property of the stem to which they are attached— the order is /-waa-d/ when
attached to inflectional stems ending in a vowel, and /-d-waa/ (or /-g-waa/) when attached to
inflectional stems ending in a consonant, for example, waabmiwaad, '(if) they see me,' but
waabmiyngidwaa, '(if) they see us (excl.)' (with a link vowel l\l inserted after the first per-
son plural suffix /-yang/, prior to attaching /-d-waa/). Note that the use of /-yang/ here to
indicate an exclusive first person plural is out of line with respect to the rest of the conjunct
paradigm, where it usually signals inclusive first person plural.
    Several inflectional combinations are unpredictable. For example, the form for a first
person singular actor and third person goal lacks a theme sign and has a completely SUPPLE-
TIVE suffix /-ag/ as the sole inflectional marker, as in waabm-ag, '(if) I see ANsg.' The form
for second person singular actor and third person goal is similarly unruly, having the form
/-ad/, waabm-ad, '(if) you (sg.) see ANsg.' There are several other places in the paradigm
where somewhat unexpected allomorphic forms appear.
    As for MODE markers in the conjunct, they are almost invariably the last element in the
inflectional complex, e.g., waabmagba(n), 'that I had seen ANsg,' with a final PRETERIT suf-
fix. The negative suffix comes immediately after the theme suffix. This produces the follow-
ing overall template.

     Stem    Theme      Negative         Local            Non-Local             Mode
                                    Person/Number       Person/Number
                                                                             Pret     Dub

7.4.1 Alternate VTA Conjunct Forms with Third Person Actors

    Some sub-dialects of Nishnaabemwin show a rather different approach to the conjunct
inflectional forms that have third person actors and first or second person (i.e., local) goals.
Basically, the conceptually simple system of the inanimate actor forms is generalized to
those inflections having third person animate actors as well as inanimate, in other words, in
all forms having local goals and third person actors. This system is thus much more like the
independent order. All inanimate actor forms involve the use of the inverse theme sign
/-igw/, to which is then attached the standard conjunct person/number suffixes that are
found on animate intransitive verbs, which makes for a very transparent morphological and
                                            7.5 VTA Imperative Order Inflectional Template • 279


conceptual system. Also, note that number in the third person actor is not distinguished, so
that the forms are the same whether the actor is singular or plural. The following table illus-
trates this inflectional system.

                       Alternate 3(p) > Local Conjunct Inflections
                   waabmigyaanh '(if) ANsglpl see(s) me'
                   waabmigyan         '(if) ANsglpl see(s) you (sg.)'
                   waabmigyaang       '(if) ANsglpl see(s) us (excl.)'
                   waabmigyang        '(if) ANsglpl see(s) us (incl.)'
                   waabmigyeg         '(if) ANsglpl see(s) you (pi.)'

7.5 VTA Imperative Order Inflectional Template

   The IMPERATIVE ORDER is relatively simple, basically using the following template.

                    I   Stem "I Theme           Mode/Number Ending           |

    One wrinkle in theme marking in the imperative is that a suffix having the form 1-i.l
appears where we would expect a non-local direct, that is, /-aa/. This suffix form shows up
in all cases of positive imperatives involving second person singular and plural actors, as in
miizhig, '(you (pi.) give Y to AN), while /-aa/ occurs with first plural (inclusive) actors, and
in prohibitives with second person actors and third person goals, e.g., gego miinaake(n),
'don't (you sg.) give it to AN.'
    Rather than tease out discrete suffixes for mode and number, I have elected to leave the
rest of the imperative ending unanalyzed.

7.5.1 The Relationship of VTA Independent Order to Noun Inflection

   Examination of the morphological components of the transitive animate independent
and conjunct order demonstrates very clearly that independent order inflection shows strik-
ing similarities to the inflection of possessed nouns, both in terms of the affixes that are
used, and in their ordering relationships. For example, both possessed nouns and indepen-
dent order verbs use person prefixes, while the conjunct order does not.

               Verb, Independent Order      nwaabmaa       'I see her/him'
               Noun Possessive              ngwis          'my son'
               Verb, Conjunct Order         waabmag        '(if) I see her/him'

   Both independent order and possessed nouns also use the same morphemes to indicate
280* 7.6 VTA Stem Classes


nominal number and obviation inflections: in the possessed forms, nominal number and
obviation markers indicate grammatical features of the possessum (ones or objects pos-
sessed); in the independent order, the same markers are used to indicate agreement features
of third person goals.

                Independent Order       nwaabmaag           'I see them'
                Noun Possessive         ngwisag             'my sons'
                Conjunct Order          waabmagwaa          '(if) I see them'

    The conjunct order form here has the theme sign /-ag/, which resembles the animate plu-
ral inflection, but it is the morpheme /-waa/ in the conjunct inflection that marks the goal as
plural.
    The independent order and possessed noun inflections show parallel behaviour in the
form of plural actor and possessor suffixes as well.

           Independent Order      nwaabmaanaanig         'we (excl.) see them'
           Possessed Form         ngwisnaanig            'our (excl.) sons'
           Conjunct Order         waabnryangdwaa         '(if) we (excl.) see them'

   Nouns can optionally be marked even for MODE categories, as we have seen, the PRET-
ERIT, for example, is used to indicate a deceased relation, such as in nmishoomsnaabniig,
'our (excl.) deceased grandfathers;' and the DUBITATIVE is used with vocative plurals, as in
nwiijkiiwenyidig, 'my friends.' Mode suffixes on nouns too bear closer resemblance to inde-
pendent order forms than they do to conjuncts.

7.6 VTA Stem Classes

indexed only in a few participle forms. So, for example, the verb miizh, 'give Y to AN,'
indexes a giver as actor and an (animate) recipient as goal, but the thing given, indicated by
Y, is not indexed on the verb.

    Based on the forms in Rhodes 1985, it appears that some speakers have reanalyzed the
imperative forms in such a way that the second person singular acting upon third person
inflection is now /-izh/, that is, the historical /zh/ which is due to alternation with /n/ has
been reanalyzed to be part of the inflection, rather than part of the stem. This element is then
added to the stem with /n/, for example, the imperative of /miiN/, 'give Y to ANsg,' is
miinizh, and the imperative of/dakobiN/, 'tie ANsg fast,' is dkobnizh for speakers having
this innovation.

    SHORT V-STEMS. Short vowel stems are those that historically contained a single short
vowel, such as shi, 'put AN (in a place)' (historically /aS/) and nshi, 'kill AN' (historically
/niS/). There are very few such stems. These stems bear an interesting relationship to the
rule of final short-vowel and glide deletion, which deletes a final short vowel or glide, pro-
ducing, for example, nwiisin, 'I (am) eat(ing),' from a stem /wiisini/. We have also seen the
prominence of the METRICAL FOOT in Nishnaabemwin, which ideally consists of a weak
syllable paired with a strong syllable, but may sometimes consist of a single strong syllable,
as in the word, gii(n), 'you.' The rule of final short vowel and glide deletion historically was
limited by a restriction on the phonological shape of a minimal independent word— if the
deletion of a final short vowel would result in a word having only one vowel, which was
short, then the rule did not apply. This rule is related to the metrical structure that is seen at
work in the operation of syncope in that the restriction on final short vowel deletion was
grounded in a requirement that a word minimally consist of at least one FOOT, and a single
short vowel didn't qualify— either one long vowel (creating a DEFECTIVE FOOT), or two
short vowels were minimally required. One place where this restriction applied was in the
form of 2s»3 imperatives for verbs that had stems whose only vowel was short. A compari-
son of such verbs with a few other verbs shows the effect of this restriction:

                             zhi              'say to AN!'
                             shi              'put AN!'
                             nshi             'kill AN!'
                             wi               'use AN; wear AN'
                             gnawaabam        'look at AN!'
                             naadmaw          'help AN!'
                             miizh            ' give Y to AN!'

    What is crucial here is that the first four verbs have a final short vowel lacking in the last
three examples. The verbs showing a final vowel all represent stems that historically con-
tained only one vowel, which was short. If we assume that there is a suffix to mark this
imperative form, consisting of /-i/, these forms are readily explained. In the cases of the last
four examples, this vowel has been deleted by the rule of final short-vowel and glide dele-
tion. In the first three examples, however, this vowel could not be deleted, because it would
have resulted in a word having only a single vowel, which was short.The following diagram
shows the basic structure of the verb meaning, 'to speak,' zhi, along with its derivation in
modern Nishnaabemwin.
284 • 7.6 VTA Stem Classes



                 Underlying Form                    i .    N       +       i
                 /N/ > /zh/ before l\l              i      zh      +       i
                 Final Short Vowel Deletion         i      zh      +       i
                   (does not apply)



                 Syncope

    These short-vowel stem verbs thus preserve the final short vowel of the imperative
inflection that is deleted for all other verbs. Note, however, that the voracious rule of syn-
cope is more than happy to leave a word with only a single short vowel, as it does in the
cases of these verbs, which end up in modern speech with only a single short vowel.
    Another adjustment that many speakers have made to these forms is to add /n/ to the
 simple imperative, so that it becomes zhin. This /n/ is reminiscent of the /-n/ suffix found on
animate intransitive second person singular imperative forms, such as wiisnin, 'eat!'
    STEMS IN /?/. Stems ending in /?/ (glottal stop), spelled «h», show variation in their 2s»3
imperative forms, being pronounced variably with final /?/, /y/, or /w/, for example, the
imperative of /zaagih/, 'love ANsg,' may be /zaagi?/, /zaagiy/, or /zaagiw/. Often the 111 is
dropped from pronunciation between vowels, but a [y] may be heard in the transition
between vowels, giving the impression of an alternation between [?] and [y], as in
baabiiyik, '(you pi.) wait for AN!' In certain inflections, glottal stop sounds distinctly like
 [w], as in baabiiw, '(you sg.) wait for AN!' (from /baabii?+i/).
     STEMS IN Cw. These are verbs that have a stem ending in a consonant followed by /w/,
 such as njaaggwaa, 'I burn ANsg up,' and ndamwaa, 'I eat ANsg.' In this class a vowel is
 inserted between the consonant and final /w/ in the simple imperative form, producing
jaagzaw and maw as the imperative (2»3s/p) forms of the two example verbs. The latter
form is one of several (dialect) variants for this verb, which also include mo and mon. These
forms show a COALESCENCE of the /-i/ of the imperative with the /w/ of the stem, /amw+i/,
 and this short vowel is retained because the verb also belongs to the Short-Vowel Stem
class.
    Coalescence of the stem-final /w/ with a suffixal /i/ results in the extensive presence of
/o/ in the paradigms of these verbs. The following examples are illustrative. Everywhere
that an inflectional suffix complex begins with an /i/, the Cw-stem verbs will show coales-
cence to /o/, though this vowel may of course be deleted by syncope.
                                                     7.6.1 Example VTA Imperative Forms • 285



                                  /waabam/, 'see AN'      /jaagizw/, 'burn AN'
             3s   »   Is   ind    nwaabmig                 njaagzog
             3'   »   3s   ind    wwaabmigoon              wjaagzogoon
             Is   »   2s   ind    gwaabmm                  gjaagzon
             3s   »   Is   conj   waabmid                 jaagzod
             2s   »   Is   imp    waabmishin              jaagzoshin

   For some speakers, verbs that end in «hw» delete the /h/, and the /w/, no longer post-con-
sonantal, does not coalesce with a following /i/, as in, e.g., nbaktewig, 'ANsg hit me,' with
underlying form /bakitehw+igw/.
   THE IRREGULAR VERB ZHI(N), 'SAY Y TO AN'. The VTA verb zhi(n), 'speak to AN' has
an underlying form /iN/, which can be clearly seen in forms such such as ndinaa, T say Y to
ANsg,' and gdizh, 'you (sg.) say to me.' The morphophonemic element /N/ is realized as
/zh/ before the theme suffix /-i/, 'first person goal,' and the theme sign l-il that appears in
imperatives having third person goals, /-i/, as in zhig (or zhik) '(you pi.) say Y to AN!'.
However, a significant irregularity in the conjugation of zhi(n) is that it has the form zero,
that is, has an empty allomorph, when it is followed by the themes /-igw/ and /-igoo/, as in
ndig, 'ANsg says to me,' where /nd-/ represents a first person prefix, and /-ig/ the theme
sign.

7.6.1 Example VTA Imperative Forms

   The table on the following page lists imperative forms provided by a speaker from Wik-
wemikong (MC) for four subclasses of transitive verbs: those ending in an /N/ (and making
the necessary changes, /S/), exemplified by /miiN/, 'give Y to AN'; short vowel stems,
exemplified by /amw/, 'eat AN'; stems in /h/, exemplified by /baabiih/, 'wait for AN'; and
/aw/ stems, exemplified by /bizindaw/, 'listen to AN'

7.7 VTA Paradigms

   Beginning on page 287, a range of VTA paradigms is provided. Actors are designated in
the row labels running down the left side of each chart, and goals in the columns. Most par-
adigms are divided in half, with singular goal forms in the upper chart, and plural goals
forms in the lower. Disallowed actor-goal combinations are signalled with an em-dash
(—) (see discussion on p. 273, above).

Transitive Inanimate Verb Inflection




   Transitive inanimate verbs (VTI) are transitive verbs which take inanimate goals.
Because of a requirement that any transitive verb have at least one animate argument, VTI
verbs do not manifest reflexive or reciprocal forms, which only arise when the subject and
object are the same (reflexives), or when they act upon each other (reciprocals).

8.1 VTI Theme Suffixes

   There are three distinct subclasses of transitive inanimate verbs, morphologically
defined, based on the element of their structure traditionally called a THEME SUFFIX (or
THEME SIGN), because it occupies a structural position analogous to that of transitive ani-
mate (VTA) theme suffixes (see discussion, Chapter 7.2.2, VTA Theme Suffixes, beginning
on page 270). If we compare pairs of transitive animate and inanimate verbs, the presence of
the theme suffix becomes clear:

                            VTA stem       VTI stem         VTI theme sign
                seeX        waabam         waaband-am             -am
                likeX       mnwenim        minwend-am             -am
                use X       aabjih         aabjit-oo              -oo
                loseX       naajih         naajit-oo              -oo
                getX        naaN           naad-i                  -i

    Note that the first two VTA and VTI stems listed here appear to be structurally related, in
that the VTI stems resemble the VTI but with a /d/ added to the end of the stem, for example,
to the VTA stem waabam, 'see AN,' /d/ is added, and the final /m/ of the stem adjusts its
place of articulation (ASSIMILATES) to become more like the /d/, so that /waabam+d/
becomes /waaband/. But after this derived stem an additional element occurs, which I have
306 • 8.1.1 Patterned Variation in Theme Suffix /-am/


indicated with /-am/ in the table above. This is a VTI theme suffix. In the case of aabjih, 'use
AN,' once more a /d/ is added to the VTA stem to produce the VTI, that is, /aabjih+d/, which
is spelled /aabjit/, with the segments /h/ and /d/ combining to produce /t/. To this VTI stem
there is added a VTI theme different from that of/waaband/, in this case /-oo/. Lastly, there is
apparently a VTI theme suffix l-il that shows up on a very small number of verbs, such as
naadin, 'fetch it.' Every transitive inanimate verb has one of these three theme suffixes asso-
ciated with it, either /am/, /oo/, or /i/, and the theme suffix never changes for a given verb. In
VTI stem structure, then, the theme suffix is essentially a basic part of the verb, and is not
nearly as contextually cued as are the VTA theme suffixes, which vary depending on the con-
figuration of actors and goals, as in nwaabmig, 'ANsg sees me,' with theme /-igw/, versus
nwaabmaa, 'I see ANsg,' with theme /-aa/. But it should not surprise us that the theme suf-
fix never changes in VTI verbs, because their action always involves a higher ranking (ani-
mate) actor acting upon a lower ranked (inanimate) goal, given that the goals of VTI verbs
are obligatorily grammatically inanimate, and given that VTI verbs cannot have inanimate
actors. So the VTI theme suffix simply means "inanimate goal acted upon by an actor that
outranks it," and thus never changes. There are three theme suffixes for VTI verbs, usually
labeled as followed:

                                    VTI Theme 1         /-am/
                                    VTI Theme 2         /-oo/
                                    VTI Theme 3         l-il

   Most VTI verbs with theme 2 have instrumental/causative finals, and as a result have
stems ending in /d/ or /t/, with a few exceptions, most notably mmoon, 'remove IN, take IN
away' (M), and related bmoon, 'remove IN, take IN away' (M). VTI theme 3 verbs are very
few in number, the most common being naadin, 'fetch IN,' and miijin, 'eat IN.' Both of
these verbs are irregular in showing (partially) suppletive relationships to their correspond-
ing VTA'S, which are naazh (/naaN/) and mo(n) (/amw/), respectively. The verb yaan, 'have
IN,' is sometimes treated as the sole member of a fourth theme class of VTi's, but it's behav-
iour is very similar to a regular /-am/ theme VTI. It is distinct, though, in having a
vowel-final stem. All other transitive stems end in consonants.

8.1.1 Patterned Variation in Theme Suffix /-am/

    The theme suffix /-am/ shows several quirks. For example, in the independent order of
transitive inanimate verbs, when the actor is singular, there appears on the verb a suffix, /-n/,
which has sometimes been analyzed as a non-plural, since it only occurs with singular
actors, or alternatively, as a marker of an inanimate goal. The theme suffix /-am/ before this
/-n/ is realized as /aa/, by a phonological process of DELETION and COMPENSATORY
                                              8.1.1 Patterned Variation in Theme Suffix /-am/ • 307



LENGTHENING. The following diagram shows what is happening.
                    1.    n      w    a   a    b       n   d   a   m   +     n

                    2.    n      w a a b n d a _
                                                                   \       + n

                    3.    n      w    aa b         n       d   a ' _        +n

   First, because both /m/ and /n/ are NASALS, problems arise, since a syllable in Nishnaa-
bemwin can only contain one nasal after the vowel. To resolve this problem, the first nasal,
the /m/ of the theme suffix, is deleted. Next, to compensate for the loss of the nasal, the
short /a/ of the stem is lengthened, as if it were actually moving into the vacated 'slot' left
by the departed /m/. This spreading of/a/ to occupy two slots lengthens it, making it long.
So, nearly everywhere in the transitive inanimate paradigm that the theme sign is followed
by a suffix that begins with a nasal, the nasal of the theme sign is lost and its vowel is com-
pensatorily lengthened. This same process applies, for example, in the plural actor forms, as
can be seen from the following forms (where the theme sign is underlined).

           lp»0       nwaabndaanaa(n)           'we (excl.) see it' (most dialects)
           lp»0       nwaabndaamin              'we (excl.) see it' (other dialects)
           2p»0       gwaabndaanaawaa           'you (pi.) see it'
           3p»0       wwaabndaanaawaa           'they see it'

   These facts can be captured with the following rule:

                     VTI /-am/ Theme Vowel Lengthening
                     The /m/ of VTI theme /-am/ is lost before a suffix
                     beginning with a nasal, and the vowel lengthens in
                     compensation

   In the second person singular actor imperative form, it appears that the /m/ of the theme
sign is deleted before the /n/ of the imperative suffix, and in this case there is no compensa-
tory lengthening of the theme sign vowel, as can be seen from the example, gnawaabndan,
'look at IN!' (which has the structure gnawaabndam+n).

                     VTI /-am/ Theme Nasal Deletion I
                     The /m/ of VTI theme /-am/ is lost before impera-
                     tive suffix /n/

  Another phonological effect of the /m/ of this theme sign is that it 'softens' (LENITES,
VOICES) FORTIS (HARD, VOICELESS) consonants associated with the negative suffix in all
308 • 8.1.1 Patterned Variation in Theme Suffix /-am/


three verbal orders (independent, conjunct, imperative). This is a consistent property of
stems ending in nasals, in all classes of verbs. Comparison of forms with theme sign /am/
versus a verb with theme sign /oo/ shows the nature of the adjustment in VTI verbs.

                          /am/ -theme          Neg. Cons. /oo/ - theme       Neg . Cons.
      I do not see IN nwaabndanziin                     z   ndaajitoosiin          s
      if I do not see IN waabndanzwaan                  z   aabjitooswaan          s
      don ' t see IN !   waabndangen !                  g   aabjitooken!           k
    In each case where there is a fortis (voiceless) consonant associated with a negative suf-
fix occurring with a verb having /-oo/ theme suffix, there is a corresponding lenis (voiced)
consonant following the /-am/ theme (realized in these forms by /an/). In these cases the
voiceless /s/ of the negative has become like the nasal in being voiced, [z], and the voiceless
/k/ of the prohibitive has become voiced [g]. The nasal too, originally /m/, has partially
ASSIMILATED to the following sound by changing its place of articulation to be DEN-
TAL/ALVEOLAR like that of/s, z/, and is spelled with an «n». There is thus voicing assimila-
tion of /s/ and /k/ to that of the preceding nasal, and place (of articulation) assimilation of
the nasal to that of the following consonant.
    These observations can be captured with the following informal rules:

                     Nasal Lenition
                     A consonant following a stem-final nasal is voiced.

                     Nasal Place Assimilation
                     A stem-final nasal consonant assimilates its place of
                     articulation to that of a following consonant.

     This rule also accounts for the form of the theme sign /-am/ when it precedes the third
person singular actor conjunct inflection /g/, as in waabndang, 'that ANsg sees IN,' where
the nasal of the theme suffix is realized as /rj/, that is, a VELAR NASAL.
     OPTIONAL Loss OF THEME SUFFIX NASAL IN INDEPENDENT NEGATIVE FORMS . Many
contemporary speakers of Nishnaabemwin pronounce and spell independent negative VTI
forms as if the nasal of the theme sign were deleted, for example, nwaabdasiin, T do not see
it,' as opposed to the more traditional form nwaabdanziin. If we hypothesize a deletion rule
at work here, then we can explain why the negative suffix continues to show an /s/, instead
of/z/, since the trigger for the change of/s/ to /z/, the nasal, is deleted. We need only order
the deletion rule before the rule of Nasal Lenition.

                VTI /-am/ Theme Nasal Deletion II (Optional)
                The /m/ of VTI theme /-am/ is lost before negative suffix /-sii/
                                      8.1.2 Glide Insertion after Theme Suffixes /-oo/ and /-i/ • 309



8.1.2 Glide Insertion after Theme Suffixes /-oo/ and /-i/

    Since the theme signs /-oo/ and /-i/ end with vowels, and many suffixes following them
begin with vowels, another problem arises, since Nishnaabemwin (and Ojibwe in general)
does not permit sequences of unlike vowels. The problem is resolved in Nishnaabemwin by
inserting a glide consonant, usually /y/, but /w/ for some speakers, between the final vowel
of the stem and the vowel of the suffix, for example, aabjitooyaanh, '(if) I use it,' versus
waabndamaanh, '(if) I see it,' with the same terminal inflectional suffix, /-aan/.

8.2 Pseudo-Intransitive (Objectless TI) Verbs

    A striking feature of the transitive inanimate verb is that there is no inflectional distinc-
tion between singular and plural goals in the CONJUNCT ORDER. Some analysts of Ojibwe
have pointed out that transitive inanimate verbs are inflectionally almost indistinguishable
from animate intransitive verbs (VAl) in the conjunct order. Furthermore, there is a class of
animate intransitive verbs that structurally resemble VTI verbs with /-am/ themes, but which
are not transitive. Often these verbs have forms identical with a VTI verb, though with an
intransitive meaning, as can be seen from the following examples:

 AIForm               Gloss                      VTI Form              Gloss
 ndi-nendam           'I decide, think, vote'    ndi-nendaan           'I think IN'
 nda-mnwendam         'I am glad, content'       nda-mnwendaan         'I like IN'
 ndebwetam            'I believe'                ndebwetaan            'I believe IN'
 ndi-naabndam         'I have a vision'          ndi-naabndaan         'I see IN in such a way'
 nda-bzindam          'I listen, obey'           nda-bzindaan          'I listen to IN'
 nnoondam             'I am able to hear, I      nnoondaan             'I hear IN'
                      hear about things'
 nda-nsitam           'I understand'             nda-nsitaan           'I understand IN'
 nda-nkwetam          'I answer'                 nda-nkwetaan          'I respond to IN'
 ndi-ntam             'I hear things so'         ndi-nitaan            'I hear x so'

   This class of verbs is sometimes called PSEUDO-INTRANSITIVES, or OBJECTLESS VTl's.
Most of these verbs have meanings relating to mental processes, sensory impressions, or
emotional states. The verbs are only 'pseudo-' in the sense that many of them structurally
resemble VTI verbs in their appearing to have a VTI theme suffix. They are inflected as ani
mate intransitive (VAl) verbs, however. Their final element corresponding to the VTI theme
/-am/ shows the same processes that it does with respect to the loss of/n/ and compensatory
lengthening before suffixes that begin with /n/, as can be seen from the following examples:
310 • 8.3 VTI Inflectional Templates


                       ndi-mnwendaamin            'we (excl.) are glad'
                       gdi-mnwendaam              'you (pi.) are glad'
                       ngii-mnwendaanaaban        'I had been glad'

   Since they inflect as VAI verbs, this class of verbs is treated in Chapter 5, grouping with
other nasal-final VAI stems, except in their behaviour before nasal-initial suffixes.

8.3 VTI Inflectional Templates

   INDEPENDENT. VTI verbs, being transitive, have theme signs, though in VTI'S the theme
signs are lexically specified and invariant for a given verb. Otherwise, their inflectional slots
correspond closely to those of the VTA verb.

     Prefix Stem      Theme       Neg.         Pron. Plural          Mode       Nominal
     ni- 1            -am Theme 1 -sn          -naan 1 -min 1        -ban pret. -an Op
     gi- 2            -oo Theme 2              -waa 2/3              -dig dub.
     «w» 3            -i Theme 3
                                                An. Obv.        3
                                                   -ini         -w

   INDEPENDENT ORDER SUFFIX /-N/. The suffix /-n/ on the end of singular (non-obviative)
actors in the independent order indicative, as in nwaabndaan, 'I see INsg,' has been vari-
ously analyzed as a non-plural suffix (since its presence is not obvious with plural actors, all
of which are indexed by suffixes beginning with a nasal) or as an inanimate third person
goal inflection. See O'Meara 1990 for more detail.
   CONJUNCT AND IMPERATIVE ORDERS. Other than PARTICIPLES, the conjunct VTI para-
digms are identical to those of VAl's. Other than the theme sign, there is no inflectional ref-
erence to properties of the goal, e.g., its NUMBER.
   Imperatives of VTl's, too, are very similar to VAl's. The theme sign /-am/, however,as
mentioned above, loses its nasal before the singular suffix /-n/, with no compensatory
lengthening of the vowel.

8.4 VTI Paradigms

    Transitive inanimate verbs with theme sign /-i/ pattern identically to those with theme
sign /-oo/ in their inflection, so there is no need to list them separately. In paradigm charts
which follow, forms for both /-am/ theme and /-oo/ theme VTI verbs are given, where they
differ.

The Derivation of Intransitive Verbs




9.1 Introduction and Background

    In this chapter I will present in some detail the internal morphological properties of
intransitive verb stems. In English, many common words consist of a single morpheme,
such as walk, run, fly, and sing. There are many words in Nishnaabemwin too which consist
of a single morpheme, most notably nouns, but the majority of verbs are made up of two or
more morphemes. For example, the following intransitive verbs clearly consist of an initial,
noun-like, element, and a final element that is sensitive to the gender of the subject, in that
the words in the Animate column are used with grammatically animate subjects, while those
in the Inanimate column represent the corresponding words used with grammatically inani-
mate subjects.

          Animate       Inanimate
    (1)   mshkikiiwi    mshkikiiwan       'be a medicine'
    (2)   mskwiiwi      mskwiiwan         'be bloody, get bloody; bleed [VAI]'
    (3)   ziitaagniwi   ziitaagniwan      'be salty'

    Each word above consists of a noun, mshkiki, 'medicine,' in (1), mskwi, 'blood,' in (2),
and ziitaagan, 'salt,' in (3), to which has been added an ending, /-wi/ to make animate
intransitive (VAI) verbs, and /-wan/ to make inanimate intransitives (VII). Evidently virtually
any noun can be used as the initial component of a verb formed in this way. We can summa-
rize this relationship with the following simple chart, in which the first component, or struc-
tural position within the word, is labelled an INITIAL, and the second, a FINAL. These are in
fact the terms used by Algonquianists in referring to these word components. The symbol N
in the chart stands for any noun.
                                                                     9.1 Introduction and Background • 319




                  INITIAL        FINAL
                  N              -wi          Animate Intransitive (VAI) Verb of Being
                  N              -wan         Inanimate Intransitive (VII) Verb of Being

    These finals represent the common pattern, namely that, when semantically feasible,
finals occur in pairs, a VAI and a VII. In the case of intransitive finals such as these, neither
paired final is typically derived from the other, e.g., in the example above, it is unlikely that
/-wi/ is derived from /-wan/ or vice versa. By contrast, transitive finals tend to show deriva-
tional relationships between animates and inanimates. See Chapter 10 for additional details.
    WORDS AND STEMS. As discussed in in the section titled "Prefixes, Suffixes, Stems, Pre-
nouns and Preverbs," beginning on page 59, basic word-stems are determined by removing
all inflectional affixes, systematically restoring all deleted short vowels, and putting the
restored form within slashes. This process allows one to more readily see relationships
between words. For example, the words bmose, 'walk along' VAI and nimse, 'walk away'
VAI, both contain the same FINAL element. The relationship between these words can be
more easily determined by the speech of those speakers who say ndanmose, 'I am walking
away,' as opposed to those who consistently say ndoo-nimse, because in the former case, the
/o/ of the final element is pronounced, just as it is bmose, and the common identity of this
element in these two words is more readily deduced. It is probable that for some speakers
consistently using the /ndoo-/ first person prefix, the /o/ of this word is never pronounced.
But based on the word's meaning, and comparison with other words having related mean-
ings and structures, such as bmose, we can determine that the form of the final is /-ose/, and
ultimately, that the form of the stem is /animose/. Determination of the stem forms of words
is made easier by knowing their pronunciation in a dialect of Ojibwe which does not have
the rule of syncope.1 So when discussing the structure of word stems in this and subsequent
chapters, I will take as the basis of analysis a somewhat abstract entity consisting of the
word minus all of its inflections, and with all short vowels restored, placed within slashes, in
order to distinguish it from actual spoken forms, which are subject to syncope. The alterna-
tive is to assume that morphemes have variable forms that are arbitrarily associated with
particular words. For example, if we assume that the stem form of nimse is /nimse/ and
bmose is /bmose/, we will have to say that the MOTION FINAL of walking has two forms, /-se/
and /-ose/, and that the former occurs in the word nimse, and the latter in bmose, with no
apparent reason for this distribution of variant forms of the final. Another possibility is to
say that for some speakers many word stems no longer have any internal structure, but this
seems unlikely. But there is no doubt that syncope is resulting in fundamental changes in
Nishnaabemwin, obscuring many relationships that were formerly much more transparent.


1. An indispensable tool for students of word structure is Nichols and Nyholm 1995, a dictionary of a non-synco-
pating dialect of Ojibwe, spoken in Minnesota.
320 • 9.1 Introduction and Background


    PREVERB LEXICALIZATION. While the basic stem form of many verbs can be straightfor-
wardly determined by removing their prefixes, suffixes, and preverbs, there are some cases
in which a preverb has become LEXICALIZED, that is, has become intimately connected with
the stem in such a way as to form a complex (compound) word-stem with it. To determine if
this is so, we must consider the meaning of the word, and the consistency with which a
given preverb is used with the word for a particular meaning. For example, the preverbal
element zhi- /izhi-/, 'to, there, in a particular way,' occurs very frequently with vast num-
bers of verbs. In the following sentence, for example, it occurs twice, once with the verb
zhiitaa, 'prepare, get ready' VAI and another with the verb mno-yaa, 'be well, be well situ-
ated' VAI.

   (1)   Kina dash gegoo zhi-zhiitaawag gonda Fair Company ge-zhi-mno-yaawaad giw
         waa-bi-zhaajig.
         'The Fair Company is preparing everything for the enjoyment of those who will
         be coming.'(AMIS.4)

    As a point of contrast, I new address the status of another preverbal element, mno-,

can clearly be seen from the two examples above (sentences (1) and (2) on page 320). This is

    In fact, many physical, emotional, and psychological states are expressed by means of
preverbs in combination with the basic verb of location, yaa. This phenomenon reflects a
consistent METAPHORICAL use of language, in which something abstract, a state of mind or
health, is expressed by means of a more concrete concept, that of being in a particular place,
of being situated in a particular location. Metaphor is discussed in more detail below (sec-
tion 9.6, beginning on page 335). Many physical and emotional states are expressed by
means of the locational verb yaa in conjunction with various preverbs, such as in
gchi-zhi-yaa, 'be proud; feel good; be wound up' (VAI), where it is not merely one, but two
preverbs that form the word. Many other words have lexicalized preverbs, for example,
nda-zhichge, 'do one's utmost' (VAI), bbaa-nendan, 'worry about IN' (VTI), bbaa-yzhaa,
'go places and stay' (VAl), gchi-nendam, 'be glad, be in good spirits,' (VAI) mno-piichbii,
'be mildly inebriated' (VAI), and aanji-giisiwe, 'menstruate' (VAI). Such expressions must
be memorized as complete units, since there is no obvious way to determine the meaning of
the complex expression on the basis of its component parts, as for example in mno-piichbii,
'be slightly inebriated,' which has preverb mno-, 'good, well,' and an apparent independent
word, *piichbii, with root /apiit/, 'to a particular extent,' and final /-bii/, '[be in a state pro-
duced] by some liquid,' as in giiwshkwebii, 'be drunk,' but with component morphemes that
literally mean, 'be in disoriented state by means of some liquid.' But there happens to be no          >
independent word *piichbii, and the complex word mno-piichbii is probably better associ-
ated with mnobii, 'be a little high [on alcohol].'
    In summary, when a preverb and verb combination have a meaning that does not repre-
sent merely the sum of their component parts, then the combination must represent a sepa-
                                                                       9.1 Introduction and Background • 323



rate word of the language, and be listed in the dictionary, with a stem form that includes
both the preverb and the verb. If a meaning can be easily determined from the combination
of components, such as in gchi-gwiiwzenswi, 'be a big boy,' (preverb gchi-, 'big'; gwiiwzens
'boy' /-wi/ VAI final, 'be a(n)...') then there is no need to list the word in the dictionary. The
same goes for preverbs that serve particular grammatical purposes in particular grammatical
contexts, such as gii-, 'past tense' or daa- 'should, could (modal).' Even the most clearly
grammatical preverbs can become lexicalized, however, as in the case of humorous expres-
sion wii-debweshkid, 'be the kind of person who always wants to have the last word' (VAI),
which has preverb wii-, 'FUTURE TENSE; VOLUNTATIVE.' This word is also interesting in the
fact that the secondary suffix /-(i)shki/, used to form so-called VERBS OF ADDICTION, is
clearly added to a comple stem containing both the preverb and verb stem. The following

    ABSTRACT AND CONCRETE FINALS. The initial and final components of stems contribute
different kinds of information to the meaning of the stem. The initial component in each
example word in (l)-(3), for example, provides a nominal concept, whose properties are
being attributed to some other entity, the subject of the verb. For example, in mshkikiiwi, 'be
a medicine' (VAI), the medicinal properties of medicine are attributed to the verb's subject,
and in ziitaagniwi, 'be salty' (VAI), the saltiness of salt is attributed to the subject. The final
elements in these words, however, serve to categorize the entire word as belonging to a par-
ticular subclass of verbs, either animate intransitive (VAI) or inanimate intransitive (vn). In
addition, they can be said to carry a meaning somewhat equivalent to the English verb 'be.'1
Generally, this is the case, namely that a final usually has the dual function of both defining
a word's part of speech class (as a verb) and subclass (as VAI, vn, VTA, or VTI), while at the
same time often adding some additional meaning, such as 'be' in these cases. For example,
mnogi, 'grow well' (VAI), has a final /-gi/ that simultaneously identifies the verb as animate
intransitive and adds the meaning component 'grow.' Finals vary in how specific the addi-
tional meaning they provide is: those which have a clearly definable additional meaning
component, such as 'grow' in the case of final /-gi/, are often called CONCRETE FINALS, and

1. In fact, Peter Denny 1984 has argued that abstract finals specify a small number of aspectual distinctions, such as
states, events, and processes. O'Meara 1990 rejects this proposal.
324 • 9.1 Introduction and Background


those which function more generally mostly to define a word's part of speech are called
ABSTRACT FINALS, though even these may have a very general meaning component, such as
'be,' as in biinzi, 'be clean' (VAI). Note that the additional meanings supplied by concrete
finals are for the most part verbal or adverbial in nature, as opposed to the nominal meaning
provided by the initial components in examples (l)-(3). Initials also often contribute adjecti-
val and adverbial meanings, but they are distinct from finals. The identity of the whole word
as a verb most directly reside in the final.
    Since the final determines the part of speech and subclass of the whole word, it is some-
times referred to as the HEAD of the word. Nishnaabemwin words almost always have their
head elements in final position, in agreement with most languages in the world.
    FINALS WITH BIPARTITE STRUCTURE. While some finals are morphologically unitary,
many have a bipartite structure, in which the first portion of the final adds some concrete
meaning, and the second portion more abstractly identifies the verbal subclass. The follow-
ing examples illustrate some correspondences.

                        VAI Final           VII Final           Gloss
                        /-gi/               /-gin/              'grow'
                        /-bizo/             /-bide/             'fly, drive'
                        /-aaboozo/          /-aaboode/          'float'
                        /-aashi/            /-aasin/            'be blown; sail'
                        /-aaso/             /-aate/             'by sunlight, by heat'
                        /-igaazo/           /-igaade/           'be X'ed' (PASSIVE)

    So, for example, the finals /-bizo/ and /-bide/ can be divided into two parts, an element
/-bi/ that contributes the meaning 'fly, drive,' shared by both the VAI and VII verbs, and ele-
ments /-zo/ and /-de/ that assign each word to the class of VAI or VII verbs, respectively.
Note that these latter components also occur in the final pairs /-aaboozo/ and /-aaboode/,
and /-igaazo/ and /-igaade/. The initial, more concrete components of complex finals are
often called PRE-FINALS (also, SIGNIFICANT PRE-FINALS), and the more abstract component
is considered to be the final proper. The following chart summarizes these structures.

                                 Pre-Final                  Final
                                 More Concrete              More Abstract
                                 /-bi/                      /-zo/
                                 /-aaboo/                   /-zo/

    Particular abstract finals often show distributional restrictions, in that they attach directly
to only a limited number of roots, and are usually more productive when used in combina-
tion with particular pre-finals. Some analysts (e.g., O'Meara) do not consider the pre-final
to be part of the final, but rather to represent a separate suffix. At the same time, there is an
intimate relationship between the pre-final and final, and the two together form a unit very
convenient for exposition, and relatively salient to speakers. In my presentation in the fol-
lowing three chapters, I will usually treat prefinal+final complexes as units, calling them
"finals," without comment.
    Many VAI verbs have uncertain analysis as to the presence of a particular abstract final.
The verbs in the following list all end in vowels, but their derivational structure is opaque at
best: aadsooke, 'tell a story'; bgizo, 'swim'; bke 'turn off (from road); boodwe, 'build a
fire'; boozi, 'get aboard, embark'; daa, 'live in some place, live there'; gbaa, 'land, go
ashore'; giiwe, 'go home'; googii, 'dive'; gpii, 'go inland'; m\vi, 'cry'; mwizo, 'pick ber-
ries'; nbaa, 'sleep'; nbo, 'die'; nese, 'breathe'; niimi, 'dance'; wiisini, 'eat.'
    PALATALIZATION AND ASSIBILATION IN VAI FINALS. Another observation to make
about the pairings of VAI and vn finals is the tendency for the relationship between the two
finals to involve PALATALIZATION, for example, /-aji/ (VAI) and /-adin/ (vn), 'by cold,' could
be analyzed as consisting of the elements /-ad-i/ and /-ad-in/, respectively, but in which the
final l-il of the VAI final causes palatalization of /d/ in its prefinal to /j/. I have already
observed (in Chapter 2) that there are in essence two types of lil (short /i/) in Nishnaabem-
win, one that palatalizes a following consonant, from PA *i, and one that doesn't, from PA
*e (short e). The VAI finals for falling, /-shin/, and being blown, /-aashi/, also appear to have
a palatalized segment, ///, where the VII equivalents have /s/, yielding /-shin/ versus /-sin/
and /-aashi/ versus /-aasin/. This is a characteristic pattern of variation of the MORPHOPHO-
NEMIC element /S/. Furthermore, the difference between VII /d/ and lil and VAI /z/ and /s/
found in some VII and VAI final pairs represents a similar phonological relationship, though
326 • 9.1 Introduction and Background


it cannot strictly be called palatalization, since a shift from lil to /s/ does not involve a more
palatal articulation. This sound shift is sometimes called ASSIBILATION, and in many lan-
guages, occurs in phonological contexts that are similar to those of palatalization.
    In sum, there appear to be very structured relationships between the segments that occur
in many VII and VAI finals, such that where the VII finals show /s/, /d/, or /t/, corresponding
VAI finals show /J7, /&$/, and /s/ respectively. The following table summarizes some of these
relationships between the two classes of finals. Careful exposition of such relationships is
beyond the scope of the present study.

    VII Final      Prefinal     Final   VAI Final     Prefinal     Final   Gloss

    /-adin/        /-ad/        /-in/   /-aji/        /-ad/        /-i/    'by cold, by ice'
    /-sin/         /-S/         /-in/   /-shin/       /-S/         /-in/   'fall, move'
    /-agwinde/     /-agwind/    /-de/   /-agwinjin/   /-agwind/    /-in/   'float'

   SUMMARY OF FINAL STRUCTURAL TYPES. To summarize, finals can be conveniently
considered to be of two structural types, abstract and concrete. Concrete finals can be fur-
ther distinguished on the basis of whether they consist of a single morphologically unana-
lyzable unit, or a combination of a more concrete prefinal (sub-final) element and a more
abstract (sub-)final element. The following chart shows the various types.

9.2 Roots and Initials

   In examining a few VERBS OF BEING at the start of this chapter, I observed that there exist
paired VAI and VII verbs with an initial + final structure. Many other verbal expressions
show similar pairings, as can be seen by inspecting the following sample list.

           Animate            Inanimate
    (10)   dkoozi             dkwaa              'be short'
    (11)   giin'zi            giinaa             'be sharp (of tongue)' [VAll; 'be sharp'
    (12)   mnotaagzi          mnotaagod          'sound good'
    (13)   ndawendaagzi       ndawendaagod       'be needed, wanted'
    (14)   ziiwmaagzi         ziiwmaagod         'smell sour'
    (15)   aazhgidshin        aazhgidsin         'lie face up'
    (16)   debweweshin        debwewesin         'ring, sound in the distance'
    (17)   bkobiise           bkobiise           'fall into the water, slip into the water'
    (18)   gtigse, gdigse     gtigse, gdigse     'roll'
    (19)   bmaashi            bmaasin            'sail along; be carried along by wind'
    (20)   zhaabbizo          zhaabbide          'drive, fly through'

    Examples (10) and (11) represent physical attributes; (12), (13), and (14), perceptual prop-
erties; and (15) through (20), either physical states or motion. In each case we find a shared
initial component, and paired finals, one for VAl's and one for VII's, except in the case of
(17) and (18), where the finals appear to be identical. The initial components in the words in
this list, however, are not nouns, as in the verbs of being in (l)-(3)) (on page 318), but rather
here seem to encode ideas similar to English adjectives, adverbs and prepositions. For
example, the initial in (10)) is /dakw-/, 'short'; in (11), /giin-/, 'sharp,' and in (12), /minw-/,
 'good.' All of these concepts correspond to English adjectives. In (19), though, the initial is
/bim/, 'along, by,' and in (14), /zhaab/, 'through,' which are like English adverbs or preposi-
tions. However, these elements are different from the nouns in examples (l)-(3) in another
way as well, in that they cannot function as independent words, but rather must be associ-
ated (bound) with a final in order to form a word. Such bound elements occurring in initial
position are often referred to as ROOTS, as opposed to the general term INITIAL, which
includes both roots and elements based on free (independent) word-stems. There are actu-
ally two quite distinct types of word-formation in Nishnaabemwin, called PRIMARY and
SECONDARY derivation. Word-formation processes that add a transparent final to a free
word-stem are secondary. The formation of verbs of being, for example, is secondary, since
a final, either /-wi/ (VAI) or /-wan/ (VII) is added to a noun to derive a verb. In primary deri-
vation, sub-components of complex words need not be free word-stems. Primary and sec-
ondary derivation are discussed in more detail in section 9.5 below.
328 • 9.2 Roots and Initials


     POST-RADICAL ELEMENTS. Sometimes different roots appear to show similar formal
extensions that may or may not have any meaning, such as /(w)aas/ in /ningodwaas/ 'six,'
and /niizhwaas/, 'seven.' Beside these extended roots exist /ningod/, 'one,' and /niizh(w)/,
 'two.' Here the extensional element might be inferred to itself be a meaningful unit meaning
 'five.' In other cases, there is no discernible meaning to extensions, as in the root meaning
 'two,' which has the extended form /niizhoo-/ in nizhootooge, 'have two ears' (VAI), along-
side unextended /niizh/, as in niizhwag, 'be two in number' (VAI). Extensional elements
such as these are called POST-RADICALS or post-radical elements. A list and discussion of
such elements in Nishnaabemwin can be found in Bloomfield 1958:128-29.
     RESTRICTED AND GENERAL ROOTS. There are said to be two basic classes of roots in
Algonquian languages, what I will call RESTRICTED ROOTS, mostly noun roots but some
verb roots as well, which enter into primary derivational relationship with medials and
finals, and GENERAL ROOTS, which occur with finals to form nouns, adverbs, and verbs. So,
for example, in mik, 'beaver,' a restricted root /amikw-/, 'beaver,' occurs, whereas in the
word mskwi, 'blood,' a general root, /miskw-/, 'red,' occurs, which is also found widely in
verbs, as in mskwegzi, 'be red (of a clothlike object)' VAI. Note, though, that the word stem
/amikw/, as opposed to the root /amikw/, can serve as a component of another word, as in
mikgamig, 'beaver lodge,' where it combines with the concrete noun final /-gamigw/,
'room; habitation.' The final /-gamigw/ freely combines with both roots and independent
word stems. Because of the freedom with which some finals accept initial elements, both
from roots (a part of a word) and word stems, the distinction between restricted and general
roots may sometimes be obscured.
     ROOT REDUPLICATION. Some initials show various processes of REDUPLICATION, as in
nnaamdabi, /nanaamadabi/ 'ANsg sits awhile, sits and sits' (VAI) beside nmadbi,
/namadabi/, 'ANsg sits.' Reduplication to express plurality is commonly found in certain
STATIVE VERBS, as in mmaachaanoon, 'they (inan.) are big' (VII), and mmaandidwag,
 'ANpl are big' (VAI). As suggested, reduplication of this sort seems to be associated with
specific roots, such as /mang/, 'big,' /dakw/, 'short,' and /ginw/, 'long.' Reduplication has
two main functions in such cases, one of which, as here, is to pluralize the SUBJECT. Another
function is to pluralize an INCORPORATED element, as in ggaangaade, 'have long legs'
(VAI). Sometimes detecting the exact form of reduplication is made more difficult in Nish-
naabemwin by the effects of the vowel-deleting rule of SYNCOPE.

   (21)   ddaakwaakgaade         'have short legs' VAI (root /dakw/ 'short')
   (22)   ggaan'gaade            'have long legs' VAI (root /ginw/ 'long')
   (23)   mmaachaanoon           'they (inan.) are big'VII (cf. mchaa'be big')
   (24)   mmaandidwag            'they (anim.) are big' VAI (cf. mdido 'be big')
   (25)   maangaashkaa           'be big waves' VII (root /mang/ 'big')
   (26)   mmaangden'gome         'have big nostrils'VAI
   (27)   mmaangnike             'have big arms' VAI
