    FINALS THAT CAN OCCUR WITHOUT INITIALS. A few VAI finals involving motion are
somewhat fluid in that they can appear with or without any initial element. Examples
include gwaashkni, 'jump' (VAI) and gzi /gozi/, 'move camp, residence' (VAI). For example,
gzi by itself means 'move camp, move [residence],' but also appears as a final in words such
as bgamoodegzi, 'arrive with one's things' (VAI) and maajiiyoodegzi, 'cart off one's belong-
ings' (VAI), which appear to have initials /bagam-/, 'arrive' and /maajii-/, 'start off,' and
possibly medial /-oode-/, 'household,' which may also be present in oodenaw, 'town,' and
the widely found dependent noun for traditional clan, /-oode/, as in ndoodem, 'my clan.'
When gwaashkni is used without an initial, it means 'climb out [of a vehicle], disembark'
(VAI) (Odawa dialect), but it also occurs in combination with initials, as in gjigwaashkni,
'jump off [a vehicle],' bkobiigwaashkni, 'jump into the water' (M), and mbigwaashkni,
'jump up,' and googiigwaashkni, 'jump and dive in,' with VAI verb googii, 'dive,' as initial.
    DEVERBAL FINALS. A few roots seem to have the capacity to attach themselves as ini-
tials to a few independent verbs, in essence, converting the independent word into a com-
plex, derived final.1 One root with this capacity is the RELATIVE ROOT /IN-/, 'in a particular
way; to, toward,' which, for example, attaches to the VAI verb nokii, /anokii/ 'work,' to pro-
duce nankii, /inanokii/ 'act in a particular way' VAI. Another example is naabdizi
/inaabadizi/, 'be put to a particular use, be useful in a particular way' VAI, which is derived
by attaching /IN-/ to the independent VAI verb aabdizi, 'be useful; be used.' Another root
which shows this behaviour is relative root /ond-/, 'from, source,' as in ndagoode,
/ondagoode/ 'it falls form a certain place' (vn), which has the free verb goode /agoode/,
 'hang,' as a derived final. The root /dagw-/, 'together,' attaches directly to the transitive ani-
mate (VTA) verb maw /amw/, 'eat AN' to produce dgamaw /dagamw/ 'eat AN with some-
thing else.'
    As can be seen from these several examples, the independent verbs capable of becoming
derived (deverbal) finals often begin with the sounds /a/ or /aa/, and even among verbs
beginning with these sounds, only a very few submit to this sort of treatment.
    In the most extreme cases the boundaries between preverbs and roots is somewhat fluid
and arbitrary. For example, alongside naabdizi, /inaabdizi/ 'be used in a particular way'
(VAI), with relative root /iN-/ in root position and an independent verb functioning as a
DERIVED FINAL, there is zhi-yaa /izhi-ayaa/, 'feel a certain way,' in which the relative 'root'

example he cites is /inaabandang/, 'he sees it so,' which he analyzes as having a complex final consisting of prefi-
nal /aab/, 'see,' and VTI final /and/.

shows up as a preverb, zhi- /izhi-/, because the verb /ayaa/ does not have the capacity to
function as a derived final, even though it begins with /a/. The preverb form /izhi-/ arises
from attachment of particle (adverb) final l-il to the relative root /iN-/, and subsequent PAL-

('way') expression relating to the basic verb, whether aabdizi, 'be used' (VAI) or yaa, 'be
(in a location)' (VAI).
    Another productive deverbal final comes from the VAI verb baapi, 'laugh.' When serving
as a final, the verb loses its initial consonant, as can be seen from examples such as
boonaapi, 'stop laughing' (VAI) and maadaapi, 'start laughing' (VAI).
    The verb mooshkine, 'be full' (VAI/Vll) appears to become a deverbal final in
aabtooshkne, 'be half full' (VAI/VH), in which case it loses its initial /m/, a very common
process with noun derivation.

9.3 Medials

   INCORPORATED NOUN MEDIALS. One last word component remains to be introduced,
that of the MEDIAL. Medials, as their name suggests, appear between initials and finals, in
the structural 'middle' of a word, as in the following examples, both of which are VAI verbs:

    (33) dewnike        'have an ache in one's arm'
    (34) bookjaane      'have a broken nose'

   These words have a similar structure, consisting of an initial, medial and final.

                      INITIAL             MEDIAL          FINAL
                      dew 'sore'          nik 'arm        e 'have/VAl'
                      book 'broken'       jaan 'nose'     e 'have/VAl'

    Medials are typically NOMINAL in character, as in these cases, where they are very simi-
lar in form and function to BODY-PART DEPENDENT NOUNS. Other medials fall into
well-defined subclasses as well, including (INDEPENDENT) INCORPORATED NOUNS, NOUN
CLASSIFIERS, and ENVIRONMENTAL MEDIALS, among others. Incorporated nouns are (usu-
ally) independent (free) nominal elements inside a word that correspond to the goal (object)
of a transitive verbal action. The following examples illustrate verbs with incorporated
nouns.
                                                                                  9.3 Medials* 331


        Word                             INITIAL               MEDIAL               FINAL
        naajmiijme 'fetch food'          /naad/   'fetch'      miijim 'food'        e VAI
        moon'hapnii 'dig potatoes'       /moonah/ 'dig'        /apiny/ 'potato'     e VAI

    The first example contains the incorporated element, miijim, 'food,' which is an indepen-
dent noun; the second contains the noun pin /apiny/ 'potato,' in medial position. The final
lyl of the noun stem and the Id of the final coalesce to /ii/.
    CLASSIFICATORY MEDIALS. There is a rather large set of medials which classify objects
on the basis of various physical properties. A prominent set of these reflects an ancient sys-
tem of NOUN CLASSIFICATION, in which nouns are classified by their physical properties of
shape, substance, and consistency. The following CLASSIFIERS are common.

                     Classifier Medials
                     -aabiig-     stringlike
                     -aabik-      metal/stone/plastic (inorganic solid)
                     -aak(w)-     wooden, pole-like (organic solid)
                     -eg-, -iig-  sheetlike, cloth-like
                     -minag-      round, berry-like

    These morphemes create a system of classification that indexes properties of flexibility
and dimensionality. For example, classifiers /-aabiig-/ and /-aak-/ both refer to long,
two-dimensional objects, but differ as to the relative flexibility of the objects. The finals
/-aabiig-/ and /-eg-, -iig-/ both refer to relatively flexible objects, but differ in that the latter
group refers to objects having two dimensions, that is, sheetlike objects. Another basis of
contrast in these medials can be seen in the distinction between /-aak-/ and /-aabik-/, the
former referring to organic (solid, non-flexible) objects, such as bones and branches, and the
latter to inorganic (solid, non-flexible) objects, such as rocks and metal objects of manufac-
ture.
    Peter Denny (1976) has pointed out that the classifier system of Ojibwe (of which Nish-
naabemwin is a dialect group) has categories for classes of raw materials traditionally used
in manufacture. The following table shows these relationships.

                     Traditional Technology & Classificatory Medials
                     -aabiig-      vines, ropes
                     -aabik-       rocks, stone
                     -aak-         wooden poles, branches
                     -eg-, -iig-   sheets of bark
                     -minag-       berries
332 • 9.4 Basic Word Structure


    Although classificatory medials occur widely, they are most commonly used contras-
tively with a limited set of descriptive roots, such as /ginw-/, 'be long,' as in gnwegzi, 'be a
long clothlike object' (VAl), or gnwaakzi, 'be a long sticklike object' (VAI), and
gnwaabiigzi, 'be a long stringlike object.'
    ENVIRONMENTAL MEDIALS. There is an extensive set of medial-like elements referring
to natural features, such as snow conditions /-aagonag-/, hills /-adin-/, and rivers /-itigwe-/.
These medials most commonly occur in impersonal inanimate intransitive (VII) verbs, such
as shpaagnagaa, 'be deep snow' and bmadnaa, 'be a range of hills,' though some occasion-
ally show up in other verb constructions as well, e.g., bmaagnagii, 'walk by in deep snow'
(VAI). These elements are sometimes analyzed as PRE-FINALS1, because their distribution is
often restricted to occurrence with a very limited number of finals, suggesting that they
form a unit with the finals they occur with. I treat them in this work as medials because they
often have some correspondence with nouns or noun finals, as in /-itigw-e-/, 'river,' which
shows up as a noun final on mnitig, 'an island in a river.' These elements are discussed in
detail in section 9.11.1, beginning on page 365.
    OTHER CLASSIFICATORY MEDIALS. There are many other classificatory medials, such as
/-isag-/, which refers to wood, wood products, and floors, as in, for example, bkosgaa
/bakosagaa/ 'be a hump in the floor, be a piece of the floor sticking up' (VII). Closely related
is the medial /-is-/, 'wood,' which occurs in mnise /manise/, 'cut firewood' (VAI). Some of
these medials blur the distinction between the classificatory system and incorporated nouns.
    PRE-MEDIALS AND POST-MEDIALS. Medials often appear to have internal structure. For
example, several medials have a terminal element /-ag/, as in /-aagon-ag-/, 'snow,' /-is-ag-/,
 'wood, floor,' and /-min-ag-/, 'berry; round object.' Such isolatable elements are sometimes
called POST-MEDIALS. Several medials have /aa/ before the obviously nominal portion of the
medial, as in /-aa-gon-ag/, 'snow' (compare goon, 'snow') and /-aa-gam/, 'water body'
(compare gchigmi, 'ocean, large lake,' with /gam-i/). This and similar elements are some-
times called PRE-MEDIALS.

9.4 Basic Word Structure

   In summary, intransitive verbs typically consist of an initial and final element, though
some words also have a medial component. The initial component is generally of the nature
of a modifier, providing information similar to English adjectives and adverbs. Initials may
consist of an element that is itself a word, as in mshkikiiwi (mshkiki+wi), 'be a medicine'
(VAI), which contains the initial mshkiki, 'medicine,' or represent components that are not of
themselves words, as in mnotaagzi, (/minw+itaagozi/), 'sound good' (VAI), which contains
the initial /minw/, 'good.' Initials of this latter type are called ROOTS, which can be a bit
misleading, since it is the final that determines the part of speech of the whole word and
thus acts like the head or root element of the word. The class of initials is much larger in


1. Thanks to John O'Meara for pointing this out to me.
                                                                  9.4 Basic Word Structure • 333



membership than that of finals. There is only a relatively small number of finals, but there is
no logical limit to the number of initials, and the rate at which new initials are formed is
much higher than that of finals. In this way, too, initials are similar to English adjectives and
adverbs, which are also OPEN classes of words, meaning that new members can be freely
added to them when necessary. In the same way, new initials can readily occur in Nishnaa-
bemwin, and initials can represent components that are themselves morphologically com-
plex, including independent words in the language.
   We have also seen that many finals occur in pairs, one forming animate intransitive (VAl)
verbs, and one forming corresponding inanimate intransitive (vil) verbs. The following
chart summarizes the usual properties of each structural component within the word.

              INITIAL (ROOT)        MEDIAL          FINAL
              Primary               Nominal         Part of Speech Category /
               • adjectival         • body part     Verbal Meanings
               « adverbial          • classifier    defines part of speech (abstract
              Secondary             • goal noun     final) and may add additional
               • nominal                            meaning (concrete final)
               • verbal

    A more articulated word structure takes cognizance of the following structural elements,
which often grade into one another and show variable analysis by different theorists. Each
of these components and sub-components is discussed below.

                Initial                      Medial                             Final
       Root     Post-Radical      Pre-Medial Medial Post-Medial           Pre-Final Final

    INTERNAL WORD-STRUCTURE. Arguments can be made that within the word initials and
classificatory medials show a closer connection to each other than either does to the final.
For example, certain roots appear to select for the presence of medial classifiers, such as
/ginw-/, 'long,' and /dakw-/, 'short,' whereas other roots, such as /aabad-/, 'be useful, be
used' and /-ishp-/, 'high,' tend to occur in words lacking classifiers. Also, Rhodes 1981
points out that many initials that occur in verbs of breaking tend to be associated with spe-
cific classes of objects, such as /book-/, which is especially associated with the breaking of
sticklike objects, and /baashk-/, which is associated with three-dimensional objects. But we
rarely find finals that are associated with particular classes of objects, though in some cases,
such as the element /-bii/, 'liquid, by means of liquid,' as in giiwshkwebii, 'be drunk' (VAl)
(with initial /giiwashkw-/, 'be dizzy, disoriented,' the boundary does blur somewhat.
    These observations suggest that initials and medials are more closely linked to each
other than either is with finals. Perhaps this is true of roots and classificatory medials. On
the other hand, certain medials seem to select for particular forms of finals, suggesting a
close link between medials and finals. For example, the body part medials that end in /n/

often show up with a ZERO-FINAL, that is, with no apparent final at all, as in gzhiibaawgan,
'have an itchy back' (M), with body part medial /-aawgan-/ 'back,' and gaagiijgondaagan,
'have a sore throat' (M), with body part medial /-gondaagan-/, 'throat.' See also the forms in
9.11.13.2 below, which suggest medial + final fusion.
    Preverbs show variable structural affinity in derivation. In the structure of verbs such as
mno-zhi-yaa, 'be healthy' (VAI) and myagi-zhi-yaa, 'act strange,' the first preverb in each
case would seem to be attached to a stem consisting of a preverb and verb, as articulated in

9.5 Primary and Secondary Derivation

    There are two kinds (or levels) of derivation, or word-forming processes, in Nishnaabe-
mwin, PRIMARY DERIVATION and SECONDARY DERIVATION. Primary derivation involves the
formation of word stems using a ternary word-structure template, consisting of an initial, a
medial, and a final. So, for example, the word gaagiijndbe, 'have a sore head' (VAI), has ini-
tial /gaagiij/ 'sore,' medial /-ndib-/ 'head' and final /-e/ VAI. Secondary word-formation cre-
ates new words by adding a final to an initial that is itself an independent word-stem in the
language. An example is gaagiijndbekaazo, 'pretend to have a sore head' (VAI), which adds
secondary derivational final /-kaazo/, 'pretend to...,' to the word-stem previously discussed.
Secondary derivation has a binary structural template (initial-final). What is tricky about
distinguishing primary and secondary derivation is that independent word-stems can serve
as components in primary derivation as well as in secondary. For example, the final /-aadizi/
is used in primary derivation to create VAI verbs pertaining to living, such as bmaadzi, 'live,'
with bound root /bim/, 'along, by.' However, the word gookooshwaadzi, 'live like a pig'
(VAI) has a derived initial that is formed by adding /w/ to the independent word-stem
                                                 9.6 Meaning, Word Structure, and Metaphor • 335



gookoosh, 'pig.' While it is thus sometimes hard to distinguish between primary and sec-
ondary derivation, the distinction is fundamental to Nishnaabemwin word-formation. Sec-
ondary derivation tends to be much more productive than primary derivation, and produces
meanings that are more transparently derivable from the meanings of the component parts.
COMPOUNDING, a very common process involving the combining of two word stems, is also
a process of secondary derivation.

9.6 Meaning, Word Structure, and Metaphor

    Given that Nishnaabemwin words have component parts, each of which may contribute
a meaning to the word as a whole, we can ask what relationships exist between the mean-
ings of word components and the meanings of the words of which they are constituents. In
some cases, the meaning of a word is relatively straightforwardly determinable from its
components, especially in cases of secondary derivation, as in niniiwi, 'be a man' (VAI),
with noun initial nini /ininiw/ 'man' and VAI final /-wi/, 'be,' orjiimaanke, 'make a boat'
(VAI), with noun initial jiimaan, 'boat,' and VAI final /-ke/, 'make, gather.' Many cases of
primary derivation also show meanings computable in this way as well, such as gwekshin,
'turn around while lying,' with initial /gwek-/, 'turn,' and VAI final /-shin/, 'fall, lie,' or even
giiwshkweyaaso, 'be dizzy from the heat of the sun,' with initial /giiwshkwe-/, 'be dizzy, be
disoriented,' and VAI final /-aaso/, 'by action of sunlight.' However, many words have mean-
ings that cannot be determined in this way, for example, giiwshkwebii, 'be drunk,' which
consists of the elements /giiwshkwe-/, 'dizzy, disoriented' and VAI final /-bii/, 'having
something to do with a liquid.' Being disoriented because of a liquid is not the same as
being drunk. The element /-bii/ seems to have developed a secondary meaning, 'alcohol,'
though, as in words such as mnobii, 'be slightly inebriated' (VAI), though here again there
are problems of interpretation, since the initial /minw-/ has the meaning, 'good, well,' so the
component parts suggest a meaning something along the lines of 'be (feeling) good by
means of alcohol.' A similar process of specialization appears to have developed with the
VAI motion final /-aaboozo/, 'move along the surface of water, float,' as in waabnaaboozo,
 'drink (alcohol) until dawn' (VAI), with a derived initial /waaban/, 'be dawn, be day' (VII).
Compare this word with bmaaboozo, 'float along, float by' (VAI), which is not used in refer-
ence to alcohol. Consider also the word aangwaazim, 'coax AN, reassure AN by talking.'
On the basis of words such as aangwaadzi, 'be sane, be well-behaved,' we can surmise that
the meaning of the initial is something like 'be mentally sound.' The final in this case seems
to be /-im/, an INSTRUMENTAL CAUSATIVE FINAL (see next chapter) meaning 'using speech.'
So the 'literal' meaning of aangwaazim is 'make AN be mentally sound by talking to
him/her,' which is different from coaxing, which involves an element of persuasion, and
reassuring, which implies an element of restoring confidence. There is thus a relatively
clear relationship between the meaning of aangwaazim and the meaning of its component
parts, but it is not a direct one. This is the way it is with many words in Nishnaabemwin.
336 • 9.6 Meaning, Word Structure, and Metaphor


      Other words show more abstract relationships between the meaning of the word as a
 whole and the meaning of its component parts. For example, the word ggwejim, 'ask AN
  something, question AN' has an initial component /gagwed/ which means something like
  'try' or 'test.' The final here is again the causative instrumental final /-(i)m/, which means
  something such as 'cause by using speech,' so the component parts of ggwejim suggest that
 its literal meaning is 'test someone by means of speech.' But this is quite diiferent in mean-
 ing from 'asking,' though of course, again, we can see a connection between the constituent
 parts of the word and its meaning as a whole. Another example is the word mnozo, 'cook, be
  cooked' (VAI), which consists of the initial /minw/, 'good, well,' and the VAI final /-(i)zo/
  'be in a state by means of the application of heat.' All of these examples point to a common
 trend in Nishnaabemwin, namely that when words have meanings that are not simply the
  sum of their component parts, it is usually because the whole word has a meaning that is
 more specific than what is suggested by the component meanings.
      In some cases, word components are used metaphorically. By this I mean that, rather
 than establishing a direct relationship of meaning components to the meaning of a word as a
 whole, an abstract concept is expressed by associating it with a more concrete concept. For
 example, in Nishnaabemwin, the concept of taking a liking to someone is expressed by the
 combination of the root /odaap/, 'take,' and the final, /-enim/, 'in thought,' that is,
 daapenim, 'take a liking to AN, take AN to one's heart' (VTA). One does not literally take
 someone in one's mind in liking them; rather, the meaning relationship is that of metaphor,
 in this case by expressing the relatively abstract concept of liking someone is by means of
 the more concrete concept of physical embrace. Other abstract concepts are expressed simi-
 larly, as, for example, when the concept of caring about someone is expressed by means of
 the DIRECTIONAL ROOT /him/, 'by, along,' in concert with the finals /enim/ (VTA) and
/end+am/ (VTI), 'mental perception, by means of thought,' producing VTA bmenim, 'care for
 AN,' and VTI bmendan. A different kind of mental engagement is expressed metaphorically
 with the DISTRIBUTIVE directional root /babaam/, derived from /bim/ by distributive REDU-
PLICATION, resulting in VTA bbaamenim, 'bother AN, worry about AN, pay attention to
AN,' and its corresponding VTI form, bbaamendan.
     In some cases, the meaning of a word simply cannot be related to its component parts, as
in dzhim, 'gossip about AN,' which evidently consists of the RELATIVE ROOT /daN/, 'in a
particular place,' and the final /-im/, 'cause using speech.' There is no way that the meaning
 'gossip about AN' can be directly or even easily metaphorically derived from components
that together mean 'cause AN to be in a particular place using speech.'
     Thus, while we can recognize component parts of a word, assuming we do so correctly,
we cannot always say that these parts constructively contribute to the meaning of the word
as a whole. This is the case with many words in Nishnaabemwin, though perhaps the major-
ity of words have meanings that relate in some reasonably consistent way to the meanings
of their component parts. Also, words can have completely figurative interpretations, and
commonly do, as in Odawa wewebtoogese VAI, which is used to mean 'eat quickly, eat like
a pig,' but which literally means, 'make one's ears move back and forth' (/weweb-/ 'swing,
move back and forth'; /-toog-e-/, 'ear(s)'; /-se/ 'move; act; process'). Here again, there is no
                        9.7 Nishnaabemwin Ambiguity in Stative/Inchoative Senses of Verbs • 337



 straightforward relationship between the meaning of the word its component parts.
     It is sometimes not possible to determine whether a word has component parts. For
 example, the vn verbs for the seasons, bboon, 'winter' and niibin, 'summer,' both end with
 an /n/. Is this a final— it is not easy to know, because the elements remaining when /n/ is
 removed, /biboo/ and /niibi/, do not constitute recognizable morphemes. The VII verbs for
 spring, mnookmi, and autumn, dgwaagi, both end in /i/. Again we cannot readily determine
 the structure of these words without extensive comparative study. Sometimes a word may
 appear to have a recognizable component, but the suggested component does not fit regular
patterns of word formation. For example, I have heard an explanation of the VAI verb
jiibaakwe, 'cook, prepare food,' as involving the presence of the animate noun kwe,
 'woman,' as a final component, since it was generally women who prepared food in tradi-
 tional Nishnaabemwin society. But VAI verbs are never formed by putting a noun in final
position, so this etymology is ruled out on structural grounds. This, of course, says nothing
 of other ends that might be achieved by such explanations, and etymologies such as this one
 are popular pedagogical tools.

9.7 Nishnaabemwin Ambiguity in Stative/Inchoative Senses of Verbs

    Nishnaabemwin, in keeping with other dialects of Ojibwe, does not usually make a dis-
tinction between the onset and progress of an event and its resultant state. English uses the
verb become in order to focus on the transition into a state, as in 'she became a doctor,' as
opposed to the state itself, 'she is a doctor.' In Nishnaabemwin the two aspects of a verb
reflecting a state or the shift into it are not typically morphologically distinguished, and the
meaning of such verbs is ambiguous, resolved only on the basis of how the word is used in a
particular context. Thus, the basic verb of identity aawi, 'be an X' (VAI) can refer to an
ongoing state or a transition into that state, as in the following examples:

   (7)   Gbeyhiing gii-bbaa-nokii naangim go biimskwaabkagewnini gii-aawid.

         'He went around working for a long time until he became an engineer on a tug.'

          Gbeyhiing av 'for a long time'; gii-bbaa-nokii vai ind SsProx 'ANSG went around
          working'; naangim av 'until'; biimskwaabkagewnini na 3sProx 'engineer on a tugboat';
          gii-aawid vai conj SsProx '(CONJ) ANSG was/became.' (AK13.25)


   (8)   Boodewaadmii gii-aawi aw nmishoomis Wisconsin odi gii-dnizwag.

         'My grandfather was a Potawatomi, they lived there in Wisconsin.' (AK15.1)

          Boodewaadmii na SsProx 'Potawatomi'; gii-aawi vai ind SsProx 'ANSG was'; awpr
          SsProx 'that'; nmishoomis nad ls(SsProx) 'my grandfather'; odi av 'there'; gii-dnizwag
          vai ind SpProx 'ANPL lived there.'
338 • 9.8 The Structure of Morphemes; Link Vowels and Consonants


   The ambiguity between STATIVE and INCEPTIVE interpretations of words results in many
words having variable meanings in translation, such as VAI nbo, which means both 'die' and
the resulting state, 'be dead,' VAI bookjaane, which means 'break one's nose' as well as
'have a broken nose,'1 and VAI mnozo, which means both 'be cooking' and 'be cooked.'
    Some finals appear to have more of a processual meaning than others, though. For exam-
ple, consider the contrast between ziiwzi, 'be sour' VAI and ziiwshin, 'be sour, become sour'
VAI. In the latter case there is a greater sense of process than in the former, though both can
be used as statives or inchoatives.

9,8 The Structure of Morphemes; Link Vowels and Consonants

    Simple (primary, root) initials, medials, and finals have somewhat characteristic phono-
logical shapes. For example, most verbal roots consist of from one to three syllables, and
many common ones have a monosyllabic CVVC or CVCw structure, as in /boon-/, 'stop,'
/giizh-/, 'finish,' /maad-/, 'start,' and /web-/, 'begin,' which are comprised of CVVC sylla-
bles, and /dakw-/, 'short,' /ginw-/, 'long,' /minw-/, 'good,' and /dagw-/, 'together,' which all
have a CVCw structure. Roots can end in consonant clusters, as in /ishp-/, 'high,'
/zhooshkw-/, 'slippery, smooth,'/miskw-/, 'red,'/mang-/, 'big,' and/wiimb-/, 'hollow.'The
phoneme /w/ shows an unusually high representation as a root-final consonant, both after
consonants, as in /miskw-/, 'red,' /bikw-/, 'bump(y),' and /dakw-/, 'short,' and less com-
monly, after vowels, as in /mashkaw-/, 'hard, strong,' and /ozaaw-/, 'yellow, brown.' Roots
may begin with vowels, as in /anim-/, 'away from speaker,' /ishp-/, 'high,' /ond-/, 'from,
source,' and /aabt-/, 'half.' Very few roots in the language have initial /ii/, Id or /oo/; /ii/ and
/oo/ are not common initial elements in any roots in the language, either verbal, particle, or
nominal. When roots are three syllables long, it is common for the third syllable to contain
/e/, or occasionally, /oo/, as in /niboode-/, 'lonely, depressing,' /makade-/, 'black,'
/bagone-/, '(have a) hole,' and /aanikoo-/, 'link(ed).'
    Sometimes when morphemes are juxtaposed, combinations of consonants and vowels
arise that violate the basic PHONOTACTIC patterns of the language, that is, the phonologi-
cally acceptable sequences of consonants and vowels within a word. For example, the com-
ponents of the word meaning 'fetch food,' naajmiijme, on the basis of the comparison of
many words, can be determined to be the following:

                                      INITIAL        MEDIAL          FINAL
                                      /naad/         /miijim/        Id
                                      fetch          food            VAI




1. Some speakers prefer to add /-shin/ for a specifically process reading, regardless of whether or not falling is
involved. So the system may be changing for some words, and distinct stative and process interpretations develop-
ing for particular words.
                             9.8 The Structure of Morphemes; Link Vowels and Consonants • 339



    A problem that arises here is that the initial ends with a consonant and the medial begins
with one, and the combination of/d/ + /m/ was not found historically in the language, prior
to syncope. To accommodate the basic phonotactic requirements of the language a simple
short vowel HI, is inserted between the initial and the medial, producing /naad+i+miijim+e/.
This III, called a LINK VOWEL, causes the preceding /d/ to PALATALIZE as well, shifting its
pronunciation from /d/ to /j/, producing /naaj+i+miijim+e/. This form can be compared to
another word having the same initial, but with a medial that does not require a link vowel,
naadsabii /naadasabii/, 'go check one's net,' which has the following structure:

                             INITIAL       MEDIAL         FINAL
                             /naad/        /asaby/        Id
                             fetch         net            VAI


    Because the medial in this case begins with a vowel, /a/, there is no need for a link
vowel, since the combination /d/ + /a/ is an acceptable sequence of phonemes in Nishnaabe-
mwin. Tracing the behaviour and effects of link vowels is sometimes tricky, however,
because of SYNCOPE, which freely deletes unstressed vowels, and produces combinations of
consonants that historically were not found in the language. But on the basis of comparison
of large sets of words sharing morphemes, it is often possible to determine the presence of
link vowels, even when they are not pronounced because of syncope. For example, in the
word naadsabii, we know that a weak vowel has been deleted by the very fact that an /a/
appears as the next vowel after /aa/— some other vowel must be filling the weak position,
and is itself being deleted, in this case the first /a/ of the UNDERLYING FORM for 'net,'
/asaby/. Note that this vowel is also deleted in the usual pronunciation of the word when it
stands alone, sab /asaby/, since it is also situated in a weak position. Ultimately the pronun-
ciation of Nishnaabemwin words is based on many different levels of phonological pattern-
ing, including the underlying level, before syncope applies, and the level of pronunciation,
after syncope applies.
    LINK VOWEL /o/. In the cases of stems ending in /n/ or /m/, that is, NASAL consonants,
the link vowel often appears to be /o/, as in dgoshnoomgad, 'arrive' (vil), which is formed
from VAI verb /dagoshin/, 'arrive' and VII final Amagad/. Because two nasal consonants
stand adjacent in /dagoshin+magad/, a link vowel is evidently inserted. This vowel is then
lengthened before the final /-magad/, producing /oo/. One reason that nasal-final stems
might show link vowel /o/ has to do with the INFLECTION of such verbs, particularly the
THIRD PERSON PLURAL and OBVIATIVE INDEPENDENT ORDER (VAI) forms, which have the
structure /dagoshin+w+ag/ and /dagoshin+w+an/, respectively, but which are pronounced
(and spelled) as dgoshnoog and dgoshnoon, due to a COALESCENCE of/w+a/ to /oo/ after a
consonant. Perhaps speakers of Nishnaabemwin have interpreted the /oo/ in these forms to
be a link vowel.
   LINK CONSONANTS. Sometimes it happens in the juxtaposing of morphemes that two
long vowels stand side by side, as in the word for 'INsg has a hole,' bgoneyaa, which has
340 • 9.8 The Structure of Morphemes; Link Vowels and Consonants


the following morphological structure:

                                      INITIAL       FINAL
                                      bagone        aa
                                      hole          vii

    Nishnaabemwin does not generally allow the pronunciation of two long vowels in a row,
without an intervening consonant, so in this case, a LINK CONSONANT is inserted, lyl. How-
ever, there seems to be some unpredictable variation in the form of link consonants. For
example, the link consonant in maajiiwaaboozo, 'float away, start floating away' (VAI)
appears to be /w/, rather than lyl, since its component parts are initial /maajii/, 'start, begin,'
and VAI final /-boozo/, 'float,' though it may also be that the /w/ here is a derivational ele-
ment used for unknown reasons to derive (or mark) a specific initial, /majiiw/. The VAI verb
maajiihoode, 'start to crawl off, crawl off,' appears to have a link consonant /h/ (glottal
 stop), which can be compared with biindgeyoode, 'crawl inside,' which has the more com-
mon linker, lyl.
    LINK CONSONANT /d/ WITH PERSONAL PREFIXES. Link consonants between initials and
finals must be distinguished from the element /d/ that occurs with personal prefixes, as in
gdaakoz, 'you are ill' (with VAI verb /aakozi/), which has the second person prefix /gid/,
which is reduced by syncope to Vgd/, as opposed to gniim, 'you are dancing,' (with VAI verb
/niimi/) where the prefix is /gi/, reduced by syncope to /g/. The link consonant /d/ only
occurs with personal prefixes.
    LOSS OF SHORT VOWELS. When the joining of two morphemes juxtaposes a short vowel
and a long vowel, the short vowel is deleted, as in bkemo, 'the road forks' (VII), which con-
tains the morphemes /bake+amo/. This word can be compared with zhaashdamo, 'be a slip-
pery road' (VII), and namo, 'be a road leading in a particular direction' (VII), both of which
show the /a/ of vii final /amo/.
    LENGTHENING OF SHORT VOWELS. Short vowels lengthen before some finals, for exam-
ple, wiisni, 'eat' (vai) lengthens its final vowel to /ii/ in construction with /-mgad/,
wiisniimgad, 'it eats' (vii). Noun stems that end in /i/, such as mshkiki, 'medicine' (Nl), or
/iw/, such as nini /ininiw, aniniw/, 'man' (NA), are particularly prone to showing their final
short l\l lengthened when serving as initials, as in mshkikiiwi, 'be a medicine, be medicinal'
(VAI) and niniiwi, 'be a man' (VAI).
    SHORTENING OF LONG VOWELS. Very occasionally, long vowels are shortened in deriva-
tional processes, as in VTA giiwshkwebin (~zh), 'get AN drunk,' which has as initial VAI
verb giiwshkwebii, 'be drunk,' but the final vowel of the initial appears to have been short-
ened from /ii/ to lit.
    VOWEL SHIFTS. Another process that occasionally occurs involves an alternation of a
stem-final vowel between /ii/ or /aa/ and /e/, or Id and /aa/. For example, the classificatory
medial /-iig-/ has a variant /-eg-/ that occurs after initials ending in /w/, as in VAI mskwegzi,
'be red (of cloth),' and VAI gnwegzi, 'be long (of cloth),' alongside VAI bbagiigzi, 'be light,
                                      9.9 Problems in Identifying and Segmenting Morphemes • 341



be thin (of cloth).' An example of/aa/ to Id correspondence can be seen by comparing VAI
nbaa, 'sleep,' with the causative form, nbeh, 'put AN to bed, make AN go to bed' (VTA).
Alongside the VAI verb mnikwe, 'drink,' is VTI mnikwaadan, 'use s.t. to get a drink,' show-
ing a shift from Id to /aa/ in the transitive form.
    LOSS OF CONSONANTS. Occasionally, when morphemes combine, consonants are lost,
as in zaagdaabiishin, 'come out (stringlike object)' (VAI), which contains a form of the clas-
sificatory medial /-aabiig-/ that lacks a final /g/. Also, stem-initial /m/ is lost when the stem
is used as a suffix in derivational forms, as can be seen in the correspondence between
VAI/VII mooshkne, 'be full,' and VAl/vn aabtooshkne, 'be half-full.'

9.9 Problems in Identifying and Segmenting Morphemes

   The presence of link vowels and link consonants creates potential indeterminacies in the
segmenting of words into their component morphemes. For example, both of the following
words have the same final element:

                                   biin'zi       'be clean' (VAI)
                                   niinmizi      'be weak' (VAI)

    A question immediately arises as to which morpheme, if any, the HI after the /m/ in
niinmizi should be assigned. There are three possibilities:

   1. The lil belongs with the initial, /niinami+zi/.
   2. The lil belongs with the final, /niinam+izi/.
   3. The lil is a link vowel, /niinam+i+zi/.

    Often, when there is a large set of words sharing a given morpheme, its exact form can
be determined on the basis of comparison. Sometimes we can appeal to general patterns
concerning of shape of morphemes filling particular slots in a word, such as, for example,
the observation that most initials end in consonants or long vowels. Sometimes the effect a
given segment has on neighbouring sounds allows us to make an educated guess. For exam-
ple, we saw in the case of naajmiijme, 'ANsg fetches food,' that the link vowel causes the
/d/ of the initial /naad/ to PALATALIZE, converting it to /j/.We would then assume that link
vowels should have this effect on any preceding /d/. However, in the case of the word
aabdizi, 'be useful,' the final /d/ of the initial /aabad/, 'useful,' does not show palatalization
(to /j/) before the lil. This fact allows us to analyze HI as part of the final, which is then /-izi/.
Recall that there are two kinds of short lil in Nishnaabemwin, those that palatalize a follow-
ing consonant, which come historically from Proto-Algonquian */i/, and those which do
not, which come from Proto-Algonquian */e/ (short e). More commonly the link vowel
comes from PA *i, while the HI in /-izi/ evidently comes from PA */e/. While overly simple,
when there is uncertainty, I will assume that /i/'s from PA *i are link vowels, and that those
342 -9.10 Paired VAI and VII Finals


from PA *e are not. Goddard 1990, however, argues that link vowels come from both histor-
ical sources. Very little is at stake in this grammar.
    In summary, accurately segmenting words into their component morphemes is a com-
plex task involving the careful study of many words sharing the same morphemes, looking
for structural patterns in morpheme shapes, and examining the phonological behaviour of
adjacent segments. In the lists which follow, I strive to be as accurate as possible in my
determinations, but there are undoubtedly errors, simply because I lack diagnostic forms
and the depth of knowledge in the language necessary to recognize all patterns.

9.10 Paired VAI and VII Finals

   I begin the presentation of intransitive verb structure with organized lists of paired VAI
and VII finals, followed by those that are specific to vil verbs, and lastly, examine VAI finals
that do not have VII correspondents. In all charts presented below, where both VAI and vn
forms are listed, the VAI forms are listed to the left of the VII. I will focus on the more pro-
ductive finals, or those which belong to productive families (semantic groups) of finals.
Those wishing a more exhaustive list of finals can consult Bloomfield 1958.

9.10.1 Attributive (Descriptive) Expressions

    Most ATTRIBUTIVE (ADJECTIVAL, descriptive) concepts are expressed by means of
intransitive verbs having a DESCRIPTIVE INITIAL (or complex initial), an optional classifica-
tory medial, and a final sensitive to gender. The most common VAI descriptive final is /-izi/,
which may be paired with VII finals /-aa/, /-an/, or /-ad/. In cases where the stem ends in a
long vowel, the first /i/ of /-izi/ is deleted; in cases where the stem ends in a long vowel, lyl
is inserted before vn /-aa/. Note that the initial III of the VAI final does not cause palataliza-
tion of a root-final /d/, as can be seen from the form aabdizi, 'be useful, be used' (VAI),
which has root /aab[a]d/.

'fly, drive, run (of machines).' For more information on motion finals, see section 9.12.1,
beginning on page 374, which deals specifically with those associated with animate intran-

9.10.4 Goal Focus Verbs with Instrumental Causative Finals

    Some finals specify an INSTRUMENT or an AMBIENT FORCE (that is, action of the wind,
the sun, ice or cold, etc.) acting upon the subject of the verb, and the verb refers to the state
or motion resulting from application of the instrument or force, for example, mshkawji,
'freeze, be frozen' (lit., 'be made hard by cold'), which has the final element /-aji/, 'be acted
upon by ice, by cold.' Instrumental finals are prominent in the structure of many transitive
verbs, but many occur with intransitive GOAL FOCUS VERBS associated with the correspond-
ing transitives, in which the SUBJECT of the INTRANSITIVE is the GOAL of the TRANSITIVE
CAUSATIVE. They are thus somewhat PASSIVE in their semantics. Some relatively common
intransitive verbs with these structures are those involving the instrumentality of falling (VAI
-shin/vil -sin), the wind (VAI -aashi/vil -aasin), cold (VAI -aji/VH -adin), and heat (VAI
-zo/vn -de). These forms are particularly interesting, given that Nishnaabemwin does not
allow a transitive predication to fill both macroroles with an inanimate.

   14        VAI /-shin/     VII /-sin/        'fall, happen, lie, be situated. /

    The finals /-shin/ and /-sin/ seem prototypically used with verbs pertaining to motion
and/or location involving the concept of falling, or that of its resultant state, lying in a par-
ticular way or in particular orientation. Most of these verbs have morphologically related
CAUSATIVE TRANSITIVE verbs associated with them, and often represent the state that results
from the application of the causative action upon them. For example, the verbs aazhgidshin
(VAI) and aazhgidsin (vn) 'lie face up,' have associated causatives aazhgidshim (VTA) and
aazhgidsidoon (vti), 'place X face up.'
    The VII final /-sin/ can be added as a secondary final to some stative verbs to produce a
process reading, e.g., dkaagami, 'be cold (of liquids)' VII, versus dkaagmisin, 'cool off (of
liquids)' VII.
    CLASSIFICATORY MEDIALS sometimes occur with these finals, as in mnwegshin, 'be
smooth, even' (VAI), in which case the medial /-eg-/ specifies that the subject is a sheetlike,
or clothlike object. However, medials may contribute other kinds of meaning as well, as in
zhaashaabkishin, 'slip, slide on a stone surface,' where the medial /-aabik-/ indicates the
nature of the surface on which the action takes place.
    Another element found in words with this final, as well as with many others, is /-wewe/,
which indicates that sound is involved in the verbal predication, as in debweweshin, 'ring,
sounds in the distance' (VAI) and dpweweshin, 'be heard through some opening' (VAI).
While there is evidence for analyzing the element /-wewe/ as a post-radical, and these
examples thus as being formed with a (derived) initial, the transparency and prevalence of
/-wewe/ suggests that it has something of the status of an independent unit.

9.10.5 Object of Perception Verbs

    Object-of-perception verbs are those which describe an entity in terms of the way it is
perceived by the senses, such as mnotaagzi, 'sound good' (VAI) or mnopgwad, 'taste good'
(vn). There are classes of object-of-perception verbs for each of the senses of taste, hearing,
sight, and smell, as well as for thought processes. The sense of touch is given little explicit
lexical representation in Nishnaabemwin (and Ojibwe in general).
                                                          9.10.5 Object of Perception Verbs • 357



   The finals used with these verbs are complex, consisting of a morphological element that
resembles the PASSIVE morpheme, /-igw/ or /-igoo/, presumably because these verbs are a
type of GOAL FOCUS VERB, derived from TRANSITIVE constructions (see VERBS OF PERCEP-
TION, in section 10.6 of the following chapter). The component parts of the different final
complexes appear to be as follows, though I am somewhat uncertain of the precise analysis.

               VAI Structure            VAI Form       VII Structure             VII Form
    thought    -end -aw -igw -zi        -endaagzi      -end -aw -igw -ad         -endaagod
    sound      -it -aw -igw -zi         -itaagzi       -it -aw -igw -ad          -itaagod
    smell      -im -aw -igw -zi         -imaagzi       -im -aw -igw -ad          -imaagod
    sight      -in -aw -igw -zi         -inaagzi       -in -aw -igw -ad          -inaagod
    taste      -ip -igw -zi             -ipigozi       -ip -igw -ad              -ipigod

    Based on the verb of thought final complex /-end-aw-igw/, it appears that the INTRANSI-
TIVE FINALS of both the VAI and vn forms are formed from a VTl-like final structure, in that
the VTI final for verbs of thought is /-end+am/, while the VTA is /-enim/. Both intransitive
finals have /-end/, like the VTI. However the element /-aw/ is typically associated with VTA
finals, as in nitwaad, 'hear AN in a certain way,' with VTA final /-itaw/, compared to VTI
nitang, 'with final /-it+am/. So the relationships between forms is not straightforward.

9.10.6 Overt Lexical Passive Verbs

    The final complexes /-igaazo/ and /-igaade/ are used to derive PASSiVElike VAI and VII
 verbs, respectively. These complex finals may consist of the elements /-ig-aw-(i)zo/, though
 once again it isn't clear what the element /-aw/ might contribute to their meaning or struc-
ture. The element /-ig/ resembles the PASSIVE morpheme of transitive verbs, /-igoo/, and the
INVERSE form used with actions involving third persons, /-igw/, though it seems to lack the
 final /w/ found in both of the other forms. The elements /-zo/ and /-de/ resemble other
 (ABSTRACT) INTRANSITIVE finals. As with verbs of thought, above, the stem used with both
VAI and VII forms appears to be derived from the VTI stem, minus its theme suffix. So, for
example, associated with VTA.jaa.gzaw /jaagzw/ and VTI jaagzan, 'burn X' are VAI
jaagzigaazo and VII jaagzigaade, both of which lack any evidence of the /w/ of the VTA
final.

   24       VAI /-igaazo/     VII /-igaade/    'beXed...'

    (340)   gbaakwigaazo       gbaakwigaade       'be closed; be blocked off
    (341)   gtigaazo           gtigaade           'be planted'
    (342)   jaagzigaazo        jaagzigaade        'be burnt out'
    (343)   nsaaknigaazo       nsaaknigaade       'be opened'

9.10.7 Other Paired Intransitive Finals

   There are other paired finals that are not easily classified into notional groups in the
same way that the preceding finals have been. I list a couple of these in this section, though
the list is obviously by no means complete.
360 • 9.10.8 Paired Forms with Identical VAI and VII Finals



   25       VAI /-aanzo/     VII /-aande/       'be coloured...'

Verbs specifying various colours can be formed by adding these finals to NOUN STEMS, as in
(361), where giizhig, 'sky' (Nl) occurs, and (363), where miin, 'berry' (Nl), occurs. In other
cases, these finals are added to ROOTS, as in (365), where relative root /iN-/ occurs as initial.
Verbs with these finals often have a PASSIVE sense, in which their colour is implied to have
come about through the action of an ACTOR. They are thus a kind of GOAL FOCUS construc-
tion. They appear too to be related to the final pair VAl/vil /-aanzhe/, 'shine, with lights on.'

   31       VAI /-wi/        VII /-wan/         'be N-y, be a(n) N' (existential be)

    These finals of secondary derivation create denominal verbs of being, or verbs of attribu-

distinct NA and NI forms to serve as bases, such as in (395) and (396) (which have elements

tial to derive either an VAI or VII verb. So, for example, in (396), the VAI verb form has NA
shkihaa, 'new thing,' as initial, and the vn verb form has NI shkihii, 'new thing,' as initial. In
the other cases, corresponding to English N-y constructions, the appropriate final is added
to an inanimate noun.

9.11 Inanimate Intransitive Verbs

   In this section we will examine finals whose semantics makes them appropriate only to
inanimates. Many of these concepts have to do with states of the weather, landscape, sea-
sons, days, and the properties of liquids.
                                                                   9.11.1 Impersonal Verbs • 365



9.11.1 Impersonal Verbs

   There is a rich set of IMPERSONAL verb forms that are used to describe features of land-
scape and weather. Impersonal verbs are those which do usually have an explicit subject,
cannot be made plural, and generally have no participial forms, as in the following.

       *Shpaagnagaa maanda ki. I 'This land is deep in snow.'

   Instead, impersonal verbs are quite similar to English weather constructions which use
the dummy subject it, as in, 'it's raining,' or 'it's snowing.'

   Impersonal landscape verbs tend to have a structure as follows.

        Descriptive Initial    Environmental Medial -aa Final

   Most of these verbs have a medial (or pre-final) element specifying what feature of land-
scape is being described, for example, /-aagonag-/, 'snow,' /-akamig-/, 'ground, land,' and
/-adin-/, 'hill, mountain.' Often there are free nouns that correspond to these medials
(pre-finals) in meaning, but the morphological relationship between them and the corre-
sponding free noun is usually very weak, as can be seen from the following examples.

                     Medial/PF       Independent Noun
     'snow'          /-aagonag-/     goon, 'snow'
     'lake, water'   /-gam-/         zaaghigan 'lake'; nbiish 'water'; gamii 'lake' CL
     'hill'          /-adin-/        (no shared common term), wajiw in other Ojibwe
     'grass'         /-ashk(w)-/     miizhashk, 'blade of grass, stalk of hay'
     'leaves'        /-bag-/         niibiish, 'leaf

    Some of these elements show up in noun derivation, however, associated with NOUN
FINALS, as in the case of/-ashk(w)-/, which occurs in miizhashk Ni 'blade of grass,' and
pakweyashk NA 'cattail,' and /-bag-/, which shows up in ziiwbag NI 'rhubarb,' and nimkiibag
NI 'poison ivy.' They usually occur with an abstract nominalizing final /-w/.
    Note also that these impersonal verbs never have forms referring to people or animals as
the medial element, such as 'be fish there' or 'have animals in a certain way' (both poten-
tially used to describe some geographical area). Rather it appears that impersonal verbs
always pertain to either features of inert landscape, such as snow, ice, and hills, or to vegeta-
tion, such as grass, leaves, bushes, and trees.
    The initial elements of impersonal verbs are usually descriptive, that is, rather like
English adjectives of physical description, for example, /ishp-/, 'high,' and /dak-/, 'cold,'
though they may also be numbers, RELATIVE ROOTS, DIRECTIONAL ROOTS, or evaluative
366 • 9.11.1.1 Impersonal Verbs of General Conditions of Landscape


morphemes, such as /minw-/, 'good.' A few examples illustrate:

    (417)    relative root    piitaagnagaa    'be snow of a certain depth' (VII)
    (418)    directional      bmadnaa         'be a ridge of hills going along' (VII)
    (419)    evaluative       mnokmigaa       'be good/level ground' (VII)
    (420)    numeric          niizhgon'gad    'be two days ago, two days since' (vn)

    In some cases, as illustrated in (418), there appear to be metaphors of motion not unlike
those found in English, so there are expressions such as bmadnaa, literally, 'there are hills
going along, hills going by,' that is, an initial indicating direction of movement is used with
stationary objects such as a ridge. The only way a ridge can be said to 'go along,' is by hav-
ing physical extension over space.
    In the following sections I will outline some of the more common impersonal verbs,
grouped into broad semantic classes.

9.11.4 The Augment /-magad/ or /-migad/

    VII verbs can be readily derived from VAI verbs by addition of the final /-magad/ (or
sometimes /-migad/), as in the following examples. Note that stem-final short vowels usu-
ally lengthen before /-magad/, as in (546), and that /oo/ appears after nasal stems, as in (544).

    (544)    dgoshinoomgad          'arrive (from VAI dgoshin)'
    (545)    giizhiitaamgad         'be finished; be ready (from VAI giizhiitaa)'
    (546)    kidoomgad              'mean, say (from VAI kido)'
    (547)    maajaamgad             'leave (from VAI maajaa)'
    (548)    nokiimgad              'work (from VAI nokii)'
    (549)    zhiwoomgad             'take shape' (Od)

   The ending /-magad/ can also be redundantly added to VII verbs that end in a vowel, as in
gsinaamgad' from gsinaa, 'be cold (weather),' and temgad, from te, 'be [in a certain

9.12.5 Verbs Describing Body Part Attributes

   Attributes of body parts and states pertaining to body parts are expressed by means of
animate intransitive verbs in which the relevant body part is indexed with the appropriate
medial, and the possessor of the body part functions as the subject of the verb. The follow-
ing example illustrates the basic construction.

                       yekgaade                 yek-       -gaad-          -e
                       'have tired legs'        tired      leg             have

   If the body part represents a rigid object, especially a limb, hand, or foot, the classifica-
tory medial /-aakw-/, 'rigid organic solid,' sometimes occurs as well. The following exam-
ple illustrates this construction.

         ddaakwaakgaade         dadaakw-                          -aakw-          -gaad-   -e
         'have short legs'      short (redup of /dakw-/)          rigid organic   leg      have

    The presence of /-aakw-/ is optional, so that the lexeme ddaakgaade, lacking the ele-
ment, also occurs. This example also illustrates the use of DISTRIBUTIVE REDUPLICATION
with descriptive concepts such as /dakw-/, 'short' when the body part referent is plural, as it
commonly is, given that human bodies show bilateral symmetry. The pattern of reduplica-
tion has the form /CaCaa/, where C is the first consonant of the descriptive initial, in this
case /dakw-/, 'short.' If the stem begins with a vowel, such as /akw-/, 'be of such extent,' the
pattern of reduplication is /ayaa/, as in yaakwaakgaade, 'have legs of a certain length,' with
RELATIVE ROOT /akw-/, 'extent, degree.'
   The final element in these body part possessor verbs is /-e/, which merges with
stem-final /y/ to produce /ii/, e.g., gaagiijninjii, 'ANsg has sore hands,' with body part
medial /ninjy-/. A few body part medials, most of which end in /n/, are followed by what is
sometimes called a ZERO-FINAL, as in bookwaawgan, 'break one's back,' and
gaagiidaawgan, 'have a sore back.'
   Stems describing parts of the body may themselves function as initials, as in
shkaakdiyebi, 'have a tired backside (from sitting),' which has the VAI verb shkaakdiye,
'have a tired backside,' as initial, and a final, /-abi/, 'sitting.' Such constructions are dis-
cussed in the next section.
386 • 9.12.5 Verbs Describing Body Part Attributes


   Some body part medials have forms, or alternative forms, that are different from their
corresponding DEPENDENT NOUN forms. These include the following, among others:

                   Nominal Form            Medial Form           Gloss
                   -kaad                   -gaad-                'leg'
                   -ndib, -shtigwaan       -ndib-, -kwe-         'head'
                   -masad                  -ashkad-, -masad-     'stomach'
                   -dengway                -iingwe-              'face'
                   -bikon                  -aawgan-, -bikon-     'back'

   94      VAI /-BP Medial-e/        'have a<body part> that is...'

    The following verbs are also irregular, in that they lack an INCORPORATING FINAL (or

   Note also the interesting internal structure of the word mngijiimnagzi, 'be fat; have a
paunch,' which contains a medial element /-jii-/, 'belly,' along with the berrylike (round
object) classifier /-minag-/, to which is then added the customary descriptive VAI final /-izi/.

ing secondary Vll-final /-(y)aa/ to a VAI form, as in ggaanwaakgaadeyaa, 'have long legs'
(Od).

9.12.6 Bodily Actions and Movements

   Body part medials are also used in various expressions referring to actions or orienta-
tions of the body and its parts. These verbs encompass concepts such as washing, injury,
and positioning or orienting, among others. Because of the systematic ambiguity that exists
in Nishnaabemwin between states and the actions associated with entering the state, many
verbs are, at least for some speakers, ambiguous in their meanings between states and the
processes/events that give rise to the state, such as bookjaane, which for some speakers
means both 'have a broken nose,' and 'break one's nose.'

   (829)    baapiingwe        'smile' /-iingw-/ 'face'
   (830)    bookgaade         'break a leg, have a broken leg' /-gaad-/ 'leg'
   (831)    bookjaane         'break one's nose, have a broken nose' /-jaan-/ 'nose'
   (832)    booknike          'break an arm, have a broken arm' /-nik-/ 'arm'
   (833)    gziibiiggwewe     'wash one's neck' /-gwew-/ 'neck'
   (834)    gziibiigninjii    'wash one's hands' /-ninjy-/ 'hand'
   (835)    gziibiigzide      'wash one's feet' /-zid-/ 'foot'

9.12.9 Physical Actions of Parts of the Body with /-ni/

  97        VAI /-ni/          'act upon «a body part>

    Physical actions applied to body parts are commonly expressed in construction with the
final /-ni/. These forms show an interesting morphological structure, in that they have /-e/
(with variant liil after stems ending in /y/), following the body part, to which is then suffixed
/-ni/, but differ from processes of SECONDARY DERIVATION in that the complex initial is
often not itself a free word. Thus, for example, boodaakwenjiini, 'put one's hands into the
water,' appears to consist of a word boodaakwenjii, 'have one's hands in the water,' to
which is added /-ni/, but there is no free word ^boodaakwenjii.

    (857)    aazhgidkweni         'throw one's head back' /-ikw-/ 'head'
    (858)    biimskokweni         'turn/twist one's head around'

    (860)    boodaakwezdeni       'put one's feet into the water' /-zid-/ 'foot'
    (861)    daatgikweni          'tilt one's head backwards'
    (862)    dpikweni             'stick one's head through an opening'

9.12.10 Middle Verbs with /-ho/

    A few verbs, typically involving action upon the body with an instrument, show final

e.g., (877) has a corresponding VTA, nskwew, 'comb AN's hair.' Some forms, such as (874)
and (876) are REFLEXIVES based on transitive verbs; verbs of this sort, in which an actor acts
upon her/himself, are sometimes called MIDDLES.

9.12.13 Verbs of Speaking

   103      VAI /-mo/          'speech, speaking'

9.12.17 Actor-Focus Detransitivizing Finals

    A very common derivational process is that of DETRANSITIVIZATION, which derives an
INTRANSITIVE verb from a TRANSITIVE, by eliminating or suppressing the GOAL role, which
simultaneously focuses on the ACTOR by making it the only role. Both transitive animate
(VTA) and transitive inanimate (VTI) verbs may be detransitivized. Detransitivization is par-
ticularly important in Nishnaabemwin, as only intransitive verbs may derive nouns, as in
naadmaagewin, 'help, aid,' derived from VTA naadmaw, 'help AN,' by the addition of
detransitivizing suffix /-ge/, then adding NOMINALIZING suffix /-win/.

9.12.17.1 Actor Focus Detransitive /-ge/

  127       VAI /-ge/        actor focus detransitive

   The suffix /-ge/, often preceded by LINK VOWEL /i/, is added to a host of transitive stems
to produce DETRANSITIVE actor focus verbs. Transitive stems that end in /-aw/ coalesce
/-aw/ and /-i-ge/ to produce /-aage/, as in the following examples.

   (1089) aankanootmaage         'interpret'
   (1090) bkinaage               'win a contest'
   (1091) bzindaage              'listen (to people)'
   (1092)    dngishkaage         'kick people'
   (1093) jiibaakwaage           'do the cooking; be the cook (for others)'
   (1094)    mgoshkaajiikaage    'be a bother'
   (1095) naadmaage              'help people'
   (1096)    nataage             'play a certain game; gamble thus'
   (1097) nbendaage              'sleep over'
   (1098) nitaage                'hear people say thus'
   (1099) nootaage               'repeat what was heard'
   (1100)    ntaage              'kill; butcher; commit murder'
   (1101)    taage               'play at a game; gamble'
404 • 9.12.17.1 Actor Focus Detransitive /-ge/



    (1102)   wiindmaage             'tell, relate, report'

    The formjiibaakwaage, 'do the cooking, be the cook (for others)' illustrates another
aspect of detransitive verbs, namely that they inherit some sense of the semantic role rela-
tionships of the transitive verbs they are derived from, even though the roles can no longer
be explicitly stated. The verbjiibaakwaage, for example, is derived from a benefactive verb,
jiibaakwaw, 'cook for AN,' and the detransitive verb retains some sense of doing cooking
 explicitly for the benefit of others. Similar effects can be seen with verbs that have incorpo-
rated elements, such as the following, all of which have the medial element /-ndib-/, 'head,'
 and which, as intransitive forms, retain the notion of action applied to the head of the goal.

    (1103) bgaskiigndibehge           'knock people on the head'
    (1104) bgaskndibehge              'slap people on the head'
    (1105) bkitendbehge               'beat people on the head'

    Many transitive verbs have incorporated elements that refer to an inanimate goal that is
made secondary in the PREDICATION, for example, daanzhewen, 'dim the lights on AN,' in
which the lights are secondary, or naadaabkinan, 'collect payment for IN,' in which the
payment is secondary. When the PRIMARY GOAL role is absorbed through detransitivization,
these SECONDARY GOALS might appear to become more primary, as, for example, in
daanzhewebjige, 'dim the light, turn down the lights,' and naadaabkin'ge, 'collect pay-
ment.' Note however, that these secondary goals only seem salient because of the English
glosses; more precise glosses for these two intransitives might be 'do light-dimming,' and
'do payment-collecting,' respectively, where there is no overt object, but rather a compound
verb that includes the notion of the secondary goal within the meaning of the verb itself,
rather than as an independent entity.

   The final /-(i)ge/ is also used in combination with a VTI element /-wit/ in borrowed words
having to do with the use of technology, such as print-wichge, type-wichge,
photocopy-wichge, videotape-wichge, tape-wichge (audiotape, videotape), vacuum-wichge,
and staple-wichge. Evidently these verbs are modeled on a VTI stem with a general instru-
mental final which is then detransitivized with /-(i)ge/. They can be compared to borrowed
verbs formed with /-(n)wi/, such as skiinwi, 'ski,' skidoonwi, 'skidoo, and gas-up-wi.

blance to transitive forms. In (1145), for example, the derivational structure is evidently

ending in /-gamigw/, and in certain verbs such as biindge, 'enter (a structure).'

    (1144) koge       'assemble (of groups)'
    (1145) zhige      'build a house'

9.12.17.2 Actor Focus Detransitive /-iwe/, Human Goal

   128       VAI /-(i)we/      actor focus detransitive, human goal

    The DETRANSITIVIZING suffix /-(i)we/ is most commonly attached to VTA stems that end
in /h/, /N/, /S/, and sometimes /n/, and derives intransitive verbs that apply to unspecified
human goals. Thus, for example baabiihwe, 'wait' can only be used in reference to waiting
                                                  9.12.17.3 Actor Focus Detransitive /-aaso/ • 407


for people, and would not be appropriately used if the object of one's waiting were not peo-
ple. The suffix thus detransitivizes, but at the same time leaves a trace of the goal's seman-
tics (as human, animate), in the meaning of the intransitive.
    Stems ending in /N/ and /S/ usually show PALATALIZATION to /zh/ and /sh/ before this
suffix, due to the presence of III. For example, the stem /bimidaabaaN/ + /iwe/ produces
bmidaabaazhwe, 'drag, haul people around; drive a taxi.' Note, though, that dkonwe, 'hold,
arrest people,' (1148), fails to show palatalization. In other dialects, however, its final /n/ is
not /N/ (see, e.g., Nichols and Nyholm 1995:41).

    (1146)   baabiihwe              ' wait (for people)'
    (1147)   bmidaabaazhwe          'drag/haul people around; drive a taxi'
    (1148)   dkonwe                 'hold, arrest people'
    (1149)   gnagjiibzhiwe          'tickle (someone)'
    (1150)   maajiiwzhiwe           'take people away'
    (1151)   maajiizhwe             'take people away'
    (1152)   moozhhowe              'give haircuts'
    (1153)   nbwaachhiwe            'visit (people)'
    (1154)   niimhiwe               'give/hold a dance'
    (1155)   njihwe                 'fight for some reason'
    (1156)   njin'zhiwe             'fight/cause harm for some reason'
    (1157)   nshiwe                 'kill; commit murder'
    (1158)   nsitamoohwe            'explain things to people (by illustrating)'

   The form miigwe, 'give' has a suppletive stem, derived as it is from miinaad, 'give some-
thing to AN' (stem /miiN/). A form based on wiijiiw, 'go with AN,' appears irregular, but
has its form due to the simplification of consonants that occurs with syncope, adjusting
from /wiijiiwiwe/ to /wiijiiwe/.

    (1159) wiijiiwe                 'go along with/accompany others'

9.12.17.3 Actor Focus Detransitive /-aaso/

   129       VAIAaaso/         actor focus detransitive

    A small number of verbs, based on TRANSITIVE INANIMATE (VTI) STEMS, take a final
/-aaso/ to derive DETRANSITIVE forms. The VTI theme suffix (/-am/ or /-oo/) is not present in
the derived form. The form mookdaaso, 'whittle,' lacks a transitive correspondent in many
dialects of Anishinaabemowin.
408 • 9.12.18 Reflexive /-idizo/



              VAI Form       VAI Gloss          VTI Form       VTI Gloss
    (1160)    gkendaaso      'be intelligent'   /gikend+am/ 'know s.t.'

9.12.18 Reflexive /-idizo/

   130       VAI /-idizo/      reflexive

    REFLEXIVE verbs are those in which an actor acts upon himself or herself, as in
bdakhodzo, 'prick oneself.' Such verbs are freely made from any transitive animate (VTA)
verb, by attaching the complex /-idizo/ to the bare VTA stem. Only transitive animate verbs
can have reflexive forms; transitive inanimate (VTI) verbs never do, because of the rule that
transitive relations must always involve at least one animate, as either ACTOR or GOAL, and a
transitive inanimate reflexive would have to have an inanimate actor and goal. VTA stems
ending in /-aw/ show COALESCENCE with the reflexive suffix to produce /-aadizo/, as in
(1165), below (from stem /biidaw/, 'bring something for AN'). Other aspects of morpholog-
ical behaviour are as with the RECIPROCAL, which is discussed below. Reflexive verbs are
INTRANSITIVE in Nishnaabemwin. The reflexive suffix appears to be complex, made up of
an element /-idi/ that also seems to be present in the motion final /-bahidi/, 'run as a group'
and in the reciprocal, /-idi/. In reflexive and reciprocal constructions, its usage suggests the
absorption of the goal role, rendering the verb intransitive. The additional element /-zo/ on
reflexive forms is a common VAI final (see e.g., finals 24 and 25, above, p. 359).
    The following examples illustrate a few reflexive forms. Several of these forms have spe-
cialized meanings, especially "middle" senses in which the actor acts on his/her own behalf.

    (1164)    bdakhodzo            'prick oneself
    (1165)    biidaadzo            'bring s.t. for one's own use'
    (1166)    gg wepnandzo         'make every effort; try very hard (in spite of illness)'
    (1167)    gtaamg wendizo       'think that one is the greatest' (W, CL)
    (1168)    dbendizo             'be on one's own'
    (1169)    gziing wehdizo       'wash/wipe one's face'

   Although the reflexive is extremely productive, and its meaning transparent, there are
occasional irregularities, as in the following example, where the reflexive form appears to
be based on a VTA stem /nawapwaankodaw/, instead of the attested VTA stem
/nawapwaankaw/.
                                                                  9.12.19 Reciprocal /-idi/ • 409



   (1170)    nwapwaankaw        nwapwaankodaadzo           'pack a lunch for oneself

9.12.19 Reciprocal /-idi/

  131       VAI/-(i)di/       reciprocal

   The RECIPROCAL, in which the ACTOR and GOAL act upon each other concurrently, is
formed by the addition of /-(i)di/ to the VTA stem. Stems ending in /m/, such as (1173) and
(1176) below, attach /-di/ without the initial link vowel, I'll. VTA stems ending in /aw/ show
COALESCENCE with /-i-di/ to produce /aadi/, as in (1171) and (1178) below. A few reciprocals
do not seem to have corresponding productive VTA forms, such as (1172) below.

   (1171)   ggweji-bkinaadi    'compete against AN' (< bkinaw 'beat/win against AN')
   (1172)   ggwejkandi         'race against AN'
   (1173)   giikaandi          'be engaged in a quarrel with AN' (< giikaam 'yell at AN')
   (1174)   maawnjihdi         'assemble'(<maawnjih'gather AN together')
   (1175)   miigaadi           'fight each other' (< miigaazh 'fight against AN')
   (1176)   ndaapnendi         'quarrel with e.o. for a reason < ndaapnem 'quarrel w/ AN'
   (1177)   njinnidi           'fight with/harm each other for some reason'
   (1178)   taadi              'bet one another, gamble with one another' (Od) < /ataw/
   (1179)   webiichgedi        'race each other'
   (1180)   wiijiindi          'accompany each other' (< wiijiiw 'accompany AN')

9.12.20 Incorporated Goal Verbs

    There is a group of verbs which INCORPORATE the NOMINAL goal of the action into the
verb itself, as a medial, as in the following examples. The derived verb is invariably
inflected as an intransitive.

             VAI                 Gloss                         Goal Noun        Gloss
    (1181) moonhapnii            'pick/dig potatoes'           /apiny/          'potato'
    (1182) baapiiwkizneshin      'brush off one's shoes'       /makizin/        'shoe'
    (1183) naajmiijme            'fetch food'                  /miijim/         'food'
    (1184) gezbinaagne           'clear the dishes'            /onaagan/        'dish'

   These verbs share a similar structure, consisting of a transitive initial component, a nom-
inal medial element corresponding to a free noun, and a final element l-d that generally
occurs after noun medials, such as the body part terms in descriptive verbs of body parts,
410 • 9.12.20 Incorporated Goal Verbs


e.g., m(n)gizde, 'have a big foot' (from /mang+i+zid+e/), which has a medial body part term

in /apiny/, 'potato,' in (1181), above.

9.12.20.1 Special (Lexicalized) Medials
   There are some verbs that have a structure like that of an incorporating verb, but which
have medials that do not correspond to presently used independent nouns. The following
examples illustrate.

   137     Medial /-aabikw-/       money

    (1197) naadaabkwe                'go get one's money'
    (1198) gindaabkwe                'count one's money'
    (1199) maawndowaabkwe            'collect money, pool money'

   The independent word for money is zhoon'yaa. The medial /-aabikw-/ is related to the
inorganic classifier /-aabik/, and suggests an older period of history in which money was
more commonly in the form of coins than paper currency.

  138      Medial/-is-/         '(fire)wood'

   (1200) mnise                      'chop firewood; cut firewood'
   (1201) bgidnise                   'put wood in the fire'

    For some speakers the general independent word for firewood is msan, plural msanan;
for other speakers mshi is the singular and msan is the PLURAL. In this case, it appears that
the independent noun arose from the use of a GENERALIZED POSSESSOR FORM with prefix
/m-/, with a structure /m-is-i/, with inanimate noun final l-il. This medial would seem to be
related to medial /-isag-/, 'floor,' as well.
412 • 9.12.20.2 Other Quasi-Incorporating Verbs



   139     Medial /-konay-/       'clothing'

    (1202) biiskon'ye            'put on clothes'
    (1203) giiskon'ye            'take off clothes'
    (1204) msko-kon'ye           'wear red clothes

    There is no widely-used general independent term for clothing. At Wikwemikong,
gwiwin (plural gwiwnan or gwinan) is used. Gwinaanan (plural) is used at CL and R, and
ndahiiman, lit., 'my things,' at W and CL. Many speakers now have /w/ in place of tradi-
tional /y/ in /-konay-/, so will say, e.g., biiskonwe for (1202).

9.12.20.2 Other Quasi-Incorporating Verbs
    In addition to the incorporating verbs mentioned above, there are verbs with transitive
initials, but which lack the incorporating final /-e/. The medials in these verbs bear no rela-
tion to independent nouns with equivalent meanings. It might be best in these cases to ana-
lyze the medial+final complex as some type of complex final. Some examples follow:

   140     VAI /-aawaso/       'take care of, attend to children'

 binoojiinh, though a specialized form for child also occurs in niijaan 'si, 'be pregnant, have

    (1206) gzhaawso             'baby-sit, take care of one's children'

    (1208) nbehaawso            'put the children to bed'
    (1209) shamaawso            'feed one's offspring'

   141      VAI /-aawazo/      'attend to a group of people, things'

    These verbs are possibly built on a COMPLEX INITIAL, structurally consisting of some ini-
tial, such as biindge-, 'enter, inside' in combination with the verbal element /aawad, aawaz/,
'haul' (compare aawdoon, 'haul s.t. (inan.) and aawazh, 'haul s.t. (an.)), to which is then
added a VAI final, /o/. But I have no evidence to support such an analysis.

9.12.21 VAI Finals Used in Secondary Derivation

   Several finals occurring in VAI verbs are only used in secondary derivation. I list some of
the more common and productive ones in this section.

9.12.21.1 Verbs of Feigning, Pretending

  145       VAIAkaazo/        'pretend to V; pretend to be (a) N'

   VAI final /-kaazo/ can be added to virtually any VAI verb to derive a VERB OF PRETEND-
ING (also sometimes called a VERB OF FEIGNING). Such forms always represent secondary
derivation, since the initial component is always a free (independent) word. The final vow-
414 • 9.12.21.1 Verbs of Feigning, Pretending


els of the initial component show variable adjustment when /-kaazo/ is added. Some stems
ending in /aa/, for example, nbaa, 'sleep,' change their final vowel to /e/, producing
nbekaazo; however, the vowel /aa/ is retained with initial ndamtaa, 'be busy.' In the cases of
verbs ending in I'll, sometimes there is lengthening of the final vowel, as in (1232) and (1233),
whereas in yekgaabwikaazo, 'pretend to be tired from standing,' and mwikaazo, 'pretend to
cry,' there is no lengthening. Stems that end in /o/ consistently show lengthening, as in
(1230).

   (1221)     aakshkadekaazo         'pretend to have a stomach-ache' « aakshkade
   (1222)    aakziikaazo             'pretend to be sick' « aakzi
   (1223)    gajiikaazo              'pretend to be shy' « gaji
   (1224)    gdimaagziikaazo         'pretend to be poor' « gdimaagzi
   (1225)    giiwshkwebiikaazo       'pretend to be drunk' « giiwshkwebii

   (1232)     niinmiziikaazo         'pretend to be weak' « niinmizi
   (1233)    nshkaadziikaazo         'pretend to be angry' « nshkaadzi
   (1234)    wiidgemaagnikaazo       'pretend to be married' « wiidgemaagan (NA)
   (1235)    wiisniikaazo            'pretend to eat' « wiisni
   (1236)    yekgaabwikaazo          'pretend to be tired standing' « yekgaabwi

9.12.21.3 Verbs of Possession

  147        VAINPoss/-i/       'have N'


   Verbs of possession are formed by adding final l-\l to a THIRD PERSON POSSESSED NOMI-
NAL THEME. Nouns forming possessed themes with suffix /-im/ show the suffix in their cor-
responding verbs of possession, as in (1260), while those that lack it may not, as in (1263).
Stems that end in /w/ merge it with the final /-i/.to produce /o/, as in (1259). Stems that take
augment /-aa/ in their locative forms show the augment in verbs of possession, as in (1267)
and (1269), which have locatives nmasdaang and nzidaang, respectively. Words that have
SUPPLETIVE possessive stems, such as nimosh, 'dog,' and binoojiinh, 'child,' use the posses-
sive stems to form verbs of possession, as can be seen from (1261) and (1268). Verbs of pos-
session relating to body parts use the possessed form of the noun, as opposed to the medial
form, as can be seen from (1122), which has a medial form /-gaad-/ as opposed to possessed
stem /+kaad/.
