   POSSESSION WITH EXISTENTIAL YAA. It is also possible to indicate possession with VAI
yaa, 'be (in a location), exist,' as in the following example:

   (10)   Yaawan wgwisan.

          'Sine has a son.' (lit. 'HerlHis son exists.') (AM39.151)

          Yaawan vai ind 3obv 'ANobv exists'; wgwisan nod 3sProx(3obv) 'ANsg's son.'


    TRANSITIVE VERBS OF POSSESSION. Possession may also be expressed with transitive
verbs yaawaad (VTA, stem /ayaaw/) and yaang (VTI, stem /ayaam/), which are related to the
intransitive existential/locational verb yaa, illustrated in example (10), above. The following
examples illustrate the use of transitive forms.

   (11) Gaa wii gii-yaawaasiiwaan dbahgiiswaanan zhaazhi go Nishnaabeg.

          The Indians of old had no clocks or watches.' (AM27.1)

          Gaa wii av 'not'; gii-yaawaasiiwaan vta ind neg 3pProx>3obv 'ANpl did not have
          ANobv'; dbahgiiswaanan na 3obv 'clock/watch'; zhaazhi av 'long ago'; go av 'indeed';
          Nishnaabeg na 3pProx 'Indians.'


   (12) Gye go mii gii-wiidgemaad, gye go mii wiiba gii-yaawaawaad binoojiinyan.

          'Then he married her; and soon they had children.' (AM28.6)

          Gye av 'and'; go av 'indeed'; mii av 'then'; gii-wiidgemaad vta conj 3sProx>3obv
          '(CONJ) ANsg married ANobv'; gye av 'and'; go av 'indeed'; mii av 'then'; wiiba av
          'soon'; gii-yaawaawaad vai conj 3pProx>3obv '(CONJ) ANpl had ANobv';
          binoojiinyan na 3obv 'child(ren).'


   (13) Bngiishenh ge nii ndayaan mtigwaakiins maa endaayaan.

          'I too have a small plot of wooded land there where I dwell.' (AM 15.11)

          Bngiishenh av 'a little'; ge av 'also'; miprpers Isg T; ndayaan vti ind ls>0s 'I have
          INsg'; mtigwaakiins ni Os 'stand of trees'; maa av 'there'; endaayaan vai ic conj Is
          '(CCNJ) where I live.'
418 • 9.12.21.4 Verbs of Constructive Application


   (14) Wedi waa-ni-bmiseg mil iw fair wii-yaamwaad giw Nishnaabeg maa Waabow
        Island.
          'Next week the Indians on Walpole Island are going to hold a fair.' (AMI7.1)

          Wedi av 'next'; waa-ni-bmiseg vii ic conj 0 '(CCNJ) IN will occur in time' (week); mii

   Fluent speakers have clear preferences as to whether derived (intransitive) verbs of pos-
session as opposed to transitive verbs of possession are more appropriate for given refer-
ents.
   PARTICIPIAL VERBS OF KIN RELATIONSHIP. Some kin relations are expressed by PARTI-
CIPIALIZED VERBS OF POSSESSION, such as weniijaanid, 'mother,' which derives from
/oniijaani/, 'have a child,' with SUPPLETIVE possessed noun stem /-niijaan/, 'child.' By com-
parison, the verb nahaangshiimi, 'have a son-in-law' VAI (M), does not show the INITIAL
CHANGE associated with participles, clearly marking it as a verb of possession form.
   The verb form woosi, 'have a father' (CL, W) is somewhat unusual in its possessive
theme, in apparently having a third person (POSSESSOR) prefix /w/, which does not occur
with the simple third person possessed noun, oosan, 'ANsg's father.' Related to this word is
the form weyoosid, 'a man's child' NA, which appears to add third person prefix /o-/ to the
stem /oos/, producing /oyoos/, which is then undergoes INITIAL CHANGE to become
/weyoos/.

9.12.21.4 Verbs of Constructive Application

   148      VAI N/-ke/          'gather N, hunt N, work with N, etc.'

    The final /-ke/ takes a noun as its INITIAL and derives verbs that generally involve gather-
ing or harvesting when the noun is a plant or agricultural product; hunting, when the noun is
an animal; manufacture, when the noun is an object of manufacture; and manipulation for
useful purpose, when the noun represents a manipulable object, including such things as
semaa, 'tobacco,' gaaway, 'porcupine quills,' and even mnidoo, 'spirit being.' Generalizing,
this final can be said to standardly derive verbs of constructive social activity as applied to
whatever the initial represents. In some cases, though, meanings are not entirely predictable
from the nature of the noun referent, such as with bkwaakdoke, which does mean 'make a
ball,' but generally, 'play ball,' though of course the same word could be used with the
former meaning. And when the noun referents are nini, 'man,' or kwe, 'woman,' in combi-
nation with the preverb nda-, 'look to [do something],' the meaning is that of lascivious pur-
suit of the opposite sex. This is quite interesting, because in these cases, the meaning is a
specialized composition involving a PREVERB, an INITIAL, and a FINAL.
                                                       9.12.21.4 Verbs of Constructive Application • 419



   This final is quite productive, occurring with many borrowed words, such as in the fol-
lowing example. Note too toast-ke, 'make toast,' and homework-ke, 'do homework' (M).

   (15) A: Gojiing gga-wiisnimi. B: Mii gsha, gga-picnickemi.
         'A: "We'll eat outside." B: "For sure, we'll have a picnic.'" (ED)

            Gojiing av 'out of doors'; gga-wiisnimi vai ind 21 'we (incl.) will eat'. Mii av 'so'; gsha
            av 'indeed'; gga-picnickemi vai ind21 'we (incl.) will have a picnic.'

   (1271)     bkwaakdoke               'play ball'
   (1272)     dehminke                  'pick strawberries'
   (1273)     gaawyike                  'do quill-work'
   (1274)     giigoonyke                'go fishing'
   (1275) jiigke                        'hunt fishers' (n.b., the animal)
   (1276) jiimaanke                     'make boats/canoes'
   (1277)     kokmidaaske               'make socks' (Od)

   (1279)     mdaaske                   'make socks'

9.13 Roots and Initials

    The elements that function as initials are semantically varied, though in some cases there
are rather obvious semi-paradigmatic groupings of related concepts. In the following notes I
list some notional groupings of initials, particularly those that are more common. My pre-
sentation doesn't begin to account for the richness of Nishnaabemwin initials, and is offered
only as a pointer to a rich area of language that is largely neglected in this study.

9.13.1 Directional Roots

   There is a set of four DIRECTIONAL ROOTS that orient motion events to some reference
point, often the speaker's location, or some reference point established within the discourse.
These elements are discussed elsewhere, e.g., in their PREVERB forms in Chapter 3.9.2.3, in
their LOCATIVE functions in Chapter 15.2.3, and in their use as TENSE/ASPECTUAL markers
in Chapter 16.2.8. Here I provide a few examples of their usage in intransitive verbs.

                                      Directional Roots
              /biid-/, /biij-/            'toward, come and. . . '
              /anim-/                     'away, go (away) and. . . '
              /him-/                      'along, go along and. . . '
              /bibaam-/, /babaam-/        'around, go around and. . . '

             Directional root /biid-/, 'toward speaker, come and...'
    (1295)   biidaagmose          'walk this way in snowshoes'
    (1296)   biidaasmabi          'sit facing this way'
    (1297)   biijdiyeshin         'lie with one's rearend facing this way'
    (1298)   biij wine            'come carrying things'

             Directional root /anim-/, 'away from speaker, go and...'
    (1299) nimaajmo               'walk away talking about something'
    (1300) nimaanzhe              'head off with lights on' (of vehicles)'
    (1301) nimwewetoo             'head off making noise'

             Directional root /him-/, 'along, by, go along and...'
    (1302) bmaanzhe              'go [along] with lights on' (of vehicles)
    (1303) bmaashi               'sail [along], be blown [along] by the wind'
    (1304) bmademo               'go [along] crying'
                                                                      9.13.2 Relative Roots-421



              Directional root /babaam-/, /bibaam-/, 'go around...'
    (1305) bbaamaajmo               'spread a rumour'(lit.,'talk around')
    (1306) bbaamdaabaazo            'drag one's family around, drag one's things around'
    (1307) bbaamgaa                 'dance around'

9.13.2 Relative Roots

   RELATIVE ROOTS are used to specify various relations between a verb and some element,
which may serve to indicate the predicate's source, reason, manner, location, quantity,
degree, or extent. They are discussed elsewhere as well, e.g., Chapter 3.9.2.2, Chapter 13.3,
and Chapter 17.1. The following chart provides the basic (UNDERLYING) form of each ROOT,
along with a number of "written" forms, representing the various ALLOMORPHIC variants of
each root.

      Basic Form          Written Forms            Gloss
      /iN-/               /i-/, /in-/, /izh-/      'to; in such a way'
      /ond-/              /ond-/, /onj-/           'from, source, reason'
      /apiit-/            /apiit-/, /apiich-/      'extent; particular amount'
      /akw-/              /akw-/                   'extent; particular degree'
      /daN-/              /dan-/, /dazh-/          'there, in that location'
      /daSw-/             /dasw-/, /dash-/         'so many; particular number'

    The relative root /iN-/ shows considerable variation in the way it attaches to finals. In
some cases it surfaces as /in-/, as in naabdizi /inaabadizi/, 'be put to a certain use' (VAI) and
nendam /inendam/, 'decide to do [something]; think; vote' (VAI). In certain cases in which
/iN-/ is attached to finals that begin with the consonant /b/, and perhaps historically /g/, the
/N/ is realized only as a STRENGTHENING of the initial consonant of the final, for example, as
in pizo, 'drive in a particular way, drive along a particular route' (VAI), from /iN+bizo/,
patoo, 'run in a particular way, run along a particular route' (VAI), from /iN+batoo/, and
pahwe, 'run from something in a particular way, run from something to a particular place'
(VAI), from /iN+bahiwe/. The relative root /iN-/ is also present in the verb kido /ikido/, 'say
something' (VAI), where it appears to be combined with /gido/, which perhaps shows up in
the word giigdo /giigido/, 'talk, speak,' which also shows REDUPLICATION.

9.14 Summary Notes on Roots and Preverbs

   In summary, Nishnaabemwin words have four well-defined DERIVATIONAL positions:

                              Preverb   Initial Medial Final

    The boundary between the preverb and initial position is relatively porous, and some ele-
ments show variable representation depending on the nature of the material they are associ-
ated with. For example, the aspectual element /maad/, 'start,' appears as preverb maajii- in
maajii-giigdo, 'begin to talk/speak,' but as an initial in maadaapi, 'start to laugh.' Preverbs
seem to be readily formed from roots by the addition of/-i/ or /-ii/, and there is no logical
limit to the number of preverbs that may occur in a word. For example, there are six in the
tongue twister Gga-gchi-niisaakye-zaagji-ziinkiigmaane-bskiigdigwe-bmiboojgesahin, T11
throw you down the hill so hard the snot will come out of your nose and your knees will
buckle.' Some of these preverbs are themselves complex elements with meanings such as
'be flowing with snot,' and 'have buckled knees.' As with all areas of Nishnaabemwin gram-
mar, the language is so rich in resources that I can only begin to address things in this mono-
graph. Many common preverbs, such as the DIRECTIONALS, have somewhat different
PREVERB and ROOT forms, and there is at least one directional preverb that has no root form.
A few other preverbs have no root forms, most notably TENSE and MODAL markers such as
/ga-/, FUTURE, /wii-/, VOLITIONAL FUTURE, and /daa-/, MODAL. The ubiquitous preverb
gchi-, 'great, extreme,' doesn't appear to have a productive root correspondent. All of the
relative roots have preverb forms, which are commonly used. The relative root /iN/ some-
times forms an initial in construction with verbs, especially those that begin with /a/ or /aa/,
as in naabdizi, 'be put to a certain use,' where /iN/ is attached to aabdizi, 'be useful,' and
nankii, 'act in a certain way, works in a certain way' where /iN/ is attached to nokii, 'work.'

9.15 Additional Reading

   The linguistic topics in this chapter and the following two have been studied in consider-
able detail by many scholars, including Bloomfield (1958 and 1962), Goddard (1990),
                                                                 9.15 Additional Reading • 425


Johnston (1978), Nichols (1980), O'Meara (1990), and Rhodes (1976a). Bloomfield 1958
gives the most articulated list of word-components for Nishnaabemwin, since it is a gram-
mar based on Andrew Medler's speech. Bloomfield 1962 is a truly virtuoso piece of detailed
analysis, but is written in a telegraphic style that make it of use only to the most dedicated
and persevering students. Basil Johnston's language course (Johnston 1978) and lexicon
(Johnston 1979) provide very useful and stimulating thematically organized groupings of
Nishnaabemwin vocabulary as well, with a native speaker's perspective. Perusing any dic-
tionary (Rhodes 1985, Nichols and Nyholm 1995, McGregor 1987) of Nishnaabemwin or a
related dialect of Ojibwe will reward the student with many gems. Piggott and Grafstein
1983, a dictionary with a large corpus of words representing Manitoulin Island Odawa, has
a valuable listing of words sorted on the basis of their spellings from the end of the word
forward, so that words with the same finals are listed together. While the spelling system
that Piggott and Grafstein use is quite different from the modern standard, conversion is
very easy.

The Derivation of Transitive Verbs




10.1 Introduction

   In this chapter we will examine the internal structure of TRANSITIVE verbs. A transitive
predication typically involves action by an ACTOR on a GOAL, as in the following examples.

                                VTA                             VTI
               (1) waabam              'see AN'     waabndan       'see IN'
               (2) aabjih              'use AN'     aabjitoon      'use IN'
               (3) noondaw             'hear AN'    noondan        'hear IN'
               (4) mo, maw, mon        'eat AN'     miijin         'eat IN'

    Both actors and goals may be animate, or either the actor or the goal may be inanimate,
but both cannot be inanimate— a transitive predication in Nishnaabemwin must have at
least one animate argument. Most commonly actors, as initiators and controllers of actions,
are animate. Transitive verbs typically come in pairs, distinguished according to the gram-
matical gender of their goals. Transitive verbs with animate goals are transitive animate
(VTA or TA), and those with inanimate goals are transitive inanimate (VTI or TI). In this
grammar, transitive verbs are often cited in their imperative forms used with a singular sec-
ond person actor acting upon a third person animate goal (singular or plural), as in gnawaa-
bam, 'look at AN' (VTA) or an inanimate goal (VTI), as in gnawaabndan, 'look at IN'
Rhodes 1985 cites transitive verbs with conjunct order inflection, with an animate third per-
son singular actor and a third person obviative goal, e.g., gnawaabmaad. I use both of these
citation forms depending on their relative usefulness to a given point of discussion.
    Like intransitive verbs (see Chapter 9), transitive verbs often show paired sets (VTA and
VTI) differing only on the basis of their FINALS, as in examples (1) through (3) above. This
chapter focuses on the rich internal structure of transitive verbs.
                                                                  10.2 The Structure of Transitive Verbs • 427



10.2 The Structure of Transitive Verbs

    Transitive verbs, like intransitives, have a basic PRIMARY DERIVATIONAL structure con-
sisting of INITIAL, optional MEDIAL, and FINAL components. The initial position is
open-ended as to what may fill it, and may contain a wide variety of elements, such as
/aand-/, 'change,' (e.g., aandkwen, 'move AN's head over'), /giishk-/, 'sever(ed), sheer'
(e.g., giishknem, 'bite AN off cleanly in one's mouth)' /aabad-/, 'be used' (e.g., aabjitoon,
'use IN, put IN to use), and thousands of others. In some constructions, such as causatives
made from VAI verbs, independent word stems may serve as initials, as in mwih, 'make AN
cry,' with VAI mwi, 'cry,' as initial, and baapih, 'laugh at AN,' with VAI baapi, 'laugh,' as
initial.
    VARIATION IN ROOT FORMS. Many ROOTS have forms that vary in their final consonant,
depending on what final they are attached to. Some roots in particular show an alternation
between final /d/, /j/ (IPA /d3/), and /z/ (or /s/, or both), as illustrated by these examples:

                                         Variant Forms of Roots
              Gloss                Ending in /d/ Ending in /j/             Ending in /z/, /s/
              'push'               gaand          gaanj                    gaanz
              'face up'            aazhgid        aazhgij                  aazhgiz
              'heavy'              gwiid          gwiij                    gwnz
              'try'                ggwed          ggwej                    ggwez
              'wake'               mad            maj                      maz
              'triumph'            zhaagood       zhaagooj                 zhaagooz
              'grab'               nwad           nwaj                     nwaz
              'weak, timid'        zhaagood       zhaagooj                 zhaagooz, zhaagoos

   A few examples are provided here to illustrate these patterns. As with the examples
throughout this chapter, VTA forms are given to the left of VTI forms.1

                                                  Root /gaand/, 'push'
        (5)   /d/ gaandin, ~zh              gaandnan                 'push X' (with an instrument)
        (6)   /j/ gaanj webshkaw            gaanj webshkan          'push X' (with foot or body)
        (7)   /z/ gaanzkaw                  gaanzkan                'push against X' (with foot, body)

    (20)      /j/    majwebin ~zh     'wake AN by shaking them'
    (21)      /z/    mazom            'wake AN by talking'
    (22)      /z/    mazkaw           'wake AN by bumping into them'

    As can be seen, particular finals seem to be associated with particular forms of these
roots that show variation in their final consonants. The alternation between /d/ and /j/ can
sometimes be explained in terms of the phonological process of PALATALIZATION, dis-
cussed in Chapter 2.8.1.8, Palatalization, beginning on page 86. The alternation between /d/
and /z/, though, cannot, since /z/ seems to occur before /o/, as in (21) and palatalization usu-
ally only applies in the vicinity of high front vowels (lil or /ii/) or the glide /y/. The finals
/-ikaw/, 'cause using foot or body' and /-om/, 'cause with speech,' both require stem vari-
 ants in final /z/.
    LEXICAL REDUPLICATION IN ROOTS. Many roots show REDUPLICATION in transitive
 contexts, usually expressing such things as repeated or extensive action applied to a goal, or
 the plurality of actors. Reduplication is always PREFIXAL. One reduplicative pattern involves
 copying an initial consonant and forming a syllable with the vowel /aa/, as in naanookgwin-
jim, 'soak AN in order to soften,' (VTA) which can be compared with the unreduplicated
 root in nookzi, 'be soft' (VAI) (root /nook/, 'soft'), waawiindmaw, 'promise AN something'
                                                       10.2 The Structure of Transitive Verbs • 429



(VTA), as opposed to unreduplicated wiindmaw, 'tell AN something, advise AN of some-
thing' (VTA) (root/wiind(amaw)/, baabaapnodaw, 'make fun of AN,' beside baapi, 'laugh'
(VAI), and waawaabam, 'stare at AN,' beside waabam, 'see AN' The form baapaashkzaw,
'shoot at AN (plural subject)' (VTA) compared to baashkzaw, 'shoot at AN' (VTA), illus-
trates another aspect of this pattern of reduplication, namely that root-initial OBSTRUENTS
such as /b/ are sometimes made FORTIS (i.e., become their corresponding 'hard' correspon-
dent, in this case /p/) as part of the reduplicative process.
    Another pattern replaces a CiV(C2) initial syllable with the pattern C1aC1aa(C2), that is,
substitutes an initial IAMBIC (weak-strong) METRICAL FOOT, as in nnaandweh
/nanaandaweh/, 'take care of AN; fix AN; cure AN' (VTA), compared with ndawzi
/nandawizi/, 'try and get Y' (VAIO), with root /nandaw/. Compare also nhishin, 'adjust one-
self in a lying position' (VAI) with nnaahshim, 'fix AN, repair AN' (VTA). This reduplicative
pattern is also evident in the VAI pair, nmadbi, 'sit,' and nnaamdabi, 'sit a while, sit and sit.'
It is also commonly used in DISTRIBUTIVE REDUPLICATION of attributes, as in mmaangnike,
/mamaangnike/, 'have big arms,' with root /mang/, 'big.'
    Lastly, some roots show apparent copying of an initial consonant and formation of a syl-
lable with /a/, as in nnangwebizh, /nanangwebizh/, 'shake AN' (VTA), nnagmotaw
/nanagamotaw/, 'sing and sing for AN' (VTA), beside n'gamtaw, /nagamotaw/, 'sing for
AN' (VTA), ddangshkaw, 'kick AN repeatedly' /dadangishkaw/ (VTA), beside dngishkaw,
'kick AN' /dangishkaw/ (VTA), and shekshim /zhazhekshim/, 'arrange AN in a row' (VTA).
This last example also illustrates how the operation of syncope can obscure historical redu-
plications of this sort, since the short vowel of the reduplicated syllable is lost by syncope,
and there is subsequent fusion of the juxtaposed lenis sibilant consonants /zh+zh/ (IPA /3/)
into /sh/ (IPA /J7). This reduplicative pattern is probably also present in words such as
mmaadnan, /mamaadnan/ 'move IN, wiggle IN (of parts of the body)' (VTI), and
mmigwebdoon, /mamigwebdoon/, 'grab IN and shake it' (VTI). Reduplicative patterns of all
three kinds illustrated here occur with both transitive and intransitive stems.
    MEDIALS. Medials are nominal in character, and may consist of either NOUN CLASSIFI-
ERS, BODY PART TERMS, or free NOUN STEMS, as in the following examples.

      Classifier    gnwaabiigm ~zh            'lengthen AN' (of strings) (vta)
      Classifier    zhaabwz/ghan              'tear a hole through IN' (of cloth) (vti)
      Body Part     baazgogaadeshkaw          'scratch AN on the leg' (vta) leg /-gaad-/
      Body Part     bookwaabdegnaam           'hit AN and break AN's tooth' (vta)
      Nominal       n&gkizhen                 'stick AN into coals' (vta) coal: kakzhe
      Nominal       ndoimw/:maa(ni)zh         'groom AN; pick AN's lice' (vta)
                                              'my louse' /nd+ikom/

    Intransitive verbs not uncommonly have free nouns as medials, as in naajmiijme, 'ANsg
fetches food,' with the independent noun miijim, 'food' as medial, but such nouns are rarely
found as medials in transitive verbs. The reason for this is straightforward. In intransitive
430 • 10.2 The Structure of Transitive Verbs


verbs with independent noun medials, the medial often functions as the internalized GOAL
of the verb. If the goal is inside the verb, the verb becomes intransitive, since it then retains
only one overt, external SEMANTIC MACROROLE, that of the S-ROLE (SUBJECT) (see extensive
discussion of these concepts in Chapter 13). Incorporated elements often seem to absorb the
semantic roles associated with them. A transitive verb makes overt inflectional reference to
at most two roles, an actor and a goal. If a goal is incorporated into the verb, the verb
becomes intransitive, because one role has been absorbed; if it isn't incorporated, the verb
remains transitive. A verb usually has only a single inflectional goal, and so does not usually
have both an incorporated goal and an independent goal. In the two examples of nominal
medials above, the medials do not function as primary goals of the transitive verb—in the
case of negkizhen, 'stick AN into coals,' the medial specifies the coals as a location or latent
instrument; in the case of ndomaakmaa(ni)zh, 'pick AN's lice,' the medial element makes
reference to the lice, but the overt goal of the verb is the recipient of the grooming, not the
lice. Note too that in this case, the medial /-aakom-/ has a rather different form from that of
the free noun, which has the form /-ikom/ (NAD), with a PRE-MEDIAL element /-aa-/, sug-
gesting that the noun has undergone explicit medialization. There also exist forms such as
naadaabikinmaw, 'collect payment for something from AN,' which has a classificatory
medial /-aabik-/, 'inorganic solid,' that makes reference to the physical properties of the
coins that were traditionally collected in payment. Another example is gnwegtamaw, 'make
something (sheetlike) long(er) for AN,' which has the classificatory medial /-eg-/, sheetlike
object. It is interesting that ditransitive verbs rarely show a medial indexed for properties of
the entity or entities filling the semantic role of patient.
    FINALS. Transitive finals define a verb's class, and its subclass, as either transitive ani-
mate (VTA) or transitive inanimate (VTI). Just as with intransitive verbs, many transitive
verbs occur in pairs, one used with animate goals and the other with inanimates. Unlike the
usual case with intransitive finals, though, it often appears that one of a pair of transitive
finals is derived from the other, as can be seen from the following examples.

           VTA Final      VTI Final Meaning                             Relationship
           -shkaw         -shk      'cause (using foot or body)'        TA = TI + aw
           -kaw           -k        'cause (in the body)                TA = TI + aw
           -m             -nd       'cause using speech'                TI = TA+ d
           -am            -and      'cause using mouth/teeth'           TI = TA + d
           -aganaam       -aganaand 'cause using great force'           TI = TA + d

    In the first two examples, the VTA final seems to be derived from the VTI by the addition
of /-aw/, while in the last three, the reverse is found: the VTI appears derived from the VTA
by the addition of /-d/. Note that in all three of these cases the /-m/ of the VTA final ASSIMI-
LATES to /n/ before /d/. Some analysts assert, on theoretical grounds of generality, that the
direction of derivation in these final pairs is always from the VTA to the VTI, and that
VTA-stems which end in finals /-w/ and /-aw/ undergo TRUNCATION, that is, are shortened, in
                                                                    10.2 The Structure of Transitive Verbs • 431



the derivation of corresponding VTl's. Such issues are discussed in detail in O'Meara 1990,
in which the transitive finals of Delaware are analyzed as falling into four groups, based on
the final suffix forming the VTA stem, and the relationship between the VTA and associated
VTI form. These four classes are outlined in the table below. Subscripted «f» indicates a spe-
cific final, while subscripted «n» indicates several finals ending in the designated segment.

                            Delaware Transitive Finals (from O'Meara 1990)
                            Class        TA           TI      Tl-theme
                              I   (PF) +Wf            —       +am
                               II     (PF)      +awf           —           +am
                              III     (PF)      +In            +t          +'m, +am, +00
                              IV      (PF)      +mn, +h        +m+t

    These finals are abstract, meaning that their function is to define the lexical sub-class of
the words they appear in, rather than provide additional lexical meaning. These finals can be
added directly to a stem or appear in combination with a variety of prefinals. Prefinals spec-
ify such notions as causation, instrument, sensory stimulus, motion, and many others. Simi-
lar observations can be made about Nishnaabemwin transitive finals, namely, that while
many quite specific final complexes exist, they ultimately involve only a very small number
of abstract finals, quite parallel to the Delaware, which the reader can readily discern by
examining the list of finals in this chapter or in the index. Transitive finals all end in conso-
nants or /w/, as they do in Menominee (Bloomfield 1962:329)
    THE RELATIONSHIP OF TRANSITIVE AND INTRANSITIVE FINALS. Transitive finals often
show structured relationships to the finals of semantically related intransitive verbs. So, for
example, corresponding to transitive verbs with finals TA /-shim/ and TI /-sid+oo/, are
intransitives AI /-shin/ and II /-sin/. The animate finals can be analyzed as sharing pre-final
/-sh/, and the inanimate, prefinal /-s/, to which is added an abstract final, /-in/ for the AI and
II, and /-m/ for the TA and /-id+oo/ for the TI.1 Such word families are common.

                          Class      Prefinal      Final         Example          Gloss
                           VTA         /-S/        Aim/          bngishim         'drop AN'
                           VAI         /-S/        /-in/AI       bngishin         'fall'
                            VII         /-S/       /-in/n        bngisin           'fall'
                            VTT         /-s/       /-id+oo/      bngisdoon         'drop IN'

    Another example of a word family, with variable finals.



1. As in so many cases, it is not entirely clear where to assign the vowel /i/ in these forms.
432 • 10.2 The Structure of Transitive Verbs


           (23)     VTA     /nisooN/       /-N/     nsoo(ni)zh    'corner AN, trap AN'
           (24)     VTI     /nisood-oo/    /-d/     nsoodoon      'corner IN, trap IN'
           (25) VAI         /nisoozi/      l-7.il   nsoozi        'be cornered, be trapped'
           (26) VII         /nisoode/      /-de/    nsoode        'be cornered, be trapped'

    Relationships between transitive and intransitive finals are treated in Chapter 9.
    IDENTIFYING WORD COMPONENTS. Word components can be identified only by careful
comparison of large amounts of vocabulary, and looking for structured relationships of form
and meaning. Fortunately for students of Nishnaabemwin, the work of linguists such as
Glyne Piggott (Piggott and Grafstein 1983) and Richard Rhodes (Rhodes 1985) has pro-
duced a very strong foundation for the study of lexical structure in the language. Almost all
of the examples provided here come from these sources.
    Finals are identified by examining the structure of words and determining what initial
and medial elements are present, though there is often much uncertainty in fine details of
analysis. Consider, for example, the following words (with VTA forms in the first column,
and VTI in the second, as throughout this chapter).

                  (27)   dgon ~zh         dgonan        'include X with others'
                  (28)   dgojiin ~zh      dgojiinan     'carry X with others'
                  (29)   gwekin ~zh       gweknan       'turn X around; turn X over'
                  (30)   gwekjiin ~zh     gwekjiinan    'turn X around; turn X over'

   In (27) and (28), there appears to be an initial /dgo-/, which, based on the analysis of
many words having this component, would seem to have a meaning 'together, with others.'
Examination of a variety of inflected forms suggests that the basic form of this initial is
/dagw-/. The following forms provide evidence for such an analysis.

   (a) ndagnaa             'I include AN'                 Shows presence of /a/ in /dagw-/
   (b) dgwamwag            '(if) I eat AN with something' Shows final segment is /w/ in /dagw-/

     Similarly, examination of the pairs of words (29) and (30) suggests that their initial is
/gwek-/. Next, we try to isolate the FINALS in these words. Here we run into problems. First,
it is not clear if the final in dgon and gwekin is /-in/ or /-n/. If we take the latter analysis, then
we must assume that the III is a LINK VOWEL. When the vowel in question is /i/, it is often
very hard to know whether it belongs to the final or not, since this is indeed the common
link vowel. If the vowel is /a/ or /o/, however, we can be reasonably certain that the vowel
belongs to the final, though in the case of dgon, we recognize a structure /dagw+in/ or
/dagw+i+n/, which, in either case shows a short o, /o/, on the basis of COALESCENCE of the
root-final /w/ with the following vowel, that is /w+i/ becomes /o/.
                                                                      10.3 Basic Causatives • 433


    Another problem that we face with the set of words in (27) through (30) is what to do
with the string /-jii-/ that shows up in two of them. Do we analyze this element as a separate
unit, perhaps the MEDIAL /-jii-/ (which may mean either 'belly, middle,' or more commonly
add some extremely idiosyncratic meaning, if any) or as constituting part of a separate set of
finals, TA AjiiN/ (or /-jiin/) and TI /-jiin+am/, related to TA /-N/ (or /-n/) and TI /-n+am/, but
distinct from them? Are these pre-final elements? Based on the difference of meaning in
(27) and (28), it might appear that this set of finals has the meaning 'carry,' but when we
examine (29) and (30), we find that these two sets of words have identical meanings, but one
set has /jii/ and the other doesn't. To resolve issues like these we must examine large groups
of words containing the elements in question and look for patterns of form and meaning. In
some cases, there may be only a few words recorded in the language which manifest the
items of interest, leaving the correct analysis forever uncertain, or requiring resort to the
study of cognate forms in sister languages. Analytic investigations into the structure of
vocabulary can ultimately be an almost limitless pursuit. In this grammar, I have settled for
a compromise between a desire for reasonable scholarship and a desire to complete my
work in a reasonable amount of time. I present what I believe to be the most common deri-
vational elements, and leave exhaustive analysis to others.
    In this chapter then, I will lay out some of the more common transitive verb sets, orga-
nized according to a preliminary analysis of the classes of finals that occur, into rough
notional groupings, rather than on the basis of formal features. Those wishing to pursue the
study of transitive finals should consult Rhodes 1976, Bloomfield 1958, Todd 1970, and
Bloomfield 1962, and, especially, O'Meara 1990.

10.3 Basic Causatives

    The first group of finals we will examine are those that produce verbs of unadorned CAU-
SATION, that is, those which do not additionally specify a particular instrument, manner, or
location involved in the causative act, but simply indicate unembroidered causation. The
following finals belong to this class.

                                  Simple Causative Finals
                                  VTA     VTI         Gloss
                                  -ah     -at+oo      'cause'
                                  -ih     -it+oo
                                  -sah    -sat+oo     'cause'
                                  -sih    -sit+oo
                                   -IN    -in+am      'cause'

    Note that VTI finals are given in combination with their THEME SUFFIXES, which are
almost always either /-am/ or /-oo/. These suffixes are discussed in more detail in Chapter 8
(p. 305ff.).
434 • 10.3 Basic Causatives


   1       TA /-ih/, /-ah/      TI /-it+oo/, /-at+oo/      'cause, act on X'

    Simple VTA causatives, that is, those which lack specification of an instrument or loca-
tion, are formed by adding final /-ih/ (or /-ah/) to either bound or free stems, and the corre-
sponding TI finals are formed by adding /-d/ or /-t/ to the VTA finals. The combination of
/h+d/ (or /h+t/) is realized as /t/ in the VTI forms. The VTI stems are then followed by the
VTI2 theme suffix, /-oo/. This VTI final is perhaps present in the many VTI'S made from
English borrowings, such asfaxwitoon, vacuumwitoon, photocopywitoon, printwitoon,
typewitoon, tapewitoon (audio or video), pavewitoon, and insulatewitoon. (examples, MC).
    The HI of these finals causes palatalization of an immediately preceding /d/ or /N/, as, for
example, in aanjih, 'change AN,' with initial element /aand/, 'change,' which can be com-
pared with a form showing the same root with unchanged /d/, in aandshin, 'AN lies some-
where else,' and zaagjih, 'bring AN out, take AN out,' with initial /zaagad/ (or /zaagid/),
 'out,' which occurs unchanged in zaagdaabiise 'AN/IN comes out (of strings).' Examples of
causative forms built on primary stems follow.

            VTA               VTI
    (31)     aanjih           aanjtoon         'change X'
    (32)     giizhih          giizhtoon        'finish (doing/making) X'
    (33)     gjih             gjitoon          'try/test X'
    (34)     gshkih           gshkitoon        'control/manage X'
    (35)     maawnjih         maawnjitoon      'store up/collect X'
    (36)     moozhih          moozhtoon        'feel the touch of X'
    (37)     naajih           naajtoon         'lose X'
    (38)     wiikjih          wiikjitoon       'urge X; try to get X (to do s.t.)'
    (39)     nih              nitoon           'lose X'
    (40)     zaagjih          zaagjitoon       'take X out; cause X to go outside'
    (41)     zhaagoojih       zhaagoojtoon     'beat/overcome X'
    (42)     zhih             zhitoon          'make X (e.g. car, mitten)'

   Roots that occur with intransitive finals /-izi/ VAI and /-ad/ VII also appear with these
causative finals, as in the following examples. Relevant VAI forms are also provided.

             VTA             VAI         VTI
    (43)     aabjih          aabdizi      aabjitoon     'use X; put X to use'
    (44)     biinih          biinzi       biintoon      'clean X; make X clean'
    (45)     wiinih          wiinzi       wiintoon      'dirty X; make X dirty'

medial /-eg/, 'sheet-like.'

           VTA          VAI             VTI
    (46)   dkwegih      dkwegzi         dkwegtoon          'shorten X'(sheet-like obj.)

   Other causative forms suggest derivation from fully formed VAI verbs, though the mean-

           VTA           VAI            VTI
    (49)   bbaamgaah     bbaamgaa       bbaamgaatoon       'cause X to spin; whirl X around'

    In the forms above, both VTA and VTI stems are formed with free VAI verbs as initials. In

           VTA         VII        VTI
    (53)   shpaah      shpaa      shpaatoon        'raise X; make X high(er)'
    (54)   gnwaah      gnwaa      gnwaatoon        'make X long(er)/tall(er)'

   VTA forms can also evidently be made with VAI2 or VTI stems as initials, in which case
the animate agent or experiencer of the VTI serves as the goal of the causative verb, and the

causative. The following examples all involve VTI or VAl2 stems with theme sign /-am/. A

10.4 Instrumental Causative Finals

    A number of transitive finals have senses that involve causation by means of particular
instrumentalities, or simply involve the use of particular instruments. These are commonly
called INSTRUMENTAL-CAUSATIVE finals, or sometimes simply INSTRUMENTAL finals.1
Instruments may include parts of the body, with specific finals designating three distinct
areas: the mouth, the hand, and the foot or body. This set of finals I call BODILY INSTRUMEN-
TAL CAUSATIVE FINALS, because they do not involve an instrument external to the body. The
following table lists the more common of these.

                                   Internal Instrumental Causative Finals
              TA            TI              Gloss
              -m            -nd+am          'cause using speech'
              -am           -and+am         'causing using the mouth/teeth'
               -biN         -bid+oo         'cause using force; cause using the hand; pull'
              -shkaw        -shk+am         'cause using foot/body'
              -kaw          -k+am           'cause using the body'


   Overlapping with this set of finals are several that can be used to assert causation taking
place in or on the region for which an instrumental body part final exists. I call these
BODY-INTERNAL INSTRUMENTAL CAUSATIVE FINALS.

                                 Insternal-Site Instrumental Causative Finals
                           TA            TI                 Gloss
                            -anem        -anend+am          'cause in the mouth'


1. These notes owe a great debt to Rhodes 1976, though errors of representation of a difficult area of grammar are
my own responsibility. See Rhodes 1980 and Rhodes 1981 for more detailed analysis than provided here.
                          10.4.1 Instrumental Causatives Involving Specific Parts of the Body • 439



                       -shkaw      —               'cause in the body'
                       -kaw        —               'cause in the body'
                       -zaw        —               'cause in the body'

   Another group of finals involves the use of implements of traditional technology. Most
of such VTA finals end in abstract final /-w/. I am calling these EXTERNAL INSTRUMENTAL
CAUSATIVE FINALS, as they involve the use of tools external to the body.

                            External Instrumental (Causative) Finals
       TA         TI              Gloss
       -ahw       -ah+am          'cause using an instrument'
       -apiN      -apid+oo        'tie X, use rope on X'
       -zw        -z+am           'cause using heat' (fire)
       -aakizw    -aakiz+am       'cause using fire, cause using a flame' (fire)
       -biihw     -biih+am        'draw, write'
       -booN      -bood+oo        'cause using a sawing action' (saw)
       -gahw      -gah+am         'cause using an axe/instrument' (axe)
       -izhw      -izh+am         'cause using a cutting edge' (knife)
       -koN       -kod+am         'cause using a cutting action' (knife)

   Another set of finals sometimes listed with the instrumental finals involves the use of
force, or striking. Perhaps similar is the final pair /-shim/ and /-sid+oo/, which often express
a notion, 'cause by dropping,' or alternatively, 'cause to lie (down).' I label this group
ACTION-BASED INSTRUMENTAL CAUSATIVE FINALS, since it is not so much the instrument
that is used in the action that is designated by the final, but rather, the way (manner) in
which force is applied to the goal. Many instrumental finals, of course, have associative ele-
ments of action and instrument, since the use of particular instruments entails particular
forms of action.

                          Action-Based Instrumental Causative Finals
       TA            TI              Gloss
       -aganaam      -aganaand+am 'cause by exerting great force; hit, strike'
       -shim         -sid+oo              'cause by dropping'

    Several sets of finals refer to causation located in places which happen also to be speci-

  12    TAAanem/         TI /-anend+am/        'cause in the mouth'

   (231) ndaapnem                  'quarrel with AN, reproach AN (for a specified reason)'

  13    TA /-ishkaw/          TI /-ishk+am/            'cause in, on the body'

    The VTA forms occur only in the INVERSE, that is, generally involve the ingestion of a
substance which produces some usually unpleasant effect. Many of these forms have a VAI
verb as initial, representing the condition created by the action of the ingested substance, as
in aakziishkaw, 'make AN sick,' with initial aakzi, 'be sick,' (VAI), with a lengthened final
vowel when serving as initial. Note, however, that zaagaateshkaw, 'shine on AN (of the
sun),' has a vn verb form as initial, zaagaate, 'be bright out, be bright sun,' and also has a
VTI form.

   17       TA/-zw/      TI/-z+am/        'heat X, use heat on X'

   There are two sets of finals that specify heat or flame as instrument:

                  TA            TI              Gloss
                  -zw           -z+am            'heat X, use heat on X'
                  -aakzw        -aakz+am         'use a flame on X'

   These final pairs appear to differ only by the presence of classificatory medial /-aak-/ in
the second set. In some cases of lexical pairs, /-aak-/ functions as an intensifier, as can be
                                            10.4.2.1 External Instrumental Causative Finals • 449



seen from the following pairs.

    (280) jaagzaw           jaagzan             'burn X'
    (281) jaagaakzaw        jaagaakzan          'burn X completely'

    (283) giishkaakzaw     giishkaakzan        'cut X with a blowtorch; cut X with a flame'

intent:

    (284) bgonezaw     bgonezan                'heat X and have a hole develop'
    (285) bgoneyaakzaw bgoneyaakzan            'burn a hole in X'

  In other cases, the difference seems to be whether the instrument is direct flame, in
which case the finals with /-aak-/ are used, or the instrumentality simply involves heat, in
which case finals without /-aak-/ are used.

    (287) baasaakzaw        baasaakzan         put X in a flame and have it crack

    (289) daashkaakzaw      daashkaakzan        put X in a flame and have it split

10.7 Accompaniment and Benefactive (Applicative) Finals

  Several finals exist which derive VTA verbs having goals that represent various kinds of
OBLIQUE, or peripheral, semantic roles. These derived goals are similar to those expressed in
English by means of prepositions such as 'with,' as in wiidabim, 'sit with AN,' and 'for,' as
462 • 10.7.1 Accompaniment (Comitative) Verbs


in zhitmaw, 'make something for AN.' These finals seem always to produce VTA verbs in
which the derived goal is a human being or other living creature. When the derived verb has
a transitive initial, features of the original goal of the verb, almost always representing
something notionally non-living, are no longer marked inflectionally on the verb. These
verbs thus seem to often involve some sense of 'promotion' of some grammatically oblique
animate entity to the role of goal, supplanting the original, usually inanimate, goal. A rather
similar phenomenon occurs syntactically in English, where beneficiaries, that is, those ben-
efitting from some action become direct objects, and appear directly after the verb, as in 'I
made Mary Ann some muffins.' If the beneficiary does not occur directly after the verb, it
must be identified with the preposition for, as in 'I made some muffins for Mary Ann.' In
Nishnaabemwin, the only way to represent the BENEFICIARY is by making it the goal of a
derived BENEFACTIVE VERB. The original goal is demoted to a very peripheral grammatical
role, in which case it no longer receives any inflectional reference on the verb it is associ-
ated with, except possibly in participles of which it is the focus.

10.7.1 Accompaniment (Comitative) Verbs

   37      TA /wiid-X-m /       'do X with someone'

    To express accompaniment, or co-participation in an activity (traditionally called COMI-
TATIVES), the initial /wiid-/, 'together' is used in combination with various finals to derive
initials, which are then combined with final /-m/. In the following examples, the final asso-
ciated with /wiid-/ is a bound form, producing a complex initial, which is then combined
with final /-m/. When the final begins with a consonant, a link vowel /-if is inserted, which
causes palatalization of the final /d/ of /wiid/, to /j/. In a couple of cases, such as wiijsem,
'walk with AN,' (from /wiid-ose-m/), the root /wiid/ appears to have been reanalyzed as
/wiij/, perhaps on analogy with the common prenoun, (w)iiji-, 'one's fellow,' as in
«w«/-Nishnaabe, 'my fellow Indian' (W, CL).

   (587)   wiidsem          'walk with AN'          /-ose/        'walk'
   (588)   wiijbatoom       'run around with AN'    /-batoo/      'run'
   (589)   wiijbiim         'get drunk with AN'     /-bii/        'involving a liquid'
   (590)   wiijgaam         'dance with AN'         /-gaa/        'dance'
   (591)   wiidgem          'marry/live with AN'    /-ige/        'involving a building'?

    In other cases, a DEVERBAL final occurs, which resembles, but is not identical to, an
independent VAI verb. In both cases the initial fuses with the deverbal element in such a way
as to absorb some of its initial segments.
                                                                     10.7.2 Benefactives/Applicatives • 463



    (592)    wiidoopom 'eat with AN'                 /oopo/ /adoopo/                'eat from something'
    (593)    wiipem    'sleep with AN'               /be/   /nibaa/,/nibe/          'sleep'

   In other cases, a deverbal final retains a form identical to its independent form.

    (594) wiidbim                'sit with AN'               /abi/            'be, sit somewhere'

    In some cases, the verbal element is evidently incapable of forming a final complex, and
so must be structurally an initial, which forces the element /wiid/ into a preverb position,
where it appears as wiiji-, due to the presence of preverb-deriving final /-i/, which causes
palatalization of the final consonant of /wiid/. The following examples illustrate preverb
wiiji- constructions.

    (595) wiiji-mnikwem           'drink with AN'
    (596) wiiji-nokiim            'work with AN'
    (597) wiiji-yaam              'be/live with AN'

    The form wiiji-nokiim, 'work with AN,' has a variant, wiijnokiim, in which case /wiij-/
fills initial position, rather than being a preverb.
    The forms wiijgaabwitwaad, 'stand with AN,' and wiijgendwaad, 'live with AN' (also
wiidgendwaad) are exceptional in showing the APPLICATIVE FINAL COMPLEX /-taw/, instead
of/-m/.
    One last form deserves mention, wiijkiwenyim, 'befriend AN,' which seems to be formed
on the basis of analogy with the verbs listed above, though in this case, the initial is
/wiijkiwenh/, 'brother, friend,' a dependent noun, and /wiij/ is part of this noun.

10.7.2 Benefactives/Applicatives

   38       TA /-amaw /         benefactive, applicative

    The final /-amaw/ can be added freely to VTI stems to derive a benefactive verb, in which
the actor carries out the action specified by the VTI stem, for the benefit of an animate goal,
usually a person. While these verbs often entail a semantic patient, i.e., an object manipu-
lated for someone's benefit, there is usually no inflectional reference to this entity on the
verb. As with other cases of derivation involving VTI stems, the theme suffixes /-am/ and
/-oo/ do not appear in the derived forms.1 Benefactives can also be derived from VAI verbs,
in which case a nonce transitive stem seems to be created by suffixing VTI final /-t/ to the

/am/-theme VTI verbs.

    In some cases, there exist synonyms reflecting different strategies for forming benefac-

10.8 Verbs with Body Part Medials

   Many VTA verbs express action by an agent upon a particular part of a goal's body, for
example, booknikebizh, 'break AN's arm,' and baazgogaadebizh, 'scratch AN on the leg.'
468 • 10.8 Verbs with Body Part Medials


These verbs contain body part medials, such as /-nik-/, 'arm,' and /-gaad-/, 'leg,' in the two
examples here. However, their structures cannot be analyzed as simply initial + medial +
final, since the medials are followed by the morpheme /-e/, which represents a VAI final in
words such as booknike, 'AN has a broken arm,' and gzhiibgaade, 'have an itch on one's
leg.' One possible analysis of these verbs is that they represent the addition of a transitive
final to an initial that is itself an independent word, as in booknikebizh, 'break AN's arm,'
which could be analyzed as /booknike+bizh/. In other words, the suggestion might be that a
VTA final has been added to an initial which has the same form as a VAI verb. The problem
with such an analysis is that many VTA verbs with body part medials do not show forms that
correspond to any VAI verbs. For example, in the case of gaanjgaadeshkaw, 'push AN's leg
[with foot or body]' there is no corresponding VAI verb, *gaanjgaade, 'have one's leg
pushed; have a pushed leg.' Therefore, we must assume one of the following structures for
these VTA verbs. In the first, /-e/ functions as some kind of medializing suffix attached to
/-gaad-/, 'leg'; in the second, it derives a complex initial consisting of/gaanj-/ plus /-gaad-/.

                   Initial   Medial       Final
                   gaanj     gaad+e       shkaw

                   Initial           Final
                   gaanjgaad+e       shkaw

  The following examples illustrate several body part medials occurring in a variety of
VTA verbs. No doubt such a list could be extended indefinitely.

10.9 Verbs with Classificatory Medials

    Classificatory medials also occur in transitive verbs, typically indicating the class of the
patient role, as in dkwaabiigkozh, 'cut AN short(er) (of strings),' or specifying an instrument
or other prop involved in some way in the action, as in niisaabiigin, 'let AN down on a
rope,' and naadaabkin, 'collect payment for AN,' the latter with mineral medial /aabik/, in
reference to the coins involved in payment. These medials do not seem very common. A few
example words with different Classificatory medials follow.

    Other medials show up in some transitive forms, but these usually involve medials that
are best analyzed as belonging to an independent word stem which is serving as a complex
initial. This is true, for example, of the medial /-konay-/, 'clothing,' in the following forms,
e.g., (784), where aanzkon'ye, 'changes (one's) clothes' (VAI), serves as an initial to vta final
/-h/, 'causative.'

           VTA Form                    VAI Form          VTA Gloss
    (784) aanzkon'yeh, ~y              aanzkon'ye         'make AN change clothes'
    (785) biiskon'yeh, ~y              biiskon'ye         'dress AN'
    (786) giiskon'yeb(n)izh            giiskon'ye         'pull AN's clothes off'

   A medial of liquids /-aagam-/ occurs in a few transitive forms.

    (787) ndaahaagmin            ndaawaagminan          'stir X (of liquids)'
    (788) ndaahaagmaw            ndaahaagmahan          'stirX with instrument (of liquids)'

10.11 Other Transitive Finals

   Many other transitive finals exist in addition to those listed above. Some are simply

The Derivation of Nouns and Adverbs




    Chapters 9 and 10 presented analyses of the derivational morphology of intransitive and
transitive verbs, and in this chapter we briefly examine the derivational structure of nouns
and adverbs. These last two word classes are grouped together here solely for convenience,
as they do not particularly share structure or content that motivates their treatment as a
definable sub-grouping of parts of speech.

11.1 Nouns

     NOUN ROOTS AND GENERAL ROOTS. There are two basic classes of ROOTS in the PRI-
MARY DERIVATION of WORD STEMS in Nishnaabemwin, NOUN ROOTS and GENERAL ROOTS.
Noun roots are used exclusively with nouns, and general roots are used with any word
(stem) category, whether nouns, verbs, or adverbs. Nouns thus stand apart from other word
classes in their derivational properties, in that there is a set of roots that is uniquely associ-
ated with them in primary derivation.
     STEM FORMS. As with my discussion of both transitive and intransitive verbs, I will have
occasion to refer to the stem form of a noun, which almost always consists of the basic word
minus its inflections, and with all short vowels represented, that is, the hypothetical form of
the stem before the application of syncope. Many nouns also show a final /y/ or /w/ in their
stem forms that is not pronounced in the simple singular, but which can be recognized on
the basis of the stem's phonological properties in the presence of various suffixes. Stem
forms are usually represented within slashes in this grammar. For example, the stem form of
the word for 'snake,' gnebig, is /ginebigw/ NA; for 'net,' sab, it is /asaby/ NA; for 'man,'
mm, it is /aniniw/ or /ininiw/ NA, subject to dialect variation.
     THE PHONOLOGICAL STRUCTURE OF NOUN STEMS. Traditionally, as with all words in
Nishnaabemwin, independent noun stems did not begin with either fortis consonants (/p/,
/t/, /k/, /ch/, /s/, /sh/) or clusters of two or more consonants. In modern Nishnaabemwin, of
course, many words are pronounced with fortis initial segments and with initial consonant
clusters, due to the deletion, by syncope, of word-initial short vowels, as in, for example,
478* 11.1 Nouns


pin, 'potato,' from stem /opiny/ (or /apiny/), and shkode, 'fire,' with stem /ishkode/ (or
/ashkode/). Probably for some speakers, who may have reanalyzed some of these words so
that they no longer begin with vowels, the old constraints on word-initial consonants no
longer hold.
    Historically, a few DEPENDENT NOUN STEMS began with fortis consonants or consonant
clusters, such as /+kaad/, 'leg' NID, and /+shkiinzhigw/, 'eye' NID. While stem-initial, these
fortis consonants and clusters never occurred word-initially, however, because dependent
nouns always have a possessive prefix.
    UNANALYZABLE PRIMARY NOUNS. Large numbers of common nouns, especially ani-
mate nouns, show indivisible ROOT forms, such as bzhiki, 'cow' and bzhiw, 'lynx.' Such
nouns are thus rather different in structure than common verbs, which typically, though not
always, have a relatively straightforward initial+final structure, in which the final deter-
mines the part of speech (stem-class) and sub-class of the word as a whole, as in aabdizi,
'be useful' VAI, with root /aabad-/, 'useful, used,' and FINAL /-izi/, 'be' (VAI). Many com-
mon nouns are not straightforwardly analyzable as having component parts, though some
show historical relics that point to an earlier morphological system that is no longer produc-
tive.
    PRIMARY COMPLEX NOUN STEMS. Other primary nouns have identifiable structural
components, such as getehii, 'old thing' Nl and getehaa, 'old thing' NA, both of which share
an INITIAL (root) component, /gete-/, 'old,' but differ in their finals (/-hii/ and /-haa/, respec-
tively), and wiingashk, 'sweetgrass' NI and pakweyashk, 'cattail' NA, both of which have
noun final element /-ashkw/, 'grass, reed,' which seems to be related to mshkiki
/mashkikiw/, 'medicine' NI.
    SECONDARY COMPLEX NOUN STEMS. Some nouns consist of an independent nominal
stem to which a concrete noun final has been attached, such as goonaaboo 'melted snow
water' NI, with the independent noun goon, 'snow' NA as initial, and concrete noun final
/-aaboo/, 'liquid'; and zhgaagwinzh, 'onion' NA, consisting of the independent word
zhgaag, 'skunk' NA, as initial, and concrete noun final /-winzhy/, 'plant.'
    In some cases, noun finals are added in secondary derivation to initials that are animate
intransitive (VAI) verbs, to derive nouns associated with the verbal action or state specified
by the verb, as in the noun nbaagan, 'bed' NI, which has as initial VAI verb nbaa, 'sleep,' to
which is attached noun final /-gan/. The noun final /-win/ is also sometimes used to derive
nouns referring to physical objects, as in dnakiiwin, 'town, village' NI, with initial dnakii,
'live in a certain place' VAI, and migiiwin, 'scabs, leprosy,' with initial migii, 'have scabs,
have open sores' VAI. In other cases, /-win/ is used to derive ABSTRACT NOUNS of states,
actions, and events, as in yekziwin, 'tiredness, fatigue' NI, with initial yekzi, 'be tired' VAI,
and niimwin, 'dance' NI, with initial niimi, 'dance' VAI. This process of deriving nouns from
intransitive verbs by means of nominalizing suffixes such as /-win/ and /-gan/ most com-
monly produces nouns of inanimate gender. It is especially productive in the formation of
the names of manufactured objects.
    PARTICIPIAL NOUNS AND DEPARTICIPIAL NOUNS. Some nouns are derived from verbs
by means of PARTICIPIALIZATION, that is, by using special verb PARTICIPLE INFLECTIONS to
                                                                               11.1 Nouns* 479


identify individuals and groups on the basis of verbal actions or states associated with them.
So, for example, baatewaagmiseg, 'beer' Nl, which is the participial form of the inanimate
intransitive (VII) verb biitewaagamse, 'be/become foamy liquid,' and nesoobgak, 'clover'
NI, which is the participial form of VII verb nsoobgad /nisoobagad/, 'have three leaves.'
Note that there is usually semantic specialization in such words, as can be seen, for exam-
ple, with nesoobgak, 'clover,' since many plants besides clover have three leaves. And liq-
uids other than beer can be foamy. Words of this sort are structurally true participles, in that
they show both INITIAL CHANGE and PARTICIPIAL VERBAL (suffix) INFLECTION. Other parti-
ciple-like forms in some dialects of Nishnaabemwin show initial change of a verbal stem,
but lack participial inflectional suffixes, as in dekaashiinh, 'tourist' NA, with initial change
of VAI verb dkaashi, 'be carefree, have fun' /dakaashi/, and esbikenh, 'spider' NA, with ini-
tial change of VAI verb sabke, 'make a net' /asabike/. In both cases, too, a CONTEMPTIVE
SUFFIX appears on the noun. I designate words formed in this way as DEPARTICIPIAL NOUNS.
    The definition of a STEM as a word minus its inflectional affixes does not work well with
participles, since true participles are only nominal by virtue of showing special inflections
and being used as nouns. The uninflected stem of a true participle is always derivationally a
verb. In the case of departicipial nominals such as dekaashiinh, initial change functions der-
ivationally, creating a new stem, rather than inflectionally, as it does in most uses with verbs.
    COMPOUND NOUNS. COMPOUND NOUNS are those containing one or more word STEMS,
such as in mshkikiiwnini, 'male doctor' NA, which consists of the component stems mshkiki
/mashkikiw/, 'medicine' Nl, and mm/ininiw, aniniw/, 'man' NA. Compounds always consist
of exactly two stem elements, though these elements may themselves be compounds, as in
mshkode-bzhiki-wiiyaas, 'buffalo meat,' which has the compound mshkode-bihiki, 'buffalo'
NA as its first element, and wiiyaas, 'meat' Nl as its second. The GRAMMATICAL PROPERTIES
of the compound as a whole are usually those of the stem element on the right, as in the
example of mshkikiiwnini, in which the right element is of animate gender, a property which
it passes on to the compound as a whole. Furthermore, the right element usually defines the
notional class to which the referents of the whole*word belong. So, for example, in the case
of mashkode-bzhiki-wiiyaas, we note that the right element is wiiyaas, 'meat,' and that the
whole word represents a kind of meat.
    PRENOUNS IN COMPOUND STEMS. Some stem forms may include PRENOUNS, in cases
where the meaning of the prenoun plus noun combination cannot be straightforwardly
determined from the meanings of its component parts. For example, at Curve Lake, the
combination of prenoun mji- 'bad,' and animate noun gnoozhe, 'fish,' means 'muskellunge,'
a particular kind of fish, and not simply 'bad fish,' as is suggested by the individual mean-
ings of mji- and gnoozhe. The stem form of this word is /maji-ginoozhe/, which can be
determined by examining a variety of word-forms having different inflections, such as
nmaji-gnoozhem, 'my muskellunge,' which reveals the presence of a short vowel, /a/, in the
prenoun.
    A prenoun in combination with a noun represents a type of compound, since the result-
ing complex word-stem consists of two separate stems. The prenoun stem always modifies
the noun stem it is attached to, but acts as a word-domain with respect to the vowel deleting
480 • 11.2 Unanalyzable Primary Nouns


rule of syncope, in that its last vowel is never deleted, just as if it were the last vowel of a
word. This can be seen from a word such as waabi-mnoomin, 'white rice' (stem
/waabi-manoomin/ Nl), in which the short vowel l\l of waabi-, 'white,' is not deleted, even
though it immediately follows a syllable containing a long vowel, and is not the last vowel
in the composite word. Furthermore, the short vowel immediately following /i/, the /a/ of
noun stem /manoomin/, 'rice,' is itself deleted, in this case because it represents the first
short vowel of a new phonological word. These phonological features of prenouns and pre-
verbs are treated in more detail in Chapter 2.6.4, Prefixes, Suffixes, Stems, Prenouns and
Preverbs, beginning on page 59.
    SUMMARY OF NOUN STRUCTURAL STEM TYPES. To summarize, the following types of
NOUN STEM structures occur in Nishnaabemwin, and will be treated in this chapter. In the
table below, 1C stands for INITIAL CHANGE.

             Noun Stem Structures
             Primary (Simple) Noun Stems
                                 Root
                                 Root       + Concrete Noun Final
             Secondary (Complex) Noun Stems
                                 Stem       + Concrete Noun Final
                                 Stem       + Abstract Noun Final
             Participial Nouns
                                 IC/Stem    + Contemptive Noun Final
                                 IC/Stem    + Participial Inflectional Suffixes
             Compound Noun Stems
                                 Stem       + Stem

11.2 Unanalyzable Primary Nouns

   Many nouns cannot be confidently divided into meaningful component parts, and must
thus be considered single, indivisible units. There is however, some uncertainty as to how to
categorize these single units occurring as stems, whether they should be considered roots,
medials, or finals. I will take up the discussion of this problem briefly, below. As examples,
the words in the following representative list of animal terms do not appear to have recog-
nizable component parts in contemporary Nishnaabemwin, and so must be interpreted as
Unanalyzable primary nouns.

                         (2)     bzhiw       NA    'wildcat, lynx'

    STEM-FINAL /w/ WITH ANIMATE NOUNS AND NOUN FINALS. A large number of animate
nouns, and some inanimate nouns, have stems ending in /w/, suggesting that at one time this
was a meaningful structural component of such words, perhaps an ABSTRACT NOUN FINAL
that classified the stem as belong to the word class of nouns or sub-class of animate nouns.
One clue in determining the stem-shape of a noun is its plural form. The basic animate noun
plural inflectional suffix is /-ag/, which shows up transparently on some words, such as
waagshag, 'foxes.' When the animate plural suffix appears to be something other than /-ag/,
it is always because of the influence of a stem-final /w/ or /y/ that is not pronounced in the
singular form. For example, bzhiki, 'cow,' has a plural bzhikwag, suggesting that its stem
has a final /w/, /bizhikiw+ag/; the plural of jiig, 'fisher,' is jiigog, suggesting its stem is
/ojiigw+ag/, and the plural of mooz, 'moose,' is moozoog, suggesting that it too has a final
/w/, /moozw+ag/. In these last two cases, however, the final /w/ of the stem and the /a/ of the
plural suffix COALESCE to either /o/ or /oo/. Note, too, that there do exist a few nouns that do
not lose stem-final /w/ in their singular forms, such as bzhiw, 'lynx' NA, and bgiw, 'gum,
pitch' NA. See Chapter 4 for extensive discussion of noun stem-classes. The following list
provides a representative sample of Nishnaabemwin person and animal terms having stems
that end in /w/.

           Singular             Plural                       Stem                Gloss
    (14)   bzhiki               bzhikwag                     /bizhikiw/          'cow'
    (15)   bzhiw                bzhiwag                      /bizhiw/            'lynx'
    (16)   dikmeg               dikmegog                     /adikamegw/         'whitefish'
482 • 11.2 Unanalyzable Primary Nouns



           Singular           Plural                      Stem                  Gloss

    It is unlikely that final /w/ is a meaningful component in these words in contemporary
Nishnaabemwin.
    INITIAL DERIVING-/W/. When used to form derived initials, some word-stems ending in
vowels show the presence of an element /w/, which can cause an immediately preceding
short vowel to lengthen. For example, the VAI verb aakozi, 'be ill,' occurs in the noun
aakziiwgamig, 'hospital,' as an initial attached to the NOUN FINAL /-gamigw/, though with
an EXTENDED FORM, /aakziiw-/. This /w/ is sometimes called EXTENSIONAL-/W/.
    GENDER MARKERS /-a/ AND /-i/. In Chapter 4.3 (p. 177), I discuss a few nouns which
show vestiges of Proto-Algonquian gender-related markers, */-a/ animate, as in mkwa (or
mko, with coalescence of/w/ + /a/ to /o/J, 'bear' and nka, 'Canada goose') and */-i/ inani-
mate (as in mshi, 'piece of wood' and mskwi, 'blood'). While terms such as mkwa and nka
may end with the historical animate marker, the overwhelming majority of animate nouns
now lack it, for example, waagosh, 'fox' and mik, 'beaver.' It seems best to consider the /a/
and I'll of these few nouns as simply historical relics that have no place in the word structure
patterns of contemporary words.
    DEPENDENT NOUNS AS DERIVATIONAL UNITS. Sometimes DEPENDENT NOUNS, particu-
larly body part terms and kin relations, occur as component parts of simple and compound
nouns. Though it often hard to tell, due to the action of syncope, dependent nouns used as
word elements often occur with inflection for a THIRD PERSON POSSESSOR. An example is
                                                        11.3 An Assortment of Noun Finals • 483



shkiinzhgokaajganan, 'eyeglasses' Nl (W, CL), which has as a component the third person
possessed form of the word for 'eye,' /oshkiinzhigw/.
    FUNCTIONAL SHIFT. A few words shift their part of speech from that of a verb to a noun,
with no apparent change in form. An area of vocabulary where this is common is that of
names. For example, the name Gchi-Negaw, 'Sands' a Potawatomi family name used on
Walpole Island, is based on an inanimate noun, negaw, 'sand,' but when used to name
human beings, the word is animate. Names of individuals and ethnic, national and racial
groups are always animate, even when they are derived from inanimate stems. This shift
from one part of speech to another without any overt change in the word class is sometimes
called FUNCTIONAL SHIFT, conversion, or ZERO-DERIVATION.
    The following nouns referring to different kinds of clouds all correspond to vn IMPER-
SONAL VERBS describing various cloud formations.

    (32)   nimkiiwaankod      Nl   'thundercloud'
    (33)   waabaankod         Nl   'grey cloud; white cloud' Od
    (34)   mskwaankod         Nl   'red cloud'

    In these cases, however, the noun stem crucially ends in /w/, as can be seen from plural
forms such as nimkiiwaankodoon, 'thunderclouds,' suggesting an ABSTRACT FINAL, /-w/,
which can be used to derive nouns from verbs. This /w/ then coalesces with the /a/ of the
plural suffix /-an/ to produce /oo/. Similar in its behaviour is the word for 'day,' giizhgad Nl
(W, CL), which appears to have the same form as the corresponding VII verb, but which has
a plural giizhgadoon, suggesting a stem ending in /w/.
    TRUNCATED FORMS. A few noun forms evidence TRUNCATION, the shortening of a
word, in which case, some derivational elements may be lost or obscured. For example, the
word mskwaandib, 'copperhead snake' NA, ends with the body part element /aandib/,
'head,' which does not typically occur in final position. The fact that the plural is
mskwaandbag reveals that there is no /w/ at the end of this stem either. A word with a
related meaning and structure, mskondbe, 'be a redhead' VAI, shows the more customary
way to identify individuals on the basis of physical attributes, as does mtigndibe, 'be a
blockhead' VAI, which has as initial the stem /mi tig w/, 'wood' NL

11.3 An Assortment of Noun Finals

    In this section I will present a variety of noun finals, initially some of the more common
finals used clearly in primary derivation, that is, in the derivation of words that usually have
initials that are not independent word-stems. In secondary derivation, all initials are inde-
pendent word-stems. The distinction is somewhat harder to make in nouns than it is in
verbs, though, and I have not adhered to any rigorous classification in the organization of
the notes which follow.
484 • 11.3.1 General Animate and Inanimate Noun Finals


11.3.1 General Animate and Inanimate Noun Finals

   1       NA /-haa/    NI /-hii/      'an X thing,' where X = initial

   Small sets of nouns and pronouns are formed with the noun finals /-haa/, designating an
animate entity, and /-hii/, the corresponding inanimate entity. The initials in these nouns are
usually descriptive, such as /gete-/, 'old,' /oshk-/, 'new,' and /gagwetaan-/, 'extreme, mar-
velous.' Note, however, that the inanimate final also occurs with a noun initial maantaanish,
'sheep,' NA though the precise analysis of the form listed below is uncertain.


           Animate Noun (NA) Inanimate Noun (NI) Gloss
    (35)   ggwetaan'haa             ggwetaan'hii           'a very beautiful thing'
    (36)   getehaa                  getehii               'old thing'
    (37)                            maantaan'shiiyhii      'woolen goods'
    (38)    shkihaa                 shkihii                'a new thing'

   These finals also evidently occur in PAUSAL PRONOUNS, which are used as filler words in
conversation when one has momentarily forgotten a name or noun referring to a particular
person or thing. The following examples illustrate such forms (plural suffixes are given as
well).

            Animate        Inanimate Gloss
    (39)    nahaa,-g       nahii,-n      'whatchamacall'em'W
    (40)    —              nihii, -n     'whatchamacallit' M, CL

11.3.3 Noun Finals Pertaining to Fauna

   A few concrete NOUN FINALS refer to particular classes of fauna, such as fish. As with the
preceding group, most of these finals end in a glide, usually /w/, suggesting an abstract final.

   10       NA /-amegw/        'fish'

11.3.4 Other Noun Finals

   12      Nl /-aaboo/       'liquid'

and shkodewaaboo, 'whiskey,' with stem /ishkode/, 'fire' Nl. A couple of words ending in
consonants also show /w/, sometimes called EXTENSIONAL-/W/, between the initial and
final, as in wiiyaaswaaboo, 'broth, gravy,' with initial wiiyaas, 'meat' Nl, and in
nbiiskwaaboo, 'liquid,' with initial nbiish, '(portable quantity of) water' Nl.

   13       N /-aaby/, /-eyaaby/     'rope; string; chain' (stringlike)

    This noun final is probably related to noun final /-by/. It is mostly used in secondary der-
ivation to designate ropes and strings associated with the referent of the noun serving as ini-
tial. So, for example, mtigwaab, 'archery bow,' with final /-aaby/ attached to stem /mitigw/,
'stick' or 'tree.' The extended form /-eyaaby/ in general Anishinaabemowin most com-
monly appears after noun stems ending in /n/, as it does in one of the examples I have for
Nishnaabemwin, goodkikwaaneyaab, 'chain for hanging a cooking pot' Nl. This final com-
plex also shows an obvious relationship to the classificatory medial /-aabii(g)-/, which
occurs in words such as gnwaabiigzi, 'be long (of stringlike things)' VAI, and dkwaabiigzi,
'be short (of stringlike things)' VAI, suggesting that the medial is a complex of/-aaby-ag-/.
It is probably related as well to the final element /(a)by/ in words such as sab, 'net' NA and
wiigob, 'basswood bark' NA.

   14       Nl /-gamigw/      'building; habitation' (all Nl)

   The noun final /-gamigw/ is extremely productive, used to name buildings, their parts,
and even the habitations of animals and insects. Almost all initials are independent
word-stems, and can be NOUNS (usually animate) or ANIMATE INTRANSITIVE (VAI) VERBS. A
few forms with roots occur, such as /miskw-/, 'red,' in mskogmig, 'red house,' and
/gagwetaan-/, 'extreme, marvelous,' in ggwetaan'gamig, 'very impressive building.' An ele-
ment /w/ commonly occurs with initials ending in VOWELS, whether VAI verbs, as in (142)
and (146), or nouns, as in (144) and (154). Initials representing stems that end in /Cy/, such as
/mikomy/, 'ice,' and /asiny/, 'stone,' show the VOCALIZATION and LENGTHENING of the final
GLIDE /y/, resulting in /ii/, perhaps under the influence of extensional-/w/, as in (161). A cou-
ple of INITIALS ending in /sh/ show the addition of/ii/ and extensional-/w/, e.g. (158), with
492 »11.3.4 Other Noun Finals


noun initial maashtaanish, 'sheep' (stem /maashtaanish/) and (175), with noun initial
nimosh, 'dog' (stem /animosh/). Note, however, nimosh with only link vowel lit in (174).
Noun initials that end in /iw/, such as bzhiki, 'cow' (stem /bizhikiw/), lose final /w/, but
lengthen the final /i/ to /ii/ by virtue of a following extensional-/w/. Verbs ending in short III
or /o/, i.e., in a SHORT VOWEL, show lengthened final vowels with extensional-/w/ in the
same way, as in (142) and (156) for I'll and (152) for /o/. Note however, that the noun ki, 'land,
earth,' does not show lengthening of its final vowel (157).

PLURALITY is SEMANTICALLY relevant, as in mshigamig, 'woodshed,' which has as initial
the singular form for a piece of firewood, mshi NI, and en'googmig, 'anthill,' which has as

11.4 Diminutives and Contemptives

   There are many suffixes, occurring especially with animate nouns, that have a DIMINU-
TIVE, CONTEMPTIVE, or PEJORATIVE structure, but which generally lack such meanings in
contemporary usage. In other words a diminutive flavour persists.

11.4.1 Productive Diminutive /-ens/ and Contemptive /-enh/

   16      N /-ens/       'diminutive'

    A common component of many words is the diminutive suffix /-(e)ns/. Virtually any
noun can easily be made diminutive by the addition of this suffix, but some items of vocab-
ulary occur only in diminutive form, typically those having referents that are perceived as
physically small or juvenile relative to some standard, for example bebiins 'baby' NA,
maamaateshiins, 'firefly' NA, and en'goons 'ant' NA. In other cases, items of vocabulary
with distinctly different meanings are distinguished on the basis of the presence or absence
of a diminutive suffix. For example, bgaan Nl without a diminutive means 'hickory nut, gen-
eral word for nuts' (Od), but with the diminutive, bgaanens Nl, refers specifically to a pea-
nut; mnidoo NA without a diminutive means 'spirit being with spiritual power,' but with a
diminutive, mnidoons NA, means 'insect.' In the case of zhoomin 'grape' Nl, and
zhoomnens, 'raisin' NA, there is also a change of grammatical gender. Examples of this sort
are very easy to find, and many more are presented in Chapter 4.6, beginning on page 185.
   The following list provides examples of vocabulary showing diminutive suffixes.

   (186)    biiwaabkoons             Nl   'telephone'
   (187)    bkwaakdoons              Nl   'little ball; pill' [cf. bkwaakod Nl 'ball']

11.4.2 Other Diminutives and Contemptives

    Many other suffixes and suffix complexes occur that have something of a diminutive fla-
vour, though it is often very difficult to be certain of their presence, their segmentation, or
their contribution to the present meaning of the nouns they occur in. Often these represent
combinations of diminutives, pejoratives, or Contemptives. In this section I list a few exam-
ples. I am uncertain about the analysis of many. Susceptible consonants sometimes show
palatalization, and the suffixes themselves usually have alveolar or alveopalatal fricative or
affricate consonants, such as /s/, /sh/ (IPA /J7) and /j/ (IPA /ds/).
