11.5 Nouns Finals with Classifiers and Classifier-like Elements

    Several finals with classifiers or classifier-like elements occur, and are commonly added
secondarily to independent noun stems, though forms with roots occur as well. All such
finals show a final /w/, suggesting that these components are a combination of a classifica-
tory medial and an abstract noun final. These finals do service in allowing for the specifica-
tion of accessory concepts, such as waasechganiigin, 'curtain' Nl, with the final for cloth,
/-iiginw/, and \vaasechganaabik, 'glass, window pane' NI, both of which are attached to the
independent noun, waasechgan, 'window' NI.

      23      N /-aabikw/    'metal, glass, plastic' (inorganic solid)

   This final is used to refer to objects representing inorganic solids, such as glass, stone, or
metal. It has become specialized in some uses to refer to money, as it commonly does when
a number serves as initial, as in bezhgwaabik, 'one dollar' NI, and niizhwaabik, 'two dollars'
NI.


      (290)   bezhgwaabik            NI     'one dollar'

11.5.1 Classificatory Elements on Verbs of Counting

    Traditionally Anishinaabemowin had a large set of classifiers that were used in counting
objects, such as bezhgwaatig, 'one stick; one bottle,' which has the number bezhig, 'one' as
initial, and the Classificatory element /-aatig/, referring to wooden objects. Some of these
classifiers are still used, though their use has diminished in recent years. They are presented
in detail in Chapter 17.

11.6 Nominalizers

   There are several suffixes which DERIVE NOUNS from VERBS. Verbal stems are almost
always animate intransitive (VAl) verbs, though a few examples of other verb classes occur
as well. Sometimes it is difficult to know exactly what the form of the nominalizing suffix
should be, whether /-n/, /-gan/, or /-aagan/.

   26      N /-n/       Nominalizer

    Many nouns "of instrument or product" (Nichols 1980:78) are formed by adding final
/-n/ to VAl verbs ending in DETRANSITIVIZING suffix /-ge/, formed from VTI verbs. In such
cases, the final Id of the stem changes to /a/, as in bkitehgan, 'hammer, instrument for hit-
ting' Ni, from VAl verb bkitehge, 'hit, strike.' In many cases, it is unlikely that the logical
VAI verb stem corresponding to the noun form is presently used in the language, if it ever
was, such as in bezhgoobiihgan, 'ace,' which is theoretically derived from an VAI verb
*bezhgoobiihge, 'do writing involving the concept "one" in some way.' This is commonly
the case, and sometimes creates uncertainty as to the proper analysis of such words.
    The grammatical gender of nouns derived by the addition of nominalizers is determined
by the semantic properties of their referents, that is, by general conventions of animacy in
Nishnaabemwin. Most such nouns, because they name inert objects, are inanimate, but a
few are animate, such as those naming playing cards, for example, bezhgoobiihgan, 'ace.'
Gambling instruments are often animate.
    All of the following nouns appear to be derived from VAI verbs formed by adding detran-
sitivizing suffix /-ge/ to transitive verbs having instrumental causative finals ending in /-h/.

    (335) aazhdeyaakbiihgan        NI    'something with an X on it' M

   John Nichols has pointed out that a significant difference between Nishnaabemwin
abstract nouns and those of English is that in the latter language complex abstract nominals
are common, such as the anticipation of the rejection of the proposal by the committee. One
reason for this is that English allows abstract nominals to be formed from transitive verbs,
with their objects then specified by means of of phrase, such as of the rejection and of the
508 • 11.7 Reduplication in Nouns


proposal, as in the example provided above. Nishnaabemwin abstract nouns are formed
almost exclusively from intransitive verbs, which generally do not have objects, and as
such, do not allow for the complex constructions of English.

11.7 Reduplication in Nouns

    Some words naming animals and other fauna show apparent REDUPLICATION, but it is
not systematic, and often gives little evidence of being meaningful, as in the following
forms, all of which are animate nouns. There are fairly obvious motivations for a few words,
as in the case of butterflies, which flap their wings in a repetitive manner. By contrast, nei-
ther the form nor the behaviour of the mouse seems to motivate reduplication, and indeed
the word is variable in its behaviour in different communities, showing forms both with and
without reduplication, as in waawaabgonoojiinh (CL) and waabgonoojiinh (M). Reduplica-
tion does show some apparent semantic motivation, however, in its prominence in the
names of birds.
    The following tables provide examples of reduplication in the names of birds, insects,

   It is difficult to know in the case of terms for animals whether repeated syllables actually
constitute deliberate reduplication or are only serendipitous. In the case of bird names, how-
ever, the process is so common that it must be deliberate. Some names of birds are rather
obviously ONOMATOPOEIC, as in (436) and (438) above (see below as well); others redupli-
cate an action or descriptive root, such as (439), which has the root /gwaashkon/, 'jump,' and
(445), which has the root /miskw-/, 'red.' Several reduplicative patterns are used.

• Reduplication of a C(w)VV syllable, e.g., (436), (439), (444), (447).
• Reduplication of a C(w)VV unit, and addition of /n/, e.g., (435), (440), (443)
• Reduplication of the C of the first syllable with vowel /e/, e.g., (445), (446), (448), (459),
  (461), (462).
• Reduplication pattern CV(V)h, which causes STRENGTHENING of ROOT consonant, e.g.,
510 • 11.8 Participles and Deverbal Nouns


    (434), (437), (438), (442), (453), and (455).
•   Reduplication of a CVC unit, e.g., (441)

   ONOMATOPOEIA. Reduplication in bird names is often for the effect of producing ono-
matopoeia, that is, the naming of a creature on the basis of the way it sounds. Another
vocabulary item that illustrates onomatopoeia is the word for 'chicken,' which shows con-
siderable dialect variation, as can be seen from the follow variant forms.

    (469) baagaakwenh              'chicken' CL
    (470)    baaghaakwaanh ' chicken'W
    (471) baaghaakwenh             'chicken' M

11.8 Participles and Deverbal Nouns

    PARTICIPLES are special verb forms which function as nouns, such as e-wepjiged, 'batter
(baseball)' NA (W), and e-kandood, 'fielder (baseball)' NA (M). Participles show INITIAL
CHANGE, and are inflected in the CONJUNCT ORDER, but take endings that resemble noun
endings more than their corresponding conjunct verbal suffixes. For example, the plural
e-wepjigejig, 'batters,' has an animate plural suffix /-ig/ that resembles the animate noun
plural suffix /-ag/ more than the customary animate third person conjunct suffix /-waa/
found on verbs, as in wepjigewaad, '(when/if/that) they hit.' Participles are thus hybrids,
consisting of verbal bases, showing much verbal inflection, but having some noun-like
inflectional features, and functioning as nouns in sentences.
    DEVERBAL NOUNS. Nishnaabemwin has another construction in which verbs are used to
derive nouns, such as in gekaanh, 'old person,' which is based on the VAI verb gkaa /gikaa/,
'be old.' In this case, though, the derived form does not retain verbal features, other than in
showing initial change. I designate words having this derivational form as DEVERBAL
NOUNS, since they are nouns derived from verbs.
    In the following sections I will present examples of the two types of participial construc-
tion found in Nishnaabemwin.

11.8.1 True Participles

   True participles are easy to recognize, since they are fundamentally verbal, and retain
verbal features such as conjunct order inflection, which means that they always have a ver-
bal suffix of some sort, though noun-like endings may appear as well. So, for example, in an
obviative form such as wepjigen'jin, 'batter(s) obv.,' we find the ending /-ini-j-in/, in which
the first element /-ini/ is a verbal inflectional marker of OBVIATION, the element /-j/ a (PALA-
TALIZED) third person animate conjunct order verbal inflectional marker, and the last com-
ponent, /-in/ a NOMINAL inflectional marker of obviation. The form is thus doubly,
redundantly marked for obviation, once with a verbal suffix and once with a nominal suffix.
                                                                     11.8.1 True Participles • 511



These facts underscore the dual nature of participles as both verbal and nominal.
   Participles also show obligatory INITIAL CHANGE. Many participles have a PREVERB /e-/,
perhaps an initial changed form of the preverb /a-/, which seems often to function as a rather
general SUBORDINATOR, and so can have a variety of English interpretations, including
'who...,' 'where...,'and 'when....'
   Participles arise all the time in normal conversation, but are not listed in the dictionary as
nominal forms, because such usage is completely predictable from the meaning of the word
that is participialized. A couple of examples will illustrate this point.

   (1)   Semaan gii-miinaawag giw kiwenziinyag gaa-bi-zhaajig.
         'The old men who had come were given tobacco.' (AK10.6)

          Semaan na 3obv 'tobacco'; gii-miinaawag vta indx»3pProx 'ANpl were given Y'; giwpr
          SpProx 'those'; kiwenziinyag na BpProx 'old men'; gaa-bi-zhaajig vai ic conjpart
          BpProx '(CCNJ) who (ANpl) came.'


   (2)   Mii naa gaa-zhichgewaad giw nishnaabeggaa-niigaan'zijig.

         This is what the Indians who were leaders did.' (AK5.1)

          Mii av 'it's'; naa av 'indeed'; gaa-zhichgewaad vai ic conj BpProx '(CCNJ) what ANpl
          did'; giw/?r SpProx 'those'; nishnaabeg na SpProx 'Indians'; gaa-niigaan'zijig vai ic
          conj part 3pProx 'who (ANpl) were leaders.'


    Here the speaker has simply chosen to identify individuals on the basis of some verbal
notion, in these examples either with verb bi-zhaa, 'come' (VAI) or niigaan'zi, 'be a leader,
take the lead' (VAI). The meaning 'who had come' in (1) follows completely predictably
from the verbal components gaa-, past tense (with initial change), bi-zhaa, 'come' and the
VAI participial ending /-jig/, signifying proximate animate third person plural.
    In other cases, however, participials may come to represent a consistent and conven-
tional way of expressing a concept, and so, may need to be listed in the dictionary. Often the
meanings of the component parts of the participle suggest a meaning that is more general
than the concept the participle comes to identify, so a semantic process of specialization
(also called narrowing) takes place. For example, the term for 'clover,' nesoobgakNlJvu, is
a participle based on a VII verb nsoobgad /nisoobagad/, 'have three leaves,' which consists
of INITIAL /nisw-/, 'three,' MEDIAL /-bag-/, 'leaf,' and vn FINAL /-ad/, 'have, be.' The mean-
ing 'that which has three leaves' makes perfect sense as a means of identifying clover. Note,
however, that many plants other than clover have three leaves, and that the general particip-
ial word meaning 'that which has three leaves,' has come to represent a particular kind of
plant having three leaves, clover. This is not to say that this word could not be used as a gen-
eral participle in the context where its more general meaning was also applicable, certainly
it could. But the point here is that a significant number of Nishnaabemwin speakers consis-
512* 11.8.1 True Participles


tently identify the plant in question with the participial expression nesoobgak, and so it must
be listed in the dictionary with the particular meaning of 'clover.'

    One particularly intriguing participial form is that of shwaachgwaasang, 'applique' NI
(W), which appears to have an English borrowing 'swatch,' in initial position, to which a
final complex /-gwaas+am/, a hybrid of the VAI final /-gwaaso/ and TI final /-gwaad+am/
has been added. The element swatch- fortuitously looks as if it were an initial changed vari-
ant of a fictional root */sooch/, as well. This is truly an example of creative word formation.
    REDUPLICATED PARTICIPLES. The word for 'banana' at Walpole Island (listed as rare by
Rhodes), wewaagaag, appears to show reduplication of the initial syllable of the VII verb
waagaa, 'bend, warp, curve,' creating an extra syllable by reduplication of the first conso-
nant and providing the short vowel /a/, producing /wawaagaa/, which is then subjected to
initial change to produce /wewaagaa/. This type of reduplication also shows up in a few
other words, of uncertain origin, though some are possibly of participial origin, or DEVER-

    DE-PARTICIPIALIZED NOUNS. The form waasgan, 'pepper' NI (CL), appears to have lost
its CONJUNCT VERBAL INFLECTION and thereby become an ordinary noun. Other dialects of
Nishnaabemwin have this word with a final (inflectional) /-g/, waasgang, evidently a parti-
cipial form of the VII verb wiisgan, 'be bitter.'
    Another example is the expression endzhi-mzinaatesjige, 'movie theatre' M, which has a
plural, endzhi-mzinaatesjigengin, but a locative form, endzhi-mzinaatesjigeng. Locatives,
formed by suffixation of this sort, are nominal inflections. However, the word also shows
presence of RELATIVE PREVERB dzhi-, 'at a particular place,' with INITIAL CHANGE to
endzhi- associated with the ITERATIVE inflection it carries (signalled by the suffix -in), rep-
resenting canonically verbal behaviour. This word is thus quite a hybrid between nominal
and verbal forms.

11.9 Compound Nouns

    COMPOUND NOUNS are quite common in Nishnaabemwin. A compound is a word made
up of two relatively independent word-stems, though in Nishnaabemwin, as with other dia-
lects of Anishinaabemowin, this criterion is blurred by the fact that PRENOUNS behave PHO-
NOLOGICALLY as semi-independent words, in that their last VOWEL is never affected by
SYNCOPE, as if it were at the end of a 'word.' MORPHOLOGICALLY, however, prenouns are
not autonomous words, because they cannot stand alone as separate words. Compounds in
Nishnaabemwin always consist of exactly two elements at their most immediate ("highest")
level, and when not EXOCENTRIC, are always RIGHT-HEADED, that is, the element on the
right almost always determines the primary morphological, syntactic, and semantic proper-
ties of the word. For example, the compound jiibaakwe-kik, 'cooking pot,' consists of two
elements: on the left, an animate intransitive (VAI) verb, jiibaakwe, 'cook, prepare food,'
and on the right, an animate noun (NA) kik, 'pot, ashcan, kettle.' It is the element on the right
that determines the part of speech of the whole word, and the compound jiibaakwe-kik is
thus a noun. Furthermore, because kik is of animate gender, a compound with kik as its pri-
mary element will also be animate. This is commonly the case in Nishnaabemwin except for
a few exocentric compounds, such as Gchi-Mookmaan, 'American.' In this case, the ele-
ment on the right is an inanimate noun, mookmaan, 'knife,' but the compound as a whole is
an animate noun, meaning 'Big-Knife,' perhaps originally in reference to the sabres worn
by U.S. cavalrymen. This feature of gender anomaly, however, is not a property of com-
pounds per se, but of naming conventions in the language in general. Names of people are
invariably animate nouns, though they may be based on words that are not inherently ani-
mate, or even nouns, such as Biidaankod, 'Cloud Approaching,' which is a VII verb when
not used as a name, though it can be argued that the name has a final /w/ that derives nouns
516 • 11.9 Compound Nouns


from VII verbs, which would then serve as the head of the word. Compounds that have the
 same gender as their right element are said to be ENDOCENTRIC, that is, have their heads
inside of them, and those that do not, EXOCENTRIC. Another example of an exocentric com-
pound is ziiwtaagni-gookoosh, 'salt pork,' NI, which has an animate noun in right position,
but which, as a compound word, is inanimate. Generally it is the case in Nishnaabemwin
that compounds are endocentric, that is, have the same morphological properties as their
right (head) elements.
     Another property of compounds clearly demonstrating that the right element is the head
can be seen from INFLECTED forms of compounds. For example, the form njiibaakwe-kik (or
alternatively njiibaakwe-kikom), which means 'my cooking pot,' appears to have a FIRST
PERSON PREFIX (/n/) on the verb jiibaakwe, creating njiibaakwe, which, when the word is
not in a compound, would be interpreted to mean, 'I am cooking.' However, the person pre-
fix in a compound is never understood to apply to the first element, such as the verb
jiibaakwe in this case, but rather to the compound as a whole, and because the compound is
 a noun, the person prefix is understood to represent a possessor prefix, and thus add the
 meaning, 'my.' It is important to note, however, that the possessive prefix is attached to the
 compound as a whole, and not to its head word, and from forms such as
 njiibaakwe-kik(mi)naan, 'our (excl.) cooking pot,' it can be seen that possessive suffixes are
 added to the end of the compound as a whole as well.
     Another feature of compounds is that the left element loses all of its morphological
properties. For example, the verb jiibaakwe can be inflected with PAST TENSE, as in
gii-jiibaakwe, 'ANsg cooked, prepared food.' However, when jiibaakwe is the first element
 of a compound, it cannot be inflected for tense, that is, one cannot say *gii-jiibaakwe-kik,
perhaps, for example, if one wanted to refer to a cooking pot that was used one hundred
 years ago, or to a cooking pot that had recently been converted into a plantholder. The only
 way to relate time to the compound jiibaakwe-kik is to use the PRETERIT suffix /-ban/, as dis-
 cussed in Chapter Section 4.11, page 206ff.
     Semantically, too, it is clear that the right element is the head, in that the term
jiibaakwe-kik refers to a kind of pot, rather than to a kind of cooking, which we might
 expect if the left element, the verb jiibaakwe, were the head.
     THE BINARY NATURE OF COMPOUNDS. Nishnaabemwin compounds can consist of more
 than two word-elements, but in such cases, the elements always show sub-grouping into
 units of two. So, for example, in the case of Gchi-Mookmaan-Ki, 'United States,' there are
 three elements, a PRENOUN gchi-, 'great, big,' an inanimate noun (NI), mookmaan, 'knife,'
 and another inanimate noun, ki, 'land, earth.' These three elements are not related to each
 other in the same way, however, because the elements Gchi- and Mookmaan combine to
 form the compound Gchi-Mookmaan, 'American,' and this compound noun is then used as
 the left element of another compound, in which the right element is this time ki, 'land.' The
 following diagram illustrates the relationships between the elements of this word.
                                                                    11.9 Compound Nouns • 517




   THE CLASSIFICATION OF COMPOUNDS BY PHONOLOGICAL LINKAGE. Compounds show
four distinct kinds of PHONOLOGICAL LINKAGE between their elements.
    1. The most loosely bound compounds simply juxtapose free words, and have no explicit
linkage, as in the following examples:

    (522)   shkode-daabaan           NA 'train' W (lit, 'fire-vehicle')
    (523)   waasgang-kosmaan         NI    'bell pepper' (lit., 'pepper-squash')
    (524)   waawan-kokbinaagan       NI    'Easter basket' W (lit., 'egg-basket')
    (525)   wiigwaas-makak           NI    'birchbark box'

    2. Another type of linkage involves the addition of I'll to the end of the first member of
the compound. In these cases, noun stems ending in /Cy/, such as /opiny/ (or /apiny/),
'potato,' VOCALIZE the lyl to /i/ and lengthen it, as in pinii-mshkimod, 'potato sack' NI.
Stems ending in /iw/, such as /ininiw/ (or /aniniw/), 'man,' show loss of /w/ and lengthening
of the final /i/ to /ii/, as in ninii-miiknod, 'man's trousers, man's underwear' NI. The word
zhmaaganish, 'soldier' Od also acts as if it ended in /iw/. This compound-formation process
is especially common with noun stems ending in /Cy/. The following examples illustrate
compounds showing this degree of linkage.

    (526)   mkomii-mkak              NI   'freezer' (lit., 'ice box')
    (527)   ninii-miiknod            NI   'man's trousers'
    (528)   pinii-mnidoons           NA 'cutworm; potato bug'
    (529)   pinii-mshkimod           NI   'sack for potatoes'
    (530)   sinii-waagaakod          NI    'stoneaxe'
    (531)   zhmaagni-gimaa           NA 'jack' (lit. 'soldier-leader')
518 • 11.9 Compound Nouns


    (532)   zhmaagni-wesiinh        NA 'wasp' (lit., 'soldier-animal')
   (533)    zhmaagnishii-gimaa      NA 'leader of soldiers (e.g. captain, general)'
   (534)    ziiwtaagni-gookoosh     NI    'salt pork'

    3. A tight linkage between compound elements occurs in words such as mshkikiiwnini,
'herbal remedy specialist, medicine man' NA, which shows EXTENSIONAL-/W/ and the
lengthening of a preceding vowel that always accompanies it. This behaviour is quite com-
mon with compounds having nini, 'man,' as head. Other words showing the same pattern
are daakewnini, 'helmsman' NA and kawaabiiwnini, 'guard, watchman' NA.
    4. Some compounds in Nishnaabemwin involve root elements that are not quite pre-
nouns, since they lack the derivational suffix /-i/. Compare, for example, the two words
waabi-mnoomin, 'white rice' NI, which has a derivationally straightforward prenoun ele-
ment, waabi-, and waab-signaak, 'bobolink' (NA), which has a prenominal element that is
identical to the root form meaning 'white,' Avaab/. Several prenominal units specifying
colours, as well as other prenouns, appear in this root form in compounds. Words such as
zaaw-bmide, 'butter' NI suggest that these elements are in fact prenouns, because the first
short vowel of the right stem element, /bimide/, is deleted by syncope, which it would not
be if the stem form of the first element were /waabi/, and its last segment, /i/, was being
deleted by syncope.
    THE CLASSIFICATION OF COMPOUNDS ON THE BASIS OF THEIR LEFT ELEMENTS.
Another way of classifying compounds is on the basis of the basic part of speech class of
the element that serves as the left component. This element may be a prenoun, a noun, or an
intransitive verb, most commonly an animate intransitive (VAl) verb, but occasionally an
INANIMATE INTRANSITIVE (vil) verb. I will treat each of these types in turn.
    PRENOUN + NOUN COMPOUNDS. Compounds consisting of a PRENOUN and a NOUN are
quite common. The following table lists examples.

   (535)    bgoji-bzhiki             NA     'buffalo'

11.10 A Brief Introduction to Adverb Finals

    In this section I will briefly outline a few ADVERB FINALS. Adverbs represent the least
unified part of speech class in Nishnaabemwin, consisting of words that correspond to
English ADVERBS, PREPOSITIONS, CONJUNCTIONS, and INTERJECTIONS. The class of adverbs
basically consists of all of those words that are not NOUNS, PRONOUNS, or VERBS, outside of
NUMBERS and a very small set of words classed by Rhodes as PARTICLES (see Chapter 3 for
discussion of adverbs). Numbers are treated at length in Chapter 17, so will not be consid-
ered here. My discussion is quite limited, and the reader should consult Bloomfield 1958 for
a more comprehensive treatment of adverb finals.
    THE GENERAL STRUCTURE OF ADVERBS. As with nouns and verbs, many adverbs show
evidence of having internal structure, and some of these structural components correspond
to elements found in nouns and verbs. For example, there is a fairly large set of locational
adverbs that incorporate familiar noun-like elements found in verbs as medials or finals, and
in nouns as concrete noun finals. Examples of the latter include naamaatig, 'under a tree'
(Od), jiigaatig, 'near the woods; near the wall,' and gidaatig, 'at the top of a tree; on a log.'
Each of these words ends with the element, /-aatig/, which appears to have the meaning
'tree; wood; log' and is almost identical to a final used with nouns, as in waagaakdaatig,
'axe handle.' On the other hand, the locational adverbs gidaajwan, 'upstream' and
niisaajwan, 'downstream,' have a final element similar to that found in INANIMATE INTRAN-
SITIVE (VII) verbs such as maajjiwan, 'start to flow,' bmijwan, 'flow along' and gzhiijwan,
'flow quickly.' The only difference in this case is that the adverb final /-aajwan/ appears to
have a leading element /aa/ not found in the corresponding verb final /-jiwan/.
                                                              11.10.1 Some Adverb Finals • 523


    Further evidence of the structure of adverbs can easily be seen by comparing sets having
related meanings, as in the following list.

    (626)   gidaa         'up; on'
    (627)   gidaagon      'on the snow'
    (628)   gidaajwan     'upstream'
    (629)   gidaaki       'up the hill'
    (630)   gidaatig      'at the top of a tree; on a log'
    (631)   gidbag        'on the roof'
    (632)   gidbiig       'on top of the water'
    (633)   gidgamig      'on top of the building'
    (634)   gidkamig      'on the earth, on the ground'
    (635)   gidsag        'on the floor'(W, CL)
    (636)   gijyahii      'on [top of s.t.]; on top of s.t.
    (637)   gijyahiing    'on [top of s.t.]; on top of s.t.

    Here we can easily determine that there is an initial component, having the shape /gid-/
or /gij-/, which means 'on top of; upon; up.' The variation in form between the final /d/ of
/gid-/ and the final /j/ of /gij-/ can be explained on the basis of PALATALIZATION. Removal
of the initial component reveals a variety of finals with meanings ranging from the fairly
ABSTRACT, as in gidaa, 'up, on,' with final /aa/ functioning only to create an adverb, to
those with quite CONCRETE meanings, such as /-brig/, 'water,' as in gidbiig, 'on top of (the)
water,' and /-gamig/, as in gidgamig, 'on top of (the) building.'

/-dbik/, 'nights,' e.g., ngodbik, 'for one night' (with root /ngo(d)/, 'one'), and /-bboon/,
 'years,' e.g., ngo-bboon, 'one year.' These and many other units of time are discussed in
more detail in Chapters 16 and 17. These words are sometimes analyzed as nouns.

11.12 Deriving Preverbs and Prenouns

    Preverbs and prenouns are commonly derived by the addition of final l-il to a root or
other initial. This final PALATALIZES a susceptible stem-final consonant. For example, RELA-
TIVE PREVERBS zhi-, 'manner, to,' /izhi-/ and nji- /onji-/, 'from, source,' are formed from rel-
ative roots /iN/ and /ond/, respectively. Final /-i/ shows standard phonological behaviour
with respect to glides, e.g., fuses with a stem-final /w/ to become /o/, as in mno-, 'good,
well,' from stem /minw/, 'good.'

11.13 Additional Reading

    An excellent source for those interested in the structure of Ojibwe nouns is Nichols
1980. Bloomfield 1958 and 1962 are also very useful, though they are both quite schematic
in their treatment. Goddard 1990 represents a significant revision of Bloomfield's analyses
of Algonquian word structure. O'Meara 1990 is also very valuable.
12
Nominals and Pronominals




12.1 Introduction

    Noun phrases can consist of a solitary noun or PRONOUN, two nouns in APPOSITION, or a
group of words HEADED by a noun or pronoun. They may represent a name (proper noun) or
a COMMON NOUN. They may show POSSESSION, as in ndoo-nmemag, 'my sturgeon (pi.),' or
be qualified by one or more PRENOUNS, as in bgoji-mnoomin, 'wild rice.' They may be
quantified by specific numeral QUANTIFIERS, as in bezhig jiimaan, 'one boat,' and
ngodwewaan mkiznan, 'one pair of shoes,' or by more general quantifiers, such as kina (also
gkina), 'all,' and aanind (also aaning), 'some,' or qualified by the NEGATIVE pronoun, gaa
wiya (also gaa waya), 'no one.' They may show further specification by RELATIVE CLAUSES,
that is verbal expressions used as modifiers or identifiers of participants in verbal actions,
such as in giw kiwenziinyag gaa-bi-zhaajig, 'those old men who came,' which has the rela-
tive clause gaa-bi-zhaajig, 'who (pi.) came,' modifying and further delimiting the class
identified by the noun kiwenziinyag, 'old men.' All of these strategies for forming noun
phrases will be discussed in this chapter.
    Nishnaabemwin also has a wealth of PRONOUNS which can either stand in the place of
noun phrases, occur together with nouns, or provide various kinds of emphasis or focus.
PERSONAL PRONOUNS identify individuals on the basis of their conversational roles as
speakers (first person), addressees (second person), or topics of conversation (third person).
A rich and well-used set of DEMONSTRATIVE PRONOUNS exist which are indexed to agree
with their associated nouns for the grammatical categories of gender, number, and obvia-
tion. The inanimate singular demonstrative pronouns, especially iw (or wi), 'that,' is used in
many SYNTACTIC constructions as a pronominal substitute for an entire CLAUSE or SEN-
TENCE, rather similarly to the way that English it is used, as in 'Helen didn't know it, but I'd
already baked her birthday cake,' or English that, as in 'I know that you love autumn.'
There are also INDEFINITE PRONOUNS indexed only for gender but not number or obviation,
similar to the English pronouns 'someone' and 'something.' These pronouns are also used
to form negative pronouns, analogous to English 'no one' and 'nothing,' and universal pro-
528 • 12.2 Some Terminology


nouns, roughly like English 'everyone' and 'everything.' SUBSTITUTIVE PRONOUNS such as
nahii function as placeholders and generics in conversation. These and several other kinds
of pronouns are treated in this chapter.
    We have also seen in the previous chapters that there is a rich system for the INFLEC-
TIONAL marking of actors and goals on verbs, by means of PREFIXES and SUFFIXES. The
inflectional system is so rich that it is not uncommon for verbs to be used without any asso-
ciated noun phrases or pronouns, since the inflections alone allow the determination of who
or what is involved in the verbal action, event, or state. In addition to the three person cate-
gories mentioned above, there also exist generalized actor forms, used when reference is to
general activity rather than to that of specific individuals.
    PHYSICAL AND LINGUISTIC CONTEXTS. To clarify several issues pertaining to the use of
nouns and pronouns, I will distinguish between the PHYSICAL CONTEXT, which is defined as
the spatial, temporal, and social context in which the communicative act of using language
takes place, and the LINGUISTIC CONTEXT, which is wholly within language, and refers to
the context in which a given word or sentence occurs relative to other words and sentences
in a communicative event. The physical context thus consists of people and objects, is situ-
ated in time and space, but can be referred to linguistically, such as when a speaker says
maaba gwiiwzens, 'this boy,' and indicates a particular boy in the immediate physical con-
text. The physical context often provides the means of interpreting DEICTIC words such as
maanda, 'this (inan.)' and iw 'that (inan.),' maanpii, 'here,' and odi, 'there,' and noongo(m),
'now,' since these words are defined on the basis of some reference point, usually the
speaker's location and the time of speaking. Many of these words can have discourse-inter-
nal meanings as well, as we will see.
    In language use there is typically a rich interplay of physical context and linguistic con-
text, and every language has many ways to introduce and maintain "characters" in a dis-
course. In this chapter we will examine some of the ways in which Nishnaabemwin
speakers do so, using the rich assortment of linguistic resources the language provides,
including nouns, pronouns, prenouns, inflections, and more elaborate devices such as pos-
sessive constructions and relative clauses.

12.2 Some Terminology

     The following terms are used extensively throughout this chapter, in quite specific ways.
First a NOUN PHRASE is a grouping of words consisting of a noun as the main unit (or HEAD)
of the group, possibly modified by such categories of words and phrases as numbers, pro-
nouns, and relative clauses, as in, for example, niizh ninwag, 'two men,' giw ninwag, 'those
men,' and giw niizh ninwag gaa-ngamjig, 'those two men who sang.'
     NOMINAL. The term NOMINAL is sometimes used to refer to the grammatical properties
of nouns. This is the case when the term "nominal" is itself used as an adjective, as when,
for example, the PARTICIPIAL inflectional endings /-ig/ and /-in/, as in bemaadzijig, 'people'
(lit., 'those who live'), and bemaadzin'jin, 'person/people (obv.),' are said to be NOMINAL,
because of their similarity to the animate plural and obviative suffixes found on nouns. The
                                                    12.3 Ways of Identifying Discourse Entities • 529


term NOMINAL, when used itself as a noun, specifies any word or phrase functioning as a
noun phrase, whether a noun, pronoun, or a relative clause. For example, mik, 'beaver,' aw
mik, 'that beaver,' wiinwaa, 'they/them,' giw niizh mikog, 'those two beavers,' and
waasnijig, 'those eating,' can all be nominals.
    RELATIVE CLAUSES. RELATIVE CLAUSES describe characters on the basis of some
verb-based modifying description, as in naagaaniid, '(the one) who leads' (VAI), where
someone is identified on the basis of leading, or gaa-bi-mwinewaajig, '(the ones) who come
attacking them (anim.)' (VTA), where characters are identified on the basis of their action in
coming to attack. Nishnaabemwin relative clauses usually have participial verbs as their
heads (main elements), and these verbs show both nominal and verbal inflectional features.
Participles are verbal constructions which function as nouns. They are discussed at length
below.
    In the following sections we will examine the means available to speakers for identifying
characters in conversation and other kinds of discourse. These include verbal affixation,
pronouns, simple nouns, noun phrases, and relative clauses.

12.3 Ways of Identifying Discourse Entities

    The entities being referred to in speech are often called referents, and the linguistic act of
associating these entities to particular language forms is called reference. I will refer to
words or phrases that are used to identify individuals and groups as referring expressions.
    VERBAL MARKING ALONE. The simplest way to identify participants is INFLECTION-
ALLY, that is, by means of combinations of prefixes and suffixes on verbs, without any inde-
pendent nominal expression. This is the normal means of introducing first and second
persons, singular and plural, as mentioned above, whose reference is determined or under-
stood from the conversational context, as in the following examples, both of which appear
as the first sentences of various episodic narratives.

   (1)   E-shki-waabmag aw Gchi-mookmaan maa ddibew ziibing ngii-zeghig.
         'The first time that 1 saw a white man there by the bank of the river, he frightened
         i»c.'(AM3.1)

          E-shki-waabmag vta ic conj ls»3sProx '(CCNJ) when I first saw ANsg'; aw pr 3sProx
          'that'; Gchi-mookmaanna SsProx 'white American'; maa av 'there'; ddibew av 'on the
          bank'; ziibing ni 0 loc 'by the river'; ngii-zeghig vta ind3sProx»ls 'ANsg frightened
          me.'
530 • 12.3 Ways of Identifying Discourse Entities


   (2)   Mewnzha gaa-zhiwebziyaan gii-waabmangid aw meko-bmased.
          'A long time ago it happened to me that we saw this bear-walker (witch).'

          Mewnzha av 'long ago'; gaa-zhiwebziyaan vai ic conj Is '(CCNJ) what happened to
          me'; gii-waabmangid vta conj lp»3sProx '(CONJ) we saw ANsg'; aw/?r SsProx 'that';
          meko-bmased vai ic conj part SsProx '(CCNJ) ANsg who is a bear walker.' (AK8.1)

    Sentence (2) can be contrasted with a narrative about a third person, which requires
introduction of the protagonists by means of separate nominals, though even here, reference
may be in part contextually determined by the speaker, since the identity of textual charac-
ters may be on the basis of their kinship or social relations with the speaker (or addressee),
as in the following.

   (3)   Mewnzha aw nmishoomis gaa-zhiwebzinid niw wdedeman miinwaa niw
         wdoodooman.
         'What happened to my. grandfather's father and mother, long ago.' (AK2.1)

          Mewnzha av 'long ago'; a\vpr3sProx 'that'; nmishoomis nad ls(3sProx) 'my
          grandfather'; gaa-zhiwebzinid vai ic conj 3obv '(CCNJ) what happenened to ANobv';
          niwpr 3obv 'that/those'; wdedeman na 3sProx(3obv) 'ANso'S father'; miinwaa av
          'and'; niwpr 3obv 'that/those'; wdoodooman na 3sProx(3obv) 'ANSG'S mother.'

   VOCATIVES. By using a VOCATIVE form, that is, a term of direct address, a speaker can
simultaneously address and identify one or more individuals, as in the following example.
Vocative plurals have a distinct ending, /-dig/ (or /-dog/), formally related to the INDEPEN-
DENT ORDER DUBITATIVE VERBAL MODE.

   (4)    Nooshenh, bi-zhaan maampii. I 'Come here, (my) grandchild.7 (AM39.717)

          Nooshenh nad (we)1 ls(3sProx) 'my grandchild'; bi-zhaan vai imp 2s 'come hither';
          maampii av 'here.'
          1. The vocative form of this term is commonly noozis, but here the term-of-reference is used in a voca-
         tive context.


   (5)   Boozhoo nwiijkiwenydig giinwaa mnik bezndaageyeg.
         'Good-day, my friends, as many of you as who are listening.' (SO6.189)1

          Boozhoo av 'hello'; nwiijkiwenydig nadvoc ls(2p) 'you my friends'; giinwaa pr pers
          2p 'you'; mnik av 'as many as'; bezndaageyeg vai ic conj 2p 'you (pi) who are listening.'
                                                          12.3 Ways of Identifying Discourse Entities • 531


   IDENTIFICATION INVOLVING VERBAL INFLECTION IN TANDEM WITH SEPARATE NOMI-
NALS. It is also possible to have plural forms which include both discourse LOCAL (first and
second person) and discourse NON-LOCAL (third person) referents. First and second person
plural can both include reference to third persons. In such cases, third person referents may
be introduced by means of explicit nominals in clauses having verbs with first or second
person plural inflections. The following examples are illustrative. In both sentences, the
verb is inflected for first person plural exclusive, but a separate nominal occurs as well, in
the first, niijkiwenh, 'my friend,' and in the second, niidgemaagan, 'my wife.'

    (6)     Niijkiwenh ngii-nmadbimi endzhi-bgizwaad.
           'My friend and I sat at the bathing beach.' (AM39.578)

            Niijkiwenh na Is(SsProx) 'my friend'; ngii-nmadbimi vai ind Ip 'we (excl.) sat';
            endzhi-bgizwaad vai ic conj SpProx '(CCNJ) where ANpl swim.'

    (7)     Niidgemaagan nnanaamdabmi biindig wiigwaaming.
           'My wife and I are sitting inside the house.' (AM39.41)

            Niidgemaagan nad ls(3sProx) 'my spouse'; nnanaamdabmi vai redup ind Ip 'we
            (excl.) are sitting'; biindig av 'inside'; wiigwaaming ni 0 loc 'in house.'

    Once a third person referent has been introduced and established in the discourse con-
text, an additional third person can be introduced in a new clause or sentence, and the verb
inflected for plural, thus including reference to both the previously introduced third person
and the new one. For example, prior to the occurrence of both of the example sentences
below, a third person referent has already been well established in the discourse.

    (8)    Mii gwa eta go niizhiwaapa aniw ogwisan bimaadiziwaad.
           'There were only the two of them living, his son and he.' (AW9.41)

            Mii av 'and'; gwa av 'indeed'; eta av 'only'; niizhiwaapa vai indpret SpProx 'ANpl
            were two in number'; aniwpr 3obv 'that/those'; ogwisan nad 3sProx(3obv) 'ANso's
            son(s)'; bimaadiziwaad vai conj SpProx '(CONJ) ANpl lived.'




1. While speakers and addressees are normally physically and temporally contiguous, the nature of contemporary
linguistic recording sometimes gives rise to rather unnatural speech contexts, such as that in which a narrator may
be required to imagine an audience who may hear him or her at a later date by means of electronic recording, and
whom he may address in absentia, which is the case in this sentence.
532 • 12.3 Ways of Identifying Discourse Entities


   (9)   Mil sa gii-minozekwed gii-wiisiniwaad. I Then she cooked and they ate.'
          Mii av 'and'; gii-minozekwed vai conj SsProx '(CONJ) ANsg cooked'; gii-wiisiniwaad
          vai conj SpProx '(CONJ) ANpl ate.' (AW14.95)

    In (8), an explicit third person nominal form is added, a kinship term with a third person
possessor, aniw ogwisan, 'that son of his.' The head of the possessed nominal expression,
ogwisan, is obligatorily obviative, though both associated verbs are inflected as third person
plural proximates, niizhiwaapa, 'they (prox.) were two in number,' and bimaadiziwaad,
'they (prox.) live.' In (9), the verbal inflection simply switches from singular to plural in the
sequential clauses.
    NOMINAL EXPRESSIONS. More commonly in discourse, however, third person characters
are introduced and identified expressly by means of nominals, as in the following examples,
where noun phrases consisting of demonstrative pronouns modifying nouns are used.

   (10) "Dbik-giisong giiwenh gii-baa-zhaa wa Gchi-mookmaan" naajmo wa
        kiwenziinh.
          '"Some American allegedly went to the moon," some old man tells the story.'

          Dbik-giisong na loc 3 'to the moon'; giiwenh av 'allegedly'; gii-baa-zhaa vai ind SsProx
          'ANsg went around'; wa/?r SsProx 'this'; Gchi-mookmaan na SsProx 'white American';
          naajmo vai ind SsProx 'ANsg relates'; wa pr SsProx 'that'; kiwenziinh na SsProx 'old
          man.'(FFl.l)

   (11) Megwaa ko mekdekewaad giw Nishnaabeg gii-ndo-gkendmowaad gegoo.
         'Back in the days when th(os)e Indians used to fast, they sought to obtain knowl-
         edge of something.'(AM23.1)


          Megwaa av 'while'; ko av 'used to'; mekdekewaad vai ic conj SpProx '(CCNJ) when
          ANpl fasted'; giwpr SpProx 'those'; Nishnaabeg na SpProx 'Indians';
          gii-ndo-gkendmowaad vti conj 3pProx»0 '(CONJ) ANsg sought to know IN'; gegoo pr
          indefO 'something.'

    Once characters have been introduced and identified, they can subsequently be referred
to by means of verbal inflection alone. For this reason, personal pronouns in particular are
much less commonly used than in English. The inflections on verbs fill a role very similar to
that played by English personal pronouns. The following example represents a very com-
mon pattern, in which reference to the grammatical subjects is solely by means of verbal
inflection. There are no personal pronouns, nor any another type of nominal to identify the
subject.
                                            12.3.1 Making Reference to Generalized Activity • 533


   (12) Naabndamwin wgii-aabjitoonaawaa. Gii-naabndamHY«w/ dash gegoo mil iw
        giishpin wdaapnaawaad niw sa waa-zhwennugwoo/in.
         'They made use of dream visions. When they had dreamt anything, the question

          Naabndamwin ni Os 'dream vision'; wgii-aabjitoonaawaa vti ind3pProx»Os 'ANpl
          used INsg.' Gii-naabndamwaad vti conj 3pProx»0 '(CONJ) ANpl dreamed IN'; dash av
          'then'; gegoo pr indefO 'something'; mii av 'and'; iw prOs 'that'; giishpin av 'if;

12.3.1 Making Reference to Generalized Activity

    Specific resources exist to make reference to general activities or experience, that is,
those that are normal or common, representing customary activity. In these cases the
emphasis is less on who undertakes the activity, than the fact of the activity itself. There are
several ways to make statements of generalized activity, including the use of unspecified
subject inflections, second person forms, third person plural forms, expressions with indefi-
nite pronouns, and generic reference, all of which are discussed below.
    GENERALIZED SUBJECT INFLECTIONS. Specific generalized activity inflectional markers
exist in Nishnaabemwin for the grammatical subjects of animate intransitive (VAI) and tran-
sitive inanimate (VTI) verbs. The following examples illustrate the use of these inflections.

   (13) Eshkam znagad wii-debnaming iw waa-boodweng.
         'It is getting harder and harder/or one to obtain that with which one might make
         afire: (AM 15.15)

          Eshkam av 'increasingly'; znagad vii ind Os 'INsg is difficult'; wii-debnaming vti conj
          x»0 '(CONJ) that one will get IN'; \\v pr Os 'that'; waa-boodweng vai ic conj x '(CCNJ)
          one makes fire.'

   (14) Aabdeg sa gwagchi-nakiim wii gwa miinwaazhoon'yaakem gwa aanwi.
         'One indeed works hard, (N.B. in the auto industry) and, thankfully, one does
         make a lot of money.' (JF)

          Aabdeg av 'necessarily'; gwa av 'indeed'; gchi-nakiim vai indx 'there is much work';
          wii av 'indeed'; gwa av 'indeed'; miinwaa av 'also'; zhoon'yaakem vai indx 'there is
          money making'; gwa av 'indeed'; aanwi av 'besides.'
534 • 12.3.1 Making Reference to Generalized Activity


    SECOND PERSON INFLECTIONS. Just as with English, the second person can be used to
refer to general activity or experience as well. Both singular and plural second person forms
occur in this function.

   (15) Mil maa naa gaa-zhi-debweyendmowaad giw nishnaabeg giishpin waabmad aw
        baanaabe. Waya da-nbo maa endaayan. Mjihiiwan giishpin ngoding waabmad
        baanaabe.
          'See, that's what the Indians believed if you (sg.) see a mermaid. Someone will
          die there where you (sg.) live. It's a bad omen if you (sg.) ever see a mermaid.'

          Mii av 'that's'; maa av 'in that case'; gaa-zhi-debweyendmowaad vti ic conj 3pProx»0
          '(CCNJ) ANpl believed IN'; giw pr 3pProx 'those'; nishnaabeg na 3pProx 'Indians';
          giishpin av 'if; waabmad vta conj 2s»3sProx '(CONJ) you (SG) see ANsg'; awpr
          3sProx 'that'; baanaabe na 3sProx 'mermaid.' Waya/?r indef3sProx 'someone'; da-nbo
          vai ind 3sProx 'ANsg will die'; maa av 'there'; endaayan vai ic conj 2s '(CCNJ) where
          you (SG) live.' Mjihiiwan vii ind Os 'INsg is an ill omen'; giishpin av 'if; ngoding av
          'sometime'; waabmad vta conj 2s»3sProx '(CONJ) you (SG) see ANsg'; baanaabe na
          3sProx 'mermaid.' (AK4.11)


   (16)   "Gii-mzhwaagniwi," gii-zhinkaajgewag wi pii; nango wii go naa gnimaa
          'gii-mzhikoozo,' gdaa-kidom.
          '"Gii-mzhwaagniwi," that's the term they used then; nowadays perhaps you (pi.)
          would say, "gii-mzhikoozo."' (SO6.46)

           Gii-mzhwaagniwi vta/ai indx»3sProx'ANsg was wounded'; gii-zhinkaajgewag vaio
           ind SpProx 'ANpl called Y so'; wi pr Os 'that'; pii av 'time'; nango av 'nowadays'; wii av
           'however'; gnimaa av 'probably'; gdaa-kidom vai ind 2p 'you (pi) would say.'

        kawe-giizhoos\\ingaa-shkwaa-mdoodoojinlTER.

          about'; pane av 'always.'

    Another kind of reference related to that of generic nouns is non-specific reference. By
non-specific reference, I mean reference that simply mentions the existence of something
without referring to specific individuals. In the following sentence, for example, the words

ticular berries and fish, but rather make vague, general reference to these things as groups.

          pr Os 'that'; zaaghigan ni Os 'lake'; miinwaa av 'and'; baatiindoon vii ind Op 'INpl are
          abundant'; miinan ni Op 'blueberries'; giigoonyag na SpProx 'fish PL'; ge av 'also';
          yaawag vai ind3pProx 'ANpl are there'; maa av 'there'; zaaghigning ni 0 loc 'in lake.'

12.3.2 Indefinites

    The terms definite and indefinite are used to characterize the English articles the and
a(n), respectively. The definite article is typically used when the identity of the referent of a
noun phrase is known, either because it is familiar or can be inferred from context or from"
our assumptions about the nature of the world; otherwise, the indefinite article is used. In
English narrative the indefinite article is typically used to introduce characters, while the
definite article is used with referents that have already been introduced. Nishnaabemwi
does not use specific indefinite or definite articles, but instead has a variety of other devices
to introduce characters and maintain reference to them.
    INDEFINITES WITH BEZHIG. Nominal phrases containing bezhig, 'one,' can be used to
introduce characters in a discourse, as in the following examples:

   (27) Aanii-sh mii sa gii-maajaad giiwenh bezhig nini, gii-zhaad wadi
        ziisbaakdokaaning.
          'So a certain man set off alone, and went over there to the sugar camp.' (SOI .8)

          Aanii-sh av well; mii av 'then'; gii-maajaad vai conj SsProx '(CONJ) ANsg left';
          giiwenh av 'reportedly'; bezhig nm 'a certain; one'; nini na SsProx 'man'; gii-zhaad vai
          conj SsProx '(CONJ) ANsg went there'; wadi av 'there'; ziisbaakdokaaning ni loc 0 'to
          the sugaring place.'
                                                                           12.3.2 Indefinites* 539



   (28) Nbwaanwihaanaa wadi wii-nsangid bezhig mnidoo, mii sa
        gaa-zhi-mkwenmigooyan wii-bbaa-wiijiiwyaang, wii-wa-naadmawyaang."
        'We have tried in vain to kill a manitou over there, and we thought you would
        come along with us and help.'" (SO4.11)

         Nbwaanwihaanaa vta ind lp»3sProx 'we tried in vain to do to ANsg'; wadi av 'there';
         wii-nsangid vta conj lp»3sProx 'we want to kill ANsg'; bezhig nm 'one, a certain';
         mnidoo no, 3sProx 'manitou'; mii av 'and'; gaa-zhi-mkwenmigooyan vta ic conj lp»2s
         'we thought of you'; wii-bbaa-wiijiiwyaang vta conj 2s»lp 'you would come along with
         us'; wii-wa-naadmawyaang vta conj 2s»lp 'you would go and help us.'


   The construction miinwaa bezhig, 'another one,' is very common, too, for introducing
additional characters to those already introduced.

   (29) Jiimaaning ngii-boozmi miinwaa bezhig kwe, gii-bbaa-yaamwaad iw
        bgoji-mnoomin widi waabshkokiing.
        'We went in a canoe, along with another woman, and they went about gathering
        wild rice there in the marsh.' (AM5.2)

         'and'; bezhig nm 'a certain; one'; kwe na SsProx 'woman'; gii-bbaa-yaamwaad vti conj

         ni Os 'wild rice'; widi av 'over there'; waabshkokiing ni 0 loc 'in the marsh.'


   (30) Aanii-sh mii sa gmaapiich go miinwaa bezhig bmaadgaad go wesiinh, aanii-sh mii

          ANobv'; nishnaaben na 3obv 'lndian(s).'

          '(CCNJ) where I live.'

   (36) Aw dash gwiiwzens gii-zhaa odi gidaaki gii-wi-boodaajged, mii dash

           3pProx 'those'; nishnaabeg na 3pProx 'Indians.'

          ANobv'; gii-bi-giiwewdamwaad vta conj 3sProx»3obv '(CONJ) ANsg brought them

          grandmother(s)'; mii av 'and'; dash av 'then'; niwpr3obv 'that/those'; gaa-mnazwaajin
          vta ic conj 3sProx»3obv '(CCNJ) what (ANobv) ANsg cooked'; gii-mwaawaad vta conj

12.3.3 Mass Nouns

   MASS NOUNS, that is those representing things that are usually expressed as undifferenti-
ated substances or materials, are typically used without demonstratives.

   (40) Ggizheb dash ngii-naadin nbiish. I 'In the morning I fetched water.' (AM 10.5)
           Ggizheb av 'in the morning'; dash av 'then'; ngii-naadin vti ind ls»0s 'I fetched INsg';
           nbiish ni Os 'water.'

   (41)   Maajiigi mdaamin. I "The corn is growing.' (AM39.84)
           Maajiigi vai ind 3sProx 'ANsg is growing'; mdaamin na SsProx 'corn.'

   Mass nouns also typically occur with verbs inflected as singulars.

   (42) Baatiino semaa. I 'There is lots of tobacco.' (AM39.112)

           Baatiino vai ind SsProx 'ANsg is abundant'; semaa na SsProx 'tobacco.'

   (43) Baatiinad wiiyaas. I "There is plenty of meat.' (AM39.242)

           Baatiinad vii ind Os 'INsg is abundant'; wiiyaas ni Os 'meat.'
                                                                               12.3.3 Mass Nouns • 543


   (44) Nbaatiintoon wiisniwin. I "I have lots of food.' (AM39.168)

         Nbaatiintoon vti ind ls»0s 'I have lots of INsg'; wiisniwin ni Os 'food.'

   Compare the forms above to the following verbs having plural COUNT NOUNS, and plural
verbs.

   (45) Gii-baatiinwag bemaadzijig. I 'There were many people.' (AM39.653)

          Gii-baatiinwag vai indBpProx 'they were many'; bemaadzijig vai ic conjpart 3pProx
          '(CCNJ) people (lit :ANpl who live).'

   (46) Baatiindoon siniin. I "There are many stones.' (AM39.249)

          Baatiindoon vii ind Op 'INpl are abundant'; siniin ni Op 'stones.'

   Mass nouns may also have a PARTITIVE sense in their usage, referring to some portion of
the group specified by the noun.

   (47) Wgii-mkaanan gwiwnan. I 'He found (some) clothes' (AM39.413)

          Wgii-mkaanan vti ind3sProx»Op 'ANsg found INpl'; gwiwnan ni Op 'garments.'

   (48) Wgii-miijin bkwezhgan. I 'He ate (some) bread.' (AM39.183)

          Wgii-miijin vti ind 3sProx»Os 'ANsg ate INsg'; bkwezhgan ni Os 'bread.'

    This partitive sense is also evident in the glosses of many mass nouns in Rhodes 1985,
e.g., bkwezhgan, 'bread, (a piece) of bread,' mkom, 'ice, a piece of ice,' semaa, 'tobacco, a
wad of tobacco,' mdaamin, 'corn, a kernel of corn.' However, there can also be reference to
a specific quantum, in which case a demonstrative can occur, as in the following example.

   (49) Mii dash gaa-nag, Waabndamog ow nbiish e-zhnaagwak.
         'I said to him, "Look at the way this water looks.'" (AM 10.13) [NB, different
         from maanda, usual word for 'this' (inan.)]

          Mii av 'and'; dash av 'then'; gaa-nag vta ic conj ls»3sProx '(CONJ) I said to ANsg';
          Waabndamog vti imp 2p 'look at IN'; ow/?r Os 'this'; nbiish ni Os 'water'; e-zhnaagwak
          vii ic conj 0 '(CCNJ) how IN looks.'


  PARTICIPLES freely occur with mass nouns. In the following example, the noun
mdaamin, 'corn,' is separated from its associated participle by the verb.
544 • 12.3.3 Mass Nouns


   (50) Mdaamin naazh gaazhiingwed. I 'Fetch corn which is ripe' (AM39.783)

         Mdaamin na 3sProx 'corn'; naazh vta imp 2s»3 'go get AN'; gaazhiingwed vai ic conj
         part SsProx '(CCNJ) ANsg which is ripe.'

    Mass nouns such as mdaamin, 'corn,' can also occasionally occur in the plural, as in the
following example.

   (51) Kina gegoo da-temgad netaawging, jiisan, eshoonyan, mskodiisminag, piniig,
        mdaamnag, bnagzignag, mnijiimin.
         'There will be everything that is raised: turnips, cabbages, beans, potatoes, Indian

          'potatoes'; mdaamnag na SpProx 'corn (pi)'; bnagzignag na SpProx 'hard shell corn
          (pi)'; mnijiimin ni Os 'pea.'


    Mass nouns may also be used with a demonstrative, even upon introduction into a dis-

          'children'; mii av 'and'; iwpr Os 'that'; gii-biijmaamaawaad vta conj 3pProx»3obv
          '(CONJ) ANpl smelled ANobv'; niwpr 3obv 'that/those'; semaan na 3obv 'tobacco.'
                                                                   12.3.4 Definite Expressions • 545



   (53) Mil dash aw nishnaabe gii-jekaakhang gii-biidood iw wiigwaas, mii dash
        gii-wzhitood niw wiigwaasnaagnan nooj eyaan'gokwaan'gin.
         'And then the man went into the bush and brought some birchbark, so he made

12.3.4 Definite Expressions

    DEFINITE EXPRESSIONS are those referring to referents that have already been established
in the discourse, or can be readily identified on the basis of knowledge shared by those par-
ticipating in the discourse, either through shared cultural knowledge or through personal
experience.
    NOUNS WITH DEMONSTRATIVES. A very common construction in Nishnaabemwin is
that of a nominal expression consisting of a demonstrative pronoun and a noun. This con-
struction is customarily used with definite expressions, though demonstrative pronouns also
commonly occur with indefinites as well, as was shown in the previous section. The follow-
ing examples illustrate some definite expressions.
546 • 12.3.4 Definite Expressions


   (55)   Aw maa mandaagnini mii maaba aw sajiindiisiinh ezhnikaazod. (AM23.13)

          'Thatfine gentleman, you must know, it's this one that's called the bluejay.'

          Awpr 3sProx 'that'; maa av 'in that case'; mandaagnini na SsProx 'gentleman'; mii av
          'it's'; maabapr SsProx 'this'; avfpr 3sProx 'that'; jiindiisiinh na SsProx 'bluejay';
          ezhnikaazod vai ic conj SsProx '(CCNJ) ANsg is called so.'


   (56) Mii dash gii-waabmag maaba Menomini girl dzhi-gziibiignang waasechganan.

          'There I saw this Menomini girl washing windows.' (AM8.31)

          Mii av 'and'; dash av 'then'; gii-waabmag vta conj ls»3sProx '(CONJ) I saw ANsg';
          maaba pr SsProx 'this'; dzhi-gziibiignang vti conj 3sProx»0 '(CONJ) ANsg was
          washing IN there'; waasechganan ni Op 'windows.'


    AGREEMENT BETWEEN DEMONSTRATIVES AND ASSOCIATED NOUNS. Demonstratives
customarily agree with the nouns they are associated with in gender, number, and obviation
(for animates). For example, in the following sentence, the demonstrative giwi, 'those'
agrees in gender (animate), number (plural), and obviation (proximate) with its associated
nouns Nishnaabeg, 'people,' and Nimkiig, 'Thunderers.'

   (57) Gii-yaawag-sh giiwenh go iidig wadi giwi Nishnaabeg Nimkiig.

          'Those Thunder People were over there.' (SO4.22)

          Gii-yaawag-sh vai ind SpProx 'ANpl were there'; giiwenh av 'allegedly'; iidig av 'it
          seems'; wadi av 'there'; giwipr SpProx 'those'; Nishnaabeg na SpProx 'Indians';
          Nimkiig na SpProx 'Thunderers.'


    Uncommonly, agreement requirements may be relaxed, as in the following example,
where the proximate animate plural demonstrative gonda modifies the obviative possessed
noun, wdooshkniigman, 'his (young) men.' The associated verb, gii-nibaawag, 'they slept,'
is also proximate. Here it cannot be the case that the third person plural is being used due to
the reference including Nibakom, who is proximate, because the following clause explicitly
excludes him.
                                                                    12.3.4 Definite Expressions • 547



   (58) Gii-nbaawag dash giiwenh gonda Niibaakhom wdooshkniigiman, Niibaakhom
        gaawiin nibaasii.
         'So these (prox.) young men of Nibakom's went to sleep; Nibakom himself didn't
         sleep.'(SO6.157)

          Gii-nbaawag vai indSpProx 'ANpl were sleeping'; dash av 'then'; giiwenh av
          'reportedly'; gonda pr na SpProx 'these'; Niibaakhom na 3sProx 'Niibaakhom';
          wdooshkniigiman na 3sProx(3obv) 'ANSG'S young man/men'; Niibaakhom na SsProx
          'Niibaakhom'; gaawiin av 'not'; nbaasii vai ind neg SsProx 'ANsg does not sleep.'


    LOCATIVE NOMINALS AND DEMONSTRATIVES. Nouns inflected as locatives, particularl
inanimates, tend to lack demonstratives even when their reference is definite, that is where
reference is to a particular (discourse-established) place, as in the following examples.
Nouns inflected for location resemble locative adverbs, and this too undoubtedly contributes
to their lacking demonstratives.

   (59) Maanda mkokbinaagan, ni-zhaan maa gtigaaning gwyak, enaabiishing aw
        mdaamin. (AK6.2)
         'Here's a basket, go there into the garden where the corn lies in a straight row.'

          Maanda pr Os 'this'; mkokbinaagan ni Os 'basket'; ni-zhaan vai imp 2s '(you SG) go
          there'; maa av 'there'; gtigaaning ni 0 loc 'in garden'; gwyak av 'straight'; enaabiishing
          vai ic conj SsProx '(CCNJ) where ANsg lies'; aw pr 3sProx 'that'; mdaamin na SsProx
          'corn.'


   (60) Gii-giimoozaabid maa waasechganing mii gii-waabndang nsawhigan gii-wzhitood
        maa shkweyaang maa wttgwaaming. Mii dash epiichi-yaad odi shpimsagong mii
        iw gii-ningsenig iw wiigwaam aapji dash gii-zegzi.
         'She peeked out a window and saw that he had made a tepee there at the back of
        the house. And while she was upstairs, the house shook and she was very afraid'
        (AK11.9-10)

         Gii-giimoozaabid vai conj SsProx '(CONJ) ANsg peeked'; maa av 'there';
         waasechganing ni 0 loc 'in window'; mii av 'and'; gii-waabndang vti conj 3sProx»0
         '(CONJ) ANsg saw IN'; nsawhigan ni Os 'conical lodge'; gii-wzhitood vti conj3sProx»0
         '(CONJ) ANsg made IN'; maa av 'there'; shkweyaang av 'behind'; maa av 'there';
         wiigwaaming ni 0 loc 'in wigwam.'


   NAMES. Names can be used to identify characters as well. Names may involve those
known only within a local context, such as in (61), or those known by common cultural
548 • 12.3.4 Definite Expressions


knowledge, as in (62), where the culture hero/trickster Nenabush is introduced. Both of
these sentences introduce discourses.

   (61) Geget sa naa gii-waawiizhi-yaa go This Week.
         That Joe Williams (we called him 'This Week') was really a riot.' (NS2.1)

          Geget av 'truly'; gii-waawiizhi-yaa vai ind 3sProx 'ANsg was hilarious.'


   (62) Nenbozh giiwenh gii-bmosegban ddibew.
         'It is said that Nenabush was walking along the bank of a stream.' (AM35.1)

          Nenbozh no. 3sProx 'Nenabush'; giiwenh av 'reportedly'; gii-bmosegban vai indpdub
          SsProx 'ANsg was allegedly walking along'; ddibew av 'on the river bank.'


   Names are also often modified by demonstratives, as in the following examples:

   (63) Mii sa gaa-kidod wa Niibaakhom. I 'That's what (that) Nibakom said.' (SO6.87)

          Mii av 'that's'; gaa-kidod vai ic conj SsProx '(CCNJ) what ANsg said'; \vapr SsProx
          'this'; Niibaakhom na SsProx 'Niibaakhom.'


   (64) Gii-zegzi dash aw Nenbozh. I 'That Nenabush was frightened.' (AM35.23)

          Gii-zegzi vai ind SsProx 'ANsg was frightened'; dash av 'then'; aw/??- SsProx 'that';
          Nenbozh na SsProx 'Nenabush.'


   (65) Maaba dash Nenbozh gii-zegzi. I Then this Nenabush was frightened.'

          Maabapr SsProx 'this'; dash av 'then'; Nenbozh na SsProx 'Nenabush'; gii-zegzi vai
          ind SsProx 'ANsg was frightened.' (AM36.19)

    NOMINAL COLLECTIVES. The names of more abstract or collective entities, such as coun-
tries, can also be modified by demonstratives:

   (66) Mii sa go maanda Genada wii-mkanding, giishpin bkinwind
        zhaagnaashii-gchi-gimaa.

         '(This) Canada would certainly be seized, if the English general was beaten.'

          Mii av 'and'; maanda pr Os 'this'; Genada ni Os 'Canada'; wii-mkanding vti conj x»0
          '(CONJ) IN will be taken'; giishpin av 'if; bkinwind via conj x SsProx '(CONJ) ANsg is
          defeated'; zhaagnaashii-gchi-gimaa na SsProx 'the English leader.' (SO6.94)
                                                                 12.3.4 Definite Expressions • 549


   ASSOCIATIVE PARTICIPANTS. Once a character is introduced, associated characters can
be introduced on the basis of cultural knowledge of conventional social relationships. For
example, in Ms. Soney's brief anecdote about Joe Williams, after her initial sentence ((61)
above), the next sentence shifts to a plural actor, who are understood to be Joe Williams and
his wife.

   (67) Wgii-baatiin'haawaan binoojiinyan. I 'They had lots of kids' (NS2.2)

          Wgii-baatiin'haawaan vta ind 3pProx»3obv 'ANpl had many ANobv'; binoojiinyan na
          3obv 'child(ren).'

   In her next sentence, Ms. Soney broadens the reference group to Joe Williams' family:

   (68) Wiikaa-sh go naa wiiyaas wgti-yaanaawaa. I 'So they only rarely had meat.'

          Wiikaa av 'rarely' dash av 'then'; wiiyaas ni0(s) 'meat'; wgii-yaanaawaa vaio
          3pProx»0 'ANpl had INsg.' (NS2.3)

   The following example explicitly identifies and introduces two third person participants,
then in the next sentence uses a verb inflected for third person plural along with a singular
noun phrase, aw gitigewinini, 'that farmer.' Bloomfield translates this NPfsing] + V[plur] as
'the farmer and his wife.'

   (69) (a) Bezhig aw akwe gii-aawi animoshishan gaa-ogitiziimimaad, miinawaa bezhig
        aw anini. (b) Mii dash aw gitigewinini ogii-manezinaawaa giziibiigahigan.
         '(a) This one woman was a person who had a dog as a parent, and this one man.
         (b) This farmer and his wife ran short of soap.' (AW15.6-7)

          (a) Bezhig nm 'a certain; one'; aw/?r SsProx 'that'; akwe na 3sProx 'woman'; gii-aawi
          vai ind SsProx 'ANsg was'; animoshishan na pej 3spej 'worthless dog';
          gaa-ogitiziimimaad vta ic conj 3sProx»3obv '(CCNJ) whom (ANobv) ANsg has as a

          'man.' (b) Mii av 'and'; dash av 'then'; awpr SsProx 'that'; gitigewinini na SsProx
          'farmer'; ogii-manezinaawaa vaio ind3pProx»Os 'ANpl ran short of INsg';
          giziibiigahigan ni Os 'soap.'


    Another example has a singular noun phrase, maaba Niibaakhom, 'this Nibakom' (a
prominent Odawa war chief at the turn of the nineteenth century) with an associated verb
inflected for plural, gchi-miigaazwaad, 'they were fighting hard,' referring to Nibakom and
his men.

   (70) Megwaa-sh go maaba Niibaakhom gchi-miigaazwaad, mii-sh gii-gkendmowaad.

    ORDERING OF DEMONSTRATIVE AND NOUN. The most common ordering pattern is for
the demonstrative to directly precede the noun it is associated with. In some cases, though,
the two constituents may be separated, in which case the demonstrative is usually to the left
of the noun, that is, occurs earlier in the clause or sentence. In the following examples, the
discourse particles dash, which always comes second in its clause, and sa, intervene
between the demonstrative and noun.

   (71) Giw dash kwewag wgii-gnawenmaawaan niw binoojiinyan.
           'And the women took care of the children.' (AK2.3)

            Giwpr SpProx 'those'; dash av 'and'; kwewag na SpProx 'women';
            wgii-gnawenmaawaan vta ind 3pProx»3obv 'ANpl took care of ANobv'; niw pr 3obv
            'that/those'; binoojiinyan na 3obv 'child(ren).'

   (72) Ambe gegoo zhichgen, wi-nda-waabam aw sajiiskiiwnini..."
           '"Now do something, go and look for the shaking tent diviner...'" (AK11.5)

            Ambe av 'come on'; gegoo pr indefO 'something'; zhichgen vai imp 2s '(you SG) do so';
            wi-nda-waabam vta imp 2s»3 'you SG go see AN'; aw pr 3sProx 'that'; jiiskiiwnini na
            3sProx 'shaking tent diviner'; odi av 'there'

   In the following example, a RELATIVE CLAUSE (PARTICIPLE) intervenes between the
demonstrative and noun. The position of the participle is somewhat unusual, in that clausal
modifiers typically follow the nouns they modify. Richard Rhodes has pointed out that such
pre-nominal relatives tend to consist of a single word.1

   (73) Bekish gii-bmi-giigoonyke gii-ndawenjge ge gii-shamaad niw bekden'jin
        nishnaaben.
        'Besides he fished as he went along and he went hunting, giving food to those
        Indians who were hungry! (AK5.11)

         fishing'; gii-ndawenjge vai indSsProx 'ANsg hunted'; ge av 'and'; gii-shamaad vta conj
         3sProx»3obv '(CONJ) ANsg fed ANobv'; niw/?r 3obv 'that/those'; bekden'jin vai ic
         conj part Oobv '(CCNJ) ANobv who are hungry'; nishnaaben na 3obv 'lndian(s).'


   (74) Miinwaa wgii-bshanzhehaan gye go miinwaa wgii-wiiwkwejiinaan iw
        nembiiwegdinig bbagwayaanenh, mil dash gii-giizhtood.
         'She whipped it again and wrapped it in a damp piece of cotton cloth, and then
         she finished it.'(AM26.11)

         'and'; miinwaa av 'also'; wgii-wiiwkwejiinaan vti ind3sPmx»Os 'ANsg wrapped INsg
         up'; i\v pr Os 'that'; nembiiwegdinig vii ic conj part 0 '(CCNJ) which INobv is wet
         cloth'; bbagwayaanenh ni Os 'thin cloth'; mii av 'and'; dash av 'then'; gii-giizhtood vti
         conj 3sProx»0 '(CONJ) ANsg finished IN.'


   In the following sentence, a demonstrative pronoun referring to another participant
occurs between a demonstrative and its associated noun. This is possible because the inter-
vening demonstrative is proximate, while the demonstrative and noun of the interrupted
phrase are both marked as obviative.

   (75) Gii-mnozwaan giiwenh gora'H>/BH>aA giigoonyan^, gii-mwaad.

         'ThatA (fellow) evidently cooked thatEfish^, and ate it.' (SO3.15)

         vta conj 3sProx»3obv '(CONJ) ANsg ate ANobv.'


    FLOATING (FRONTING) OF DEMONSTRATIVES. As with other modifiers of nouns, demon-
stratives can move in front of verbs associated with the noun phrase, which often remains
post-verbal, as in the following examples:

   (76) Mil maaba gaa-kidod zhaagnaashii-gchi-gimaa.

           zhaagnaashii-gchi-gimaa na SsProx 'English (white) leader.'


   (77)   'Aanii pii-sh maaba gaa-ndinad giigoonh? I 'Where did you get this fish?'

           '(CCNJ) that you SG got ANsg from'; giigoonh na SsProx 'fish.' (SO3.8)


   DEMONSTRATIVES WITH CONJOINED NOUN PHRASES. A single demonstrative pronoun
can serve to modify both elements of a conjoined noun phrase, such as in (78) below, or both
nominals in parallel constructions, as in (79). In most cases, the demonstrative occurs before
the first noun phrase in the conjoined group.

   (78)   Mii maa naa eta iw gaa-wndaadziwaad, niw miinan miinwaa mshkiigminan kina
          gegoo wgii-zgaknaanaawaa,...

          and cranberries and everything,...' (AK17.11)

           Mii av 'and'; maa av 'there'; eta av 'only'; iw pr Os 'that'; gaa-wndaadziwaad vai ic
           conj SpProx '(CCNJ) ANpl lived by means of Y'; niw pr Op 'those'; miinan ni Op
           'blueberries'; miinwaa av 'and'; mshkiigminan ni Op 'cranberries'; kina av 'every';
           gegoo pr indefO 'thing'; wgii-zgaknaanaawaa vti ind 3pProx»Os 'ANpl harvested IN.'


   (79) Maaba gwiiwzens giigoonykenid niw wdedeman wdoodooman ge
        wgii-wiiji-yaawaan niw ookmisan. (AK13.1)

          This boy stayed with his grandmother while his father and mother were fishing.'

          Maaba pr SsProx 'this'; gwiiwzens na SsProx 'boy'; giigoonykenid vai conj Sobv
          '(CONJ) ANobv fished'; niwpr Sobv 'that/those'; wdedeman na SsProx(Sobv) 'ANso's
          father'; wdoodooman na 3sProx(3obv) 'ANSG'S mother'; ge av 'also';
          wgii-wiiji-yaawaan vta ind 3sProx»3obv 'ANsg stayed with ANobv'; niw pr Sobv
          'that/those'; ookmisan na SsProx(Sobv) 'ANSG'S grandmother.'

   (80) Bezhig shkiniigkwe wdayaan mtig-naagan gye iw mtigo-emkwaan.

         Bezhig nm 'a certain'; shkiniigkwe na SsProx 'young woman'; wdayaan vti ind
         3sProx»Os 'ANsg has INsg'; mtig-naagan ni Os 'wooden bowl'; gye av 'and'; iwpr Os
         'that'; mtigo-emkwaan ni Os 'wooden ladle.'


   In other cases, both nouns may be marked with an identical demonstrative.

   (81) Mewnzha aw nmishoomis gaa-zhiwebzinid niw wdedeman miinwaa niw

   (83) Aapji dash gii-mkadekewag naan'godnong giw dash shkinweg gye go

   DEMONSTRATIVES WITH POSSESSED NOUNS. Demonstratives are very common modifi-
ers of possessed nouns in Nishnaabemwin.

   (84) Mewnzha aw nmishoomis gaa-zhiwebzinid niw wdedeman miinwaa niw
        wdoodooman.
         'A long time ago this happened to my grandfather's father and mother.' (lit., 'that
         grandfather of mine's that father of his and that mother of his') (AK2.1)

          niwpr 3obv 'that/those'; wdedeman na 3sProx(3obv) 'ANSG'S father'; miinwaa av
          'and'; niwpr 3obv 'that/those'; wdoodooman na 3sProx(3obv) 'ANSG'S mother.'


   (85) Mil dash ngoding enmahe-giizhgak wgii-bi-ndawaabmaan aw kwe niw wdaansan
        odi namhewgamgong.
         'Then one time when it was Sunday a woman came there to the church to look for
         her daughter: (AK3.3)

          IN be Sunday'; wgii-bi-ndawaabmaan vta ind3sProx»3obv 'ANsg came to look for
