          wdaansan na 3sProx(3obv) 'ANsG's daughter'; odi av 'there'; namhewgamgong ni 0
          loc 'at the church.'


   DEFINITE REFERENCE BY DEMONSTRATIVES ALONE. Once characters are established in
a discourse, they can then be referred to solely by means of verbal inflections, or by a com-
bination of verbal inflections and demonstrative pronouns. Establishment of reference may
                                                                  12.3.4 Definite Expressions • 555



be due to the proximity and immediacy of the referents in the internal context of the story,
as in the following examples.

   (86) Mii sa maaba ge-wiidgemag," kido sa giiwenh.

         'This is the one that I'll marry," she said.' (SO2.7)

          Mii av 'it's'; maabapr 3sProx 'this'; ge-wiidgemag vta ic conj ls»3sProx '(CCNJ) who
          (ANsg) I will marry'; giiwenh av 'reportedly.'


   (87) Aanpiish naa gonda gaa-ndindwaa? I 'Where did you get theseT (SO2.14)

          Aanpiish av 'where'; gondaprna 3pProx 'these'; gaa-ndindwaa vta ic conj 2s»3pProx
          '(CCNJ) that you got ANpl from.'

    DEMONSTRATIVES WITH RELATIVE CLAUSES. Relative clauses commonly occur in asso-
ciation with demonstrative pronouns. The first example below is interesting in that the only
reference to weeds prior to their reference with a demonstrative and relative clause is by
means of the medial element /-ashkw/, 'plant, grass,' in moonshkwe, 'weed (verb).'

   (88) Mii dash maaba nishnaabe moonshkwed maa wii-gtiged mii gii-ni-kosdood niw
        gaa-bkojbidoojin, ...

         'And this Indian was weeding intending to make a garden there and he piled up
         those which he pulled out,...' (AK16.3)

         Mii av 'and'; dash av 'then'; maaba pr SsProx 'this'; nishnaabe na 3sProx 'Indian';
         moon'shkwed vai conj 3sProx '(CONJ) ANsg weeds'; maa av 'there'; wii-gtiged vai
         conj SsProx '(CONJ) ANsg intended to garden'; mii av 'and'; gii-ni-kosdood vti conj
         3sProx»0 '(CONJ) ANsg heaped IN up'; niwpr Op 'those'; gaa-bkojbidoojin vti ic conj
         part 3sProx»Op '(CCNJ) which (INpl) ANsg pulled out.'


   (89) E-ni-dgoshnaan wiinaagmi iw nbiish e-ndhamaang.

         'When I got there, it was dirty, that (place) from which we got water.' (AM 10.7)

          E-ni-dgoshnaan vai ic conj Is '(CCNJ) when I arrived there'; wiinaagmi vii ind Os 'the
          water is dirty'; iw pr Os 'that'; nbiish ni Os 'water'; e-ndhamaang vti ic conj lp»0
          '(CCNJ) where we got IN from.'


    PROXIMAL VERSUS DISTAL DEMONSTRATIVES. PROXIMAL DEMONSTRATIVES are used
to specify objects in close proximity to the speaker, or in close proximity relative to some
other point of reference. DISTAL DEMONSTRATIVES are used to specify objects that are rela-
556 • 12.3.4 Definite Expressions


lively farther away. Examples occur throughout this chapter. A further degree of remoteness
is indicated with the invariant word wedi, 'over there, yonder' (also wadi), as in the follow-
ing.

   (90) Gyak maaba nimosh, wedi dash bezhig dkonge.
         'This dog is well-behaved, but that one (over there) bites.' (AM39.65)

          Gyak av 'proper'; maabapr SsProx 'this'; nimosh na SsProx 'dog'; wedi na SsProx
          'over there'; dash av 'but'; bezhig nm 'one'; dkonge vai ind SsProx 'ANsg bites.'


   (91) Wedi ge gii gga-miijin, maanda dash ge nii nga-miijin waawan.
         'You may eat that egg (over there), and I shall eat this one.' (AM39.174)

          Wedi ni 0 'that over there'; ge av 'as for'; giiprpers 2s 'you'; gga-miijin vti ind 2s»0s
          'you will eat INsg'; maanda pr Os 'this'; dash av 'however'; ge av 'as for'; nii prpers Is
          'I/me'; nga-miijin vti ind ls»0s 'I will eat INsg'; waawan ni Os 'egg.'

   THE OPTIONALITY OF DEMONSTRATIVES. While demonstratives occur with great fre-
quency in Nishnaabemwin, they generally seem to be optional in many cases, and further-
more, the distinction between the PROXIMAL and DISTAL is subtle, often rather like the
discourse use of 'this' and 'that' in English, where, for example, each of the following
might be said in similar contexts:

   (a)   And then that guy had the nerve to try to shake my hand...
   (b)   And then this guy has/had the nerve to try to shake my hand ...
    Compare the behaviour of demonstratives in the following three sentences, all from dif-
ferent versions of Andrew Medler's telling of the same story. The proximal form, maaba,
occurs with present tense.

   (92) Gaa wgikenmaasiin manj ge-kidgwen maaba noos.
         'She does not know what (this) my father might say.' (AM4.10)

          Gaa av 'not'; wgikenmaasiin vta ind 3sProx»3obv neg 'ANsg does not know about
          ANobv'; manj av 'however it may be'; ge-kidgwen vai ic conj dub SsProx '(CCNJ) what
          ANsg might say'; maaba pr SsProx 'this'; noos na Is(SsProx) 'my father.'
                                                                 12.3.4 Definite Expressions • 557



   (93) Gaa wgii-gkenmaasiin manj ge-kidgwen aw noos.

         'She did not know what (that) my father would say.' (AM5.12)

          Gaa av 'not'; wgii-gkenmaasiin vta ind 3sProx»3obv neg 'ANsg did not know about
          ANobv'; manj av 'however it may be'; ge-kidgwen vai ic conj dub 3sProx '(CCNJ) what
          ANsg might say'; awpr SsProx 'that'; noos na Is(SsProx) 'my father.'


   (94) Gye gaa wgii-gkenmaasiin manj iidig ge-kidgwen sa noos.

         'She did not know what () my father would say.' (AM6.10)

          Gye av 'and'; gaa av 'not'; wgii-gkenmaasiin vta ind 3sProx»3obv neg 'ANsg did not
          know about ANobv'; manj av 'however it may be'; iidig av 'perhaps'; ge-kidgwen vai ic
          conj dub 3sProx '(CCNJ) what ANsg might say'; noos na ls(3sProx) 'my father.'


   The presence or absence of demonstratives in Nishnaabemwin is quite variable in run-
ning narrative. It is easy to find sentences such as these which differ in the variable presence
of a demonstrative. This seems to particularly be the case with POSSESSED NOUNS, as evi-
denced by the following examples as well.

   (95) Ngii-nkwetwaa dash ji-zhaayaambaanh giishpin bgidniwaad ngitziimag.

         'I answered him that I would go if my parents permitted me to go.' (AM8.3)

          Ngii-nkwetwaa vta ind ls»3sProx 'I answered ANsg'; dash av 'then';
          ji-zhaayaambaanh vai ic conj pret Is '(CCNJ) I would go there'; giishpin av 'if;
          bgidniwaad vta conj 3pProx»ls '(CONJ) ANpl would let me'; ngitziimag nad
          ls(3pProx) 'my parents.'


   (96) Ngii-nkwetwaa dash da-zhaayaambaan giishpin bgidniwaad giw ngitziimag.

         'I answered him that I would go if my parents permitted me.' (AM9.3)

          Ngii-nkwetwaa vta ind ls»3sProx 'I answered ANsg'; dash av 'then';
          ji-zhaayaambaanh vai ic conj pret Is '(CCNJ) I would go there'; giishpin av 'if;
          bgidniwaad vta conj 3pProx»ls '(CONJ) ANpl would let me'; giwpr 3p 'those';
          ngitziimag nad ls(3pProx) 'my parents.'


    DISCOURSE USES OF PROXIMAL AND DISTAL DEMONSTRATIVES. Proximal demonstra-
tives (words equivalent to English 'this' and 'these') tend to be used more often in narra-
tives in reference to the story's protagonist, that is, the character from whose perspective the
story is told. For example, in a cautionary tale about a young man who is taught bear-walk-
558 • 12.3.4 Definite Expressions


ing by his grandmother, and later pays for his knowledge with his life, Alice King structures
her story from the perspective of the boy, and all uses of proximal demonstratives are in ref-
erence to the boy, as in the following examples.

   (97) Gii-nbowan wgitziiman maaba gwiiwzens, ntam gii-nbowan oosan mii dash
        giiwenh egod niw wdoodooman, gchi-aakziwan giiwenh, "Maawndoopdoon niw
        gdayhiiman maajaan odi ji-wi-wiij-yaawad aw gookmis.
         'This boy's parents died, first his father and then (that) his mother reportedly said
         to him (she was reportedly very sick), ...' (AK14.la)

          Gii-nbowan vai ind3obv 'ANobv died'; wgitziimanna 3sProx(3obv) 'ANsg's parents';
          maabapr SsProx 'this'; gwiiwzens na SsProx 'boy'; ntam av 'first'; gii-nbowan vai ind
          3obv 'ANobv died'; oosan nod 3sProx(3obv) 'ANsg's father'; mii av 'and'; dash av
          'then'; giiwenh av 'reportedly'; egod vta ic conj 3sProx»ls '(CCNJ) ANobv said to
          ANsg'; niwpr 3obv 'that/those'; wdoodooman na 3sProx(3obv) 'ANSG'S mother';
          gchi-aakziwan vai ind3obv 'ANsg is very ill'; giiwenh av 'reportedly'.'


   (98) Mii dash gii-gkinoohmawaad gbeyhiing go mii-sh gii-mkwendang maaba
        gwiiwzens, mii dash iw ngoding nshike-yaad, gii-ndomaa aw mdimooyenh
        ji-wi-wiidookwaad niw getgen'jin.
         'And so she taught him for a long time and this boy remembered it, and then one
         time when he's alone, that old woman was invited to go and help those who were
         gardening.' (AK14.9)

          Mii av 'and'; dash av 'so'; gii-gkinoohmawaad vta conj 3sProx»3obv '(CONJ) ANsg
          taught ANobv'; gbeyhiing av 'for a long time'; mii-sh av 'and then'; gii-mkwendang vti
          conj 3sProx»0 '(CONJ) ANsg remembered IN'; maaba pr SsProx 'this'; gwiiwzens na
          SsProx 'boy'; mii av 'and'; dash av 'then'; iwpr Os 'that'; ngoding av 'one time';
          nshike-yaad vai conj 3sProx '(CONJ) ANsg was alone'; gii-ndomaa vta indx»3sProx
           'ANsg was summoned'; awpr SsProx 'that'; mdimooyenh na SsProx 'old woman';
          ji-wi-wiidookwaad vta conj 3sProx»3obv '(CONJ) ANsg go and help ANobv'; niwpr
          3obv 'that/those'; getgen'jin vai ic conj part 3obv '(CCNJ) ANobv who is/are gardening.'


    Another striking usage of proximal demonstratives is found in Sam Osawamick's telling
of a traditional story of a man who foolishly eats a suspicious fish, despite the warnings of a
friend, and as a result turns into a fish. To make the action more vivid and immediate,
Osawamick's protagonists consistently refer to the fish with the proximal demonstrative.
The frequency of its usage in this short passage is striking as well, underscoring its rhetori-
cal function.
                                                                     12.3.4 Definite Expressions • 559



   (99) (a) Mil dash giiwenh gii-naadid nbiish wa, giigoonyan giiwenh wbi-dgojiinaan.
        (b) "Aanii pii-sh maaba gaa-ndinad giigoonh?"
        (c) "Wadi sa ngii-mkawaa, ndahbaaning."
        (d) "Gaa wii maaba gdaa-mwaasii."

         '(a) So that fellow went and got some water, but he's holding a fish also.

    It is less common for a proximal demonstrative to be used with an inanimate noun in this
way, or with an obviated animate noun. The use of proximal forms lends immediacy to the
reference. It is more common when the verbs are in present tense, too, which represents
another common way of making a discourse more immediate.

          indpdub 3sProx 'ANsg allegedly lived there'; Nenbozh na 3sProx 'Nenabush.'

          'woman/women'; bi-dnaangidoonnid vai conj 3obv '(CONJ) ANobv come talking.'

   .. .and the next nominal reference...

   (105) Mii dash gaa-kidwaad giw kwewag, Gaag maanpii yaa wiimbnakdoonying.

   (107) Mil dash gii-bkonaad niw waawaashkeshwan. I Then he skinned that deer.'

          Mii av 'and'; dash av 'then'; gii-bkonaad vta conj 3sProx»3obv '(CONJ) ANsg skinned
          ANobv'; niwpr 3obv 'that/those'; waawaashkeshwan na 3obv 'deer.' (AM35.30)

    So the absence of a demonstrative in these stories is somewhat equivalent to English
indefinite reference, used for introducing characters into a story, at least for those that enter
the story in the grammatical role of goals. While it would be nice if this generalization con-
sistently held, it obviously does not. Characters in goal roles are frequently introduced into
narratives with demonstratives. In another Nenabush story, twice told by Mr. Medler, ducks
are introduced as goals, and in both recountings of the story, have demonstratives, as in the
following example:

   (108) Wgii-waabmaan niibna niw zhiishiiban. I 'He saw many ducks' (AM37.6)
          Wgii-waabmaan vta ind3sProx»3obv 'ANsg saw ANobv'; niibna av 'many'; niw/?r
          3obv 'that/those'; zhiishiiban na 3obv 'duck(s).'

   As to the use of a proximal demonstrative (equivalent to English 'this' or 'these'), this
choice at least sometimes seems to be a matter of empathy or focus. For example, note that
Mr. Medler uses maaba, 'this' (anim.) in the sentence above containing a CONTEMPTIVE
form of the name Nenbozhoonh (103), which also indicates sympathy for the character.
Another place where Mr. Medler uses maaba is in two very parallel references to a partridge
who is outraged at the abuse one of her chicks receives from Nenabush. Twice Mr. Medler
uses the proximal demonstrative, perhaps to foreground her indignation and the likelihood
of her seeking revenge, which motivates the action of the story.

   (109) Mii dash gii-nshkaadzid maaba gchi-bne.
         'Then this big partridge was angry.' (AM36.12 and AM36.15)

          Mii av 'and'; dash av 'so'; gii-nshkaadzid vai conj 3sProx '(CONJ) ANsg was angry';
          maabapr SsProx 'this'; gchi-bne na 3sProx 'big partridge.'


  In another version of the same story, the same proximal reference occurs again, and once
more, the statement is reiterated.

   (110) Aapji dash gii-nshkaadzi maaba gchi-bne. I 'This big partridge was very angry.'

          Aapji av 'really'; dash av 'then'; gii-nshkaadzi vai ind 3sProx 'ANsg was angry';
          maaba pr SsProx 'this'; gchi-bne na 3sProx 'big partridge.' (AM35.15)
                                                                   12.3.4 Definite Expressions • 563


   (111) Gii-nshkaadzi dash maaba gchi-bne. I 'This big partridge was angry.' (AM35.18)
   Another point in favor of an empathy and focus analysis of the use of proximals is that
proximal obviatives seem relatively uncommon, which makes sense, given that obviation is
a backgrounding strategy, suggesting the distancing of a character.

12.3.5 Nominal Possessive Constructions

   In POSSESSIVE CONSTRUCTIONS, a POSSESSED noun (called a POSSESSUM) is modified by
another nominal representing its POSSESSOR. Usually only animates can be possessors, and
any possessed animate must be inflected for obviation. The grammatical features of person
and number of the possessor are coded inflectionally on the possessum. In the following
sentence, for example, the person and number features of the possessor, first person plural
inclusive, are coded on the two possessums, gdakiimnaa, 'our land,' and
gwiijkiwenynaanig, 'our friends,' by means of the second person prefix /gi(d)-/ and the first
person plural suffix /-naany/.

   (122) Gwii-mkamgoomi gdakiimnaa, giishpin bwaa-naadmawngwaa gonda
         gwiijkiwenynaanig.
         'Our land will be taken from us, if we fail to help these friends of ours.' (SO6.18)

          Gwii-mkamgoomi vta indx»21 'we will be robbed ofY'; gdakiimnaa ni 21(0s) 'our
          land'; giishpin av 'if; bwaa-naadmawngwaa vta conj 21»3pProx '(CONJ) we fail to
          help ANpl'; gonda prna SpProx 'these'; gwiijkiwenynaanig nad 21(3pProx) 'our
          friends.'


    The obviative status of the possessor may be coded on the possessum as well. In the fol-
lowing example, Naadweswag, 'Iroquois (pi.)' is proximate, and zaazbaakdoken'jin, 'those
who make sugar,' an obviative participle (from zuzbaakdoke, 'make sugar' VAI). When the
latter functions as possessor of ziizbaakod, 'sugar,' the possessum is marked with the obvia-
tive possessor suffix /-iniw/.

   (123) Memdage go zaazbaakdokejin aw Wjibwe, mil iw pii giw Naadweswag widi
         gii-bi-zhaawaad maanpii nikekmig gii-bi-mkamaawaad niw zaazbaakdoken'jin iw
         sa wziizbaakdomni.

         'Especially when the Ojibwe were making sugar, that was when those Hurons
         would come over to this side of the water to rob the sugar makers of their sugar.'

12.3.6 Conjoined Noun Phrases

    Noun phrases can be conjoined either with a CONNECTING ADVERB/CONJUNCTION, such
as miinwaa or gye, or with no connective. Conjoined goals (objects) seem somewhat more
frequent than conjoined subjects, though both are common. Often when the goal is a con-
joined noun phrase, the verb shows agreement for a singular object, as in (133) and (80)
(above, p. 553). In (135), a conjoined actor shows singular inflection on the verb as well.

   (133) Ngii-zaaghaa nookmis gye go aw nmishoomis.

         'I loved my grandmother and my grandfather.' (AM2.3)

          Ngii-zaaghaa vta ind ls»3sProx 'I loved ANsg'; nookmis nad ls(3sPwx) 'my
          grandmother'; gye av 'and'; awpr 3sProx 'that'; nmishoomis nad ls(3sProx) 'my
          grandfather.'


   (134) Gii-naningishkaa okaading onikaang.

         'He had a palsy in his leg and in his arm.' (AW6.32)

         Gii-naningishkaa vai ind SsProx 'ANsg had palsy'; okaading nid loc 3sProx(0) 'in
         ANsg's leg'; onikaang nid loc 3sProx(0) 'in ANsg's arm.'
                                                              12.3.6 Conjoined Noun Phrases • 569



   (135) Zhaazhi go megwaa binoojiinywiyaan ngii-maajiinig aw ngashi gye bezhig kwe
         gii-wa-yaamwaad iw bgoji-mnoomin.
         'Long ago, when I was a little child, my mother and another woman took me
         along as they went to get wild rice.' (AM4.1)

          Zhaazhi av 'long ago'; megwaaav 'while'; binoojiinywiyaan vai conj Is '(CONJ) I was
          a child'; ngii-maajiinig via ind3sProx»ls 'ANsg took me along'; aw pr SsProx 'that';
          ngashi nad Is(SsProx) 'my mother'; gye av 'and'; bezhig nm 'one; a certain'; kwe na
          SsProx 'woman'; gii-wa-yaamwaad vta 3pProx»0 '(CONJ) ANpl went to get it'; \vtpr Os
          'that'; bgoji-mnoominni Os 'wild rice.'


    When more than two noun phrases are conjoined, the last one is customarily preceded by
a conjoining adverb such as gye or miinwaa, as illustrated by (136), below. In some cases, as
in (137), below, more than one conjoining adverb may be used. In (149), however, on p. 573,

   Conjunction of various grammatical constituents is also discussed in Chapter 18.

12.3.7 Demonstrative Presentationals (Asserting Immediate Location)

    Demonstratives function prominently in a special construction used to present individu-
als and objects to another, roughly equivalent to the English expression, 'Here's a...,' used
when presenting something to someone, such as 'Here's a plate to eat with,' or with a verb,
to associate the subject to a specific and immediate location, such as in English, 'Here she
is!' or 'Here she lies!' In Nishnaabemwin, a proximal (near-form) demonstrative is used, in
association with either a noun or a verb. These presentationals have the form: Demonstra-
tive + (Emphatic Particle) + Verb or Noun

   (138) Maanda sa naagaans. I 'Here's a dish.' (AM39.852)
          Maanda pr Os 'this'; naagaans ni Os 'cup.'

   (139) Maanda mkokbinaagan. Ni-zhaan maa gtigaaning gwyak, enaabiishing aw
         mdaamin. (AK6.2)
         'Here's a basket. Go there into the garden where the corn lies in a straight row.'

          Maandapr Os 'this'; mkokbinaagan ni Os 'basket'; ni-zhaan vai imp 2s '(you SG) go
          there'; maa av 'there'; gtigaaning ni 0 he 'to garden'; gwyak av 'straight'; enaabiishing
          vai ic conj SsProx '(CCNJ) where ANsg lies'; aw pr SsProx 'that'; mdaamin na SsProx
          'corn.'


   (140) Oonh, maaba dash! I 'Oh, so here it is!' (upon finding a missing cat) (JF)

          Oonh av 'oh'; maaba pr SsProx 'this'; dash av 'then.'

   If a verb is present, it is inflected for CHANGED CONJUNCT ORDER.

   (141) Maaba go zhengishing. I 'Here she is, lying down.' (AW16.32)

          Maaba pr SsProx 'this'; zhengishing vai ic conj SsProx '(CCNJ) ANsg is lying.'

   (142) Maaba go ebid. I 'But here she is, at rest.' (AW16.40)

          Maaba pr SsProx 'this'; ebid vai ic conj SsProx '(CCNJ) ANsg is here.'

12.3.8 Quantificational Modifiers of Nouns

   Nominals may also be quantified by specific numeral quantifiers.

   (143) Wgii-wiindmaagoon dash niw zhaagnaashan gii-nsaawaad nswi dkonwewninwan.

         'They told him that those whites had killed three policemen.' (AK2.11)

          Wgii-wiindmaagoon vta ind3obv»3sProx 'ANobv told ANsg'; dash av 'then'; niwpr
          3obv 'that/those'; zhaagnaashan na 3obv 'white(s)'; gii-nsaawaad vta conj
          3pProx»3obv '(CONJ) ANpl killed ANobv'; dkonwewninwan na 3obv 'policeman/men.'


   (144) Niizh nga-yaanan bwiin, I 'I shall have two paddles.' (AM39.411)

          Niizh nm 'two'; nga-yaanan vti ind ls»0p 'I will have INpl'; bwiin ni Op 'paddles.'

    These two examples represent the most common orderings of quantifier and noun, in
(143), the quantifier directly precedes the noun it is associated with and both occur after the
verb; in (144), the quantifier has "floated" to a position before the verb, reflecting another
very common pattern. Quantifier-float seems more common with verbs inflected for INDE-
PENDENT ORDER than those inflected for CONJUNCT.
    Less commonly, other configurations occur in texts as well, such as the following, in
which the nominal precedes the verb and the numeral quantifying it follows. Note that this
sentence is introducing the characters referred to, shkinweg, 'young men,' and it is probably
for this reason that the noun is fronted.

   (145) Ngoding shkinweg gii-gkinoohmaagziwag niizh maa gkinoohmaadiiwgamgong,
         bezhig dash aw Gchi-mookmaani-shkinwe gye bezhig Nishnaabens.
         'Once two young men studied there at the University, one young white American,
         and one young Indian.' (AM30.1)

          Ngoding av 'once'; shkinweg na SpProx 'young men'; gii-gkinoohmaagziwag vai ind
          3pProx 'ANpl were in school'; niizh nm 'two'; maa av 'there';
          gkinoohmaadiiwgamgong ni 0 loc 'to/at the school'; bezhig nm 'one'; dash av 'then';
          awpr SsProx 'that'; Gchi-mookmaani-shkinwe na 3sProx 'young white American'; gye
          av 'and'; bezhig nm 'one'; Nishnaabens na BsProx 'young Indian.'


   In the following example, both the number and noun appear before the verb.
572 • 12.3.8 Quantificational Modifiers of Nouns


   (146) Mil ge eta bezhig nwi yaamwaadv; gaa gegoo waa-miijwaad.
          'And they havey only one shell, and nothing for them to eat,...' (AK7.8)

          Mii av 'and'; ge av 'also'; eta av 'only'; bezhig nm 'one'; nwi ni Os 'bullet'; yaamwaad
          vti conj 3pProx»0 '(CONJ) ANpl have IN'; gaa av 'not'; gegoopr indefO 'anything';
          waa-miijwaad vti ic conj part 3pProx»0 '(CCNJ) what ANpl will eat N.'

   In the following, both the number and a goal noun follow the verb as well as its actor, aw
gwiiwzens, 'that boy.'

   (147) Mii dash giiwenh gii-waabndang aw sa gwiiwzens niizh jiimaanan biidaasninig
         gchi-mookmaan-zhmaagnishag giw wii-miigaanaawaad niw Canadians.
         'And then reportedly this boy saw two boats sailing toward them, they were

          Mii av 'and'; dash av 'so'; giiwenh av 'reportedly'; gii-waabndang vti conj 3sProx»0
           '(CONJ) ANsg saw IN'; aw pr 3sProx 'that'; gwiiwzens na 3sProx 'boy'; niizh nm 'two';
          jiimaanan ni Op 'boats'; biidaasninig vii conj Oobv '(CONJ) INobv come sailing';

          wii-miigaanaawaad vta conj 3pProx»3obv '(CONJ) ANpl intend to fight ANobv'; niw
          pr 3obv 'that/those.'

    CLASSIFIERS AND NUMERAL QUANTIFIERS. Traditionally, a system of CLASSIFIERS
existed which was used with numbers describing objects of different shape and substance.
The system is discussed at length in Baraga 1850. In example (137), above (p. 569), the clas-
sificatory number bezhgwaatig, 'one wooden-object,' is used to enumerate the noun wishkii,
'whiskey.' This usage recalls a time when liquor was stored in wooden containers.
    GENERAL QUANTIFIERS. In addition to specific numeric quantifiers, non-numeric gen-
eral quantifiers occur as well, including bngii, 'a few,' aanind, 'some, others' (also aanin,
aaning), and niibwa, 'many,' (also niibna). The following examples illustrate such quantifi-
ers, which can occur with or without a head noun. Examples (148) and (149) have no head
noun associated with the quantifier, while (150) and (151) do.

   (148) Bngii dash eta maanoo gii-ni-maajiibhiwewan maanoo.
         'Only a few of them were able to run away.' (AM31.39)

          Bngii av 'a few'; dash av 'but'; eta av 'only'; maanoo av 'nevertheless';
          gii-ni-maajiibhiwewan vai ind 3obv 'ANobv ran away from there'; maanoo av
          'nevertheless.'

As with numeric quantifiers, general quantifiers can float to a position before the verb.

    DEMONSTRATIVES WITH QUANTIFIERS. Both explicit numeral quantifiers and non-
numeric quantifiers can occur in noun phrases having demonstratives. The demonstrative
and quantifier vary in their relative order. When the demonstrative follows the quantifier, as
in the following examples, the meaning seems to most commonly be partitive, in which the
quantifier specifies a part or portion of the group specified by the demonstrative + noun
combination.

   (153) Mii dash miinwaa gii-maawnjidoowaad gaa-bskaabiiwaad mii dash gaa-kidwaad,
         "Gaawiin nii-bgidnanziimin maanpii endnizyaang," aaning dash giw nishnaabeg,
         "Gaawiin niinwind...
         'And then they assembled again when they returned and they said, "We will not
         give up this place where we live," but some of the Indians, "Not us... (AK15.6a)

          Mii av 'and'; dash av 'then'; miinwaa av 'again'; gii-maawnjidoowaad vai conj SpProx
          '(CONJ) ANpl assembled'; gaa-bskaabiiwaad vai ic conj 3pProx '(CCNJ) when ANpl
          came back'; mii av 'and'; dash av 'then'; gaa-kidwaad vai ic conj SpProx '(CCNJ) ANpl
          said'; Gaawiin av 'not'; nii-bgidnanziimin vti ind lp»0 'we do not want to give IN up';
          maanpii av 'here'; endnizyaang vai ic conj Ip '(CCNJ) where we live'; aaning av
          'some'; dash av 'but'; gjvfprSpProx 'those'; nishnaabeg na SpProx 'Indians'; Gaawiin
          av 'not'; niinwindprpers Ip 'we/us/our.'


   (154) Wgii-gnoonaan maanda niw ndoodooman, wgii-miinaan neyaab aaning iw
         bagoowyaan, miinwaa ngodwewaan wgii-miinaan niw mkiznan.
         'She talked to my mother about this, and she [my mother] gave her back some of
         that cloth and gave her one pair of shoes.' (AK3.14)

          Wgii-gnoonaan vta ind3sProx»3obv 'ANsg spoke to ANobv'; maandapr Os 'this'; niw
          pr 3obv 'that/those'; ndoodooman na ls(3obv) 'my mother'; wgii-miinaan vta ind
          3sProx»3obv 'ANsg gave Y to ANobv'; neyaab av 'back'; aaning av 'some'; iwpr Os
          'that'; bagoowyaan ni Os 'cloth'; miinwaa av 'and'; ngodwewaan ni 0 'one pair';
          wgii-miinaan vta ind 3sProx»3obv 'ANsg gave Y to ANobv'; mwpr Op 'those';
          mkiznan ni Op 'shoes.'


    However, when the demonstrative precedes the quantifier, the meaning is usually inclu-
sive, rather than partitive.

    The quantifier kina (gkina), 'all,' merges the distinction between partitive and non-parti-
tive senses, since it is universally inclusive. Perhaps for this reason, kina never occurs

    (157) Giishpin naadmawyan mii go ji-giizhiitaayaan moonwagwaa kina giwpiniig.

           'If you help me I will get done digging up all those potatoes.' (AM39.489)

            Giishpin av 'if; naadmawyan vta conj 2s»ls '(CONJ) you help me'; mii av 'then';
            ji-giizhiitaayaan vai conj Is '(CONJ) I could finish'; moonwagwaa vta conj ls»3pProx
             '(CONJ) I dig ANpl'; kina av 'all'; giw/?r SpProx 'those'; piniig na 3pProx 'potatoes.'

            'these'; gii-zhaawag vai ind3pProx 'ANpl went there.' (SO6.15)

    QUANTIFIERS AND RELATIVE ROOTS. Quantifiers can be associated with elements other
than nouns, which induce their own ordering patterns. In the following sentence, for exam-
ple, the number mdaaswi-shi-niizh, 'twelve,' is not directly associated with a noun but with
RELATIVE ROOTS /iN-/ in nakdesin, 'be placed in such a way,' and /akw-/ in kooksin, 'be
arranged in rows to such depth.' In both cases the number precedes the verb containing the
relative root, which both have as their subject, nanda wiigwaaman, 'those tents' (Nl, plural),
intervening between the number and the verb. In this construction, the number is only indi-
rectly modifying the noun phrase, nanda wiigwaaman, by means of the verb's relative root.

   (168) "Mii go wi mdaaswi-shi-niizh nanda wiigwaaman nakdesnoon miinwaa-sh
         mdaaswi-shi-niizh kooksinoon, mii ge go kina baashkzignan nengodwaaswi
         naksinoon," gii-kidwag gonda.
         "Those tents are twelve rows wide and twelve rows deep, and all six guns placed
         upright in a row in each tent," these (two) said.'(SO6.141)

          Mii av 'and'; wipr Os 'that'; mdaaswi-shi-niizh nm 'twelve'; nanda pr Op 'these';
          wiigwaaman ni Op 'wigwams'; nakdesnoon vii ind Op 'INpl are standing'; miinwaa-sh
          av 'and then'; mdaaswi-shi-niizh nm 'twelve'; kooksinoon vii ind Op 'INpl are arranged
          in rows to such extent'; mii av 'and'; ge av 'also'; kina av 'all'; baashkzignan ni Op
          'rifles'; nengodwaaswi nm 'six by six'; naksinoon vii ind Op 'INpl are arranged so';
          gonda pr na 3pProx 'these.'

12.3.9 Relative Clauses

    Verbs in relative clauses are usually marked with special participial verbal inflections
that show CONJUNCT ORDER verb inflection, INITIAL CHANGE and in many forms making
reference to third persons, distinctive noun-like inflections. For example, the simple con-
junct third person plural form of the VAI verb bmaadzi, 'live, be alive,' is bmaadziwaad,
 '(when) they live,' with conjunct order inflectional suffix complex, /-waad/, consisting of an
animate third person suffix /-d/ preceded by a verbal animate plural suffix /-waa/; the corre-
sponding participle form is bemaadzijig, 'those who live,' which has a suffix complex /-jig/,
consisting once more of the verbal animate third person suffix /-d/ (though palatalized to /j/)
and a noun-like plural suffix /-ig/. At the same time, relative clauses have all of the inflec-
tional possibilities of a verb, such as tense and verbal mode, and thus represent a very rich,
hybrid form having properties of both nominals and verbs. For example, the following sen-
tence contains a participle form making reference to fishermen of the future:

   (169) Gchi-zaaghigan zhonda ge-dgog, mii zhonda ge-bi-zhaawaad ge-giigoonykejig.
          'There will be a big lake here; this is where those who will fish will come.'
        '(S03.35)

          Gchi-zaaghigan ni Os 'big lake'; zhonda av 'here'; ge-dgog vii ic conj 0 '(CCNJ) 0 will
          be there'; mii av 'and'; zhonda av 'here'; ge-bi-zhaawaad vai ic conj SpProx '(CCNJ)
          ANpl will come'; ge-giigoonykejig vai ic conj part SpProx '(CCNJ) ANpl who will fish.'

   Nishnaabemwin relative clauses have properties reminiscent of both relative clauses and
to a small extent, GERUNDS (verbal nouns), in English. Relative clauses in Nishnaabemwin
do not require association with (i.e., the presence of) an explicit (head) noun, as can be seen
from the following examples.

   (170) Mii dash bekaanak gii-wiiwjiinid.
         Then she wrapped me in something else' (lit., wrapped me in 'which is differ-
         ent'). (AM5.8)

          Mii av 'and'; dash av 'then'; bekaanak vii ic conj part 0 '(CCNJ) IN which is something
          else'; gii-wiiwjiinid vta conj 3sProx»ls '(CONJ) ANsg wrapped me in IN.'

   (171) Zhwenmishnaang dash debenminaang.
         'Have Thou pity on us now Who art Lord of us (lit., 'who own us') (AM12.8)

          Zhwenmishnaang vta imp 2s»lp 'have pity on us (excl)'; dash av 'then'; debenminaang
          vta ic conj part 2s»lp '(CCNJ) you who own us (excl).'
580 • 12.3.9 Relative Clauses


    However, it is also quite common for relative clauses to modify a nominal such as a noun
or a demonstrative pronoun, and typically the relative clause follows the nominal it modi-
fies. The following examples illustrate.

   (172) Mii dash giw zhaagnaashag bezhgoongzhiin gaa-aabjihaajig kina
         gaa-zhi-gmoodwaad niw bkwezhganan.
         'But those whites who were using the horses stole all the bread.' (AK2.7)

          Mii av 'and'; dash av 'then'; giwprSpProx 'those'; zhaagnaashag na 3pProx
          'whitemen'; bezhgoongzhiin na 3obv 'horse(s)'; gaa-aabjihaajig vta ic conj part
          3pProx»3obv '(CCNJ) who (ANpl) were using ANobv'; kina av 'all';
          gaa-zhi-gmoodwaad vai ic conj SpProx '(CCNJ) ANpl thus stole (Y)'; niw pr 3obv
          'that/those'; bkwezhganan na 3obv 'bread.'

   (173) Kina dash gii-goojgaazwag giw gaa-nsaajig niw dkonwewninwan.
         'But all of those who killed the policemen were hanged.' (AK2.17)

          Kina av 'all'; dash av 'then'; gii-goojgaazwag vai conj SpProx 'ANpl were hanged'; giw
          pr SpProx 'those'; gaa-nsaajig vta ic conj part 3pProx»3obv '(CCNJ) ANpl who killed
          ANobv'; nivfpr 3obv 'that/those'; dkonwewninwan na 3obv 'policeman/men.'

   (174) Gaa waya ekwaabid nwaabmaasii. I 'I do not see anyone keeping watch:
          Gaaav 'not'; wayapr indefSsProx 'anyone'; ekwaabid vai ic conj part 3sProx '(CCNJ)
          who ANsg was keeping watch'; nwaabmaasii vta ind ls»3sProx neg 'I don't see ANsg.'
          (AM8.33)

   However, other orders of elements are possible too. Occasionally, the relative clause pre-
cedes the nominal it modifies, with no apparent difference in meaning. Often in these cases,
the relative clauses consists of a single word.

   (175) Mii dash pii giiwewaad giw niizh nishnaabeg, mii dash ekdod aw bezhig,
         "Aanii-sh ge-zhichgeyamban giishpin waabmaawgibnen gechi-gnaajwid kweT
         'And when these two Indians were going home, one of them said, "What would
         you do if you should see a woman who is very beautifulT" (AK4.3)
                                                                       12.3.9 Relative Clauses • 581



          Mii av 'and'; dash av 'then'; awpr 3sProx 'that'; nishnaabe na 3sProx 'Indian';
          gii-jekaakhang vai conj SsProx '(CONJ) ANsg went into the woods'; gii-biidood vti
          conj 3sProx»0 '(CONJ) ANsg brought IN'; iw/?r Os 'that'; wiigwaas ni Os 'birchbark';
          mii av 'and'; dash av 'then'; gii-wzhitood vti conj 3sProx»0 '(CONJ) ANsg made IN';
          niwpr Op 'those'; wiigwaasnaagnan ni Op 'birchbark dishes'; nooj av 'various';
          eyaan'gokwaan'gin vii ic conj part Op '(CCNJ) which (INpl) are different sizes.'

    Rhodes 1996:6 refers to such single-word constructions as "light term relative clauses,"
using "term" to designate a core grammatical role of a verb, such as subject, primary object,
or secondary object. Rhodes suggests that this preverbal order reflects a general tendency
for the order modifier-head in Nishnaabemwin. Keenen 1985:144 points out that post-nom-
inal relative clauses are almost the only type found in verb-initial languages, though a few
languages such as Tagalog sometimes allow relative clauses to occur prenominally, but only
when they are structurally very simple, thus showing behaviour very similar to that of Nish-
naabemwin, which is said to be verb-initial in its most pragmatically unmarked ordering.
    A construction with the order demonstrative + relative clause + N, in which the relative
clause is sandwiched between a demonstrative and the head noun, occurs several times in
the texts of Alice King, though Mary Ann Corbiere considers such forms "most unusual and
atypical" (p.c.) with regard to their use on Manitoulin Island.

   (176) Bekish gii-bmi-giigoonyke, gii-ndawenjge ge, gii-shamaad niw bekden'jin
         nishnaaben.
         'Besides he fished as he went along, he went hunting as well, giving food to those
         Indians who were hungry' (AK5.11)

          Bekish av 'at the same time'; gii-bmi-giigoonyke vai ind SsProx 'ANsg went along
          fishing'; gii-ndawenjge vai ind SsProx 'ANsg hunted'; ge av 'also'; gii-shamaad vta
          conj 3sProx»3obv '(CONJ) ANsg fed ANobv'; niwprSobv 'that/those'; bekden'jin vai
          ic conj part Oobv '(CCNJ) ANobv who are hungry'; nishnaaben na 3obv 'lndian(s).'


   (177) Mii dash noongo iw wenji-yaawaad giw ngoji debendaagzisgog nishnaabeg.
         'And now that's why there are those Indians who don't belong anywhere'

          Mii av 'and'; dash av 'then'; noongo av 'nowadays'; iw pr Os 'that'; wenji-yaawaad vai
          ic conj 3pProx '(CCNJ) why there are ANpl'; giw pr SpProx 'those'; ngoji av
          'anywhere'; debendaagziSGog vai ic conj part 3pProx neg '(CCNJ) who ANpl don't
          belong to a group'; nishnaabeg na SpProx 'Indians.' (AK9.10)


   NON-CONTIGUOUS RELATIVE CLAUSES. The noun or pronoun associated with a relative
clause need not be adjacent to it, as can be seen from the following examples. In the first,

the relative clause waa-aabjitoowaad, 'which they were going to use,' follows the noun it is

the end. In this way Nishnaabemwin behaves similarly to English.

   (178) Mii dash gii-zhitoowaad iw mshkikwaaboo waa-aabjitoowaad.

          3pProx»Os 'ANpl made IN'; waa-aabjitoowaad vti ic conj part 3pProx»0 '(CCNJ) which
          ANpl will use IN.'

    GRAMMATICAL ROLES WHICH CAN RELATIVIZE. A prominent grammatical aspect of
relative clauses cross-linguistically concerns which grammatical roles can relativize. For
example, in the following sentence, the relative clause is bebaa-wiijiiwag, 'whom (ANsg) I
was going with,' and the relativized grammatical role is that of the goal of the transitive verb
wiijiiw, 'accompany AN' (VTA).

   (186) Ngii-naadmaag gwiiwzens bebaa-wiijiiwag.
          'A boy I was going with helped me.' (AM7.5)

          Ngii-naadmaag vta ind3sProx»ls 'ANsg helped me'; gwiiwzens na SsProx 'boy';
          bebaa-wiijiiwag vta ic conjpart ls»3sProx '(CCNJ) whom (ANsg) I was going around
          with.'

    There do not seem to be any restrictions on the grammatical relation of a nominal having
a relative clause associated with it. Nominals filling the roles of grammatical actors (sub-
jects), goals (objects), recipients (indirect objects), complements of relative roots, and other
relations can all freely have relative clauses associated with them. Rhodes 1996:5 makes the
same observation: "relative clauses can be formed on any nominal whose grammatical func-
tion is licensed by the verb of the clause." The following examples illustrate the relativiza-
tion of other grammatical roles, including subject of transitive in (187), subject of
intransitive in (188), object of possessor in (189), and relative root complement in (190).

   (187) Kina dash gii-goojgaazwag giw gaa-nsaajig niw dkonwewninwan.
         'But all of those who killed the policemen were hanged.' (AK2.17)

          Kina av all'; dash av 'but'; gii-goojgaazwag vai indSpProx 'ANpl were hanged'; giwpr
          SpProx 'those'; gaa-nsaajig vti ic conjpart 3pProx»3obv '(CCNJ) who (ANpl) killed
          ANobv'; niw pr 3obv 'that/those'; dkonweninwan na 3obv 'police.'

   (188) Mii naa gaa-zhichgewaad giw nishnaabeg gaa-niigaanzijig.
         'This is what those Indians who were leaders did.' (AK5.1)

          Mii av and'; naa av 'emphatic'; gaa-zhichgewaad vai conj ic part SpProx 'what ANpl
          did'; giw pr 3pProx 'those'; nishnaabeg na 'Indians'; gaa-niigaanzijig vai conj ic part
          SpProx 'who (ANpl) were leaders.'
                                                                      12.3.9 Relative Clauses • 585


   (189) Mil wa nini dakweman gaa-bkinaagen'jin mbingoo.
         That's the man whose wife won at bingo.' (MC)

          'ANsg's woman, wife'; gaa-bkinaagen'jin vai ic conjpart3obv 'who (ANobv) won';
          mbingoo ni? Os 'bingo.'

    ADJUNCT RELATIVE CLAUSES. Rhodes 1996:9-10 also discusses relative clauses formed
on adjuncts, such as locational and temporal expressions. Rhodes notes that 'relative clauses
formed on locative adjuncts show a special construction that the corresponding non-relative
form does not share. A locative relative root is present in the relative clause form which is
absent from the non-relative from, and the nominal head appears in either the locative
inflectional form or not, depending on its position in the syntax of the external clause.' The
following examples, taken from Rhodes (pp. 9-10), illustrate a head inflected for locative
(201), with wiigwaam, 'shelter,' inflected for locative, and a head in a non-locative, (202), in
which niimhidiiwgamig, 'dancehall,' is not inflected for locative.
588 • 12.3.9 Relative Clauses


   (201) ... waa-dzhi-mkadekewaad wiigwaaming. I '... in the shelter where they would fast.'
          waa-dzhi-mkadekewaad vai ic conj SpProx '(CCNJ) where ANpl will fast';
          miigwaaming ni 0 loc 'in the shelter.' (AM23.3)

   (202) ... iw niimhidiiwgamig waa-dzhi-niimwaad giw waa-bi-zhaajig.
         '... in the dancehall where those who would be coming would dance.' (AM 16.14)

          iw/?r Os 'that'; niimhidiiwgamig ni Os 'dancehall'; waa-dzhi-niimwaad vai ic conj part
          SpProx '(CCNJ) ANpl would dance'giwpr SpProx 'those'; waa-bi-zhaajig vai ic conj
          part SpPwx '(CCNJ) who (anpl) would come.'

   Rhodes 1996:10 also discusses temporal adjunct relative clauses, pointing out that 'tem-

   (203) Mii dash pii beskaabiiyaang, ... I 'But when we got back...' (AK3.9)

          '(CCNJ) we (excl) got back.'

          ANobv'; niwprSobv 'that/those'; bnewan naSobv 'partridge.'

   (205) Mii ngoding bbaa-miinkeyaang mii gii-megwaashkwaangdwaa giw nishnaabeg
         gaa-wnikewaad iidog wdaabjichganwaan iw wii-wiisniwaad.
         'Once when we were out berrying we happened to meet these Indians who had
         apparently forgotten their utensils for eating.' (AK17.1)

         Mii av 'and'; ngoding av 'once'; bbaa-miinkeyaang vai conj Ip '(CONJ) we were going
         around gathering berries'; mii av 'then'; gii-megwaashkwaangdwaa vta conj lp»3pProx
         '(CONJ) we encountered ANpl'; giw/?r 3pProx 'those'; nishnaabeg na 3pProx 'Indians';
         gaa-wnikewaad vaio ic conj SpProx '(CCNJ) when ANpl forgot (Y)'; iidog av 'it seems';
         wdaabjichganwaan ni 3pProx(Op) 'their utensils'; iw/?r Os 'that'; wii-wiisniwaad vai
         conj SpProx '(CONJ) ANpl will eat.'

   However, nominals can precede the verb even in relative clauses, as in (172), above (p.
580). In the following example, both orders occur, in parallel constructions.

   (206) Ntam go iw piniig wii-biwaad mii-sh miinwaa gookoosh mii-sh gii-ni-wzhitood
         niw wiigwaas-naagaansan niibiishaaboo waa-dzhi-mnikwewaad miinwaa

         'ANpl will be present'; mii-sh av 'and then'; miinwaa av 'also'; gookoosh na SsProx
         'pig'; mii-sh av 'and then'; gii-ni-wzhitood vti conj 3sProx»0 '(CONJ) ANsg made IN';

    VARIATION IN RELATIVE CLAUSE FORMS. Sometimes speakers do not use full particip-
ial inflection in relative clause constructions. For example, in the following, the regular
changed conjunct form, gaa-bi-waabmaad occurs, rather than the participle form,
gaa-bi-waabmaajin.

   (207) Aapji go jina ngii-gnoonaa wa," gii-kido-sh giiwenh miinwaa bezhig
         zhmaagnishii-gimaa wa gaa-bi-waabmaad niwi.
         'I only spoke to him for a short while," said the other officer, who had come to see
         him.' (SO6.60)

         Aapji av 'really'; jina av 'a short time'; ngii-gnoonaa vta ind ls»3sProx 'I spoke to
         ANsg'; wa/?r SsProx 'this'; dash av 'then'; giiwenh av 'reportedly'; miinwaa av 'and';
         bezhig nm 'one'; zhmaagnishii-gimaa na SsProx 'military leader'; v/apr SsProx 'this';
         gaa-bi-waabmaad vta ic conj 3sProx»3obv '(CCNJ) ANsg came and saw ANobv'; niwi
         pr na Sobv 'that/those.'

   The following example, from the same speaker, shows the traditional participle form
used in such contexts.

   (208) Aanii-sh mii sa gmaapiich go miinwaa bezhig bmaadgaad go wesiinh, aanii-sh mii
         go nendmaad goyaabmaajin go bmaadgaanid.
         'Well, a little later, another animal swims by; well, he calls out to the one he sees
         swimming by.' (SOS. 10)

          Aaniish av 'well'; mii av 'then'; gmaapiich av 'after awhile'; miinwaa av 'again';
          bezhig nm 'one'; bmaadgaad vai conj 3sProx '(CONJ) ANsg swims along'; wesiinh na
          BsProx 'animal'; aaniish av 'well'; mii av 'then'; go nendmaad vta ic conj 3sProx»3obv
          '(CCNJ) ANsg summoned ANobv'; yaabmaajin vta ic conj part 3sProx»3obv '(CCNJ)
          ANobv whom ANsg saw'; bmaadgaanid vai conj 3obv '(CONJ) as ANobv swims along.'


   The same kind of variation occurred within the speech of Andrew Medler, as attested by
the following examples, the first with a true participle, the second, not.

   (209) Gye go wgii-dbaajmaan niw shkiniigkwen gaa-msawenmaajin niw shkinwen.

         'He also told of a young woman who took a shine to a young man.' (AM29.3)

          Gye av 'and'; wgii-dbaajmaan vta ind 3sProx»3obv 'ANsg told about ANobv'; niw pr
          3obv 'that/those'; shkiniigkwen na 3obv 'young woman'; gaa-msawenmaajin vta ic
          conj part 3sProx»3obv '(CCNJ) who ANsg longed for ANobv'; niw pr 3obv 'that/those';
          shkinwen na 3obv 'young man.'


   (210) Niin aw gaa-waabmaad waawaashkeshwan.

         'I am the one who saw the deer.' (AM39.641)

          Niinprpers Is T; aw pr 3sProx 'that'; gaa-waabmaad vta ic conj 3sProx»3obv
          '(CCNJ) ANsg who saw ANobv'; waawaashkeshwan na 3obv 'deer.'


   Even more extreme variation can be seen in (205), above (p. 588), where a demonstrative
pronoun iw, 'that' (inan.) is used, and a plain conjunct, future tense form of the verb wiisni,
'eat' (VAI), with a rough meaning 'when ANpl will eat.' This construction seems to serve a
function similar to that of a relative clause. Andrew Medler also uses a form with a plain
conjunct VII form, yaanig, 'INobv is/are there,' in a function rather like a relative clause, as
a modifier of niw siniin, 'those stones' (Nl).

   (211) Pii dash gaa-wwenbid niwyaanig niw siniin wgii-ziignaanaawaa iw

12.3.10 Compound Nominals

   Compound nominals are common, consisting of two identically inflected nouns used in
conjunction, and often modified by a single demonstrative which precedes both nouns. Note
that in the examples below, both nouns are independently inflected for nominal features of
plural or obviative.

   (212) Wgii-ggwejmaan niw kiwenziinyan wii-giishpnadmawaad iw wiikwebjigan manj
         go maanda msawenmaad niw shkinwen mandaagninwan.
        'She asked that old man to let her buy that love medicine from him, since she was
        so very much in love with that young man-handsome one.' (AM29.4)

         Wgii-ggwejmaan vta 3sProx»3obv 'ANsg asked ANobv'; niw/?r 3obv 'that/those';
         kiwenziinyan na 3obv 'old man/men'; wii-giishpnadmawaad vta conj 3sProx»3obv
         '(CONJ) ANsg buy Y from ANobv'; i\vpr Os 'that'; wiikwebjigan ni Os 'love medicine';
         manj av 'however it may be'; maandapr Os 'this'; msawenmaad vta conj 3sProx»3obv
         '(CONJ) ANsg longed for ANobv'; mw pr 3obv 'that/those'; shkinwen na 3obv 'young
         man/men'; mandaagninwan na 3obv 'gentleman/men.'


   (213) Gii-yaawag-sh giiwenh go iidig wadi giwi Nishnaabeg Nimkiig.
         'Apparently, there did exist over there, those Thunder People.' (SO4.22)

         Gii-yaawag vai ind3pProx 'ANpl were there'; dash av 'then'; giiwenh av 'reportedly';
         iidig av 'it seems'; wadi av 'there'; giwipr 3pProx 'those'; Nishnaabeg na SpProx
         'Indians'; Nimkiig na 3pProx Thunderers.'

12.3.11 Qualification of a Nominal with Prenouns

   The concepts expressed in English by means of adjectives are often encoded in Nishnaa-
bemwin in intransitive verbs, as in the following examples, with verb gaachiinh, 'be small'
(VAI) in (214), and waabshkizi, 'be white' (VAI) in (215). See also Chapter 9.

   (214) Aapji shkwaaj egaachiinynijin, Aanii dash giin ezhnikaazyan? wgii-naan.

         To the smallest one, in the end, he said, "And what is your name, you?'"
         (AM35.6)

          Aapji av 'really'; shkwaaj av 'last'; egaachiinynijin vai ic conjpart 3obv '(CCNJ) who
          ANobv was small'; Aanii av 'how'; dash av 'then'; giinprpers 2s 'you'; ezhnikaazyan
          vai ic conj 2s '(CCNJ) you SG are so named'; wgii-naan vta ind 3sProx»3obv 'ANsg said
          to ANobv.'


   (215) Waaboozoonh gii-ggwejmaa wegdagwen wenji-waabshkizgwen.

         'Rabbit was asked why he was white of color.' (AM34.2)

          Waaboozoonh na 3sProx 'rabbit'; gii-ggwejmaa vta indx»3sProx 'ANsg was asked';
          wegdagwenpr dub 0 'whatever'; wenji-waabshkizgwen vai ic conj dub 3sProx '(CCNJ)
          why might ANsg be white in color.'


    However, there are also many prenouns which serve to qualify a noun in some way, by
far the most common being gchi-, 'great, large, big'. The following examples illustrate the
use of adjectival prenouns.

   (216) Gchi-dikmeg ngii-debnaa. I 'I caught a big whitefish" (MC5.4.)

          Gchi-dikmeg na 3sProx 'whitefish'; ngii-debnaa vta ind ls»3sProx 'I caught ANsg.'

   (217) Ngii-wzhitmaag aw ngashi \vshki-goodaas ge-biiskamaan go eta
         ji-wi-namhaayaan.

         'My mother made me a new dress to wear only for going to church.' (AK3.2)

          Ngii-wzhitmaag vta ind3sProx»ls 'ANsg made for me'; awpr 3sProx 'that'; ngashi nad
          ls(3sProx) 'my mother'; wshki-goodaas ni Os 'new dress'; ge-biiskamaan vti ic conj
          ls»0 '(CCNJ) that (IN) I will wear'; eta av 'only'; ji-wi-namhaayaan vai conj Is
          '(CONJ) should I go to church.'

12.3.12 Dnawa, 'Kind of Constructions

   The pronominal element dnawa is used in expressions of kind or type, almost always in
conjunction with an antecedent pronoun, as in the following examples:

   (218) Maaba dnawa biindaakwaazh. I 'Smoke this kind of tobacco.' (AM39.784)
         Maabapr SsProx 'this'; dnawaprsim 3/0 'kind'; biindaakwaazh vta imp 2s»3 'smoke
         AN.'

   (219) Gaa dash iw dnawa nokiiwin ngii-ndawendnziin.
         'But I did not want that kind of work.' (AM8.17)

         Gaa av 'not'; dash av 'then'; iw pr Os 'that'; dnawa pr sim 3/0 'kind'; nokiiwin ni Os
         'work'; ngii-ndawendnziin vti ind ls»0 neg 'I did not want INsg.'

   This pronoun is inflected for number and obviation by some speakers, as in the following

   (220) Wegnesh dnawan daabaanan gaa-giishpnanaajin? I 'What kind of car did sine buy?'
         Wegnesh pr inter 3/0 'what'; dnawan prsim 3obv 'kind'; daabaanan na 3obv 'car';
         gaa-giishpnanaajin vta ic conjpart 3sProx»3obv 'that [ANobv] ANsg bought.' (MC)

   In the stories of Angeline Williams, dowa is found instead of dnawa, in conjunction with
the interrogative pronouns wenesh (animate) and wegone (inanimate).

   (221) Wenesh dowa giigoonh waa-amwad izhi-giigoonh?
         ' What kind of fish do you want to eat?' (AW14.48)

         Wenesh pr inter 3/0 'who'; dowa per sim 3 'kind'; giigoonh na SsProx 'fish';
         waa-amwad vta ic conj 2s»3sProx '(CCNJ) you want to eat ANsg'; izhi-giigoonh na
         SsProx 'such fish.'

   Note too the following, in which the pronoun has the form, anindowa.

   (222) Mii iw animoshishan wegitiziimimaad anindowa gaa-aawid.
         'That one person was of the kind that have a dog as one parent.' (AW15.3)

         Mii av 'and'; iwprOs 'that'; animoshishan napej3spej 'worthless dog';
         wegitiziimimaad vta ic conj 3sProx»3obv '(CCNJ) ANsg who has ANobv for parent';
         anindowa pr sim 'kind'; gaa-aawid vai ic conj 3sProx '(CCNJ) that ANsg was.'

12.3.13 Substitutionary Pronouns

   Substitutionary, or general, pronouns are extremely common in conversation, peppering
discourse at every turn. These pronouns deserve a monograph unto themselves, but only a
couple of examples are provided here. A list of common forms can be found in Chapter 3,
though there is undoubtedly more variation than I represent.

   (223) «Na'ii, eshkam go niibna notes ndoo-ni-maawndoobiiyaanan nawach gegoo
         waa-kwejminaa, dictionary-ing nikeyiing.»
         'Well, I'm gradually accumulating more notes of various things that I want to ask
         you about the dictionary.' (MC)

          Na'iipr ni Os 'uh'; eshkam av 'increasingly; niibna av 'many';
          ndoo-ni-maawndoobiiyaanan vti ind ls>0p 'I am accumulating INpl'; nawach av
          'more'; gegoo pr ni Os 'thing'; waa-kwejminaa vta ic conj ls>2s '(CCNJ) which I want
          to ask you (sg); dictionary-ing ni 0 loc 'in the dictionary'; nikeyiing av 'pertaining to.'


   (224) Nahii noongo gaa-ggwejmigoowaanh, Obatanga miinwaa Obakamiga edming.
         Nahiin giiwenh nanda, zaaghigaansan White River miinwaa Hornepayne
         nikeyiing etegin.

         'Uh, today I was asked what Obatanga and Obakamiga mean (in Nishnaabem-
         win). Uh, apparently these are small rivers located in the direction of White River
         and Hornepayne.' (MC)

          Nahiiprpaus Os 'uh'; noongo av 'today'; gaa-ggwejmigoowaanh vta ic conj x»Is
          '(CCNJ) I was asked'; miinwaa av 'and'; edming vti ic conj x»0 'what X means of IN.'
          Nahiin prpaus Op 'uh'; giiwenh av 'reportedly'; nanda pr Op 'these'; zaaghigaansan ni
          Op 'creeks'; miinwaa av 'and'; nikeyiing av 'in that direction'; etegin vii ic conj Op
          'where INpl are.'


12.3.14 Indefinite, Universal, and Negative Pronouns

    Indefinite (existential), universal and negative pronouns all use the basic pronominal
waya (also wiya and awiyd) for animates and gegoo (also gegoori) for inanimates. All three
of these pronominals occur in the following sentence:

   (225) Gaawiin waya gga-aanwenmaasii, kina waya gga-wiijkiweymaa miinwaa
         gga-wiidookwaa waya iw giishpin ndawendang ji-wiidookwind.
         'You are not to look down on anyone, you are to be friendly to everyone and help
         anyone if he wants people to help him.' (AK6.8)
                                               12.3.14 Indefinite, Universal, and Negative Pronouns • 595



            Gaawiin av 'not'; waya/?r indef 3sProx 'anyone'; gga-aanwenmaasii vta ind 2s»3sProx
            'you SG will look down on ANsg'; kina av 'every'; waya/?r indef 3sProx '(some)one';
            gga-wiijkiweymaa vta ind 2s»3sProx 'you SG will be friendly to ANsg'; miinwaa av
            'and'; gga-wiidookwaa vta ind 2s»3sProx 'you SG will help ANsg'; wayapr indef
            3sProx 'anyone'; iwpr Os 'that'; giishpin av 'if; ndawendang vti conj 3sProx»0
            '(CONJ) ANsg wants IN'; ji-wiidookwind vta conjx»3sProx '(CONJ) ANsg should be
            helped.'

   Many speakers do not inflect these pronouns for number or obviation, as can be seen
from the following examples. In the first, way a modifies an obviated participle
(bemaadzin 'jin), and the second gaa awiya modifies a plural noun, Anishinaabeg.

   (226) Mii-sh giiwenh gii-dbaajmod gaa-zhiwebzid, waya1 iidig gii-maajiiwnigod
         bemaadzin'jin.
           Then he related what had happened to him, how some people had taken him off

            ANsg'; wayapr indef 3sProx 'someone'; iidig av 'perhaps'; gii-maajiiwnigod vta conj
            3obv»3sProx '(CONJ) ANobv took ANsg away'; bemaadzin'jin vai ic conj part 3obv
            '(CCNJ) ANobv who live' (people).


   (227) Mii dash gaa-igod: "Gaa na awiya Anishinaabeg ningwaji ji-danakiiwaad?"

           They said to him, "Aren't there any people living anywhere?'" (AW19.5)

            Mii av 'and'; dash av 'then'; gaa-igod vta ic conj3obv»3sProx '(CCNJ) ANobv said to
            ANsg'; Gaa av 'not'; na av 'yes/no question'; awiyapr indef 3 'anyone'; Anishinaabeg
            na 3pProx 'people'; ningwaji av 'anywhere'; ji-danakiiwaad vai conj 3pProx '(CONJ)
            ANpl might be living there.'

598 • 12.3.14 Indefinite, Universal, and Negative Pronouns


    NEGATIVE PRONOUNS. The negative pronoun essentially defines an empty set, that is,
specifies that no one or nothing meets some criterion. These pronouns have the negative
word gaawii(n) (often written as two words, gaa wii(n)) or gaa in conjunction with the
indefinite pronouns, producing gaawii(n) waya (or awiyd) and gaawii(n) gegoo(n) for ani-
mates and inanimates respectively. Gaawii(n) is usually among the first words in its clause,
and always precedes the pronoun, though it may be separated from it by intervening mate-
rial. Often the pronoun follows the verb and the negative precedes, and the negative adverb
seems associated with both the verb and the pronoun. All verbs having negative arguments
are themselves inflected as negative. The following examples illustrate the basic usage of
these pronouns.

   (237) Gaa wii ndoo-giishkhanziin aapji gegoo. I 'I do not cut down anything at all.'
          Gaa av 'not'; wii av 'not'; ndoo-giishkhanziin vti ind ls»0s neg 'I do not cut IN down';
          aapji av 'really'; gegooprindefO 'anything.' (AMIS.13)

   Negatives can be used with nominals to convey the meaning 'not any,' or 'no X.' The
verb is inflected as negative.

   (240) Ge wiin dash zhaazhi go giw gaa-bi-nbojig gaa mi gegoo mzinhigan
         gii-yaasnoon.

   NEGATIVE EXISTENTIALS. A striking feature of negatives in Nishnaabemwin is the fact
that simple NEGATIVE EXISTENTIAL assertions are often verbless.

   (241) Gaawii wiya wiijkiwenywaan; kina gii-gjibhiwengoba.

          friend(s)'; kina av 'all'; gii-gjibhiwengoba vai indpdub 3obv 'ANobv evidently had
          fled.'


   (242) Gkina ngii-bkinaag iw nzhoon'yaam, gaa dash gegoo noongwazhoon'yaa.

          'that'; nzhoon'yaam ni ls(0s) 'my money'; gaa av 'not'; dash av 'then'; gegoo pr indefO
          'anything'; noongwa av 'now'; zhoon'yaa ni Os 'money.'


   Gaa wii gegoo, literally, 'nothing,' can be used predicationally to mean 'it's nothing, it
doesn't matter,' as in the following example:

   (243) Gaa wii gegoo noonde-nboyan, gga-bmaajhin miinwaa, mookseyan.

          '(CONJ) you die before the goal is reached'; gga-bmaajhin vta ind ls»2s 'I will revive

    A relative clause associated with a verbless negative predication does not show negative

   UNIVERSAL PRONOUNS. The universal quantifier is kina (or gakina), which may be com-
bined with the pronouns waya (or awiya) and gegoo, to produce kina \vaya and kina gegoo,
with the respective meanings 'everyone' and 'everything.' The following examples illustrate
the use of these constructions.

   (246) Gaawiin waya gga-aanwenmaasii, kina waya gga-wiijkiweymaa miinwaa
         gga-wiidookwaa waya iw giishpin ndawendang ji-wiidookwind.
         'You are not to look down on anyone, you are to be friendly to everyone and help
         anyone if he wants people to help him.' (AK6.8)

          Gaawiin av 'not'; wayapr indefSsProx 'anyone'; gga-aanwenmaasii vta ind 2s»3sProx
          'you SG will look down on ANsg'; kina av 'every'; wayapr indef3sProx '(any)one';
          gga-wiijkiweymaa vta ind 2s»3sProx 'you SG will be friendly to ANsg'; miinwaa av
          'and'; gga-wiidookwaa vta ind 2s»3sProx 'you SG will help ANsg'; waya pr indef
          3sProx 'anyone'; i\v pr Os 'that'; giishpin av 'if; ndawendang vti conj 3sProx»0
          '(CONJ) ANsg wants IN'; ji-wiidookwind vta conj xSsProx '(CONJ) ANsg should be
          helped.'


   (247) Mii maa naa eta iw gaa-wndaadziwaad, niw miinan miinwaa mshkiigminan kina
         gegoo wgii-zgaknaanaawaa, wgii-gkendaanaawaa maa naa iw ezhi-znagdinig iw
         bboon. (AK17.11)
         'And this is the only way they made a living, they harvested blueberries and cran-
         berries and everything, indeed they knew how hard it was for them in winter.'
                                          12.3.14 Indefinite, Universal, and Negative Pronouns • 601



          Mil av 'it's'; maa av 'indeed'; eta av 'only'; iwpr Os 'that'; gaa-wndaadziwaad vai ic
          conj SpProx '(CCNJ) ANpl lived by means of; niwpr Op 'those'; miinan ni Op
          'blueberries'; miinwaa av 'and'; mshkiigminan ni Op 'cranberries'; kina av 'every';
          gegoopr indefO 'thing'; wgii-zgaknaanaawaa vti ind 3pProx»Os 'ANpl harvested IN';
          wgii-gkendaanaawaa vti ind3pProx»Os 'ANpl knew INsg'; maa av 'indeed'; iwpr Os
          'that'; ezhi-znagdinig vii ic conj Oobv '(CONJ) how difficult INobv is'; iwpr Os 'that';
          bboon ni Os 'winter.'

   ABSENCE OF PRONOMINALS. When universal quantification is applied to first and second
persons, there is no pronominal (wiyd), perhaps because the third person feature of the pro-
noun clashes with first or second person. Rather, kina (gakina) is used alone, as in the fol-
lowing.

   (248) Baamaa-sh ggii-gkenminim zhaazhi kina gaa-bi-maajaayeg.
         'It was somewhat later that I realized that you all had already left.' (SO6.82)

          Baamaa av 'later'; dash av 'then'; ggii-gkenminim vta ind ls»2p 'I knew of you (pi)';
          zhaazhi av 'long ago'; kina av 'all'; gaa-bi-maajaayeg vai ic conj 2p '(CCNJ) you (pi)
          had left.'


   (249) Kina dash gnandmigoom da-bi-zhaayeg mnik ge-gshkitooyeg ji-bi-waabndameg
         ge wii ennokiid aw Nishnaabe maa wdankiiwning.
         'You are all invited, as many of you as will be able, to come and see the ways of
         the Indian there on his reservation.' (AMIS.6)

          Kina av 'all'; dash av 'then'; gnandmigoom vta indx»2p 'you (pi) are invited';
          da-bi-zhaayeg vai conj 2p '(CONJ) you (pi) will come'; mnik av 'as many as';
          ge-gshkitooyeg vti conj 2p»0 '(CCNJ) you (pi) will be able to do IN'; ji-bi-waabndameg
          vti conj 2p»0 '(CONJ) you (pi) could come and see IN'; ge av 'as for'; wiiprpers 3s
          's/he'; ennokiid vai ic conj 3sProx '(CCNJ) how ANsg works so'; awpr 3sProx 'that';
          Nishnaabe na SsProx 'Indian'; maa av 'there'; wdankiiwning ni 3sProx(0) loc 'at
          ANsg's place of residence.'


    When third person objects being quantified are known from the linguistic or physical
context, kina may occur without a noun or pronoun as well, apparently quantifying the pro-
nominal argument of the verb as it must when it binds first and second persons. This might
be considered equivalent to the English distinction between 'everyone/everything' and the
use of 'all' as a pronominal form, though in English it is usually restricted to subjects,
whereas in Nishnaabemwin it applies most commonly to absolutives (subjects of intransi-
tive verbs and goals of transitive verbs), but occasionally to transitive actors as well. Forms
602 • 12.3.14 Indefinite, Universal, and Negative Pronouns


lacking the pronoun are particularly common in Nishnaabemwin when the referent is ani-
mate, in fact only one example of kina waya occurs in the combined texts of Andrew
Medler, Sam Osawamick, and Alice King. The following examples illustrate the more com-
monly found construction in these materials.

   (250) Mii go kina gii-nsaawaad. I 'They had killed them all: (SO6.163)
          Mii av 'and'; kina av 'all'; gii-nsaawaad vta conj 3pProx»3obv '(CONJ) ANpl killed
          ANobv.'

   (251) Gii-biindged kina go. I 'In fact, they all went in.' [N.B. Note singular verb]
          Gii-biindged vai conj SsProx '(CONJ) ANsg entered'; kina av 'all.' (SO6.179)

    When kina modifies a noun, it usually precedes the noun, which frequently has no asso-
ciated demonstrative, though the reference is definite and specific. This construction is per-
haps more common with inanimate nouns.

   (252) Mii-sh giiwenh zhiwi kina kosing kanan, kanenyan.
         'So all the bones were piled up there, those old bones' (SO2.40)

          Mii-sh av 'and then'; giiwenh av 'reportedly'; zhiwi av 'there'; kina av 'all'; kosing vii
          conj 0 '(CONJ) IN is in a pile'; kanan ni(d) Op 'bones'; kanenyan ni(d) contemp Op 'old
          bones.'


   (253) Mii giiwenh go kina baashkzignan zhiwi-sh teg. I 'All the guns were there.'
          Mii av 'and'; giiwenh av 'reportedly'; kina av 'all'; baashkzignan ni Op 'rifles'; zhiwi
          av 'there'; dash av 'then'; teg viz conj 0 '(CONJ) IN are there.' (SO6.130)

    However, constructions with demonstratives are common too. In such cases, the quanti-
fier always precedes the demonstrative, which in turn, always precedes the noun it modifies.
It is customary, but not obligatory, for the quantifier to precede the verb, regardless of the
position the noun phrase it is associated with.

   (254) Mii go wadi gaazhiitaawaad, mii go kina giizhiitaawaad wadi nanda
         wiijkiwenywaan.
         'When they (one group) were finished over there, all those companions of theirs
         were finished also.' (SO6.162)
                                         12.3.14 Indefinite, Universal, and Negative Pronouns • 603



         Mil av 'and'; wadi av 'there'; gaazhiitaawaad vai conj SpProx '(CCNJ) when ANpl
         finished'; mii av 'then'; kina av 'all'; giizhiitaawaad vai conj 3pProx '(CONJ) ANpl
         finished'; wadi av 'there'; nandapr3obv 'this/these'; wiijkiwenywaan na 3pProx(3obv)
         'ANpl's friend(s).'

   (255) Kina dashniw wdadaawenaawaan. I 'All these (things) they sell,' (AM15.3)

         Kina av 'all'; dash av 'then'; niwpr Op 'those'; wdadaawenaawaan vaio ind 3p»0p
         'ANpl sell INpl.'

   The variable presence of the demonstrative is made particularly clear by the examples of
the following two sentences from two versions of the same story by Andrew Medler:

   (256) Aapji dash gii-mno-bmaadzi, gye go kina gii-maajaamgadni wdakjiwin.

         Aapji av 'really'; dash av 'then'; gii-mno-bmaadzi vai indSsProx 'ANsg felt well'; gye
         av 'and'; kina av 'all'; gii-maajaamgadni vii ind OobvSg 'INobvSg was gone';
         wdakjiwin ni 3sProx(Os) 'ANSG'S cold.'


   (257) Aapji gii-mno-bmaadzi gye kina iw sa wdaakziwin gii-maajaamgadni.

         'He felt very good, and his illness was entirely gone.' (AM21.19)

         Aapji av 'really'; gii-mno-bmaadzi vai indSsProx 'ANsg felt well'; gye av 'and'; kina

          0 '(CCNJ) the extent of IN's length'; i w p r O s 'that'; sabaab ni Os 'cord.'

   (270) Aaniish mii sa go gii-dbaajmod wa shkiniigish, mii sa go maanda

          SsProx 'this'; mdimooyenh na SsProx 'old woman'; wgwisan na SsProx(Sobv) 'ANSG'S

    In the following example, the quantifier appears to directly modify the verb, rather than

can apply to either the totality of the snow or the achievement of its complete melting.
Undoubtedly many subtleties of this sort exist in Nishnaabemwin as well, and my discus-
sion once again only skims the surface of a very rich area of grammar.

   RELATIVE CLAUSES WITH KINA GEGOO. Relative clauses may be used with kina gegoo.
The ordering relationship between the relative clause and the quantificational expression is
variable.

   (275) Gye go netaawgitoowaad kina gegoo wii-temgad, jiisan, piniig, mdaamnag,
         mskodiisminag, gye go iw bkwezhgaans, gye go mnoomin, mnijiimin,

          Gye av 'and'; go netaawgitoowaad vti ic conjpart SpProx 0 '(CCNJ) which ANpl raise

         mdaamnag, bnagzignag, mnijiimin.

         'There will be everything that is raised: turnips, cabbages, beans, potatoes, Indian

          Kina av 'every'; gegoo pr indefO 'thing'; da-temgad vii indOs 'INsg will be there';
          netaawging vii ic conj part 0 '(CCNJ) which (IN) grows to maturity'; jiisan ni Op

   As with waya, 'someone, anyone,' the expression kina gegoo, 'everything,' can be used

   (277) Kina gegoo wii-yaamgadoon niw games, waa-ggwejkandijig bezhgoogzhiig.

          Kina av 'every'; gegoo pr indefO 'thing'; wii-yaamgadoon vii ind Op 'INpl will be
          there'; mwprOp 'those'; waa-ggwejkandijig vai ic conj part SpProx '(CCNJ) who ANpl

12.3.15 Personal Pronouns

    Personal pronouns identify participants on the basis of their roles in the communicative
context as speakers, addressees, or topics of comment. They are closely related to the per-
son and number affixes that occur on independent order verbs and on possessed nouns.
There are personal pronouns for each combination of the three conversational roles (person)
and two number categories. But DEVIATION (proximate and obviative), though inflectionally
indexed on the verb, is more a NOMINAL than PRONOMINAL category, and can only be intro-
duced in the context of nominals. There are no obviative personal pronouns, nor even are
there third person personal pronouns that are distinctly animate or inanimate. In some dia-
lects of Anishinaabemowin, all third person personal pronouns are animate, but in Nishnaa-
bemwin it appears that at least for some speakers they can be inanimate as well. In all
dialects of Anishinaabemowin, including Nishnaabemwin, first and second person pronouns
are always animate, and verbs that take exclusively inanimate subjects (VII verbs) or inani-
mate goals (VTI verbs) have no first or second person forms for roles filled by inanimate ref-
erents. Pronominal person categories also pattern differently from nominals in their
grammatical traits, e.g., second and third person pronominals share a plural, /-waa/, which
is opposed to first person /-naany/.
    In English, personal pronouns are used to signal primary grammatical relations, a func-
tion fulfilled in Nishnaabemwin by means of verbal affixes, as we have seen. Nishnaabem-
win personal pronouns are used in two identifiable contexts: first, in syntactic contexts
where verbs are not used, either because of the nature of the construction itself, or because
of a contextual ellipsis of a verb; secondly, personal pronouns are commonly used in con-
texts of focus or emphasis. In such uses, they often have meanings corresponding to com-
pound English pronominal expressions such as 'you yourself or 'your own,' though
English also expresses equivalent ideas by means of prosodic emphasis.
    VERBLESS POSSESSION FORMULAS. Verbless statements and questions involving owner-
ship, possession, or relationship commonly show pronouns, as in the following example:

   (278) Aapii dash giin gwiiwkwaan? I 'And you, where is your hat?' (AM39.853)
          Aapii av 'where'; dash av 'then'; giinprpers 2s 'you'; gwiiwkwaan ni 2s(0s) 'your hat.'

   Often, though, no pronoun occurs.

   (279) Aaniipiish ndoopwaagan? I 'Where is mypipeT (AM39.855)

          Aaniipiish av 'where'; ndoopwaagan na ls(3sProx) 'my pipe.'


    DIRECT ADDRESS. Personal pronouns may be used in formal contexts of direct address,
as in the following examples, which contain both vocative plural forms and second person
plural pronouns. The first example occurs at the end of a long formal, historical account
610 • 12.3.15 Personal Pronouns


given by a Manitoulin Island oral historian, and the last example is the opening sentence of
a formal speech.

   (280) Boozhoo nwiijkiwenydig giinwaa mnik bezndaageyeg.
         'Good-day, my friends, as many of you (pi.) who are listening. '(SO6.189)

          Boozhoo av 'hello'; nwiijkiwenydig nad voc ls(2p) 'you my friends'; giinwaa prpers
          2p 'you'; mnik av 'as many as'; bezndaageyeg vai ic conj 2p 'you (pi) who are listening.'


   (281) Mandaagkwedig gye giinwaa mandaagninwidog!
         'Ladies and (you,) gentlemen!' (AM 18.1)

          Mandaagkwedig na 2p voc 'ladies'; gye av 'and'; giinwaa prpers 2p 'you';
          mandaagninwidog na voc 2p 'gentlemen.'


    Sentence (280) shows a common focusing strategy, that of using a pronoun modified by a
restrictive relative clause in order to delimit a particular subgroup, as does the following.

   (282) Mii maanda sa ge-waabndameg giinwaa waa-bi-zhaayeg.
         'Such are the things you will see, you who will come there.' (AM 18.18)

          Mii av 'it's'; maandapr Os 'this'; ge-waabndameg vti ic conj 2p»0 '(CCNJ) you (pi)
          will see IN'; giinwaa prpers 2p 'you (pi)'; waa-bi-zhaayeg vai ic conj part 2p '(CCNJ)
          you (pi) who will come here.'

   In commands, the use of pronouns seems to add force to the command.

   (283) Aa, mii go ge giinwaa maajaag! I 'Come on! All of you, leave!' (SO5.67)
          Aa av 'well'; mii av 'then'; ge av 'also'; giinwaa prpers 2p 'you (pi)'; maajaag vai imp
          2p '(you pi) leave.'

   SUBSTANTIVE QUESTIONS. Personal pronouns are also common in SUBSTANTIVE QUES-
TIONS, which, of course, also involve direct address. Such questions share an imperative fea-
ture with commands, since they are essentially commands to provide verbal information.

   (284) Aapji shkwaaj egaachiinynijin, Aanii dash giin ezhnikaazyan? wgii-naan.
         'To the smallest one, in the end, he said, "And what is your name, JOM?'"
                                                                      12.3.15 Personal Pronouns • 611



          Aapji av 'really'; shkwaaj av 'last'; egaachiinynijin vai ic conj part 3obv '(CCNJ) who
          ANobv was small'; Aanii av 'how'; dash av 'then'; gjinprpers 2s 'you'; ezhnikaazyan
          vai ic conj 2s '(CCNJ) you SG are so named'; wgii-naan vta ind3sProx»3obv 'ANsg said
          to ANobv.' (AM35.6)

   (285) Gomaapii "Weneshgwn ayaawiyan?" I 'After a bit, "Who arejww?" (AW19.154)

          Gomaapii av 'after awhile'; Weneshpr inter 3/0 'who'; giinprpers 2s 'you.'

   There are many other contexts where personal pronouns are used.

   (286) Wgii-naan niw sa shkiniigkwen, Gego dash zhgadenmaaken maaba shkinwe. (b)
         Giin maa gdizhchigaanaa sa ji-mdaagwenmik.
         'He said to the young woman, "And do not be too impatient to have that young
         man. (b) You (yourself) will bring it about that he will be the one to desire you.'"

          Wgii-naan vta ind3sProx»3obv 'ANsg said to ANobv'; niwpr 3obv 'that/those';
          shkiniigkwen na 3obv 'young woman'; Gego av 'don't'; dash av 'then';
          zhgadenmaaken vta imp 2s»3sProx neg 'do not 2s be impatient with AN'; maaba pr
          3sProx 'this'; shkinwe na 3sProx 'young man.' (b) Giin pr pers 2s 'you'; maa av 'there';
          gdizhchigaanaa vta ind 2s»3sProx 'you SG work on ANsg'; ji-mdaagwenmik vta conj
          3sProx»2s '(CONJ) ANsg would like you.' (AM29.7)


   (287) Bngiishenh wgii-gaadaajmotwaan wiinwaa nishnaabewwaad wii-daapnigaazwaad,
         mii gchi-mookmaan gaa-kidod.

         'He concealed a little in telling him that, since they were Indians, they would be
         seized according to what the American had said.' (SO6.13)

          Bngiishenh av 'a little'; wgii-gaadaajmotwaan vta ind 3sProx»3obv 'ANsg made an
          incomplete report to ANobv'; wiinwaa pr pers 3p 'ANpl'; nishnaabewwaad vai conj
          SpProx '(CONJ) ANpl were Indians'; wii-daapnigaazwaad vai conj SpProx '(CONJ)
          ANpl would be seized'; mii av 'that's'; gchi-mookmaan na SsProx 'American';
          gaa-kidod vai ic conj 3sProx '(CCNJ) ANsg said.'

   PERSONAL PRONOUNS WITH OTHER NOUNS OR PRONOUNS (APPOSITION). Personal pro-
nouns also occur in sentences with nouns and other pronouns making reference to the same
characters that the personal pronouns do, creating a situation that is typically translated into
English as an APPOSITIVE. In the first example below, the pronoun wiinwaa, 'they,' occurs
with the animate noun nishnaabeg, 'Indians,' and in the second wiinwaa occurs with the
demonstrative pronoun giwi, 'those (anim.).' These constructions commonly involve the
conjunctive element ge, 'also, and,' or the disjunctive element, eta, 'only.'
612 • 12.3.15 Personal Pronouns


   (288) Wiinwaa go eta nishnaabeg zhiwi miigaazwag.

         'Only they, the Indians, were left to fight.' (SO6.34)

          Wiinwaaprpers 3p 'ANpl'; eta av 'only'; nishnaabeg na SpProx 'Indians'; zhiwi av
          'there'; miigaazwag vai ind SpProx 'ANpl fight.'


   (289) Mil go ge wiinwaa giizhiitaawaad giwi. I 'And those, they too were finished also.'

          Mii av 'and'; ge av 'also'; wiinwaa prpers 3p 'ANpl'; giizhiitaawaad vai conj SpProx
          '(CONJ) ANpl finish'; giwi pr SpProx 'those.' (SO6.186)

    PERSONAL PRONOUNS AND FOCUS/EMPHASIS. Personal pronouns are also used in con-
texts of particular emphasis, which is often implicitly or explicitly contrastive as well. In the
following account by Sam Osawamick, a man is visited by friends who request his help in a
dangerous task. In order to avoid his obligations, the man makes reference to his state of ill
health, several times using the first person singular pronoun to draw attention to his particu-
lar state, and to contrast himself with those going:

   (290) A: "Gwii-wiikjiwnigoo wii-bbaa-wiijiiwyaang. (b) Nbwaanwihaanaa wadi
         wii-nsangid bezhig mnidoo, mii sa gaa-zhi-mkwenmigooyan
         wii-bbaa-wiijiiwyaang, wii-wa-naadmawyaang."

         A: "We will ask you to accompany us. (b) We have tried in vain to kill a monster
         over there, and we thought you would come along with us and help."

          Gwii-wiikjiwnigoo vta ind lp[x]»2s 'we will invite you'; wii-bbaa-wiijiiwyaang vta
          conj 2s»lp 'you will come along with us.' (b) Nbwaanwihaanaa vta ind lp»3sProx 'we
          tried in vain to do to ANsg'; wadi av 'there'; wii-nsangid vta conj lp»3sProx 'we want to
          kill ANsg'; bezhig nm 'a certain'; mnidoo na SsProx 'manitou'; mii av 'and';
          gaa-zhi-mkwenmigooyan vta ic conj lp»2s 'we thought of you'; wii-bbaa-wiijiiwyaang
          vta conj 2s»lp 'you will come along with us'; wii-wa-naadmawyaang vta conj 2s»lp
          'you will go and help us.'


         B: (c) "Oonh, oonh, gaa nii\ (d) Ngoji ndaa-de-zhaasii. (e) Ndaakoz nii, gaawaanh
         nii go naa ndizhwebiz.

         B: (c) "Oh, not me\ (d) I won't be able to go anywhere, (e) / am sick, 7 am hardly
         able to do anything." (SO4.10-14)
                                                                  12.3.15 Personal Pronouns • 613



         (c) Oonh av 'oh'; oonh av 'oh'; Gaa av 'not'; nilprpers Is 'I.' (d) Ngoji av 'anywhere';
         ndaa-de-zhaasii vai ind Is neg 'I won't be able to go.' (e) Ndaakoz vai ind Is 'I am ill';
         mi pr pers Is T; gaawaanh av 'barely'; mi pr pers Is T; ndizhwebiz vai ind Is 'I do

   Pronouns are common when the speaker wishes to draw attention to himself or herself.

   (291) Mii dash aw bezhig nishnaabe gii-maajaad wii-ndawaabmaad niw,

        'And this one Indian went away to look for them, "I'll intercept them myself"'

   (292) "Niin giwi gdan'shinaabemag nwii-gnawenmaag," wgii-goon.
         "(b) Gaawiin! Niin go nwii-gnawenmaag."
        "7 am going to take charge of those Indians of yours," he said to him.
        "(b) Oh no (you're not)! / will look after them myself!" (SO6.10-11)

         Niin pr pers Is 'I myself; giwi pr 3pProx 'those'; gdan'shinaabemag na 2s(3pProx)
         'your Indians'; nwii-gnawenmaag vta ind ls»3pProx 'I will take charge of ANpl';
