         Is T; go nwii-gnawenmaag vta ind ls»3pProx 'I will take charge of ANpl.'

  EMPHATIC PARTICLES WITH PRONOUNS. The assertive emphatic particle sa is very com-
mon with emphatic uses of pronouns, as we would expect.

   (293) Gun sa ggii-mmaazhiiwii, gaa-nji-mzhkoozyaan.
        'You played your part very badly, and that's why I got wounded.' (SO6.79)

         Giinprpers 2s 'you'; ggii-mmaazhiiwii vai ind2s 'you did poorly';
         gaa-nji-mzhikoozyaan vai ic conj Is '(CCNJ) why I was wounded.'

   The EMPHATIC PARTICLE go is also very common in clauses with pronouns, as well as
the particle combination go naa.
614 • 12.3.15 Personal Pronouns


   (294) Wiinwaa go eta nishnaabeg zhiwi miigaazwag.
         'Only they, the Indians, were left to fight.' (SO6.34)

          Wiinwaaprpers 3p 'ANpl'; etaav 'only'; nishnaabegna SpProx 'Indians'; zhiwi av
          'there'; miigaazwag vai ind SpProx 'ANpl fight.'

   See also (290), above, for an example with nil, 'I.'
   FOCUS CONSTRUCTIONS WITH Mil. Personal pronouns are also used in focusing contexts
with the predicative element mii, as in the following example.

   (295) Giishpin eyaagin waa-nankiing widi Girls Quarters mii go niin widi
         ezhnaazhkaagooyaan ji-waabndamaan wegdagwen iidig nendwendaagdogwen.
         'Whenever there was any work to be done over in the Girls' Quarters, / was the
         one to be sent there to see what it might be that was wanted.' (AM8.24)

          Giishpin av 'if; eyaagin vii conj 0 iter '(CCNJ) there was ever'; waa-nankiing vai ic
          conjx '(CCNJ) one will do work'; widi av 'over there'; mii av 'it's'; go mm prpers Is
          T; widi av 'over there'; ezhnaazhkaagooyaan vta ic conj part Is '(CCNJ) I who was
          sent'; ji-waabndamaan vti conj ls»0 '(CCNJ) I will see IN'; wegdagwenpr dub 0
          'whatever'; iidig av 'perhaps'; nendwendaagdogwen vii ic conj part dub 0 '(CCNJ) what
          IN might be wanted.'

   GE CONSTRUCTIONS. A common construction in Nishnaabemwin is the combination ge
plus a personal pronoun. Ge is probably related to the ADVERB gye, 'and, also' (also often
written ge), though in combination with a pronoun it forms a single word, as can be seen
from the fact that the combination ge+pronoun is followed by the yes/no question particle
na, which is encliticized to the first word in a sentence.

   (296) Ge giin na gwii-wiisin? I 'Do you too want to eat?' (AM39.35)
          Ge av 'also'; giin prpers 2s 'you'; na av 'yes/no ques.'; gwii-wiisin vai ind 2s 'you want
          to eat.'

    The combination ge+pronoun has a variety of meanings linking the action or state of
one participant to that of another, sometimes COORDINATELY, with a meaning something
like 'too, also,' and sometimes CONTRASTIVELY, with meanings roughly equivalent to
English 'as for..., on the other hand...' and similar notions. The following examples illus-
trate some of the uses of ge with personal pronouns.
    In a COORDINATE FUNCTION, a single occurrence of ge + pronoun:
                                                                       12.3.15 Personal Pronouns • 615


      (297) Mil dash ge nii gii-boozyaan. I 'So then /, too, got on board the train.' (AM8.9)
             Mii av 'and'; dash av 'so'; ge av 'also'; niiprpers Is T; gii-boozyaan vai conj Is
             '(CONJ) I got on board.'

      (298) Ge gtinwaa wii-saanwezyeg ngii-shkonaag.
            'I spared them so that you, too, might have some amusement.'" (AM31.46)

             Ge av 'also'; giinwaa pr pers 2p 'you'; wii-saanwezyeg vai conj 2p '(CONJ) you pi will
             amuse yourselves'; ngii-shkonaag vta ind ls»3pProx 'I spared ANpl.'

      Parallel coordinate expressions exist as well, such as the following:

      (299) Wedi ge gii gga-miijin, maanda dash ge nii nga-miijin waawan.
            'You may eat that (one), and / shall eat this egg.' (AM39.174)

             Wedi ni 0 'that over there'; ge av 'as for'; gii pr pers 2s 'you'; gga-miijin vti ind 2s»0s
             'you will eat INsg'; maanda prOs 'this'; dash av 'however'; ge av 'as for'; nil pr pers Is
             T; nga-miijin vti ind ls»0s 'I will eat INsg'; waawan ni Os 'egg.'

    In a disjunctive, or contrastive function, often two occurrences of ge + pronoun occur,
and it is common for the second member of the contrastive pair to be set off with the con-
trastive particle dash (or its partner wiiri) as well, according to the following form:

         (ge-)pronoun.. .(ge)-pronoun dash/wiin...

      The particle dash is often reduced to an enclitic -sh attached to the word which precedes
it.

      (300) Nen'shike-sh go wadi ge gii gdooshkniigiimag bkaan, ge nii-sh wadi
            ndooshkniigiimag bkaan.
            'Each group will be on its own, you and your men over there by yourselves, and
            me with my men over there by ourselves.' (SO6.100)

             Nen'shike av 'separately'; dash av 'then'; wadi av 'there'; ge av 'as for'; gii pr pers 2s
             'you'; gdooshkniigiimag na 2s(3pProx) 'your young men'; bkaan av 'different'; ge av
             'as for'; mi pr pers Is T; dash av 'then'; wadi av 'there'; ndooshkniigiimag na
             ls(3pProx) 'my young men'; bkaan av 'different.'
616 • 12.3.15 Personal Pronouns


   (301) Mil iw ezhitwaawaad gaye nii niniijaanisag. (b) Niin wiin gaa wii
         nindizhitwaasii.
         'My children, too, have that religion, (b) But / do not have it.' (AW20.24-25)

          Mil av 'it's'; i\v pr Os 'that'; ezhitwaawaad vai ic conj BpProx '(CCNJ) which AN pi
          practice religion'; gaye av 'as for'; miprpers Is T; niniijaanisag nad Is(SpProx) 'my
          children.' (b) Niinprpers Is T; wiin av 'however'; gaa av 'not'; wii av 'not';
          nindizhitwaasii vai ind neg Is 'I do not practice religion.'


    When the pronoun is third person, it is very common for a noun or demonstrative pro-
noun with the same reference to occur in the clause with the pronoun. The pronoun almost
invariably precedes the nominal it is associated with. In the following example, the nominal
(participial) expression niw waa-bi-taagwaajin, 'those (obv.) coming whom they (prox.)
will play against' is used in conjunction with the ge-personal pronoun construction, ge
wiinwaa, 'they.' Although the participle is clearly obviative, the pronoun cannot show obvi-
ation, but does show plurality, which is not available to animate obviatives, since number
(singular versus plural) is neutralized in such forms.

   (302) Gye go giw sa waa-bkwaakdwejig ge wiinwaa sa wii-bi-dgoshnoon niw
         waa-bi-taagwaajin.
         'And as for those (prox.) looking forward to playing baseball, they will also
         arrive, those (obv.) whom they (prox.) will play.' (AM 18.9)

          Gye av 'and'; giwpr 3pProx 'those'; waa-bkwaakdwejig vai ic conj part SpProx
          '(CCNJ) who ANpl will play baseball'; ge av 'also'; wiinwaaprpers 3p 'they';
          wii-bi-dgoshnoon vai ind 3obv 'ANobv will arrive here'; niw pr 3obv 'that/those';
          waa-bi-taagwaajin vta ic conj part 3pProx»3obv '(CCNJ) who ANpl will play against
          ANobv.'


   In the following example, the pronoun ge wiinawaa occurs with the nominal expression
giw shkinweg, 'those young people,' and the associated transitive inanimate verb,
wii-gkendmowaad, 'they will have knowledge of it,' is inflected for a third person plural
actor as well, creating triple reference in the clause. Personal pronouns thus clearly do not
merely substitute for nominals in these constructions. The emphatic particle sa is also com-
mon in such contexts, often following the demonstrative pronoun of the nominal phrase.

   (303) Mii maanda gaa-zhiwebak sa shkweyaang ge-giizhgak ge wiinwaa giw sa
         shkinweg wii-gkendmowaad gegoo gye go iw waa-mno-aabjitoowaad.
         This happened so that in the days to come they also, those young men, also
         might have some knowledge and something of which they could make good use.'
                                                                    12.3.15 Personal Pronouns • 617



          Mii av 'it's'; maandaprOs 'this'; gaa-zhiwebak vii conj 0 '(CCNJ) that (IN) happened';
          shkweyaang av 'following'; ge-giizhgak vii ic conj 0 '(CCNJ) will be day'; ge av 'also';
          wiinwaa pr pers 3p 'ANpl'; giwpr 3pProx 'those'; shkinweg na 3pProx 'young men';
          wii-gkendmowaad vti conj 3pProx»0 '(CONJ) ANpl will know IN'; gegoopr indefO
          'something'; gye av 'and'; iw pr Os 'that'; waa-mno-aabjitoowaad vti ic conj part
          3pProx»0 '(CCNJ) which (IN) ANpl will make good use of.' (AM23.9)

   Additional examples:

   (304) Mii go ge wiinwaa giizhiitaawaad giwi. I 'Those over there were finished also.'
          Mii av 'and'; ge av 'also'; wiinwaaprpers 3p 'ANpl'; giizhiitaawaad vai conj 3pProx
          '(CONJ) ANpl finish'; giwi pr 3pProx 'those.' (SO6.186)

   (305) Gii-gdimaagzi ge wiin aw kwe. I 'She was very poor as for her, the woman.'
          Gii-gdimaagzi vai ind3sProx 'ANsg was poor'; ge av 'also'; wiin prpers 3s 'she'; aw/?r
          3sProx 'that'; kwe na SsProx 'woman.' (AK3.15)

   GE Wll AS A FIXED EXPRESSION. For some speakers the combination ge wii appears to
be turning into a fixed expression that means 'also.' In such usage its form is invariant, and
may also account for the use of wii(n) with reference to inanimate third persons.

   (306) Naan'godnongge wii ndoo-bbaa-bmakzhiwemi.
         'Sometimes we also go paddling around.' (TN)

          Naan'godnong av 'sometimes'; gewii av 'also'; ndoo-bbaa-bmakzhiwemi vai ind Ip
          'we paddle around.'

   (307) Niwiitaawsensag ge wii ndoo-ni-nkawenaanaanig.
         'We pick up my little cousins also, along the way.' (TN)

          Niwiitaawsensag nad ls(3pProx) 'my cousins'; gewii av 'also';

12.4 Proximate and Obviative: Foregrounding and Backgrounding

    (DEVIATION is one of the most interesting discourse phenomena in Nishnaabemwin. Its
workings are relatively simple: within a given clause, only one third person animate referent
can be in the foreground at a time; all other third person referents are backgrounded by
making them obviative, which is marked by suffixes on animate nouns and by inflection on
verbs. The foregrounded referent is said to be PROXIMATE. A referent can only be back-
grounded (OBVIATED) in the presence of a foregrounded (proximate) referent, so a story, for
example, can't begin with an obviated referent representing a character that the storyteller
wishes to keep in the background. Only an animate third person can trigger obviation, inan-
imates cannot, though they themselves can be obviated by an animate. Obviation has been
called a system of disjoint reference, a way of grammatically distinguishing the animate
third person arguments of a predicate or a possessed noun phrase.
    Animate nouns all have obviative forms, which can readily be derived from their plurals
by changing the last consonant of the plural to /n/, e.g., the plural form of kik, 'kettle,' is
kikoog, and the obviative is kikoon. The following sentence shows a typical example of an
obviated animate noun.

   (331) Giw dash kwewag wgii-gnawenmaawaan niw binoojiinyan.
         The women took care of the children.' (AK2.3)

          Giwpr 3pProx 'those'; dash av 'and'; kwewag na 3pProx 'women';
          wgii-gnawenmaawaan vta ind 3pProx»3obv 'ANpl took care of ANobv'; niw pr 3obv
          'that/those'; binoojiinyan na 3obv 'child(ren).'


    The inflection of obviative forms is covered in detail in Chapter 4. Here, though, note
that the noun binoojiinyan, 'child/children,' carries an obviative suffix, and has an obviative
demonstrative pronoun associated with it, niw.
    Inanimate nouns are not inflected for obviation, but verbs associated with them can be
inflected to show obviation. The following examples illustrate this, from two tellings of the
same story by Andrew Medler. In both examples, the inanimate intransitive verb (VII)
maajaamgad, 'leave,' is inflected for obviation; in the first it is inflected with INDEPENDENT
624 • 12.4 Proximate and Obviative: Foregrounding and Backgrounding


ORDER inflection (spelled «ni»), and in the second, with inflection for the CONJUNCT order
(spelled «nig»).

   (332) Aapji dash gii-mno-bmaadzi, gye go kina gii-maajaamgadnioQ^ wdakjiwin.
         'He felt very well and all his cold had gone away.' (AM19.15)

          Aapji av 'really'; dash av 'then'; gii-mno-bmaadzi vai ind SsProx 'ANsg felt well'; gye
          av 'and'; kina av 'all'; gii-maajaamgadni vii ind Oobv 'INobv was gone'; wdakjiwin ni
          3sProx(Os) 'ANSG'S cold.'


   (333) Gegzhebaawgak gii-wnishkaa, gye go mii iw gii-mno-bmaadzid,
         gii-maajaamgadnigQw wdaakziwin.
         'When morning came he got up, and now he felt well and his illness had gone.'
         (AM20.12)

          Gegzhebaawgak vii ic conj 0 '(CCNJ) when IN was morning'; gii-wnishkaa vai ind
          SsProx 'ANsg got up'; gye av 'and'; mii av 'it's'; ivrpr Os 'that'; gii-mno-bmaadzid vai
          conj SsProx '(CONJ) ANsg felt well'; gii-maajaamgadnig vii conj Oobv '(CONJ) INobv
          left'; wdaakziwin ni 3sProx(Os) 'ANSG'S illness.'


   Unspecified actors do not obviate the subjects of third person passive verbs.

   (334) Gchi-gnawaabmaa wa Aanmaa Nishnaabemod.
         'People looked with some surprise at the German speaking Indian.' (FF04.25)

          Gchi-gnawaabmaa vta ind x»3sProx 'ANsg was looked at with surprise'; wa pr SsProx
          'that'; Aanmaa na 'German'; Nishnaabemod vai conj SsProx '(CONJ) ANsg speaks
          Ojibwe.'


    Obviation can be used to disambiguate the participants in subordinate clauses in relation
to those in a main clause. In the following sentence, for example, it is clear that it is the
ducks that are floating around, and not Nenabush (the actor), since the verb in the subordi-
nate clause is obviative, in agreement with the ducks in the main clause.

   (335) Wgii-waabmaan dash niw zhiishiibanOBV niibna bbaa-gomnidQ^y.
         'He (Nenabush) saw many ducks (obv.) as they (obv.) floated about.' (AM38.6)
                           12.4 Proximate and Obviative: Foregrounding and Backgrounding • 625



         Wgii-waabmaan vta ind3sProx»3obv 'ANsg saw ANobv'; dash av 'then'; niwprSobv
         'that/those'; zhiishiiban na 3obv 'duck(s)'; niibna av 'many'; bbaa-gomnid vai conj
         3obv '(CONJ) ANobv float about.' / bbaa-gomod vai conj 3sProx '(CONJ) ANsg floats
         about.'

   To change the reference in the subordinate clause to that of Nenabush, one need only
change the verb of the subordinate clause to proximate:

   (336) Wgii-waabmaan dash niw zhiishiiban niibna bbaa-gomod.
         'He (Nenabush) saw many ducks (obv.) as he (prox.) floated about.' (AM38.6
         (modified))

         Wgii-waabmaan vta ind 3sProx»3obv 'ANsg saw ANobv'; dash av 'then'; niw prSobv

         3obv '(CONJ) ANobv float about.' / bbaa-gomod vai conj 3sProx '(CONJ) ANsg floats
         about.'


    OBLIGATORY DEVIATION. Obviation is obligatory in two contexts. First, any third per-
son possessed by another third person must be obviative. For many speakers, only animate
nouns can be possessors. Animate nouns, of course, show their obviation status with an
obviative suffix, but as mentioned, inanimate nouns may indirectly show their obviative sta-
tus through verb inflection. In the following sentence, for example, an (animate) possessor
triggers obviative inflectional marking on an inanimate intransitive verb (VII) of which the
inanimate possessed noun is subject:

   (337) Pii dash go naawkweg gaawaanh beshaabiigmoni0QV iw
         wmakdewshkiinzhgwaan.
         'But when it is noon, his pupil (NB of eye) is only a very narrow line.' (AM27.4)

          Pii av 'when'; dash av 'then'; naawkweg vii conj 0 '(CONJ) it is noon'; gaawaanh av
          'barely'; beshaabiigmoni vii indOobv 'INobv be a narrow stringlike object'; i w p r O s
          'that'; wmakdewshkiinzhgwaan ni 3sProx(Os) 'ANSG'S pupil of eye.'


   The following example illustrates obviation of animate possessed nouns, both kinship
terms, /daan/, 'daughter,' and /gwis/, 'son.'
626 • 12.4 Proximate and Obviative: Foregrounding and Backgrounding


   (338) Mil dash gii-maajii-yaawaad binoojiinyan aw nookmis, gii-nsiwan raw
         wdaanwaan gii-bezhgowan dash wgwiswaan.

         'And then my grandmother started having children, their daughters were three
         and their son was one.' (AK11.22)

          Mii av 'and'; dash av 'then'; gii-maajii-yaawaad vta conj 3sProx»3obv '(CONJ) ANsg
          began to have ANobv'; binoojiinyan na 3obv 'child(ren)'; awpr SsProx 'that'; nookmis
          nad Is(SsProx) 'my grandmother'; gii-nsiwan vai ind 3obv 'ANobv were three in
          number'; niwpr 3obv 'that/those'; wdaanwaan na 3pProx(3obv) 'ANpl's daughter(s)';
          gii-bezhgowan vai ind 3obv 'ANobv was one in number'; dash av 'on the other hand';
          wgwiswaan na 3pProx(3obv) 'ANpl's son(s).'


    Richard Rhodes (1991:104) points out that possessor obviatives behave distinctly from
non-possessor obviatives in often showing proximate APPOSITIVES, as in (339), below, and in
triggering verb agreement only when they are the subjects of verbs, almost always intransi-
tive verbs in contemporary usage, as opposed to objects. Example (340) illustrates an object
(goal) possessed noun, wgwiiwzensmiwaan, 'their son(s),' which fails to trigger verb agree-
ment, and (341), the object, wmiignan, 'ANsg's feather(s),' which also functions as an object
(goal).

   (339) Mdimooyenh go naa gii-naanwan niwiOBV wgwisanOBV, shkinwensagPROX,
         shkinwegPROX.

         'There was an old woman with five sons, boys and teenagers.' (SO)

          Mdimooyenh na 3sProx 'old woman'; go naa pc 'emphatic'; gii-naanwan vai ind 3obv
          'ANobv were five in number'; niwipr 3obv 'that/those'; wgwisan na 3sProx(3obv)
          'ANsg's son(s)'; shkinwensag na SpProx 'boys'; shkinweg na SpProx 'young men.'


   (340) NwaabmaaPROX SG GOAL wgwiiwzensimiwaanOBV. I 'I see their son.' (AM39.288)

         Nwaabmaa vta ind ls»3sProx "I see ANsg'; wgwiiwzensmiwaan nad 3pProx(3obv)
         'ANpl's son(s).'


   (341) Ngii-bshkobnaagPROX pL GOAL wmiignanOBV aw zhiishiibenh.

         'I plucked that duck's feathers.'(AM39.288)

         Ngii-bshkobnaag vta ind ls»3pProx "I plucked ANpl'; wmiignan nad 3sProx(3obv)
         'ANsg'sfeather(s)'; aw pr 3sProx 'that'; zhiishiibenh na 3sProx 'duck.'
                           12.4 Proximate and Obviative: Foregrounding and Backgrounding • 627


     The other context in which obviation is obligatory is that of the third person participants
filling the semantic roles associated with a single verb: only one can be the proximate, and
the rest must be obviative. This restriction is most obviously seen at work in transitive ani-
mate verbs (VTA), which by definition have at least two semantic roles, both an animate
actor and goal, and when both roles are filled by third persons, one of them must be obvia-
tive. The following example illustrates.

   (342) Bezhig dash aw nishnaabe wgii-nsidtawaan z/raagnoas/wzn.
         'And this one Indian understood white people.' (AK2.10)

          Bezhig nm 'a certain'; dash av 'then'; awpr SsProx 'that'; nishnaabe na 3sProx
          'Indian'; wgii-nsidtawaan vta ind3sProx»3obv 'ANsg understood ANobv';
          zhaagnaashan na 3obv 'white(s).'

    The verb nsidtawaad, 'understand AN,' has two semantic roles associated with it, an
actor, the one(s) who understand(s), and a goal, the one(s) who is/are understood. Here,
there are two noun phrases associated with the verb wgii-nsidtawaan, an actor, bezhig aw
nishnaabe, 'one of the Indians,' which is proximate, and zhaagnaashan, 'white person/peo-
ple,' which is obviative, clearly marked as such by the obviative suffix /-an/.
    The same rule applies for ditransitive verbs, that is, those that have two objects, such as
miinaad, 'give something to AN.' Only one nominal associated with the verb can be proxi-
mate, and the others must be obviative. When there is a third person giver (ACTOR) or
receiver (GOAL), mention of the object transferred (THEME) requires that it be obviative. The
following example illustrates.

   (343) Semaan gii-miinaawag giw kiwenziinyag gaa-bi-zhaajig.
         'The old men who had come were given tobacco.' (AK10.6)

          Semaan na 3obv 'tobacco'; gii-miinaawag vta indx»3pProx 'ANpl were given Y'; giw
          pr 3pProx 'those'; kiwenziinyag na SpProx 'old men'; gaa-bi-zhaajig vai ic conjpart
          3pProx 'who (ANpl) came.'

   Here the old men, giw kiwenziinyag, is a proximate nominal; the object transferred,
semaan, 'tobacco' NA, is marked as obviative.
   Rhodes (1991:103) points out that subjects (actors) control obviation of objects (goals)
and that objects control obviation in obliques (non-goal objects), i.e., that the control of
obviation follows the conventional hierarchy of grammatical relations.
   It is important to realize that it is not the presence of overt nominals in association with a
verb that trigger the requirements of obviation. The role-fillers associated with a verb need
not have overt expression in order to trigger obviation. Consider the following:
628 • 12.4 Proximate and Obviative: Foregrounding and Backgrounding


   (344) Mil dash gii-bkonaad niw waawaashkeshwan. \ 'Then he skinned that deer.'
          Mii av 'and'; dash av 'then'; gii-bkonaad vta conj3sProx»3obv '(CONJ) ANsg skinned
          ANobv'; niwpr 3obv 'that/those'; waawaashkeshwan na 3obv 'deer.' (AM35.30)

    The verb bkonaad, 'skin AN,' is transitive animate (VTA), and thus has two semantic
roles associated with it, a skinner, filling the role of actor, and whatever is skinned, filling
the role of goal. If both roles are filled by a third person, one of them must be obviative, and
indeed, in this case, there is an obviative nominal, niw waawaashkeshwan, 'that/those deer
(obv.).' There is only one explicit nominal, niw waawaashkeshwan. and the actor is
expressed only by inflections on the verb, namely the suffix complex /-aad/, which indicates
that a third-person proximate actor is acting on a third-person animate obviative goal. Obvi-
ation is checked in the role structure of the verb itself, in the inflection, and the explicit
nominals are then marked in accordance with the inflection. Consider also the following
sentence.

   (345) Mii dash maaba nishnaabe gii-giisaadenmaad [mii dash gii-biidmawaad niw
         waabgan-pwaagnan miinwaa semaan].
          'And this Indian felt sorry for her and he brought her a clay pipe and also
         tobacco.'

          Mii av 'and'; dash av 'then'; maabapr 3sProx 'this'; nishnaabe na 3sProx 'Indian';
          gii-giisaadenmaad vta conj 3sProx»3obv '(CONJ) ANsg felt sad for ANobv'; mii av
          'and'; dash av 'then'; gii-biidmawaad vta conj 3sProx»3obv '(CONJ) ANsg broughtY
          for ANobv'; nivtprSobv 'that/those'; waabgan-pwaagnan na 3obv 'clay pipe(s)';
          miinwaa av 'and'; semaan na 3obv 'tobacco.' (AK12.4)

    This sentence has two transitive verbs, gii-giisaadenmaad, 'feel sorry for AN,' and
gii-biidmawaad, 'bring something to AN.' For our purposes, we are interested in the latter,
which has two object roles associated with it, one, representing the object(s) brought, and a
second, representing the one(s) to whom the object is brought. In addition there is an actor
role, that of the bringer. We can summarize these roles as follows, using a chart that lists the
SEMANTIC ROLES associated with the verb:

              biidmawaad         Actor        Goal                   Theme
                                 bringer      one(s) brought to      thing(s) brought

   Now if we examine (345), above, we see that it is only the theme that is expressed with
an overt nominal, namely, niw waabgan-pwaagnan miinwaa semaan, 'that clay pipe and
tobacco.' But both nouns, waabgan-pwaagan and semaa are marked with obviative suffixes,
and the inflectional marking on the verb clearly shows that there are other third persons fill-
                           12.4 Proximate and Obviative: Foregrounding and Backgrounding • 629


ing this verb's semantic roles. The actor is filled by a third person animate singular proxi-
mate, and the goal is filled by a third person animate obviative. This is all communicated by
means of the suffix /-aad/, and if it is understood from context who is being talked about,
there is no need for overt nominals in such sentences. So, to summarize, using a semantic
role chart:

     biidmawaad     Actor                Goal                    Theme
                    animate third per- animate third person      niw waabgan-pwaagnan
                    son singular proxi- obviative                miinwaa semaan (obvia-
                    mate                                         tive)
                                      /-aad/

    So the nouns in niw waabgan-pwaagan miinwaa semaan, 'that clay pipe and tobacco,'
must be marked as obviative because they are animate nouns filling a theme (thing trans-
ferred) semantic role of a verb that has another role, in this case an actor role, filled by a
proximate. This fact is signalled solely by the inflection on the verb, /-aad/.
    OPTIONAL DEVIATION. The subject of a matrix clause can optionally obviate the subject
of an adjunct (clause of time, location, manner, etc.) or complement subordinate clause. For
example, in example (335), above (p. 624), the subordinate verb, bbaa-gomnid, 'as ANobv
floated about,' is obviative, made so by the subject of the main verb, wgii-waabmaan,
'ANsg saw ANobv.' Richard Rhodes (1991:107) suggests that the application of obviation
in these seemingly optional contexts is guided by the relative discourse-level topicality of
both the trigger and target of obviation, in that more topical elements tend to induce more
obviation and be more resistant to obviation, while less topical elements have the opposite
behaviour. Rhodes also observes the following contrasts:

   (346) Ngii-mbwaachhig gaa-bi-gsinaa(*ni)g. I 'He visited me when it got cold.' (RV)
          Ngii-mbwaachhig vta ind3sProx»ls 'ANsg visited me'; gaa-bi-gsinaa(*ni)g vii ic conj
          0 'when IN(obv) came to be cold.'

   (347) Miish gii-mbwaachhid gaa-bi-gsinaa(ni)g. I 'He visited me when it got cold.' (RV)
          Miish av 'and so'; gii-mbwaachhid vta conj 3sProx»ls 'ANsg visited me';
          gaa-bi-gsinaa(*ni)g vii ic conj 0 'when IN(obv) came to be cold.'

   In the first sentence optional obviation of the verb in the temporal adjunct clause,
gaa-bi-gsinaag, 'when IN got cold,' signalled by the suffix /-ini/, is not allowed, while in
the second it is. The main verb in (346), ngii-mbwaachhig, has an inverse form, signalled by
the inverse theme sign, /-igw/. The conjunct equivalent in sentence (347), gii-mbwaachhid,
does not have an inverse, but a first person object theme sign, /-i/, followed by a third person
subject suffix /-d/. These two sentences also illustrate how the inverse patterns somewhat
630 • 12.4 Proximate and Obviative: Foregrounding and Backgrounding


differently in the independent and conjunct orders. Rhodes argues that inverse forms actu-
ally reverse grammatical relations, so the third person argument in (346), even though it is
an agent, is not a subject, and thus cannot control obviation in the adjunct clause. However,
for some speakers, optional obviation can occur with either independent or conjunct in these
cases, as in the following:

   (348) Ngii-baabiitookdamaag gaa-mnadenig. I 'S/he sliced it for me once itOBV was done.'
          Ngii-baabiitookdamaag vta conj 3sProx»ls 'ANsg sliced Y for me'; gaa-mnadenig vii

   (349) Mii-sh gii-baabiitookdamwid gaa-mnadenig.

    OBVIATION AND FIRST AND SECOND PERSONS. Obviation only occurs in the context of
two third persons. If the actor or goal of a simple transitive verb is first or second person,
and there is a single unpossessed third person filling the other role, then that third person
need not be obviative, though it can be if it happens to be obviative due to its being pos-
sessed by a third person possessor, or if it represents a perpetuation of obviation assigned in
the preceding discourse.
    The same is true of possessed nouns— if the possessor is first or second person, singular
or plural, the noun referring to the person or thing possessed is not required to be obviative.
There are thus possessed forms such as noos, 'my father' (proximate), but oosan, 'her/his
father,' (obviative); ngwis, 'my son' (proximate) but wgwisan, 'her/his son' (obviative).
Nouns possessed by first and second persons can be obviative, just like any other noun, in
the proper context in which a different third person is proximate, as in the following sen-
tence:

   (350) Wgii-gnoonaan raw ndoodooman aw kwe, . . . .
         'That woman talked to my mother....' (AK3.14a)

          Wgii-gnoonaan vta ind 3sProx»3obv 'ANsg spoke to ANobv'; niw pr 3obv 'that/those';
          ndoodooman na ls(3obv) 'my mother'; aw pr 3sProx 'that'; kwe na 3sProx 'woman.'

   Here there are two third person nominals, aw kwe, 'that woman,' which is proximate,
and niw ndoodooman, 'that mother of mine,' which is obviative— this can be seen by virtue
of the obviative suffix it carries, /-an/. But the expression ndoodooman is not obviative
because it is possessed, but because it is in a grammatical context where another third per-
                            12.4 Proximate and Obviative: Foregrounding and Backgrounding • 631



son, aw kwe, has been given proximate status, and so must be obviative.
    DETERMINING WHICH CHARACTERS ARE PROXIMATE AND WHICH ARE OBVIATIVE.
With regard to possessive constructions with third person possessors, there is no choice as
to which of the possessor or possessum is obviative—it is obligatorily the possessum. So, in
expressions such as maaba nini wgwisan, 'this man's son(s),' the term for son, /gwis/ must
be marked as obviative, because it is "possessed" by a grammatical third person the man,
maaba nini.
    In transitive verbs, however, there is more freedom as to what is proximate and what is
obviative. In the most typical case, it is the actor that is proximate, and the goal that is obvi-
ative, as in the following:

   (351) Giw dash kwewag wgii-gnawenmaawaan niw binoojiinyan.

         "Th(os)e women took care of the children.' (AK2.3)

          Givrpr SpProx 'those'; dash av 'then'; kwewag na SpProx 'women';
          wgii-gnawenmaawaan vta ind 3pProx»3obv 'ANpl took care of ANobv'; niw pr 3obv
          'that/those'; binoojiinyan na 3obv 'child(ren).'


   Here, giw kwewag, 'those women,' fills the actor role, and niw binoojiinyan, 'that/those
child/ren,' fills the role of goal. However, it is possible to reverse the obviation roles by
making the following changes:

   (352) Niw dash kwewan wgii-gnawenmigwaan giw binoojiinyag.

          'The woman/women (obv.) took care of the children (prox.).' (AK2.3)

          Niw pr 3obv 'that/those'; dash av 'then'; kwewan na 3obv ' woman/women';
          wgii-gnawenmigwaan vta ind 3obv»3pProx 'ANobv took care of ANpl'; giw pr SpProx
          'those'; binoojiinyag na SpProx 'children.'


   To bring about this reversal of obviation, three sets of changes had to be made:

• the suffixes on the nouns are changed, changing binoojiinyan (obviative) to binoojiinyag
  (proximate, plural), and kwewag (proximate, plural) to kwewan (obviative).
• the demonstrative pronouns are changed to match the obviation status of their associated
  nominals, changing niw (obviative) to giw (proximate plural) and vice versa.
• the verbal inflection is changed from gnawenmaawaan to gnawenmigwaan.

   The last change, the change in the verb's inflection, deserves further comment. Analyz-
ing the verbal suffix complexes of the two verb forms into their component parts, we find
the following elements:
632 • 12.4 Proximate and Obviative: Foregrounding and Backgrounding


                                      Suffixes
                    Stem              Theme Suffix         Plural Suffix        Obviative Suffix
                    gnawenim          -aa                  -waa                 -an
                                      -ig                  -waa                 -an

    By breaking down the inflectional suffix complex, it is clear that just the theme suffix has
changed: when the actor is proximate, the theme suffix is /-aa/, and when the goal is proxi-
mate, the theme suffix is /-ig/. The traditional terms for these theme suffixes are direct for
/-aa/ and inverse for /-igw/.1 We can now summarize, as follows:

                      Obviation and Theme Suffixes for Third Persons in TA Verbs
               If the ACTOR is PROXIMATE...
                   then the GOAL must then OBVIATIVE...
                   and the THEME SUFFIX is DIRECT, /-aa/
               If the GOAL is PROXIMATE...
                   then the ACTOR must then be OBVIATIVE...
                   and the THEME SUFFIX is INVERSE, /-igw/

   So a speaker always has a choice as to which of the actor or goal is made proximate, but
there is a grammatical requirement that whichever of them isn't is then made obviative, and
the verb bears a theme suffix that indicates whether it is the actor or the goal that is proxi-
mate.
   THE POSSESSOR CONSTRAINT (RHODES 1992). Rhodes 1992 examines restrictions on
possessor relations within a single clause. Consider, for example, the following sentence:

    (353) John wgii-waabmaan wgwisan. I 'John saw his son.' (RV)

             wgii-waabmaan vta ind 3sProx»3obv 'ANsg saw ANobv'; wgwisan na 3sProx(3obv)
             'ANSG'S son(s).'

   In this sentence John is both the actor (subject) of the transitive verb wgii-waabmaan,
and the possessor of the goal (object), wgwisan, 'his son.' It is also possible to use an
inverse theme suffix and give the son the actor (subject) role.

    (354) John wgii-waabmigoon wgwisan. I 'Johna's son (obv.) saw hima.' (RV)

             wgii-waabmigoon vta ind 3obv»3sProx 'ANobv saw ANsg'; wgwisan na 3sProx(3obv)
             'ANSG'S son(s).'


1. The suffix actually has the form /-igw/, with a final /w/ that is often deleted or fuses with a following /i/ to pro-
duce /o/.
                           12.4 Proximate and Obviative: Foregrounding and Backgrounding • 633



   However, we cannot make John's son the subject and John the object, and use a direct
theme suffix:

   (355) *Wgwisan wgii-waabmaan Johnan. I 'Hisa son saw Johna.' (RV)
          *Wgwisan na 3sProx(3obv) 'ANSG'S son(s)'; wgii-waabmaan vta ind 3sProx»3obv
          'ANsg saw ANobv'; Johnan na 3obv 'John (obv).'

  Because the son, the subject, is possessed by the object, John, the sentence is ungram-
matical. The following sentence is also disallowed, when the father is John.

   (356) *John wgwisan wgii-waabmaan oosan. I 'Johna's sonb saw hisb fathera.' (RV)
          *John na 3sProx 'John'; wgwisan na 3sProx(3obv) 'ANSG'S son(s)'; wgii-waabmaan
          vta ind 3sProx»3obv 'ANsg saw ANobv'; oosan nad 3sProx(3obv)'ANsg's father.'

   Here the problem is once again that the subject is possessed by the object. Now consider
the following two sentences.

   (357) John wgii-waabmaan noosan. I 'John (prox.) saw ray father (obv.)'
          John na 3sProx 'John'; wgii-waabmaan vta ind3sProx»3obv 'ANsg saw ANobv';
          noosan nad ls(3obv) 'my father.'

   (358) John wgii-waabmigoon noosan. I 'My father (obv.) saw John (prox.).'
          John na 3sProx 'John'; wgii-waabmigoon vta ind 3obv»3sProx 'ANobv saw ANsg';
          noosan nad ls(3obv) 'my father.'

   Here, even though the goal, noosan, 'my father (obv.),' is possessed and obviative, both
sentences are grammatical, because noosan is not possessed by John. Richard Rhodes
(1993:4) has formulated the restrictions on possessor relations within a clause in his Pos-
sessor (Clausemate) Constraint, which he states as follows:

         No clause (in Ottawa) is grammatical which contains a nominal, n^ pos-
         sessed by a third person, p, and a nominal coreferential with p, n2, unless
         the grammatical relation borne by n2 outranks that borne by HI on th rela-
         tional hierarchy in final relations.

    While this constraint is cast in the theoretical trappings of relational grammar, Rhodes
clarifies by stating that "in the simplest cases this means that if the subject is possessed by
the object, the clause is ungrammatical ... or if the primary object is possessed by the sec-
ondary object, then the clause is ungrammatical" (p. 4). Discussion of grammatical relations
can be found in Chapter 18.6, beginning on page 957.

    DEVIATION AND VAIO VERBS. In transitive animate (VTA) verbs with third persons fill-
ing both the actor and goal roles, which of the actor or goal is filled by a proximate can be
determined by inspecting the inflectional theme suffix and the obviation status of any asso-
ciated nominals. The following example illustrates this:

   (359) Wgii-ggwejmaan dash niw ngitziiman maaba Gchi-mookmaan.
           Then this American asked my parents.' (AM8.4)

            Wgii-ggwejmaan vta 3sProx»3obv 'ANsg asked ANobv'; dash av 'then'; m\vpr 3obv
            'that/those'; ngitziiman nod ls(3obv) 'my parents'; maaba pr SsProx 'this';
            Gchi-mookmaan no. SsProx 'white American.'

    The verb form wgii-ggwejmaan, has a direct theme suffix, /-aa/, indicating that the actor
is proximate and the goal is obviative. The nominal maaba Gchi-mookmaan, 'this Ameri-
can,' is proximate, and niw ngitziiman, 'that/those parent(s) of mine,' is marked as obvia-
tive. So it is the American who is the actor and the parents who are the goal. The transitive
animate theme suffix is thus very important in these determinations. Now consider the fol-
lowing sentence, which does not have a transitive animate verb:

   (360) Gii-bootaagewag giw kwewag niw mdaamnan iw wii-bkwezhgankewaad.
           'The women ground up the corn when they were going to make bread.' (AK2.4)

            Gii-bootaagewag vai indSpProx 'ANpl ground (Y)'; gi\vpr SpProx 'those'; kwewag na
            SpProx 'women'; riivrprSobv 'that/those'; mdaamnan na 3obv 'corn'; iwprOs 'that';
            wii-bkwezhgankewaad vai conj SpProx '(CONJ) ANpl will make bread.'

    Here the verb is bootaage, 'grind (something) up,' which is an animate intransitive verb
that takes an optional object (VAIO).1 There are two nominals associated with this verb, giw
kwewag, 'those women,' which is animate and proximate (we know from the plural suffix
on the noun and the form of the demonstrative pronoun, giw), and niw mdaamnan, 'that
corn,' which is proximate and obviative (we know from the obviative suffix and the form of
the demonstrative pronoun, niw). Here, however, the verb lacks a theme suffix, and a ques-
tion arises as to how we can know which of these nominals is the actor and which is the
goal. The answer is rather obvious: we know from the circumstances of life, that women
customarily grind up corn, but corn does not grind up women. This is a pragmatic determi-
nation, that is, one based on our knowledge of the state of the world. But the fact that the
actors and goals of VAIO verbs cannot be determined by strictly grammatical means, such as
with a theme suffix, has imposed interesting restrictions on what kinds of things can play a
goal role in these verbs. For one, the goal-like role cannot be filled by a first or second per-

1. The dialect represented here does not show inflection of VAIO'S for goals in the independent order.
                            12.4 Proximate and Obviative: Foregrounding and Backgrounding • 635



son, singular or plural. One reason for this is that first and second persons, the participants
in conversation, are usually human, and since humans tend to be both agents, active doers in
the world, and goals, the recipients of the actions of others, there is much more ambiguity
about their status in a given verbal event than say that of corn, which is rarely if ever an
active doer, but in transitive contexts almost always functions as the object of actions carried
out by others. So disallowing first and second persons as the goals in VAIO verbs helps to
limit potential ambiguity. Most such verbs indeed do have non-living things as their goals,
which allows one to easily determine actor and goal relationships on the basis of PRAGMAT-
ICS.
    PROXIMATE AND OBVIATIVE MARKING. Three very important parts of speech are com-
monly marked to show proximate and obviative status. These are animate nouns, animate
demonstrative pronouns, and all classes of verbs. The following sentence illustrates how
important such marking is. All bolded words show obviative inflectional marking.

   (361) Gii-nbowan wgitziiman maaba gwiiwzens, ntam gii-nbowan oosan mii dash
         giiwenh egod niw wdoodooman, gchi-aakziwan giiwenh, "Maawndoopdoon niw
         gdayhiiman maajaan odi ji-wi-wiij-yaawad aw gookmis."

         there with your grandmother.'" (AK14.1)

          Gii-nbowan vai ind3obv 'ANobv died'; wgitziiman na 3sProx(3obv) 'ANsg's parents';
          maabapr 3sProx 'this'; gwiiwzens na SsProx 'boy'; ntam av 'first'; gii-nbowan vai ind
          3obv 'ANobv died'; oosan nod3sPmx(3obv) 'ANsg's father'; mii av 'and'; dash av
          'then'; giiwenh av 'reportedly'; egod vta ic conj 3sProx»ls '(CCNJ) ANobv said to

    The storyteller has elected to give proximal status to a nominal referring to a boy, which
is indicated by the form, maaba gwiiwzens, 'this boy.' The nominal wgitziiman, 'his par-
ent(s)' carries an obviative suffix, and the animate intransitive verb (vai) of which it is a sub-

«wan». In the next clause, the expression gii-nbowan oosan, 'his father died,' once again

obviative. Next is niw odoodooman, gchi-aakziwan, 'that mother (obv.) of his, she (obv.) is

third person obviative (actor) acting on an animate third person singular proximate (goal).
So, since we know that maaba gwiiwzens, 'this boy,' is the proximate third person, and
wdoodooman, 'his mother,' is obviative, we can readily determine from the inflection on the
verb spelled «god» that it is the mother speaking to the boy. And because of all of this rich
inflectional action going on, clearly determining actors, goals, and the subjects of intransi-
tive verbs, the order of words in the sentence is relatively free, much freer than in English,
which lacks the inflectional resources of Nishnaabemwin.
    Inanimate intransitive verbs (VII) are also sometimes marked for obviation. Such obvia-
tion can apply to both possessed and unpossessed inanimates, the latter of which must
acquire obviative status by serving as goals of transitive (VTI) verbs. However, even imper-
sonal verbs can be obviated if they are subordinated to a verb containing an animate third
person actor or goal. The following example illustrates such obviation of impersonal verbs,
in its having an obviative (conjunct order inflection) form of the verb dbikad, 'be dark, be
night.'

   (362) Mii dash gii-bi-giiwewaad debkadnig dash gii-dgoshnoog.
         'And they came home and arrived just at dark (obv.)' (AK7.14)

          Mii av 'and'; dash av 'then'; gii-bi-giiwewaad vai conjSpProx '(CONJ) ANpl came
          back home'; debkadnig vii ic conj Oobv '(CCNJ) when INobv was dark'; dash av 'then';
          gii-dgoshnoog vai ind SpProx 'ANpl arrived.'


     The impersonal verb is marked obviative because it is being used in the context of a
proximate third person, the animate plural subject of gii-bi-giiwewaad, 'ANpl came back
home,' and gii-dgoshnoog, 'ANpl arrived.' Explicit marking of obviation on inanimate
verbs such as this tends to be optional. Once a participant has been obviated, its obvious sta-
tus can persist in following sentences, even in those verbs of which it is the sole argument,
i.e., in intransitive (vn) verbs. An interesting example is found in the sequence of sentences

   Mr. Medler tells this story twice. In the other version, the verb te, 'be in a place' (VII)
shows an independent order obviative just as in sentences 6 and 8 above. The same partici-
ple as in sentence 11 also occurs, though in the second version it is not obviated. Still, the
consistency of usage with verbs such as te suggests that there are grammatical and discourse
principles at work that must await a more adequate accounting.
   DISCOURSE USES OF DEVIATION. In many dialects of Anishinaabemowin, obviation is
used as a powerful foregrounding and backgrounding device, allowing storytellers to align
their perspective and empathy with particular characters in a narrative. As a small taste of
638 • 12.4 Proximate and Obviative: Foregrounding and Backgrounding


how this is done, we will briefly examine a story told by Andrew Medler, about a young
man who fasts and receives the blessing of a mirror being. Later, when the young man's
community is attacked, the assistance of the mirror manitou enables him to vanquish the
enemy. The story is told from the perspective of the young man, and when the enemy
comes, they are represented with obviative forms. The following sentence is used to
announce the arrival of the enemy:

   (364) Mii dash gaa-aazhoo-ggizhebaawgak maaba nini gii-noondwaad aazhi go
         bi-yaanid niw waa-nsigjin.
         'When the next morning came, this man heard them come who were coming to
         kill him.'(AM31.27)

          Mii av 'and'; dash av 'then'; gaa-aazhoo-ggizhebaawgak vii ic conj 0 '(CCNJ) when the
          next morning came'; maabapr SsProx 'this'; nini na 3sProx 'man'; gii-noondwaad vta
          conj 3sProx»3obv '(CONJ) ANsg heard ANobv'; aazhi av 'now'; bi-yaanid vai conj
          3obv '(CONJ) ANobv (was) coming'; niwpr 3obv 'that/those'; waa-nsigjin vta ic conj
          part 3obv»3sProx '(CCNJ) who (ANobv) wanted to kill ANsg.'


    First, note that the young man is identified with the proximate nominal phrase, maaba
nini, 'this man,' which is the actor of a transitive verb gii-noondwaad. This verb carries the
inflectional suffix complex /-aad/, which indicates an animate singular proximate actor act-
ing upon an animate obviative goal (in a subordinate clause, since the inflection is conjunct
order). The next verb is bi-ayaanid, a VAI, which has inflection /-nid/ indicating an animate
obviative subject, and then there is the nominal expression niw waa-nsigjin, which consists
of an animate obviative demonstrative pronoun, niw, and a transitive animate participle,
nsigjin. This participle has an inverse theme suffix, here spelled «ig», indicating that it has
an obviative actor and a proximate goal. The proximate goal is the man, and the obviative
actor are his attackers. The point here is that Mr. Medler continues to keep the man proxi-
mate even as he puts the attackers into a very active role, coming to kill him; There is no
grammatical requirement that he do this, rather it represents a storytelling strategy of per-
spective and empathy, in which his allegiance and sympathies are aligned with the man. He
keeps the man in the foreground, when several sentences later, the attackers arrive:

   (365) Mii dash aazhi go gii-bi-dgoshninid niw waa-miigaan'gojin.
         'Now they (obv) arrived who were going to fight him (prox).' (AM31.29)

          Mii av 'and'; dash av 'then'; aazhi av 'now'; gii-bi-dgoshninid vai conj 3obv '(CONJ)
          ANobv arrived here'; niwpr 3obv 'that/those'; waa-miigaan'gojin vta ic conj part
          3obv»3sProx '(CCNJ) who ANobv will fight ANsg.'
                           12.4 Proximate and Obviative: Foregrounding and Backgrounding • 639



    Here, the first verb, gii-bi-dgoshninid, is an animate intransitive (VAI), referring to the
arrival of the enemy, and it is inflected for an obviative subject. There are no obviation
requirements on this verb, however, so Mr. Medler has the grammatical liberty to shift the
enemy to proximate if he wishes, but instead he elects to keep them obviative, that is, to
background them, even though they are rather obviously the active aggressors at this point
in the story. The subject of this verb is the nominal niw waa-miigaan'gojin, 'those (obv.)
who (obv.) intended to fight him (prox.),' clearly casting the enemy in the obviative while at
the same time making them the actors, by using an inverse verb form. This is classic dis-
course-based use of obviation.
    OBVIATION IN SUBORDINATE CLAUSES. Proximates in main clauses sometimes obviate
the subjects of subordinate clauses. This is true of both complement and adjunct clauses. In
the following sentence, for example, an inanimate intransitive (vn) verb in a complement
clause is obviated by a third person plural actor in the main verb, wgii-gkendaanaawaa,
'they (anim. prox.) knew it.'

   (366) Aapji dash aanind Nishnaabeg gii-gtaamgozwag, gye go wgii-gkendaanaawaa
         gegoo, gye go wgii-gkendaanaawaaMMN sa [waa-bi-dgoshnoomgadnig
         niigaan]sm.
         'Some Indians were very formidable and they knew things, and they knew [what
         (obv) was to arrive in the future].' (AM23.23)

          Aapji av 'really'; dash av 'then'; aanind av 'some'; Nishnaabeg na SpProx 'Indians';
          gii-gtaamgozwag vai indSpProx 'ANpl were formidable'; gye av 'and';
          wgii-gkendaanaawaa vti ind 3pProx»Os 'ANpl knew INsg'; gegoo pr indefO
          'something'; gye av 'and'; wgii-gkendaanaawaa vti ind 3pProx»Os 'ANpl knew INsg';
          waa-bi-dgoshnoomgadnig vii ic conjpart Oobv '(CCNJ) that INobv which would arrive';
          niigaan av 'in the future.'


    In the following example, two VII impersonal verbs in subordinate clauses are obviated

   PROXIMATE SHIFTS. Contemporary speakers sometimes show rapid shifts in the proxi-
mate and obviative status of verbal participants, freely changing status across clauses. Con-
sider, for example, the following sentence:
642 • 12.4 Proximate and Obviative: Foregrounding and Backgrounding


   (373) Mii-sh giiwenh gii-dbaajmowaad [gaa-zhichged wamdimooyenh].

         Then they reported what the old lady did.' (SO2.33)

          Mii-sh av 'and then'; giiwenh av 'reportedly'; gii-dbaajmowaad vai conjSpProx
          '(CONJ) ANpl told the news'; gaa-zhichged vai ic conj SsProx '(CCNJ) what ANsg did';
          wapr SsProx 'this'; mdimooyenh na SsProx 'old woman.'


    Here, the subject of the verb of speaking, gii-dbaajmowaad are an old woman's sons,
and the verb is proximate. In the associated subordinate clause, the subject shifts to the old
woman, who is also proximate. So obviation shifts within this sentence.
    In the following sentence, a mermaid is introduced (as a woman), and is obviative in the
first clause (niw kwewan... zhngishninid), obviative in the second clause (by virtue of verb
gaa-zhi-baaphigwaad, 'ANobv smiled at ANpl (always proximate),' but shifting to proxi-
mate in the third clause (by virtue of verb gii-ni-zhooshkboozod, 'ANsg (always prox.) slid
off'), without explanation.

   (374) Mii dash iw gaa-zhi-waabmaawaad niw kwewan maa ddibew zhngishninid, mii
         dash iw gaa-zhi-baaphigwaad, mii ge go gii-ni-zhooshkboozod maa nbiing.
         'And when they saw this woman lying there on the shore, she smiled at them and
         she slid there into the water.' (AK4.4)

          Mii av 'and'; dash av 'then'; iwpr Os 'that'; gaa-zhi-waabmaawaad vta ic conj
          3pProx»3obv '(CCNJ) when ANpl thus saw ANobv'; niwpr 3obv 'that/those'; kwewan
          na 3obv 'woman/women'; maa av 'there'; ddibew av 'on the shore'; zhngishninid vai
          conj 3obv '(CONJ) ANobv lie'; mii av 'so'; dash av 'then'; iw pr Os 'that';
          gaa-zhi-baaphigwaad vta ic conj3obv»3pProx '(CCNJ) ANobv smiled at ANpl'; mii av
          'and'; ge av 'also'; gii-ni-zhooshkboozod vai conj 3sProx '(CONJ) ANsg slid off away';
          maa av 'there'; nbiing ni 0 he 'into the water.'

   In the following sentence, the focal character (a young woman) starts out obviative in a
when-clause (and there is no proximate), flips to proximate in the next clause when another
person tells her something, and then there is a flip to a proximate animate noun in the indi-
rect discourse, giw mskomnag, 'those raspberries,' though here there is no obviative. So
every verb shows different obviation status.

12.5 Examining a Short Narrative

    As a summary, we will examine a short narrative text in order to illustrate and discuss
Nishnaabemwin referring expressions. The text, which appears on the following page, was
told by Andrew Medler, and is about a man who catches a cold while traveling, and is then
cured by undergoing treatment in a sweat lodge.1 The following characters and props
appear in this story:

                              mm                      na     man
                              Nishnaabeg              na    'Indians'
                              mshkikwaaboo            ni    'medicine'
                              mdoodoo-siniin          ni    'sweat rocks'
                              gwiwnan                 ni    'cloths'
                              dkajwin                 ni    'cold' (illness)

    The story opens with the identification of a man by means of the expression bezhig nini,
'a certain man,' employing the discourse-specialized use of the numeral term bezhig, 'one.'
This is the only nominal reference to this character in the whole story— throughout the
remainder, in fourteen references, reference is solely by means of verbal inflections. In the
third sentence, some Indians who doctor the man are introduced, by means of the expres-
sion giw Nishnaabeg, 'those Indians,' in a common pattern of using a distal demonstrative
modifier, giw, 'those,' when introducing plural characters. As with the man, this is the only

    Two inanimate, instrument props also occur in the story. The first is medicine made by
the Indians to assist in the man's cure, introduced with the expression iw mshkikwaaboo
waa-aabjitoowaad, 'that medicine which they were planning to use,' in sentence 4, having
the structure demonstrative pronoun + noun + relative clause, the standard form for this con-
struction. Unlike the man and the Indians, though, all clauses making reference to the medi-
cine contain an overt nominal expression of it, in sentences 5, 7, and 8, in the first case with
an expression almost identical to the introductory, iw mshkikwaaboo gaa-aabjitoowaad,
'that medicine which they used.' In sentences 7 and 8, iw mshkikwaaboo, 'that medicine' is
used.
    Another prop in this narrative are sweat-rocks, mdoodoo-siniin, mentioned in sentences
5 and 7. In sentence 7, the stones are referred to by means of a locational existential form
                                                                 12.6 Additional Reading • 645


which resembles a participle, raw yaanig niw siniin, 'those stones being there,' but which is
not strictly speaking a participle because it shows neither initial change nor plurality.
   The last nominal in this text, wdakjiwin, 'his cold,' a nominalized possessed form,
occurs in the last sentence. This word represents a nominalization of a verb occurring in
sentence 2, dkaji, 'have a cold (illness). The verb associated with it, maajaamgadni, 'it
(had) left,' an inanimate intransitive verb (vii), is inflected for obviation (backgrounding).
   Several aspects of the means of making reference used in this text are worth comment.
First, although there are seven transitive verbs, in none of them are both actor and goal
expressed with overt nominals. In particular, in two sentences involving the verb of speak-
ing zhi, 'say to AN' (6, 10), neither the actor nor goal are overtly expressed, and it is only
from context, and by the fact that the verbs are inflected for third person plural actors, as
opposed to a singular actor, that we know that it is the Indians and not the man speaking.
There are no obviative animate nouns in this text, all are proximate.
   Three relative clauses occur, in each case applying to an inanimate noun, for example, iw
mshkikwaaboo waa-aabjitoowaad, 'that medicine which they would use' (sentence 4).

12.6 Additional Reading

    Unfortunately, I have not had the opportunity to delve into Nishnaabemwin discourse to
any depth in this grammar. A richly annotated collection of texts told by Andrew Medler of
Walpole Island is available in Valentine 1998, ed., and the many other textual resources
cited in Chapter 1. Rhodes 1993, 1996 and many other papers cited in the references lay out
valuable foundations for the study of the areas of grammar treated in this chapter, as well as
providing a rich array of insights into particulars. Tomlin and Rhodes 1979 provides many
wonderful insights into Ojibwe discourse, republished in Payne 1992. Spielmann 1998 pro-
vides an accessible introduction to many approaches to discourse study, using Nishnaabem-
win and Algonquin examples. Nichols and Ogg, eds., 1996 contains many papers treating
discourse structure, including R. Valentine 1996, L. Valentine 1996, Russell 1996, and
Dahlstrom 1996. Many aspects of the discourse of Fox, a sister language of Nishnaabem-
win, have been treated by Ives Goddard in a series of papers, e.g., Goddard 1984, 1988, and
1990b.

    (1) What do you guys think of those who went and competed for Canada? (2) Who did

Verbs and Their Semantic Roles




   This chapter introduces concepts associated with the meaning structures of verbs, partic-
ularly with regard to a small number of universal semantic (meaning) relationships that
exist between verbs and the noun phrases and other elements associated with them. I begin
with a detailed discussion of the various semantic roles pertinent to Nishnaabemwin verbs,
and conclude with an account of the strategies that exist in the language for altering the
number of semantic roles associated with a verb.

13.1 Semantic Roles

    In simple terms, when considering the kinds of meaning associated with different parts
of speech, NOMINALS are used to represent people and things, and verbs to express states,
attributes, events, and actions that pertain to the people and things represented by nominals.
I will use the term PREDICATION to refer to the basic meaning relationships which a verb
shows with associated nominals. Depending on what aspects of an action or event that a
speaker wishes to focus on, verbs with different SEMANTIC ROLE relationships can be used.
A verb such as wiisni, 'eat' (VAI) has only one semantic role associated with it; in the case
of mwaad and miijid, there are two semantic roles, that of the eater, and also, whatever is
eaten. The verbs mwaad and miijid are thus TRANSITIVE, because there is a "transfer" of
action from the eater to the eaten; the verb wiisni is INTRANSITIVE, because there is only a
single SEMANTIC ROLE, and therefore there cannot be any transfer of action.

               INTRANSITIVE Verb      A single semantic role           wiisni
               TRANSITIVE Verb        Two (or more) semantic roles     mwaad, miijid

    The differences between transitive and intransitive verbs are discussed in more detail in
Chapter 3.4.1, page 130 and following. The nominal roles integral to the meaning of a verb
(predicate) are called its SEMANTIC ROLES. The following chart summarizes the semantic
roles associated with the verbs of eating discussed here. An 'x' in a box means that a given
648 • 13.1.1 Macroroles (Actor and Goal), Agent and Patient


semantic role (eater or eaten) is part of the meaning of the designated verb. Those verbs that
have two roles, mwaad and miijid, are transitive, while those that have one, wiisni and
wiisniimgad, are intransitive.

                                                 Eater Role    Eaten Role
                           mwaad           vta   X             x [animate]
                           miijid          vti   X             x [inanimate]
                           wiisni          vai   x [animate] —
                           wiisniimgad     vii   x [inanimate] —

   SEMANTIC ROLES, INFLECTION, NOUNS, PRONOUNS, AND NOUN PHRASES. In English,
the semantic roles of verbs are usually filled by means of independent words such as PRO-
NOUNS and NOUNS. Consider, for example, the following sentence, where the English gloss
contains the pronoun T to represent the role of the eater.

    (1)   Aankonaanyan pane ngii-miijnan.
          'I always ate crackers.' (AM33.10)

          Aankonaanyan ni Op 'crackers'; pane av 'always'; ngii-miijnan vti ind ls»0p 'I ate
          INpl.'


    In Nishnaabemwin, however, semantic roles are typically expressed by means of
INFLECTIONS on verbs. For example, in (1), the filler of the role of eater is signalled only by
the prefix on the verb ngii-miijnan, 'I ate them (inanimate),' which is «n». And in this sen-
tence, the role of the thing eaten is indicated by two distinct elements, the inflection on the
verb as well as an independent noun, aankonaanyan, 'crackers.' When independent nouns
related to a verb's semantic roles occur, they do not replace the inflections on the verb— the
inflections are present regardless of whether or not there are separate nominals associated
with the semantic roles. In Nishnaabemwin there are no uninflected verbs, and no infinitive
verbs.

13.1.1 Macroroles (Actor and Goal), Agent and Patient

    Verbs, whether transitive or intransitive, take a particular perspective on the event they
represent. For example, each of the following verbs has two semantic roles associated with
it, one that is more actively involved in initiating the verbal event, and one that is less
actively involved.
                                      13.1.1 Macroroles (Actor and Goal), Agent and Patient • 649



             Verb           Gloss                    More Active Role     Less Active Role
             nsaad          'kill AN'                one(s) killing       thing(s) killed
             mwaad          'eat AN'                 one(s) eating        thing(s) eaten
             aabjihaad      'use AN'                 one(s) using         thing(s) used
             niisnaad       'put AN down'            one(s) putting       thing(s) put
             waabmaad       'see AN'                 one(s) seeing        thing(s) seen
             mnopwaad       'like the taste of AN'   one(s) tasting       thing(s) tasted

     In the case of mwaad, 'eat AN,' it is the eater that represents the more active role, and
the thing eaten that is the less active. When the more active role represents a willful initiator
of action, usually controlling the action in some way, the role is that of AGENT, and the less
active role, representing the entity changed or affected by the agent, is that of PATIENT. In
the situation of eating, for example, the patient no longer exists in its previous form. The
most straightforward cases of verbs having agents and patients involve meanings entailing a
violent and metamorphic effect on the patient, such as eating, breaking, tearing, shredding,
assaulting, killing, or destroying.
    In other cases, though, the role relationships are not so readily cast in terms of agency.
For example, in the case of mnopwaad, 'like the taste of AN,' there is less of a deliberate
choice on the part of the one tasting— one either likes the taste of something or not, and the
preference is more of a reaction than a deliberate action. Such verbs are often analyzed as
having a semantic role of EXPERIENCER, distinct from that of agent, and involve less agency
and control in their application. But volition may be involved in tasting, if one actively
chooses to commit the act of tasting something. And the role associated with the taster is
certainly more active than that of whatever is being tasted. The important grammatical point
is that Nishnaabemwin aligns the taster in mnopwaad with the eater in the case of mwaad,
'eat AN,' and the thing tasted with the thing eaten. That is, in the case of transitive verbs,
there are two primary role slots, and Nishnaabemwin, like other languages, linguistically
casts the events, actions, and states that make up experience into a very limited system
involving only a few categories. Traditionally in Algonquian studies, the two primary role
slots of a transitive verb's PREDICATE are called ACTORS, for the more active, controlling
role, and GOALS, for the less active. I call these role slots MACROROLES, because they sub-
sume more specific roles. Agents and experiencers, for example, are both usually cast in the
macrorole of actor. The goal role, too, subsumes several more specific roles, including for
example, the BENEFICIARY of a verbal action such as zhitmawaad, 'make something for
AN,' and the RECIPIENT of a verbal action such as miinaad, 'give something to AN.' What is
particularly important about the actor and goal macroroles in Nishnaabemwin is that the sta-
tus of a verb as VTA or VTI is based on the animacy of whatever is filling the goal macrorole.
So, for example, the animacy of the object exchanged is irrelevant to the verbal subclassifi-
cation of miinaad, 'give Y to AN,' because the recipient semantic role is filling the goal
macrorole, and the receiver must be animate, and the verb is therefore VTA. This can easily
be seen by examining a couple of examples, sentences (2) and (3), below. In the first, the
word for the thing given, mskomnag, 'raspberries,' is grammatically animate, and in the sec-
650 • 13.1.2 The Semantic Roles and Macrorole of Intransitive Verbs


ond it is grammatically inanimate, dehminan, 'strawberries.' Yet in both cases, the verb is
VTA, because the recipient fills the goal macrorole, and the recipient must be animate. In
fact, there is no inflectional marking (or indexing) of any grammatical features of the object
that is given, such as whether it is singular or plural (its number), or proximate or obviative.

   (2)   Ggii-miinin mskomnag. I 'I gave you raspberries.' (mskomin 'raspberry' NA)
          Ggii-miinin vta ind ls»2s 'I gave Y to you'; mskomnag na BpProx 'raspberries.'


   (3)   Ggii-miinin dehminan. I 'I gave you strawberries.' (dehmin, 'strawberry' NI)
          Ggii-miinin vta ind ls»2s 'I gave Y to you'; dehminan ni Op 'strawberries.'

    There are many other areas of grammar where Nishnaabemwin organizes patterns
around the semantic properties of entities. For example, in the choice of a person prefix for
transitive verbs inflected in the independent order, a strict topicality hierarchy applies, in
which second person outranks first, which, in turn, outranks third. Another context where
semantic properties interact with grammar involves the grammatical gender of the fillers of
the roles of transitive predications, where, in Nishnaabemwin, one of the roles must be filled
by a grammatically animate entity, commonly a human. So, for example, there are no VTI
forms to specify an inanimate actor acting upon an inanimate goal, as in English expres-
sions such as 'the wind blew the leaf along.' Where such concepts exist in Nishnaabemwin,
they are expressed by intransitive verbs, in which the agent, or more properly, the FORCE
(see below), is encoded in an INTRANSITIVE INSTRUMENTAL FINAL, as in bmaasin, 'be
blown along by the wind' VII, which has a final /-aasin/, 'be acted upon by the wind.' This
organization of grammar around semantic properties is a striking feature of Nishnaabem-
win, a primary principle of the language, and a key to understanding much of its grammati-
cal patterning. For this reason, we will examine how semantic roles are expressed in
Nishnaabemwin in some detail in the sections which follow.

                                               Macroroles
                          Actor     More active role   Agent, Experiencer
                          Goal      Less active role   Patient, Beneficiary

13.1.2 The Semantic Roles and Macrorole of Intransitive Verbs

   Intransitive verbs are those that prototypically have only a single semantic role in their
predicates, such as wiisni, 'eat' (VAI), and bmose, 'walk along' (VAI). However, intransitive
verbs show an immense variety in the nature of the single semantic role associated with
them, which may be an agent, a patient, or almost any other role. For example, in the case of
wiisni, 'eat' (VAI) the semantic role is that of an agent. For mnopgozi, 'taste good' (VAI),
however, the sole role is that of a patient. Since agents typically map to the actor role of
                                                               13.1.3 Semantic Role Charts • 651


transitive verbs and patients to the goal role, intransitive verbs cut across the distinction
between actor and goal roles that apply to transitive verbs. This suggests that there is moti-
vation for introducing a third macrorole to refer to the supercategory comprised of semantic
roles associated with intransitive verbs. I will call this macrorole the S-ROLE to distinguish it
from the macroroles associated with transitive verbs (ACTOR and GOAL). We thus have three
macroroles, as outlined in the following table.

                       Macrorole      Specifying...
                       Actor          More active role in a transitive predication
                        Goal          Less active role in a transitive predication
                        S-Role        Single role in an intransitive predication

13.1.3 Semantic Role Charts

   A specification of a verb's semantic roles constitutes part of its PREDICATE STRUCTURE.
To introduce predicate structures, consider the following sentence.

   (4)   Wshki-nbagsagoon wminpawaawaan giw gaagog.

          'The porcupines like to eat new lumber.' (AK1.9)

          Wshki-nbagsagoon na 3obv 'new lumber'; wminpawaawaan vta ind3pProx»3obv
          'ANpl like the taste of ANobv'; giwprSpProx 'those'; gaagog na SpProx 'porcupines.'


    The chart on the following page lays out the grammatical features of the elements of this
sentence. It shows that there are two noun phrases, wshki-nbagsagoon, 'new board(s),'
which is the obviative (backgrounded) form ofwshki-nbagsag, an animate noun; the second
noun phrase is proximate (foregrounded), giw gaagog, 'those porcupines,' which has as its
head the plural form of the animate noun gaag, 'porcupine.' The verb in the sentence is
wminpawaawaan, which is listed in the dictionary as mnopwaad, 'have AN taste good to
one, like the taste of AN.' There are two semantic roles associated with this verb, an experi-
encer (taster) and a patient (or theme) (the thing(s) tasted). As to macroroles, the experi-
encer is the actor and the patient is the goal. Because there are two roles associated with the
verb, it is transitive, and, more specifically, it is transitive animate (VTA) because the goal is
animate (wshki-nbagsag). There are inflections on the verb, signalled by the prefix-suffix
combination w_aawaan, which indicate that a third person proximate plural actor is acting
upon an animate obviative goal. The inflections indicate only these bare grammatical cate-
gories, "proximate third person plural actor," but the associated noun phrase, giw gaagog,
'those porcupines,' more specifically identifies who (or what) the third person plural inflec-
tion refers to.

     The same is true of the goal—the inflections simply identify an animate obviative
goal—the noun wshki-nbagsagoon identifies this goal more specifically as newly cut lum-
ber. The inflections on the verb and the associated noun phrases work together, and they
must AGREE in their grammatical features. The following semantic role chart summarizes
the predicate relations at work:

          PREDICATE                  ACTOR                 GOAL
          VTA wminpawaawaan          EXPERIENCER           PATIENT
          'like the taste of AN'                  INFL w_aawaan

          (4)                        giw gaagog            wshki-nbagsagoon

    The leftmost column contains the predicate, in this case, the verb form, along with its
verbal subclass, here VTA. Additional columns are provided for each semantic role associ-
ated with the predicate. The semantic roles are also classified according to their macrorole
status, as either actors or goals. Here the experiencer fills the macrorole of actor, and the
patient, that of goal. For each semantic role, there is a specification of the grammatical form
of the item filling it, which always includes an inflection (abbreviated as INFL), but may
have associated pronouns or NOUN PHRASES (abbreviated as NPi or NPa, depending on their
grammatical gender) as well. The box containing INFL is spread across the columns for
actor and goal because inflections (INFL) code actors and goal properties relationally, that
is, they often encode both macroroles compositionally, as they do here, with the indepen-
dent order inflection combination, \v_aawaan. The nominals associated with a particular
(macro)role are given in the lowest box in each role column. Here, for example, the actor
role has associated with it the NP, giw gaagog, 'those porcupines,' and the goal role,

wshki-nbagsagoon, 'new lumber.' A reference number in the lower left corner indexes the
associated example sentence.
   The following sentence provides another example.

   (5)   Mii sa giiwenh gaa-god maaba nmishoomis, "Mshi-gnebig sa aw emwaad niw

   We are interested in the predicate, "Mshi-gnebig sa aw emwaad niw gniijaansan."

                         PREDICATE           ACTOR           GOAL
                         VTA emwaad          AGENT           PATIENT
                         'eat AN'                         INFL _aad
                                             NPa[prox]        NPa[obv]
                         (5)                 mshi-gnebig      niw gniijaan'san

   The verb is VTA, and its agent role is filled by an animate noun (NPa), mshi-gnebig,
'great serpent, mythic serpent'; its patient role is filled by the animate noun phrase, niw
gniijaan'san, 'those children of yours.' In this sentence, then, both roles are explicitly real-
ized by independent nouns, but both are also indicated by means of inflections on the verb,
the conjunct order suffix complex, _aad.

13.1.4 Incorporation of Patients

   Nishnaabemwin has many verbs which have patients INCORPORATED inside of them,
such as naajmiijme, 'go get food' (VAI) [with the incorporated noun /miijim/, 'food'], and
mnise, 'cut firewood' (VAI) [with the medial element /-is-/ 'domestically useful wood'].
These verbs are both intransitive, meaning that, for purposes of inflection, they have a single
semantic role, that of an agent, because the patient role has, in a sense, been absorbed inside
the verb. Most incorporating verbs have meanings associated with the acquisition or transfer
or goods, such as the two illustrated here, and they reflect a general tendency in Nishnaabe-
mwin to grammatically background inert objects.
654 • 13.1.5 The Semantic Role of Force


13.1.5 The Semantic Role of Force

    A semantic role related to agent is that of FORCE. A force is something that brings about
results similar to those of an agent, but without willful agency, without volition. Forces are
often represented by nouns that are grammatically inanimate, though they may be animate
as well. The important feature of a force is that it is usually not considered an active, con-
scious initiator of the effect it has on the patient. As examples of prototypical forces, there is
a small set of verbs that are used to make reference to ingested substances that produce par-
ticular effects, for example, aakshkadegshkaagod, 'give AN a stomach ache,' and
gbisgishaagod, 'make AN constipated.' The semantic role of force maps into the macrorole
of actor, and the semantic role of patient, into that of goal. An example of such a verb fol-
lows.

                                              Force      Patient
                                              Actor      Goal

   (6)   Abinoojiinyag niibiwa miijiwaad aniw miinan ozhaabozogonaawaan.
          'If children eat lots of those blueberries they get diarrhoea.' (AW13.1)

          Abinoojiinyag na 3pProx 'children'; niibiwa av 'many'; miijiwaad vti conj 3pProx»0
          '(CONJ) (if) ANpl eat IN'; aniwpr Op 'those'; miinan ni Op 'blueberries';
          ozhaabozogonaawaan vtai ind Op»3pProx 'INpl gives ANpl diarrhea.'

          PREDICATE                            ACTOR         GOAL
          VTAI ozhaabozogonaawaan              FORCE         PATIENT
          'give AN diarrhoea'                           INFL o_aawaan
                                               NPi           NPa
          (6)                                  aniw miinan abinoojiinyag

    The distinction between agents and forces is important in Nishnaabemwin grammar
because verbs with forces as actors are always inflected for INVERSE inflection. The distinc-
tion between direct and inverse i's discussed in Chapter 7.2.2, beginning on page 270.
    Force is also closely related to INSTRUMENTALITY, which is very explicitly represented
in Nishnaabemwin, and there are many verb finals that specify common forces and instru-
ments, such as /-aashi/ (VAI) and /-aasin/ (VII), 'by wind action,' as in GWAASHI and
GWAASIN, 'blow down, blow over, be blown down, be blown over.' These instrumental
finals are discussed in Chapters 9 (section 9.10.4, page 349ff.) and 10 (section 10.4, page
438ff.).
    Since forces are usually inanimate, and there is a requirement that at least one argument
of a transitive verb be animate, there are no transitive inanimate (VTI) verbs that have a force
filling a macrorole.

13.1.6 The Semantic Role of Experiencer

   The semantic role of EXPERIENCER refers to a participant in the verbal action which nei-
ther controls the action nor is changed by it, but in some way experiences or senses some-
thing. The most typical experiencer role is that of a living creature, perceiving something by
means of the senses or mental process. The object perceived is given the semantic role of
PATIENT (or alternatively, THEME). So verbs of sensation, such as those of tasting, smelling,
seeing, hearing all have experiencers as one semantic role. In Nishnaabemwin the experi-
encer role maps into the macrorole of actor, and the theme, that of goal.

                                   Experiencer      Patient (or Theme)
                                   Actor            Goal

   (7)   Mii dash wi Niibaakhom zhngishing, mii gii-noondwaad bezhgoogzhiin
         biidwewebtoonid— dog! dog! dog! dog!
         'So it was that (the war chief) Nibakom was lying there; he heard the sound of a
         horse approaching— clip! clop! clip! clop!' (SO6.45)

          Mii av 'and'; dash av 'then'; wi pr Os 'that'; Niibaakhom na SsProx 'Niibaakhom';
          zhngishing vai conj SsProx '(CONJ) ANsg lies prone'; mii av 'then'; gii-noondwaad vta
          conj 3sProx»3obv '(CONJ) ANsg heard ANobv'; bezhgoogzhiin na 3obv 'horse(s)';
          biidwewebtoonid vai conj 3obv '(CONJ) ANobv come(s) making noise.'

   The semantic role chart of gii-noondwaad, in (7), is given below.

          PREDICATE           ACTOR          GOAL

          'hear AN'                    INFL _aad
