    Both transitive and intransitive verbs of mental activity sometimes have a whole predica-
tion closely associated with them, as COMPLEMENT CLAUSES. This phenomenon is discussed
more generally in Section 13.3.7, page 681, below.

13.1.7 The Semantic Roles of Recipient and Theme

    The semantic roles of RECIPIENT and THEME are involved in predications that refer to the
transfer of something. The recipient role specifies the receiver of the transfer, and the theme,
what is transferred. The source of the transfer fills the semantic role of agent, and the mac-
rorole of actor. The recipient fills the macrorole of goal, and the theme, being neither actor
656 • 13.1.7 The Semantic Roles of Recipient and Theme


nor goal, is not marked inflectionally on the verb. Verbs with both recipient and theme roles
are sometimes called DITRANSITIVES, as they have two objects, and are thus doubly-transi-
tive. The recipient role in English is customarily expressed by means of PREPOSITIONAL
PHRASES having prepositions such as from or to.

                              Agent              Theme          Recipient
                              Actor              —              Goal

   Examples of verbs having AGENT, RECIPIENT and THEME roles are miinaad, 'give [some-
thing] to AN,' and bgidnamaad, 'let AN have something'

13.1.8 VAIO Objects and Their Relationship to Ditransitive Secondary Objects

    Some dialects of Nishnaabemwin inflect VAIO verbs in the independent for features of
their goals, whether animate or inanimate, according to a pattern reminiscent of VTI (transi-
tive inanimate) goal inflection. Rhodes (1991a, 1991b) asserts that the goals of VAIO verbs
function similarly to the secondary objects (themes) of ditransitive verbs. At first glance,
this seems unlikely, since secondary objects are not inflectionally marked on ditransitive
verbs except in certain participles. However, Rhodes provides good evidence for the align-
ment of the two types of objects, and his arguments are discussed in more detail in Chapter
18.6, beginning on page 957.

13.1.9 The Semantic Role of Beneficiary (Benefactive)

   The semantic role of BENEFICIARY, also called BENEFACTIVE, specifies the role of the
one or ones benefitting from some action, that is, the one(s) for whose benefit the action is
undertaken. The semantic role of the one(s) undertaking the beneficial action is that of
agent, which maps into the macrorole of actor, and the beneficiary maps into the macrorole
of goal.

                                     Agent      Patient    Beneficiary
                                     Actor      —          Goal

   Verbs having beneficiaries filling the goal role are called BENEFACTIVE VERBS. There is
almost always a patient semantic role associated with benefactive verbs, but this role
receives no inflectional marking on the verb. For example, in the following sentence,
nbabgiwyaan, 'my shirt,' fills the role of patient, but there is no marking on the verb to
index an inanimate patient.
658 • 13.1.10 The Semantic Role of Instrument

          Awpr SsProx 'that'; kwe na SsProx 'woman'; ndazhtamaag vta ind3sProx»ls 'ANsg
          makes for me'; nbabgiwyaan ni ls(0s) 'my shirt.' (AM39.356)


                 PREDICATE             ACTOR                    GOAL

    Benefactive verbs represent another definable sub-group of DITRANSITIVES. Benefactive
relationships are expressed in English primarily by means of the preposition for to identify
the beneficiary, as in the examples above.

patient fills the goal macrorole and the instrument is not indexed at all inflectionally on the
verb, as in (14).

                                  Actor         —            Goal

13.1.10.1 Instrumental Finals

    Transitive finals allow specification of a variety of instrumental means by which an
action is brought about. The following examples illustrate some of these finals.

                       VTA Final      VTI Final    Meaning
                       -shkaw         -shk         'cause (using foot or body)'
                       -kaw           -k           'cause (in the body)
                       -m             -nd          'cause using speech'
                       -am            -and         'cause using mouth/teeth'
                       -aganaam       -aganaand    'cause using great force'

   For example, the instrumentality in the following sentence is provided by the VTA final
/-ga(h)w/, 'use an axe as instrument.'

   (16) Wgii-daashkgawaan mtigoon. I 'He split the tree with his axe.' (AM39.324)
          Wgii-daashkgawaan vta ind 3sProx»3obv 'ANsg split ANobv using axe'; mtigoon na
          3obv 'tree(s).'

   In the following the instrumentality of the hand is indicated by the VTI final /-bid+oo/:

   (17) Aabta bookbidoon. I 'Break it in half with your hand.' (AM39.746)
          Aabta av 'in half; bookbidoon vti imp 2s»0 'break IN using hand.'

means of speech, speaking, oral sound' in VTA verb boonim, 'stop talking about AN':

   (18) Aambe wii-boonmishnaang. I 'Please stop bothering us with talkl' (AM39.805)
          Aambe av 'hey'; wii-boonmishnaang vta imp 2»lp 'stop bothering us (excl.) by talking.'

   In the following, the instrumentality of a knife is provided both by explicit mention, in
mookmaanens, as well as by the VTI final /-kod+am/, 'cause using a cutting action,' on vti
verb giishkkodan, 'sever with a blade.' Note that there is no cross-referencing (inflection) on
the verb of any grammatical features of the instrument.

13.1.12 Summary of Semantic Role Relationships

   The following chart provides a summary of the semantic roles introduced so far.

          Agent            The willful initiator of an action, the "doer"
          Force            An inanimate force which brings about an action
          Patient          The recipient of the action of an agent, the "done-to"
          Theme            The role of one(s) undergoing transfer or movement
          Recipient        The role of one(s) receiving a theme
          Benefactive      The role of the one(s) benefitting from the action of an agent
          Instrument       An object used by an agent in an action to bring about the result

    DEFAULT SEMANTIC ROLE-TOMACROROLE ASSOCIATIONS. The semantic roles dis-
cussed to this point can also be summarized in terms of their default associations with the
macroroles of actor and goal. Agents and experiencers are always actors in transitive predi-
cations; patients are goals unless there is a recipient or beneficiary, in which case these
always fill the goal role and the patient is not inflectionally indexed. Themes function as
goals only when there is no recipient. If a semantic role is cast in neither macrorole, then it
is usually not inflectionally indexed on the verb at all.

                                                Actor      Goal      Unindexed
                          Agent
                          Force
                          Experiencer
                          Recipient
                          Beneficiary
                          Patient
                          Theme
                          Instrument
                             13.2 Semantic Relations of Relative Roots and Relative Preverbs • 663


   Nishnaabemwin verbal inflection rather strikingly privileges those semantic roles that
are customarily rilled by humans, such as recipient and beneficiary, over those that are not,
particularly the roles of patient and instrument. As a result, benefactive verbs and transfer
verbs are always VTA's, because the goal macrorole, which determines the verbal subclass
(VTA or VTI), is filled by the semantic role of recipient or beneficiary. Typological studies of
many languages show that the system of "object" marking found in Nishnaabemwin is not
uncommon. In this system, the "direct object" of a simple transitive verb and the "indirect
object" of a ditransitive verb are together called the PRIMARY OBJECT, as opposed to the
direct object of a ditransitive, which is called the SECONDARY OBJECT (Croft 1990:103).
Rhodes, too, in many papers on Ojibwe grammar (e.g., 1991a, 1991b, 1998), makes a fun-
damental distinction between primary and secondary objects. In Nishnaabemwin, instru-
mental notions also tend to be backgrounded by semantic incorporation into verbal finals,
where they lose all inflectional salience. Patients too, especially those nominals associated
with traditional cultural activities of everyday subsistence, are often incorporated within the
verb, a form of rhetorical backgrounding.
    With regard to intransitive verbs, I have suggested that many different semantic roles can
be associated with its one inflectional macro-role, which I call the S-Role.

13.2 Semantic Relations of Relative Roots and Relative Preverbs

   Nishnaabemwin has a set of ROOTS, which may also appear as PREVERBS, that have the
property of associating a semantic relation with a predicate. These roots are called RELA-
TIVE ROOTS because they relate the verbal predicate to something else, either a way (man-
ner) of doing something, a degree to which something is done, the number of times
something is done, or a specification of a source, place, or destination relating to the predi-
cate. For example, the verb zhichge, do something,' is a VAI verb, meaning it takes an ani-
mate S-Role (subject) and that it is intransitive—that is, is not inflectionally specified for a
goal (unless it is a VAIO, which this isn't). However, the presence of the relative root /iN/
(here spelled «zh») in this word allows for the specification of an additional goal-like (com-
plement) relation, namely, whatever is done (or the "way" of doing). This can be seen from
the following two examples.

   (25) Mii sa [maanda] gaa-zhichgewaad giw Nishnaabeg zhaazhi go.
         '[This] is what those Indians did of old.' (AM21.20)

          Mii av 'it's'; maandapr Os 'this'; gaa-zhichgewaad vai ic conjSpProx '(CCNJ) what
          ANpl did'; giwpr SpProx 'those'; Nishnaabeg na SpProx 'Indians'; zhaazhi av 'long
          ago.'
664 • 13.2 Semantic Relations of Relative Roots and Relative Preverbs


   (26)   Ggii-zhichge na dash [iw] gaa-zhi-gkinoohmoonaan ?
          'Did you do [the way] that I taught you?' (AM30.32)

          Ggii-zhichge vai ind2s 'did you (SG.) do so'; na av 'yes/no question'; dash av 'then'; iw
          pr Os 'that'; gaa-zhi-gkinoohmoonaan via ic conj ls»2s '(CCNJ) how I taught you (SG)
          to do.'


   Relative elements function similarly to prepositions and their objects in English. Rhodes
(1990) makes the general observation that they function like verbal constructions found in
Siouan languages, Chibchan and Maku, as discussed in Craig and Hale 1988. The following
semantic role-chart includes a slot for the object (complement) of a relative element.

          PREDICATE              S-Role               OBJECT OF RELATIVE
          vai zhichge           AGENT
          'do something so'      INFL_
                                 NPa                  NPi
          (25)                   giw Nishnaabeg       maanda

   Here the immediate object is the inanimate demonstrative pronoun, maanda, 'this.' But
maanda is here representing the entire discourse that has preceded this summary sentence,
in which the narrator has recounted how the Indians of old practiced sweating cures.

                     PREDICATE            S-Role        OBJECT OF RELATIVE
                     vai zhichge          AGENT
                     'do something'       INFL_
                                          —             NPi
                     (26)                               iw gaa-zhi-gkinoohmoonaan

   In example (26), a young woman has been instructed to prepare a love medicine, and her
teacher asks her if she has acted in the way that he has specified.
   When a noun (as opposed to a clause) is the complemnt of a relative root or preverb, it
typically immediately precedes the associated verb, and shows LOCATIVE CASE marking.

   (27) Mhiingning zhinaagzi gday. I 'Your (sg.) dog looks like a wolf.' (MC)
          Mhiingning na loc 3 '(like) a wolf; zhinaagzi vai indSsProx 'ANsg looks like'; gday
          nad 2s(3sProx) 'your dog.'
                                                                            13.3 Sentential Complements • 665


   (28) Mhiingning zhinaagziwag gonda nimookaajiinyig. I 'Those dogs look like wolves.'
          Mhiingning na loc 3 '(like) a wolf; zhinaagziwag vai ind SpProx 'ANpl look so';
          gondapr na SpProx 'these'; nimookaajiinyig na SpProx 'dogs.' (MC)

   The following table lays out the core Nishnaabemwin relative roots and their corre-
sponding relative preverbs. See the index for additional details for each root.

           Roots                Preverbs                 Meaning
           /akw/                ako-, ko-                'since; so far; for a long time'
           /apiit/              apiichi-, piichi-        'to the extent that. . ., in the process of. . . '
           /apiich/
           /apiis/
           /in/, /izh/          izhi-, zhi-              'like a certain thing; towards a certain place;
           /ih/1                                         in a certain direction; in a certain way; in
                                                         spite of a certain obstacle'
           /ond/, /onj/         onji-, nji-, wnji-       'from a certain direction, for a certain reason'

           /dash/
          1. Here /h/ indicates that the initial consonant of the root is made fortis, e.g., patoo, /ipatoo/, 'run
          there,' from /iN+batoo/; kido, /ikido/, 'say something' from /iN+gido/.
    Note that several common morphologically simple verbs specifying locations also act as

13.3 Sentential Complements

     Many verbs take whole CLAUSES as ARGUMENTS (COMPLEMENTS) in their predicate
 structure. Such clauses can fill the goal roles of transitive verbs, though verbs that semanti-
cally include human recipients of acts of communication typically yield the goal macrorole
to the recipient. For example, the following sentence contains a VERB OF SPEAKING,
wiindmaw, 'tell AN something,' and includes a complement clause expressing what is to be
told, in the form of an indirect statement. The inflectional goal of the main verb,
ji-wiindmawdwaa, is giw Nishnaabeg widi gaa-bi-njibaayang, 'those people where we
 (incl.) come from,' that is, those who are the recipients of the communication.
666 • 13.3 Sentential Complements


   (29) Ggizheb waabang gga-maajaajz-vwmdmawdwaa giw Nishnaabeg widi
        gaa-bi-njibaayang \ji-bi-naadmawwaadji-miigaan'gidwaa giw
        myagi-nishnaabeg].
          'Tomorrow morning you must go and tell those people where we came from [to
          come and help me fight those men of a foreign tribe].' (AM31.24)

          Ggizheb av 'in the morning'; waabang av 'tomorrow'; gga-maajaa vai ind 2s 'you (SG)
          will leave'; ji-wiindmawdwaa vta conj 2s»3pProx '(CONJ) you (SG) will tell ANpl'; giw
          pr SpProx 'those'; Nishnaabeg na 3pProx 'Indians'; widi av 'over there';
          gaa-bi-njibaayang vai ic conj 21 '(CCNJ) where we (incl.) come from';
          ji-bi-naadmawwaad vta conj 3pProx»ls '(CONJ) ANpl will come and help me';
          ji-miigaan'gidwaa vta conj 21»3p '(CONJ) we (incl.) will fight ANpl'; giwpr SpProx
           'those'; myagi-nishnaabeg na 3pProx 'alien Indians.'


   In the following example, the thought associated with a MENTAL ACTIVITY VERB is
expressed by means of a clause, which is interrupted by the verb of thinking.

   (30)   Gnimaa niiwgon wgii-gkendaan wii-bi-dgoshninid.
          'He knew [that they were probably going to come in four days].' (AM31.20)

           Gnimaa av 'probably'; niiwgon av 'four days'; wgii-gkendaan vti 3sProx»0 'ANsg
           knew IN'; wii-bi-dgoshninid vai conj 3obv '(CONJ) ANobv would arrive here.'


   These sentence-like elements that are closely associated with the fundamental meaning
of a verb are called SENTENTIAL COMPLEMENTS. In Nishnaabemwin they are usually related
by means of clauses containing verbs inflected for the conjunct inflectional order, and they
typically occur after the main verb they are associated with, though as can be seen from sen-
tence (30), above, portions of them sometimes appear before the verb. It is also not uncom-
mon with verbs of speaking or thinking for the entire clause to precede the verb, which is
almost always inflected in the independent order, as in this example.

   (31)   [Wii-boontaad giishpin washme niibna bwaa-dbahmawind] gii-kida Maanii.
          'Mary said [she 'd quit if she didn 't get paid more].' (MC)

           Wii-boontaad vai conj SsProx 'ANsg will quit'; giishpin av 'if; washme av 'more';
           niibna av 'a lot'; bwaa-dbahmawind vta conjx»3sProx 'ANsg is not paid'; gii-kida vai
           ind SsProx 'ANsg said'; Maanii na 3sPwx 'Mary.'


   There are several notional classes of verbs which take sentential complements, a repre-
sentative sampling of which are listed in the following section. In all cases, the COMPLE-
                                    13.3.1 Intransitive Verbs that Take Sentential Complements • 667



MENT-TAKING VERBS are in italics, and their corresponding sentential-complements within
square brackets.

13.3.1 Intransitive Verbs that Take Sentential Complements

   In Nishnaabemwin, many verbs that are INTRANSITIVE in their basic structure allow SEN-
TENTIAL COMPLEMENTS. These include verbs of speaking, verbs expressing thought pro-
cesses, orientational/evaluative verbs such as znagad, 'be difficult' (vii), and many others.
The following examples illustrate, with the verbs identified with subscripted CTV, for
"complement-taking verb."

   (32) Noongo giizhgak nwii-dbaajimCTV [iw Nishnaabeg maa Waabow Island fair
        wii-yaamwaad].
         Today I am going to tell [of the fact that the Indians on Walpole Island are
         going to have a fair].' (AM18.2)

          Noongo av 'now'; giizhgak vii conj 0 '(CONJ) it is day'; nwii-dbaajim vai ind Is 'I will
          tell the news'; iw^r Os 'that'; Nishnaabeg na SpProx 'Indians'; maa av 'there';
          wii-yaamwaad vti conj 3pProx»0 '(CONJ) ANpl will have IN.'


   (33) Maanii gii-dbaajmaciy [Rogeran gii-ni-boontaad}.
         'Mary gave the news [that Roger had quit]! (MC)

          Maanii na BsProx 'Mary'; gii-dbaajma vai indSsProx 'ANsg told the news'; Rogeran
          na 3obv 'Roger'; gii-ni-boontaad vai conj 3sProx 'ANsg had quit.'


   (34) Nzegizciv [wii-niibwiyaanh]. I 'I'm afraid [to get married].' (DP)
          Nzegiz vai ind Is 'I am afraid'; wii-niibwiyaanh vai conj Is '(CONJ) I will marry.'

   (35) Bngii zhiwi go ngii-znagizCTV [wii-naaghadoowaanh aanin
        gchi-zhi-giizhwewnan].
         'I had a little trouble [following some of the jargon].' (MC)

          Bngii av 'a little'; zhiwi av 'there'; go ngii-znagiz vai ind Is 'I had difficulty';
          wii-naaghadoowaanh vti conj ls»0 '(CONJ) I follow IN'; aanin av 'some';
          gchi-zhigiizhwewnan ni Op 'jargon (PL).'


   PSEUDO-INTRANSITIVES. There is a large group of animate intransitive verbs that have
the form of a transitive inanimate verb in having a VTI THEME SUFFIX, /-am/. These verbs
668 • 13.3.2 Direct and Indirect (Reported) Quotation


were called PSEUDO-INTRANSITIVES in early linguistic studies. They commonly take senten-
tial complements.

   (36)   Gii-giiwsaadendam Maanii [gaa-naadRogeran].
          'Mary regretted [what she had said to Roger].' (MC)

          Gii-giiwsaadendam vai ind SsProx 'ANsg regretted'; Maanii na 3sProx 'Mary';
          gaa-naad vta ic conj 3sProx»3obv '(CCNJ) what ANsg said to ANobv'; Rogeran na
          3obv 'Roger.'

13.3.2 Direct and Indirect (Reported) Quotation

    Just as with English, Nishnaabemwin has two distinct ways to report speech, one
DIRECT, in which the actual words spoken are given, and one INDIRECT, in which the words
of the speaker are adjusted to the situation of the report, by changing person categories and
tense, as well as other features. The following examples represent DIRECT QUOTATION,
quoting the actual words of the speaker.

   (37) Mii dash gaa-naad aw mshkikiiwnini, [Gego nendangen].
          The doctor told her, "Do not feel that way about it.'" (AM30.21)

13.3.3 Demonstrative Complementizers

   Complement clauses, as with other subordinate clauses, may be introduced with the
inanimate demonstrative pronouns maanda, 'this,' or more commonly, iw, 'that.' Such ele-
ments used to introduce complement clauses are called COMPLEMENTIZERS.

   (44) Gii-nshkaadzi aw ndawemaa [iw bbaa-yaayaan wiikaa iw dbikak]
        gii-zhmaagnishiiwi maa naa ge wiin, ngii-paktewig dash naangim go
        gii-ni-dgoshnaang endaayaan.
         'My brother got mad [that I was around late at night], he was a soldier too, and
         he hit me on the shoulder until we got to my house.' (AK8.10)

         Gii-nshkaadzi vai ind3sProx 'ANsg was angry'; awpr SsProx 'that'; ndawemaa nad
         ls(3sProx) 'my sibling-of-opposite sex'; iwpr Os 'that'; bbaa-yaayaan vai conj Is
         '(SUF) I was around'; wiikaa av 'ever'; iw/?r Os 'that'; dbikak vii conj 0 '(CONJ) IN be
         night'; gii-zhmaagnishiiwi vai ind SsProx 'ANsg was a soldier'; maa av 'there'; wiin/?r
         pers 3s 'ANsg'; ngii-paktewig vta ind3sProx»ls 'ANsg hit me repeatedly'; dash av
         'then'; naangim av 'until'; gii-ni-dgoshnaang vai conj Ip '(CONJ) we arrived there';
         endaayaan vai ic conj Is '(CCNJ) where I live.'


   (45) Mii dash nhendmaan [iw gii-gkenmag geget iw nsitang].
         'So now I felt sure [that I knew that she did really understand it].' (AM9.35)

          Mii av 'and'; dash av 'so'; nhendmaan vti conj ls»0 '(CONJ) I felt satisfied that IN was
          true'; ivf pr Os 'that'; gii-gkenmag vta conj ls»3sProx '(CONJ) I knew about ANsg';
          geget av 'truly'; ivfpr Os 'that'; nsitang vti conj 3sProx»0 '(CONJ) ANsg understood IN.'


    The optionality of iw in complement clauses can be seen by comparing example (45)
directly above with the following sentence, which lacks iw. This sentence is also interesting
in the TENSE relationship between the main verb, which is unmarked for tense, and the verb
in the complement, which is marked for past tense (with gii-).

   (46) Mii dash nhendamaan [geget sa gii-gkenmag sa Wjibwemod].
         'So now I was satisfied [that I knew she spoke Ojibwa].' (AM9.40)

          Mii av 'and'; dash av 'so'; nhendamaan vti conj ls»0 '(CONJ) I felt satisfied about IN';
          geget av 'truly'; gii-gkenmag vta conj ls»3sProx '(CONJ) I knew about ANsg';
          Wjibwemod vai conj 3sProx '(CONJ) ANsg spoke Ojibwe.'
                                           13.3.4 Tense and Modality in Complement Clauses • 671



13.3.4 Tense and Modality in Complement Clauses

    Verbs in complement clauses allow a rather free range of TENSE and MODAL PREVERBS,
including: gii-, 'past tense' (55) (p. 673), (88) (p. 680); \vii-, 'future tense, intentive' (53) (p.
672), (54) (p. 672); ji-, 'modal ('should, could, would')' (64) (p. 675), (65) (p. 675); and da-,
'modal' (47) (p. 671), (48) (p. 671). Generally, verbs in complements that represent unreal-
ized events in the past, present, or future, such as in (54) (p. 672) and (63) (p. 674), are
marked with wii-, 'future, intentive.' When the complement represents a real(ized) event or
situation, its verb is often not marked with tense. Complements representing unrealized sit-
uations, such as those of verbs of striving and trying, also often have verbs marked with
conjunct modal preverbs ji- or da- (64) (p. 675) and (65) (p. 675). Preverb ji- is also used
with complements representing actions and events which will take place in the future (70)
(p. 676). Much more analysis remains to be done on tense and modality in complements.

ment verbs in Nishnaabemwin. Verbs are grouped into very general notional categories.

13.3.8 Secondary Role VTA Verbs

   Related to sentential-complement raising verbs discussed in the previous section are VTA
verbs derived from VTI by the addition of a suffix such as /-aw/, as in gkendmaw, 'know
something about AN' Such verbs are formed by deriving a VTA verb which takes a SECOND-
ARY SEMANTIC ROLE normally filled by a human and makes it the MACRO-ROLE of GOAL.
The original goal of the VTI, which may have been a SENTENTIAL COMPLEMENT, can still
occur alongside the newly derived animate goal. And since the animate goal is often the
SUBJECT of the SENTENTIAL COMPLEMENT, there is the appearance of COPYING (see previous
section) as well.

                   vti                 vta
                   gkendam       +aw = gkendmaw             'know something about AN'

    The following example illustrates the use of such a verb. This sentence is from an oral
historical account of treaty proceedings, in which the Indians returning from treaty signing
were ambushed by others who had not signed.

         'And the Indians who did evil waited to ambush them upon their return, indeed

13.4 Changing Verbal Perspectives on a Scene

    Speakers of Nishnaabemwin have many options in choosing a way of casting a particular
action or event. Because of the rich morphological resources of the language, a notion such
as cooking can be represented in many different ways: as a transitive activity involving an
agent acting on a patient, by using a transitive verb such as mnozwaad, 'cook AN,' (VTA) or
mnozang, 'cook IN' (VTI); with a focus on the agent by using an actor-focus intransitive
verb, such as mnozekwe, 'do cooking'; with a focus on whatever's being cooked, by using a
goal-focus intransitive verb, such as mnozo, 'undergo cooking' (VAI) or mnode, 'undergo
cooking' (VII); with a focus on the goal, by using an inflectional or lexical passive form of a
transitive verb; with a focus on the beneficiary of the act of cooking, by using an applicative
(benefactive) verb, mnozmawaad, 'cook for AN.' All of the verbs listed here bear obvious
relationship to one another, underscoring a fundamental aspect of Nishnaabemwin vocabu-
lary, namely that for any given concept there is usually a family of closely related words
which can be used to cast an action or event from a number of different perspectives. When
we consider that these multiple perspectives can be combined with the many ways of mak-
ing reference, such as by verbal inflection, by demonstrative pronouns, or by full noun
phrases of greater or lesser elaboration, we begin to understand something of the limitless
richness that the language offers it speakers. And this is not to mention the vast amount of
subtlety that can be achieved with different patterns of word order, syntactic focusing, and
other rhetorical devices.

13.4.1 Decreasing the Number of Semantic Roles Associated with a Verb

   There are many ways in Nishnaabemwin to suppress characters, that is, to either down-
play or eliminate reference to some character/participant customarily associated with the
meaning of a given verbal concept. At the same time that one character is suppressed,
another is often advanced in prominence. For example, in a PASSIVE construction, the filler
of a transitive verb's actor role is not specified, defocusing the agent, but at the same time
the GOAL becomes more prominent, e.g., nwaabmigoo, 'I am seen.' In an ANTIPASSIVE, a
                                        13.4.1.1 Suppressing Actors with Inflectional Passives • 687


transitive verb's GOAL ROLE in greatly downplayed or eliminated, and the ACTOR/SUBJECT
gains in significance, as well as the verbal action itself, e.g., gnaadmaage, 'you (sg.) help.'
Another way that goals can be backgrounded is by INCORPORATING them into the verb, e.g.,
gnaadsabii, 'you (sg.) go check (your) net,' with incorporated sab, 'net.' All three of these
processes involve changing the mechanics of a transitive verb by downplaying one or
another of its roles, creating an intransitive verb as part of the bargain. In this section we
will examine the form and use of each of these three devices.

13.4.1.1 Suppressing Actors with Inflectional Passives

    Nishnaabemwin has PASSIVE forms for all PERSON and NUMBER combinations of ani-
mate goals, which like English passives, suppress the actor role. In the following passage
for example, told by Angeline Williams, a dog who has married a woman has a premonition
that the woman's brothers will soon arrive to kill the family. He informs his wife of this by
means of three progressively more specific MII-FOCUS CLAUSES, only the last of which has
an explicit NOUN PHRASE; the first clause uses a PASSIVE form. The passive is only one of
several masking devices Ms. Williams uses in these few words.

   (106) "Mii iw waabang wii-bi-nisigooyang" odinaan aniw owiidigemaaganan. (b)
         "Aanii dash?" (c) "Mii sa iw gaa-izhichigewaad gii-zagaswaawaad, mii agiw
         gidawemaag."
         "Now in the morning we (incl.) will be killed" he told his wife, (b) "How is
         that?" (she replied) (c) "That is what they have decided upon, having smoked,
         your brothers." (AW 14.140-142)

          Mii av 'it's'; iwpr Os 'that'; waabang av 'tomorrow'; wii-bi-nisigooyang vta conjx»21
          '(CONJ) we will be killed'; odinaan vta ind3sProx»3obv 'ANsg says to ANobv'; aniw
          pr Bobv 'that/those'; owiidigemaaganan na 3sProx(3obv) 'ANsg's spouse.' (b) Aanii av
          'how'; dash av 'then.' (c) Mii av 'that's'; \\vpr Os 'that'; gaa-izhichigewaad vai ic conj
          3pProx '(CCNJ) what ANpl did'; gii-zagaswaawaad vai conj 3pProx '(CONJ) ANpl
          smoked tobacco'; mii av 'it's'; agiw pr 3pProx 'those'; gidawemaag nad 2s(3pProx)
          'your brothers.'

    In another story, focusing on a removal of Indian people by the U.S. government, Ms.
Williams uses passive forms to describe the seizure of the Indians' horses. This example
shows that the SUBJECT of the passive verb can be the SECONDARY OBJECT (semantic THEME
in this case) of the active verb, as in the case of gii-mamawindwaa, 'they were taken from
them,' below.
688 • 13.4.1.1 Suppressing Actors with Inflectional Passives


   (107) Mil iw gii-mamawindwaa neyaab gii-giiwenaazha'ondwaa.
          Then they (horses) were taken from them and driven back home.' (AW18.36)

          Mil av 'and'; \vtpr Os 'that'; gii-mamawindwaa vta conjx»3pProx '(CONJ) ANpl were
          taken away'; neyaab av 'back'; gii-giiwenaazha'ondwaa vta conjx»3pProx 'ANpl were
          driven back home.'

   The following sentence shows the persistence of a non-goal semantic role under passiv-

    Unlike English, Nishnaabemwin passive constructions do not allow any indirect specifi-
cation of the actor role. In English this is done by means of a prepositional phrase with by,
as in The window was broken by the raccoon. No equivalent means of indirectly specifying
the actor in a passive exists in Nishnaabemwin. Also, transitive animate verbs that are pas-
sive are inflected as if they were animate intransitives, that is, they are inflected as if they
have a single semantic role, that of their subject (S-Role). For example, the following pas-
sive verb shows the suffix complex «wag», associated with animate intransitive third person
plural independent order forms. At the same time, the semantic role of the theme, here filled
by semaan, 'tobacco' (obv.), is preserved.

   The only INFLECTIONAL difference between passives and regular animate intransitive
verbs is that the passive retains an inflectional transitive theme suffix, here /-aa/.

                       Passivization
                       1
                         Reference to Actor is eliminated (Agent defocus)
                       1
                         Verb becomes intransitive in inflection
                       1
                         Goal of old transitive becomes S-Role (subject) of intransitive

    PERSON ASYMMETRIES IN PASSIVIZATION. Passivization of first and second persons, sin-
gular and plural, uses the theme suffix /-igoo/, which appears related to the NON-LOCAL
INVERSE THEME suffix, /-igw/. Third persons are inflectionally passivized by means of the
NON-LOCAL DIRECT THEME SUFFIX, /-aa/ in the independent order, and by the ending /-ind/
in the conjunct. This complex decomposes into an l-il of uncertain provenience, followed
perhaps by the generalized actor suffix /-m/, and what at first blush looks like the regular
conjunct animate third person inflection /-d/. Such an analysis is problematic in that the
third person suffix standardly has the alternant /-g/ following a nasal. Furthermore, third
person passives contrast with generalized actor forms in this very feature, in that the latter
have a conjunct ending, /-ng/ (see next section). At any rate, it appears that first and second
person outrank the passive trigger (unspecified actor) on the topicality hierarchy, since an
INVERSE theme /-igoo/ appears in their passives, whereas the trigger outranks third persons,
since a DIRECT theme, /-aa/, occurs. This is the motivation for the place of X, the unspecified
actor, in the ranking 2,1 > X > 3.
    GENERALIZED ACTOR FORMS. VAI and VTi1 verbs can also show defocusing of their ani-
mate roles, rather analogous to the actor defocus of a VTA verb that occurs in the passive.
This is done by means of the generalized actor suffix /-m/. This suffix indicates that the ver-
bal action is general, rather than the action of any specific, identifiable individuals. General-
ized actor forms are unlike passives in their failure to detransitivize VTI'S, which retain their
inanimate goals. Their inflectional behaviour is unusual in that the suffix /-m/ is retained in
the conjunct, as if the suffix were derivational, and an additional conjunct ending, /-g/ is
added, as can be seen in several of the examples below.

   (110) Eshkam znagad wii-debnaming iw waa-boodweng.
          'It is getting harder and harder/or one to obtain that with which one might make
          afire: (AMIS. 15)

           eshkam av 'increasingly' znagad vii indOs 'INsg is difficult'; wii-debnaming vti conj
           x»0 '(CONJ) one will obtain IN' iwprOs 'that'; waa-boodweng vaio ic conjx 'one will
           make a fire (with X).'

    LEXICAL PASSIVES. Many different classes of verbs exist with rather passive-like mean-
ings. The largest class consists of descriptive verbs referring to the sensory or mental stimuli
their subjects provide, such as mnopgozi, 'taste good,' mnonaagzi, 'look good,' and
mnotaagzi, 'sound good.' The reason that these verbs are called LEXICAL PASSIVES is that
they not only show the /-igw/ that occurs with inflectional passives, but they also have DER-
IVATIONAL elements attached, INTRANSITIVE FINALS, /-izi/ which form animate intransitive
verbs (VAI) and /-ad/, which forms inanimate intransitive verbs (Vii). The structure of these
verbs suggests that the passive morpheme has been applied to a transitive stem, to which is
then added an intransitive final. These derivational processes are not straightforward, how-
ever, and are subject to many irregularities. Sometimes the transitive stem that serves as a
base is a transitive animate (VTA) stem; other times it is a transitive inanimate (VTI) stem. In
some cases, it appears that the element /-aw/ is attached to the stem prior to the addition of
the passivizing element /-igw/; in others it is not. The tables below show possible deriva-
tions of representative forms. Sometimes too they have meanings that can not be straightfor-
wardly computed based on the meanings of their component parts. For example, the verb
gkendaagzi, 'be revealed, be known' VAI, suggests a passive formation on the basis of its
meaning; but another word with similar structure, mnwendaagzi, with root /minw-/, 'good,
well,' means not 'be thought good,' as would be expected with a passive reading, but rather
'be content, be glad.' This meaning seems rather unpredictable.
   Possible derivations of some lexical passives:

the general tendency to give grammatical prominence to humans and other living beings
over inanimates.

13.4.1.2 Suppressing Goals with Detransitives (Antipassives)

   GOALS too may be suppressed, using DETRANSITIVE VERBS, that is, verbs that have been
made morphologically intransitive by removing their GOAL role, or making it very vague.
The following sentence, for example, uses the intransitive verb gtige, 'do planting; do farm-
ing,' in which the emphasis is on the activity of farming or planting, as opposed to other
activities, and the crops that are planted or farmed are not mentioned. To make explicit ref-
erence to a goal, there exist the corresponding transitive verbs gtigaanaad, 'plant, cultivate
AN' VTA and gtigaadang, 'plant, cultivate IN' VTI. The VTA verb, for example, is used in
sentence (118), where explicit reference to the cultivation ofsemaa, 'tobacco,' is made.

13.4.1.3 Detransitivization with the Final /-iwe/

    Another detransitivizing final is /-iwe/, which is added to a transitive animate verb (VTA)
to produce an animate intransitive verb (VAI) that retains a vestigial sense of the original
goal in that it implies a sense of action directed vaguely toward human beings. For example,
from the VTA verb dkonaad, 'hold AN,' is derived VAI dkonwe, 'hold people; make an arrest,
throw people in jail,' and from VTA gkendmoohaad, 'let AN know something,' is derived
VAI gkendmoohwe, 'let people know.' This detransitivizing final suffix thus produces a verb
that, while intransitive, retains traces of its transitivity in the retention of the human feature
of its original goal. See also 9.12.17.2, Actor Focus Detransitive /-iwe/, Human Goal, begin-
ning on page 406.

13.4.1.4 Nominalization

    Another important function of DETRANSITIVIZATION is to provide input verbs for NOMI-
NALIZATION processes, that is, derivational morphological processes that make verbs into
nouns. All such nouns in Nishnaabemwin are derived from intransitive verbs, in the case of
transitive verbs by means of detransitivization. For example, the noun meaning 'writing,'
zhibiihgewin, is derived by adding the nominalizing suffix /-win/ to the VAI form zhibiihge,
'do writing,' which is itself derived from the VTI stem zhibiihang, 'write IN,' by addition of
the detransitivizing suffix /-(i)ge/. The noun meaning 'aid, assistance,' naadmaagewin, is
derived from VAI naadmaage, 'help, be a help,' which is itself derived from VTA naadmaw,
                                                        13.4.1.5 Reflexives and Reciprocals • 695


'help AN' by the addition of the detransitivizing suffix /-(i)ge/. Various nominalizing suf-
fixes are discussed in Chapter 11.6, Nominalizers, beginning on page 502.

13.4.1.5 Reflexives and Reciprocals

    Sometimes, an actor acts REFLEXIVELY, that is, upon himself or herself. English has a set
of reflexive personal pronouns for expressing reflexive activity, as in / see myself, or you see
yourself. Nishnaabemwin treats reflexives differently, essentially by detransitivizing the
transitive animate (VTA) verb by adding the VAi-deriving reflexive final complex /-idizo/, as
in waabmidzo, 'AN sees self.' There are, of course, no reflexive forms for transitive inani-
mate (VTI) verbs, since the actor of a VTI, which must be animate, is always distinct from the
goal, which must be inanimate.
    In a RECIPROCAL activity, at the same time that the actor acts upon the goal, the goal acts
upon the actor. English uses the pronominal expression each other in such contexts, as in
they see each other, or we see each other. Nishnaabemwin treats reciprocals differently, and
detransitivizes the transitive animate verb by adding the VAi-deriving reciprocal final com-
plex A(i)di/, as in waabmidwag, 'they see each other.' There are no VTI reciprocals.
    The reflexive and the reciprocal thus both deal with co-reference of actor and goal by
adding a final complex to produce an intransitive verb. These final complexes appear to be
related, in that they share the component /-id-/, to which the reflexive adds VAI final /-izo/
and the reciprocal adds the VAI final l-il.
    The following examples provide a few sentential examples of reflexives ((122) to (124)),
and reciprocals ((125) to (127)).

   (122) Mii sa gii-ni-moon'hishkwed, mii sa Niibaakhom gii-shagwezdizod.
         'So he dug out some medicinal herbs as he went along, and so Nibakom induced
         himself to vomit' (SO6.65)

          Mii av 'so'; gii-ni-moon'hishkwed vai conj3sProx '(CONJ) ANsg went and dug herbs';
          mii av 'and'; Niibaakhom na SsProx 'Niibaakhom'; gii-shagwezdizod vai conj 3sProx
          '(CONJ) ANsg made self vomit.'

   (123) Pii yaabndizod gii-nbogba. I 'When he saw himself he must have died.'
          Pii av 'when'; yaabndizod vai ic conj SsProx '(CONJ) when ANsg saw self; gii-nbogba
          vai indpdub 3sProx 'ANsg must have died.' (AM39.609)

   (124) Gwanhodzon waaboowyaan. I 'Cover yourself with the blanket.' (AM39.740)
          Gwanhodzon vai imp 2s 'cover yourself; waaboowyaan ni Os 'blanket.'

13.4.1.6 Backgrounding by Means of Incorporation of Nouns into Verbs

    Nouns referring to body parts and bodily products are customarily incorporated inside
the verb, which may be considered a form of backgrounding, since they are then not
referred to by means of independent nominals. In standard incorporation, a notional goal
shows up as a medial inside the verb. The verb, lacking an external goal, is then inflected as
an animate intransitive (VAl) verb, with the notional actor as subject. No VII verbs show
comparable incorporation, or if they do, they are extremely rare. The following examples
illustrate VAl forms.
                     13.4.1.6 Backgrounding by Means of Incorporation of Nouns into Verbs • 697


   (128) Wegne-sh wenji-niizhootwageyan? I 'Why do you have two ears?' (AM33.4)
          Wegne-sh av 'what'; wenji-niizhootwageyan vai ic conj 2s '(CCNJ) do you (SG) have
          two ears on account of.'

   (129) Waaboozoonh, wegne-sh wenji-waawyemooweyan?
         'Rabbit, why do you have round droppings?' (AM33.9)

          Waaboozoonh na 3sProx 'rabbit'; wegne-sh av 'what'; wenji-waawyemooweyan vai ic
          conj 2s '(CCNJ) do you (sg) have round droppings on account of.'

   The following chart outlines in very simple terms the workings of INCORPORATION.

                                            Incorporation
                           1
                             Goal is made a medial inside of verb
                           1
                             Verb becomes intransitive because it no longer
                             has an external goal
                           1
                             Actor is Subject of intransitive

    A number of incorporating verbs exist pertaining to the quest for, acquisition, transport,
and processing of material resources such as fish, game, and plants and their parts, or with
the acquisition, donning, doffing, or wearing of articles of clothing. A couple of examples
are moonhapnii, 'dig potatoes' (/apin, opin/, 'potato'), and naadsabii, 'check one's fishing
net' (/asaby/, 'fish net'). A variety of such verbs is presented in Chapter 9.12.20, Incorpo-
rated Goal Verbs, beginning on page 409.
    Other processes produce goal-like elements inside of a verb. For example, VERBS OF
POSSESSION (all VAI) have an INITIAL COMPONENT consisting of the possessed form of a
noun, including possessed theme /-im/ where appropriate, and bearing inflection for a third
person possessor, though this fact is sometimes obscured in Nishnaabemwin by the effect of
syncope, which deletes the initial /o/ representing the third person prefix, /o(d)-/. Some
examples are dakiimi, 'own land' (stem /odakiimi/, cf. /aki/, 'land' Nl) and nahaangshiimi,
'have a son-in-law' (stem /onahaangishiimi/, cf. /nahaangishim/ 'son-in-law' NA). The fol-
lowing two sentences show a contrast in the treatment of the noun zhoon 'yaa, 'money,' as
the base of a verb of possession, in (130), and as an independent noun, in (131).

         ji-giishpnadooyaambaa iw mtig, mil baamaa iw da-giishkwag aw mtig.

    Another common verbal derivative is the VERB OF MAKING AND GATHERING, which adds
animate intransitive (VAI) final /-(i)ke/ to a noun initial, as in mnoomnike, 'gather wild rice,'
with noun mnoomin, 'wild rice' NI as initial, and giigoonyke, 'fish,' with noun giigoonh,
'fish' NA as initial. Impersonal verbs of abundance are created by adding inanimate intransi-
tive final /-kaa/ to a noun initial, as in nimkiikaa, 'be thundering' (from noun nimkii, 'Thun-
derer' NA) and moodyikaa, 'be lots of bottles' (from mooday, 'bottle' NI). See Chapter
9.12.21.4, (p. 418) for more details. VERBS OF ABUNDANCE suffix /-kaa/ to form vn verbs,
e.g., moodyikaa, 'be an abundance of bottles' (see Chapter 9.11.3, (p. 373)),

13.4.2 Increasing the Number of Semantic Roles Associated with a Verb

    Other morphological processes add grammatical roles to a verb, or alter its role configu-
ration. The two most common processes are CAUSATIVE-FORMATION and APPLICA-
TIVE-ADVANCEMENT. I will discuss each of these processes below. I also briefly discuss
VERBS OF ACCOMPANIMENT.


13.4.2.1 Causative-formation

   This process takes an intransitive (VAI) stem as input and adds a transitive animate final
(VTA), often /-h/, to produce a causative in which the actor is an agent who acts directly or
indirectly upon a goal, causing the goal to undertake the action of the intransitive verb either
voluntarily or involuntarily. An example of a verb formed by CAUSATIVE-FORMATION is
                                                    13.4.2.2 Applicatives as Primary Objects • 699



mwihaad, 'make AN cry,' which is formed by adding the transitive animate causative final
/-h/ to the VAI verb, mwi, 'cry.' The following list provides examples.

        Causative    Gloss                            Base           Gloss                  PoS
        baatiinhaad  'have a lot of AN '              baatiino       'be many'              vai
        bbaamgaahaad 'spin AN , whirl dancing'        bbaamgaa       'dance around'         vai
        gwihaad      'clothe AN '                     gwid           'wear (Y)'             vaio
        mdoodoohaad 'give AN a steam bath'            mdoodood       'take a steam bath     vai
        mwihaad      'make AN cry'                    mwid           'cry'                  vai
        nbehaad      'put AN to bed'                  nbaad          'sleep'                vai
        niimhaad     'make AN dance'                  niimid         'dance'                vai
        nmadbihaad   'make AN sit'                    nmadbi         'sit'                  vai

   In one common verb, a VTI seems to serve as a base for causative formation,
waabndahaad, 'show Y to AN,' evidently from VTI stem /waaband-am/, 'see IN.' The fol-
lowing chart illustrates the process of causative-formation.

                                           Causative-Formation
                       1
                         Start with an intransitive (VAI) verb
                       1
                         Make it transitive by adding a VTA final, usually /-h/
                       1
                         Agent is actor of new transitive
                       1
                         Subject of old intranstive becomes goal of new transitive

    Causation involving an instrument is commonly expressed with complex finals incorpo-
rating notions of instrumentality and causation. These are discussed at length in Chapter 10.

13.4.2.2 Applicatives as Primary Objects

    Nishnaabemwin tends to give grammatical prominence to humans by inflectionally
indexing semantic roles customarily associated with them, at the expense of roles stan-
dardly filled by non-living entities. For example, all verbs involving the transfer of some-
thing, including concepts such as giving, sending, receiving, writing, ordering, and feeding,
treat the (typically) human receiver of the transfer as the grammatical goal, and these verbs
are thus all transitive animate (VTA) because the recipient is animate. It doesn't matter what
the gender of the object transferred is, it is irrelevant to the sub-classification of the verb as
VTA or VTI, because it does not function as the grammatical goal, and is not inflectionally
recognized except perhaps in certain participles. English has two ways of expressing the
roles associated with transfer verbs, as in the following examples.

   (a) Peanut mailed a book to me.
   (b) Peanut mailed me a book.
700 • 13.4.2.2 Applicatives as Primary Objects


    In the first, the recipient, grammatically called the INDIRECT OBJECT, and equivalent to
the goal in Nishnaabemwin, is expressed by means of a prepositional phrase, 'to me,' and
the DIRECT OBJECT, which follows directly after the verb, is 'a book.' In the second exam-
ple, however, it appears that the recipient ('me') is the direct object, because there is no
longer a preposition associated with it, and it is now in the direct object position directly fol-
lowing the verb.
    The treatment of recipients as primary grammatical goals is the norm in Nishnaabem-
win, and is commonly indexed with morphological changes in the verb. I call this process
APPLICATIVE-ADVANCEMENT, which indexes the recipient (primary object) as the inflec-
tional goal while ignoring the semantic theme (secondary object). Applicative is a cover
term that applies to such categories as the recipients of transfer verbs and the beneficiaries
of benefactive verbs, such as zhitmawaad, 'make something for AN,' as well as many other
peripheral semantic roles. In English, these roles are typically expressed with the help of
prepositions such as to, from, and for, though, as we have seen, they can sometimes be pro-
moted to the status of direct object, in which case they directly follow the verb and do not
have an associated preposition. Nishnaabemwin shows a similar promotion, obligatorily,
often by modifying the verb. Applicative-advancement takes as input a transitive stem, usu-
ally formally a transitive inanimate (VTI) stem, and adds the transitive animate final /-aw/ or
/-amaw/, to produce a verb in which the original actor carries out the action of the verb for
the benefit of the derived goal, or in relation to the derived goal in some way. Many verbs
involving the transfer of an object show applicative-advancement. The verb gains a new
goal, either the beneficiary, affected one(s), or recipient of a transfer. The old goal, repre-
 senting the object manipulated, remains, but is only inflectionally marked on the verb in the
most exceptional circumstances, such as in participle forms directly focusing on it. For
example, in the following sentence, the actor role is filled by aw kwe, 'that woman,' and the
goal role by first person singular, represented only by inflection on the verb. The object
being made, nbabgiwyaan, 'my shirt,' is not inflectionally indexed on the verb in any way.

   (132) Aw kwe ndazhtamaag nbabgiwyaan. I 'That woman is making me a shirt.'
           Aw pr SsProx 'that'; kwe na SsProx 'woman'; ndazhtamaag vta ind 3sProx»ls 'ANsg
           makes for me'; nbabgiwyaan ni ls(0s) 'my shirt.' (AM39.356)


   The following chart summarizes the workings of APPLICATIVE-ADVANCEMENT.

                                        Applicative-Advancement
                  Start with a transitive inanimate (VTI) verb stem
                  Make it transitive animate by adding VTA final /-aw/ or /-amaw/
                  The actor of the old transitive remains actor of new transitive
                  Goal of old (VTI) transitive loses inflectional status
                  Recipient, beneficiary, affectee becomes goal of new (VTA) transitive
                                                    13.4.2.2 Applicatives as Primary Objects • 701



    Note that a few transfer verbs do not have /-(am)aw/ in their structure, e.g., miinaad,
'give X to AN,' wihaad, 'lend X to AN,' daawmaad, 'borrow X from AN,' and gmoodmaad,
'steal X from AN.'
    To give some idea of the range of meanings associated with applicatives, the following
verbs represent a variety of examples. More detail can be found in Chapter 10.7, Accompa-
niment and Benefactive (Applicative) Finals, beginning on page 461.

           aajidaabaadwaad          'haul something for AN by dragging'
           aawshkwetmawaad          'haul hay for AN'

           bskaabwidmawaad          'bring something back for AN'

    APPLICATIVE-ADVANCEMENT APPLIED TO INTRANSITIVE BASES. Applicative-advance-
ment is also freely used in the formation of verbs from intransitive stems. For example, the
verb nshkaadziitwaad, 'be angry at AN,' is formed by adding /-taw/ to the VAI stem
/nishkaadizi/, 'be angry.' Other examples formed similarly are nokiitwaad, 'work for AN'
(VAI stem /anokii/, 'work'), dbaajmotwaad, 'talk about something to AN,' (VAI stem
/dibaajmo/ 'narrate, report'), Nishnaabemtawaad, 'speak Indian to AN' (VAI stem
/anishinaabemo/, 'speak Indian'), and debwetwaad, 'believe AN' (VAI stem /debwe/, 'be
right, speak the truth'). The element I-\J added to the VAI stem would seem to produce a
dummy (empty) VTI stem to satisfy the input requirements of the process of applica-
tive-advancement.

   (133) Wnishkaadziitwaan wiidgemaagnan.
         'S/he is angry with her/his spouse.' (AM39.322) [Cf. nshkaadzi, 'be angry' VAI]

          Wnishkaadziitwaan vta ind 3sProx»3obv 'ANsg is angry with ANobv';
          wiidgemaagnan na 3sProx(3obv) 'ANsg's spouse.'

13.4.2.3 Verbs of Accompaniment (Comitatives)

    Another process that changes the role structure of a verb by increasing its number of
roles is one that produces verbs of accompaniment (also called Comitatives). In simple
terms, this process adds VTA final /-m/, usually to a VAI verb, and prepends preverb wiiji-,
'with' (also wiij-) or its corresponding root, /wiid-/. An example is wiiji-mnikwemaad,
'drink with AN,' formed from VAI verb mnikwe, 'drink.' The formation of these verbs is
treated in detail in Chapter 10.7, Accompaniment and Benefactive (Applicative) Finals,
beginning on page 461. Other examples are wiijnokiimaad, 'work with AN,' formed from
nokii, 'work' VAI, and wiij-yaamaad, 'live with AN,' formed from yaa, 'be (in a place).'

   (135) Ngii-mkawaag dash kina mno-bmaadziwaad gonda waajnokiimgig.

          'I found those I work with here all in good health.' (AM 12.5)

          Ngii-mkawaag vta ind ls»3pProx 'I found ANpl'; dash av 'then'; kina av 'all';
          mno-bmaadziwaad vai conj SpProx '(CONJ) ANpl live well'; gonda pr na 3pProx
          'these'; waajnokiimgig vta ic conj part ls»3pProx '(CCNJ) whom I work with ANpl.'


13.5 Summary

    Concepts can be cast in a variety of ways in Nishnaabemwin, and there exist in the lan-
guage families of verbs which provide different kinds of focus on the participants in a ver-
bal event or action. The following charts provide a few illustrations of such families. Almost
any transitive animate verb (VTA) can be inflectionally passivized as well, which eliminates
the agent role and promotes the goal role to subject (S-role). Transitive inanimate verbs
(VTI) do not have inflectional passive forms that promote their goals, but a variety of lexical
passives exist which accomplish similar ends. A lexical passive is different from an inflec-
tional passive in adding a derivational final to a verb's structure, creating a different word
(lexeme), rather than merely inflecting an existing word, as an inflectional passive does.
    In the case of verbs of transfer, benefit, and other kinds of association (ditransitives), the
                                                                            13.5 Summary • 703


recipient, beneficiary, and related roles serve as the inflectional goal (the primary goal). The
object transferred (the secondary goal) is not usually inflectionally represented. I call this
phenomenon applicative-advancement, because of its correspondence to equivalent gram-
matical rules in languages such as English.
    In some cases, goals can be incorporated into medial position within a verb, producing
an intransitive verb. Other kinds of verbs have notional goals functioning as initials, e.g.,
verbs of possession, such as (w)zhoon'yaami, 'have money' VAI (W, CL).
    Causatives can be formed from intransitive verbs, as can verbs of accompaniment (com-
itatives).
    The following charts provide a few summary illustrations of word families showing dif-
ferent kinds of role-focus.

                 Verb Form          Part of Speech        Gloss
                 mnozwaad           vta                   'cook AN'
                 mnozang            vti                   'cook IN'
                 mnozmawaad         vta (benefactive)     'cook something for AN'
                 mnozod             vai (goal focus)      'cook, be cooked'
                 mnodeg             vii (goal focus)      'cook, be cooked'
                 mnozekwe           vai (actor focus)     'cook, bake'



                 Verb Form          Part of Speech        Gloss
                 dkobnaad           vta                   'tie AN fast'
                 dkobdood           vti                   'tie IN fast'
                 dkobzod            vai (goal focus)      'be tied up'
                 dkobdeg            vii (goal focus)      'be tied up'
                 dkobjiged          vai (actor focus)     'tie things; tie one's shoes'
                 dkobjigan          ni                    'tie-on ice skate'
                 dkobjigan          ni                    'bailing machine'


                 Verb Form          Part of Speech        Gloss
                 jaagzwaad          vta                   'burn AN'
                 jaagzang           vti                   'burn IN'
                 jaagzo             vai (goal focus)      'burn (up)'
                 jaagde             vii (goal focus)      'burn (up)'
                 jaagzigaazo        vai (goal focus)      'be burned out'
                 jaagzigaade        vii (goal focus)      'be burned out'

Being and Becoming




    This chapter looks at a few of the ways that Nishnaabemwin expresses the concepts of
being and becoming. Nishnaabemwin uses several distinct constructions to assert identity or
existence. These include the VERBS OF IDENTITY, aawi (VAl) and aawan (VII) and the LOCA-
TIONAL VERBS OF BEING, yaa (VAI) and yaa(mgad) (vn), and hi (VAI) and te (VII). Another
verb, dgo (VAI) and dgon (also dgomgad) (VII), can be used to specify the existence of sta-
tionary objects in a particular location. Various verbs of number exist which specify both the
existence of something and provide some quantitative measure, such as baatiino, 'be abun-
dant, be many' (VAI) and niswag, 'be three in number' (VAI). There are also a couple of
INTRANSITIVE FINALS which take NOUN INITIALS and form VERBS OF BEING (/-wi/ VAI and
/-wan/ VII) or verbs OF ABUNDANCE (/-kaa/ VII). All of these constructions are discussed
below. The following chart summarizes the constructions that are examined in this chapter.

                                       Animate              Inanimate
           identity, existence         aawi (VAI)           aawan (vn)
           identity, existence         VAI FINAL /-wi/      vn FINAL /-wan/
           location, state of being    yaa (VAI)            yaa(mgad) (vn)
           location                    dgo (VAI)            dgo(n), dgomgad (vn)
           location                    bi (VAI)             te (vii)
           quantity                    baatiino (VAI)       baatiinad (vii)
           abundance                                  VII FINAL /-kaa/

14.1 The Verbs of Identity Aawi and Aawan

   The animate intransitive verb (VAI) aawi and corresponding inanimate intransitive (VII)
aawan are mainly used to predicate IDENTITY. A predication of identity asserts that a given
individual belongs to a particular group or has a particular social role or relation, that is, it
                                                 14.1 The Verbs of Identity Aawi and Aawan • 705


classifies the subject with the formula, 'X is a Y,' as in the following example, where the
speaker's grandfather is identified as a Potawatomi.

   (1)   Boodewaadmii gii-aawi aw nmishoomis, Wisconsin odi gii-dnizwag.
         'My grandfather was a Potawatomi, they lived there in Wisconsin.' (AK15.1)

         Boodewaadmii na 3sProx 'Potawatomi'; gii-aawi vai ind 3sProx 'ANsg was'; awprn
         BsProx 'that'; nmishoomis nad Is(SsProx) 'my grandfather'; odi av 'there'; gii-dnizwag
         vai ind 3pProx 'ANpl lived there.'


   Statements of identity involve two nominals, one of which functions as a subject, and the
other as a predicate nominal. The subject may be a noun or noun phrase, a pronominal, or,
when understood from context, indicated solely by means of verbal inflection. The noun in
the role of predicate nominal usually immediately precedes the verb, perhaps because it is
customarily indefinite, and represents new information, which tends to occur early in Nish-
naabemwin clauses. The subject more commonly follows the verb, producing the following
schematic:

                      Predicate Nominal Verb            (Subject)
                      Boodewaadmii      gn-aawi         aw nmishoomis

   The following sentences provide additional examples.

   (2)   Gaa wiin Wemitigoozhiikwe gii-aawisii aw mindimooyenh Anishinaabekwe
         gii-aawi.
         That old woman was not a Frenchwoman; she was an Indian woman.' (AW 16.58)

          Gaa av 'not'; wiin av 'then'; Wemitigoozhiikwe na SsProx 'a white woman'; gii-aawisii
          vai ind neg SsProx 'ANsg was not'; a-w prn 3sProx 'that'; mindimooyenh na 3sProx 'old
          woman'; Anishinaabekwe na SsProx 'Indian woman'; gii-aawi vai ind SsProx 'ANsg
          was.'


   (3)   Gonda niizh gii-ggiinwishkwag; gaawii gonda wedaaseg aawsiiwag.
         These other two were lying; they were not really braves.' (SO6.117)

          were liars'; gaawii av 'not'; gonda prn na 3pProx 'these'; wedaaseg na 3pProx
          'warriors'; aawsiiwag vai ind neg 3pProx 'ANpl were not.'
706 • 14.1 The Verbs of Identity Aawi and Aawan

          Aabita-animosh na 'half-dog'; aawi vai ind3sProx 'ANsg is.'

   (16) Holiday na aawan waabang? I 'Is tomorrow a holiday?' (MC)

   The following examples illustrate a focus construction using aawan, in which a pronom-

verb.

   (17) Gchi-nakiiwin maanda aawan zhibiihgaadeg grammar.
         'It's a huge task this writing a grammar.' (MC)

          Gchi-nakiiwin ni Os 'a great work'; maanda prdemOs 'this'; aawan vii ind Os 'INsg is';
          zhibiihgaadeg vii conj Os '(CONJ) IN is written.'
                                   14.2 Denominal Verbs of Being with Finals /-wi/ and /-wan/. • 709


   (18) Gaawii gegoo maanda aawnzinoo bemi-mbiighigyin.

         'It's nothing, this thing that's got you ranting.' (MC)

          Gaawii gegoopr neg Os 'nothing'; maandapr dem Os 'this' aawnzinoo vii indneg Os
          'INsg is not'; bemi-mbiigigyin vta ic conj 0»2s '(CCNJ) which (IN) makes you rant.'


    As with most predicates in Ojibwe, verbs of being are systematically ambiguous
between STATIVE ('be') and INCHOATIVE ('come to be') interpretations, and so have transla-
tions equivalent to both English 'be' and 'become.' The following sentence illustrates the
latter interpretation of aawi See also the examples on p. 337.

14.2 Denominal Verbs of Being with Finals /-wi/ and /-wan/.

    A noun can also serve as a base to which is attached a verbal FINAL, -wi for animate
nouns and -wan for inanimates, to produce a DENOMINAL verb of being, which is identifica-
tional, either statively or mutatively. Inanimate verbs of being are less common, though they
are sometimes used in borrowings from English, such as in terms for the days of the week,
e.g., Sundaywan, 'it is Sunday.' Examples of inanimates from Piggott and Grafstein are
oodenaawan, 'be a town' (« oodena NI 'town') and ziitaaganiwan, 'be salty' (« ziitaagan
NI 'salt'). The following examples illustrate animates.

   (20) Washme wiin kiwenztinywi. I 'He is a still older man.' (AM39.109)

          Washme av 'more'; wiin av 'then'; kiwenziinywi vai ind3sProx 'ANsg is an old man.'

   (21) Otahaa! Mii giiwenh zhaazhi go aabta-gtigoonywid wa!

         'Goodness! He is already half-fishl' (SOS.29)

          Otahaa av 'oh my!.' Mii av 'then'; giiwenh av 'allegedly'; zhaazhi av 'already';
          aabta-giigoonywid vai conj 3sProx '(CONJ) ANsg is half become a fish'; vraprn 3sProx
          'this one.'
710 • 14.3 Locational/Existential Verbs Yaa and Yaa(mgad)


   (22) Geget sa naa gmino-gwiiwzensiw. I 'Really, now, you are a good boy.' (AM39.36)
          Geget av 'truly'; gmino-gwiiwzensiw vai ind 2s 'you are a good boy.'

    The last two examples illustrate another point about verbs of being, namely that the stem
to which the VERBAL FINAL is attached may include PRENOUNS, and the VERB FINAL can
have scope over the entire complex. So, for example, mno-gwiiwzenswi, 'be a good boy,' is
bracketed as [[mino-gwiiwzens]wi], while aabta-giigoonywi has the structure [aabta-[[gii-
goonyjwi]].
    With regard to the stative and inchoative readings of verbs of being mentioned in the pre-
vious section, with the verb forms in this section the inchoative reading seems to be the
default interpretation with past tense, while the stative is the more common default interpre-
tation with present tense, e.g., gii-dkonweniniiwi, with past tense, is more likely to be neu-
trally interpreted as 'he became a cop,' and dknonweniniiwi as 'he is a cop.' Speakers have
preferences too as to whether to use an aawi construction or VERB OF BEING, in different sit-
uations. For example, while it's possible to use ko, 'used to,' with a verb of being, as in
gii-dknoweniniiwi ko, 'he used to be a cop,' the form dkonwenini ko gii-aawi is preferred.
    Derivational aspects of denominal verbs of being are discussed in Chapter 9, beginning
on p. 363.
    DEPENDENT NOUNS such as KINSHIP TERMS can also serve as initials in the formation of
verbs of being, as in ookmiswi, 'be a grandmother,' with initial /-ookmis/, 'grandmother,'
though it is also common to use a VERB OF POSSESSION for such concepts, as in ooshenyi,
 'have a grandchild' (i.e., 'be a grandparent'), with initial /-oosheny/, 'grandchild.'.

14.3 Locational/Existential Verbs Yaa and Yaa(mgad)

   The verb yaa most commonly predicates existence restricted to a particular location,
though it is also metaphorically extended to apply to states of being, particularly those of
the mind and body. In its normal locational usage, it occurs with some specified location,
most commonly a LOCATIONAL ADVERB, such as maa, 'here,' or besho, 'near.'

   (23)   Gga-kawaabndaanmaandajiimaanmaajoas'H'aan.
          'You'll look after this boat when I'm not here.'" (AK13.22)

          Gga-kawaabndaan vti ind 2s»0s 'you SG will look after INsg'; maandapm Os 'this';
          jiimaan ni Os 'boat'; maa av 'here'; yaaswaan vai conj Is neg '(CONJ) I am not (here).'


   (24) Aaniish mnik nimshag eyaawaadl I 'How many dogs are there?' (KK1.38)
          Aaniish av 'how'; mnik av 'many'; nimshag na SpProx 'dogs'; eyaawaad vai ic conj
          SpProx '(CCNJ) ANpl are.'
                                           14.3 Locational/Existential Verbs Yaa and Yaa(mgad) • 711



   (25)   "Aakaa giiwenh go naa iidig giigoonh zhandaji-yaad ndahbaaning!"

          "That's a hell of a place for a fish to be, here in a water-hole!'" (SO3.22)

          Aakaa av 'hell of a place'; giiwenh av 'evidently'; iidig av 'perhaps'; giigoonh na
          SsProx 'fish'; zhanda av 'here'; ji-yaad vai conj 3sProx '(CONJ) ANsg would be there';
          ndahbaaning ni 0 loc 'in the water hole.'


    The verb yaa is also used as an existential, that is, to introduce characters into a dis-
course by predicating their existence, either generally or in a particular location, rather sim-
ilarly to English 'there was/were' constructions.

   (26) Aabdeg go gii-yaa aw wshkinwe gaa-nbwaakaad gaa-jepzid miinwaa
        gii-gzhiikaabtoo.
          There was sure to be a young man who was intelligent, smart and he ran fast.'

          Aabdeg av 'necessarily'; gii-yaa vai ind SsProx 'ANsg was there'; awprn 3sProx 'that';
          wshkinwe na SsProx 'young man'; gaa-nbwaakaad vai ic conj part SsProx '(CCNJ)
          who (ANsg) was wise'; gaa-jepzid vai ic conj part SsProx '(CCNJ) who ANsg was
          bright'; miinwaa av 'and'; gii-gzhiikaabtoo vai ind SsProx 'ANsg ran fast.' (AK9.1)


   (27)   Mii dash noongo iw wenji-yaawaad giw ngoji debendaagzisgog nishnaabeg.

          And now that's why there are those Indians who don't belong anywhere.'

          Mii av 'and'; dash av 'so'; noongo av 'now'; ivrprn Os 'that'; wenji-yaawaad vai ic conj
          SpProx '(CCNJ) why ANpl are'; giwpra 3pProx 'those'; ngoji av 'anywhere';
          debendaagziSGog vai ic conj part SpProx neg '(CCNJ) who (ANpl) don't belong to a
          group'; nishnaabeg na SpProx 'Indians.' (AK9.10)


   (28)   Yaa gwa Gzhe-mnidoo. I There is a God; God exists.' (MC)

          Yaa vai ind SsProx ANsg is (there)'; gwa av 'emphasis'; Gzhe-mnidoo na SsProx 'God.'

   In sentence (28), the verb must come first, since the nature of the predication is focusing
on the assertion of existence.
   YAA AND TRANSITIVE VERBS OF POSSESSION. The existential verb yaa shows a mor-
phological relationship with the standard transitive verbs of possession, yaawaad, 'have
AN' (VTA, stem /ayaaw/) and yaang, 'have IN' (VTI, stem /ayaam/). This relationship
between existentials and possessives is found very commonly among the languages of the
world. The intransitive verb yaa can also be used in notionally possessive contexts.
712 • 14.3 Locational/Existential Verbs Yaa and Yaa(mgad)


   (29)   Yaawan wgwisan. I 'He has a son.' (AM)

          Yaawan vai ind SsProx 'there is ANsg'; wgwisan nad 3sProx(3obv) 'ANsg's son.'

   YAA WITH DIRECTIONAL PREVERBS. Used in combination with the DIRECTIONAL PRE-
VERBS such as hi-, 'hither, towards,' and bbaa-, 'around, distributed location,' bi-ayaa and
bbaa-ayaa indicate motion to a location or around it. In a sense, it is as if the verbal base
serves as a empty stem to which meaningful directional elements can be attached.

   (30) Miish wa mndimooyenh bbaa-yaad, mii gii-waabmaad ninwan, mansooyan.
          This old lady was wandering around, and she saw some men, strangers.'
          (SO2.3)

          Miish av 'then'; \vapm 3sProx 'this'; mdimooyenh no. SsProx 'old woman'; bbaa-yaad
          vai conj SsProx '(CONJ) ANsg goes around'; mii av 'then'; gii-waabmaad vta conj
          SsProx 3obv '(CONJ) ANsg saw ANobv'; ninwan na Sobv 'man/men'; man'soonyan na
          3obv 'sneak(s).'

   (31) Nenbozh go sha gii-bmi-yaa. I 'Why, Nenabush came by here' (AM35.13)
          Nenbozh na SsProx 'Nenabush'; gii-bmi-yaa vai ind SsProx 'ANsg came along.'

   (32) Mii dash besho eni-yaayaan maa endnakmigzid.
          'Then I got near to where she was working.' (AM8.32)

          there'; maa av 'there'; endnakmigzid vai ic conj SsProx '(CCNJ) ANsg was busy there.'

   ZHI-YAA(MAGAD). The relative preverb zhi- (preverb form of root /iN/) denotes way or
manner, and in combination with yaa indicates a general situational state. Predicated of
humans, it generally refers to one's state of health, and when used interrogatively, implies a
condition with cause for concern, as in the following example.

14.4 Existence in a Particular Location with Dgo and Dgon (Dgomgad)

    The locational verbs dgo (VAI) and dgon (VII) are used to predicate the existence of some
relatively stationary object in a particular location, typically natural objects or plants. In ref-
erence to the latter, it is sometimes translated with 'grows,' though the idea is existence in a
particular place.

         miinwaa av 'also.'

15
Location and Manner




    In this chapter I present an introduction to the various ways that locations are specified in
Nishnaabemwin. I also look briefly at the way that the manner in which things are done can
be expressed. In the first section three locational semantic relations are outlined, fixed
(static) location, origin location, and destination location. This is followed with a look at
how various locational concepts find representation in particular locational vocabulary. Fol-
lowing this, we look at various locational adverbials, then locative nouns. Next I consider
the form of clauses used to specify locations. The chapter concludes with a brief account of
manner expressions, especially those used to express similarity or likeness.

15.1 Locational Perspectives

    Three distinct locational perspectives are prominent in Nishnaabemwin: that of simple
location, that is, fixed location in a particular place with no change of location, though there
may be other kinds of movement (i.e., movement "in place"); that of the SOURCE location of
some movement; and that of the DESTINATION location of some movement. Locational
semantic roles rarely ever fill SEMANTIC MACROROLES of ACTOR or GOAL (see Chapter 13),
so they are usually not indexed INFLECTIONALLY on the verb in Nishnaabemwin. When
nouns are used to specify locations, they usually carry a locative suffix.
    Several RELATIVE ROOTS, or their corresponding RELATIVE PREVERBS, are prominent in
location and motion (change of location) expressions, namely /daN-/, /iN-/, and /ond-/,
which prototypically have meanings corresponding to the three locational perspectives out-
lined in the previous paragraph. The following table summarizes their functions.

                                 place of location       /daN/
                                 place of destination    /iN/
                                 place of origin         /ond/
722 • 15.1 Locational Perspectives


    There are also a few locational verbs that behave like those having relative roots and pre-
verbs, in that they typically occur with, and are not complete without, some kind of loca-
tional complement, which may be an adverb, a nominal, or a clause. Examples include yaa,
'be (in a place)' (yaa(mgad)), daa, 'dwell (in a place) VAI, bi, 'sit/be in a certain place' VAI,
and te, 'sit/be in a certain place' VII.

   (1)   Maa dash e-ndhamaang dkibi [aabtawdaakiyaamgad], [besho yaag] nbis.
         'The spring from which we got the water is halfway up a hill, it is near a lake.'
         (AM 10.6)

          Maa av 'there'; dash av 'then'; e-ndhamaang vti ic conj lp»0 '(CCNJ) where we got IN
          from'; dkibi ni Os 'spring of water'; aabtawdaaki av 'halfway up a hill'; yaamgad vii ind
          Os 'INsg is there'; besho av 'nearby'; yaag vii conj 0 '(CONJ) IN is there'; nbis ni Os
          'lake.'


   (2)   Mii dash gii-bi-zhaad wshkinwe [odi endaayaan].
         'A young man came there where I live! (AK7.1)

          Mii av 'and so'; dash av 'then'; gii-bi-zhaad vai conj SsProx '(CONJ) ANsg came here';
          wshkinwe na SsProx 'young man'; odi av 'there'; endaayaan vai ic conj Is '(CCNJ)
          where I live.'


    SIMPLE (STATIC) LOCATION. The semantic relation of static location specifies the loca-
tion where an action or event takes place. If the location is indicated with a noun phrase, the
HEAD NOUN of the phrase shows locative inflection. Very often locative adverbs occur in
conjunction with locative nouns, in which case the adverb almost always precedes the asso-
ciated noun. In (3), below, for example, locative adverbs maa, 'there,' and ddibew, 'on the
bank,' occur with a locative-inflected noun, ziibing, 'on/by the river,' and in (4), maa occurs
with noun locative wninjiing, 'on ANsg's hand(s).'

   (3)    E-shki-waabmag aw Gchi-mookmaan maa ddibew ziibing ngii-zeghig.
         'The first time I saw a white man there by the bank of the river, he frightened
         me.'(AM3.1

          E-shki-waabmag via ic conj ls»3sProx '(CCNJ) when I first saw ANsg'; awprn SsProx
          'that'; Gchi-mookmaan na SsProx 'white American'; maa av 'there'; ddibew av 'on the
          bank'; ziibing ni 0 loc 'by the river'; ngii-zeghig vta ind 3sProx»ls 'ANsg frightened
          me.'
                                                                  15.1 Locational Perspectives • 723



   (4)   Mil dash iw gii-bchinaajgaazod aw nmishoomis maa wninjiing,
         niiho-bboongizgoban giiwenh iw pii.
          'And my grandfather was struck by accident there on his hand, he was reportedly
          four years old at the time.' (AK10.14)

          Mii av 'and'; dash av 'then'; iwprn Os 'that'; gii-bchinaajgaazod vai conjSsProx
          '(CONJ) ANsg was shot accidentally'; stwpm SsProx 'that'; nmishoomis nod ls(3sProx)

          niiho-bboongizgoban vai indpdub SsProx 'ANsg was allegedly four years old'; giiwenh
          av 'reportedly'; iw prn Os 'that'; pii av 'time.'


    The RELATIVE ROOT /daN-/, 'place, at' which takes the forms /dan/ or /dazh/, or its asso-
ciated RELATIVE PREVERB dzhi- /dazhi-/, frequently occurs in expressions specifying a par-

as in sentence (5), below, or some object pertinent to the location, as in (6).

   (5)    Gye go mii gii-miin'gooyaang rooms waa-dnizyaang.

           Ge av 'as for'; nii prn pers Is T; gwiwnan ni Op 'garments'; endzhi-wzhichgaadeg vii
           ic conj 0 '(CCNJ) where IN are made there'; ngii-zhiwnigoo vta indx»ls 'I was taken.'


    SOURCE LOCATION (ABLATIVE). The semantic relation of SOURCE specifies the place of
origin of a verbal activity or motion. If the source is indicated with a noun phrase, the head
noun of the phrase shows locative inflection. Very often specifications of source involve the
relative root /ond/, 'source; reason' (also /onj-/), or its associated preverb /onji-/ (or /nji-/) or
adverb, nji.

     DESTINATION LOCATION (ALLATIVE). The semantic relation of destination specifies the
locational endpoint of a verbal action or motion. If the location is indicated with a noun
phrase, the head noun of the phrase shows locative inflection, as with kikong, 'into the ket-
tle,' in (9), below. Very often the relative root /iN/, 'direction, manner,' or its associated rela-
tive preverb /zhi-/, occurs in predications involving destinations or the specification of a
"way," or manner. The root form varies between /in/, /izh/, and simple devoicing of the stem
it is attached to. The following examples illustrate a few of its hundreds of lexically specific
forms.

   pide              /iN+bide/             vii   'drive to a certain place/in a certain way"
   patoo             /iN+batoo/            vai   'run to a certain place/in a certain way'
   kido              /iN+gido/             vai   'say'
   naande            /iN+aande/            vii   'be coloured a certain way'
   namo              /iN+amo/              vii   'be road running to a certain place'
   nataage           /iN+ataage/           vai   'gamble in a certain way'
   zhidaabaan'go     /iN+idaabaanigo/      vai   'ride in a certain direction'
   zhinaagzi         /iN+inaagozi/         vai   'look a certain way'
   zhinkaazo         /iN+inikaazo/         vai   'have a certain name'

   A couple of examples illustrating the expression of destination:
