          Nbiish ni Os 'water'; wgii-toon vti ind3sPwx»Os 'ANsg put INsg'; kikong na 3 loc 'into
          kettle.'


   (10) Mii dash gwyak odi gaa-z/H-giiwewaad Neyaashii-nagmiing.
         And they went straight home to Cape Croker.' (AK10.16)

          Mii av 'so'; dash av 'then'; gwyak av 'straight'; odi av 'there'; gaa-zhi-giiwewaad vai ic
          conj SpProx '(CCNJ) ANpl went home there'; Neyaashii-nagmiing place 'to Cape
          Croker.'

    Rhodes 1990 observes that the locational complements of relative elements associated
with verbs are sensitive to defmiteness in their word-order patterns, such that complements
that are definite (old information) tend to follow the verb, while those that are indefinite
(new information) tend to precede it. Rhodes also observes that there are two classes of
exceptions to this general pattern. First, the the complements of relative roots inside of rela-
tive clauses sometimes occur to the right of their associated verbs, in order to keep the rela-
tivized verb adjacent to the noun being modified by the relative clause. The following
example (from Rhodes 1990:4) illustrates.

   (11) [Aw epgidang bkwaakod]NOM [ezhnikaazod Wellington Shognosh]RC, mii aw...
         As for the pitcher, whose name is Wellington Shognosh, he's the one...'

          Aw pr 3 sProx 'that (one)'; epgidang vti ic conj part 3sProx»0. '(CCNJ) who (ANsg)
          throws IN'; bkwaakod ni Os 'ball'; ezhnikaazod vai ic conj part SsProx '(CCNJ) who
          (ANsg) is named'; mii adv 'it's'; aw pr 3 sProx 'that (one)'. (AM17.9 partial)

   Here the relative clause, ezhnikaazod Wellington Shognosh, 'whose name is Wellington
Shognosh,' modifies the preceding nominal aw epgidang bkwaakod, 'the one who throws
the ball,' (i.e., the pitcher). Normally the name Wellington Shognosh, which is the comple-
ment of the relative root /iN/ in ezhnikaazod, 'be named X,' would appear before
ezhnikaazod, but here it follows it, in order to keep ezhnikaazod adjacent to the nominal
modified by the whole relative clause, ezhnikaazod Wellington Shognosh. Rhodes also
points out that there is also a tendency for definite noun phrase complements to precede
their verbs when they are definite 'by virtue of iaferability or common experience' (p. 4), in
contrast to corresponding non-complement definites. This points to an important fact about
word order patterns generally, namely that definiteness distinctions can be quite nuanced,
726 • 15.2 The Lexical Expression of Location


and a complete account of their relationships to ordering patterns in Nishnaabemwin awaits
a much more thorough study than I can provide here.

15.2 The Lexical Expression of Location

    Nishnaabemwin shows considerable richness and variety in the way that locational con-
cepts are realized, in part because the locative roots that are used to express them can be
used in a great variety of ways, including serving as roots of locational adverbs having clas-
sificatory and geographical finals, as in (12) to (14) below, as roots in more general locative
adverbs, as in (15), in prenouns, as in (16), and as root forms in verbs referring to specific
locational orientations, as in (17). An extensive list of locational adverbs can be found in
Chapter 3 (p. 140), and some lexical sets are listed below in Section 15.9, page 742.

   (12) Gidaaki gii-zhaa. I 'He went up on the hill.' (AM39.55) [/-aaki/ 'hill']
          Gidaaki av 'on top of hill'; gii-zhaa vai ind SsProx 'ANsg went there.'


   (13) Wgii-ni-waabmaan dash widi bnensan gidaatig nmadbinid.

         branch.' (AM36.2) [/-aatig/ 'sticklike object']

          'over there'; bnensan na 3obv 'nestling partridge(s)'; gidaatig av 'upon a branch';
          nmadbinid vai conj 3obv '(CONJ) ANobv sat.'


   (14) Miinwaa wgii-nganaawaan niw wshkinwensan ge-kawaabnijin gechi-gidaabik odi
        gii-nmadbi aw wshkinwens.
         And also they left this young man to be a lookout way up on top of a rock, and
         there this young man sat.' (AK15.9) [/-aabik/, 'rock']

15.2.3 Demonstrative Locative Adverbs

   A host of dialectally variable DEMONSTRATIVE locative adverbs exist. Such adverbs
express location in very general terms, in relation to some reference point, usually the loca-
tion of the speaker. General locative adverbs are thus like demonstrative pronouns, which
also get their reference in relation to some established reference point, usually the place of
speaking. These locationals sometimes behave like nominals, for example, in the ease with
which relative clauses are associated with them. The l.ocational wedi is labelled an animate
noun in Rhodes 1985. The following table lists the common general locative adverbs, fol-
lowed by a few examples.
734 • 15.2.3 Demonstrative Locative Adverbs

                        maanpii, maampii 'here'
                        zhonda, zhanda       'here' (Od)
                        maa                  'here; there'
                        zhiwi                'there' (M)
                        widi, odi, oodi      'there; over there'
                        wedi                 'that over there' (na)

   (44) Widi giiwednong gye go e-bngishmog gii-bi-wnjibaawag giw Naadweswag
        gaa-bi-mwinewaajig niw Wjibwen maanpii nikekmig.
         'From the North and from the West came those Iroquois to attack the Ojibwe here
         in this part of the country.' (AM23.27)

          Widi av 'over there'; giiwednong av 'in the north'; gye av 'and'; e-bngishmog vii ic conj
          0 '(CCNJ) where IN sets'; gii-bi-wnjibaawag vai ind 3pProx 'ANpl came hither from

    When demonstrative locatives are used in combination with other words, it seems that
their usual position is after the verb, often at the end of the clause containing them, though

         'So this man set off alone, and went over [there to the sugar camp].' (SO1.8)

          Aaniish av 'well'; mii av 'then'; gii-maajaad vai conj SsProx '(CONJ) ANsg left';
          giiwenh av 'so the story goes'; bezhig nurn 'a certain'; nini na SsProx 'man'; gii-zhaad
          vai conj SsProx '(CONJ) ANsg went there'; wadi av 'there'; ziisbaakdokaaning ni loc 0
          'to the sugaring place.'

   The post-verbal position of these expressions is in contrast to the use of the DEMONSTRA-
TIVE LOCATIVES alone, which seem to more freely occur both before the verb, as in (51),
below, and after it, as in (52).

   (51) Mii giiwenh zhiwi gii-gbeshwaad. I 'And so it seems that they made camp there.'

          Mii av 'and'; giiwenh av 'evidently'; zhiwi av 'there'; gii-gbeshwaad vai conj SpProx
          '(CONJ) ANpl camped.' (SO3.3)

   PRE-ADVERB WAS-,'BEYOND'. To express relatively more distant location, the
pre-adverb was-, 'beyond,' can be added to a distal demonstrative adverb, e.g., was-odi,
was-oodi, was-wadi, all of which mean 'way over there.'

15.3 General Directional Adverb Nakeyaa, Nikeyaa

    To specify general direction toward another location, or orientation with respect to
another location, the general directional adverb nakeyaa (also nikeyaa) is used. In the usage
of Andrew Medler, nakeyaa follows the word it modifies, in (53) and (54), locative noun
forms, and in (55), a locational IMPERSONAL verb (VII), e-bgandaanmak, 'where the wind
strikes.'

   (53) Gii-mbi-gwaashkni ziibiing nakeyaa. I 'He leaped up in the direction of the river.'
          Gii-mbi-gwaashkni vai ind SsProx 'ANsg jumped up'; ziibiing ni 0 loc 'toward the
          river'; nakeyaa av 'in such a direction.' (AM35.24)

   (54) Nbiing dash nikeyaa gidaaki gii-bngishin.
         'Down he fell into the water in the direction o/the foot of the bluff.' (AM36.21)

          Nbiing ni 0 loc 'into the water'; dash av 'then'; nikeyaa av 'in that direction'; gidaaki av
          'on top of hill'; gii-bngishin vai ind SsProx 'ANsg fell.'

   (55) E-bgandaanmak maanoo nakeyaa da-wnjigaabwi aw waa-wiikwebnind.
         'By all means, the person who is to be charmed must stand in the direction
         toward which the wind is blowing. '(AM30.9)

          E-bgandaanmak vii ic conj 0 '(CCNJ) where the wind strikes'; maanoo av
          'deliberately'; nakeyaa av 'in such a direction'; da-wnjigaabwi vai ind SsProx 'ANsg
          will stand back from there'; aw prn SsProx 'that'; waa-wiikwebnind via ic conj part
          x»3sProx '(CCNJ) who (ANsg) will be put under a love spell.'

15.4 Indefinite Location with Ngoji

    Indefinite location, often corresponding to English somewhere and anywhere, is indi-
cated in Nishnaabemwin with the locational adverb ngoji (also ngwaji), which commonly
precedes the verb it is associated with. The following examples illustrate its use.

   (56) Wegnesh ngwaji gaa-nji-zhaayan? I 'Why did you go off somewhere!'
         Wegneshpra inter 0 'what'; ngwaji av 'somewhere'; gaa-nji-zhaayan vai ic conj 2s
         '(CCNJ) from what did you go.' (AM39.575)


   (57) Naan'godnong gaa wii yaasii aw nini bbaa-ndawenjiged ngoji bgodkamig.
        'Sometimes the man of the family would not be at home, having gone off hunting
        somewhere in the wilds.' (AM32.2)

         Naan'godnong av 'sometimes'; gaa av 'not'; wii av 'then'; yaasii vai ind3sProx neg
         'ANsg is not there'; a\vpm SsProx 'that'; nini na 3sProx 'man'; bbaa-ndawenjiged vai
         conj SsProx '(CONJ) ANsg go around hunting'; ngoji av 'somewhere'; bgodkamig av
         'out in the wilds.'


   This adverb appears in construction with other adverbs, too, as in the following.

   (58) Ngoji waasa zhiwdoon. I 'Take it far off with you somewhere.' (AM39.748)

         Ngoji av 'somewhere'; waasa av 'far'; zhiwdoon vti imp 2s»0 'take IN.'

15.7 General Locational Adverbs

    There is a large number of locational adverbs. A representative list is provided in Chap-
ter 3 (p. 140). The following examples illustrate the use of such adverbs. When associated
with a relative root, as in (63) and (64), the adverb often directly precedes the verb; other-
wise, its position within the clause is quite variable, though Tomlin and Rhodes 1992:120
assert that the "unmarked" position of rhematic (new or particularly salient) adverbs is left-
                                          15.7.1 Locational Terms with /-yahii/ and /-yahiing/ • 739


ward, towards the beginning of the sentence, as in (63) and (64), below.

   (63) Besho endaayaan. I 'It is near [from here] to where I live.' (AM39.581)

          Besho av 'nearby'; endaayaan vai ic conj Is '(CCNJ) where I live.'

   (64) Waasa endaayaan. I 'It is far to where I live.' (AM39.580)
          Waasa av 'far'; endaayaan vai ic conj Is '(CCNJ) where I live.'

   (65) Gzhidemgad biindig, zaam. I 'It is hot indoors, too hot.' (AM39.238)

          Gzhidemgad vii Os 'INsg is hot'; biindig av 'inside'; zaam av 'too.'

   (66) Gwajiing biindaakwen. I 'Smoke out of doors' (AM39.729)

          Gwajiing av 'outside'; biindaakwen vai imp 2s 'smoke tobacco.'

   Locational adverbs can be combined into complex, multi-word expressions, as in the fol-
lowing sentence, where widi waasa giiwednong, 'there far to the north,' occurs.

   (67) Gye go maaba niikaanis gchi-waasa gaa-bi-wnjibaad Mister Snow widi waasa
        giiwednong ge wii ji-zhi-giiwed ndawaabndang neyaab miinwaa widi

          gchi-waasa av 'very far'; gaa-bi-wnjibaad vai ic conj BsProx '(CCNJ) where ANsg
          came from'; widi av 'over there'; waasa av 'far'; giiwednong av 'in the north'; ge av

          there'; ndawaabndang vti conj 3sProx»0 '(CONJ) ANsg look for IN'; neyaab av 'back';
          miinwaa av 'again'; widi av 'over there'; gaa-bi-wnji-maajaad vai ic conj 3sProx
          '(CCNJ) ANsg left from to come here.' (AM 13.2)

15.7.1 Locational Terms with /-yahii/ and /-yahiing/

   ROOTS ATTACHED TO FINAL /-YAHII/. Adverb FINAL /-yahii/ can be attached to orienta-
tional initials to produce general locational adverbs. A short, very incomplete list with
examples can be found in Chapter 11 (p. 523ff.). These adverbs are often used in association
with nouns inflected with a locative suffix, or with verbs having environmental medials (or

15.9 Some Specific Locational Vocabulary Sets

   In this section we list a few common adverbial locational vocabulary sets.
   SERIAL SEQUENCE. Serial sequence is expressed by means of niigaan, 'first,' njiiyenh,
'next,' and shkweyaang, 'last.'

   (78) Niigaan bmose. I 'He walks in the lead: (AM39.71)
          Niigaan av 'in front'; bmose vai ind 3sProx 'ANsg walks.'

   (79) Wiikaansan njiiyenh bmosewan. I 'His brother walks next in order.' (AM39.152)

          Wiikaansan nod 3sProx(3obv)'ANsg's brother'; njiiyenh av 'next in serial order';
          bmosewan vai ind 3obv 'ANobv walks.'


   (80) Shkweyaang bmose. I 'He walks in the rear.' (AM39.70)

          Shkweyaang av 'behind'; bmose vai ind SsProx 'ANsg walks.'

   CARDINAL DIRECTIONS. Cardinal directions are as follows. We have not been able to
find location terms for east and south, and speakers consulted say that they do not exist.

                        Term     Location             Direction
                        east     —                    waabnong
                        south    —                    zhaawnong
                        west     (e-)bngshimog        (e-)bngshimog
                        north    giiwedin             giiwednong

   (81) Zhiishiibag da-maajaawag zhaawnong. I 'The ducks will leave/or the south:

          Zhiishiibag na 3pProx 'ducks'; da-maajaawag vai indSpProx 'ANpl will leave';
          zhaawnong av 'to the south.' (AM39.129)

   (82) Widi giiwednong gye go e-bngishmog gii-bi-wnjibaawag giw Naadweswag
        gaa-bi-mwinewaajig niw Wjibwen maanpii nikekmig.
         'From the North and from the West came those Iroquois to attack the Ojibwe here
         in this part of the country.' (AM23.27)
                                                                       15.10 Locative Nouns • 743



          Widi av 'over there'; giiwednong av 'in the north'; gye av 'and'; e-bngishmog vii ic conj
          0 '(CCNJ) where IN sets'; gii-bi-wnjibaawag vai ind SpProx 'ANpl came hither from
          there'; giwpm SpProx 'those'; Naadweswag na SpProx 'Iroquois (pi)';
          gaa-bi-mwinewaajig vta ic conj part 3pProx»3obv '(CCNJ) who ANpl came and
          attacked ANobv'; niw/?m 3obv 'that/those'; Wjibwen na 3obv 'Ojibwe'; maanpii av
          'here'; nikekmig av 'side of the border.'

   LEFT AND RIGHT. The DEVERBAL ADVERBS ezhi-gchi-nikaayan, 'to your right,' and
ezhi-nmanj-nikaayan, 'to your left' are used to express right and left, respectively. The term
for 'right' includes the preverb gchi-, 'big, large,' and the term for 'left,' the preverb nmanj-,
of uncertain meaning.

   (83)   EzM~gehi~nikaayan ni-izhaan. I 'Go to your right' (AM39.719)
          Ezhi-gchi-nikaayan av 'on your right side'; ni-izhaan vai imp 2s 'go there.'

   (84)   Ezhi-nmanj-nikaayan ni-zhaan. I "Goto your left! (AM39.720)
          Ezhi-nmanj-nikaayan av 'on your left'; ni-zhaan vai imp 2s '(you SG) go there.'

    UPSTAIRS AND DOWNSTAIRS. Shpimsagong, 'upstairs' AV, and naamsagong 'down-
stairs' AV.

   (85)   Gii-zhaa shpimmgong. I 'He has gone upstairs! (AM39.54)
           Gii-zhaa vai ind SsProx 'ANsg went there'; shpimsagong av 'upstairs.'

   (86)   Waya na yaa shpimsagongl I 'Is anyone upstairsT (AM39.58)
          Wayapra indef3sProx 'someone'; na av 'yes/no question'; yaa vai ind SsProx 'ANsg is
          there'; shpimsagong av 'upstairs.'

    UPSTREAM AND DOWNSTREAM. Gidaajwan, 'upstream' AV and niisaajwan, 'down-
stream' AV. There are also specific motion verbs, such as godham, godho, and godkozhwe,
all of which mean 'paddle upstream,' and are VA! verbs. Cf., niiskozhwe, 'paddle down-
stream' VAI.

15.10 Locative Nouns

   Nouns can be made into locational terms by the addition of the locative suffix, /-ing/, and
variation in its form with different types of nouns is discussed at length in Chapter 4 (see
page 193). The meaning of the locative is relatively general, and translates into English with
a variety of more specific terms, such as on, in, by, and at. Locative nouns are not marked
744 • 15.10 Locative Nouns


for the regular nominal grammatical categories of number and obviation, and in this sense,
resemble locative adverbs, though they can be inflected for a possessor. Generally, locative
noun forms more commonly appear at the end of clauses containing them, a feature they
share with other locational expressions, though they may also occur initially, as in sentence
(89), below. They generally are not modified by demonstrative pronouns even when they are
definite (see Chapter 12, p. 547). The following examples illustrate the use of locative
nouns.

   (87) ... "Giiskan iw ggoodaas, gga-goodoon dash maamtigoonsing"
         '.. ."Take off your dress, you are to hang it here on a bush."' (AK3.8b)

          Giiskan vti imp 2s»0 '(you SG) take IN off'; \\vprn Os 'that'; ggoodaas ni 2s(0s) 'your SG
          dress'; gga-goodoon vti ind 2s»0s 'you SG will hang IN'; dash av 'then'; maa av 'there';
          mtigoonsing na 3 loc 'on bush.'

   (88) Gii-bi-ngodwaasooshkaawag jiimaaning, I 'They came here six in a canoe.'
          Gii-bi-ngodwaasooshkaawag vai ind 3pProx 'ANpl came hither six to a boat';
          jiimaaning ni 0 loc 'in a boat.' (AM39.128)

   (89) Daabaaning ngii-boozmi. I 'We got on a wagon." (AM39.43)
          Daabaaning na 3 loc 'into wagon'; ngii-boozmi vai ind Ip 'we (excl.) got on board.'

       Very commonly, as we might expect, locative nouns are used with verbs containing
locative roots, directional roots, or relative roots. The following examples illustrate occur-
rence with locative roots. Note that unlike the complements of relative roots, nominals asso-
ciated with locational roots do not typically appear adjacent to the root or preverb in
position before the verb.

   (90) Nii-rf&amaadgaa nbising. I 'I shall swim across the lake.' (AM39.4)
          Nii-dkamaadgaa vai ind Is 'I will swim across' [/dakam-/, 'across']; nbising ni 0 loc
          'lake (loc).'

   (91) Gu-biinjse dkibiing. I 'He stepped into a spring of water.' (AM39.67)
          Gii-biinjse vai ind 3sProx 'ANsg fell in' [/biind-/, 'in(side)']; dkibiing ni 0 loc 'into
          spring of water.'

   The following examples show verbs with RELATIVE ROOTS. Note that the locative fol-
lows the verb in (94).
                                                                          15.10 Locative Nouns • 745


   (92) Nbiingpidoon. I 'Pull it into the water.' (AM39.747)
         Nbiing ni 0 loc 'into the water'; pidoon vti imp 2s»0 'pull IN to there' [relative root /IN/].

   (93) Doopwining ngii-/M/inaan. I 'I picked it up from the table.' (AM39.385)
         Doopwining ni 0 loc '(from) the table'; ngii-ndinaan vti ind ls»0s 'I got INsg from'
         [relative root /ond/]

   (94) Nso-bboon ngii-z/iaa gkinoohmaadiiwgamgong.

   (97) Gii-dsoozo dash wnikaang. I 'He got himself caught there by his arm.' (AM35.42)

          loc 'on ANsG's arm(s).'

   (98) Nii-nokii ngitgaanensing. I 'I am going to work in my garden.' (AM39.15)
          Nii-nokii vai ind Is 'I will work'; ngitgaanensing ni dim 0 loc 'in my garden.'

  The following sentence is interesting, in that it contains the dependent noun /doon/,
'mouth,' both in an incorporated verb form, and as a free locative noun.

    DISTRIBUTED LOCATIVES. An ending /-ikaang/ occurs on nouns as a locative form usu-
ally indicating location -within an amorphous substance, such as water or sand. The nouns
which take this suffix thus tend to be mass nouns. I call such locatives distributive locatives.
This locative can be contrasted with the regular locative in sentence (101).

   (100) Wdaansan dnakmigziwan negwiikaang. I 'His daughters are playing in the sand.'

          Wdaansan na 3sProx(3obv) 'ANSG's daughter(s)'; dnakmigziwan vai ind 3obv 'ANobv
          is/are busy there'; negwiikaang ni 0 loc 'in the sand.' (AM39.155)

   (101) Gii-bmose negwiing. I 'He walked on the sand.' (AM39.69)

          Gii-bmose vai ind 3sProx 'ANsg was walking along'; negwiing ni 0 loc 'on the sand.'

  LOCATIVES WITH NOMINAL PLACENAMES. Locative suffixes are freely used with place-

   (102) Oodenaang dnakii. I 'He lives in Detroit.' (AM39.80) [oodena(w), NI 'town, city]

         I Oodenaang name ni loc 'in Detroit'; dnakii vai ind 3sProx 'ANsg lives there.'

   (103) Zhgaagong ngii-zhinaazhwaa. I 'I sent him to Chicago.' (AM39.278)

          Zhgaagong name ni loc 'to Chicago'; ngii-zhinaazhwaa vta ind ls»3sProx 'I sent
          ANsg.' [compare zhgaag, NA 'skunk']

   (104) Baawtigoong ngo-bboon dash gii-miinaawag ji-dgoshinowaad odi gaawiin dash
         giw aaning gii-debwetnziiwag gaawiin gii-nsidtaziiwag gaa dash gii-zhaasiiwag.

         'And they were given one year to arrive there at Sault Ste. Marie, but some of
         them didn't believe, they didn't understand and they didn't go.' (AK9.9)

         Baawtigoong name ni loc 'to Sault Ste. Marie'; ngo-bboon temp/ni 'one year'; dash av

         SpProx '(CONJ) ANpl will arrive'; odi av 'there'; gaawiin av 'not'; dash av 'then'; giw
         prn 3pProx 'those'; aaning av 'some'; gii-debwetnziiwag vai indSpProx neg 'ANpl did

         understand'; gaa av 'not'; dash av 'so'; gii-zhaasiiwag vai indSpProxneg 'ANpl did not
         go there.'

    However, with the names of places that represent English borrowings, the locative suffix

   (105) Maampii nikekmig ndazhi-ndaadiz, baamaa dash miinwaa ngii-wa-dnakii widi

15.11 Using Clauses to Express Location

   VERBAL EXPRESSIONS AS MODIFIERS OF LOCATIVE ADVERBS. Verbal expressions can
be used to identify or specify locations. Very commonly, such expressions serve as CLAUSAL
MODIFIERS to locational adverbs such as maanpii, 'here,' maa, 'there,' and odi, 'there.'
These locative adverbial clauses consistently follow the locative adverb they are associated
with, and usually show PLAIN CONJUNCT INFLECTION, unless the verb contains a relative
root or relative preverb, in which case the verb shows INITIAL CHANGE. For example, the
verb miizhshkoonskaag, in (110) below, lacks a relative and is in the plain conjunct, while
endzhi-zhitoowaad, in (111), has relative preverb dzhi-, 'at a certain place,' and has initial
change.

   (110) Nnanaamdabmi maa miizhshkoonskaag, nnoondwaanaanig dash bneshiinyag
         ngamwaad.
         'We (exc.) sat a while there in the grass, and we heard the birds singing.'

          Nnanaamdabmi vai redup ind Ip 'we are sitting'; maa av 'there'; miizhshkoonskaag vii
          conj 0 '(CONJ) IN be grassy'; nnoondwaanaanig vta ind lp»3p 'we heard ANpl'; dash
          av 'then'; bneshiinyag na SpProx 'birds'; ngamwaad vai conj SpProx '(CONJ) ANpl
          sing.' (AM39.532)


   (111) Mii dash gii-webtaayaan gii-naadmaageyaan maa endzhi-zhitoowaad iw
         miishkogmig.
         'Then I began to help there where they were building a barn' (AM8.21)

          Mii av 'and'; dash av 'then'; gii-webtaayaan vai conj Is '(CONJ) I began';
          gii-naadmaageyaan vai conj Is '(CONJ) I helped'; maa av 'there'; endzhi-zhitoowaad
          vti ic conj 3pProx»0 '(CCNJ) where ANpl make IN'; i\vprn Os 'that'; miishkogmig ni Os
          'barn.'
                                                   15.11 Using Clauses to Express Location • 749



   (112) Gaa-sh go wiikaa wgii-nenmaasii ji-zhaanid odi endzhi-gkinoohmoondww giw
         binoajiinyag, mil go eta gii-maajiinaazhkawaad ji-bbaa-ndawenjgenid.
        'She never allowed him to go there where the children were taught, but only sent
        him to go out hunting.' (AK13.5)

         Gaa-sh av 'not then'; wiikaa av 'ever'; wgii-nenmaasii vta ind 3sProx»3obv neg 'ANsg
         did not permit ANobv'; ji-zhaanid vai conj 3obv 'ANsg could go there'; odi av 'there';
         endzhi-gkinoohmoondwaa vta ic conjx»3pProx '(CCNJ) where ANpl were taught
         there'; gi\vprn 3pProx 'those'; binoojiinyag na 3pProx 'children'; mii av 'but'; eta av
         'only'; gii-maajiinaazhkawaad vta conj 3sProx»3obv '(CONJ) ANsg sent ANobv
         away'; ji-bbaa-ndawenjgenid vai conj 3obv '(CONJ) ANobv would go around hunting.'


   LOCATIVE EXPRESSIONS WITH RELATIVE ROOTS & PREVERBS. Verbal locative expres-
sions also occur without any associated adverb, as ADJUNCT CLAUSES showing standard
conjunct order inflection. The verbs of such expressions often have a relative root or pre-
verb, which shows initial change. Such clauses commonly follow the main clause.

   (113) Gnabaj zgimenh ngii-bdakhogdig, ngizhiibii gaa-namid.
         'A mosquito must have stung me; I am itching where it bit me.' (AM39.552)
         [RELATIVE ROOT /iN-/, 'there, to, thus'; INITIAL CHANGE: gii- > gaa-]

         Gnabaj av 'perhaps'; zgimenh na SsProx 'mosquito'; ngii-bdakhogdig vta ind dub
         3sProx»ls 'ANsg pierced me'; ngizhiibii vai ind Is 'I itch'; gaa-namid vta ic conj
         3sProx»ls '(CCNJ) where ANsg bit me.'


   (114) Niijkiwenh ngii-nmadbimi endzhi-bgizwaad.
         'My friend and I sat where they bathe (i.e., at the bathing beach).' (AM39.578)
         [RELATIVE PREVERB /dazhi-/, 'at such place,'; INITIAL CHANGE: dzhi- > endzhi-]

         Niijkiwenh na ls(3sProx) 'my friend'; ngii-nmadbimi vai ind Ip 'we sat';
         endzhi-bgizwaad vai ic conj 3pProx '(CCNJ) where ANpl swim.'


   (115) Waasa endaayaan. I 'It is far to where I live.' (AM39.580)
         [Irregular RELATIVE component /en/, akin to /iN-/, 'there, to, thus' INITIAL
         CHANGE: daa > endaa]
          Waasa av 'far'; endaayaan vai ic conj Is '(CCNJ) where I live.'


    THE LOCATIONAL (SUBORDINATING) PREVERB A-. The preverb a- occurs several times
in the recorded texts of Andrew Medler, and serves as a locational SUBORDINAI OR.
750 • 15.11 Using Clauses to Express Location


   (116) Njiiyenh ngii-nmadab a-nmadbid. I 'I sat next to him where he sat' (AM39.534)
          Njiiyenh av 'next in serial order'; ngii-nmadab vai ind Is 'I sat'; a-nmadbid vai conj
          SsProx '(CONJ) where ANsg sat.'

   (117) Ngashi gii-bi-zhaa maa a-nbaayaan gii-bi-waabmid nembaawaanen.
         'My mother came to where I was sleeping to see whether I was asleep.'

          Ngashi nod ls(3sProx) 'my mother'; gii-bi-zhaa vai ind 3sProx 'ANsg came hither';
          maa av 'there'; a-nbaayaan vai conj Is £(CONJ) where I sleep'; gii-bi-waabmid vta conj
          3sProx»ls '(CONJ) ANsg came and saw me'; nembaawaanen vai ic conj dub Is
          '(CCNJ) I might be sleeping.' (AM39.668)

   PREVERB a- can undergo INITIAL CHANGE, becoming e-.

   (118) E-bgandaanmak maanoo nakeyaa da-wnjigaabwi aw waa-wiikwebnind.
         'By all means, the person who is to be charmed must stand in the direction toward
         which the wind is blowing.' (AM30.9)

          E-bgandaanmak vii ic conj 0 '(CCNJ) where the wind strikes'; maanoo av 'by all
          means'; nakeyaa av 'in such a direction'; da-wnjigaabwi vai ind SsProx 'ANsg will
          stand back from there'; aw prn SsProx 'that'; waa-wiikwebnind vta ic conj part
          x»3sProx '(CCNJ) who (ANsg) will be put under a love spell.'

   LOCATIONAL Focus. Locations can serve as the FOCUS of mii-focus constructions.

   (119) Ngii-baashkzwaa jidmoonh, miigwa naa maampugaa-ndaakwuyaan.
         'I have shot a squirrel; it's here that I shot from.' (AM39.574)

          Ngii-baashkzwaa vta ind ls»3sProx 'I shot ANsg'; jidmoonh na SsProx 'squirrel'; mii
          av 'and'; gwa av 'indeed'; maampii av 'here'; gaa-ndaakwiiyaan vai ic conj Is '(CCNJ)
          I shot from there.'

    LOCATIVE RELATIVE CLAUSE FRAGMENTS. Rhodes 1996:11 discusses what he calls loc-
ative relative clause fragments, which "occur in positions like relative clauses and modify
the head nouns in the way that relative clauses do, but lack the locative verb yaad, 'be
(there),' which is suggested by the sense of the whole construction." He cites as an example
the following:
                                                                     15.12 Expressing Manner • 751


   (120) iw mnjikan endnizyaan. I 'the fence at my place (lit. where I live)' (AMI 1.4)
          iwpr Os 'that'; mnjikan ni Os 'fence'; endnizyaan vai ic conj Is '(CCNJ) where I live.'

   Here one might expect a participial form of the locational verb yaa, 'be (there)' VII, to
occur with iw mnjikan, 'that fence.' Rhodes further observes that the only time a locative
verb explicitly occurs is when there is no head noun, as in the following example, which has
a demonstrative pronoun giwi, but no noun.

   (121) giwi eyaajig wedi. I 'the ones who are there' (SO)
          giwi pr 3pProx 'those'; eyaajig vai ic conj part 3pProx '(CCNJ) who (ANpl) are there'
          wedi av 'there.'

15.12 Expressing Manner

   The SEMANTIC RELATION of MANNER expresses the way in which an action or event
occurs. Manner expressions very often show the relative root /iN-/, 'in such way; thus/ so, to
there,' or its associated relative preverb, /izhi-/, as in the following examples.

   (122) Ggii-zhichge na dash iw gaa-zhi-gkinoohmoonaan?
         'Did you do the way I taught you?' (AM30.32) [rel. pv. /izhi-/]

          Ggii-zhichge vai ind 2s 'did you SG do'; na av 'yes/no question'; dash av 'then'; iw prn
          Os 'that'; gaa-zhi-gkinoohmoonaan vta ic conj ls»2s '(CCNJ) how I taught you (SG) to
          do.'

   (123) Gaa wii ngii-nwesii enwewaad. [rel. rt. /iN/]
         'I did not pronounce the way they did.' (AM 1.2)

          Gaa wii av 'not'; ngii-nwesii vai ind Is neg 'I didn't speak so'; enwewaad vai ic conj
          3pProx '(CCNJ) way ANpl speak.'

   (124) Mii dash gaa-nag, Waabndamog ow nbiish ezhnaagwak.
         'I said to him, "Look at the way this water looks'" (AM10.13) [rel. rt. /iN/]

          Mii av 'and'; dash av 'then'; gaa-nag vta ic conj ls»3sProx '(CONJ) I said to ANsg';
          Waabndamog vti imp 2p 'look at IN'; owpra Os 'this'; nbiish ni Os 'water'; ezhnaagwak
          vii ic conj 0 '(CCNJ) how IN looks.'

15.12.1 Expressions of Similarity (Likeness)

     Expressions of similarity between two people or objects are made by using relative root
/iN-/ in conjunction with a rich variety of verbal finals. In the simplest form, the subject fol-
lows the verb, and the object of comparison precedes it, marked with a locative suffix, /-ing/
if it is a noun, as in the following examples.

   (129) Mhiingning zhinaagzi gday. I 'Your (sg.) dog looks like a wolf.' (MC)
          Mhiingning na 3 loc 'wolf (loc)'; zhinaagzi vai ind SsProx 'ANsg looks like'; gday nad
          2s(3sProx) 'your dog.'

   (130) Mhiingning zhinaagzi wag gonda nimookaajiinyig.
          'Those dogs look like wolves' (MC)

          Mhiingning na 3 loc 'wolf (loc)'; zhinaagziwag vai ind SpProx 'ANpl look so'; gonda
          pm na SpProx 'these'; nimookaajiinyig na SpProx 'dogs.'


   (131) Mhiingning zhinaagziwan wdayan. I 'Her dogs look like wolves.' (MC)
          Mhiingning na 3 loc 'wolf (loc)'; zhinaagziwan vai ind3obv 'ANobv look(s) like';
          wdayan nad 3sProx(3obv) 'ANsg's dog.'

    Other attributes besides appearance can be compared, using different verbs. The follow-
ing examples are representative. Example (134) is particularly interesting, in that it has a
free noun, giigoonh, 'fish,' serving as an initial to VII final /ipogod/, 'taste.'

   (132) Zhgaagong zhimaagzi gday. I 'Your (sg.) dog smells like a skunk.' (MC)

          Zhgaagong na 3 loc 'skunk (loc)'; zhimaagzi vai indSsProx 'ANsg smells like'; gday
          nad 2s(3sProx) 'your dog.'
754 • 15.12.1 Expressions of Similarity (Likeness)


   (133) Mhiingning nitaagzi gday. I 'Your (sg.) dog sounds like a wolf.' (MC)

          Mhiingning na loc 3 'wolf (loc)'; nitaagzi vai ind SsProx 'ANsg sounds like'; gday nad
          2s(3sProx) 'your dog.'

   (134) Giigoon(y)pogod maanda wiiyaas. I This meat tastes like fish.' (MC)

          Giigoon(y)pogod vii indOs 'INsg tastes like fish'; maandapr/z Os 'this'; wiiyaas ni Os

   The assertion of likeness may involve an action or situation, as in the following, which
have clauses with independent order-inflected verbs associated with the relative element.

         'Her dog smells like it encountered a skunk.' (MC)

          met ANobv'; zhimaagziwan vai indSobv 'ANobv smell(s) like'; wdayan nad
          3sProx(3obv) 'ANsg's dog(s).'
                                                        15.12.1 Expressions of Similarity (Likeness) • 755


    (140) Zhgaagon daa-gii-nkweshkwaawaan zhimaagziwag gonda nimookaanjiinyig.
           'These dogs smell like they encountered a skunk.' (MC)

            Zhgaagon na 3obv 'skunk(s)'; daa-gii-nkweshkwaawaan vta ind 3pProx»3obv 'ANpl
            met ANobv'; zhimaagziwag vai indSpProx 'ANpl smell like'; gondaprn na SpProx
            'these'; nimookaanjiinyig na SpProx 'dogs.'

    Richard Rhodes (1990:5) observes an important point about constructions involving rel-
ative elements, namely that 'there are no non-clausal relative root complements which are
referential.' To understand what he means by this, consider the preceding examples, (129)
and (130), where dogs are described as looking like wolves. Note that the reference is not to
any specific wolves, but rather to the general class of creatures named with the Nishnaabe-
mwin noun, mhiingan, 'wolf.' This is a non-referential usage, as opposed to reference that is
to a specific individual, such as maaba mhiingan, 'this wolf.'
    Because first and second persons can only be referred to by means of personal pronouns,
which are inherently referential, it is common to express comparisons with a first or second
person as the object of comparison by means of interlocked relative-root verbal expressions
such as the following. Rhodes 1990:5 observes that these structures resemble corelatives,
which are used in some languages to express the equivalents of relative clauses.1 Notice in
the example below that identical verbs are used, zhinaagozi, 'look so,' with relative root
/iNA

    (141) Ezhnaagziyaanh gdizhnaagoz. I 'You look like me.' (MC)
            Ezhnaagziyaanh vai ic conj Is '(CCNJ) as I look'; gdizhnaagoz vai ind 2s 'you look so.'

    Rhodes also notes that constructions of this type are used when a referential animate
would otherwise be the complement of a relative root, though a few common possessed
inanimates also seem to be expressed in this way, such as the widely used verbal expression
specifying the location of one's residence, e.g., endaayaanh and endaad, literally, 'where I
live' and 'where ANsg lives,' as opposed to rare nmiigwaam, 'my house' and wmiigiwaam,
'ANsg's house.'
    There are also transitive verbs (VTA and VTI) specifically involving comparison and sim-
ilarity, using the relative root /IN-/, such as now, 'resemble AN,' in the following.

   (142) Wmishoomisan dinwaan ngwis. I 'My son takes after his grandfather.' (MC)
            Wmishoomisan nad 3sProx(3obv) 'ANsg's grandfather'; dinwaan vta ind 3sProx»3obv
            'ANsg resembles ANobv'; ngwis na Is(SsProx) 'my son.'

Time and Circumstance




16.1 Expressing Time

    Nishnaabemwin has a rich system of TENSE inflection by which a verbal expression can
be set in the present, the past, or the future. It also has MODAL preverbs to indicate possibil-
ity and obligation, and a host of preverbs with associated roots that signal aspectual notions
such the beginning and end of an event or action. DIRECTIONAL preverbs can be used with
temporal meanings as well. There are also verbal inflectional MODES, indicated by suffix
inflections, which index the time in which a verbal event takes place relative to another, and
the degree of certainty with which an assertion is made, including the DUBITATIVE MODE,
PRETERIT mode and PRETERIT DUBITATIVE mode. There are ways to make subordinate
clauses that specify time relations. Distinct temporal adverbs exist as well, and there are
impersonal verbs which make reference to temporally defined concepts. In this section we
will examine all of these different resources. The following chart summarizes some of the
different ways of indicating time in Nishnaabemwin.

            Verb Tenses                       Present (doo-/da-/di-), Past (gii-),
                                              Future (wii-, da-/ga-)
            Verb Inflectional Modes           Indicative, Preterit, Dubitative,
                                              Preterit Dubitative
            Modal Preverbs                    daa-, gii-
            Directional Preverbs as Time      bi-, ani-, bmi-
            Aspectual Preverbs and Roots      maajii-, booni-, ishkwaa-, giizhi-,
                                              etc.
            Temporal Adverbs                  bjiinaago, noongwa, waabang, etc.
            Temporal Verbs                    giizhgad, naagshi, dbikad, etc.
                                              namhe-giizhgad,
            Temporal Clauses                  pii..., megwaa..., etc.
                                                                       16.2 Tense and Mood* 759



16.2 Tense and Mood

    Tense is expressed by means of distinct preverbs for past and future. Present tense was
historically not usually marked. In contemporary usage, however, what were historically
extended person prefixes are now used in present tense contexts in independent order inflec-
tion, as a means of stabilizing some of the variation in verb stems introduced by syncope.
These person prefixes thus indirectly index present tense.
    Tense preverbs occur with verbs inflected for the INDEPENDENT and CONJUNCT ORDERS;
imperative verbs have IMMEDIATE and DELAYED modes, but these modes are expressed by
means of inflectional suffixes, rather than by means of the system of tense preverbs. Verbs
inflected for conjunct order are also subject to INITIAL CHANGE, which often affects the
tense preverb, as it is frequently word-initial.
    The past tense preverb is gii-, which does not show variation in its form, though it can
undergo initial change, becoming gaa-. There are two future tense preverbs, wii-, which
usually implies volition or desire (changed form waa-), and da-/ga-, which implies "conse-
quence or obligation, rather than will" (Rhodes 1985:124). The latter future tense displays
irregular (SUPPLETIVE) ALLOMORPHY, in its independent order variation between da- and
ga-, and in the plain conjunct form, which isji- (the changed conjunct form is ge-). The fol-
lowing chart lays out the basic scheme of tense preverbs. I have also included the TENSE-
LESS SUBORDINATING PREVERB, a-, which is discussed below.

                       Independent           Plain Conjunct     Changed Conjunct
          Tenseless    —                     a-                 e-
          Present      nda-, ndi-, ndoo-
                       gda-, gdi-, gdoo-
                       wda-, wdi-, wdoo-
          Past         gii-                  gii-               gaa-
          Future       wii-                  wii-               waa-
          Future       ga-/da-               ji-                ge-

16.2.1 Present Tense

    Present tense is used to refer to verbal events taking place at the time of speaking, or at
the same time as some other temporal reference point within a discourse. Verbs in the
present tense, according to their traditional form, do not show any tense preverb, as in the
following examples: in (1), prefix /ni-/, 'first person,' is added directly to verb stem
/waabandam/, 'see IN'; in (2), prefix /gid-/, 'second person' is added to stem /ayaaw/.

   (1)   Nwaabndaan jiimaanim. I 7 see his boat.' (MC22.1.)
          Nwaabndaan vti ind ls»0s 'I see INsg'; jiimaanim ni 3sProx(Os) 'ANsg's boat.'
760 • 16.2.2 Past Tense


   (2)   Bkwezhgan na gdayaawaa ge-shamyaangban.
         'Do you have any bread you could feed us?' (AK7.12)

          Bkwezhgan na SsProx 'bread'; na av 'yes/no question'; gdayaawaa vta ind 2s»3sProx
          'you have ANsg'; ge-shamyaangban vta ic conj 2s»lp '(CCNJ) you (sg) could feed us
          (excl).'

   For many contemporary speakers, the extended person prefixes are very commonly used
in present tense contexts. Note that such prefixes are not exclusively tense markers, since
they also occur with possessed nouns. They are in complementary distribution with past and
future tense preverbs, and as such, implicitly signal present tense. These prefixes only occur
with first and second person forms of intransitive verbs, but with all persons for transitives
and VAIO verbs. Third person intransitives don't show the prefixes because historically they
had no person prefixes. And, of course, the prefixes occur only in the independent order.

   (3)   ATtfoo-mmaangshkiinzhgwe. I 7 have big eyes.' (EM)
          Ndoo-mmaangshkiinzhgwe vai ind Is 'I have big eyes.'

   (4)   Enso-biidoowaani coffee, nda-oo-nendaan creamer.
         'Whenever I bring coffee, I go and forget creamer.' (MC22.5)

          Enso-biidoowaani vai ic conj iter ls»0 'every time I bring IN'; nda-oo-nendaan vti ind
          ls»0s 'I go and forget INsg.'

   (5)   Ge-gii gsha ko gdoo-mnjiw. Miinwaa gdoo-ntaa-naadmaw.
         'You too treat me often. Andyou often help me.' (MC15.5)

          Ge-giiprpers 2s 'you too'; gsha av 'indeed'; ko av 'habitually'; gdoo-mnjiw vta ind
          2s»ls 'you treat me.' Miinwaa av 'and'; gdoo-ntaa-naadmaw vta ind 2s»ls 'you
          habitually help me.'

16.2.2 Past Tense

   Past tense is used to make reference to events that took place prior to the time of speak-
ing, or prior to some other established temporal reference point within a discourse. Past
tense is expressed in a variety of ways in Nishnaabemwin, but most commonly by means of
the preverb gii-.

    SEQUENCES OF Gil-. Much work remains to be done before we have even the beginning
of an account of the use of tense in connected discourse. In some cases, successive verbs are
each marked with gii-, while in others they are not. The following examples, representing
different versions of the same story as told by Andrew Medler show variable presence of
gii- in the dependent time clause that translates as 'long ago when I was a child.' The main
verb, ngii-(bbaa)-maajiinig, 'ANsg took me along,' is marked with independent order
inflection and past tense gii- in all three cases. In sentence (13), gii- occurs with the DEPEN-
DENT VERB, but in (14) it does not. In another recounting of the same story, it is missing as
well.

   (13) Zhaazhi go megwaa gii-binoojiinywiyaan ngii-bbaa-maajiinig aw ngashi
        bbaa-bwahmowaad bgoji-mnoomin widi waabshkokiing.
         "Long ago when I was a child, my mother took me along as they went about gath-
         ering rice in the marsh.' (AM6.1)
                                                                             16.2.2 Past Tense-763



          Zhaazhi av 'long ago'; megwaa av 'while'; gii-binoojiinywiyaan vai conj Is '(CONJ) I
          was a child'; ngii-bbaa-maajiinig vta ind3sProx»ls 'ANsg took me around'; a\vpr
          3sProx 'that'; ngashi nod ls(3sProx) 'my mother'; bbaa-bwahmowaad vti conj
          3pProx»0 '(CONJ) ANpl went around knocking IN down'; bgoji-mnoomin ni Os 'wild
          rice'; widi av 'over there'; waabshkokiing ni 0 loc 'in the marsh.'

   (14) Megwaa binoojiinywiyaan degwaagig ngii-bbaa-maajiinig aw ngashi.
         'When I was a child, one autumn my mother took me about with her.' (AM5.1)

          Megwaa av 'while'; binoojiinywiyaan vai conj Is '(CONJ) I was a child'; degwaagig vii
          ic conj 0 '(CCNJ) when IN was autumn'; ngii-bbaa-maajiinig vta ind3sProx»ls 'ANsg
          took me around'; awpr SsProx 'that'; ngashi nad ls(3sPwx) 'my mother.'


   Verbs in clauses with past time that are contemporaneous with a main or preceding verb
marked for past time, or which function as staging or elaboration of a main verb, often do
not show marking for past tense, but simply inherit their tense from the main verb they are
associated with. In example (15), below, the main verb is gii-waabmaad, which has a past
tense preverb, while the staging verb, bbaa-yaad, does not. The verb maajaa, 'set off,' as in
(16), often serves as the staging for a verb which follows it. This latter verb sometimes lacks
past tense marking, as here, though in other examples both verbs are marked. In (17), the
subordinated verb niibwinid has no past tense marker.

   (15) Mii-sh wa mdimooyenh bbaa-yaad, mii gii-waabmaad ninwan, mansooyan.
         Then as this old lady was wandering around, she saw some men, strangers.'

         'So they set off, going around in search of the tracks! (SO 1.34)

          Gii-maajaawaad vai conj 3pProx '(CONJ) ANpl went away'; bbaa-ndakwechgewaad
          vai conj SpProx '(CONJ) ANpl go around looking for tracks.'

    PAST TENSE AND IMPERSONAL VERBS. Often, impersonal verbs, such as those express-
ing time of day, geographical features, and weather conditions, do not show a past tense pre-
verb in past tense contexts. However, impersonal verbs with time reference often do show
INITIAL CHANGE, which usually indexes past occurrence of a specific instance of the state
described by the verb, and have a perfective sense, that is, indicate that the event signified
by the verb has already taken place at the time of the action/event of the main verb, and is
often translated as antecedent 'when.' The following examples illustrate.

   (18) Mii dash gii-bi-giiwewaad debkadnig dash gii-dgoshnoog.
         'And they came home and arrived just at dark.' (AK7.14)

          Mii av 'and'; dash av 'then'; gii-bi-giiwewaad vai conj SpProx '(CONJ) ANpl came
          back home'; debkadnig vii ic conj Oobv '(CCNJ) when INobv was dark'; dash av 'then';
          gii-dgoshnoog vai ind SpProx 'ANpl arrived.'

   (19) Gegzhebaawgak goon kina gii-nkaabaawe.
          'When morning came all the snow had melted away.' (AM 10.22)

          Gegzhebaawgak vii ic conj 0 '(CCNJ) IN was morning'; goon na 3sProx 'snow'; kina av
          'all'; gii-nkaabaawe vai ind SsProx 'ANsg melted away.'


   Temporal reference in impersonal verbs that does not refer to a specific instance often
does not show initial change or past tense.

   (20) Gii-nshkaadzi aw ndawemaa iw bbaa-yaayaan wiikaa iw dbikak
        gii-zhmaagnishiiwi maa naa ge wiin, ngii-bbaktewig dash naangim go
        gii-ni-dgoshnaang endaayaan.
         'My brother got mad that I was around late at night, he was a soldier too, and he
         hit me on the shoulder until we got to my house.' (AK8.10)
                                                                            16.2.2 Past Tense* 765

         Is(SsProx) 'my sibling-of-opposite-sex'; iwpr Os 'that'; bbaa-yaayaan vai conj Is
         '(CONJ) I was around'; wiikaa av 'ever; late'; iwpr Os 'that'; dbikak vii conj 0 '(CONJ)
         IN be night'; gii-zhmaagnishiiwi vai ind SsProx 'ANsg was a soldier'; maa av 'then'; ge
         av 'as for'; wiinprpers 3s 'ANsg'; ngii-paktewig vta ind3sProx»ls 'ANsg hit me
         repeatedly'; dash av 'then'; naangim av 'until'; gii-ni-dgoshnaang vai conj Ip '(CONJ)
         we arrived there'; endaayaan vai ic conj Is '(CCNJ) where I live.'

   In the following example, all verbs making reference to past events are marked with past
tense except for the impersonal verb dbikad, 'be dark, be night,' though here the verb is

cess/event reading for the verb.

   (21) Mii gM-nda-waabndamwaad wii-nbaawaad wgw-mkaanaawaa, wiigwaamens,

   More stative (time-stable) impersonal verbs, such as those describing features of land-
scape, seem to be less often explicitly marked with past tense.

   (22) Mii dash gaa-zhichged aw gaa-nsaad niw bnewan gii-zhaad maa gchi-bkwaabkaag

    INITIAL CHANGE AND PAST TENSE. In some cases verbs show INITIAL CHANGE to indi-
cate a specific instance of an event in the past, as opposed to a customary, habitual, or repet-

pit, 'when,' commonly occurs with them. Clauses of this sort are usually staging for a main
predication, providing a time specification for the main verb of the sentence.

   (42) Zhaangsimdana shi niiwin gii-dso-bboon'gizi aw nookmiSjpw nembod.
         'My grandmother was 94 years old when she died.' (AM2.2)

          Zhaangsimdana-shi-niiwin nm '94'; gii-dso-bboon'gizi vai ind SsProx 'ANsg was so
          many years old'; aw pr SsProx 'that'; nookmis nod Is(SsProx) 'my grandmother'; pii av
          'when'; nembod vai ic conj SsProx '(CCNJ) when ANsg died.'

   (43) Pii dash menookmig, Ziisbaakdoke-giizis e-goojing, gii-gsinaamgad.
         'Then when the spring was at hand, in the month of March, there was cold
         weather.' (AM 10.2)

          Pii av 'when'; dash av 'then'; menookmig vii ic conj 0 '(CCNJ) when spring came';
          Ziisbaakdoke-giizis na SsProx 'Sugar Moon'; e-goojing vai ic conj SsProx '(CCNJ)
          when ANsg was hanging'; gii-gsinaamgad vii ind 0 'the weather was cold.'

   When the event does not represent a specific occurrence in the past, INITIAL CHANGE
does not usually occur.

16.2.3 Future Tense

    There are two future tense preverbs, wii- and da-/ga-. The former functions as a VOLUN-
TATIVE in many dialects of Anishinaabemowin, that is, it is used to express desire or intent.
It often implies VOLITION in Nishnaabemwin, though there are some uses where it doesn't,
such as when it expresses futurity with impersonal verbs. The future preverb da-/ga- tends
to be used in contexts of consequence or obligation, though there is some overlap in usage.
In at least one example, both preverbs occur with the same verb, in which case wii- would
seem to have volitional or modal force.

   (46) Gga-wii-daawmin gwepjigaans, baamaa nga-biidoon waabang.
         7 want to borrow your hammer; I will bring it back tomorrow.' (AM39.106)

          Gga-wii-daawmin vta ind ls»2s 'I would like to borrow from you'; gwepjigaans ni
          2s(0s) 'your hammer'; baamaa av 'later'; nga-biidoon vti ind ls»0s 'I will bring INsg';
          waabang av 'tomorrow.'

    FUTURE PREVERB Wn-. This preverb is straightforward, showing predictable variants in
all three of its forms.

                  wii-              wii-                       waa-

   FUTURE PREVERB DA-/GA-. The preverb da-/ga- is used in contexts where futurity is
more directly associated with consequence or obligation, rather than desire or will. Ignoring
the effects of syncope, the form da- is used in the independent order when there is no person
prefix, and ga- elsewhere in the independent order. This effectively restricts the use of this
form to third person intransitive contexts. The plain conjunct form of this preverb isji-, and
the changed conjunct is preverb ge-.

         wii-baatiinod vai conj SsProx '(CONJ) ANsg will be abundant'; ge-waabndamwaad vti
         ic conj 3pProx»0 '(CCNJ) ANpl will see IN'; giw pr SpProx 'those'; ge-bi-zhaajig vai ic
         conj part SpProx '(CCNJ) who ANpl will come.' (AMI 8.11)


   Future preverb wii- is also used in a DUBITATIVE construction with MODAL da- (one of
the conjunct forms of daa-}.

   (78) Endgwen da-wii~ndawaabminang. I 'I wonder whether he'll be looking for us (inc.}!

         Endgwen av 'whether'; da-wii-ndawaabminang vta conj 3sProx»21 '(CONJ) ANsg
         maybe will be looking for us.' (AM39.93)


   (79) Endgwen da-wii-naadmoonang. I 'I wonder whether he'll help us (inc.).'

         Endgwen av 'whether'; da-wii-naadmoonang vta conj 3sProx»21 '(CONJ) ANsg
         maybe will help us.' (AM39.626)


   These can be contrasted with a past tense form:

   (80) Endgwen da-gii-waabminang. I 'I wonder whether he has seen us (inc.)!

         Endgwen av 'whether'; da-gii-waabminang vta conj 3sProx»21 '(CONJ) ANsg might
         have seen us.' (AM39.95)

   Note, however, that, corresponding to the forms with wii-, above, there are future forms
with ge- and DUBITATIVE MODE as well:

   (81) Endgwen ge-bbaa-giiwsegwen. I T wonder whether he will go hunting'

         Endgwen av 'whether'; ge-bbaa-giiwsegwen vai ic conj dub SsProx '(CCNJ) ANsg
         might go around hunting.' (AM39.674)
782 • 16.2.4 Modal Preverb Daa-


   (82) Endgwen ge~naadmawwanen. I 'I wonder whether you'll help me.' (AM39.686)

          Endgwen av 'whether'; ge-naadmawwanen via ic conj dub 2s»ls '(CCNJ) you might
          help me.'


16.2.4 Modal Preverb Daa-

   The MODAL preverb is daa-, which expresses a range of meanings related to possibility,
necessity, desire and obligation. The range of its meaning can be seen from it normal
English translations, which include could, should, would, and might. The modal shows
extreme variation in its independent, plain conjunct, and changed conjunct order forms,
respectively daa-, ji-, and da-.

              Independent Order         Plain Conjunct Changed Conjunct
              daa-                      ji-            ge- + preterit mode
                                        da-

  The form daa- is used in independent order inflections, and precedes all other preverbs.
The following examples illustrate its usage.

   (83) Aw dash kiwenziinh wgii-naan niw wgwisan, Gdaa-nkwetwaa iw maanoo
        ji-zhwenmik.
         'The old man said to his son, "You must accept this being's offer to bless you.'

          Awpr SsProx 'that'; dash av 'then'; kiwenziinh na SsProx 'old man'; wgii-naan vta ind
          3sProx»3obv ' ANsg said to ANobv'; niw pr 3obv 'that/those'; wgwisan na 3sProx(3obv)
          ' ANSG's son(s)'; Gdaa-nkwetwaa vta ind 2s»3sProx 'you must accept ANsg'; iw pr Os
          'that'; maanoo av 'by all means'; ji-zhwenmik vta conj 3sProx»2s '(CONJ) ANsg bless
          youSG.'(AM31.12)


   (84) Ndaa-ni-maajaa na gwa? I 'May IgoT (AM39.3)
          Ndaa-ni-maajaa vai ind Is 'I may set off'; na av 'yes/no question'; gwa av 'indeed.'


   (85) Gdaa-naadmoon na? I 'Should I help youT (AM39.373)

          Gdaa-naadmoon vta ind 2s»ls 'you SG could help me'; na av 'yes/no question.'
                                                                    16.2.4 Modal Preverb Daa- • 783



   (86) Aapji nbakde, Maanii. Bezhgoognzhii gwa ndaa-mwaa.
         'I'm really hungry, Mary. I could eat a horse.' (ED)

          Aapji av 'really'; nbakde vai ind Is 'I am hungry'; Maanii na 3sProx 'Mary.'
          Bezhgoognzhii na 3sProx 'a horse'; gwa av 'indeed'; ndaa-mwaa vta ind ls»3sProx 'I
          could eat ANsg.'


   The modal preverb can be used with future reference rather like English modals.

   (87) Waabang na go ndaa-bgiz gbe-giizhig? I Tomorrow can I go swimming all day?'
          Waabang av 'tomorrow'; na av 'yes/no question'; ndaa-bgiz vai ind Is 'I could swim';
          gbe-giizhig av 'all day.' (DP)

    The modal preverb is used with past tense preverb gii- in the independent order as well,
in which case it usually signals unrealized possibility. An associated conditional clause typ-
ically has its verb in the PRETERIT mode.

   (88) Giishpin wiindmawyamba gdaa-gii-naadmoon.
         'If you had told me / would have helped you.' (AM39.697

          Giishpin av 'if; wiindmawyamba vta conj pret 2s»ls '(CONJ) you SG had told me';
          gdaa-gii-naadmoon vta ind ls»2s 'I would have helped you SG.'

        ndaa-gii-baashkizwaa.
         'I saw a deer over in the woods. If I had had a gun / would have shot it.'

          Waawaashkeshi na SsProx 'deer'; ngii-waabmaa vta ind ls»3sProx 'I saw ANsg'; widi
          av 'over there'; megyaak av 'in the woods'; giishpin av 'if; yaamaambaa vtipret ls»0
          '(CONJ) I had had IN'; baashkzigan ni Os 'rifle'; ndaa-gii-baashkzwaa vta ind

   One form of daa- used in the plain conjunct is da-, used with verbs in subordinate
clauses that have time reference subsequent to that of the main verb. In most examples I
have, the main verb is a verb of speaking, and the subordinate clause represents indirect
speech.

16.2.5 Expressing Obligation

    Related to MODALITY is OBLIGATION, which is commonly expressed in Nishnaabemwin
by means of adverbial constructions. There are several adverbs for this function, including
ndawaa (also ndawaaj), aabdig (also aabdeg), and booch (also pooch, pooj). Ndawaa
expresses a range of obligation, and is glossed by Rhodes 1985:286 as 'after all, might as
well, necessarily, changing one's mind'; aabdig (also aabdeg) and booch both express
strong obligation, the former glossed by Rhodes 1985:2 as 'absolutely, necessarily' and the
latter as 'sure, must.' All three adverbs typically precede the verbs they modify. The follow-
ing are examples of ndawaa.

   (101) Ndawaa baamaa gga-biindaakwemi. I 'We (incl.) shall have to smoke later on.'
          Ndawaa av 'have to'; baamaa av 'later'; gga-biindaakwemi vai ind 21 'we will smoke
          tobacco.' (AM39.46)


   (102) Mii dash ndawaa gii-giiwewaad. I 'Then they were compelled to go home.'

          Mii av 'and'; dash av 'so'; ndawaa av 'have to'; gii-giiwewaad vai conj SpProx '(CONJ)
          ANpl went home.' (AM4.8)

   Examples of aabdig (aabdeg). Verbs associated with this adverb are usually FUTURE
TENSE.

   (103) Aambe gshkozin, ngwiiwzens. Aabdeg gwii-o-skooniw.

         'Okay, get up my son. You have to go to school.' (ED)

          Aambe av 'hey'; gshkozin vai imp 2s 'wake up!'; ngwiiwzens na Is(SsProx) 'my boy.'
788 • 16.2.5 Expressing Obligation


   (104) Aabdig go ngii-yaanan mzinhignan wii-skoonwiyaanh.

         7 had to have the books to go to school.' (FF2.9)

          Aabdig av 'necessarily'; ngii-yaanan vti ind ls»0p 'I had to have INpl'; mzinhignan ni
          Op 'books'; wii-skoonwiyaanh vai conj Is '(CONJ) I will go to school.'


   (105) Ji-bwaa-nso-dbahganek aabdeg gwii-giizhiitaami ennakiiying.

         'We (incl.) have to finish working before three o'clock.' (MC)

          Ji-bwaa-nso-dbahganek vii conj 0 'before IN be three o'clock'; aabdeg av 'necessarily';
          gwii-giizhiitaami vai ind 21 'we will finish'; ennakiiying vai ic conj 21 '(CCNJ) we
          work so.'


   The adverb aabdeg can be used with past tense, but usually in a context of future or
unrealized action, as in the following sentence, where gii-zhaawag, 'ANpl went,' is past, but
both wii-boozchigewaad, 'ANpl intend to do mailing,' and wii-disgowaad, 'ANpl intend to
receive IN,' are both future. See also (104), above.

   (106) Aabdeg oodenaang gii-zhaawag go Nishnaabeg wii-boozchigewaad, maage
         maajiibiihgan wii-disgowaad.
          'It was necessary for people to go to town if they wanted to mail something, or if
         they wanted to receive a letter.' (RN)

          Aabdeg av 'necessarily'; oodenaang ni 0 loc 'to town'; gii-zhaawag vai indSpProx
          'ANpl went there'; go nishnaabeg na 3pProx 'Indians'; wii-boozchigewaad vai conj
          SpProx '(CONJ) ANpl wanted to do mailing'; maage av 'or'; maajiibiihgan ni Os
          'letter'; wii-disgowaad vta conj Os»3pProx '(CONJ) IN encountered ANpl.'


   As with many adverbs, aabdeg can function predicatively, which results in associated
verbs showing conjunct order inflection.

   (107) Mii dash gii-bi-zhaad aw zhaagnaash mii-sh gaa-naad niw mdimooyenyan,
         "Aabdeg sa ji-gkinoohmaagzid aw gwiiwzens."
          'And this white man (Indian agent) came and he said to the old lady, "It's impera-
         tive that that boy go to school.'" (AK13.3)
                                           16.2.6 Expressing Desires and Wishes (Optatives) • 789



         Mii av 'and'; dash av 'then'; gii-bi-zhaad vai conj 3sPwx '(CONJ) ANsg came hither
         there'; awpr BsProx 'that'; zhaagnaash na SsProx 'white person'; mii-sh av 'and then';
         gaa-naad vta ic conj 3sProx»3obv '(CCNJ) ANsg said to ANobv'; niw/?r 3obv

         7 have to go pick up my mother-in-law.' (Rhodes 1985:525)

    Desire and intent are expressed by means of the future preverb wii-, which is often

   (110) Aapji WK-damin gegoo. I 'I really want to play with something.' (DP)
         Aapji av 'really'; nii-damin vaio ind Is 'I want to play (with Y)'; gegoo pr indefO
         'something.'

   (111) Gaawii ngii-gkendnziin iidig paa-m/a-wiisniwaad giwi pinii-mnidoonshensag.

          'those'; pinii-mnidoonshensag na SpProx 'potato bugs.'


   Specific TRANSITIVE VERBS of wanting exist as well, such as ndawenim, 'want AN,' and
ndawendan, 'want IN.'

   (112) Aanii-sh gaa-zhichgeyaan, aanii-sh ezhi-ndawendman ji-zhichgeyaan?

16.2.7 Expressing Habituality

    Habitual activity is expressed by means of the adverb ko (also kwa), 'customarily, gener-
ally, often,' and with the preverb ntaa-, 'be good at, often, customarily.'

   (115) Aaniish ko pii mail e-biijgaadeg? I 'When is the mail usually brought?' (MC20.19)
          Aaniish av 'how'; ko av 'usually'; pii av 'time'; e-biijgaadeg vti/ii ic conj pass 0
          '(CCNJ) that IN is brought.'
                                                  16.2.8 Directional Preverbs as Time Markers • 791


   (116) Ngwetaani-niiskendam ko maanda wiikaa zgaknanzwin.
         'I'm terribly irritated that you never put this away.' (MC22.9)

          Ngwetaani-niiskendam vai ind Is Tm terribly irritated'; ko av 'frequency'; maandapr
          Os 'this'; wiikaa av 'never'; zgaknanzwin vti conj neg 2s»0 '(CONJ) you SG do not put
          IN away.'


   (117) Gegii gsha£o gdoo-mnjiw. Miinwaa gdoo-ntaa-naadmaw.
         'You too treat (sponsor) me often. And you often help me.' (MC15.5)

          Gegii pr pers 2s 'as for you SG'; gsha av 'indeed'; ko av 'habitually'; gdoo-mnjiw vta ind
          2s»ls 'you treat me (i.e., pay for me).' Miinwaa av 'and'; gdoo-ntaa-naadmaw vta ind
          2s»ls 'you habitually help me.'

   With past tense, ko (kwa) is rather like English "used to," that is, constitutes a past habit-
ual activity that is no longer in effect.

   (118) NgK-wa-nbwaach'aa kwa. I 'I used to go and visit him.' (AM39.253)

          Ngii-wa-nbwaachhaa vta ind ls»3sProx 'I went and visited ANsg'; kwa av 'used to.'

16.2.8 Directional Preverbs as Time Markers

   Many of the directional preverbs take on a secondary sense relating to the time of an
action relative to the time of speaking, or some other reference point. The directional pre-
verb ni-, for example, specifies something that happens subsequent to the time of speaking
or some reference point, roughly translating as 'in the future course of time,' as can be seen
from the following examples:

          ANsg spoke to ANobv'; Mii av 'so'; noongo av 'now'; i\v pr Os 'that'; ge-ni-naadziyan
          vai ic conj 2s '(CCNJ) you will live so'; niigaan av 'in the future.'

   Rhodes suggests that hi- has the tense-related meaning 'in the past' and cites the exam-
ple of gaa-bi-bmiseg, 'last week.' In this sense hi- customarily appears with a past tense pre-
verb, gii- or the SUBORDINATOR gaa-, which is identical in form to the initial-changed past
tense preverb. The use of the preverb hi- seems to be especially associated with predications
that begin in the past but have relevance to the present, or to give an explicit sense of the
passage of time in the relationship between the present and past event referred to.

16.3 Aspectual Verbs and Preverbs

     Specific ASPECTUAL verbs exist in Nishnaabemwin, many capable of taking SEN-
TENCE-COMPLEMENTS, focusing on the beginning and end of a verbal action or event.
Aspect is a grammatical concept that relates to how verbal events are cast, for example,
whether they are viewed as entirely completed or in process, or whether there is a focus on
their beginning or ending. Aspectual verbs in Nishnaabemwin include maajtaa, 'begin
[doing something],' webtaa, 'start [doing something],' boontaa, 'finish, complete,'
giizhiitaa, 'finish [doing something],' and shkwaataa, 'finish [an activity].' The verbs
boontaa and shhvaataa are most commonly used without complements, with the meaning,
 'finish an activity, finish working.' Many of these roots occur as roots in other verbs as well,
such as maaddemo, 'start to cry' VAI, and boonenim, 'forget about AN' [lit., stop thinking
about AN] VTA. The root /maad/ appears to be much more common and productive than
/boon/]. The root /ishkwaa/ appears in a few adverbs, such as shkwaayaaj, 'at the end, the
last time' (W) and shkwaayhiing, 'behind.' All five roots occur in derived preverb forms,
maajii-, 'begin,' booni-, 'stop, cease,' giizhi-, 'finish,' and shkwaa-, 'finish, complete, after,'
and webi-, 'begin.' Some examples of these verbs and preverbs follow.
794 • 16.3 Aspectual Verbs and Preverbs

 6.4 Verb Mode

   Three inflectionally marked ASPECTUAL-EVIDENTIAL MODES exist in Nishnaabemwin,
the PRETERIT, the DUBITATIVE, and the PRETERIT DUBITATIVE (also called DUBITATIVE
PRETERIT). The absence of mode inflection is usually taken to represent another, unmarked,
INDICATIVE (or NEUTRAL) mode. There are two parameters of variation in the mode system,
one preterit, and the other dubitative. Preterit mode is prototypically used to indicate verbal
action that has reached a point of completion prior to some reference point, usually the
moment of speaking (the same orientational point as used for present tense). Dubitative
mode indicates doubt, uncertainty, or conjecture. The interaction of these two parameters
                                                                               16.4 Verb Mode-799


produce the four modes of Nishnaabemwin verbs, as summarized in the following chart.

                                      - dubitative    + dubitative
                         - preterit   indicative      dubitative
                         + preterit   preterit        preterit dubitative

   The dubitative modes are discussed in Section 16.9.2, Dubitative Mode, beginning on
page 832, below. Here I will only present a few examples of the preterit.

   (148) "Mewnzha gii-nboban aw gookmis, ggii-ngadmaag iw wiigwaam."
         "'Your grandmother died a long time ago, she left you her house.'" (AK13.27)

          Mewnzha av 'long ago'; gii-nboban vai indpret 3sProx 'ANsg died'; awpr SsProx
          'that'; gookmis na 2s(3sProx) 'your grandmother'; ggii-ngadmaag vta ind 3sProx»2s
          'ANsg left Y for you SG'; iw pr Os 'that'; wiigwaam ni Os 'house.'


   (149) ... wgii-gkendmawaawaan maa naa iw sa niibwa go gegoo bmiwdoonid mii-sh
         gii-nsaawaad niw miinwaa gii-mkamaawaad iw bemwidoonpan.
         '...they knew that they were carrying lots of things, they killed them and took
         away what they had been carrying! (AK10.11)

          wgii-gkendmawaawaan vta ind 3pProx»3obv ' ANpl knew Y about ANobv'; maa av
          'then'; i\vprOs 'that'; niibwa av 'lots'; gegooprindefO 'something'; bmiwdoonid vti
          conj 3obv»0 '(CONJ) ANobv carried IN'; mii-sh av 'and then'; gii-nsaawaad vta conj
          3pProx»3obv '(CONJ) ANpl killed ANobv'; niw pr 3obv 'that/those'; miinwaa av 'and'
          gii-mkamaawaad vta conj 3pProx»3obv '(CONJ) ANpl robbed ANobv of Y'; iw pr Os
          'that'; bemwidoonpan vti ic conjpartpret3obv»0 '(CCNJ) which (IN) ANobv carried

16.5 The Iterative

    Periodic activities can be marked with ITERATIVE verbal inflection, a suffix /-in/ (often
lacking the final /n/ in Odawa) that occurs in final suffix position. Verbs inflected for itera-
tive are conjunct order and also show initial change. See also the VII examples on p. 264.

   (151) Aapji dash go niibna wzagkinaanaawaa iw mnoomin gonda Nishnaabeg
         degwaagnigin zgaknamwaad iw mnoomin....
          'These Indians collected very much rice, collecting it whenever it is autumn...'

          Aapji av 'really'; dash av 'then'; go niibna av 'much'; wzagkinaanaawaa vti ind
          3pProx»0 'ANpl store INsg'; iw pr Os 'that'; mnoomin ni Os 'rice'; gonda pr na SpProx
          'these'; Nishnaabeg na SpProx 'Indians'; degwaagnigin vii ic conj 0 iter '(CCNJ)
          whenever IN is autumn'; zgaknamwaad vti conj 3pProx»0 '(CONJ) ANpl store IN'; iw
          pr Os 'that'; mnoomin ni Os 'rice' (AM6.12)

   (152) Wayayaakzijin mii go gii-mdoodoohind maa mdoodoowgamgong. Gye go mii go
         mno-bmaadzid sa gaa-shkwaa-mdoodoojin.
         'Whenever anyone fell ill he was given a steam bath there in the sweating lodge.
         Then he would be well, when[ever] he had taken the steam bath.' (AM21.21-22)

          Wayapr indefSsProx 'anyone'; yaakzijin vai ic conj SsProx iter '(CCNJ) whenever
          ANsg was ill'; mii av 'then'; gii-mdoodoohind vta conj x»3sProx 'ANsg was given a
          sweat bath'; maa av 'there'; mdoodoowgamgong ni 0 loc 'into the sweat lodge.' Gye av
          'and'; mii av 'then'; mno-bmaadzid vai conj SsProx '(CONJ) ANsg was well';
          gaa-shkwaa-mdoodoojin vai ic conj SsProx iter '(CCNJ) whenever ANsg finished taking
          a sweat bath.'
                                                          16.6 Expressions of Specific Time • 801



   Another way to indicate iteration of actions and events is with RELATIVE PREVERB dso-,
'so many times,' as in the following example.

   (153) Endso-dgoshing wnichiiwhigoon niw ninwan.

         'Every time he comes that man scolds him.' (AM39.603)

          Endso-dgoshing vai ic conjBsProx 'every time ANsg arrives'; wnichiiwhigoon vta ind

   Repetition is also expressed by means of REDUPLICATION (see Chapter 17, p.908ff.).

16.6 Expressions of Specific Time

    In this section we examine many ways to make reference to units of time such as hours,
days, weeks, months and years.
    EXPRESSING THE HOUR AND DURATIONS OF HOURS. Expressions of hourly time are
straightforward, being formed by means of the VII measurement verb dbahgned, 'be such
hour.' (All examples in this section, from MC)

   (154) Aanii-sh endso-dbahganeg? I 'What time is it?'

          Aanii-sh av 'how then'; endso-dbahganeg vii ic conj 0 '(CCNJ) IN is so many units.'

   (155) Ngo-dbahgned. I 'It's one o'clock.'

          Ngo-dbahgned vii ind nis 'IN is one o'clock.'

   (156) A/HZ/i0-dbahganed. I 'It's two o'clock.'

   (157) Afto-dbahganed. I 'It's three o'clock.'

   (158) Mlrfoaso-dbahganed. I 'It's fen o'clock.'

   (159) Mdaaswi-shi-bezhignso-dbahganed. I "It's, eleven o'clock.'

   (160) Naawkwe. I 'It's twelve o'clock noon.'

          Naawkwe vii ind nis 'INsg is noon.'

   EXPRESSING THE DAYS OF THE WEEK. There are two forms for most days of the week
an inanimate intransitive (impersonal) verb form, and an inanimate noun form, which is
usually derived from the associated verb. Noun forms tend to be preferred in some locales,
such as Walpole, while verb forms are more common elsewhere. The following charts lay
out the verb and noun forms in use for days of the week. Many days have more than one
form.
                               Verb Forms for Days of the Week
              Monday           Shkwaa-namhe-giizhgad            'after-praying day'
              Tuesday          Niizh-giizhgad                   'day two'
              Wednesday        Nso-giizhgad                     'day three'
                               Zoozep-giizhgad (M)              'Joseph-day'
                               Aabtawyihiiwan (W)               'midway'
              Thursday         Aabtawyihiiwan (W)               'midway'
              Friday           Jiibaatgo-giizhgad (M)           'cross day'
                               Naano-giizhgad                   'day five'
              Saturday         Maanii-giizhgad (M)              'Mary-day
              Sunday           Namhe-giizhgad                   'praying day'

                               Nouns Forms for Days of the Week
              Monday           Ntam-giizhgad (Od)         first day
              Tuesday          Niizhoo-giizhgad (W)             day two
              Wednesday        Nswi-giizhgad (Od)               day three
              Thursday         Aabtawewang (W)                  halfway
              Friday           Naan(oo)-giizhgad (W)            day five
              Saturday         Ngodwaasoo-giizhgad              day six
                               Zaatewang (W)                    Saturday
              Sunday           Namhewgiizhgad                   pray-day

   Some speakers freely use the English terms for days of the week, evidently attached to

   EXPRESSING THE MONTH. The month is expressed on Manitoulin Island using the
English term and the VII verb of being, aawan. This usage is particularly interesting in that
the months were traditionally of animate gender. As borrowed terms, however, the names of
the months are often grammatically inanimate, though not invariably, as I have also heard
maaba October, 'this (an.) October.'

   (189) June aawan. I 'It's June.' (MC)
          aawan vii ind Os 'INSG is.'

   (190) March ngii-bwaachhaa ngwis. I T visited my son in March.' (MC)
          ngii-bwaachhaa vta ind ls»3sProx T visited ANsg'; ngwis na ls(3sProx) 'my son.'

   Andrew Medler used a more traditional strategy for expressing the month, using agoozi,
'hang,' in reference to the appearance and phase of the moon. In this usage, the names of the
months are animate.

   (191) Pii dash menookmig, Ziisbaakdoke-giizis e-goojing, gii-gsinaamgad.
         'Then when the spring was at hand, when the Sugar-Making moon (i.e., March)
         hung aloft, there was cold weather.' (AM 10.2)

          Pii av 'when'; dash av 'then'; menookmig vii ic conj 0 '(CCNJ) when spring came';
          Ziisbaakdoke-giizis na 3sProx '(month of) March'; e-goojing vai ic conj SsProx
          '(CCNJ) when ANsg was hanging'; gii-gsinaamgad vii ind 0 'the weather was cold.'

    EXPRESSING THE DAY OF THE MONTH. The day of the month is expressed by means of
verb of date, which has a number initial and the final complex, /-gonagizi/, 'be so many
days old' (VAI). The date is expressed in this way because traditionally the month was cast
in lunar terms, with each day being a function of the number of days "old" that a given new
moon was. There are special VAI verbs used for the first and last day of the month, respec-
tively maadgiza (or maadgizo), 'be the first day of the month,' with root /maad-/, 'begin'
and shkwaagza (or shkwaagzo), 'be the last day of the month,' with root /shkwaa-/, 'after,
last.' Both of these forms have a VAI final complex /-agi(n)zo/, 'be counted.'

   (192) Nongo maadgiza. I Today is the first of the month: (MC)
          Nongo av 'today'; maadgiza vai ind SsProx 'ANsg is starting day (of month).'
810 • 16.6 Expressions of Specific Time


   (193) Niizhgon'gizi nongo. I Today is the second of the month! (MC)
          Niizhgon'gizi vai indSsProx 'ANsg is two days old'; nongo av 'today.'

   (194) Mdaasgon'gizi nongo. I Today is the tenth of the month.' (MC)

   (195) Mdaaswi-shi-niizhgon'gizi nongo. I Today is the twelfth of the month.' (MC)

   (196) Niizhtana nsognagzi nongo. I Today is the twentieth of the month' (MC)
          Niizhtana nm 'twenty'; nsognagzi vai ind SsProx 'ANsg is so many days old'; nongo av
          'today.'

   (197) Niizhtana-shi-niizhgon'gizi nongo. I "Today is the twenty-second of the month.'
          Niizhtana-shi-niizhgon'gizi vai ind SsProx 'ANsg is twenty two days old'; nongo av
          'today.'

   (198) Nsimdana nsognagzi nongo. I Today is the thirtieth of the month' (MC)

          'today.'

   (199) Shkwaagzo nongo. I Today is the last day of the month.' (MC)
          Shkwaagzo vai ind SsProx 'ANsg is the last'; nongo av 'today.'

  Another verb expressing the last day of the month is shkwaayaasge, VAI, 'be the end of a
month'

   The expression of "years ago" and "years ahead" uses a slightly different strategy from

For years in the future, ni- is used with ngo-bboon'gad, 'be one year' vii.

   EXPRESSING DAYS RELATIVE. Distinct expressions exist for yesterday, today, and
tomorrow. The day after tomorrow is expressed by adding was-, 'beyond,' to waabang,
'tomorrow,' was-waabang. The day after the day after tomorrow can be expressed by add-
ing gchi-, 'great,' to was-waabang, and days beyond that by repeating gchi-, though, obvi-
ously, in practice this is not common. An analogous pattern exists for days before, using
what appears to be a reduced form of adverb jiinaagwa, 'yesterday.' The following chart
lays out these forms.

    waabang                      'tomorrow'
    was-waabang                  'the day after tomorrow'
    gchi-was-waabang             'the day after the day after tomorrow'
    gchi-gchi-was-waabang        'the day after the day after the day after tomorrow'

    jimaago                      'yesterday'
    was-naago                    'the day before yesterday'
    gchi-was-naago               'the day before the day before yesterday'
    gchi-gchi-was-naago          'the day before the day before the day before yesterday'

   Some examples of the usage of various temporal adverbials.

          Is(SsProx) 'my son.'

16.7 Expressing Time with Temporal Adverbs

    GENERAL TEMPORAL ADVERBS. Many distinctly temporal adverbs exist to express dura-
tions of time. A lengthy list is provided in Chapter 3, Section 3.5.1, page 139. Here I present
a few examples. As can readily be seen, such adverbs are very frequently initial in their
clauses, though they can also be preceded by more strictly initial adverbs such as gaa(wiiri),
'not,' as in (256), below.

   (251) Gbeyhii gii-bbaa-nendi. i 'He was out a longtime.' (AM39.107)
          Gbeyhii av 'for a long time'; gii-bbaa-nendi vai indSsProx 'ANsg was away going
          about.'


   (252) Gbeyhiing dash gii-bmaadzi miinwaa wgii-wiidookwaan wiiji-bmaadzi.

         'For a long time he lived and he helped his fellow man.' (AK5.8)

          Gbeyhiing av 'for a long time'; dash av 'then'; gii-bmaadzi vai ind SsProx 'ANsg lived';
          miinwaa av 'and'; wgii-wiidookwaan vta ind 3sProx»3obv 'ANsg helped ANobv';
          wiiji-bmaadzi na 3sProx 'ANSG's fellow human.'


   (253) Jina dash eta teni maa shkodeng. I 'Only for a short time is it there in the fire.'

          Jina av 'a short time'; dash av 'then'; eta av 'only'; teni vii ind Oobv 'INobv is put'; maa
          av 'there'; shkodeng ni 0 loc 'in the fire.' (AM25.8)


   (254) Ngoding giiwenh naagshig oodetoo. I 'One evening he went to town.' (FF4.22)

          Ngoding av 'once'; giiwenh av 'allegedly'; naagshig vii conj 0 '(CONJ) IN is evening';
          oodetoo vai ind SsProx 'ANsg goes to town.'

   Universality of time is expressed with the adverb pane, 'always,' and opposite concept,
'never,' with a verb inflected for negative and the adverb wiikaa, 'ever.'

   (255) Aaniish naa mii sa go pane gzhaadged, gaa go naa maamda wii-wiijiiwwed,
         maajaawaad iidig gonda zaasbaakdokejig.
         'Well, he always stayed home, as he couldn't go with others, when those who
         made sugar went off.' (SO4.5)

          Aaniish av 'well'; mii av 'then'; pane av 'always'; gzhaadged vai conj SsProx '(CONJ)
          ANsg stays at home'; gaa av 'not'; maamda av 'able'; wii-wiijiiwwed vai conj SsProx
          '(CONJ) ANsg wants to accompany'; maajaawaad vai conj SpProx '(CONJ) ANpl
          leave'; iidig av 'seems'; gonda pr na SpProx 'these'; zaasbaakdokejig vai ic conj part
          SpProx '(CCNJ) ANpl who make sugar.'

   TEMPORAL AND LOCATIVE ADVERBS. Several locative adverbs do extended service, in
