16.8 Temporal Relationships Between Clauses

    Very often associated ADJUNCT clauses are not marked with any complementizer or
other adverbial element, it is only by virtue of their verbs having conjunct order inflection
that their adjunct status is formally represented. In (279), below, for example,
ziisbaakdokewaad, '(conj) ANpl make sugar,' is loosely connected with the preceding
clause, vaguely specifying purpose or contemporaneous time.

   (279) Aaniish mii sa iidig ddanziwaad go naa [ziisbaakdokewaad].
         'Well, they used to stay in a certain place [as/when they made sugar].' (SO 1.2)

          Aaniish av 'well'; mii av 'so'; iidig av 'it seems'; ddanziwaad vai conj 3pProx '(CON
          ANpl were staying there'; ziisbaakdokewaad vai conj SpProx '(CONJ) ANpl made
          sugar.'

   The clause nmadbid zhiwi, 'as/when ANsg sits there,' is similarly related to the preced-
ing clause in the following:

   (280) Mii go nendaajiihang wa kwe [nmadbid zhiwi].
         That is why this woman was stirring it [as she sat there].' (SOI. 17)

         Mii av 'and'; go nendaajiihang vti ic conj 3sProx»0 '(CCNJ) ANsg was beating IN'; wa
         pr SsProx 'this' kwe na SsProx 'woman'; nmadbid vai conj SsProx '(CONJ) ANsg sat';
         zhiwi av 'there.'

   Often linkage between clauses in narrative is extremely loose. In the following sen-
tences, for example, the two clauses are loosely linked as successive mil clauses.

   (281) [Mii-sh wa mdimooyenh bbaa-yaad], [mii gii-waabmaad ninwan, mansooyan].

   (282) [Mii sa giiwenh gaa-nbaawaad iidig nendang wa mdimooyenh], [mii sa giiwenh
         gii-nbaad iidig gewii bjiinag].
        ' When that old woman believed that they were asleep, it was only then that she

   This is the customary kind of linkage found in running narrative, with very loose,
implicit connections between clauses, especially those showing temporal relationships.

16.9 Evidentiality

    Another kind of meaning very commonly expressed in Nishnaabemwin sentences is that
of the degree of certainty with which the speaker makes an assertion. There are two primary
ways to express uncertainty, one, by using dubitative adverbs, and two, by means of inflec-
tional suffixes belonging to the DUBITATIVE or PRETERIT DUBITATIVE modes.

16.9.1 Evidential (Dubitative) Adverbs

   Several adverbs function to add an element of doubt or uncertainty to a predication.
Chief among these are giiwenh and iidig. These adverbs are commonly translated with
                                                         16.9.1 Evidential (Dubitative) Adverbs • 831



English expressions such as 'it seems,' 'evidently,' 'they say,' or 'allegedly.' Typically these
adverbs occur very early in their clauses, often as the second constituent. Verbs associated
with them are often inflected for dubitative mode, as in (288), below. The following example
illustrates the use of iidig.

   (286) Mii sa iidig wadi gii-patood wiijkiwenyan yaanid.
         'He had apparently run over to where his friends were.' (SO 1.36)

          Mii av 'and'; iidig av 'it seems'; wadi av 'there'; gii-patood vai conj 3sProx '(CONJ)
          ANsg ran there'; wiijkiwenyan nod 3sProx(3obv) 'ANSG's friend(s)'; yaanid vai conj
          3obv '(CONJ) ANobv be there.'


   EVIDENTIAL ADVERBS are used extensively by some narrators, and in traditional stories,
such narrators may use an evidential adverb with each of a majority of the sentences in their
narration. To illustrate, the following example provides the first four sentences of a narration
by Sam Osawamick, with an evidential adverb occurring with each one.

   (287) 1 Ngoding sagiiwenh nishnaabeg ziisbaakdokewag, ngoji go naa noopming,
         waasa go naa noopming. 2 Aanii-sh mii sa iidig ddanziwaad go naa
         ziisbaakdokewaad. 3 Mii-sh giiwenh ko zhaazhi gaa-zhiwebak. 4 Gii-bbaa-yaawag
         giiwenh nishnaabeg, bebaa-nda-nshiwejig. 5 Ngoji-sh go naa wadi gii-yaadgenag
         giwi, gomaa go naa dshidgenag, mii-sh giiwenh bezhig gii-noonind: "Aa-sh ge
         naa! Bbaa-ndawaatoon."
         ' 1 Once some people were evidently making sugar, somewhere inland, far inland.
         2 They evidently used to stay in a certain place and make sugar. 3 This is evidently
         what generally happened long ago. 4 Some Indians evidently used to come
         around, bent on killing people. 5 There were apparently a number of them some-
         where over there, and one of them was evidently appointed: "Come now: Go and
         get some information." '(SOI.1-5)

          (1) Ngoding av 'once'; giiwenh av 'evidently'; nishnaabeg na SpProx 'Indians';
          ziisbaakdokewag vai ind3p 'ANpl are making sugar'; ngoji av 'somewhere'; noopming
          av 'in the bush'; waasa av 'far'; noopming av 'in the bush.' (2) Aaniish av 'well'; mii av
          'and'; iidig av 'it seems'; ddanziwaad vai conj SpProx '(CONJ) ANpl were staying
          there'; ziisbaakdokewaad vai conj 3pProx '(CONJ) ANpl made sugar.' (3) Mii-sh av
          'and then'; giiwenh av 'evidently'; ko av 'used to'; zhaazhi av 'long ago'; gaa-zhiwebak
          vii conj 0 '(CCNJ) IN happened.' (4) Gii-bbaa-yaawag vai ind 3pProx 'ANpl went
          around'; giiwenh av 'evidently'; nishnaabeg na SpProx 'Indians'; bebaa-nda-nshiwejig
          vai ic conj part 3pProx '(CCNJ) ANpl who seek to murder.' (5) Ngoji av 'somewhere';
          dash av 'then'; wadi av 'there'; gii-yaadgenag vai ind dub 3pProx 'ANpl were evidently
          there'; giwipr 3pProx 'those'; gomaa av 'indeed'; dshidgenag vai ind3pProx 'ANpl are
832 • 16.9.2 Dubitative Mode


          so many'; mii-sh av 'and then'; giiwenh av 'evidently'; bezhig nm 'one'; gii-noonind vta
          conjx»3sProx '(CONJ) ANsg was commissioned'; Aa-sh ge naa expr 'Hey!; Well!';
          Bbaa-ndawaatoon vai imp 2s 'go around spying.'

16.9.2 Dubitative Mode

   Dubitative mode inflectional marking on verbs is commonly used to express doubt,
uncertainty, or speculation. Inflection is by means suffixation, with the element /dig/ (or
/dog/) very common in the independent order, and /-en/ in the conjunct.

   (288) Gnabaj way a wesiinh j>aad/g maa ndahbaaning.
         'It seems as if there may be some creature in the spring.' (AM10.11)

          Gnabaj av 'perhaps'; wayapr indefSsProx 'some'; wesiinh na SsProx 'creature'; yaadig
          vai ind dub SsProx 'ANsg might be there'; maa av 'there'; ndahbaaning ni 0 loc 'in the
          spring'

   (289) Gaawiin gii-baatiin'siiwag gnimaa go naa ngodwaasmidna gii-dchidgenag bezhig
         iw gaa-bmi-dnizwaad.
         'There were not many, perhaps sixty formed a group where they dwelled in one
         place.' (AK9.3)

          Gaawiin av 'not'; gii-baatiin'siiwag vai ind SpProx neg 'ANpl were not many in
          number'; gnimaa av 'perhaps'; ngodwaasmidna nm 'sixty'; gii-dchidgenag vai ind dub
          SpProx 'ANpl might have been in number'; bezhig nm 'one'; iw pr Os 'that';
          gaa-bmi-dnizwaad vai ic conj SpProx '(CCNJ) where ANpl lived there over time.'

   The dubitative mode is especially common with dubitative pronouns, such as wegwen,
'whoever,' and dubitative adverbs, such as manj, 'however it may be,' almost obligatory
with the former. In the conjunct, verbs having dubitative mode always show initial change.

   (290) Wegwen dash aw ge-gshkitoogwen ji-zhngwaadzig mii aw gbeyhiing
         ge-bmaadzid, da-ntaa-ndawenjge da-nbwaakaa miinwaa gwyak da-zhi-yaa.
         'And whoever may be able to keep it down he's the one who will live for a long
         time, he'll be a good hunter, he'll be clever and he'll behave right.' (AK5.6)

   ENDGWENH CONSTRUCTIONS. The dubitative adverb endgwenh (also endgwen) indicates

            over ANobv'; iidig av 'it seems'; niwipr na 3obv 'that/those'; endgwen av 'whether';

16.9.3 Preterit Dubitative Mode

   This MODE is used in a variety of contexts where there is uncertainty with respect to
events that took place in the past. It combines the concepts of PRETERIT and DUBITATIVE,
and is commonly marked by a suffix element /(go)ban/ in the INDEPENDENT ORDER and
/(go)banen/ in the CONJUNCT.

   (297) Pii iw gaa-wiidged aw nmishoomis, niw oosan gii-zhaawan odi Sucker Creek mii
         odi gii-waabmaagbanen niw kwezensan gechi-gnaajwinjin.
         'When my grandfather got married, his father had gone to Sucker Creek and there
         he must have seen this very beautiful girl.' (AK11.1)
                                                               16.9.3 Preterit Dubitative Mode • 835



         Pii av 'when'; iwpr Os 'that'; gaa-wiidged vai ic conj 3sProx '(CCNJ) when ANsg
         married'; aw pr 3sProx 'that'; nmishoomis nad Is(SsProx) 'my grandfather'; niw/?r
         3obv 'that/those'; oosan nad 3sProx(3obv) 'ANsg's father'; gii-zhaawan vai ind 3obv
         'ANobv went there'; odi av 'there'; mii av 'and'; odi av 'there'; gii-waabmaagbanen vta
         conjpdub 3sProx»3obv '(CONJ) ANsg must have seen ANobv'; nivrprSobv 'that/those';
         kwezensan na 3obv 'young woman'; gechi-gnaajwinjin vai ic conj part 3obv '(CCNJ)
         who (ANobv) was very beautiful.'

   (298) Mii dash gii-bi-maajaawaad mii dash iw gii-sweshkaawaad, Neyaashii-nagmiing
         gii-zhaa aw nmishoomis binoojiinswigban giiwenh iw pii...
         'And so they went on and then they disappeared, my grandfather went to Cape
         Croker— he must have been an infant at the...' (AK15.13a)

         Mii av 'and'; gii-bi-maajaawaad vai conj 3pProx '(CONJ) in time ANpl left'; mii av
         'and'; i\v pr Os 'that'; gii-sweshkaawaad vai conj 3pProx '(CONJ) ANpl dispersed';
         Neyaashii-nagmiing ni 0 loc 'to Cape Croker'; gii-zhaa vai ind 3sProx 'ANsg went
         there'; aw pr 3sProx 'that'; nmishoomis nad ls(3sPmx) 'my grandfather';
         binoojiinswigban vai indpdub 3sProx 'ANsg was evidently a child'; giiwenh av
         'evidently'; i\v pr Os 'that'; pii av 'time.'

   In narrative contexts, PRETERIT DUBITATIVE MODE is sometimes used in opening and
closing sentences to frame an entire discourse as representing oral traditional knowledge.
For example, in Sam Osawamick's account of a battle in the War of 1812, preterit dubitative
forms are used in both the opening and closing sentences, as illustrated below. In such
cases, the MODE markers are indexing the entire story, not necessarily the specific PREDI-
CATES (verbs) that they occur with.

   (299) Mii dash gaa-zhinaagdagbanen gchi-gindaaswin, gii-gchi-miigaadwangbanen
         ntam.
        'This is an interpretation of what it must have been like, the first time we were
        involved in a great war! (SO6.1)

         Mii av 'and'; dash av 'then'; gaa-zhinaagdagbanen vii ic conjpdub 0 '(CCNJ) IN must
         have been like'; gchi-gindaaswin ni Os 'great accounting'; gii-gchi-miigaadwangbanen
         vii conjpdub 0 '(CONJ) there was allegedly a great war'; ntam av 'first.'
836 • 16.9.3 Preterit Dubitative Mode


   (300) Mil sa gii-giizhiitaamgak gchi-miigaadwin wi pii gaa-dgogbanen.
         'So that great battle which evidently took place at that time was over.' (SO6.188)

          Mii av 'and'; gii-gizhiitaamgak'vii conj 0 '(CONJ) IN commenced'; gchi-miigaadwin ni
          Os 'great battle'; wi pr Os 'that'; pii av 'time'; gaa-dgogbanen vii ic conjpdub 0 '(CCNJ)
          that (IN) evidently took place.'

   PRETERIT DUBITATIVE IN CONTEXTS OF HYPOTHETICALITY. The PRETERIT DUBITATIVE
MODE is also commonly used with assertions that represent hypothetical or conjectural pos-
sibilities.

   (301) Mii dash pii giiwewaad giw niizh nishnaabeg, mii dash ekdod aw bezhig,

          (SG) should see ANsg'; gechi-gnaajwid vai ic conj part SsPfox ' (CCNJ) ANsg who is

   (302) Aaniish mii sa giiwenh egod: "Giishpin wii-miizhyaang giwi ggwisag, giin go

   The preterit dubitative is also used with inferences about closed events that necessarily
precede some current state of affairs, as in the following examples.

         'They have left traces that show [that they must have come here].' (AM39.710)

  There is considerable variation in Nishnaabemwin (and other dialects of Anishinaabe-

16.10 Negation

    Statements, questions and commands can be expressed either positively or negatively.
This grammatical property is sometimes called POLARITY, and a given clause is said to have
either positive polarity or negative polarity. Two primary grammatical devices are used in
negation in Nishnaabemwin, negative adverbs and negative verbal inflection. Distinct nega-
tive adverbs are used with the different verbal orders, gaa wii(n) in the INDEPENDENT
ORDER, and gego (or gegwa) in the IMPERATIVE ORDER. The CONJUNCT ORDER very com-
monly does not use an adverb, though gaa wii occasionally occurs. The form of VERBAL
INFLECTION is different for each order. While the inflectional suffixes of the INDEPENDENT
and CONJUNCT ORDERS are structurally related, being /-sii/ for the former and /-si(w)/ for
the latter, the NEGATIVE SUFFIX of the IMPERATIVE ORDER, which is /-ke/, shows no struc-
tural relationship to the negative suffix of the other two orders (n.b. /-sii/ occurs with nega-
tive first person inclusive commands, however). The following chart lays out the basic
components of negation in each verbal order. Negative inflectional forms are covered exten-
sively in the chapters on verb inflection, 5 to 8.

                 Order            Negative Adverbs       Negative Inflection
                 Independent      gaa, gaa wii(n)        /-sii/
                 Conjunct         —                      /-siw/
                 Imperative       gego, gegwa            /-ke(n)/, /-siidaa/

   Although the negative adverb gaa can appear with and without the contrastive FOCUS
element wii(n), when together, they are often treated as a single word, which can be seen
838* 16.10 Negation


from the failure of the EMPHATIC/CONTRASTIVE CLITIC element dash, and other such parti-
cles appearing in SECOND POSITION, to intervene between them.

   (305) Gaa wii dash gii-naagzisii. I 'He was not visible.' (AM31.34)

          Gaa wii av 'not'; dash av 'however'; gii-naagzisii vai ind3sProx neg 'ANsg was not
          visible.'


   (306) Gaawiin dash aw nookmis ngoji gii-zhaasii, shpimsagong odi gii-gaazod mii dash
         gii-gkendang iw nningsenig iw wiigwaam.

         'And my grandmother didn't go outside, but she hid there upstairs, and she knew
         it when the house shook.' (AK11.8)

         Gaawiin av 'not'; dash av 'then'; aw/?r 3sProx 'that'; nookmis nad ls(3sProx) 'my
         grandmother'; ngoji av 'anywhere'; gii-zhaasii vai ind 3sProx neg 'ANsg did not go
         there'; shpimsagong av 'upstairs'; odi av 'there'; gii-gaazod vai conj 3sProx '(CONJ)
         ANsg hid'; mii av ' and'; gii-gkendang vti conj 3sProx»0 ' (CONJ) ANsg knew IN'; iw
         pr Os 'that'; nningsenig vii conj Oobv ' (CONJ) INobv shakes'; iw pr Os 'that'; wiigwaam
         hi Os 'house.'


   The YES/NO QUESTION marker, na, also occurs after the combination gaa+wii(n).

   (307) Gaawii na geshkgwaaswining tesnoo? I 'Isn't it near the sewing machine?' (MC)

          Gaawii av 'not'; na av 'yes/no question'; geshkgwaaswining ni 0 loc 'by the sewing
          machine'; tesnoo vii ind neg Os 'INsg is not there.'

   Because of the close connection between gaa and wii(n), they are often written as a sin-
gle unit, as in the last two examples above.
   NEGATION OF PROPOSITIONS. The adverbs gaa (wiin) or kaa, or these adverbs in combi-
nation with expressive elements, as in kaahaa, can be used to answer negatively or deny an
entire proposition.

   (308) Gdayekoz na?— Gaa, gaa wii ndayekozisii. 'Are you tired?— No, I'm not tired.'

         Gdayekoz vai ind 2s 'you (SG) are tired'; na av 'yes/no question'; Gaa av 'no'; gaa wii
         av 'not'; ndayekozisii vai ind neg Is 'I am not tired.' (AM39.428)

   (309) Zhaazhi na ggii-ggwejmaa wii-wiidgemad wa kwe?— Kaahaa!

         (SG) asked ANsg'; wii-wiidgemad vta conj 2s»3sProx '(CONJ) you (SG) will marry
         ANsg'; wa pr 3s 'this/that'; kwe na SsProx 'woman'; Kaahaa av 'no way.'


   (310) A: "Gdoo-nji-waabndaan na ndoo-sapnigan? Ndoo-naajtoon."
         B: "Kaa. Gaawii na geshkgwaaswining tesnoo?"
         A: "Kaa, ngii-naab go zhiwi."
         A: "Have you seen my scissors? I've lost them."
         B: "No. Are they not around the sewing machine?"

         Gdoo-nji-waabndaan vti ind 2s»0s 'have you seen INsg'; na av 'yes/no question';

         looked'; zhiwi av 'there.'


   AFFIRMATION WITH ENH. An entire proposition can be affirmed with the adverb enh,
'yes.'

   (311) Giin dash, Zhenyep, ggii-bi-niibaw na wiikaa gii-shkiniigkwewyin?
         Enh, Zhaagnaash ngii-niibwitwaaba.
         'And you, Zhenyep (Virginia), did you ever marry when you were a young
         woman?—Yes, I married a white man.' (GS/EO)

         Giinprpers 2s 'you'; dash av 'then'; Zhenyep na 2s 'Virginia'; ggii-bi-niibaw vai ind
         2s 'did you (SG) marry'; na av 'yes/no question'; wiikaa av 'ever'; gii-shkiniigkwewyin
         vai conj 2s '(CONJ) you (SG) were a young woman'; Enh av 'yes'; Zhaagnaash na
         SsProx 'white person'; ngii-niibwitwaaba vta indpret ls»3sProx 'I married ANsg.'


   NEGATION OF MAIN VERBS (INDEPENDENT ORDER). Negatives of MAIN VERBS, that is,
verbs inflected with independent order inflection, are customarily made with the negative
expression gaa wii(n), which typically comes in one of two positions: either first in its
clause, or immediately before the verb. The verb carries independent order negative inflec-
tion as well. The following examples have gaa wii(n) in initial position.
840 • 16.10 Negation


   (312) Gaa wii ngoji nii-zhaasii. I 'I shall not go anywhere.' (AM39.426)

          Gaa wii av 'not'; ngoji av 'anywhere'; nii-zhaasii vai indneg Is 'I will not go (there).'

   (313) Gaa wii maampii gdaa-yaasiimi. I 'We (inc.) must not stay here.' (AM39.438)

          Gaa wii av 'not'; maampii av 'here'; gdaa-yaasiimi vai ind neg 21 'we (INCL.) must not
          be.'

   Examples of negatives with gaa wii(n) in immediately PRE-VERBAL POSITION:

   (314) Nmishoomsinaanig gaa wii wgii-yaanziinaawaan baashkzignan.
         'Our (exc.) grandfathers did not have guns.'(AM39.451)

          wgii-yaanziinaawaan vti ind neg 3pProx»Op ' ANpl did not have IN pi'; baashkzignan ni
          Op 'rifles.'

          (ANpl) were fighting ANobv'; gaa wii av 'not'; wgii-waabmaasiiwaan vta ind

   (316) «Aabdeg sa naa gnamaa gaawii geyaabi shpide-dbik gnamdabsiinaadig

         'Perhaps it's no longer necessary for you to sit up in the middle of the night writ-

          Aabdeg av 'necessarily'; gnamaa av 'perhaps'; gaawii av 'not'; geyaabi av 'anymore';

    CONTRASTIVE NEGATION. In contexts of contrast, the verb is sometimes not repeated,
and gaa or gaa wii(n) is used to indicate negation of the salient proposition. Often the con-
trastive elements dash...wiin occur as well.

   NEGATIVES WITH /ONJI-/. Negative statements in the past sometimes occur with the pre-

   (321) Miinwaa dash go gaa gnage ngii-nji-waabmaasii.
         'I did not see her again for a long time.' (AM9.37)

          Miinwaa av 'and'; dash av 'then'; gaa av 'not'; gnage av 'at all'; ngii-nji-waabmaasii
          vta ind neg ls»3sProx 'I did not see ANsg.'

   GAAWII NJIDA. The expression gaawii njida is used for the equivalent of English "I'm
sorry," and literally means, 'not on purpose.' Verbs used with it in this sense do not show
negation.

   (322) Gaawii njida, gchi-gbeyiing gii-njitaayaanh wii-nkwebiihmoonnaa.
         "Sorry, it's been a long time since I've had a chance to write back to you.' (MC)

   MANJ (IIDIG). The element manj, or more commonly, manj iidog (or manj iidig), com-

    CONSTRUCTIONS WITH BWAA-. In the second strategy of negation in subordinate
clauses, used almost exclusively by some speakers nowadays, the preverbal element bwaa-
is used, sometimes in combination with the future/modal preverbs /wii-/ or /ji-/, and the

verb is inflected with the positive conjunct. Often, constructions with bwaa-, especially

          gaa av 'not'; giiwenh av 'allegedly'; maamda av 'able.'

          wii-nsangid vta conj lp»3sProx 'we want to kill ANsg'; bezhig nm 'a certain (one)';
          mnidoo na SsProx 'manitou'; mii av 'and'; gaa-zhi-mkwenmigooyan vta ic conj lp»2s
          'we thought of you (SG)'; wii-bhaa-wiijiiwyaang vta conj 2s»lp 'you (SG) would come
          along with us'; wii-wa-naadmawyaang vta conj 2s»lp 'you (SG) would go and help us.'

    NEGATIVE QUESTIONS. Both yes/no and content questions can be negative. Negative
yes/no questions invariably have the negative element first, either gaa or gaa wii, followed
by the yes/no question particle na. Like their English equivalents, such questions are typi-
cally rhetorical.

   (361) Gaa na ggikendnziin dbikak? I 'Don't you know that it's dark (outside)?' (DP)

          Gaa av 'not'; na av 'yes/no question'; ggikendnziin vti indneg 2s»0s 'you (SG) do not
          know INsg'; dbikak vii conj 0 '(CONJ) IN be night/dark.'

   (362) Gaawiin na bdakjihgan gwii-miizhsii? I 'Aren't you going to give me a fork?'

          Gaawiin av 'not'; na av 'yes/no question'; bdakjiihgan ni Os 'fork'; gwii-miizhsii vta
          ind neg 2s»ls 'you (SG) will not give me.' (IT)

   (363) Nkwetwishin; aaniish bwaa-nkwetwiyan?
         'Answer me. Why don't you answer me?' (AM39.802)

          Nkwetwishin vta imp 2s»ls 'answer me'; aaniish av 'why'; bwaa-nkwetwiyan vta conj
          2s»ls '(CONJ) you (SG) fail to answer me.'

    NEGATION IN IMPERATIVES (PROHIBITIVES). Negative imperatives are called PROHIBI-
TIVES. These constructions use the negative adverb gego (or gegwa), and specific negative
imperative (prohibitive) verbal inflections. The negative adverb is usually in CLAUSE INITIAL
POSITION, though it may follow an INTERJECTION such as shkenaa, expressing mild exasper-
ation, or aahaaw, 'okay.'

   (364) Shkenaa, gegwa kidke wi. I 'Oh for Pete's sake, don't say that.' (DP)
          Shkenaa av 'for Pete's sake'; gegwa av 'don't'; kidke vai imp neg 2s 'don't say'; wi pr Os
          'that.'

   (365) Gegwa wiindmawaake gii-wiindmoonaanh. I 'Don't tell her that I told you!' (DP)

          Gegwa av 'don't'; wiindmawaake vta imp neg 2s»3 'don't you (sg) tell AN';
          gii-wiindmoonaanh vta conj ls»2s '(CONJ) I told you (SG).'
854« 16.10 Negation


   (366) Gego nsaaken mii go eta go iw gegoo ji-zhi-gshkihewzisig.
        'And my grandfather said to him, "Don't kill it, but only something so it won't
        have power." (n.b., in reference to harmful manitou) (AK11.20)

         Gego av 'don't'; nsaaken vta imp neg 2s»3s 'don't you sg kill ANsg'; mii av 'but'; eta av
         'only'; \vtpr Os 'that'; gegoopr indefO 'something'; ji-zhi-gshkihewzisig vai conj
         SsProx neg '(CONJ) ANsg would not be powerful'; mii av 'that's'; gaa-naad vta ic conj
         3sProx»3obv '(CCNJ) ANsg said to ANobv'; aw pr 3sProx 'that'; nmishoomis nad
         ls(3sProx) 'my grandfather'; niw pr 3obv 'that/those'; jiiskiiwninwan na 3obv
         'shaker/diviner.'


   In one textual example involving an indirect prohibition, gego is used with a negative
verb inflected for INDEPENDENT ORDER that has HORTATIVE force.

   (367) Gego gnagen waasa wiya da-njigaabwisii!
        'Let no one dare stand too far away.' (SO6.166)

         Gego av 'don't'; gnagen av 'at all'; waasa av 'far'; wiyapr indef3 'anyone';
         da-njigaabwisii vai ind neg 3sProx 'ANsg will not stand from.'


    The adverb gego can occur with EMPHATIC PARTICLES such as wiin and dash, as in the
following examples.

   (368) Wgii-naan niw sa shkiniigkwen, Gego dash zhgadenmaaken maaba shkinwe.

        'He said to the young woman, "And don't be impatient to have that young man.'

         Wgii-naan vta ind 3sProx»3obv 'ANsg said to ANobv'; niw pr 3obv 'that/those';
         shkiniigkwen na 3obv 'young woman'; Gego av 'don't'; zhgadenmaaken vta imp
         2s»3sProx neg 'do not (2s) be impatient with AN'; maaba pr 3sProx 'this'; shkinwe na
         SsProx 'young man.' (AM29.6)


   (369) Wgii-naan dash wshiimenyan, Gego wiin zegziken.
         Then he said to his young brother, "Do not be afraid.' (AM31.30)

         Wgii-naan vta ind 3sProx»3obv 'ANsg said to ANobv'; wshiimenyan nad 3sProx(3obv)
         'ANSG's younger sibling'; Gego av 'don't'; wiin av 'then'; zegziken vai imp 2s neg
         'don't you sg be afraid.'

   PREVERB AANO-. The preverb aano- is used to indicate attempts that do not succeed in
their goals, that is, that are undertaken in vain.

   (370) "Aaniish mii sa aano-nji-gnahmoonaan, aaniish mii sa gaa go maamdaa."
         'Well that's why I tried (in vain) to stop you, but you wouldn't stop.' (SOS.30)

         Aaniish av 'well'; mii av 'that's'; aano-nji-gnahmoonaan vta conj ls»2s '(CONJ) why I
         tried to warn you against'; aaniish av 'but'; mii av 'it's'; gaa av 'not'; maamda av
         'possible.'

   (371) Mii-sh aano-wepdawaawaad iidig giwi Nimkiig niwi, mii giiwenh go maanda
         neyaab miinwaa spokmigseg negwaki, mii sa gaa go maamda gashkhaasiiwaan.
        'Those Thunderers had tried in vain to hit him (the monster), but the sandy
        ground just opened and closed again and they were unable to get at him.'
        (SO4.28)

         Mii-sh av 'and then'; aano-wepdawaawaad vta conj 3pProx»3obv '(CONJ) in vain
         ANpl struck at ANobv'; iidig av 'it seems'; giwipr 3pProx 'those'; Nimkiig na SpProx
         'Thunderers'; niwipr na 3obv 'that/those'; mii av 'but'; giiwenh av 'allegedly'; maanda
         pr Os 'this'; neyaab av 'back'; miinwaa av 'again'; spokmigseg vii conj 0 '(CONJ) IN
         opened and closed'; negwaki ni Os 'sandy ground'; mii av 'and'; sa av 'indeed'; gaa av
         'not'; maamda av 'able'; gashkhaasiiwaan vta indneg 3pProx»3obv '(CONJ) ANpl
         were not able to get at ANobv.'

   This preverb is exceptional in having no distinct INITIAL CHANGED form. For example, in
the following sentence, the presence of RELATIVE preverb nji-, 'from, source,' in a
MII-CLAUSE should induce initial change, but aano- shows no change of form.

   (372) Mii sa nii aano-nji-gnahmoonaan wii-mod wa giigoonh.
         That's why I tried to stop you from eating that fish.' (SO3.20)

         Mii av 'that's'; niiprpers Is T; aano-nji-gnahmoonaan vta conj ls»2s '(CONJ) why I
         tried to warn you against'; wii-mod vta conj 2s»3sProx '(CONJ) you eat ANsg'; giigoonh
         na SsProx 'fish.'

   THE ROOT /AANW/. The morpheme /aanw/ also occurs as the ROOT in a few verbs, such
as aanwewzi, 'try in vain, be unable to manage' VAI, aanwihaad, 'try in vain to do some-
thing to AN' VTA, aanwitood, 'try in vain to do something to IN.' VTI, and aanwitoo, 'be
unable to move' VAI. The following example illustrates the use of the last verb.
856 • 16.11 Logical Relations


   (373) Gmaapii-sh giiwenh iidig gaa-ni-aanmtood wa, aanii-sh mil go naa iidig
         gii-zhaabwaakzod zhiwi wbaknaang, gii-bgaskjiihwind wi ziisbaakod.
         'Shortly after, he could not continue the journey, as he had deep burns on his back
         where he had been plastered with the sugar.' (SOI.38)

          Gmaapii-sh av 'after awhile then'; giiwenh av 'allegedly'; iidig av 'it seems';
          gaa-ni-aanwitood vti ic conj 3sProx»0 '(CCNJ) ANsg tried in vain to do IN'; wapr
          SsProx 'this'; aaniish av 'well'; mii av 'for'; iidig av 'evidently'; gii-zhaabwaakzod vai
          conj SsProx 'ANsg was burned through'; zhiwi av 'there'; wbaknaang nid 3sProx(0) loc
          'on ANSG's back'; gii-bgaskjiihwind vta conj x 3sProx '(CONJ) ANsg had been
          plastered'; wi pr 6s 'that'; ziisbaakod ni Os 'sugar.'


   THE ADVERB AANO. This root also occurs in the free adverb, aano, 'although,' used to
indicate a concession.

   (374) Aano dash go ngii-kawaabmigoog iw pit nakmigziwaad bekish sa bwahmowaad
         maanda mnoomin.
         'Although they kept an eye on me as they were busy, at the same time, they were
         gathering rice.' (AM6.2)

          Aano av 'in vain'; dash av 'then'; ngii-kawaabmigoog vta 3pProx»l 'ANpl watched
          over me'; iwpr Os 'that'; pii av 'time'; nakmigziwaad vai conj 3p '(CONJ) ANpl were
          busy'; bekish av 'at the same time'; bwahmowaad vti conj 3pProx»0 '(CONJ) ANpl
          knocked IN down'; maanda pr Os 'this'; mnoomin ni Os 'rice.'


    LEXICAL NEGATIVES. A few lexical items are formed from verbs carrying negative
inflection, for example, nsidwi-yaasik, 'be in a daze' (VAI) and ntaa-debwesik, 'be a habit-
ual liar' (VAI).

16.11 Logical Relations

  In this section I will discuss four LOGICAL RELATIONS, those which specify PURPOSE,
REASON, RESULT, and CONDITION.

16.11.1 Purpose

     The logical relation of purpose indicates the intended result of a verbal action or event.
 In Nishnaabemwin purpose relations are usually expressed by means of subordinate
clauses, often headed by the COMPLEMENTIZER iw, 'that.' Often the preverb wii-, indicating
future intent, occurs with the subordinated verb of the purpose clause, or the modal preverb
ji-, indicating possibility.
                                                                              16.11.1 Purpose* 857


   (375) Aapji dash gii-mkadekewag naan'godnong giw dash shkinweg gye go
         shkiniigkweg iw gegoo wii-gkendmowaad iw waa-bwaadmowaad.
        'Sometimes they fasted very much, those young men and women, in order to
        obtain that knowledge which they were to get in a dream.' (AM23.5)

         Aapji av 'really'; dash av 'then'; gii-mkadekewag vai indSpProx 'ANpl fasted';
         naan'godnong av 'sometimes'; giwpr SpProx 'those'; shkinweg na SpProx 'young
         men'; gye av 'and'; shkiniigkweg na SpProx 'young women'; iwpr Os 'that'; gegoopr
         indefO 'something'; wii-gkendmowaad vti conj 3pProx»0 '(CONJ) ANpl will know IN';
         iwpr Os 'that'; waa-bwaadmowaad vti ic conj 3pProx»0 '(CCNJ) ANpl will dream IN.'

   (376) Gii-bi-znagtoowag ge wiinwaa sa [gegoo ji-gkendmowaad ge sa
         waa-mno-bmaadziwaad].
        They too went to great pains [so that they might obtain knowledge and lead a
        good life].'(AM23.21)

         Gii-bi-znagtoowag vai ind SpProx 'ANpl endured hardship'; ge av 'also'; wiinwaa pr
         pers Sp ANpl'; gegoo pr indefO 'something'; ji-gkendmowaad vti conj SpProx»0
         '(CONJ) to ANpl know IN'; ge av ' and'; waa-mno-bmaadziwaad vai ic conj SpProx
         '(CCNJ) ANpl will live well.'

   (377) Miinwaa wgii-giishpnadoon [iw bagoowyaan ji-wzhitmaagooyaan iw
         wshki-goodaas].
         And she bought some material [so that a new dress could be made for me]:

         Miinwaa av 'and'; wgii-giishpnadoon vti ind 3sProx»Os 'ANsg bought INsg'; iw/?r Os
         'that'; bagoowyaan ni Os 'cloth'; ji-wzhitmaagooyaan vta conjx»l '(CONJ) Y will be
         made for me'; iw pr Os 'that'; wshki-goodaas ni Os 'new dress.' (AK3.13)

   Other means of expressing purpose exist, as in the following two sentences, which use a
subordinate clause headed by giishpin, 'if and a verb inflected for DUBITATIVE MODE (n.b.,
conjunct dubitative obligatorily shows INITIAL CHANGE).

   (378) Nbi-zhaa endaayeg [giishpin eyaawegwen].
         'I came to your (pi.) house [(to see) if you (pi.) were there]: (AM39.669)

         Nbi-zhaa vai ind Is 'I am coming'; endaayeg vai ic conj 2p '(CCNJ) where you (PL)
         live'; giishpin av 'if/whether'; eyaawegwen vai ic conj dub 2p '(CCNJ) you (PL) might
         be there.'
858* 16.11.2 Reason


   (379) Ngii-zhaa endaawaad [giishpin eyaawaagwen].
         'I went to their house [(to see) if they were there].' (AM39.670)

          Ngii-zhaa vai ind Is 'I went'; endaawaad vai ic conj SpProx '(CCNJ) where ANpl
          lived'; giishpin av 'if/whether'; eyaawaagwen vai ic conj dub 3pProx '(CCNJ) ANpl
          might be there.'


16.11.2 Reason

    The logical relation of REASON expresses the grounds for a verbal action, event, or state,
that is, the logical source or cause of some consequence. In Nishnaabemwin, reasons are
expressed by clauses in conjunction with the relative element /ond/, which may occur as a
free adverb, nji, as a preverb, nji- (also spelled «wnji-»), or root, /ond/. The most common
usage is with the preverb.

   (380) Mii wi njil I 'That's why (I did what I did)!' (MC)
          Mii pcfoc 'It's'; wi pr Os 'that'; nji av 'from; reason.'


   (381) Aapji gii-zegzi aw sa ngashi [nji iw gii-bzhineyaan da-gii-daapneyaambaan].
         'My mother was very much frightened [because when I fell out of the canoe I
         might well have got drowned}' (AM6.11)

          Aapji av 'really'; gii-zegzi vai indSsProx 'ANsg was frightened'; aw/?r SsProx 'that';
          ngashi nad ls(3sProx) 'my mother'; nji av 'on account of; iw pr Os 'that';
          gii-bzhineyaan vai conj Is '(CONJ) I had a close call'; da-gii-daapneyaambaan vai
          conj pret Is '(CONJ) I might have drowned.'


   (382) Mii dash noongo iw wenji-yaawaad giw ngoji debendaagzisgog nishnaabeg.

         'And now that's why there are those Indians who don't belong anywhere.'

          Mii av 'and'; noongo av 'nowadays'; iw/?r Os 'that'; wenji-yaawaad vai ic conj SpProx
          '(CCNJ) why ANpl are'; ^v/pr SpProx 'those'; ngoji av ' anywhere'; debendaagzisgog
          vai ic conj part SpProx neg '(CCNJ) who ANpl don't belong to a group'; nishnaabeg na
          SpProx 'Indians.' (AK9.10)


   (383) Mii niinaa \gaa-nji-ninaanh gbe-zhebaa wii-maajtaayin]. Zhaazhi
         gdaa-giizhiitaanaaba.
         'That's [why / told you all morning to get started]. You would have been finished
         by now.' (DP)
                                                                             16.11.2Reason* 859



         Mii av 'that's'; niinaa av 'to be sure'; gaa-nji-ninaanh vta ic conj ls»2s '(CCNJ) why I
         said to you sg'; gbe-zhebaa av 'all morning'; wii-maajtaayin vai conj 2s '(CONJ) you sg
         will start.' Zhaazhi av 'already'; gdaa-giizhiitaanaaba vai indpret 2s 'you sg could have
         been finished.'

    Another, more archaic construction uses the DUBITATIVE PRONOUN wegdagwen(h) with
RELATIVE PREVERB (w)nji-. The dubitative pronoun requires that an associated verb be
inflected for dubitative mode. This construction occurs in my data in embedded reason
questions.

   (384) Waaboozoonh gii-ggwejmaa [wegdagwen wenji-bshkizgwen].
         'Rabbit was asked [however it might be white of colour]' (AM34.2)

         Waaboozoonh na 3sProx 'rabbit'; gii-ggwejmaa vta ind x»3sProx 'ANsg was asked';
         wegdagwenprdub 0 'whatever'; wenji-waabshkizgwen vai ic conj dub 3sProx '(CCNJ)
         why might ANsg be white in color.'


   (385) Miinwaa gii-ggwejmaa [wegdagwen wenji-niizhootwagegwen].
         'Again it was asked [however it might have two ears].' (AM34.5)

         Miinwaa av 'again'; gii-ggwejmaa vta indx»3sProx 'ANsg was asked'; wegdagwenpr
         dub 0 'whatever'; wenji-niizhootwagegwen vai ic conj dub SsProx '(CCNJ) ANsg might
         have two ears from.'


   Questions of reason have the inanimate interrogative pronoun, wegnen (which often
fuses with focus particle dash to wegne-sh), relative preverb wnji-, 'why, because, from,'
and changed conjunct verbal inflection.

   (386) "Waaboozoonh, [wegne-sh wenji-zaawzideyan]?"
         '"Rabbit, [why have you brown feet]T' (AM34.14)

         Waaboozoonh na SsProx 'rabbit'; wegne-shprO 'what'; wenji-zaawzideyan vai ic conj
         2s '(CCNJ) do you sg have brown feet from.'


   (387) Mii dash [wenji-zaawzideyaan], I 'That is [why I have brown feet]."' (AM33.14)
         Mii av 'that's'; dash av 'then' wenji-zaawzideyaan vai ic conj Is '(CCNJ) why I have
         brown feet.'

   Negative reason-questions with preverb bwaa-, 'not' sometimes have aanii-sh, 'how,'
860* 16.11.3 Results


instead of (w)nji-, 'why.' These questions have a structure rather analogous to English ques-
tion form, 'How is it that...'

   (388) Nkwetwishin; [aanii-sh bwaa-nkwetwiyan?}
         'Answer me. [Why don't you answer me?}' (AM39.802)

          Nkwetwishin vta imp 2s»ls 'answer me'; bwaa-nkwetwiyan vta conj 2s»ls '(CONJ)
          you (SG) fail to answer me.'

   INDICATING REASONS WITH INITIAL CHANGE. In running narrative, logical connections
are sometimes indicated by means of INITIAL CHANGE. This practice reflects a general ten-
dency to leave inter-clausal relations implicit.

   (389) Mii go ambe gii-giishkzhawaad, gii-bkwemaad. liyoo, gegaa maa
         gaa-bookwaabdeshing. Gaa-wnendmaang ji-konmaang siniinsan.
         'So then right away he sliced it and took a bite. Oh my, he almost broke his teeth!
         Because we'd forgotten to take the stones out (of the chokecherries).' (IS)

          Mii av 'and'; ambe av 'immediately'; gii-giishkzhawaad vta conj 3sProx»3obv '(CONJ)
          ANsg sliced ANobv'; gii-bkwemaad vta conj 3sProx»3obv '(CONJ) ANsg took a bite of
          ANobv.' liyoo av 'oh!'; gegaa av 'almost'; maa av 'then'; gaa-bookwaabdeshing vai ic
          conj SsProx '(CONJ) ANsg broke tooth.' Gaa-wnendmaang vti ic conj lp»0 '(CCNJ) we
          (EXCL.) forgot IN'; ji-konmaang vti conj lp»0 '(CONJ) we (EXCL.) remove IN';
          siniinsan ni Op 'cherry pits.'

16.11.3 Results

   INDICATING RESULT WITH ZHI- . A direct result of a preceding action can be indicated
by RELATIVE PREVERB zhi- (/izhi-/, changed form ezhi-\ which naturally induces INITIAL
CHANGE. This construction is quite common.

   (390) Pii dash gii-bizigwiiyaan, gaa-zhi-gnabseyaang. Gaa-zhi-giikaamid
         nmishoomisimban.
         But when I stood up, we capsized (as a result). And (as a result) my late grandfa-
         ther yelled at me. (LM)

          Pii av 'when'; dash av 'but'; gii-bizigwiiyaan vai conj Is '(CONJ) I stood up';
          gaa-zhi-gnabseyaang vai ic conj Ip '(CCNJ) we (EXCL.) thus capsized';
          Gaa-zhi-giikaamid vta ic conj 3sProx»ls '(CCNJ) ANsg thus yelled at me';
          nmishoomisimban nadpret ls(SsProx) 'my late grandfather.'
                                                                           16.11.4 Conditionals • 861



   (391) Mm... mii go ezhi-bkadeyaanh dbaajmodwaa giwi piniig. Ndaa-ke-wiisin na go?

         'Mm... I'm getting hungry from your talking about the potatoes! Can I eat?'

          mii av 'well'; ezhi-bkadeyaanh vai ic conj Is '(CCNJ) I thus (become) hungry';
          dbaajmodwaa vta conj 2s»3pProx '(CONJ) you (SG) tell about ANpl'; giwi pr SpProx
          'those'; piniig na SpProx 'potatoes.' Ndaa-ke-wiisin vai ind Is 'can I eat (first)'; na av
          'yes/no ques.' (DP)


   RESULT CONSTRUCTIONS WITH DASH. In the following example, the logical relation of
RESULT is explicitly marked only by the presence of the adverb dash, 'then, as a result, so.'
This type of construction is quite common.

   (392) Maanoo, ziigniboojgan ngii-naadin taasoowgamgong. Nga-paa-ziigniboonaag
         zgimenyig gojiing, gaa dash gwaya nga-dkomgosii.

         That's all right, I went and got the bug spray from the shed. I'll go spray the mos-
         quitoes outside, so none will bite me.' (DP)

          Maanoo av 'that's alright'; ziigniboojgan ni Os 'bug spray'; ngii-naadin vti ind ls»0s 'I
          fetched INsg'; taasoowgamgong ni loc 0 'from the shed.' Nga-paa-ziigniboonaag vta
          ind ls»3pProx 'I will go around spraying ANpl'; zgimenyig na SpProx 'mosquitoes';
          gojiing av 'out of doors'; gaa av 'not'; dash av 'then'; gwaya pr indef3 'anyone';
          nga-dkomgosii vta indneg 3sProx»ls 'ANsg will not bite me.'


16.11.4 Conditionals

    CONDITIONALS specify contingency, hypotheticality, and such notions. In Nishnaabem-
win, statements of condition are typically marked by the presence of a CLAUSE-INITIAL con-
ditional adverb giishpin, 'if.' The verb associated with giishpin is invariably inflected for
PLAIN (UNCHANGED) CONJUNCT ORDER, and not infrequently, DUBITATIVE MODE.
862 • 16.11.4 Conditionals


   (393) Mil dash pii giiwewaad giw niizh nishnaabeg, mil dash ekdod aw bezhig,
         "Aanii-sh ge-zhichgeyamban [giishpin waabmaawgibnen gechi-gnaajwid kwe}T
         'And when these two Indians were going home, one of them said, "What would
         you do [if you should see a woman who is very beautiful?}"' (AK4.3)

          Mil av 'and'; dash av 'then'; pii av 'when'; giiwewaad vai conj 3pProx '(CONJ) ANpl
          go home'; giwpr SpProx 'those'; niizh nm 'two'; nishnaabeg na 3pProx 'Indians'; mii
          av 'so'; dash av 'then'; ekdod vai ic conj SsProx '(CCNJ) ANsg said'; aw pr 3sProx
          'that'; bezhig nm 'one'; Aanii-sh av 'how then'; ge-zhichgeyamban vai ic conjpret 2s
          '(CCNJ) you sg would do so'; giishpin av 'if; waabmaawgibnen vta conjpdub
          2s»3sProx '(CONJ) you sg were to see ANsg'; gechi-gnaajwid vai ic conj part SsProx
          '(CCNJ) ANsg who is very beautiful'; kwe na SsProx 'woman.'


   (394) Ki ndaa-zhitoon, giishpin naadmawyeg" wdinaan giiwenh.
         '"I can make some land, if you all help me," he (Nenabush) told them.' (SOS. 14)

          Ki ni Os 'land'; ndaa-zhitoon vti ind ls»0s 'I can make INsg'; giishpin av 'if;
          naadmawyeg vta conj 2p»ls '(CONJ) you (pi) help me'; wdinaan vta ind 3sProx»3obv
          'ANsg says to ANobv'; giiwenh av 'allegedly.'


   Future tense preverb wii- may occur with verbs in giishpin clauses:

   (395) Aaniish mii sa giiwenh egod: "Giishpin wii-miizhyaang giwi ggwisag, giin go
         gdaa-wenaabnjige zhonda wene go naa ge-wiidgemaawdibnen.
         'They said to her, "If you (will) give us your sons, you may choose anyone here
         that you might want to marry.'" (SO2.4)

          Aaniish av 'well'; mii av 'then'; giiwenh av 'allegedly'; egod vta ic conj 3sProx»ls
          '(CCNJ) ANobv said to ANsg'; Giishpin av 'if; wii-miizhyaang vta conj 2s»lp
          '(CONJ) you give us (EXCL)'; giwi pr 3pProx 'those'; ggwisag nad 2s(3pProx) 'your
          sons'; giinprpers 2s 'you'; gdaa-wenaabnjige vai ind 2s 'you can choose'; zhonda av
          'here'; wenepr inter 3 'who'; ge-wiidgemaawdibnen vta ic conjpdub 2s»3sProx
          '(CCNJ) you might marry ANsg.'


   As with so many interclausal relations, circumstance and contingency can be expressed

Quantity and Degree




    This chapter examines the many ways that quantity and degree are expressed in Nishnaa-
bemwin. Expressions of quantity, that is, those that specify "how many," customarily
involve NUMBER ROOTS, which occur in several distinct parts of speech, including INTRAN-
SITIVE NUMBER VERBS, PRENOUNS, PREVERBS, as well as independent number words. In (1)
below, for example, an amount is indicated by means of the number preverb, niizho-, 'two,'
which in (2) appears in a free number word, and in (3), as the root of an inanimate intransi-
tive verb (VII) (with INITIAL CHANGE to /naazh/). Number roots and numeric expressions are
treated in detail below.

   (1)   Mii dash pii gii-yaawaawaad niw binoojiinyan endso-jmz/*0-bboon'gak mii-sh
         gii-nbowaad giw binoojiinyag.
         'And when they had the children, every two years, those children died.' (AK11.3)

          Mii av 'and'; dash av 'then'; pii av 'then'; gii-yaawaawaad vai conj 3pProx»3obv
          '(CONJ) ANpl had ANobv'; niwpra 3obv 'that/those'; binoojiinyan na 3obv
          'child(ren)'; endso-niizho-bboon'gak vii ic conj 0 '(CCNJ) every two years'; mii-sh av
          'and then'; gii-nbowaad vai conj SpProx '(CONJ) ANpl died'; giwpra SpProx 'those';
          binoojiinyag na 3pProx 'children.'
866 • 17.1 Relative Roots


   (2)   Mil dash giiwenh gii-waabndang aw sa gwiiwzens niizh jiimaanan biidaasninig
         gchi-mookmaan-zhmaagnishag giw wii-miigaanaawaad niw Canadians.
         'And then reportedly this boy saw two boats sailing toward them, they were Amer-
         ican soldiers intending to fight the Canadians.' (AK15.10)

          Mii av 'and'; dash av 'then'; giiwenh av 'reportedly'; gii-waabndang vti conj 3sProx»0
          '(CONJ) ANsg saw IN'; awpra SsProx 'that'; sa av 'indeed'; gwiiwzens na 3sProx
          'boy'; niizhnm 'two'; jiimaananni Op 'boats'; biidaasninig vii conjOobv '(CONJ)
          INobv come sailing'; gchi-mookmaan-zhmaagnishag na SpProx 'American soldiers';
          giwpra 3pProx 'those'; wii-miigaanaawaad vta conj 3pProx»3obv '(CONJ) ANpl
          intend to fight ANobv'; niwprn 3obv 'that/those.'


   (3)   Gaawiin gii-bskaabiisiiwag baamaa naazhgon'gak wgii-bminaazhkwaawaan niw
         waagshan, gii-biindgebhiwewan dash m'aa siniing.
         'They didn't return, later for two days they went along chasing that fox, but he ran
         inside there in some rocks.' (AK7.4)

          Gaawiin av 'not'; gii-bskaabiisiiwag vai ind SpProx neg 'ANpl did not come back';
          baamaa av 'later'; naazhgon'gak vii ic conj 0 '(CONJ) IN was two days';
          wgii-bminaazhkwaawaan vta ind 3pProx»3obv 'ANpl chased ANobv'; niw prn 3obv
          'that/those'; waagshan na 3obv 'fox(es)'; gii-biindgebhiwewan vai ind 3obv 'ANobv ran
          inside'; dash av 'then'; maa av 'there'; siniing ni 0 loc 'in rock.'


    GENERAL QUANTIFIERS. Quantity can also be expressed with general quantifying
adverbs, such as kina, 'all,' niibwa (or niibnd), 'much, a lot, many,' and bngii, 'a few.' Gen-
eral quantifiers such as these are treated in more detail in Chapter 12 (beginning on p. 572),
and are not mentioned further in this chapter. In the following sections I will first discuss
several RELATIVE ROOTS pertinent to quantity and degree expressions, then examine the
adverb mnik, '(such) amount,' which commonly occurs in expressions of quantity and
degree. This is followed by a rather extensive account of various numeric expressions, fol-
lowed by several sets of distinct quantitative expressions in the language. I end the chapter
with a brief account of quantity-related uses of REDUPLICATION.

17.1 Relative Roots

    Several RELATIVE ROOTS commonly appear in quantitative expressions, outlined in the
following table.
                                                                         17.1 Relative Roots • 867

           /apiit/, /apiich/, /apiis/ /apiichi-/              'to such extent'

   /DASw/. The RELATIVE ROOT /daSw/ (also /dash/), 'so many,' or its associated RELATIVE

   (4)   Ji-gshkitoowaad ji-bmasewaad nsimdana dso-dbahaabaan ji-bi-giiwewaad.

    /AKW/. The RELATIVE ROOT /akw/ or its associated RELATIVE PREVERB, /ako-/ some-

17.2 Degree Adverbs and Preverbs

    General expressions of marked intensity are also expressed by means of DEGREE
ADVERBS, such as aapji, 'really, extremely,' and zaam, 'too.' The preverb gchi-, 'extremely,'
is also common.

   (17) Gaawii nii, zaam niibna zhaazhi ngii-wiisin. I 'Not me, I already ate too much." (KK)

          Gaawii av 'not'; nii prn pers Is 'i'; zaam av 'too'; niibna av 'much'; zhaazhi av
          'already'; ngii-wiisin vai ind Is 'I ate.'

   (18) Gc/H-mnise giiwenh, aapji go gchi-nokii.

         'He cut lots of wood, and he really works hard.' (SO4.54)

          Gchi-mnise vai indSsProx 'ANsg gets lots of firewood'; giiwenh av 'reportedly'; aapji
          av 'really'; gchi-nokii vai ind 3sProx 'ANsg works hard.'


17.3 Quantification with Mnik

   The adverb mnik, 'so many,' is commonly used in contexts involving quantification. In
the first set of examples, mnik occurs with specific quantificational expressions. In most
cases, mnik immediately precedes the verb, or is separated from it only by emphatic parti-
cles.

   (19) Giishpin mkoonsag biindgewaad, ngodwaaso-namhe-giizhgad mnik
        wii-gsinaamgad.

         'If the cubs return to the den, there will be six more weeks of cold weather.' (KK)

          Giishpin av 'if; mkoonsag na dim SpProx 'bear cubs'; biindgewaad vai conj 3pProx
          '(CONJ) ANpl enter'; ngodwaaso-namhe-giizhgad ni 0 'six weeks'; mnik av 'amount';
          wii-gsinaamgad vii ind Os 'INsg will be cold.'
872 • 17.3 Quantification with Mnik


   (20) Aakzi-sh giiwenh maaba Nishnaabe; niizhwaaso-bboon giiwenh mnik aakzi.
         'This man was very sick; he was sick for seven years.' (SO4.2)

          Aakzi-sh vai ind3sProx 'ANsg is ill'; giiwenh av 'allegedly'; maabaprn 3sProx 'this';
          Nishnaabe na 3sProx 'Indian'; niizhwaaso-bboon ni nm 0 'seven years'; giiwenh av
          'reportedly'; mnik av 'amount'; aakzi vai indBsProx 'ANsg is ill.'

   Mnik can also be used to mean 'as many,' 'as much,' or 'as long.'

   (21) Mnik go naa geshkhaad go naa zhiwi gii-maawndoonaadgenan, mil sa zhiwi
        gii-bkodbid.
         'He piled up as many of them as he could and sat there on top of them.' (SO5.4)

          Mnik av 'as many as'; geshkhaad vta ic conj 3sProx»3obv '(CCNJ) ANsg was able to do
          with ANobv'; zhiwi av 'there'; gii-maawndoonaadgenan vta ind dub 3sProx»3obv
          'ANsg evidently piled up ANobv'; mii av 'and'; sa av 'indeed'; zhiwi av 'there';
          gii-bkodbid vai conj 3sProx '(CONJ) ANsg sat on top.'


   (22) "Mii-sh go eta go mnik gaa-gkendmaan," kido sa giiwenh wa zhashkoonh.
         'That's as much as I am aware of," said the muskrat.' (SOS.41)

          Mii-sh av 'and then'; eta av 'only'; mnik av 'as much as'; gaa-gkendmaan vti ic conj
          ls»0 '(CCNJ) that (IN) I know'; kido vai ind BsProx 'ANsg says'; giiwenh av
          'reportedly'; waprn BsProx 'that'; zhashkoonh na 3sProx 'muskrat.'

   (23) Mii dash go mnik gaa-bmaadzid gii-zgaswaa pii go naa jaanmendang.
         And for as long as she was alive she smoked whenever she was worried.'

         Mii av 'and'; dash av 'then'; mnik av 'as much as'; gaa-bmaadzid vai ic conj BsProx
          '(CCNJ) ANsg lived'; gii-zgaswaa vai ind SsProx ANsg smoked'; pii av 'when';
         jaanmendang vai conj 3sProx '(CONJ) ANsg was worried.' (AK12.6)


  Mnik can be used in conjunction with dshing, '(so many) times.'

  (24) Aaniish manj go naa iidig mnik dshing gaa-googiigwen wa, de-mnik sa go iidig
       ogii-maawnjitoon wi kiins.
         'Well, it's not known how many times he dived, probably as often as was neces-
         sary to gather up the little bits of earth.' (SOS.46)
                                                  17.4 Numbers and Number Expressions • 873


       Aaniish av 'well'; manj av 'however it may be'; iidig av 'evidently'; mnik av 'amount';
       dshing av 'so many times'; gaa-googiigwen vai ic conj dub 3sProx '(CCNJ) ANsg may
       have dived'; waprn SsProx 'that'; de-mnik av 'sufficient amount'; iidig av 'evidently';
       ogii-maawnjitoon vti ind3sProx»Os 'ANsg gathered up INsg'; wiprn Os 'that'; kiins ni
       Os 'bit of earth.'

 Mnik is also used in questions that ask 'how much' or 'how many.'

       'How many children will be getting on?' (KK)

 Mnik can occur with the COMPARATIVE ELEMENT nwaj, 'more.'

 (27) Aaniish mil sa giiwenh gii-googiid zhashkoonh, nwaj dash giiwenh weweni
      wgii-biidoon mnik ki, gii-bi-mooksed miinwaa.

   CARDINAL NUMBERS. The following charts lay out the traditional number system of

       ngo-                     /ngod/  1                    bezhig                      'one'

       niiwoo-                  /niiw/                       niiwin                      'four'
       naano-                   /naan(an)/                   naanan, naanin              'five'
       ngodwaasoo-              /ningodwaas(w)/              ngodwaaswi                  'six'
       niizhwaasoo-             /niizhwaas(w)/               niizhwaaswi                 'seven'
       nshwaasoo-               /nishwaas(w)/                nshwaaswi                   'eight'
       zhaangsoo-               /zhaangs(w)/                 zhaangswi                   'nine'
       mdaaso-                  /midaas(w)/                  mdaaswi                     'ten'
      1. The root form in other dialects is /ningod-/, and Rhodes gives some examples which use this
      form, e.g., with first person prefixes, as in nningdwewaan'giz, 'I form a single group.' In common
      usage, the short l\l in the first SYLLABLE would SYNCOPATE, and the two /n/'s in sequence then
      simplify to a single segment.


   The number system is presently BASE TEN (also called decimal), and begins recounting
at eleven, using mdaaswi, 'ten,' with CONJUNCTIVE element -shi, 'and,' to which is then
added the appropriate number, as in the following examples.

                                   mdaaswi-shi-bezhig          'eleven'
                                   mdaaswi-shi-niizh           'twelve'
                                   mdaaswi-shi-nswi            'thirteen'

   There are remnants of a BASE FIVE (also called quintenary) system in the numbers six
through eight, in that six appears to contain a traditional ROOT for one, seven that of two,
and eight that of three. The FINAL /(w)aaswi/, 'five,' that appears in these numbers is also
found in mdaaswi, 'ten,' and perhaps vestiges in zhaangswi, 'nine.' The following chart lays
out these relationships.

                              ngodwaaswi          'six'       ngod       'one'
                              niizhwaaswi         'seven'     niizh      'two'
                              nshwaaswi           'eight'     nswi       'three'

   The tens from twenty through ninety are formed by addition of a FINAL element
/-midana/, 'tens,' to the numbers for two through nine, with small adjustments in some
cases. The word niizhdana, 'twenty,' lacks the /mi/ of/midana/, for example.
                                                 17.4 Numbers and Number Expressions • 875



                             niizhdana            'twenty'
                             nsimdana             'thirty'
                             niimdana             'forty'
                             naanmidna            'fifty'
                             ngodwaasmidna        'sixty'
                             niizhwaasmidna       'seventy
                             nshwaasmidna         'eighty'
                             zhaangsimdana        'ninety'

higher numbers.

    CLASSIFIERS. Traditional Nishnaabemwin has a set of CLASSIFIERS which classify
objects according to their physical properties. The most common classifiers are /-aatig/,
'wooden, pole-like,' /-eg/, 'clothlike,' /-aabik/, 'metal, glass, plastic, stone,' and /-aabiig/,
'stringlike,' though others exist as well (see discussion in Chapter 9, beginning on page
331). These classifiers are used in counting in the traditional language, basically by adding
the appropriate classifier to a NUMERAL ROOT to produce a classifier-sensitive number.
Nowadays the most commonly used classifier is /-aabik/, used in counting money. The fol-
lowing table provides examples of CLASSIFICATORY NUMERALS.

              stick                cloth            metal, glass, coin   string, row
    one       ngodwaatig           ngodweg          ngodwaabik           ngodwaabiig
              bezhgwaatig          bezhgweg         bezhgwaabik          bezhgwaabiig
    two       niizhwaatig          niizhweg         niizhwaabik          niizhwaabiig
    three     nswaatig             nsweg            nswaabik             nswaabiig
    four      niiwaatig            niiweg           niiwaabik            niiwaabiig
    five      naanwaatig           naanweg          naanwaabik           naanwaabiig
    six       ngodwaaswaatig       ngodwaasweg      ngodwaaswaabik       ngodwaaswaabiig
    seven     niizhwaaswaatig      niizhwaasweg     niizhwaaswaabik      niizhwaaswaabiig
    eight     nshwaaswaatig        nshwaasweg       nshwaaswaabik        nshwaaswaabiig
    nine      zhaangswaatig        zhwaangsweg      zhaangswaabik        zhaangswaabiig
    ten       mdaaswaatig          mdaasweg         mdaaswaabik          mdaaswaabiig

    Classifiers, in the form of CLASSIFICATORY MEDIALS, can be combined with numbers
and intransitive verb finals to produce verbs of number that are sensitive to the classification
of the objects being counted. For example, NUMERAL ROOT /niizhw-/, 'two,' plus classifica-
tory medial /-aakw/, 'wooden, pole-like,' plus VAI FINAL /-izi/, produces niizhwaakziwag,
'be two pole-like objects' (VAIP). The corresponding VHP form is niizhwaakodoon.

                     stick       cloth      metal, glass  string, row
             two     niizhwaakzi niizhwegzi niizhwaabkizi niizhwaabiigzi
             three   nswaakzi    nswegzi    nswaabkizi    nswaabiigzi

   A variety of other classifying finals occur which are used with numeral roots. The fol-
lowing list has been culled from Rhodes 1985. Categories of classification include, among

boats), and temporal durations (day, night, year).

17.5 Various Expressions of Quantity and Degree

   In this section I provide examples of many common quantitative or degree expressions. .
  EXPRESSING AGE. Age is expressed with VAI verb bboon'gizi, /biboonagizi/, for ani-
mates, and bboon 'gad /biboonagadV VII, for inanimates, in combination with an appropriate
number preverb, or alternatively, they can be analyzed as having number ROOTS and a
                                             17.5 Various Expressions of Quantity and Degree • 887



MEDIAL derived in some way from /biboon/, 'winter,' by the addition of POST-MEDIAL /-ag/.
Preverbs and roots behave differently under syncope, in that the final vowels of preverbs are
not subject to syncope, which should theoretically allow one to distinguish their use as pre-
verbs or roots—but in these words the tests yield conflicting results. For example, in (67),
below, mdaas-bboon 'gizwaad, 'ANpl are ten years old,' should have either the final vowel
of /midaaso/ or the initial vowel of/biboonagizi/, but here has neither.
    For numbers larger than ten, dso-, 'so many,' typically occurs directly before the verb, as
in (69) and (70), below. In (69), the number mdaaso-shi-niizh, 'twelve,' is preceded by a
changed form of the preverb ni- (/ani-/), eni-, enclosing the number within the verb.

   (67) Mii pii giw gwiiwzensag mdaas-bboon 'gizwaad, mii ndawenjgewaad giw
        nishnaabeg ndawaabmaawaad niw mskwaadeswan.
         'When the boys are ten years old, the Indians go hunting and looking for turtles.'

          Mii av 'and'; pii av 'when'; giwpra BpProx 'those'; gwiiwzensag na SpProx 'boys';
          mdaas-bboon'gizwaad vai conj SpProx '(CONJ) ANpl were ten years old'; mii av
          'then'; ndawenjgewaad vai conj SpProx '(CCNJ) VAI CONJ SpPROX'; giw prn 3pProx
          'those'; nishnaabeg na SpProx 'Indians'; ndawaabmaawaad vta conj 3pProx»3obv
          '(CONJ) ANpl look for ANobv'; mw prn Sobv 'that/those'; mskwaadeswan na Sobv
          'turtle(s).' (AK5.2)


   (68) Mii dash iw gii-bchinaajgaazod aw nmishoomis maa wninjiing,
        niiyo-bboon'gizgoban giiwenh iw pii.
         'And my grandfather was struck by accident there on his hand, he was reportedly
        four years old at the time.' (AK10.14)

          Mii av 'and'; dash av 'then'; iwprn Os 'that'; gii-bchinaajgaazod vai conj SsProx
          '(CONJ) ANsg was shot accidentally'; awprn SsProx 'that'; nmishoomis nad Is(SsProx)
          'my grandfather'; maa av 'there'; wninjiing ni 3sProx(0) loc 'on ANSG's hand';
          niiyo-bboon'gizgoban vai indpdub 3sProx 'ANsg was evidently four years old'; giiwenh
          av 'evidently'; iw prn Os 'that'; pii av 'time.'
888 • 17.5 Various Expressions of Quantity and Degree


   (69) Pii dash aazhgo iw eni-mdaaso-shi-niizh-dso-bboon'gizid mii iw ngoding
        debkaag gii-gshkozid.

          'And when he was getting to be twelve years old it happened one time that he
          woke up at night.'(AK13.7)

           Pii av 'when'; dash av 'and'; aazhgo av 'already indeed'; iwprnOs 'that'; eni-
           mdaaso-shi-niizh-dso-bhoon'gizid vai ic conj SsProx '(CCNJ) when ANsg was twelve
           years old'; mii av 'then'; iwpra Os 'that'; ngoding av 'one time'; debkaag vii ic conj 0
           '(CCNJ) when IN was night'; gii-gshkozid vai conj SsProx '(CONJ) ANsg woke up.'


   (70) Mii dash gaa-zhichgewaad mewnzha gii-wi-wiidookaadwaad iw gtigewaad, mii
        dash aazhgo iw mdaaswi-shi-naanan dso-bboon'gizid maaba gwiiwzens mii-sh
        gaa-nankiid aw mdimooyenh gii-mko-bmased.

          'This is what they did long ago, they helped each other when they farmed, and
          when the boy was fifteen years old, this was how the old woman worked: she
          bear-walked (was a witch).' (AK14.7)

           Mii av 'and'; dash av 'so'; gaa-zhichgewaad vai ic conj SpProx '(CCNJ) what ANpl
           did'; mewnzha av long ago'; gii-wi-wiidookaadwaad vta/vai recip SpProx '(CONJ)
           ANpl went and helped each other'; iwpra Os 'that'; gtigewaad vai conj SpProx '(CONJ)
           ANpl farmed'; mii av 'and'; dash av 'so'; aazhgo av 'now indeed'; iwpra Os 'that';
           mdaaswi-shi-naanan nm 'fifteen'; dso-bboon'gizid vai conj SsProx '(CONJ) ANsg was
           so many years old'; maabaprn SsProx 'this'; gwiiwzens naSsProx 'boy'; mii-sh av 'and
           then'; gaa-nankiid vaiic conj SsProx '(CCNJ) ANsg worked so'; aw prn SsProx 'that';
           mdimooyenh na SsProx 'old woman'; gii-mko-bmased vai conj SsProx '(CONJ) ANsg
           bear-walked.'


   (71) Niizhwaak dso-bboon gaa-fco-zhiwebak maanda.
           'It was two hundred years ago that this happened.' (AK18.8)

            Niizhwaak nm 'two hundred'; daso-bboon ni 'so many years'; gaa-ko-zhiwebak vii ic
            conj 0 '(CCNJ) such extent IN happened'; maanda prn Os 'this.'

          '(CCNJ) you SG walked such extent.'

   (99)   Waasa ngii-ko-zhigaadese. I 'I walked a long way.'

   EXPRESSIONS OF TEMPERATURE. In this section I list a few expressions pertaining to
degree of temperature.

   (126) Aaniish epiichi-gsinaag? I 'How cold is it (the weather)?'

          Aaniish av 'how'; epiichi-gsinaag vii ic conj 0 '(CCNJ) IN is to such extent cold
          weather.'

          piichi-gsinaa vii ind Os 'INsg is cold weather to such extent.'

          nongo av 'today'; aawan vii ind Os 'IN is.'

   (129) Washme nongo gsinaa pii dash jiinaago. I 'It's colder today than it was yesterday.'

          Washme av 'more'; nongo av 'today'; gsinaa vii ind Os 'INsg is cold'; pii av 'than'; dash
          av'as for'; jiinaago av'yesterday.'

          Aaniish av 'how'; epiichi-gsinaagba vii icpdub 0 '(CCNJ) IN (weather) was evidently
          cold to such degree'; gii-zaagjiitman vat conj 2s '(CONJ) you SG went out.'


   (131) Aaniish epiitaateg? I 'How hot is it (weather)? (assumes sun is shining)'

   EXPRESSIONS OF LINEAR EXTENT. Concepts such as height and length are commonly

17.6 Comparison

    COMPARATIVE constructions typically use the following formula. The examples which
follow illustrate.

       washme (or ooshme)          <standard>                     pii dash     <NP>
       washme                      waasa (temgad) Toronto         pii dash     North Bay
       more                        farther INsg.is Toronto        than
       washme                      mBill gnoozi                   pii dash     niin
       more                        Bill is tall                   than         I

  (194) Washme ndoo-gnooz pii dash mBill. I 'I am taller than Bill.' (DP)

         Washme av 'more'; ndoo-gnooz vai ind Is 'I am tall'; pii av 'than'; dash av 'then';
         mBill na SsProx 'Bill.'


  (195) Washme mBill dkoozi pii dash niin. I 'Bill is shorter than me.'

         Washme av 'more'; mBill na SsProx 'Bill'; dkoozi vai ind SsProx 'ANsg is short'; pii av
         'than'; dashav 'then'; niin prn pers Is 'I.'
                                                                           17.6 Comparison • 905


   (196) Washme ndoo-dkooz pii dash mBill. I 'I am shorter than Bill.'
          Washme av 'more'; ndoo-dkooz vai ind Is 'I am short'; pii av 'than'; dash av 'then';
          mBill na 3sProx 'Bill.'

   (197) Niin go ooshme ngii-agaj pii dash giin. I 'I was more embarrassed than you (sg.)'

          Niinprnpers Is T; ooshme av 'more'; ngii-agaj vai ind Is 'I was embarrassed'; pii av
          'than'; dash av 'then'; giin prn pers 2s 'you.' (DP)

   (198) Washme wiin kiwenziinywi. I 'He is a still older man.' (AM39.109)

          Washme av 'more'; naangan vii ind Os 'INsg is light(weight)'; maanda pra Os 'this';
          mkak ni Os 'box'; pii av 'than'; dash av 'then'; \viprn Os 'that'; bezhig nm 'one.'

   Just as in English, much of this construction can be omitted if it is understood from con-
text.

   (199) A: "Wiindmawshin," kida, aapji go gdoo-nda-gkenjigeshkiw, mamaa.
         B: Gegii nii go naa. A: Giin go ooshme.
         'A: "Tell me," she says— you're so nosy, momma.
         B: And so are you. A: And you are more!' (DP)

          Wiindmawshin vta imp 2s»ls 'tell me'; kida vai indSsProx 'ANsg says'; aapji av
          'really'; gdoo-nda-gkenjigeshkiw vta ind 2s»ls 'you (sg) are chronically nosy with
          regard to me'; mamaa na(d) 'momma'; Gegii prn pers 2s 'you (sg) too'; nii go naa expr
          'for sure'; Giin prn pers 2s 'you' ooshme av 'more.'

   Another way of expressing the comparative is with nwanj, 'more' (also nwaj). Note that
as well as modifying verbal expressions, nwanj can be associated with (predicative) nomi-
nals in verbless clauses, such as in (202) and (203).

   (200) Nwanj maanda gchi-doopwin, maanda nwanj gaachin.
         'This table is bigger, and this one is smaller.' (AM39.228)

          Nwanj av 'more'; maanda prn Os 'this'; gchi-doopwin ni Os 'big table'; maanda prn Os
          'this'; nwanj av 'more'; gaachin vii ind Os 'INsg is small.'


   (201) Nwanj bngii ddaakzidewag. I They have smaller feet.' (AM39.133)

          Nwanj av 'more'; bngii av 'a little'; ddaakzidewag vai redup ind SpProx 'ANpl have
          short feet.'
906 • 17.6 Comparison


   (202) Nwanj shkiniigi. I 'He is younger.' (AM39.85)

         Nwanj av 'more'; shkiniigi na SsProx 'young man.'

   (203) Maantaanshiinyi nwanj niibna nagnde. I 'Woolen things cost more.' (AM39.208)

         Maantaanshiinyi ni Os 'woolen thing'; nwanj av 'more'; niibna av 'much'; nagnde vii
         ind Os 'INsg cost such.'

   (204) Aaniish mil sa giiwenh gii-googiid zhashkoonh, nwqj dash giiwenh weweni
         wgii-biitoon mnik ki, gii-bi-mooksed miinwaa.

        ' So the muskrat went down again, and, when he surfaced, he brought back much
        more earth.' (SOS.45)

         Aaniish av 'well'; mii av 'so'; giiwenh av 'reportedly'; gii-googiid vai conj SsProx
         '(CONJ) ANsg dove'; zhashkoonh na SsProx 'muskrat'; nwaj av 'more'; dash av 'then';
         giiwenh av 'reportedly'; weweni av 'properly'; wgii-biidoon vti ind 3sPmx»Os 'ANsg
         brought INsg'; mnik av 'amount'; ki ni Os 'land'; gii-bi-mooksed vai conj SsProx
         '(CONJ) ANsg surfaced'; miinwaa av 'again.'


   EQUATION. Equality according to some standard of reference is indicated as in the fol-
lowing, with the adverb naasaab, 'same (way).'

   (205) Naasaab aapiitnigdoon nanda mkakoon. I These boxes weigh the same! (MC)

         Naasaab av 'equivalently'; aapiitnigdoon vii redup ind Op 'INpl weigh such amount';
         nandaprn Op 'these'; mkakoon ni Op 'boxes.'

   (206) Gaawii naasaab aapiitnigsinoon nanda mkakoon.

         'These boxes don't weigh the same.'

         Gaawii av 'not'; naasaab av 'equivalently'; aapiitnigsinoon vii redup ind neg Op 'INpl
         do not weigh such amount'; nanda prn Op 'these'; mkakoon ni Op 'boxes.'


   Comparisons involving specific expressions of measure can also be made, as in the fol-
lowing example.
                                                                           17.6 Comparison • 907



   (207) Naano-dbaabiishkoojgan noondaash piitnigod maanda mkak pii dash wi bezhig.

        'This box is 5 pounds lighter than that one.' (MC)

17.7 The Semantic Functions of Reduplication

    Several related concepts are expressed by means of REDUPLICATION. These include PLU-
RALITY, INTENSITY, REPETITION (ITERATION), and DISTRIBUTION in time or space. It is easy
to see how these concepts are related, in that plural actors undertaking similar actions neces-
sarily repeat the action, and typically distribute its occurrence through time. The application
of multiple actors to the same action also produces added intensity. In many cases where
reduplication is used, more than one of these concepts may be operative at the same time.
The following examples illustrate some text-based uses of REDUPLICATION. Reduplicative
forms are identified within the word-for-word annotations.

   PLURALITY OF SUBJECT

   (213) Kosmaanan aapji memaachaagin da-tenoon.

         'Pumpkins which are very large will be there.' (AM 16.12)

          Kosmaanan ni Op 'pumpkins'; aapji av 'really'; memaachaagin viiic conj part 0 redup
          '(CCNJ) which IN are big' base form /michaa/; da-tenoon vii ind Op 'INpl will be there.'


   (214) Niidgemaagan nnanaamdabmi biindig wiigwaaming.

    THE PHONOLOGICAL PATTERNS OF REDUPLICATION. There seem to be four basic phono-
logical patterns of reduplication, as illustrated in the following table. All reduplication in
Nishnaabemwin is prefixal. The form of this prefix is variable, made by copying the first
consonant of the stem and adding a vowel, either /a/ or /aa/. In this table, C stands for the
initial consonant in a word, and V for a vowel in the initial syllable.
914 • 17.7 The Semantic Functions of Reduplication



          Pattern   Comments
     a.   Ca        —
     b.   Caa       —
     c.   CaCaa     Only with select descriptive roots having the form /CiX/
     d.   CVVh      Lexically specific and extremely variable in form

    Pattern (c) represents a canonical weak-strong iambic foot. Pattern (d), as noted, is spe-
cific to particular items of vocabulary, though these are rather consistent across dialects of
Anishinaabemowin. Its reduplicant vowel varies between /ii/ and /aa/ and it strengthens the
consonant of the stem (making a lenis into its fortis correspondent).
