Syntax and Communicative Functions




    This chapter examines the SYNTAX of Nishnaabemwin, that is, the patterns in the lan-
guage for putting words and PHRASES together to form CLAUSES and SENTENCES. It begins
with a discussion and illustration of how central inflection is in the grammatical workings of
Nishnaabemwin. Next, the various grammatical categories associated with each of the main
parts of speech are presented. This is followed by a brief discussion of phrases and clauses,
where it is argued that these multi-word structures are less rigid in their behaviour than cor-
responding English expressions. Next we examine in some detail the structures and func-
tions associated with the very prominent particle mil. After this, we look at the how
questions and commands are expressed. We then briefly look at COORDINATION and DIS-
JUNCTION, followed by an even briefer look at a few of the many EXPRESSIVE PARTICLES in
the language.

18.1 Introduction

    Language can be viewed both in terms of MEANINGS and STRUCTURES. Every language
encodes a set of meanings in its MORPHEMES and WORDS, and various idiomatic express-
sions. These elements are then combined to form meaningful messages, ranging from sim-
ple statements to complex discourses such as conversations, speeches and narratives. All
languages share similarities both in the meanings that they encode, and in the structural pat-
terns that are used to represent them. For example, all languages have the two WORD
CLASSES (PARTS OF SPEECH) of NOUNS and VERBS, the former referring to people and
objects, and the latter to states, processes and actions. All languages structure the meanings
of verbs in terms of a small set of common SEMANTIC ROLES such as AGENTS, PATIENTS,
EXPERffiNCERS, and INSTRUMENTS. All languages have the GRAMMATICAL PERSON catego-
ries of first, second and third. But the way in which these linguistic categories are expressed
varies from one language to another. One significant way that languages vary is in the gram-
matical features that are associated with different classes of words, and an important com-
ponent of a grammatical description of a language is a thorough accounting of these
                                                                            18.1 Introduction-917


features and their use. For example, among many other features, nouns in Nishnaabemwin
have grammatical GENDER (ANIMATE or INANIMATE), grammatical NUMBER (SINGULAR or
PLURAL), and are specified for the backgrounding feature of DEVIATION as either PROXI-
MATE (foregrounded) or OBVIATIVE (backgrounded); verbs must have INFLECTIONAL repre-
sentation of the PERSON, NUMBER and DEVIATION status of a SUBJECT (or S-ROLE, to use my
term from Chapter 13), even those verbs that, logically speaking, have no subject, such as
IMPERSONAL verbs, e.g., gii-zoogpo 'it was snowing.' In these cases a surrogate morpholog-
ical subject is provided, much as the dummy subject "it" is provided in the equivalent
expressions in English. Other grammatical features associated with verbs include the per-
son, number, and obviation features of their GOALS, if they are TRANSITIVE, their status as
POSITIVE or NEGATIVE, and their INFLECTIONAL MODE (e.g., PRETERIT or DUBITATIVE),
among many others. A simple example will illustrate how important these various grammat-
ical concepts are to the workings of Nishnaabemwin grammar. Consider the following sen-
tence:

   (1)   Nmishoomsinaanig gaawii wgii-aabjitoosiinaawaan baashkzignan.
         'Our (excl.) grandfathers did not use guns.' (RV, from AM39.451)

          Nmishoomsinaanig na Ip(SpProx) 'our (excl.) grandfathers'; gaawii av 'not';
          wgii-aabjitoosiinaawaan vti ind neg 3p»0p 'ANpl did not use INpl'; baashkzignan ni Op
          'rifles.'


    The verb in this example is listed in the dictionary as aabjitood, and marked as VTI, that
is, as a transitive verb requiring a grammatically inanimate goal (object). Were the object
grammatically animate, the related transitive animate (VTA) verb, aabjihaad, would have to
be used. The VTI form is chosen here because the goal is baashkzignan, 'guns,' an inanimate
noun. This "paired-verb" feature of Nishnaabemwin, in which many transitive concepts
have paired VTA and VTI verbs, is completely unlike English, since English transitive verbs
do not show any distinctions on the basis of the grammatical properties of their objects. Fur-
thermore, the Nishnaabemwin verb has several inflectional markings, a prefix, here spelled
«w», and a suffix complex, spelled «siinaawaan». The prefix and suffixes taken together sig-
nal a huge amount of information, namely that the actor (subject) is third person (animate)
plural (nmishoomisnaanig, 'our grandfathers'), and the goal (object) is third person inani-
mate plural (baashkzignan, 'guns'), and that the verb is being used as the main verb in the
sentence it occurs in, since the inflectional markings belong to the INDEPENDENT ORDER of
verbal inflection. The suffix component spelled «sii» indicates that the verb is negative. The
preverb /gii-/ indicates that the verb is past tense. There are no special modal suffixes to
mark this verb as preterit mode or as dubitative mode, so the assumption is that this sen-
tence is a simple, straightforward assertion. To summarize, the verb shows the following
grammatically relevant properties:
918 • 18.1 Introduction


•   It is a transitive inanimate verb (VTI). This is shown: first, by its internal (DERIVATIONAL)
    structure, in that it has the TRANSITIVE INANIMATE FINAL and THEME SIGN /-(i)too/; sec-
    ond, by the particular THIRD PERSON PLURAL SUFFIX used, /-naawaa/, which only occurs
    With TRANSITIVE INANIMATE VERBS and, Optionally, ANIMATE INTRANSITIVE + OBJECT
  (VAIO) forms.
• It is inflectionally marked for a third person animate plural subject (actor).
• It is inflectionally marked for a third person inanimate plural object (goal).
• It is inflectionally marked as negative.
• It is inflectionally marked as independent order by virtue of its negative suffix and sub-
  ject and object prefix and suffixes.
• It is inflectionally marked for past tense.
• It lacks any marking for verb mode, so is modally neutral (indicative).

    By contrast, the English verb use is not marked for any grammatical features, and the
grammatical features marked on the Nishnaabemwin verb are expressed in English by
means of a sentence with pronouns, 'they (an.) did not use them (inanimate).'
    Turning to associated nouns in this sentence, the subject (actor) of the verb is
nmishoomsinaanig, 'our (excl.) grandfathers,' which is based on the animate dependent
noun, /mishoomis/, 'grandfather.' The noun has inflectional marking for a first person plural
exclusive possessor, that is, 'our, but not yours,' and is also marked as animate third person
plural, all of this by means of the prefix/suffix complex spelled «n_naanig». The goal
(object) of this verb is baashkzignan, 'guns,' which is a plural inanimate noun, marked as
such by the suffix spelled «an».
    In addition, there is a negative adverb, gaawii, which requires that an associated verb
show inflectional marking for negation, which, as we have seen, it does, by virtue of the suf-
fix spelled «sii». The presence of gaawii also suggests that the associated verb is in an inde-
pendent clause, since gaawii does not customarily occur with verbs in dependent clauses
(though there are occasional exceptions to this).
    Comparing English and Nishnaabemwin, then, interesting similarities and differences
become apparent. First, both languages have words to express the concepts of 'use', 'gun,'
and 'grandfather,' though the last Nishnaabemwin term often refers to ancestors in general,
so enters into a different set of meaning relationships than the English word does. Note also
that this term in Nishnaabemwin belongs to a sub-class of words, dependent nouns, that
usually require a possessor/specifier of relationship. English does not distinguish nouns as
to whether they are inherently possessed or not. Note, too, that in Nishnaabemwin,
«mishoomis» is a grammatically animate noun, and «baashkzigan» a grammatically inani-
mate noun. English does not have such a gender distinction, though it does distinguish
nouns on the basis of sexual gender and animacy, in that the appropriate pronoun when
making reference to a grandfather is the masculine pronoun he, and to a gun, the neuter pro-
noun, it. In both languages, it is only third person forms that are distinguished on the basis
of gender: there are no gender specific terms for first and second persons in either language.
    Another significant difference between the languages, as mentioned above, is that Nish-
                                                                        18.1 Introduction* 919


naabemwin has paired transitive verbs meaning 'use x,' one used when making reference to
using something that is grammatically animate, and another used in reference to using
something that is grammatically inanimate. There is no variation in English verb forms
according to whether associated direct objects are masculine, feminine, or neuter.
    Both languages have a way to express negation: English by means of the adverb not and
the supporting verb, do; in Nishnaabemwin, by means of the adverb gaawii(n), and a suffix
on the verb, here spelled «sii». In both languages the negative adverb occurs in a position
directly before the verb, suggesting a close association between the verb and negation. Both
languages have a means of expressing past tense: in English, by means of a special past
tense form of the verb, did, and in Nishnaabemwin by means of the preyerb, gii-. In both
languages, though, the marking of tense also occurs in very close association with the verb.
    As for the nouns in the sentence, both languages have a means of expressing plurality, in
English by means of a suffix, spelled the same way on both nouns, «s» (grandfather-«s» and
gun«s»), and in Nishnaabemwin, by means of a suffix spelled «ig» on nmishoomisnaanig,
 'our (excl.) grandfathers,' and a suffix spelled «an» on baashkizganan, 'guns.' The differ-
ence in form here points again to a central grammatical distinction in Nishnaabemwin, the
two grammatical genders of the language, animate and inanimate, which form their plurals
with different suffixes. While English has a plural, formed by suffixation, it is not sensitive
to distinctions of either grammatical or natural gender.
    As to the expression of possession; (or more precisely in this case, kin relationship), in
English it is done by the separate pronominal word, our, whereas in Nishnaabemwin, pos-
session is shown by means of inflectional prefixes and suffixes on the possessed noun. Fur-
thermore, Nishnaabemwin makes a distinction between two distinct conceptualizations of
 'our,' one including the one(s) spoken to, and the other excluding the addressee(s). It is not
possible in Nishnaabemwin to refer to the concept 'our' without making this distinction; but
English does not usually even make such a distinction.
    The last, but very significant, distinction between the languages involves the way that
various relationships among words, grammatical relations, are expressed. For example, we
can ask how the subject and object are determined in English, that is, how does one know
which of the two noun phrases in the sentence represents the user and which represents the
items used. In English, it is the order of the words in the sentence that consistently provides
this information, in that the subject, in this case, 'our grandfathers,' customarily precedes
the verb, and the object, here 'guns,' follows it. If the order is reversed to Guns used our
grandfathers, the meaning is quite different, and it now appears that the subject is 'guns'
and the object, 'our grandfathers,' or the sentence is interpreted as showing poetic license in
violating the normal rules of grammar. In Nishnaabemwin, however, as we have seen, many
grammatical properties of the so-called subject and object are morphologically marked
directly on the verb, in the form of prefixes and suffixes. In Nishnaabemwin, there is a dif-
ferent set of prefixes and suffixes for virtually every person and number combination of sub-
ject (better, actor and S-role) and object (better, goal), producing literally thousands of
distinct verb forms. And because the verb form carries so much information about the actor
and goal, the order of associated nouns is relatively free, and changing their order does not
920 • 18.1 Introduction


change the interpretation of what the actor and goal are, but rather, the relative discourse
prominence of each in this particular sentence. The richness of morphological marking on
the verb allows for relative freedom in the ordering of associated nominals. Morphology is
thus very important in Nishnaabemwin, far more so than in English, where restrictive order-
ings of words accomplish similar ends.
    At the same time that we acknowledge that the ordering of words in Nishnaabemwin
sentences is relatively free, we recognize that the negative adverb gaawii is rather restricted
in its occurrence within the clause, in that it must precede the verb, usually as either the first
word in the clause or coming directly before the verb. Furthermore, while the order of verb,
actor and goal, are relatively free in Nishnaabemwin, certain orders are very infrequent. The
most unlikely orders are those in which both the actor and goal precede the verb; the most
common orders are those in which the actor comes later in the sentence than the goal. The
study of such grammatical relationships between words is called syntax. In this chapter we
will examine the main syntactic properties of Nishnaabemwin.
    The following chart summarizes some of the differences between English and Nishnaa-

fact that many grammatical features in Nishnaabemwin are expressed by means of inflec-
tional prefixes and suffixes, whereas in English the same information tends to be provided
by separate words and the ordering of words.

18.3 Grammatical Features of Nouns, Pronouns, Verbs, and Adverbs

    The following sections provide summaries of the grammatical features relevant to each
of the main parts of speech, nouns, pronouns, and verbs. A table is provided for each part of
speech, listing its relevant grammatical features, and its possible values for each feature.

18.3.1 Nouns

   Here I provide a summary of grammatical features pertaining to nouns (see Chapter 4).

      Nouns
                 Gender       Animate or Inanimate
                 Number       Singular or Plural
                 Obviation    Proximate [foregrounded] or Obviative (backgrounded)
                 (Possessor)  Person of Possessor (First, Second, or Third)
                              Number of Possessor (Singular or Plural)
                              Obviation of Possessor (Proximate or Obviative)
                 (Locative)   Locative
                 (Preterit)   Preterit
                 (Vocative)   Singular or Plural
                 [Diminutive] Diminutive
                 [Contempt] Contemptive or Pejorative
                                                                             18.3.1 Nouns'923


    Some of these features are mutually exclusive, that is, the presence of one precludes the
presence of the other. For example, vocatives, representing terms of direct address, can't be
in the locative, nor can they have possessors other than first person, e.g., nmishoo, 'grandfa-
ther (of mine).' And while cross-referencing on verbs shows that inanimate nouns can be
obviative, only animate nouns are explicitly marked as obviative with suffixes on the noun
itself. And obviative animate nouns neutralize the number distinction between singular and
plural.
    The locative suffix usually neutralizes the grammatical distinctions of number (singular
versus plural) and obviation (proximate versus obviative), as the locative doesn't usually
appear with plural or obviative suffixes.
    The features of diminutive and contemptive are not, strictly speaking, grammatical prop-
erties, since these features never result in any kind of special grammatical behaviour such as
a particular word order or cross-referencing on the verb. They are listed here because they
are so common (productive), and because they are often taught in conjunction with more
directly grammatical categories.
    FEATURES DISTINGUISHING ANIMATE AND INANIMATE NOUNS. Animate and inanimate
nouns show many fundamentally important differences in their grammatical behaviour,
making the distinction between them central to Nishnaabemwin grammar. I list a few of the
more important differences here.
• Animate nouns are the subjects of animate intransitive (VAI) verbs, and inanimate nouns
    are the subjects of inanimate intransitive (VII) verbs. For example, to assert that a man
    (nini NA) is big, one says, mdido nini, with a VAI verb, but to assert that a boat (jiimaan
    Nl) is big, one says, mchaa(mgad) jiimaan, with the corresponding VII verb.
• Animate nouns are the goals of transitive animate (VTA) verbs, and inanimate nouns are
    the goals of transitive inanimate (VTI) verbs. For example, to say, I see the man, one says,
    Nini nwaabmaa, with a VTA verb, but to say, / see the boat, one says, Jiimaan nwaabn=
    daan, with the corresponding VTI verb.
• Animate and inanimate nouns have distinct sets of associated pronouns. Animate nouns
    use the demonstrative pronouns maaba, 'this' (or aw or wa, for some speakers) as in
    maaba nini, but inanimate nouns use the pronoun maanda (or ow, for some speakers), as
    in maanda jiimaan. Other kinds of pronouns, too, such as indefinite pronouns, also show
    variation according to whether they are associated with animate or inanimate nouns. For
    indefinite pronouns, the animate form is waya or wiya, and the inanimate, gegoo.
• Animate nouns have inflection for backgrounded (obviative) forms, but inanimate nouns
    do not. So, for example, one says, kwe wgii-waabmaan niw ninwan, 'the woman saw
    that man,' but kwe wgii-waabndaan iw (or wf) jiimaan, 'the woman saw that boat.' In
    the case of the animate goal noun, nini, because the man is backgrounded, an obviative
    suffix /-an/ occurs on the noun. While a suffix /-an/ can also be used with inanimate
    nouns, it always indicates plurality, as injiimaanan, 'boats,' and never obviative status.
    There are also distinct obviative forms of demonstrative pronouns associated with ani-
    mate nouns, e.g., niw, 'that/those (anim. obv.), but no such forms for inanimate nouns.
    Note, however, that verbs associated with inanimate nouns may show obviation.
924* 18.3.2 Pronouns


• A verbal predication involving more than one semantic role must have at least one ani-
  mate participant, that is to say, a predication can have at most one inanimate participant.
  So, for example, transitive inanimate verbs (VTI) always have animate actors, because
  the goals of these verbs are obligatorily inanimate. There is a special class of animate
  intransitive verbs that optionally takes inflection for goals (these verbs are labeled VAIO
  verbs), but there is no class of inanimate intransitive verbs (vn) that does so.
• Inanimate nouns can sometimes shift their gender to animate, but animate nouns almost
  never shift to inanimate. The shift in gender generally occurs when conventionally inan-
  imate objects take on animate properties, such as the capacity for motion or speech.

18.3.2 Pronouns

    There are two distinct sub-types of pronouns: personal pronouns and nominal pronouns.
Nominal pronouns are those that behave like nouns, especially in being indexed for the
nominal grammatical features of gender, number and obviation. Demonstrative pronouns
are the most prominent nominal pronouns, and many other nominal pronouns show reduced
grammatical features, such as lacking a plural or obviative. This group I call the reduced
nominal pronouns.
    PERSONAL PRONOUNS. Personal pronouns are the only pronouns that may be indexed as
first or second person, and they also have distinctive plural markings and do not show obvi-
ation, that is, there are no special obviative (backgrounded) forms of personal pronouns.
Personal pronouns show formal similarity to the person prefixes that are used with verb
inflection of the independent order.
    The following chart lays out the grammatical categories of personal pronouns, and their
possible values.

                Personal F'ronouns
                            Person       First, Second, Third
                                           First Person Plural Inclusive
                                           First Person Plural Exclusive
                            Number       Singular, Plural
                            Gender       Animate, (Inanimate)

    DEMONSTRATIVE (NOMINAL) PRONOUNS. Demonstrative pronouns are indexed for the
nominal features of gender (animate and inanimate), number (singular and plural), and
obviation (proximate and obviative). They are also indexed for distance, similarly to
English demonstrative pronouns, so that there is a proximal (or near) form, and a distal (or
distant) form. As with nominal pronouns (discussed below), demonstrative pronouns lack
many features associated with full nouns, in that the pronouns lack locatives, vocatives, pos-
sessive forms, diminutives, and pejoratives.
                                                                          18.3.3 Verbs • 925


         Demonsti ative Pronouns
                   Person      Third
                   Gender      Animate, Inanimate
                    Number        Singular, Plural
                    Obviation     Proximate, Obviative (backgrounded)
                    Distance      Near (proximal), Far (distal), Remote

    Pausal pronouns are also indexed for nominal features: gender, number and obviation.
    REDUCED (NOMINAL) PRONOUNS. Many nominal pronouns vary among speakers as to
whether they show features of number (singular or plural) and obviation (proximate or obvi-
ative). As with demonstratives, all nominal pronouns are third person. Sub-classes of nomi-
nal pronouns include indefinite pronouns, interrogative pronouns, substitutive pronouns,
and dubitative pronouns. All of these are treated in various detail in Chapters 3 and 12.
Verbs associated with dubitative pronouns usually show dubitative mode inflection, and
verbs associated with interrogative pronouns always show conjunct order inflection.

         Nomin al Pronouns
                   Person       Third
                   Gender       Animate, Inanimate
                   Number       (Singular, Plural)
                   Obviation    (Proximate, Obviative)

    Restrictions limit the interaction of some of the categories listed above. For example,
inanimate intransitive verbs (VII) can only have third person subjects, and transitive inani-

have inflection for goals, and these only in the independent and imperative orders. Inverse
only transitive verbs (VTAI) can only have animate goals, almost always living beings. All of
these facts are discussed in detail in Chapters 5 through 8.

18.3.4 Adverbs

    Adverbs can be classified according to a couple of parameters. One that is pertinent to
inflection classifies adverbs on the basis of whether or not verbs occurring in clauses with

type is provided here. The first example has the adverb giishpin, which requires that an
associated verb, in this case waabmad, 'you (sg.) see ANsg,' be inflected for the conjunct
order. The independent order inflection of this form is gwaabmaa.

   (3)   Mjihiiwan giishpin ngoding waabmad baanaabe.
         'It's a bad omen if you ever see a mermaid.' (AK4.13)

18.4 Phrases, Clauses, and Sentences

    PHRASES. Classes of words differ in the constituency relationships that they enter into
with other words. For example, nouns often form phrases in association with elements that
modify them in some way. Most commonly, nouns are modified by demonstrative pronouns,
possessors, or quantificational terms, such as numbers and more general quantifiers. The
following examples illustrate these various types of modification.
                                                        18.4 Phrases, Clauses, and Sentences • 931



    (a)   aw noos                  'that father of mine'     demonstrative pronoun + N
    (b)   Zhaabdiis wgwisan        'John's son'              possessor noun + N
    (c)   niizh kwewag             'two women'               number + N
    (d)   giw niizh nishnaabeg     'those two Indians'       demonstrative + number + N
    (e)   gkina giw piniig         'all of those potatoes'   quantifier + demonstrative + N

    In all of these examples, modifying elements belonging to particular word (part of
speech) classes occur before the nouns they are associated with, forming phrasal groupings,
in which the noun is the main element of the phrase. The central element of a phrase is com-
monly called the HEAD of that phrase, and the whole phrase is named for the head element.
So, for example, all of the examples above are classified as NOUN PHRASES, because their
head elements are nouns. Noun phrases in Nishnaabemwin often show a particular ordering
relationship between their elements, in that the modifier usually precedes the head noun,
though it is frequently separated from it.
    The constituency and ordering relationships that exist among a sentence's phrasal group-
ings can be captured by means of phrase structure diagrams, such as the following.

                                       Noun Phrase (NP)
                              Modifier                 Head
                              Noun Possessor           Noun
                              Demonstrative Pronoun
                              Number Quantifier
                              General Quantifier

    This diagram indicates that a noun phrase, abbreviated NP, is made up of a head noun
preceded by a modifier. The modifier may be a noun possessor, a demonstrative pronoun, a
number, or a general quantifier. Phrase structure diagrams provide several kinds of informa-
tion about a language's phrases, their constituency, and the ordering of constituents. Con-
stituency indicates what categories of words make up the phrasal group, and ordering
indicates the order in which these occur relative to each other. In Chapter 12, it is shown that
the order varies, depending on the scope of each element, for example giw niizh ninwag,
'those two men,' with a demonstrative preceding a number, versus niizh giw ninwag, 'two of
those men,' with the number preceding the demonstrative. But even here there is variation,
and context tends to play a bigger role than in the equivalent English expressions.
    To complete this structural account of noun phrases, we need to also specify the typical
position of relative clauses, which normally follow the noun they modify, as in the follow-
ing example.
932 • 18.4 Phrases, Clauses, and Sentences


    (5)    Semaan gii-miinaawag giw [kiwenziinyag]^                 [gaa-bi-zhaajig]RQlCi.
           'Those [old men]^ [who had come]RelQ were given tobacco.' (AK10.6)

            Semaan na 3obv 'tobacco'; gii-miinaawag vta indx»3pProx 'ANpl were given Y'; giw
            prn SpProx 'those'; kiwenziinyag na 3pProx 'old men'; gaa-bi-zhaajig vai ic conjpart
            SpProx 'who (ANpl) came.'


   Given this information, we can modify our basic noun phrase structural template, recog-
nizing that it represents general tendencies rather than a rigid rule.

                      Modifiers                         Head       Clausal Modifier

                      General Quantifier

    CLAUSES. Clauses constitute another central unit of syntactic structure. Prototypically, a
clause is a verb and all associated words, typically the noun phrases (NP's) filling the verb's
semantic roles, and associated adverbs and particles. The following sentence contains a sin-
gle clause, consisting of a transitive verb and the two noun phrases filling its macro-roles of
actor and goal. The first noun phrase consists of a single noun, and the second a combina-
tion of a demonstrative pronoun and a noun.

   (7)   Wshki-nbagsagoon wminpawaawaan giw gaagog.
         'Porcupines like to eat new lumber.' (AK1.9)

          Wshki-nbagsagoon na 3obv 'new lumber'; wminpawaawaan vta ind 3pProx»3obv
          'ANpl like the taste of ANobv'; giw/?m SpProx 'those'; gaagog na SpProx 'porcupines.

   The following diagram shows one possible structural analysis of this sentence:

                                               Clause
                 NP                                            NP
                 N                       V                     Dem      N .
                 Wshki-nbagsagoon        wminpawaawaan         giw      gaagog

   This diagram specifies that the clause consists of two noun phrases (NP's) and a verb
(V). The first noun phrase consists of just a noun, and the second, of a demonstrative pro-
noun and a noun. We could make a schemata of the following sort:

   Clause = NP V NP

   Examining this simple structure, we see something that looks like English, a language in
which clauses consistently have the form [Subject NP]-Verb-[Object NP], sometimes abbre-
viated as SVO order. We note, however, that the relations in the Nishnaabemwin sentence
934 • 18.4 Phrases, Clauses, and Sentences


are opposite, with an order of [Object NP]-Verb-[Subject NP] (OVS). However, this order
does not remotely have the centrality that SVO order does in English, because, in Nishnaa-
bemwin, many different orderings of elements in the clause are possible. Consider the
ordering in the following sentences, keeping in mind at the same time that the English trans-
lations are consistently SVO:

   (8)   VOS       [Wjiigdahaan]v [iw wiigwaam]o [aw kwe]s.
                   That woman is sweeping out that house.' (AM39.398)

                    Wjiigdahaan vti ind 3sProx»Os 'ANsg sweeps out INsg'; iw prn Os 'that';
                    wiigwaam ni Os 'house'; aw prn 3sProx 'that'; kwe na 3sProx 'woman.'


   (9)   VSO       [Gii-bootaagewag]v [giw kwewag]s [niw mdaamnanJo iw
                   wii-bkwezhgankewaad.
                   'The women ground up the corn when they were going to make bread.'
                   (AK2.4)

                    Gii-bootaagewag vai ind SpProx 'ANpl ground (Y)'; giw prn SpProx 'those';
                    kwewag na SpProx 'women'; niw prn 3obv 'that/those'; mdaamnan na 3obv
                    'corn'; iw prn Os 'that'; wii-bkwezhgankewaad vai conj 3pProx '(CONJ) ANpl
                    will make bread.'


   (10) SVO        [Giw dash kwewag]s [wgii-gnawenmaawaan]v [niw binoojiinyan]o.
                   The women took care of the children.' (AK2.3)

                    Giw/?ra SpProx 'those'; dash av 'and'; kwewag na SpProx 'women';
                    wgii-gnawenmaawaan vta ind 3pProx»3obv 'ANpl took care of ANobv'; niw
                    prn Sobv 'that/those'; binoojiinyan na Sobv 'child(ren).'


    There are thus many different orderings of the elements corresponding to English sub-
jects, verbs, and objects. In carrying out syntactic research, Richard Rhodes determined that
orders that were verb-initial were preferred in Nishnaabemwin (VOS and VSO), and that
verb-medial orders SVO and OVS were also acceptable, but that verb-final orders SOV and
OSV were dispreferred. While Rhodes' observations generally hold, one must be careful in
making generalizations about acceptable orderings since verb-final sentences are certainly
found, as in the following example.
                                                      18.4 Phrases, Clauses, and Sentences • 935


   (11) Nmishoomsimban niizh bezhigoongzhiin ogii-yaawaan.
         'My late grandfather had two horses.' (SS)

          Nmishoomsimban nadpret ls(3sProx) 'my late grandfather'; niizh nm 'two';
          bezhigoongzhiin no. 3obv 'horse(s)'; ogii-yaawaan via ind 3sPmx(3obv) 'ANsg had
          ANobv.'

   Among verb-initial orders, VOS is preferred, and among verb-medial, SVO is preferred,
suggesting that a preferred pattern is for the object (goal) to follow directly after the verb.
However, this cannot be a hard and fast rule, since VSO and OSV are also allowed. Rhodes
asserts that the most basic, pragmatically neutral, order is VOS.
   The preference for verb-initial orderings applies only to transitive verbs, too, since both
orders of V and S are common with intransitive verbs. In the following examples, SV order
appears in (12), and VS in (13).

   (12) [NdawemaaJs [ntaa-gshkigwaaso]v- I 'My sister (man speaking) sews well.'
          Ndawemaa na ls(3sProx) 'my sibling-of-opposite-sex'; ntaa-gshkigwaaso vai ind
          SsProx 'ANsg is good at sewing.' (AM39.121)

   (13) [Ntaa-gshkigwaaso]y [nnahaangnikwem]s. I 'My daughter-in-law sews well.'
          Ntaa-gshkigwaaso vai ind 3sProx 'ANsg is good at sewing'; nnahaangnikwem nad
          ls(3sProx) 'my daughter-in-law.' (AM39.122)

    And if only one nominal occurs with a transitive verb, either order of verb and nominal
is allowed, including verb-final. In (14), below OV order occurs, and in (15), VO.

   (14) [Mkiznan]o [gdaa-wi-zhitoonan]v. I 'You can earn shoes.'" (AK3.6)
          Mkiznan ni Op 'shoes'; gdaa-wi-zhitoonan vti ind 2s»0p 'you (SG) can earn INpl.'

   (15) [Wgii-mskwadsaanJv [mjigkan]o. I 'He painted the fence red.' (AM39.3)
          Wgii-mskwadsaan vti ind 3sProx»Os 'ANsg painted INsg red'; mjigkan ni Os 'fence.'

    All of this suggests that phrase structure diagrams of the sort commonly used for English
clauses are not very useful for Nishnaabemwin, since the order of words is so variable, so
diagrams as such can be downright misleading. English uses ordering to signal which NP is
the subject, and which is the object, but Nishnaabemwin usually does this by means of
inflections on the verb. We can summarize our findings so far with the following statements
of preference.
936 • 18.4 Phrases, Clauses, and Sentences


    When both the actor and goal are expressed in a clause:

•   Nishnaabemwin    tends to prefer verb-initial orders (VOS and VSO)
•   Nishnaabemwin    also allows verb-medial orders (SVO and OVS)
•   Nishnaabemwin    greatly disprefers verb-final orders (SOV and OSV)
•   Nishnaabemwin    tends to prefer orders in which O directly follows V (VOS and SVO)

   THE ORDER OF SECONDARY OBJECTS (THEMES). Many verbs are DITRANSITIVE, that is,

    RELATIVE ELEMENTS AND WORD ORDER. Those nominals and other expressions that
represent the objects of RELATIVE ROOTS and PREVERBS usually come directly before the
verb they are associated with. Consider the following textual sample, from the introduction
to a story by Rose Nadjiwon of Cape Croker.

   (23) a. Neyaashiinigamiing ndoon/baa,
        b. 'Cape Croker' zftmkaade, Zhaagnaashiiwnikaadeg.
        c. Rose Nadjiwon ndiz/mikaaz.
        d. Maanda waa-naajmoyaan, geget gii-z/w'webdagban.
        e. Kaa wiin dash naa kina ngikendziin.
        f. Megwaaj dash go naa gaa-zhiwebdagbanen, nga-naajim.

         'a. I come from "Point of Land into the Water,"
         b. "Cape Croker" it's called, it is called in English.
         c. Rose Nadjiwon is my name.
         d. [This which I'm going to tell about], it supposedly really happened.
         e. But I don't know every detail.
         f. [So I'm giving only an approximation] of what might have happened.' (RN)

          a. Neyaashiinigamiing niplace 'Cape Croker'; ndoonjbaa vai ind Is 'I hail form'; b.
          zhinkaade vii ind Os 'INsg is called'; Zhaagnaashiiwnikaadeg vii conj 0 'IN has such
          name in English'; c. ndizhnikaaz vai ind Is 'I am so named'; d. Maanda prn Os 'this';
          waa-naajmoyaan vai ic conj Is '(CCNJ) which I will relate'; geget av 'truly';

    In the (a) clause, Neyaashiinigamiing directly precedes the verb ndoonjibaa, which has
the relative root /onj-/, 'from'; the verbs in the (b) and (c) clauses contain the relative root
/izh-/ (from /iN-/); the verb in the (d) clause contains the same root, in the form /in/, and the
same verb appears again in the (f) clause. Interestingly, in the (d) line, there are two verbs
with relative roots, because gii-zhiwebdagban, 'it supposedly happened,' also has a relative
root. Associated with this relative root is the whole clausal expression, Maanda

containing the relative root it is associated with. This is true of all of these examples,
namely that a noun or clause serving as the object of a relative root precedes the verb con-
taining the root.
    There is one context where the object of a relative root consistently follows the verb. For
objects that represent locations, when these occur with a demonstrative locative adverb such
as maa, 'there' or widi 'over there,' they consistently come at the end of their clauses, fol-
lowing the verb containing the relative root. In both of the following sentences, for example,
the verb containing a relative root is ihaa, 'go there' (VAI).

          there is high rock hill'; gii-wi-namhaad vai conj SsProx '(CONJ) ANsg went and
          prayed.'


   (25) Aaniish mii sa gii-maajaad giiwenh bezhig nini, gii-zhaad [wadi
        ziisbaakdokaaning].
         'So this man set off alone, and went [over there to the sugar camp].' (SOI.8)

    This is perhaps less a fact about the objects of relative roots than the behaviour of defi-

940 • 18.4.1 Gender, Number, and Obviation


18.4.1 Gender, Number, and Obviation

    Distinctions of gender (animate and inanimate), number (singular and plural), and obvi-
ation (proximate and obviative) provide a powerful set of grammatical tools for interpreting
the grammatical relations in Nishnaabemwin sentences. In this section we'll briefly exam-
ine how these tools are used. Consider the following sentence:

   (26) Giw dash kwewag wgii-gnawenmaawaan niw binoojiinyan.
          'The women took care of the children.'(AK2.3)

          Giw prn SpProx 'those'; dash av 'then'; kwewag na SpProx 'women';
          wgii-gnawenmaawaan vta ind 3pProx»3obv 'ANpl took care of ANobv'; niw prn 3obv
          'that/those'; binoojiinyan na 3obv 'child(ren).'

  First we can recognize three basic constituents in this sentence, along with their gram-
matical properties, as outlined in the following chart.

    giw kwewag               wgii-gnawenmaawaan                   niw binoojiinyan
    — animate noun (na)      — transitive animate verb (vta)      — animate noun (na)
    — plural proximate       — «w_aawaan» indicates:              — obviative
                             • animate 3rd plural actor
                             • animate 3rd obviative goal

    The verb is transitive animate (VTA), meaning that it two semantic roles, which will be
marked on the verb as actor and goal, and the goal must be animate. Furthermore, there is an
(independent order) inflectional complex, «w_aawaan», that indicates that this verb has a
third person plural (proximate) actor, and a third person obviative goal. So, inspecting the
rest of the clause, we find one animate third person plural noun phrase, giw kwewag, 'those
women,' and one animate third person obviative noun phrase, niw binoojiinyan, 'that/those
child(ren).' The only possible interpretation is that giw kwewag represents the actor, and niw
binoojiinyan, the goal. This determination is made on the basis of the interaction between
plural and obviative marking on the nouns (and their associated demonstratives), and the
inflection on the verb, together with the fact that both nouns are animate, and that the verb is
VTA. Note that at no point do we need to appeal to any kind of word order rules, though
there is one consistency in the word order, namely that the demonstrative pronouns directly
precede the nouns they modify, which is the normal, but not the only, ordering.

18.4.2 Proximity

   The following sentence presents another aspect of word order in Nish
sentence is about Nenabush spotting a deer up on a hill.
                                                                             18.4.3 Pragmatics • 941


   (27) Wgii-waabmaan dash waawaashkeshwan niibwinid gidaaki.
         'He saw a deer standing there at the top of the bluff.' (AM35.27)

          Wgii-waabmaan vta ind 3sProx»3obv 'ANsg saw ANobv'; dash av 'then';
          waawaashkeshwan na 3obv 'deer'; niibwinid vai conj 3obv '(CONJ) ANobv stand';
          gidaaki av 'on top of hill.'

    Consider the locational adverb gidaaki, 'on a hill, up the hill,' which occurs as the last
word in this sentence. How does one determine that it is referring to where the deer was
standing rather than to where Nenabush sees from? The answer is that unless there is good
reason for doing otherwise, adverbs are associated with the verbs that they are closest to, in
this case, niibwinid. This way of interpreting word relationships might be called a principle
of proximity. This principle, in association with the rich inflectional system of Nishnaabem-
win, allows for the easy interpretation of most sentences.

18.4.3 Pragmatics

    In some cases, since word order is very free in Nishnaabemwin, and the proper relation
of one word to another is determined on the basis of common sense, that is, pragmatically,
based on one's knowledge of the way the world normally works. Consider, for example,
how a speaker of Nishnaabemwin might figure out what the role of the word niizh, 'two,' is
in the following sentence.

   (28) Ngoding shkinweg gii-gkinoohmaagziwag niizh maa gkinoohmaadiiwgamgong...
         'Once (upon a time) two young men studied there at the University...' (AM30.1)

          Ngoding av 'once'; shkinweg na SpProx 'young men'; gii-gkinoohmaagziwag vai ind
          SpProx 'ANpl were in school'; niizh nm 'two'; maa av 'there';
          gkinoohmaadiiwgamgong ni 0 loc 'at the school.'

    Here there is a number situated after a verb, adjacent to no noun which it might be mod-
ifying and not in the usual pre-verbal (fronted) position of displaced quantifiers. We note
however that the verb is animate intransitive (VAI), and has a plural subject, which is known
from the inflectional suffix complex spelled «wag». Preceding the verb is a nominal,
shkinweg, an animate noun (NA) that is marked plural by virtue of the suffix spelled «g». So
given that we have an animate intransitive verb inflected for a plural subject, and a plural
animate noun, it is reasonable then to consider that the animate noun is the subject of the
VAI verb. Since the subject is plural, it is then entirely reasonable to associate the number
two, niizh, with the plural subject nominal, producing the interpretation 'two young men
were studying.' There is really no other practical interpretation.
942 • 18.4.3 Pragmatics


   Common sense also allows us to easily interpret sentences such as the following:

   (29)   Mii dash gii-miinaad aw nishnaabe niw bkwezhganan.
          'And the Indian gave them some bread.' (AK7.13)

          Mii av 'and'; dash av 'then'; gii-miinaad vta conj 3sProx»3obv 'ANsg gave ANobv Y';
          awpra SsProx 'that'; nishnaabe na SsProx 'Indian'; niwpm 3obv 'that/those';
          bkwezhganan na 3obv 'bread.'

    Stretching things to the point of absurdity for the purposes of illustration, this sentence
has two possible readings, one of which is the translation provided. The second is: "And the
Indian gave (something) to the bread." The verb form miinaad is inflected to indicate that an
animate third person singular proximate gave (something) to an animate third person obvia-
tive. Now it just so happens that niw bkwezhiganan, 'that bread,' is an animate third person
obviative (n.b. bkwezhigan is animate in Alice King's dialect), strictly speaking, it would be
possible for the bread to be the recipient of the giving, rather than the thing given. But the
whole idea of giving something to a loaf of bread makes little sense, so this interpretation is
ruled out on the basis of its impracticality. Furthermore, the sentence that directly precedes
this one is:

   (30)   Mii-sh gii-nkweshkwaawaad niw nishnaaben, mii dash enaawaad, "Bkwezhgan na
          gdayaawaa ge-shamyaangban."
          'And then they met this Indian and they said to him, "Do you have any bread that
          you might give us to eat?'" (AK7.12)

          Mii-sh av 'and then'; gii-nkweshkwaawaad vta conj 3pProx»3obv '(CONJ) ANpl met
          ANobv'; niw prn 3obv 'that/those'; nishnaaben na 3obv 'lndian(s)'; mii av 'and'; dash
          av 'then'; enaawaad vta ic conj 3pProx»3obv '(CCNJ) ANpl said to ANobv';
          Bkwezhgan na 3sProx i 'bread'; na av 'yes/no question'; gdayaawaa vta ind 2p»3sPwx
          'do you (pi) have ANsg'; ge-shamyaangiban vta ic conjpret 2p»lp '(CCNJ) you (pi)
          might feed us (excl).'

   So the appropriate reading is also encouraged by this context. Note also that transfer
verbs (VTA) such as miinaad, 'give something to AN,' generally require that their goals
(recipients) be living creatures, which also greatly facilitates the utility of logical deduction
("common sense") as an interpretive tool.
   In the following example, the determination of actor and goal of the last clause is not
possible on the basis any grammatical cues, such as the verb's inflection, because both noun
phrases associated with it are OBVIATIVE. The sentence is easily interpreted, however, on the
basis of our knowledge of the world, namely our knowledge that snakes are prone to bite
                         18.4.4 Complex Sentences and the Independent and Conjunct Orders • 943



people, but people don't often bite snakes. The story context also invites correct interpreta-
tion, since one (here, a friend) is unlikely to bite what one does not see (a snake).

   (31) Wgii-waabmaan gnebgoon, wiijkiwenyan dash gaa wiin; [wiijkiwenyangoai
        wgii-dkamgoon niw gnebgoonactor].
         'He saw the snake, but his friend not. That snake bit his friend.' (AM39.359)

          Wgii-waabmaan vta ind 3sProx»3obv 'ANsg saw ANobv'; gnebgoon na 3obv
          'snake(s)'; wiijkiwenyan nad3sPwx(3obv) 'ANsg's friend(s)'; dash av 'but'; gaa wiin
          av 'not'; wiijkiwenyan nad 3sProx(3obv) 'ANsg's friend(s)'; wgii-dkamgoon vta ind
          3obv»3sProx 'ANobv bit ANsg'; niv/prn 3obv 'that/those'; gnebgoon na 3obv 'snake(s).'


18.4.4 Complex Sentences and the Independent and Conjunct Orders

    Many sentences contain more than one verb, and therefore, more than one clause. The
following sentence, for example, contains two verbs, giizhgaatenig, 'moonlight shines
brightly (obv)' VII, and wganwaabmaan, 'ANsg looks at ANobv' VTA.

   (32) Giizhgaatenig giiwenh wganwaabmaan niwi giisoon.
         'Once, when moonlight is shining brightly, he looks at the moon.' (FF1.4)

          Giizhgaatenig vii conj Oobv '(CONJ) IN was day-bright'; giiwenh av 'allegedly';
          wganwaabmaan vta ind3sProx»3obv 'ANsg looks at ANobv'; niwi;?rn na 3obv 'nao';
          giisoon na 3obv 'moon(s).'


    In grammatical terms, the main verb here is wganwaabmaan, which provides the main
assertion of the sentence, and giizhgaatenig is subordinated to it, providing a context, a cir-
cumstance, a setting for the main action. In English, this subordination is accomplished by
placing the conjunction when at the beginning of the clause. In the Nishnaabemwin sen-
tence, however, there is no subordinating conjunction. None is needed, because Nishnaabe-
mwin makes use of an inflectional strategy for distinguishing verbs in main clauses from
those in subordinate clauses. Two distinct inflectional orders, or systems, exist in the lan-
guage. Inflection refers to the system of prefixes and suffixes on the verb that signal the
grammatical properties of their actors, goals, and S-roles (subjects).The independent order
is typically used with a verb that is the main verb of a sentence. The conjunct order is used
with verbs that are subordinated, either by virtue of being associated with a predicative
word such as mil, or by virtue of being associated with the main verb, either as a comple-
ment, or as an adverbial clause specifying time, manner, location, circumstance, condition,
reason, purpose, and the like. Often the only way of knowing that a clause is functioning in
one of these secondary functions is by virtue of the verb showing conjunct order inflection.
In the example above, (32), giizhgaatenig has a conjunct order suffix complex spelled «nig»,
944 • 18.4.4 Complex Sentences and the Independent and Conjunct Orders


which indicates an inanimate intransitive verb (VII), obviative (backgrounded), in a subordi-
nate clause; the verb wganwaabmaan has an independent order prefix/suffix complex
«w-_-aan» that indicates a third person singular proximate (foregrounded) actor acting upon
an animate third person obviative (backgrounded) goal, on the main verb of a clause. It is
perhaps a bit surprising how much information is coded in these short prefixes and suffixes,
but that is the nature of the system. And there are hundreds, if not thousands, of different
prefix and suffix combinations. For every independent order form there is a corresponding
conjunct form, though conjunct inflections tend to downplay number (singular versus plu-
ral) in inanimates, and so lack some of the inflectional distinctions of the independent. The
following table illustrates a few examples of corresponding independent and conjunct order
forms:

                          Independent                   Conjunct
    'I see you (sg.)'     gwaabamin         g _in       waabminaan(h)       _ inaan(h)
    'you (sg.) see me'    gwaabam           g -         waabmiyin           _iyin
    'I see it (in.)'      nwaabndaan        n _n        waabndmaan(h)       _ aan(h)
    'I see them (in.)'    nwaabndaanan      n _nan      waabndamaan(h)      _ aan(h)
    'you (pi) dive'       ggoogiim          g _m        googiiyeg           _yeg
    'they (an.) dive'     googiiwag           _wag      googiiwaad          _ waad

   The independent and conjunct inflectional orders can be distinguished on the basis of
several features, including, but not limited to, the following:

• Their inflections for actors, goals and subjects are different. In particular, only the inde-
  pendent order has person prefixes. The behaviour of inverse forms is different as well.
• Plurality of inanimate goals of transitives and inanimate subjects of intransitives is not
  marked in the conjunct.
• Their inflection for negation is different: the independent uses the negative adverb
  gaawii(n) along with negative inflection, but the conjunct typically uses only negative
  inflection, or special negative preverbs not used in the independent, such as bwaa-.
• Their inflections for preterit, dubitative, and preterit dubitative modes are different.
• The forms of their tense and modal preverbs are different.
• Only the conjunct can occur with complementizing preverbs such as a-
• Only the conjunct has initial change.
• Only the conjunct has participles and inflectional iteratives.
• Conjunct clauses are more consistently verb-initial than independent clauses.

  As another example, consider the following sentence, from a story about the trickster
Nenabush sneaking up on some ducks through the water.
               18.4.5 Headedness and Head-Marking in Nishnaabemwin Clauses and Phrases • 945



   (33) Mil dash maa gaa-nji-googiid gii-nakzhiwed widi yaanid.
         'Then he dived from there and swam over to where they (obv) were.' (AM37.7)

          Mii av 'and'; dash av 'then'; maa av 'there'; gaa-nji-googiid vai ic conjSsProx '(CCNJ)
          ANsg dived from there'; gii-nakzhiwed vai conj SsProx '(CONJ) ANsg swam there';
          widi av 'over there'; yaanid vai conj 3obv '(CONJ) ANobv be there.'


    There are three verbs in this sentence, gaa-nji-googiid, 'where ANsg dived from,' VAI,
gii-nakziwed, 'ANsg paddled there' VAI, and yaanid, 'ANobv were there' VAI. All three are
inflected for conjunct order, which can be inferred from their inflectional suffixes, and addi-
tionally, by the presence of initial change in the case of the first form. The following chart
provides details.

                            Conjunct order traits...
      gaa-nji-googiid           shows initial change, in gii- to gaa-
                                animate 3rd person singular proximate infl. suffix /-d/
                                [independent order form is gii-nji-googii]
      gii-nakzhiwed             animate 3rd person singular proximate infl. suffix /-d/
                                [independent order form is gii-nakzhiwe]
                            1
      yaanid                    animate 3rd person obviative infl. suffix /-nid/
                                [independent order form is yaawan]

    The reason that the first verb has conjunct inflection is that it is associated with the pred-
icative element mii, as is the second verb. Predicative elements function like main verbs in
that they require that any verb associated with them to be treated as a subordinate, which, in
Nishnaabemwin, means conjunct order inflection. The last verb, yaanid, is in a clause spec-
ifying the destination of the swimming, that is, is subordinate because it is specifying a
location related to the main verb. Note that not a single verb in this complex sentence has a
pronoun or nominal associated with it, the participants are understood entirely on the basis
of prior proximate and obviative assignment in the discourse.

18.4.5 Headedness and Head-Marking in Nishnaabemwin Clauses and Phrases

   The fact that the verb is marked for the grammatical features of actors and goals, and that
these features also signal the type of clause (main or subordinate), suggests that the verb is
the head, or more prominent element, of the Nishnaabemwin clause. Furthermore, it is the
verb which carries indications of tense, mode, and mood, grammatical concepts that argu-
ably apply to the whole proposition expressed by the clause. Even obviation, which is
marked on nouns only if they are animate, is marked on the verb for both animates and inan-
imates.
946 • 18.4.6 Subordinators (Complementizers)


   In a Nishnaabemwin noun phrase, it is also the main (head) noun that carries important
grammatical features, such as the features of a possessor. In both phrases and clauses, then,
Nishnaabemwin tends to mark important grammatical features on the head.

18.4.6 Subordinators (Complementizers)

    While the most important mark of a verb's status as subordinate is its having conjunct
order inflection, Nishnaabemwin also has a few other ways to indicate subordination, which
I discuss in this section.
    PREVERB A-. The preverb a- (changed form, e-) is sometimes used on a verb to indicate
that it is in a subordinate clause. The following examples illustrate its usage.

   (34) Pii dash debshkooseg ngii-zhaami widi a-bmi-noogbizod aw mshkode-daabaan.
         'When the time came we went to there where the train comes to a stop (i.e., the
         railway station).' (AM8.7)

          Pii av 'when'; dash av 'then'; debshkooseg vii ic conj 0 '(CCNJ) the IN time came
          around'; ngii-zhaami vai ind Ip 'we went there'; widi av 'over there'; a-bmi-noogbizod
          vai conj SsProx '(CONJ) where ANsg stops running'; aw prn SsProx 'that';
          mshkode-daabaan na SsProx 'train (lit., 'fire vehicle').'


   (35) Aanii dash e-aawyaanh! I 'So who am IT [NB, the last line of a riddle] (CN)

          Aanii av 'how'; dash av 'then'; e-aawyaanh vai ic conj Is '(CCNJ) that I am.'

   (36) E-ni-dbikak mii gii-noondwangdwaa Nimkiig, ge go gii-gchi-nimkiikaag.
         'When night came we heard the Thunders, and there was a great thunderstorm.'

          E-ni-dbikak vii ic conj 0 '(CCNJ) when night came'; mii av 'so then';
          gii-noondwangdwaa vta conj lp»3pProx '(CONJ) we EXCL heard ANpl'; Nimkiig na
          SpProx 'Thunderers'; ge av 'and'; gii-gchi-nimkiikaag vii conj 0 '(CONJ) there was a
          great thunderstorm.' (AM10.21)


   All of the verbs marked with e- show conjunct order inflection. In many cases modern
use of e- as a separate preverb arose from the reanalysis of older initial changed forms. For
example, e- in e-ni-dbikak, 'when night came,' historically comes from an initial changed
form of preverb ani-, 'in course of time, progress to...,' which would show initial change to
eni-. But since syncope would often eliminate the initial vowel in the unchanged form, the
basic form of the directional preverb has come to be /ni-/ for many speakers, who then inter-
pret the Id associated with the initial-changed form as a separate preverb. Historically, there
was indeed such a preverb, which shows up unchanged in sentence (34) above.
                                                      18.4.6 Subordinates (Complementizers) • 947



   Other preverbs serve as subordinators. These are presented in Chapter 3.8.2.9, Subordi-
nating Preverbs, beginning on page 166.
   DEMONSTRATIVE iw. The demonstrative pronoun iw, 'that' (inan.), is also sometimes
used to demarcate subordinate clauses, rather like the English use of that in similar gram-
matical contexts.

   (37) Nwaabndaan go gmaapiich [iw mmaazkaag iw biiwaabkoons].
          'In time I see [that the wire moving].' (AM14.5)

          Nwaabndaan vti ind ls»0s 'I see INsg'; gmaapiich av 'after awhile'; iwprn Os 'that';
          mmaazkaag vii conj 0 '(CONJ) that IN moves'; iwprn Os 'that'; biiwaabkoons ni Os
          'wire.'


   (38)   .. .mii dash gaa-wnji-yaawaawaad niw kikoon [iw gii-jiibaakwewaad].

          '.. .and that's why they had those pots [when they were cooking]' (AK17.4)

          mii av 'that's'; dash av 'then'; gaa-wnji-yaawaawaad vta ic conj 3pProx»3obv '(CCNJ)
          why ANpl had ANobv'; niw prn 3obv 'that/those'; kikoon na 3obv 'pot(s)'; iw prn Os
          'that'; gii-jiibaakwewaad vai conj 3pProx '(CONJ) ANpl cooked.'


    ADVERBIAL SUBORDINATORS. Several adverbs function as subordinators, so that verbs
in clauses associated with them show conjunct order inflection. The most important of these
is mii, discussed at length below, but others include giishpin, 'if,' pii, 'when,' when it heads
its clause, and megwaa, when it has the meaning 'while.'

   (39) Ngii-nkwetwaa dash ji-zhaayaambaa [giishpin bgidniwaad ngitziimag].
          'I answered him that I would go [if my parents permitted me to go].' (AM8.3)

          Ngii-nkwetwaa vta ind ls»3sProx 'I answered ANsg'; dash av 'then'; ji-zhaayaambaa
          vai conj pret Is '(CONJ) that I would go'; giishpin av 'if; bgidniwaad vta conj
          3pProx»ls '(CONJ) ANpl would let me'; ngitziimag nad Is(SpProx) 'my parents.'


   (40) [Pii dash ezhaayaang odi], aazhgo wgii-gdaanaawaa giw gaagog.

          '[But when we went there], the porcupines had already eaten it up.' (AK1.7)

          Pii av 'when'; dash av 'then'; ezhaayaang vai ic conj Ip '(CCNJ) we (excl) went there';
          odi av 'there'; aazhgo av 'already indeed'; wgii-gdaanaawaa vti ind3pPwx»0 'ANpl ate
          INsg up'; giwprn 3pProx 'those'; gaagog na 3pProx 'porcupines.'

   Since verbs specifying background information such as time and location often appear

adverbs, such as megwaa, 'while,' and naangim, 'until,' the verb always shows conjunct

18.4.9 Main Verbs Inflected with Conjunct Order

    In running narrative, the main verbs of sentences sometimes show conjunct order inflec-
tion, that is, they behave like verbs in subordinate clauses. Consider, for example, (52),
below, the opening sentences of a narrative. In the first sentence the presence of conjunct
order inflection on gaa-zhichgewaad is explainable on the basis of association with predica-
tive particle mil In the second sentence, however, there are three verbs, gii-nsaawaad,
gii-zhiiwtaagnawaawaad, and wii-aabjihaawaad, all of which show conjunct order inflec-
tion. The conjunct inflection of the first verb can be explained as being due to its being in a
when-clause, gii-nsaawaad niw nmegsan, 'when they killed sturgeon.' The conjunct inflec-
tion of the last verb, wii-aabjihaawaad, can be explained on the basis of its being in a pur-
pose-clause, 'in order to use them.' But there is no structural explanation for the conjunct
inflection of the middle verb, gii-zhiiwtaagnawaawaad, 'they salted them.'

   (52) 1 Mewnzha giw nishnaabeg mii gaa-zhichgewaad iw dgwaagig. 2 Gii-nsaawaad
        niw nmegsan gii-zhiiwtaagnawaawaad wii-aabjihaawaad iw bboon.
         ' 1 Long ago this is what the Indians did in the fall. 2 They killed sturgeon and
         salted them in order to use them in the winter.' (AK4.1-2)

          Mewnzha av 'long ago'; giwpra SpProx 'those'; nishnaabeg na SpProx 'Indians'; mii
          av 'then'; gaa-zhichgewaad vai ic conj SpProx '(CCNJ) what ANpl did'; iwprn Os 'that';
          dgwaagig vii conj 0 '(CONJ) IN be fall'; Gii-nsaawaad vta conj 3pProx»3obv '(CONJ)
          ANpl killed ANobv'; niw/?ra 3obv 'that/those'; nmegsan na 3obv 'trout';
          gii-zhiiwtaagnawaawaad vta conj 3pProx»3obv '(CONJ) ANpl salted ANobv';
          wii-aabjihaawaad vta conj 3pProx»3obv '(CONJ) ANpl will use ANobv'; iw prn Os
          'that'; bboon ni Os 'winter.'


   The reason that the verb gii-zhiiwtaagnawaawaad is conjunct in this sentence is simply
that sentences in running narrative sometimes act as if they were subordinated to the whole
narrative, or form tight units with adjacent sentences.

18.5 The Role of Word Order in Nishnaabemwin

   Because word order is not used in Nishnaabemwin to determine grammatical relations
such as subject and object, it is free to serve other functions. Richard Rhodes and Russ
Tomlin (Tomlin and Rhodes 1979) have studied Nishnaabemwin word order extensively,
and have concluded that word order is used to keep track of the information status of the dif-
ferent elements of a sentence. For example, when nominals are introduced into a narrative,
952 • 18.5 The Role of Word Order in Nishnaabemwin


they tend to occur before the verb. When nominals are subsequently referred to, they tend to
occur after the verb. The verb is thus a kind of pivot, which is used to index whether infor-
mation is new (in which case it comes before the verb) or old (in which case it comes after
the verb). In addition, Rhodes hypothesizes that there is a position before the verb for focus-
ing, or giving greater emphasis to information. This is the position to which fronted ele-
ments of split noun phrases, such as quantifiers, are moved, as in the following example:

   (53) Nswi gii-bi-zhaamgadoonjwmaanaw mnishenying.
         "Three canoes came to the island.' (AM39.248)

          Nswi nm 'three'; gii-bi-zhaamgadoon vii indOp 'INpl came'; jiimaanan ni Op 'boats';
          mnishenying ni 0 loc 'to the island.'

    New or contrastive information comes before the verb, and old, non-contrastive informa-
tion comes after it. When new characters are introduced into a narrative, a noun phrase
referring to them often appears before the verb. The example, (54), at the top of the follow-
ing page, illustrates, from a story by Rose Nadjiwon of Cape Croker. In sentence [1] here,
the character of Johnny Angus Sr. is introduced, by means of a noun phrase maaba bezhig
nishnaabe, 'a certain Indian,' which occurs before the verb. In sentence [2], horses are men-
tioned, by means of a noun placed before the verb. In sentences [3] and [5], however, inani-
mate objects (props) are introduced, raw bezhgoogzhi-piknan, 'those harnesses' (NI), and iw
mjidwe-mzinigan, 'that mail-order catalogue' (NI). In both cases, the noun phrase follows
the verb. This is evidently because these objects are not very prominent in the action of the
discourse. It is very common for words referring to props in a story to be introduced after
the verb. Note, though, that in the discourse above, another reference to new harnesses,
shki-ahiin, 'new ones,' appears before the verb (in sentence [3]).
    TOPIC AND Focus. Two very important concepts in discourse study are TOPIC and
FOCUS. Topic is a rather vague but intuitive notion often defined as "what the discourse is
about," or, with reference to individual sentences within a discourse, "what the sentence is
about." Within a given span of discourse, a speaker (or writer) will make particular charac-
ters the main topic(s). At any time, there is the option of shifting to a new topic. Many lan-
guages have special word orders that are used in association with topic shifts, and typically
such word orders put the nominal referring to the new topic in a position before the verb. We
have seen above that Nishnaabemwin often puts newly introduced topics before the verb.

   (54) [1] Mii dash maaba bezhig nishnaabe Johnny Angus (Sr.) gii-zhinkaazo, mii niw
        "Ojibwens" oosbaniin, shkinawe go naa maanda iw pii aawgoban. [2]
        Bezhgoogzhiin go naa gii-yaawaagban. [3] Aapji dash go naa aazhgo
        pakshkaanwidgenan niw sa bezhgoogzhii-piknan, aabdeg dash naa shki-ahiin
        wii-mjidwedog. [4] Gaa dash dayaanziin wiin iw sa mjidwe-mzinigan.

         '[1] And so, there was a man named Johnny Angus, he's the one whose father was
         named Ojibwens; he was a young man at this time. [2] He evidently had horses.
         [3] But evidently the harnesses were wearing out, and he had to order new ones.
         [4] But he didn't have a mail-order catalogue! (RN)

          Mii av 'and'; dash av 'then'; maabapra SsProx 'this'; bezhig nm 'one'; nishnaabe na
          3sProx 'Indian'; gii-zhinkaazo vai ind SsProx 'ANsg was named'; mii av 'it's'; niwprn
          3obv 'that/those'; Ojibwens na SsProx 'Ojibwens'; oosbaniin nadpret 3sProx(3obv)

          Bezhgoogzhiin na 3obv 'horse(s)'; gii-yaawaagban vta indpdub 3sProx»3obv 'ANsg
          evidently had ANobv'; Aapji av 'really'; dash av 'then'; aazhgo av 'now indeed';
          pakshkaanwidgenan vai inddub 3obv 'ANobv are evidently wearing out'; niw prn Op
          'those'; bezhgoogzhii-piknan ni Op 'horse harnesses'; aabdeg av 'necessarily'; dash av
          'then'; shki-ahiin ni Op 'new ones'; wii-mjidwedog vai ind dub SsProx 'ANsg evidently
          wants to order by mail'; Gaa av 'not'; dash av 'but'; dayaanziin vti ind neg 3sProx»Os
          'ANsg does not have INsg'; wiin av 'then'; iwprn Os 'that'; mjidwe-mzinigan ni Os 'mail

    Another important discourse concept is that of FOCUS. Focus simply refers to the giving
of special prominence to some constituent within a sentence, and is typically "new informa-
tion asserted against the background of a presupposed proposition" (Dahlstrom 1995:10).
Nishnaabemwin has special focus constructions using mii, discussed elsewhere in this chap-
ter, but there is also arguably a focus position within the sentence in Nishnaabemwin,
namely directly before the verb. It is in this position that (fronted) quantifiers, indefinite pro-
nouns, and other elements being given special prominence occur. Often focused elements
have emphatic particles associated with them, such as sa, as in the following example:

   (55) Jiimaanfocus sa gga-wzhitoomin ge-zhiwdooyang odi.
          'We'll make a boat that we'll take there.' (AK1.5)

          Jiimaan ni Os 'boat'; gga-wzhitoomin vti ind 21 »0 'we (incl) will make IN';
          ge-zhiwdooyang vti ic conj 21 »0 '(CCNJ) which (IN) we (incl) will take there'; odi av
          'there.'


   In a thoughtful study of word order in Meskwaki, a language related to Nishnaabemwin,
Amy Dahlstrom (Dahlstrom 1995) has suggested that sentences have the following struc-
ture, in which topic and focus positions are distinguished:
954 • 18.5 The Role of Word Order in Nishnaabemwin




    While both topic and focus positions are before the verb, the topic occurs to the left of
the negative element and the focus to the right of it. Topic is very loosely attached to the
clause it is associated with, and so is treated by Dahlstrom as a syntactic sister to the whole
sentence, by means of a special construction called an S-bar (indicated with S'), which has
as its two daughters the Topic and the Clause (indicated with S).
    The following sentence illustrates the use of both topic and focus. It comes as the fifth
one in a discourse in which Alice King explains an object lesson that young women reach-

focus can occur between the negative element and the verb, though, as Dahlstrom's work
suggests, the focus immediately precedes the verb, and the topic is to the left of it.

    SUMMARY. There are many subtleties to the notion of topic, and much work remains to

18.6 Grammatical Relations in Nishnaabemwin

    In an exciting series of papers cast in the theoretical framework of relational grammar,
Rhodes (e.g., 1998a, 1998b, 1997, 1996, 1991a, 1991b) has laid out much of the basic syn-
tax of Nishnaabemwin (especially the Odawa dialect). Rhodes lays out five principal gram-
matical relations in Ojibwe, including subjects, primary objects, secondary objects,
complements of relative roots, and obliques. These relations are ranked in the order listed
here, from highest to lowest. Primary objects are the inflectional goals of VTA and VTI verbs;
secondary objects are the inflected goals of VAIO verbs and the non-goal roles associated
with ditransitive (VTA) verbs; obliques in Nishnaabemwin are restricted to temporals, loca-
tives, and instrumentals. Primary object marking is shown by the presence of theme signs
and pronominal agreement inflection, while both primary and secondary objects show
agreement for what Rhodes calls n-registration, that is, the n's that mark agreement in VAIO
and VTI verbs in the independent order. Secondary objects can only be third person, first and
second person are excluded. Secondary objects also show fewer features of agreement than
do primary objects.
    Rhodes argues that the secondary objects of ditransitives align grammatically with the
objects of VAIO verbs, on the basis of inflectional patterns that show up when a primary
object (of a ditransitive) is lost. Invariably, the secondary ditransitive object is treated inflec-
tionally as an ordinary secondary object (i.e., like the object of a VAIO). The following
example illustrates. Here, the base VTA verb shamaad, 'feed Y to AN,' shows an incorpo-
rated primary object, realized as /-aawaso/, 'child(ren),' within the verb. The derived verb
shows secondary object agreement for an inanimate singular object, reflecting inflectional
indexing of the inanimate object, nboob, 'soup.'
958 • 18.6 Grammatical Relations in Nishnaabemwin


   (62) Wgii-shamaawson nboob. I 'She fed her children soup.'

          Wgii-shamaawson vtaA>aio ind SsProx »0s 'ANsg fed children INsg'; nboob ni Os
          'soup.'

    The two types of objects also share the properties of not being passivizable, and restric-
tion to third person.
    Rhodes distinguishes relative root complements from other obliques on the basis of sev-
eral features, the most important of which is that the complements of relative roots show
understood definite reference when the complement is not formally specified, as do subjects
and primary/secondary objects. The idea here is that in a clause containing a verb but no
explicit nominals, the inflection on the verb is interpreted as definite. So, for example, a sen-
tence such as Mii dash gii-bmi-dkajid, 'And he caught a cold (in the course of his travels),'
has no overt nominal, and the verb, dkaji, 'catch/have a cold,' is marked with a third person
singular animate subject suffix, dkaji-d. In such cases, the referent is interpreted as definite,
that is, as referring to a specific individual who has been previously identified in the dis-
course. The same applies to the complements of relative roots, as in Baamaa go ga-zhaami,
'Afterwards we'll go there' (baamaa av 'afterwards'; ga-zhaami, 'we (incl) will go there')
where the concept expressed in English as 'there,' is understood in Nishnaabemwin to refer
to a definite location, just as the verbal inflection in dkajid, above, is understood to refer to a
definite individual. Rhodes also argues that the complements of relative roots can some-
times advance (move up in the relational hierarchy) to secondary objects (Rhodes 1991a:5).
    With respect to OBLIQUES, Rhodes distinguishes two basic types, those that are central to
the semantics of the verb, and those that are not. The first type is exemplified by the verb
boozi, 'board (a vehicle),' where the specification of the vehicle is optional, but central to
the semantics of the notion of boarding. The second type of oblique occurs in Aapji
gii-gzhaate iw pii, 'It was very hot out at that time' (Aapji av 'very' gii-gzhaate vii 'IN was
hot' iw pii ni 'that time'), where iw pii is not at all central to the notion of being hot. Rhodes
suggests that this latter type of oblique modifies the clause and not the verbal predication, so
focuses his discussion on demonstrating that the first type of oblique, the semantically more
central, is grammatically different in its behaviour from relative root complements. He
argues that when such an oblique is not explicitly stated, it cannot receive a definite inter-
pretation, e.g., ngii-booz, 'I got on' cannot be interpreted as 'I got on it.'
    Rhodes also shows how relative root complements align in their grammatical behaviour-
with subjects and primary and secondary objects. These last three show verb agreement, but
other grammatical relations do not, including relative root complements. Primary and sec-
ondary objects allow quantifier floating, but relative root complements do not. The comple-
ments of relative roots are distinctively marked, with locative case. Relative root
complements are like subjects and objects, however, in being targets of grammatical
advancement. Basically, being a target of advancement means that a language provides
means to advance an element having a lower grammatical relation to that of a higher one.
For example, primary (direct) objects advance to subject by means of the rule of passiviza-
                                                   18.6 Grammatical Relations in Nishnaabemwin • 959



tion; secondary objects advance to the role of primary object by means of the various appli-
cative processes discussed in this chapter. Rhodes demonstrates that oblique heads are
advanced to relative root complements in relative clause constructions. So, for example, in
the following relative clause, modifying the locational noun, wiigwaaming, 'in the shelter,'
the relative preverb dzhi-, 'in such place, at,' appears in the relativized verb.

   (63)   ...waa-dzhi-mkadekewaad wiigwaaming.
          '...in the shelter where they would fast' (AM23.3)

           waa-dzhi-mkadekewaad vai conj ic SpProx '(CCNJ) where ANpl would fast';
           miigwaaming ni 0 /oc'in (the) shelter.'


   Rhodes demonstrates that this is the obligatory way to form relative clauses on all
obliques that are not temporals. Rhodes summarizes his argument with the following table
showing the variable grammatical properties of the different grammatical relations in Nish-
naabemwin.

18.6.1 Semantic and Syntactic Relations Revisited

   Rhodes 1994 lays out four patterns of alignment between syntactic and semantic roles
in Nishnaabemwin. These four patterns, labelled with roman numerals, are outlined in the
chart below. Within each pattern, there are two groupings, which I have labelled A and B.
                                                 18.6.1 Semantic and Syntactic Relations Revisited • 961



                                            A                            B
                          I            1
                                agent of direct                      2
                                                             patient of direct
                                patient of inverse           agent of inverse
                                patient of passive
                          II    agent of direct              patient of direct
                                agent of inverse             patient of inverse
                                                             patient of passive
                          III   agent of direct              patient of direct
                                agent of inverse             patient of inverse
                                patient of passive
                          IV    agent of direct              patient of direct

                         2. Rhodes includes theme and recipient with patient in all of

    The concepts of direct and inverse are discussed at length in Chapter 7 (beginning on
page 7.2.2, beginning on page 270). The semantic roles of agent, patient, experiencer, etc.
are treated in Chapter 13. The basic issue concerns whether clauses containing inverse verb
forms have the same surface grammatical relations as their underlying grammatical rela-
tions. Some analysts, such as Rhodes, argue that the grammatical relations are reversed,
while others, such as Dahlstrom (1987), contend that they are not. Crucial to this discussion
has been the grammatical behaviour of passives, which are clearly underlying objects but
surface subjects, and whether or not the notional objects of inverses behave like passives.
Rhodes believes that this approach has led to inconsistent results, and shows that there are at
least four distinct alignment patterns, as outlined above. Rhodes maintains that these pat-
terns can only be convincingly accounted for if one assumes that grammatical relations are
reversed in clauses containing inverse verb forms.1

   Pattern I, above, governs five distinct syntactic phenomena:

1.1 The A roles must be filled by animates; B roles can be filled by either animates or inani-
    mates.
1.2 The A roles control obviation of all other arguments (including primary objects); B roles
    can only control obviation of secondary objects.
1.3 The A roles occupy the same slot in pragmatically neutral word order in ditransitive
    predications with three expressed nominals; B roles occupy the same slot in neutral word

    findings, in which speakers were queried for all possible post-verbal arrangements of

    binoojiinyan, 'The woman fed the child(ren) blueberries.'1 Sentences with three overt
    noun phrases such as this are decidedly rare in Nishnaabemwin. Speaker preferences for
    both inanimate and animate themes (secondary objects) are given, in descending order of
    preference (A roles are in boldface, B roles in small caps).^

                                     Direct                    Inverse
                            a.       P theme agent RECIP P theme recip AGENT
                            b.       P agent theme RECIP P recip theme AGENT
                            c. ?     P theme RECIP agent        P theme AGENT recip
                            d. ?     P RECIP theme agent        P AGENT theme recip
                            e. ?* P RECIP agent theme          P AGENT recip theme
                            f.   *   P agent RECIP theme P recip AGENT theme

                                     Animate Secondary Object
                                     Direct                     Inverse

                           f.    * P theme agent RECIP P theme recip AGENT

1.4 The A roles can raise (copy); B roles cannot. (See Chapter 13.3.7, beginning on page
    681, for a discussion of raising/copying.)
1.5 The A roles control obviation in the subjects of adjunct clauses; B roles do not.
