II. 1 The A roles are bound by the aspectual preverb booni-, 'stop'; B roles are not.

   Pattern III governs four syntactic phenomena

111.1 The A roles cannot bind floated quantifiers; B roles can bind floated quantifiers.
111.2 The A roles are bound by the directional preverb hi-, 'hither'; B roles are not.
111.3 For some speakers, the A roles can raise/copy; B roles cannot.
111.4 For some speakers, the A roles control obviation in adjunct clauses; B roles do not

   Pattern IV governs one syntactic phenomenon.

IV. 1 Verbs with objects show -n(aa) inflection (the n-registration suffix in independent
    order found on VTl's and VAIO's) except where B roles are animate.

    Rhodes suggests that these phenomena can be accounted for if we consider the grammat-
ical relations of inverse predications to be reversed from those of direct. In pattern I the A
roles then express subjects, while the B roles express primary objects. In Pattern II, the A
roles express agents, and the B roles patients. In Pattern IV, the A roles are ERGATIVES, and
the B roles are ABSOLUTIVES. Rhodes interprets Pattern III to distinguish first available sub-
jects (A) from non-distinguished argument subjects (B), meaning very roughly that group A
represents the preferred candidates for subject status, and group B the less preferred.
    I have included this summary of Rhodes 1994 for several reasons. First, Rhodes'
research demonstrates the subtleties at play in Nishnaabemwin, and the complex interplay
of syntactic, morphological, and semantic features of grammar. Secondly, Rhodes' research
demonstrates that the grammatical relations subject and object have an obvious place in the
grammar of Nishnaabemwin, though they are far less central than in a language such as
English. Thirdly, Rhodes' research points to many promising areas of future study in Nish-
naabemwin grammar, such as the scope of various classes of preverbs.

18.7 Expressions with Mii

    The predicative adverb mil, which is extremely common in narrative, has two primary
functions. The first is simply to serve as a marker of normal discourse sequencing, that is, to
advance a narrative, rather like English, "and then..." as used in common narration, though
word orders within mil clauses can reflect varying degrees of prominence. The second func-
tion of mii is as a focusing element, somewhat like the English, "It was a..." (called a
cleft-construction) or "what X was..." (called a pseudo-cleft construction). In this section
we will examine each of these functions.

18.7.1 Mii as a Discourse Sequencer

   In its function as a discourse sequencing predicative adverb, mii is followed by a clause
having a verb marked with conjunct order inflection. If the verb contains a relative root, it
usually shows changed conjunct. The normal, unmarked order is probably for the verb to
964 • 18.7.1 Mii as a Discourse Sequencer


directly follow mil, though a few clitic particles such as sa, go, and dash can intervene, and
evidential particles such as giiwenh or iidig can follow the clitics. The following sentences
are very typical.

   (64) Mii go iidig gii-zhaabwaakzod, mii sa iidig gii-ni-nbod.
         'So he was badly burnt, and died along the way.' (SO 1.40)

          Mii av 'and'; iidig av 'it seems'; gii-zhaabwaakzod vai conj 3sProx 'ANsg was burned
          through'; mii av 'and'; iidig av 'it seems'; gii-ni-nbod vai conj SsProx '(CONJ) ANsg
          died along the way.'

         'This is what the old lady told her children.' (SO2.20)

          ANsg related to ANobv'; mdimooyenh na SsProx 'old woman'; niwi prn na 3obv 'nao';
          wniijaansan na 3sProx(3obv) 'ANsg's child(ren).'

    When desired, a nominal can be the first major constituent in the mil-clause, which

18.7.2 Mii in Focusing Constructions

  Mii can also serve as a focusing device in constructions using relative clauses, rather like
English clefted-sentences, such as "It was a linguist that rescued the cat." Some Nishnaabe-
mwin mii constructions used in this way have the following structure:

             Mii     Focused Item (Demonstrative Pronoun) Relative Clause

    The focused item can be either a noun phrase or a pronoun. The following examples all
have a noun in the focused position. Examples (90) and (91) represent what is sometimes
called exhaustive listing focus (Payne 1997:269), in which the speaker asserts the unique-
ness of the focused element in the context specified by the rest of the sentence. In sentence
(104), for example, the speaker asserts that at a particular wilderness location where some
men had left a boat, upon returning they found only the keel and nothing else; the rest of the
boat had been eaten by porcupines. Exhaustive listing focus almost always involves the use
of eta, 'only, just.' In sentence (91) some men come upon a lodge expecting to find a mother
who had betrayed her sons, but instead find only a pile of ashes. Here it is not so much an
                                                          18.7.2 Mil in Focusing Constructions • 971



exhaustive list that is being focused, but the unexpectedness of the situation, though the
ashes represent a suitable end to such a deceitful mother.

   (90) Mii go eta [datgaagon]
                    NP = [gaa-teg]RC.

         'It was only [the backbone (keel) that was there]' (AK1.8)

         Mii av 'it's'; eta av 'only'; datgaagon ni Os 'keel'; gaa-teg vii ic conjpart 0 '(CCNJ)
         which IN was there.'


   (91) Mii go eta [bngwi]^ = [eksing]RC!
         'It was only [ashes that were piled up]\' (SO2.36)

         Mii av 'it's'; eta av 'only'; bngwi ni Os 'ash'; eksing vii ic conj 0 'which (IN) is piled up.'


   The following examples simply assert with added emphasis a particular component of a
proposition.

   (92) Mii naw naa wiin [baanaaben]^ = [niw gaa-waabmaawaajin]RC.
         'It was apparently [a mermaid that they saw].' (AK4.5)

         Mii av 'it's'; naw naa wiin av 'indeed'; baanaaben na 3obv 'mermaid(s)'; niwprn 3obv
         'that/those'; gaa-waabmaawaajin vta ic conj part 3pProx»3obv '(CCNJ) which (ANobv)
         ANpl saw ANobv.'


   (93) Mii [maa naa pit iw]^p = \gaa-maadseg iw freaty]RC, gaa-wnji-miinndwaa niw
        zhoonyaan.

        'That was at that time that the treaty started, that's why they were given those

          'that.'


   The following example has a personal pronoun in foeus:

   (97) Giishpin eyaagin waa-nankiing widi Girls Quarters mii go niin widi

18.7.3 Mii with Independent Order

    Occasionally, in narratives, verbs in construction with mii show independent order

   (98) Mii sa wi ge sa ge naa mno-yaa. I 'Right away he feels fine.' (SO4.44)
         Mii av 'and'; vriprn Os 'that'; ge av 'and'; ge av 'even'; mno-yaa vai indSsProx 'ANsg is

18.8 Identificational Constructions

    There are many constructions which are used to explicitly assert the identity of persons
or things. One common identificational construction has the following form, where NP
stands for noun phrase, and may be a noun, pronoun, or any other nominal expression.
             NP sa (go, wii)       DEM       (Relative Clause)
974 • 18.9 Communicative Functions


   (100) Mil sa giiwenh gaa-god maaba nmishoomis, "Mshi-gnebig sa aw emwaad niw
         gniijaansan"
         'And, reportedly, the other said to my grandfather, "The great snake is the one
         who is eating your children."' (AK11.14)

          Mil av 'and'; giiwenh av 'allegedly'; gaa-god vta ic conj 3obv»3sProx '(CCNJ) ANobv
          said to ANsg'; maabaprn SsProx 'this'; nmishoomis nod ls(3sProx) 'my grandfather';

          3sProx»3obv '(CCNJ) who (ANsg) is eating ANobv'; niw prn 3obv 'that/those';
          gniijaansan na 2s(3obv) 'your SG child(ren).'

   (101) Meko-bmased sa aw. I 'She's a bear-walker!' (AK13.11)
         Meko-bmased vai ic conj part SsProx '(CCNJ) ANsg who is a bear walker'; aw prn
         SsProx 'that one.'

   (102) Giigoonh sa wii maaba! I 'This is just a fish!' (SO3.12)
          Giigoonh na SsProx 'fish'; wii av 'then'; maaba prn SsProx 'this.'

   (103) Gun sa aw gaa-niimid. \ 'You're the one who danced.' (AM39.636)
          Gimprnpers 2s 'you'; aw prn SsProx 'that'; gaa-niimid vai ic conj part SsProx '(CCNJ)
          who (ANsg) danced.'

18.9 Communicative Functions

   There are basically three things that can be done with language: make statements, ask
questions, and give commands. These are sometimes described as the basic communicative
functions of language, DECLARATIVE, INTERROGATIVE, and IMPERATIVE.

                          Declarative       — Make a statement
                                            — Express an emotional state
                          Interrogative     — Ask a yes/no question
                                            — Ask a substantive question
                          Imperative        — Give a command

   In Nishnaabemwin, each of these functions may be expressed positively or negatively.
Negation is discussed at length in Chapter 16.10, beginning on page 837.1 have addressed
declarative statements extensively throughout this chapter, so I will not treat them here. In
the following sections we will look at interrogative and imperative constructions
                                                       18.9.1 Asking Questions (Interrogatives) • 975



18.9.1 Asking Questions (Interrogatives)

    There are two kinds of questions in Nishnaabemwin, YES/NO QUESTIONS (also called
POLAR QUESTIONS), and CONTENT QUESTIONS (also called SUBSTANTIVE QUESTIONS). These
two types are formed quite differently, and will be treated separately in the sections which
follow.

18.9.1.1 Yes/No (Polar) Questions

   A distinct form exists in Nishnaabemwin for questions that invite a simple positive or
negative response, called yes/no questions or polar questions. These questions are most
commonly formed by putting the question particle na after the word being questioned, and
using question intonation.

   (104) Mno-kwaabiigad na sabaabiins?
         'Is the string long enough' (lit., is the string a good length)? (MC)

          Mno-kwaabiigad vii ind Os 'INsg (stringlike) is of suitable length'; na av 'yes/no
          question'; sabaabiins ni Os 'string.'


   (105) Waya na giigoonh ggii-debnaa? I 'Did you catch any fish?' (MC5.3)

          Wayapra indefSsProx 'any'; na av 'yes/no question'; giigoonh na SsProx 'fish';
          ggii-debnaa vta ind 2s»3sProx 'you did catch ANsg.'

    The question word na comes after the first word, even in phrasal units, such as maanda
jiimaan, 'this boat,' as in the following:

   (106) Maanda na jiimaan ggii-aabjitoon? I 'Did you use this boat?' (RV/MC)

          Maandaprn Os 'this'; na av 'yes/no question'; jiimaan ni Os 'boat'; ggii-aabjitoon vti
          ind 2s»0s 'you (sg) used INsg.'

    English multi-word borrowings are treated as single units for purposes of questioning,
as in the following, where the noun compound hamburger patties is treated as a unit, which
na then follows. The same is true of multi-word names, such as Mary Ann Corbiere.

   (107) Hamburger patties na biwag? I 'Are there hamburger pattiesT (MC8.26)

          na av 'yes/no question'; biwag vai ind BpProx 'ANpl are there.'
976 • 18.9.1.1 Yes/No (Polar) Questions


   In yes/no questions, the expression that occurs before na represents the point of focus in
the question. In the following sentence, for example, a little girl questions her grand-
mother's instructions to fetch coal oil in preparation for a trip into the garden to kill potato
bugs, and asks if she is to burn up the potato bugs. The verbal expression nii-jaagzwaag, 'I
will burn ANpl' is initial.

   (108) A: Taa taa haa! Nii-jaagzwaag na giwi pinii-mnidooshensag?
         B: Kaa, gaawimka-jaagzwaasiig.
         A: 'For goodness sakes, am I going to burn the potato bugs?'
         B: 'No, you will not burn them- (DP)

          Taa taa haa av 'oh my!'; Nii-jaagzwaag vta ind ls»3pProx 'I will burn ANpl up'; na av
          'yes/no question'; giwipra SpProx 'those'; pinii-mnidooshensag na 3pProx 'potato
          bugs'; Kaa av 'no'; gaawiin av 'not'; ka-jaagzwaasiig vta ind neg 2s»3pProx 'you (SG)
          will not burn up ANpl.'


   However, an entire proposition can also be questioned, in which case regular word order
prevails, such as in (109), where a time adverb occurs before na, (110) where sentence-com-
plement taking verb (gnandwenirri) precedes its complement (ji-nsag), and (111), where an
indefinite pronoun leads the clause, as is typical.

   (109) Waabang na go ndaa-bgiz gbe-giizhig? I 'Tomorrow can I go swimming all day?'
          Waabang av 'tomorrow'; na av 'yes/no question'; ndaa-bgiz vai ind Is 'I could swim';
          gbe-giizhig av 'all day.' (DP)

   (110) Gnandwenim na ji-nsag? I 'Do you want me to kill him?' (AK11.18)

          Gnandwenim vta ind 2s»ls 'you SG want of me'; na av 'yes/no question'; ji-nsag vta
          conj ls»3sProx '(CONJ) I should kill ANsg.'


   (111) Nii-gziibiigzhe,gwaya na zaaghmoogmigong yaa?

         T want to take a shower, is anyone in the bathroom?' (ED)

          Nii-gziibiigzhe vai ind Is 'I want to shower'; gwaya prn inde/3 'anyone'; na av 'yes/no
          question'; zaaghmoogmigong ni 0 loc 'in the bathroom'; yaa vai ind 3sProx ANsg is (in
          a location).'


   Politeness can be expressed by means of modal preverbs:
                                                          18.9.1.1 Yes/No (Polar) Questions • 977


   (112) Nookmis, iM/o0-ke-paa-wiidookaaz na go ntam?
         'Grandma, can I go and play first?' (DP)

         Nookmis nad Is(SsProx) 'my grandmother'; ndaa-ke-paa-wiidookaaz vai ind Is 'can I
         first go around playing'; na av 'yes/no question'; ntam av 'first.'


   Yes/no questions can also be asked without using na, simply by using question intona-
tion, as in English.

   (113) Mii sa go naa eta msawnawad aw John? I 'Oh, so you've got the hots for John?'
         Mii av 'it's'; eta av 'only'; msawnawad vta conj 2s»3sProx '(CONJ) you (SG) long for
         ANsg'; awpra SsProx 'that.' (IS)

   NEGATIVE YES/NO QUESTIONS. Negative yes/no questions are very common in Nish-
naabemwin. These sentences invariably have the negative adverb in sentence-initial posi-
tion, to which na can be attached. Such questions invite a positive answer.

   (114) Gaa na gwii-wiidgemaasii? I 'Don't you want to marry her?' (DP)

         Gaa av 'not'; na av 'yes/no question'; gwii-wiidgemaasii vta indneg 2s»3sProx 'you
         (SG) do not want to marry ANsg.'

   (115) Gaa na gegoo ggii-yaanziin zhoonyaans wii-wiisniyin?
         'Did you not have money that you could eat with?' (MO)

         Gaa av 'not'; na av 'yes/no question'; gegooprn indefO '(any)thing'; ggii-yaanziin vti
         indneg 2s»0s 'you (SG) did not have INsg'; zhoonyaans ni Os 'money'; wii-wiisniyin vai
         conj 2s '(CONJ) you (SG) could eat.'

   (116) Gaawiin na bdakjihgan gwii-miizhsii? I 'Aren't you going to give me a fork?' (IT)
         Gaawiin av 'not'; na av 'yes/no question'; bdakjihgan ni Os 'fork'; gwii-miizhsii vta ind
         neg 2s»ls 'you (SG) will not give me.'

   Such questions sometimes lack the element na, but have question intonation.
978 • 18.9.1.1 Yes/No (Polar) Questions


   (117) Gaawii go weyiib gnandwendnziinan gdoo-lexicography mzinhignan?
         'You don't want your lexicography books (back) soon?' (MC)

          Gaawii av 'not'; weyiib av 'right away'; gnandwendnziinan vti indneg 2s»0p 'you (SG)
          do not want INpl'; gdoo-lexicography ni 2s(0s) 'your (SG) lexicography'; mzinhignan ni
          Op 'books.'

   TAG QUESTIONS. Tag questions can be asked with emphatic particle naa.

   (118) Geget go znagad, naa? I 'It really is difficult, isn't it?' (MC)
          Geget av 'truly'; gopt 'indeed'; znagad vii indOs 'INsg is difficult'; naapt tag

   The following example is intentionally humourous in its phonological repetitiveness.

   (119) Gdaa-naanaanaa, Aanaa, naa? I 'We should fetch Anna, shouldn't we?' (MC)
          Gdaa-naanaanaa vta ind21»3sProx 'we (incl.) should fetch ANsg'; Aanaa na name
          3sProx 'Anna'; naa pt tag

    ALTERNATIVE QUESTIONS. When alternatives are offered with yes/no questions, the
linkage seems to be implicit.

   (120) Nga-nsaa na, gnimaa gegoo iw gaawiin geyaabi gegoo ji-zhi-gshkihewzisig."
         'Am I to kill him, or perhaps something so that he no longer has any power?'"
         (AK11.19)

          Nga-nsaa vta ind ls»3sProx 'I will kill ANsg'; na av 'yes/no question'; gnimaa av
          'perhaps'; gegooprn indefO 'something'; iv/ prn Os 'that'; gaawiin av 'not'; geyaabi av
          'anymore'; gegoo prn indefO 'anything'; ji-zhi-gshkihewzisig vai conj SsProx neg
          '(CONJ) ANsg would not be powerful.'

    YES/NO QUESTIONS WITH-MII. Yes/no questions can be formed with the predicative par-
ticle, mil Verbs in construction with mil are usually conjunct. These constructions are
mostly used for ratification of a conjecture or logical inference, and expect an affirmative
answer.

   (121) Mil na wii-boontaayang? I 'Is this when we (incl.) stop working?' (AM39.485)
          Mii av 'it's'; na av 'yes/no question'; wii-boontaayang vai conj 21 '(CONJ) we (incl.)
          will stop working.'
                                                         18.9.1.2 Substantive Content Questions • 979


   (122) Mil na go de-minik? I 'Is that enough? (n.b. examples for grammar)? (MC)
          Mii av 'it's'; na av 'yes/no question'; de-minik av 'sufficiently many.'

   (123) Mii na gegeti? I 'Is that right?' (MC5.5)
          Mii av 'it's'; na av 'yes/no question'; gegeti av 'right.'

18.9.1.2 Substantive Content Questions

    CONTENT QUESTIONS are those that ask for information such as who, what, when, where,
why, and how. In Nishnaabemwin, such questions have an interrogative pronoun or adverb,
which almost always occurs clause-initially, and is predicative, so the verb is inflected for
conjunct order. There is quite a bit of dialect variation in the form of the interrogatives. The
contrastive focus particle dash occurs very often in content questions, and in some cases has
indissolubly fused to the interrogative element, producing interrogative forms ending in
/sh/, such as wenesh, 'who' (anim) and wegnesh, 'what' (inan). In more formal contexts,
these are sometimes spelled with a hyphen, e.g., wene-sh.
    Rhodes 1998 presents a useful overview of content questions, which I summarize here.
The basic question words in Ottawa are wenen, 'who/what (an.),' wegne(n) (or for some
speakers wenen, 'what (in.),' aanii(n), 'how,' aanii-sh pitch, 'when,' and aanii pii/aapii
 'where.' There are two basic types of content questions, those having a verb (which is
always in the conjunct), and those having no verb. Verbless content questions are of two
types, equative and locational. Content questions with verbs can be further divided into
those in which the question word serves as a complement of a relative root, and those in
which it does not. Sentence (132) below exemplifies a verbless equational content question
and (160) a verbless locational question; (138) a verbal question with a relative root, and
(124) a verbal question lacking a relative root. All verbal content questions are inflected for
changed conjunct, with the exception of those formed on aapii, 'where,' questions, when it
is used to question static location as opposed to movement (see (148) to (151) below, for
examples without initial change). Rhodes also presents evidence that content questions are
not derived from relative clauses, as has been asserted by Truitner and Dunnigan (1972) and
Johns (1980) for western dialects of Ojibwe, because such constructions would predict par-
ticipial forms, which are not standardly used in Nishnaabemwin content questions, though
they do occur, as in (127) and (134), below.
    QUESTIONING WHO. Questions asking for the identity of an animate being use the inter-
rogative pronoun wenen, 'who' (also wene) which often has fused to it the emphatic focus-
sing particle dash, producing wenesh.

   (124) Wenesh dbaajmind? I 'Who is being narrated about?' (MT)
          Weneshprn inter 3/0 'who'; dbaajmind vta conjx»3sProx '(CONJ) ANsg is related of.'
980 • 18.9.1.2 Substantive Content Questions


   (125) "Wenesh naa ge-daamngid niw biitoosijiganan?" kido kwezens.
         "'Who are we going to sell the pie to?" one of the girls said.' (IS)

          Weneshprn inter3/0 'who'; ge-daamngid vta ic conj 21»3sProx '(CCNJ) we (incl.) will
          sell Y to ANsg'; niwpm 3obv 'that/those'; biitoosijiganan na 3obv 'pie(s)'; kido vai ind
          SsProx 'ANsg says'; kwezens na SsProx 'young woman.'

   (126) Wenesh gaa-bkobiised? I 'Who fell into the water?' (MT)
          Wenesh prn inter 3/0 'who'; gaa-bkobiised vai ic conj SsProx '(CCNJ) who (ANsg) fell
          in the water.'

   The interrogative pronoun is not inflected for plural number or obviation, though verbs
associated with it are.

   (127) Wenen ge-wa-wiidgemaajin? I 'Who (obv.) is he going to marry?' (RN)
          Wenenpra inter 3 'who'; ge-wa-wiidgemaajin vta ic conj part 3sProx»3obv '(CCNJ)
          who (ANobv) will ANsg marry.'

   A speaker from Walpole Island formed an identity question with question word aanii,
'how, in what way.'

   (128) Aanii dash e-aawyaanh? I 'So who am I/ what am I a           ?' (CN) (n.b. last line of a riddle)
          Aanii av 'how, in what way'; e-aawyaanh vai ic conj part? -7s'(CCNJ) I am.'

    QUESTIONING OWNERSHIP. The interrogative pronoun wenesh is used as a possessive
interrogative, too.

   (129) Wenesh maanda debendang zhibiihgaans? I 'Whose pencil is this?' (AM39.647)
          Wenesh prn inter 3/0 'who'; maanda prn Os 'this'; debendang vti ic conj 3sProx»0
          '(CCNJ) ANsg owns IN'; zhibiihgaans ni Os 'pencil.'

    QUESTIONING KIND. Questions as to the kind or sort of an object use wenesh in con-
struction with a similative pronoun such as dnawa, 'kind.'

   (130) Wenesh dnawa bneshiinh? I 'What fcwrf o/bird is it?' (AM39.857)
          Wenesh prn inter 3/0 'who'; dnawa prn sim 3/0 'kind'; bneshiinh na 3sProx 'bird.'
                                                                                     18.9.1.2 Substantive Content Questions • 981


    QUESTIONING WHAT. Questions regarding inanimates are expressed by means of the
interrogative pronoun wegnen, or with clitic dash, wegnesh. A variant of this pronoun is
ogonen.

   (131) Wegnesh ge-biidwiyan? I 'What are you going to bring me?' (AM39.648)

              Wegneshprn inter 0 'what'; ge-biidwiyan vta ic conj 2s»ls '(CCNJ) you (SG) will bring
              me.'


   (132) Wegnesh iw? I 'What is that?' (AM39.858)

              Wegnesh prn inter 0 'what'; iw prn Os 'that.'

   (133) "Ogonen gaa-aabajitoowan?" I 'What did you use?' (JC)

              Ogonen inter 'what'; gaa-aabajitoowan vti ic conj 2s»0 '(CCNJ) you (SG) used IN.'

   (134) Wane-sh niw genwaabndangin? I 'What (things) is he looking at?' (PI1.53)

              Wane-sh/?rn inter 0 'what'; niw prn Op 'those'; genwaabndangin vti ic conj part
              3sProx»Op '(CCNJ) which (INpl) ANsg looks at.'

    QUESTIONING WHICH. To question which, the interrogative pronoun of the appropriate
gender is used in conjunction with the nominal whose scope is being delimited. For exam-
ple, in the following sentence, the nominal is a pseudo-participle, waajnakiimad, 'whom
you (sg.) work with.'

   (135) Wegnesh waajnakiimad ewaanji-bshigenmad?(135) Wegnesh waajnakiimad ewaanji-bshigenmad?

             'Which of your co-workers do you like the best?' (MC)

              Wegnesh prn inter 3 'who'; waajnakiimad vta ic conj 2s»3sProx '(CCNJ) whom (ANsg)
              you work with'; ewaanji-bshigenmad vta ic conj 2s»3sProx '(CCNJ) you (sg) most like
              ANsg.'


   The following example has an inanimate.

   (136) Wegnesh doopwin ewaanji-bshigendman?

             'Which table do you like the best?' (MC)

              Wegneshpm inter 3 'who'; doopwinni Os 'table'; ewaanji-bshigendman vti ic conj
              2s»0 '(CCNJ) you (sg) most like IN.'
982 • 18.9.1.2 Substantive Content Questions


    The following example illustrates the query of a particular manner, using the locational
interrogative aapiish, 'where,' along with the indefinite locational, nikeyiing, 'direction.'

   (137) Aapiish nikeyiing ge-ni-zhaawngoba?
         'Which way should we go?' (MC)

          Aapiish av inter 'where'; nikeyiing av 'direction'; ge-ni-zhaawngoba vai ic conjpret 21
          '(CCNJ) we (incl.) should go there' (ge-, future + preterit to indicate contingency)


    QUESTIONING ACTIONS. Verbal actions or events are usually questioned by means of the
interrogative adverb aanii(n) (also aanii-sh), 'how, in what way,' in conjunction with rela-
tive root /iN-/ or relative preverb zhi- /izhi-/. Because of the relative element, associated
verbs show initial change.

   (138) Aanii-sh naa gaa-z/wwebziyan. I 'What happened to you?' (SO5.39)
          Aanii-sh av 'how then'; gaa-zhiwebziyan vai ic conj 2s '(CCNJ) ANsg has such happen.'

   (139) A: Miinwaa dash shkwaa-gziinaagneying ka-taadmi. BiAaniish ge-zhi-taadyingl
         'A: After we wash the dishes, we'll play cards. B: What shall weplayT

          Miinwaa av 'next'; dash av 'then'; shkwaa-gziinaagneying vai conj 21 '(CONJ) after
          we (incl.) wash dishes'; ka-taadmi vai ind 21 'we (incl.) will play cards'; Aaniish av
          'how'; ge-zhi-taadying vai ic conj 21 '(CCNJ) we (incl.) will thus play cards.'

   (140) Aanii-sh endoodman zhoon'yaa? I 'What did you do with the money?' (FF2.19)
          Aanii-sh av 'how then'; endoodman vti ic conj 2s»0 '(CCNJ) you (SG) did to IN';
          zhoon'yaa ni Os 'money.'

  When questioning the complement of a sentential-complement verb, the comple-
ment-taking verb shows zhi- if its complement does.

   (141) Aanii-sh gaa-zhichgeyaan, aanii-sh ez/M-ndawendman ji-z/zichgeyaan?
         'What shall I do, what do you want me to do?' (AK11.17)

          Aanii-sh av 'how then'; gaa-zhichgeyaan vai ic conj Is '(CCNJ) which I may do';
          ezhi-ndawendman vti ic conj 2s»0 '(CCNJ) you SG thus want IN'; ji-zhichgeyaan vai
          conj Is '(CONJ) I will do.'
                                                     18.9.1.2 Substantive Content Questions • 983



    QUESTIONING How (MANNER QUESTIONS). Many common expressions in Nishnaabem-
win have the form of manner questions, because the verbs associated with them contain the
relative root /iN/, 'thus, so, in such a way, to(ward).' Manner questions are formed using the
word for 'how,' usually aaniish or aaniin, in conjunction with this relative root or its corre-
sponding preverb, zhi-. Initial change is obligatory, because of the presence of the relative
element.

   (142) Aaniish ez/wnkaazyan? \ 'What is your name?' (AM39.557)

          Aaniish av 'how'; ezhinkaazyan vai ic conj 2s '(CCNJ) you (SG) are named so.'


   (143) Aaniish gaa-Mdyan? \ 'What did you say?' (AM39.558) [n.b., verb: /iN+gido/]

          Aaniish av 'how'; gaa-kidyan vai ic conj 2s '(CCNJ) you (SG) speak so.'


   (144) Aanti-sh waa-naabjitooyan iw bgamaagan? \ 'How are you going to use that club?'

    QUESTIONING WHERE, WHERE TO, AND WHERE FROM. Questions of location that do not

motion toward a goal usually have the relative root /iN/ (preverb /izhi-/); questions of
motion from a source usually have relative root /ond/ (preverb /onji-/).
    The following examples illustrate static-location content questions.

    QUESTIONING WHY. The reason for an action or event can be queried by using the inter-

as tenseless complementizer e- plus nji-.

  INDIRECT QUESTIONS. Questions can serve as the complements of sentential-comple-
ment verbs.

   CONVENTIONAL EXPRESSIONS. Several common conventional expressions represent

   (191) Aanii! or Aaniishnaa! I 'Hi!'
          Aanii av 'how'; Aaniish av 'how'; naa av 'indeed.'

          Aanii av 'how'; giiyenh av 'evidently.'

    TOPIC SHIFT "How ABOUT" QUESTIONS. In a context in which several people or objects

          Maanpii av 'here'; toon vti imp 2s»0 '(you SG) put IN'; \viprn Os 'that'; mkak ni Os
          'box'; Maandaprn Os 'this'; dash av 'as for'; pabwin ni Os 'chair'; Maanpii av 'here';
          toon vti imp 2s»0 '(you SG) put IN'; gewii av 'also'; \viprn Os 'that'; Maaba prn 3sProx
          'this'; dash av 'as for'; zhiishiib-kik na SsProx 'kettle.'

   (194) Giin dashl Gdoo-nji-giigoonke na?
         'How about you! Have you gone fishing lately?' (MC5.6)

          Giinprnpers 2s 'you'; dash av 'as for'; Gdoo-nji-giigoonke vai ind 2s 'have you gone
          fishing'; na av 'yes/no questions.'

    ECHO QUESTIONS. In running conversation, Nishnaabemwin allows ECHO QUESTIONS
similar to those of English, in which the question word is not at the front of the sentence, but

         B: Wii-ggwejmag weneshl

18.9.2 Issuing Commands (Imperatives)

    Commands are marked by the presence of imperative verbal inflection. Commands may
be positive or negative. Negative commands are also called prohibitives. Command forms
exist for transitive animate (VTA), transitive inanimate (VTi), and animate intransitive verb
forms (VAI). Only person combinations that include second person have command forms, so
there are no inanimate intransitive (VII) command forms.
    The distinguishing feature of commands is that their verbs carry imperative inflection,
which is outlined in detail in chapters 5, 7 and 8. Here I will simply provide a few examples
of common constructions. As (196) and (197) show, goals can come either before or after the
imperative verb. There is a tendency for verbs to appear in initial position.

   (196) Nbiish mnahshin. I "Give me a drink of water.' (AM39.801)
          Nbiish ni Os 'water'; mnahshin vta imp 2s»ls '(you SG) give me a drink.'

   (197) Miizhgon naa iw wiiwkwaan. I "(Youpi) Give her/him her/his hat!' (AM39.800)
          Miizhgon vta imp 2p»3 '(you PL) give AN'; iwpra Os 'that'; wiiwkwaan ni Os 'hat.'

   (198) Zhngishnin doopwining. I "Lie down on the table.' (AM39.760)

          Zhngishnin vai imp 2s '(you SG) lie (prone)'; doopwining ni 0 loc 'on the table.'
992 • 18.9.2 Issuing Commands (Imperatives)


   Complement-taking verbs show their complements in the conjunct. Note that in both
cases below the complement follows.

   (199) Boontaan iw ggiibaadziyan. I 'Stop being so bad.' (AM39.722)
          Boontaan vai imp 2s '(you so) stop'; iwpm Os 'that'; ggiibaadziyan vai conj 2s '(CONJ)
          you (SG) be wicked.'

   (200) Zhichgen ge gii ezhchiged. I 'Do the way he does.' (AM39.727)
          Zhichgen vai imp 2s '(you SG) do so'; ge cnj 'as for'; giiprnpers 2s 'you'; ezhchiged vai
          ic conj part 3sProx '(CCNJ) as ANsg does so.'

   PROHIBITIVES (NEGATIVE COMMANDS). PROHIBITIVES use negative adverb gego (also
gegwa) and negative imperative inflection.

   (201) Gego wii gii bi-zhaafcen maampii. I 'Don't you come here.' (AM39.831)

          Gego av 'don't'; wii av 'then'; giipmpers 2s 'you'; bi-zhaaken vai imp neg 2s '(you SG)
          don't come here'; maampii av 'here.'

   (202) Gegwa zhichgefon iw. I 'Don't do that.' (AM39.832)

          Gegwa av 'don't'; zhichgeken vai imp neg 2s 'don't (you SG) do so'; iwpra Os 'that.'

   (203) Gego wii maa nmadbikegon, gzaagaasom; gawaakwaag zhaag; wiigwaaming
         zhaag.
         'Do (you pi.) not sit here; you are right in the sun. Go where it is shady. Go inside
         the house.' (AM39.836)

          Gego av 'don't'; wii av 'then'; maa av 'there'; nmadbikegon vai imp neg 2p '(you PL) do
          not sit'; gzaagaasom vai ind 2p 'you PL have the sun shining on you'; gawaakwaag vii
          conj 0 '(CONJ) IN is shady'; zhaag vai imp 2p '(you PL) go there'; wiigwaaming ni 0 loc
          'house (loc)'; zhaag vai imp 2p '(you PL) go there.'

   (204) Gego wii-gsaafcen giw nimoog; gaa wii gegoo gdaa-doodaagsiig.
         'Don't be afraid of those dogs; they won't do anything to you.' (AM39.843)

          Gego av 'don't'; wii-gsaaken vta imp neg 2s»3 '(you SG) don't fear AN'; giwprn SpProx
          'those'; nimoog na SpProx 'dogs'; gaa av 'not'; wii av 'then'; gegoo pm indefO
          'anything'; gdaa-doodaagsiig vta ind neg 3pProx»2s 'ANpl will not do to you (SG).'
                                                     18.9.2 Issuing Commands (Imperatives) • 993



  (205) Mii-sh gaa-zhi-giigdod aw, "Gego doodwish'kegon iw, gaawiin niin
        gwii-mji-doodoosnoonim.

         'And then he spoke thus, "Don't do that to me, I'm not going to harm you people.'

         Mii-sh av 'and then'; gaa-zhi-giigdod vai ic conj SsProx '(CCNJ) ANsg spoke'; awprn
         SsProx 'that'; Gego av 'don't'; doodwish'kegon vta imp 2p neg 'don't (you PL) do Y to

         vta ind ls»2p neg 'I do not want to do harm to you PL.' (AK14.14)


    DELAYED IMPERATIVES. There is a DELAYED MODE for positive imperatives, allowing
for the issue of a command to be carried out at a later time.

   (206) Baamaa waabang bi-zhaakan, mii dash da-wiijiiwnaan.

         'Come tomorrow, then I will go with you.' (AM39.828)

         Baamaa av 'later'; waabang av 'tomorrow'; bi-zhaakan vai imp del 2s '(you SG) come
         later'; mii av 'and'; dash av 'then'; da-wiijiiwnaan vta conj ls»2s '(CONJ) I will go with
         you SG.'


   (207) Baamaa biidookan. I 'Bring it later on.' (AM39.829)

         Baamaa av 'later'; biidookan vti imp del 2s»0s '(you SG) bring IN later.'


   (208) Baamaa go naa wiindmawshikan. I "Tell me about it later on.' (AM39.830)

         Baamaa av 'later'; wiindmawshikan vta imp del 2s»ls '(you SG) tell me about Y later.'

    HORTATIVES. HORTATIVES are commands that include the speaker, and only exist for
first person plural inclusives.

   (209) Aaw dash wiisnidaa. I 'Well, let us eat: (AM39.773)

         Aaw av 'okay'; dash av 'then'; wiisnidaa vai imp 21 'let's eat.'


   (210) Bekaayaadaa maampii. I 'Let us stay right here.' (AM39.769)

         Bekaa av 'hold on'; yaadaa vai imp 21 'let's remain'; maampii av 'here.'

   DIRECTIONALS WITH COMMANDS. Verbs inflected for imperative commonly have DIREC-
TIONAL PREVERBS.

   (211) Noozhshenh, fo'-zhaan maampii. I 'Come here, grandchild.' (AM39.717)
          Noozhshenh nad Is(SsProx) 'my grandchild'; bi-zhaan vai imp 2s '(you SG) come
          hither'; maampii av 'here.'

   (212) M'-maajiiwizh. I Take them away with you.' (SO2.11)

          Ni-maajiiwizh vta imp 2s»3 '(you SG) take AN away.'

   (213) M-gnawenmishnaang niigaan giizhgadoon!
         'Continue Thou to keep us in Thy care through the days ahead!' (AMI 1.10)

          Ni-gnawenmishnaang vta imp 2s»lp '(you SG) take care of us in the course of time';
          niigaan av 'in the future'; giizhgadoon ni Op 'days.'

   (214) Wfa-nda-gkenim aaniin naa endshiwaad giwi eyaajig wadi.
         'Go find out how many of them there are over there.' (SO 1.7)

          Wa-nda-gkenim vta imp 2s»3 'go and find out'; aaniin av 'how'; endshiwaad vai ic conj
          SpProx '(CCNJ) as many as ANpl were'; giwi/?rn SpProx 'those'; eyaajig vai ic conj part
          SpProx '(CCNJ) who ANpl were there'; wadi av 'there.'

   (215) Wewiibtaan, aazha kinoomaage-daabaan biijbizo. Wi-boozin!
         'Hurry up, the school bus is coming. Go get on!' (EM)

          Wewiibtaan vai imp 2s '(you SG) hurry'; aazha av 'now'; kinoomaage-daabaan na
          SsProx 'school bus'; biijbizo vai ind SsProx 'ANsg arrives motoring'; Wi-boozin vai imp
          2s '(you SG) go and get on board.'

   Wit- WITH COMMANDS. In the recorded materials of Andrew Medler, the FUTURE PRE-
VERB wii- appears to be used with commands. Many contemporary speakers reject such
usage. Rhodes (p.c.) suggests that WH in these cases is perhaps an emphatic mistakenly
identified as a preverb. The usage of wii- as a means of adding politeness seems possible,
though, and I include a couple of examples here for the record. See also (204), above.

   (216) Aambe ww-nishkaan. I 'Do please get up (from lying).'(AM39.716)
          Aambe av 'hey'; wii-nishkaan vai imp 2s '(you SG) please get up.'
                                                       18.9.2 Issuing Commands (Imperatives) • 995


   (217) Gwajiing ww-ni-zhaadaa. I 'Let us go out of doors.' (AM39.768)

         Gwajiing av 'outside'; wii-ni-zhaadaa vai imp 2p 'let us please go out.'

   FUTURE TENSE AS IMPERATIVE. Often the FUTURE TENSE is used with imperative force.

   (218) Gego nendken ji-gziibiigdooneyin. Gookooshag gaye gwii-shamaag, bkadewag.
         'Don't forget to brush your teeth. Feed the pigs too, they're hungry.' (SS)

         Gego av 'don't'; nendken vti imp neg 2s»0 'don't (you SG) forget IN';
         ji-gziibiigdooneyin vai conj 2s '(CONJ) you SG brush your teeth'; Gookooshag na
         3pProx 'pigs'; gaye av 'also'; gwii-shamaag via ind2s»3pProx 'you (SG) will feed ANpl'
         [future tense preverb, wii-]; bkadewag vai ind SpProx 'ANpl are hungry.'


   (219) Wewiibtaan. Pii giizhiitaayin, gga-biiskon'ye, mii dashji-bi-wiisniyin.
         'Hurry. When you're done, get dressed, then come and eat.' (ED)

         Wewiibtaan vai imp 2s 'hurry up'; Pii av 'when'; giizhiitaayin vai conj 2s '(CONJ) you
         (sg) finish'; gga-biiskon'ye vai ind 2s 'you (sg) will dress' [future tense preverb, ga-]; mii
         av 'and'; dash av 'then'; ji-bi-wiisniyin vai conj 2s '(CONJ) you (sg) should come and
         eat.'

    COMMANDS WITH MIL Imperative forms of verbs can appear with the discourse element
mii, especially when the command represents the outcome or result of some previously
mentioned situation.

   (220) Mii go maajaan ambe! I 'So go away immediately!' (SO3.37)
         Mii av 'so'; maajaan vai imp 2s '(you SG) go away'; ambe av 'immediately.'

   COMPLEX CONSTRUCTIONS WITH IMPERATIVES. Imperatives can appear in complex
clauses, having all the richness of statements and questions.

   (221) Ooke, wewebzidaa jibwaa-mdwesing tetaagan.
         'Okay, let's go for a swing before the bell rings.' (ED)

         Ooke av 'okay'; wewebzidaa vai imp 21 'let's swing'; jibwaa-mdwesing vii conj 0
         '(CONJ) before IN rings'; tetaagan ni Os 'bell.'
996 • 18.10 Coordination


   (222) Mil dash gaa-naad aw nmishoomis, "Gego nsaaken, mii go eta go iw gegoo
         ji-zhi-gshkihewzisig," mil gaa-naad aw nmishoomis niw jiiskiiwninwan.
         'And my grandfather said to him, "Don't kill it, but only something so it won't
         have power," that's what my grandfather said to the shaking tent shaman.'
         (AK11.20)

          Mil av 'and'; dash av 'then'; gaa-naad vta ic conj 3sProx»3obv '(CCNJ) ANsg said to
          ANobv'; avrprn SsProx 'that'; nmishoomis nod ls(3sProx) 'my grandfather'; Gego av
          'don't'; nsaaken vta imp 2s»3s neg 'don't you SG kill ANsg'; mii av 'but'; eta av 'only';
          iwprn Os 'that'; gegooprn indefO 'something'; ji-zhi-gshkihewzisig vai conj 3sProx neg
          '(CONJ) ANsg would not be powerful'; mii av 'that's'; gaa-naad vta ic conj
          3sProx»3obv '(CCNJ) ANsg said to ANobv'; aw prn 3sProx 'that'; nmishoomis nod
          ls(3sProx) 'my grandfather'; raw prn 3obv 'that/those'; jiiskiiwninwan na 3obv 'shaker.'


18.10 Coordination

    Coordination is the linking together of like elements, typically noun phrases, clauses,
and sentences. English most commonly coordinates words and phrases by means of the con-
junction and; Nishnaabemwin has coordinative adverbs, the most common being gye (or
ge), along with miinwaa.
    COORDINATION OF NOUN PHRASES. The basic structural features of coordination are
outlined in Chapter 12.3.6, page 568. Here I will mention a few additional aspects of nomi-
nal coordination.
    In coordination of noun phrases, it seems to be the case that when there is a difference of
grammatical gender in the noun phrases, the first one determines the gender of associated
verbs. In the following sentence, for example bkwezhigan, 'bread,' is animate in Rama dia-
lect, though doodooshaaboo, 'milk,' is inanimate. The associated verb ji-naanag, 'that I
fetch ANsg,' is a VTA, and is inflected for a singular goal.

   (223) Eni-naagshig nookmisban ngii-gwejimig daawewgamigongj/-zft««yaan
         ji-naanag bkwezhigan miinwaa doodooshaaboo.
         'In the evening, my late grandmother asked me to go to the store to fetch bread
         and milk.' (SS)

          Eni-naagshig vii ic conj 0 '(CCNJ) in time evening came on'; nookmisban napret
          ls(3sProx) 'my late grandmother'; ngii-gwejimig vta ind3sProx»ls 'ANsg asked me';
          daawewgamigong ni 0 loc 'to the store1; ji-zhaayaan vai conj Is '(CONJ) I go there';
          ji-naanag vta conj ls»3sProx '(CONJ) I get ANsg'; bkwezhigan na 3sProx 'bread';
          miinwaa av 'and'; doodooshaaboo ni Os 'milk.'
                                                                             18.10 Coordination* 997


    The following sentence shows the same strategy, that of having the verb inflect to agree
with only one of the coordinated noun phrases, in this case, again, the first one, naapaane,
'flour,' which is animate at Rama.

   (224) Pii e-dgoshnaan odi endaad, mii sa ekidod, "Maajaayok, wi-ndawaabndamok
         zasweminan, niin dash nga-giizhiitaahwaa naapaane giye mbisijigan"
         'When I arrived there where she lived, she said, "Take off, go and look for
         chokecherries, and I'll prepare the flour and yeast (i.e., make the crust)." (IS)

          Pii av 'when'; e-dgoshnaan vai ic conj Is '(CCNJ) when I arrived'; odi av 'there';
          endaad vai ic conj SsProx '(CCNJ) where ANsg lived'; mii av 'then'; ekidod vai ic conj
          SsProx '(CCNJ) ANsg said'; Maajaayok vai imp 2p '(you PL) set off;
          wi-ndawaabndamok vti imp 2p»0 '(you PL) go and look for IN'; zasweminan ni Op
          'chokecherries'; niinpmpers Is T; dash av 'however'; nga-giizhiitaahwaa vta ind
          ls»3sProx 'I will prepare ANsg'; naapaane na SsProx 'flour'; giye av 'and'; mbisijigan
          ni Os 'yeast.'


   A first person can be coordinated with a third person by means of first person exclusive
verb inflection.

   (225) Ngii-oo-giigookemi nwendaagan miina nwiijkiyenaa, Gchi-mookmaanking
         gii-bi-njibaa nwendaagan.
         'We went fishing, my relative and a friend of ours, my relative came from the
         U.S.' (RD)

          Ngii-oo-giigookemi vai ind Ip 'we (excl.) went and fished'; nwendaagan na ls(3sPwx)
          'my relative'; miina av 'and'; nwiijkiyenaa nad lp(3sProx) 'our (excl.) friend';
          Gchi-mookmaankiing ni 0 loc 'United States (loc)'; gii-bi-njibaa vai indSsProx 'ANsg
          came from there'; nwendaagan na Is(SsProx) 'my relative.'


   It is of course also possible to use an explicit pronoun niin in such cases, as in the fol-
lowing example, which occurs at the beginning of an anecdotal reminiscence.
998 • 18.10 Coordination


   (226) Mewnzha odi Rama, gnamaa go naa midaaswi gii-nsa-boonigizyaan, niin
         miinwaa niizh naanind kwezensag aapji nwii-zhooniyaakemin...

         'Long ago there in Rama, when I was perhaps ten years old, / and two other girls
         (we) really wanted to make some money.' (IS)

          Mewnzha av 'long ago'; odi av 'there'; gnamaa av 'perhaps'; midaaswi nm 'ten';
          gii-nsa-boonigizyaan vai conj Is '(CONJ) I was so many years old'; niinprnpers Is T;
          miinwaa av 'and'; niizh nm 'two'; naanind av 'some'; kwezensag na SpProx 'girls';
          aapji av 'really'; nwii-zhooniyaakemin vai ind Ip 'we (excl.) want to make money.'


   Constructions with ge, 'also, too' + PRONOUN can be used to coordinate.

   (227) Owedi ge gii gga-miijin, maanda dash ge nii nga-miijin waawan.

         'You may eat that egg, and I shall eat this one.' (AM39.174)

          Owedi ni dem Os 'that over there'; ge av 'as for'; gii prn pers 2s 'you'; gga-miijin vti ind
          2s»0s 'you will eat INsg'; maanda prn Os 'this'; dash av 'and'; ge av 'as for'; nii prn
          pers Is T; nga-miijin vti ind ls»0s 'I will eat INsg'; waawan ni Os 'egg.'


   Locative nouns can be coordinated with gye (go).

   (228) Gye go mtigoon wgiishkboodoonaawaan, mii dash daawewaad Oodenaang gye go
         maa Island.

         'Also they saw wood and sell it in Detroit or on the Island' (AMIS. 10)

          Gye av 'and'; mtigoon ni op 'wood (PL)'; wgiishkboodoonaawaan vti ind 3pProx»Op
          'ANpl ripsaw INpl'; mii av 'and'; dash av 'then'; daawewaad vai conj SpProx '(CONJ)
          ANpl sell Y'; Oodenaang ni 0 loc 'in Detroit' (lit., 'in town'); gye av 'or'; maa av 'there.'


   COORDINATION OF CLAUSES. Clauses may be coordinated with the conjunctive adverbs
gye and miinwaa, the former being more common.

   (229) Gaawaanh dash ngii-debnig gye gii-gwaabiignid.

         'With difficulty she got hold of me and drew me out of the water.' (AM4.5)

          Gaawaanh av 'barely'; dash av 'however'; ngii-debnig vta ind3sProx»ls 'ANsg
          reached me'; gye av 'and'; gii-gwaabiignid vta conj 3sProx»ls '(CONJ) ANsg fished me
          out of the water.'
                                                                           18.10 Coordination* 999



   (230) Mil odi gii-mkamaang iw zaaghigan, miinwaa baatiindoon miinan, giigoonyag ge
         yaawag maa zaaghigning.
         'And there we found this lake, and there were lots of berries, and there were also
         fish there at the lake.' (AK1.3)

          Mii av 'and'; odi av 'there'; gii-mkamaang vti conj lp '(CONJ) we (excl) found IN'; iw
          prn Os 'that'; zaaghigan ni Os 'lake'; miinwaa av 'and'; baatiindoon vii ind Op 'INpl are
          abundant'; miinan ni Op 'blueberries'; giigoonyag na SpProx 'fish (PL)'; ge av 'and';
          yaawag vai ind SpProx 'ANpl are there'; maa av 'there'; zaaghigning ni 0 loc 'in lake.'


   The following example shows coordinated PURPOSE CLAUSES.

   (231) Gchi-gzheb nga-maajaa \ji-wi-daaweyaan giw mskomnag miinwaa
        ji-yaamoonaan niw mkiznan].
         'Very early I'll go [to sell the raspberries and to buy you the shoes].' (AK3.12)

          Gchi-gzheb av 'very early in morning'; nga-maajaa vai ind Is 'I will leave';
          ji-wi-daaweyaan vai conj Is '(CONJ) I will go and sell Y'; giwpm SpProx 'those';
          mskomnag na SpProx 'raspberries'; miinwaa av 'and'; ji-yaamoonaan vta conj ls»2s
           '(CONJ) I will get for you'; niw prn Op 'those'; mkiznan ni Op 'shoes.'


    Often clauses are put in sequence by means of alternations between independent and
conjunct order inflection of their verbs, as in sentence (232), or by inflecting the MAIN verb
as conjunct, as in (233).


   (232) Mii dash gii-giiwebtooyaan, [gii-wiindmawag]CONJ aw ngashi.
         'Then I ran home and told my mother about it.' (AM3.5)

          Mii av 'and'; dash av 'then'; gii-giiwebtooyaan vai conj Is '(CONJ) when I'd run
          home'; gii-wiindmawag vta conj ls»3sProx '(CONJ) I told ANsg'; aw prn SsProx 'that';
          ngashi nad Is(SsProx) 'my mother.'


    In other cases, there is no explicit marker of coordination.This is especially true of verbs
in construction with the verb maajaa, 'set off VAI, which often functions serially, as in the
following example.
1000 • 18.10 Coordination


   (233) Mil dash gii-maajaayaang (_) gii-zhaayaang widi school.

         Then we set out and went to the school.' (AM8.12)

          Mii av 'and'; dash av 'then'; gii-maajaayaang vai conj Ip '(CONJ) we (excl) left';
          gii-zhaayaang vai conj Ip '(CONJ) we (excl) went there'; widi av 'over there.'


   (234) Gaa maamda wii-wiijiiwaad zaasbaakdoken'jin, aaniish naa aakzi sa (_) niinmizi,
         (_) skanzi.

         'He couldn't go with those who made sugar, as he was so sick, so weak and
         gaunt.' (SO4.6)

         Gaa av 'not'; maamda av 'able'; wii-wiijiiwaad vta conj 3sProx»3obv '(CONJ) ANsg
         will accompany ANobv'; zaasbaakdoken'jin vai ic conj part 3obv '(CCNJ) those
         (ANobv) who were making sugar'; aaniish av 'because'; aakzi vai indSsProx 'ANsg is
         ill'; niinmizi vai indSsProx 'ANsg is weak'; skanzi vai indSsProx 'ANsg is gaunt.'


    A sentence can show a relationship with a previous sentence by beginning with gye, typ-
ically in combination with particle go, or with miinwaa.

   (235) Gye go mii gii-miin'gooyaang rooms waa-dnizyaang.

         'And then we were given rooms in which we were to stay.' (AM8.14)

         Gye av 'and'; mii av 'then'; gii-miin'gooyaang vta conjx»lp 'we (excl) were given';
         waa-dnizyaang vai conj Ip '(CCNJ) we (excl) will stay there.'


   (236) Gye go mii gii-aanskonyeyaang, gye go mii gii-miingooyaang niw rooms
         waa-dnizyaang.

        'And then we changed our clothes and we were given the rooms in which we
        were to stay.' (AM9.14)


         Gye av 'and'; mii av 'then'; gii-aanskonyeyaang vai conj Ip '(CONJ) we (excl)
         changed clothes'; gye av 'and'; mii av 'and'; gii-miin'gooyaang vta conj x»lp 'we
         (excl) were given'; niwprn Op 'those'; waa-dnizyaang vai conj Ip '(CCNJ) we (excl)
         will stay there.'
                                                                          18.11 Disjunction* 1001



   (237) Miinwaa wgii-giishpnadoon iw bagoowyaan ji-wzhitmaagooyaan iw
         wshki-goodaas.
         "And she bought some material so that a new dress could be made for me.'
         (AK3.13)

          Miinwaa av 'and'; wgii-giishpnadoon vti ind3sProx»Os 'ANsg bought INsg'; iv/prn Os
          'that'; bagoowyaan ni Os 'cloth'; ji-wzhitmaagooyaan vta conjx»l '(CONJ) Y will be
          made for me'; iwprn Os 'that'; wshki-goodaas ni Os 'new dress.'


  When an action is the logical consequence or result of another, they may be linked by
means of dash, 'then,' in the clause of the second action.

   (238) Mtigoon ngii-biindgadoonan, niidgemaagan dash gii-boodwe.
         'I brought the wood inside, (and) then my wife made a fire.' (AM39.177)

          Mtigoon ni op 'wood (PL)'; ngii-biindgadoonan vti ind ls»0p 'I brought INpl inside';
          niidgemaagan nad Is(SsProx) 'my spouse'; dash av 'then'; gii-boodwe vai ind 3sProx
          'ANsg made fire.'


   (239) Ngii-bgijwebnaan, gii-baashksin dash iw waawan.

         'I dropped it, and that egg broke.' (AM39.382)

          Ngii-bgijwebnaan vti ind ls»0s 'I dropped INsg'; gii-baashksin vii ind Os 'INsg became
          broken'; dash av 'then'; iwprn Os 'that'; waawan ni Os 'egg.'


   (240) Niikaanenh ngii-gaandhog, mii dash gii-bkobiiseyaan.

         'My brother gave me a push, and then I fell into the water.' (AM39.482)

          Niikaanenh nad ls(3sProx) 'my brother'; ngii-gaandhog vta ind 3sProx»ls 'ANsg
          pushed me'; mii av 'and'; dash av 'then'; gii-bkobiiseyaan vai conj Is '(CONJ) I fell
          into water.'


18.11 Disjunction

   Disjunction is the juxtaposing of things in such a way as to present them as alternatives.
Disjunction is typically expressed by means of the adverb maage, 'or.' Both noun phrases
and clauses can be disjunctively related with maage.
1002 • 18.12 Expressing Feelings and Attitudes


   (241) Biidoon waawnoon. Nga-zaasaanan. Bezhig na              aage niizh?
         'Bring the eggs. I'll fry them. One or two?' (IT)

          Biidoon vti imp 2s»0 'bring (you SG) IN'; waawnoon ni Op 'eggs'; Nga-zaasaanan vti
          ind ls»0p 'I will fry INpl'; Bezhig nm 'one'; na av 'yes/no ques'; maage av 'or'; niizh
          nm 'two.'

   (242) Wegnesh washme e-gzigong, maanda maage oodi wi?
         'Which box is heavier, this one or that one?' (MC2.7)

          Wegneshprn inter 0 'what'; washme av 'more'; e-gzigong vii ic conj 0 '(CCNJ) IN is
          heavy'; maanda prn Os 'this'; maage av 'or'; oodi av 'there'; wipra Os 'that.'

   (243) A: Gbe-dbik gii-migi aw gdayensim. Aaniin dash?
         B: Ngikendziin. Gnamaa go naa wiya gii-bi-zhaadog maage gii-bkadedog.
         'A: Your little dog barked all night. Why? B: I don't know. Maybe someone came
         or maybe it was hungry.'

          Gbe-dbik av 'all night'; gii-migi vai ind SsProx 'ANsg barked'; aw prn SsProx 'that';
          gdayensim nod 2s(3sProx) 'your (SG) little dog'; Aaniin av 'how'; dash av 'then';
          Ngikendziin vti ind neg ls»0s 'I don't know INsg'; Gnamaa av 'perhaps'; wiya prn indef
          3 'someone'; gii-bi-zhaadog vai ind dub SsProx 'ANsg might have come hither'; maage
          av 'or'; gii-bkadedog vai ind dub 3sProx 'ANsg maybe was hungry.'

   (244) Gaawiin na bdakjihgan gwii-miizhsii? Maage nninjiinsan nga-nakaaznan?
         'Aren't you going to give me a fork? Or shall I use my fingers?' (IT)

          Gaawiin av 'not'; na av 'yes/no question'; bdakjihgan ni Os 'fork'; gwii-miizhsii vta ind
          neg 2s»ls 'you (SG) will not give me'; Maage av 'or'; nninjiinsan nid ls(0p) 'my
          fingers'; nga-nakaaznan vaio ind ls»0p 'I will use INpl.'

18.12 Expressing Feelings and Attitudes

   Nishnaabemwin is an extremely expressive language, replete with many expressions
designed to communicate strong feelings. For example, the word esnaa is often used in this
way.
                                                  18.12 Expressing Feelings and Attitudes • 1003



(245) Oonh... emaa ngwetaani-gtim nookmis, zaam gzhide.

      'Oh, I am so lazy, grandma, it's too hot!' (DP)

       Oonh av 'oh'; esnaa av 'really'; ngwetaani-gtim vai ind Is 'I am lazy'; nookmis nad
       ls(3sProx) 'my grandmother'; zaam av 'too'; gzhide vii ind Os 'it is hot weather.'


(246) Esnaa mno-giizhgad. I 'It's such a nice day.' (BP)

       Esnaa av 'really'; mno-giizhgad vii ind Os 'INsg is a nice day.'


(247) A: Waawan nigo gdaa-zaasgokwaadmaw? Miinwaa doodooshaaboo ngodnaagaans
      nigwa gdaa-ziignamaw? B: Esnaa maaba gwiizhenzhish I Aaniish mnik
      waawnoon ge-zaasgokwaadmoonaanh?
      A: 'Could you fry me an egg? And also pour me a glass of milk?'
      B: 'Gee, this little boy! How many eggs do you want me to fry for you?' (IT)

       Waawan ni Os 'egg'; nigo av 'yes/no question'; gdaa-zaasgokwaadmaw vta ind ls»2s
       'should I fry Y for you (SG)'; Miinwaa av 'and'; doodooshaaboo ni Os 'milk';
       ngodnaagaans ni meas 0 'one cup'; nigwa av 'yes/no question'; gdaa-ziignamaw vta
       ind ls»2s 'should I pour Y for you (SG)'; Esnaa av 'really'; maaba prn SsProx 'this';
       gwiizhenzhish napej SsProx 'bad boy'; Aaniish av 'how'; mnik av 'many'; waawnoon
       ni Op 'eggs'; ge-zaasgokwaadmoonaanh vta ic conj ls»2s '(CCNJ) I will fry Y for you
       (SG).'


(248) A: Aapji go nbakde. Gaawiin ndoonji-wiisnisii eko-dgoshnaanh maampii
      kinoomaagegamgong.
      B: Esnaa giishaach\ Gaa na gegoo ggii-yaanziin zhoonyaans wii-wiisniyin?

      A: 'I'm really hungry. I haven't eaten since I got here to school.'
      B: 'That's too bad! Didn't you have money that you could eat with?' (MO)

       Aapji av 'really'; nbakde vai ind Is 'I am hungry'; Gaawiin av 'not'; ndoonji-wiisnisii
       vai ind neg Is 'I did not eat'; eko-dgoshnaanh vai ic conj Is '(CCNJ) since I arrived';
       maampii av 'here'; kinoomaagegamgong ni 0 loc 'at school'; Esnaa av 'really';
       giishaach av.'too bad'; Gaa av 'not'; na av 'yes/no question'; gegoo prn indefO 'any';
       ggii-yaanziin vti ind neg 2s»0s 'you (SG) did not have INsg'; zhoonyaans ni Os 'money';
       wii-wiisniyin vai conj 2s '(CONJ) you (SG) could eat.'


Many other expressive adverbs exist as well.
1004 • 18.13 Baby Talk and Verbs of Compassion


   (249) Aa, Otaayaal Niibaakhom, ggii-mzhikooz.

         'Oh! Nibakom! So you were wounded!' (SO6.48)

          Aa av 'well'; Otaayaa av 'oh my'; Niibaakhom na SsProx 'Niibaakhom';
          ggii-mzhikooz vai ind 2s 'you (SG) were wounded.'


   (250) Otaahaa, gii-nimgaashin giiwenh wa nini.
         'Wow! That man had left a trail along the way.' (SO 1.35)

          Otaahaa av 'oh my!'; gii-nimgaashin vai ind SsProx 'ANsg went away leaving a trail';
          giiwenh av 'allegedly'; wapra SsProx 'that'; nini na SsProx 'man.'


   (251) Otaahaal Mil giiwenh zhaazhi go aabta-giigoonywid wa!

         'Goodness! He is already half-fish!' (SO3.29)

          'that one.'


18.13 Baby Talk and Verbs of Compassion

   When talking to babies, the suffix /-ishi/ can be added to a verb to produce a diminutive
verb, as in the following example, where /-ishi/ is added to waawnigaazi, 'look cute.' The
/z/of the verb palatalizes to/zh/(IPA/3/).

   (252) Gesnaa waawninaagzhishibiibiishens! I 'What a cute little baby!'
          Gesnaa av 'exceedingly'; waawninaagzhishi vai dim ind SsProx 'little ANsg looks cute';
          biibiishens na dim SsProx 'little baby.'

    In other cases, endearment is signalled by a weakening of /ch/ (IPA /t J7) to /sh/ (IPA /J7)
in gaachiinyi, 'be small,' which becomes gaashiinyi.

   (253) Zaam gsha go naa gaashiinyi! I 'Oh my, slhe's just too little!'
          Zaam av 'too'; gsha av emphatic particle; go naa av emphatic particles; gaashiinyi
          vai ind SsProx 'ANsg is small.'

18.14 Additional Reading

Glossary




   «»            see ANGLE BRACKETS.

   []            see SQUARE BRACKETS.

  //             see SLASHES.

ABSOLUTIVE       See ERGATIVE.

ABSTRACT        Designating an analysis that seeks to capture broad linguistic gener-
                alizations, traditionally by positing UNDERLYING FORMS and a bat-
                tery of RULES to get from the underlying forms to actually
                pronounced forms, as opposed to an analysis that is more superficial
                but also more specific. For example, an abstract analysis of ANIMATE
                NOUN PLURAL formation posits a single form for the plural suffix,
                /-ag/, which interacts PHONOLOGICALLY with NOUN STEMS to create
                the variant forms that noun plurals show. A less abstract analysis
                simply asserts that the noun plural SUFFIX can have variable forms
                such as /-ag/, /-g/, /-wag/, /-oog/ and /-iig/. Both approaches have
                their value in the teaching of grammar.

ABSTRACT NOUN A NOUN referring to a concept rather than a physical object. Most
              abstract nouns in Nishnaabemwin are DERIVED from VERBS. Exam-
              ple: naadmaagewin, 'help,' and goopesewin, '[religious] confes-
              sion.'
                                                                      ADJUNCT CLAUSE •      1007



ABSTRACT STEM A linguistically determined form of a NOUN or VERB that allows for
SHAPE         its different INFLECTIONAL forms to be produced relatively straight-
              forwardly by LINGUISTIC RULES. For example, the abstract stem
              shape of the noun nini, 'man,' is /ininiw/ (or /aniniw/ for some
              speakers). This stem has a final /w/ does not appear in the simple
              SINGULAR form, but is present in the PLURAL ninwag; its absence in
              the singular can be explained by a very general rule that deletes
              WORD-FINAL /w/ and lyl.

ACTIVE VOICE     Designating a TRANSITIVE VERB form which casts the SEMANTIC
                 AGENT or EXPEREENCER in the semantic MACROROLE of ACTOR.
                 Example: Gii-ni-waabmaan Nenbozh bnensan, 'Nenabush saw
                 some birds.' Here Nenabush has the SEMANTIC ROLE of EXPERI-
                 ENCER, and is cast as the ACTOR (MACROROLE) in the verbal PREDI-
                 CATION. The birds have the semantic role of PATIENT, and are cast in
                 the MACROROLE of GOAL. Compare PASSIVE VOICE.

ACTOR            In a TRANSITIVE PREDICATION, the SEMANTIC MACROROLE associ-
                 ated with the initiator of an action, the causer of the action, or the
                 experiencer of a thought or sensation. For example, in the predica-
                 tion, Mooz nwaabmaa, 'I see a moose,' the actor is FIRST PERSON
                 SINGULAR, translated as 'I.' The ACTOR MACROROLE often corre-
                 sponds to the English SUBJECT of ACTIVE VOICE sentences. Compare
                 GOAL.

ADJECTIVE        In English, a word associated with a NOUN which expresses some
                 attribute of the noun, e.g., in the phrase red rose, red is an adjective
                 modifying the noun rose. In Nishnaabemwin, descriptive concepts
                 are expressed by means of DESCRIPTIVE VERBS and PRENOUNS, for
                 example, mskwaa(mgad), TNsg is red' (VII), and msko-disgan, 'red
                 paint' (Nl).

ADJUNCT          Specifying a SUBORDINATE (DEPENDENT) CLAUSE that is not filling a
CLAUSE           basic SEMANTIC ROLE requirement of an associated verb (that is, is
                 not a COMPLEMENT), but instead provides auxiliary information such
                 as the time, manner, or location of the action or event of the main
                 verb. Adjunct clauses are generally ADVERBIAL in nature. Example:
                 Ngizhiibii gaa-namid, T am itching where ANsg bit me.' Here
                 gaa-namid, 'where ANsg bit me,' specifies a location relevant to the
                 MAIN VERB, ngizhiibii, 'I am itching.' Adjunct clauses almost always
                 have verbs INFLECTED for CONJUNCT ORDER. Compare COMPLE-
                 MENT CLAUSE.
1008   • ADVERB



ADVERB            A word that modifies a VERB, clause, sentence, or another adverb,
                  usually by indicating aspects of location, time, degree, or MANNER.
                  For example, noopming, 'inland, in the bush,' wiiba, 'right away,'
                  jiinaago, 'yesterday,' and aapji, 'really.' In the sentence Naamkamig
                  nji-nakii, ANsg works underground,' the term naamkatnig, 'under-
                  ground" is an adverb, though it corresponds to a NOUN in English.

AFFIX             A general term to refer to a PREFIX or a SUFFIX that is attached to a
                  STEM. For example, in nwiisnimi, 'we (excl.) are eating, both /ni-/,
                  FIRST PERSON (INDEPENDENT ORDER), and /-mi/, FIRST PERSON PLU-
                  RAL (INDEPENDENT ORDER), are affixes, the former a prefix and the
                  latter a suffix. See PREFIX, SUFFIX, STEM.

AFFIXATION        The process of attaching a PREFIX or SUFFIX to a STEM.

AFFIXED           Attached as a PREFIX or SUFFIX to a STEM.

AFFRICATE         A CONSONANT sound made by momentarily stopping the flow of air
                  somewhere in the vocal tract, and then releasing it with a short
                  period of turbulence (producing a FRICATIVE). The affricates of
                  Nishnaabemwin are /ds/ «j» and /tJV «ch». Compare STOP, FRICA-
                  TIVE, NASAL, GLIDE.

AGENT             The willful, conscious initiator of an action or event. Usually cast in
                  the MACROROLE of ACTOR in a TRANSITIVE PREDICATION, and as the
                  S-ROLE (SUBJECT) of an INTRANSITIVE. For example, in
                  baashkzwaad, 'shoot AN,' the AGENT is the shooter, as it is in
                  baashkzige, 'do shooting.' See SEMANTIC ROLE, FORCE.

AGE-STRATIFIED Designating speech forms that show variation on the basis of age.
               For example, among Nishnaabemwin speakers, older speakers tend
               to have richer vocabularies and grammatical structures than younger
               speakers, due in part to language attrition.

AGREE             See AGREEMENT.
                                                               ALVEOLAR RIDGE •      1009



AGREEMENT    Cross-indexing between parts of speech for GRAMMATICAL FEA-
             TURES. For example, in the phrase giw ninwag, 'those men,' the
             DEMONSTRATIVE PRONOUN giw reflects ANIMATE PLURAL PROXI-
             MATE (foregrounded) GRAMMATICAL features. The NOUN that this
             DEMONSTRATIVE is associated with, ninwag, is also ANIMATE PLU-
             RAL PROXIMATE. The PRONOUN thus AGREES (has the same) GRAM-
             MATICAL FEATURES as the NOUN that it is modifying.

Ai VERB      An intransitive verb having an animate subject. In this work, usually
             abbreviated VAI.

ALGONQUIAN   The LANGUAGE FAMILY to which Nishnaabemwin belongs. The
             Algonquian family includes the languages Cree, Delaware, Micmac,
             Blackfoot, Cheyenne, Fox, Menominee, Potawatomi, Naskapi, and
             many others.

ALGONQUIN    A DIALECT of Anishinaabemowin (Ojibwe) spoken in Quebec, and
             the adjacent area of Eastern Ontario.

ALLOMORPHS   The variant forms that a MORPHEME has. For example, /-ag/, /-iig/,
             /-oog/ and /-g/ can be said to be allomorphs of the ANIMATE PLURAL
             SUFFIX appearing on NOUNS; and /miizh/ and /miin/ are allomorphs
             of the VTA VERB miinaad, 'give Y to AN.'

ALLOPHONES   The variant pronunciations that a given PHONEME can have in a par-
             ticular language. For example, two of the allophones of/g/ in Nish-
             naabemwin are [g] and [k], the latter being the pronunciation of/g/
             at the end of a word or before a VOICELESS CONSONANT. For exam-
             ple, in the word waagosh, 'fox,' the phoneme /g/ has the allophone
             [g], as opposed to its pronunciation in waagshan, 'fox (obv.),' where
             it shows the allophone [k].

ALLOPHONY    Pertaining to ALLOPHONES.

ALVEOLAR     Referring to a CONSONANT sound pronounced by putting the tongue
             tip on the bony ridge behind the upper front teeth. For example /s/,
             /n/ and /d/ as pronounced by many Nishnaabemwin speakers.

ALVEOLAR     The bony ridge behind the upper front teeth, where the tongue tip is
RIDGE        located for many speakers in articulating the CONSONANTS /d/, /t/,
             /z/, /s/, and /n/.
1010 • ALVEOPALATAL


ALVEOPALATAL    Of CONSONANTS, referring to those made in the region between the
                ALVEOLAR RIDGE and the HARD PALATE, /zh/ and /sh/.

ANALYTIC        Characterizing an approach to language that proceeds by breaking
                down units of language into their component parts. For example, the
                verb form nwaabmignaanig, 'ANpl see us (excl.)' can be analyzed
                into the component MORPHEMES /ni+waabam+igw+naan+igw/.
                Compare SYNTHETIC.

ANGLE BRACK-    The characters « and », used in the grammar to identify letters as
ETS             opposed to sounds, for example, «b» represents the written letter
                that begins the words bean and boodwe.

ANIMATE         One of two GRAMMATICAL GENDERS, or CLASSES OF NOUNS, the
                other being INANIMATE. Membership in the animate grammatical
                class is largely based on meanings, in that living things, including
                humans, animals, spirits, trees, and most plants are included in the
                animate classes of nouns. See also INANIMATE.

ANISHINAABE-    The self-designation of the language group called in English Ojibwe
MOWIN           (also Ojibwa, Ojibway).

ANTECEDENT      In grammar, usually referring to a NOUN PHRASE or other expression
                that is co-referenced with and precedes another. In normal conversa-
                tion, things being talked about have to be identified; once they are
                identified, they can be referred to with general PRONOUNS and VER-
                BAL INFLECTIONS. The term antecedent is used to identify some
                more explicit identifier to which a subsequent PRONOUN or INFLEC-
                TION is associated in order to have its reference properly identified.
                So, for example, a storyteller may identify a character at the begin-
                ning of a story as bezhig nini, 'a certain man,' and afterwards use
                only VERBAL INFLECTIONS to refer to the same individual. In order
                to properly identify who the verbal inflections are referring to, how-
                ever, there must be recourse to the original, ANTECEDENT NOUN
                PHRASE, bezhig nini.
                                                                       ARBITRARY • 1011



ANTIPASSIVE   Designating a process that reduces the number of SEMANTIC ROLES
              of a VERB by taking away the GOAL MACROROLE. So a TRANSITIVE
              VERB becomes INTRANSITIVE, since the GOAL can no longer be fully
              specified. Called ANTIPASSIVE because it has the opposite effect of
              the PASSIVE, which promotes the goal to S-ROLE (SUBJECT) status.
              Examples: AI suffix /-(i)ge/, as in baashkizge, 'do shooting,'; AI suf-
              fix /-iwe/, as in dknowe, 'hold (people), make an arrest.'

APPLICATIVE   A general term referring to the various SEMANTIC ROLES of a VERB
              that are not AGENTS, EXPERIENCERS or PATIENTS, but especially
              RECIPIENTS and BENEFACTIVES. While the patient is often the default
              SEMANTIC ROLE to be associated with the GOAL, many languages
              have rules which allow the "promotion" of human applicatives to the
              (MACROROLE) status of GOAL, as in English, / gave Myrna a book,
              where the RECIPIENT Myrna is in the position of a DIRECT OBJECT
              (the English equivalent of a goal). In Nishnaabemwin promotion of
              human APPLICATIVES is largely obligatory, so transfer verbs are
              almost always VTA if a RECIPIENT is mentioned.

APPLICATIVE   To promote an APPLICATIVE to the MACROROLE of GOAL. See APPLI-
ADVANCEMENT   CATIVE.


APPOSITIVE    A grammatical construction involving two nominals used together to
              refer to the same entity, such as wiinwaa Nishnaabeg, 'they, the
              Indians.'

ARBITRARY     A linguistic relationship between form and meaning is arbitrary if
              the relationship is based on convention rather than on any formal
              (iconic) correspondence between the objects. The relationship
              between the pronunciation and meaning of words is mostly arbitrary
              in human language. For example, the words mik and beaver bear no
              principled or structured relationship to the animal, so that one can-
              not say that one word is in some way a more "natural" way to desig-
              nate it. However, the name gaagaagi for 'crow' or 'raven' is not
              arbitrary, because the name in some way actually resembles a fea-
              ture of the object, namely, the sound it makes.
1012 • ARGUMENT



ARGUMENT          Designating any NOMINAL or PRONOMINAL element filling the
                  SEMANTIC ROLES associated with a verb or relative element. For
                  example, the expression Wiiyaas gii- miijin Zhaabdiis, 'John ate
                  meat,' has two arguments, wiiyaas, 'meat,' and Zhaabdiis, 'John.'
                  This is an especially tricky linguistic term, because it has a com-
                  pletely unrelated meaning in normal language use.

ASPECT            Referring to the way a verbal action, event, or state is cast— in Nish-
                  naabemwin, especially with reference to its beginning or ending.
                  Specific PREVERBS and VERBS exist in the language for focussing on
                  the beginning and end of an event, such as maajtaa and maajii- 'start
                  (to)...' There are also special MODES, the PRETERIT and PRETERIT
                  DUBITATIVE, to make reference to completed action. See MODE.

ASSIMILATION      The process of one sound becoming like another either in whole or
                  in part. For example, the sound /g/ in waagosh, 'fox,' DEVOICES to
                  [k] in the word waagshag, 'foxes,' due its being adjacent to a voice-
                  less sound, /sh/ (IPA /S/).

ASPIRATION        A puff of air accompanying the release of some VOICELESS STOP
                  CONSONANTS, as with the /p/ in English pit.

BACK              Characterizing a VOWEL produced with the tongue placed relatively
                  far back in the mouth. The back vowels of Nishnaabemwin are /a/,
                  /aa/, /o/, and /oo/. Compare FRONT.

BACKGROUND        To make less prominent. In Nishnaabemwin, backgrounded NOMI-
                  NALS are often made OBVIATIVE. An element can also be back-
                  grounded by INCORPORATING it. See especially OBVIATIVE.

BACKNESS          A way by which vowels are classified, relating to how different vow-
                  els are pronounced, involving the degree to which the tongue body is
                  moved forward or back in the mouth to pronounce the vowel. See
                  FRONT, MID, BACK.

BASE              In morphology, a working term to refer to the form that a given mor-
                  phological operation applies to, such as PREFIXATION or INITIAL
                  CHANGE. For example, the plural of a noun is formed by adding a
                  suffix to the singular, which thus serves as the base for the operation
                  of plural suffixation. See LEXEME, MORPHOSYNTACTIC WORD, STEM.
                                                                   BODY PART TERM •      1013



BASE FIVE      A counting system that goes to five and then "starts over," treating
               six as five plus one. There are vestiges of such a system in Nishnaa-
               bemwin. Another term for this is quintenary. See BASE TEN.

BASE FORM      A form of a word in which all MORPHEMES are specified in their
               basic shapes. For example, the base form of dgoshnoog, 'they are
               leaving,' is /dagoshin+w+ag/, which then undergoes PHONOLOGICAL
               and MORPHOLOGICAL RULES to derive the pronounced form.

BASE TEN       A counting system that goes to ten and then "starts over," treating
               eleven as ten plus one. This is the basic system presently in effect in
               Nishnaabemwin and in English, though there is evidence in Nish-
               naabemwin that it long ago also had a BASE FIVE system.

BASIC WORD     see STEM

BENEFACTIVE    An expression or construction involving the undertaking of an action
               for the benefit of another, such as zhitmaw, 'make something for s.o.'
               (VTA). In Nishnaabemwin all benefactive verbs are VTA.

BENEFICIARY    A SEMANTIC ROLE, that of the person(s) benefitting from the actions
               of another, the one for whom something is done. Since beneficiaries
               are almost always human, and Nishnaabemwin grammar gives
               prominence to humans, beneficiaries are usually cast in the MAC-
               ROROLE Of GOAL.

BILABIAL       Of CONSONANT sounds, articulated by putting the lips together. In
               Nishnaabemwin, the bilabial consonants are /b/, /p/, /m/, and /w/.

BILINGUALISM   A situation in which individuals speak more than one language.
               Change to a language often comes from the influence of languages
               through bilingualism. Most Nishnaabemwin speakers are bilingual,
               speaking English and Nishnaabemwin. This results in much BOR-
               ROWING from English.

BODY PART      A noun used to specify a part of the body, such as nkaad, 'my leg,'
TERM           or nzid, 'my foot.' Body part terms are almost all DEPENDENT NOUNS
               in Nishnaabemwin. They also have MEDIAL forms that appear in
               body part descriptive verbs, such as mnogaade, 'have nice legs'
               (VAI), with medial /-gaad-/, 'leg,' and other verbs.
1014 • BORROWING



BORROWING          The process in which one language takes an item of vocabulary from
                   another language, to use as its own word. For example, English has
                   borrowed the words moose and moccasin from some Algonquian
                   language. Conversely, Nishnaabemwin has borrowed the word truck
                   from English. Often words borrowed from English in Nishnaabem-
                   win retain their English spelling, as with «truck». They may also
                   become more or less adapted to the pronunciation patterns of the
                   host language, as in Zhaabdiis, a name borrowed into Nishnaabem-
                   win from French, Jean Baptiste. An alternative to borrowing is
                   COINING.

CARDINAL           A number that represents a specific amount as opposed to a ranking,
NUMBER             such as bezhig, 'one,' niizh, 'two,' and nswi, 'three.' Compare ORDI-
                   NAL NUMBER.

CAUSATIVE          A word or expression which indicates an ACTOR who makes a GOAL
                   do something, or causes a goal to undergo some process or event.
                   For example, the VTA VERB nbeh, 'put AN to bed,' is CAUSATIVE,
                   and has a structure meaning, 'make AN sleep.' One productive way
                   that causatives are formed in Nishnaabemwin is by adding TA FINAL
                   /-h/ to a VAI verb stem.

CENTRAL            Used to refer to the ALGONQUIAN languages which are not PLAINS,
ALGONQUIAN         and not EASTERN, that is, those which are spoken, or were histori-
                   cally spoken, in the vicinity of the Great Lakes, and in the Sub-Arc-
                   tic. Nishnaabemwin is a Central Algonquian language.

CHAINING           Also called DIALECT CHAINING. The process of slow language varia-
                   tion from one community to the next, creating close similarity
                   between adjacent communities, but increasing divergence as com-
                   munities are farther apart. A very common phenomenon in aborigi-
                   nal languages.

CHANGED            A VERB form showing INITIAL CHANGE (and CONJUNCT INFLECTION,
CONJUNCT           but initial change only applies to conjuncts). For example, the sec-
                   ond verb (with gaa-) in Pii dash gii-bzigwiiyaan,
                   gaa-zhi-gnabseyaang, '(but) when I stood up, we capsized,' is in
                   CHANGED CONJUNCT and the first, PLAIN CONJUNCT. Compare PLAIN
                   CONJUNCT.
                                                                                COALESCE • 1015



CHIPPEWA         L A dialect of ANISHINAABEMOWIN (Ojibwe) presently spoken in
                 Minnesota and adjacent areas. 2. Referring to non-Odawa dialects of
                 Anishinaabemowin historically spoken in Michigan. Many
                 Chippewa people relocated to Canada in the nineteenth century, and
                 constitute one of the sub-dialects of Nishnaabemwin.

CITATION FORM    Of all the many INFLECTIONS that a NOUN or VERB can have, the one
                 listed as a main entry in the dictionary is called its citation form. So,
                 for example, most NOUNS are listed in their FIRST PERSON SINGULAR
                 PROXIMATE form, such as kwe, 'woman,' as opposed to a PLURAL,
                 kwewag, or an OBVIATIVE, kwewan.

CLASSES OF       See NOUN CLASSES.
NOUNS

CLASSIFICA-      A MEDIAL that is a CLASSIFIER, such as /-eg-/ in dkwegad, 'be short
TORY MEDIAL      (of cloth) (VII).'

CLASSIFICA-  A number with a classifier attached, as in bezhgwaabik, 'one (metal)
TORY NUMERAL object,' which has classifier /aabik/ attached to bezhig, 'one.'

CLASSIFIER       A linguistic element that classifies NOUNS into SEMANTIC categories.
                 In Nishnaabemwin, there are several classifiers, such as /aabiig/,
