                 'stringlike,' as in dkwaabiigad, 'be short (of strings).' Other classifi-
                 ers include /aabik/, 'inorganic solid,' /aatig/, 'organic solid,' /iig, eg/,
                 'clothlike,' and /minag/, 'round, berrylike.'

CLAUSE           A VERB with its associated ADVERBS and NOMINALS. A simple sen-
                 tence may have only one clause, while a complex sentence usually
                 has more than one.

CLITIC           A PARTICLE or other ADVERBIAL word that fuses PHONOLOGICALLY
                 with an adjacent word. Clitics in Nishnaabemwin include dash and
                 go, among others.

CLUSTER          A group of two or more CONSONANTS.

COALESCE         See COALESCENCE.
1016 • COALESCENCE



COALESCENCE     In PHONOLOGY and MORPHOLOGY, any process which takes two sep-
                arate entities, usually sounds, and fuses them together into a single
                entity. For example, many linguists would analyze the /oo/ of the
                word kikoog, 'kettles, pots,' as involving a coalescence of /w/ and
                /a/, in a basic (UNDERLYING) form /kikw+ag/.

COGNATES        Two words in SISTER LANGUAGES that come from the same word in
                their parent language. For example, the Cree word amisk and the
                Nishnaabemwin word mik, 'beaver,' are cognates.

COINING         Making up a new word for a new concept in the language. For exam-
                ple, a snowmobile is called gidaagon bembizod, ' 'that (ANsg) which
                races along upon the snow,' by some Nishnaabemwin speakers. An
                alternative to coining is BORROWING.

COMITATIVE      See VERB OF ACCOMPANIMENT.

COMMUNICA-      The act of speaking, conventionally defined as involving a speaker
TIVE ACT        (FIRST PERSON), an addressee (SECOND PERSON), and topics of con-
                 versation (THIRD PERSON).

COMMUNICA-      Knowledge of how to use language appropriately in different social
TIVE COMPE-     settings and for different social purposes or ends. Compare GRAM-
TENCE           MATICAL COMPETENCE.

COMMUNITY       The pattern of language shared by the speakers of a particular com-
LANGUAGE        munity, including what LANGUAGES and DIALECTS are spoken, and
USAGE           the particular vocabulary, pronunction, etc.

COMPARATIVE     Referring to linguistic forms which explicitly compare things, or
                express one thing in comparison to another. For example, in English
                SUFFIX -er can be added to ADJECTIVES to make a comparative form,
                such as bigger and older. Some Nishnaabemwin speakers use nwaj,
                'more,' in comparative constructions.

COMPARATIVE     Used to define a method of historical language study that compares
METHOD          related languages in order to determine their common ancestry. This
                method is based upon finding systematic phonological correlations
                in core vocabulary.
                                                               CONJUGATION TABLE •      1017



COMPENSATORY A PHONOLOGICAL PROCESS, in which a sound adjacent to one that is
LENGTHENING  deleted becomes lengthened, to compensate for the loss of the
             deleted segment. For example, the form, nwaabndaan, 'I see INsg,'
             is often analyzed as having a basic structure /ni+waaband+am+n/,
             and the /m/ of the THEME SUFFIX /-am/ is deleted before the follow-
             ing /n/, and to compensate for the loss of this segment, the short /a/
             of the theme sign lengthens to /aa/.

COMPLEMENT       Referring to something that completes another thing. In grammar,
                 most frequently in reference to NOUN PHRASES and CLAUSES that
                 serve as GOALS of TRANSITIVE VERBS. Example: Gii-waabmaan
                 Zhaabdiis moozoon, 'John saw a moose,' has as complement of
                 gii-waabmaan the NOUN (PHRASE) moozoon; Maanii gii-dbaajma
                 [Rogeran gii-ni-boontaad], 'Mary said that Roger had quit,' has as a
                 SENTENTIAL COMPLEMENT of gii-dbaajma, the material in brackets.
                 In Nishnaabemwin, complement clauses of verbs of speaking often
                 do not appear as the goal of the verb, because the person addressed
                 is made the explicit grammatical goal. See also ADJUNCT CLAUSE.

COMPLEX          A sentence containing more than one VERB, that is, a multi-clausal
SENTENCE         sentence. See CLAUSE.

COMPOUND         1. A word made up of two or more independent stems, such as
                 bzhiki-wiiyaas, 'beef,' which contains bzhiki, 'cow,' and wiiyaas,
                 'meat.' 2. Any expression that consists of two or more of the same
                 type of elements joined together, e.g., giw waabgan-pwaagnag
                 miinwaa semaan, 'those clay pipes and tobacco,' which joins
                 together two nouns.

CONCRETE NOUN A noun that refers to physical objects, including living beings as
              well as inanimate objects. Compare ABSTRACT NOUN.

CONDITION(AL)    A clause expressing a condition, typically, in Nishnaabemwin, with
CLAUSE           giishpin, 'if.' Example: Giishpin bwaa-ndamtaayaambaanh,
                 ndaa-gii-zhaa, 'If I weren't busy, I'd go there.'

CONJUGATION      An orderly presentation of the INFLECTIONAL forms of a verb, usu-
TABLE            ally organized according -to PERSON and NUMBER categories. See
                 PARADIGM.
1018 • CONJUNCT ORDER



CONJUNCT         One of three INFLECTIONAL SYSTEMS on VERBS for indicating the
ORDER           grammatical properties (PERSON, NUMBER, GENDER, and OBVIA-
                TION) of ACTORS and GOALS. The conjunct order system is used
                when the verb is in a question sentence asking who, what, when,
                where, why and how, and when the verb is part of a sentence that
                specifies such things as the condition, location, or time of the main
                verb. For example, giishpin wiisniyaanh..., 'if I eat...' is conjunct
                order. See ORDER, INDEPENDENT ORDER, IMPERATIVE ORDER.

CONJUNCTION     1. An expression that links things together, such as shi in Nishnaabe-
                mwin numbers, e.g., mdaaswi-shi-niizh, 'twelve'; 2. A part of
                speech that links phrases and clauses together, such as English and
                and when. The equivalent Nishnaabemwin terms are usually classi-
                fied as ADVERBS, which is somewhat misleading.

CONSONANT       One of the two basic classes of sounds in language, the other being
                VOWELS. Consonants are generally produced by obstructing the flow
                of air from the lungs in particular ways at particular locations. Con-
                sonants are classified on the basis of their PLACE OF ARTICULATION,
                MANNER OF ARTICULATION, and the STATE OF THE GLOTTIS (VOICED
                 or UNVOICED). The basic classes of consonants in Nishnaabemwin
                 are STOPS, FRICATIVE, AFFRICATES, NASALS, and GLIDES.

CONSONANT        See CLUSTER.
CLUSTER

CONSTITUENT     Any identifiable unit within a SYNTACTIC structural complex. Con-
                stituents are different at different levels within a structure. For exam-
                ple, the expression niizh kwewag, 'two women,' can be considered a
                NOUN PHRASE constituent, itself consisting of two constituents,
                niizh, 'two,' a number, and kwewag, 'women,' a noun. In the sen-
                tence Niizh kwewag gii-ni-giiwewag, 'Two women went home,'
                niizh kwewag is a noun phrase (constituent) of the whole sentence,
                and gii-ni-giiwewag, (possibly) a VERB PHRASE. See also CONSTITU-
                ENCY.

CONSTITUENCY    In SYNTAX, refers to an account of the words and phrases that make
                up a larger syntactic unit. For example, a NOUN PHRASE in Nishnaa-
                bemwin can have as constituents (members) a DEMONSTRATIVE
                PRONOUN, a NUMBER, a HEAD NOUN, and a RELATIVE CLAUSE.
                                                                               DEICTIC "1019



CONTEMPTIVE      A special form of a noun reflecting the speaker's attitude toward the
                 object being referred to, communicating vaguely negative or dis-
                 missive attitudes, such as 'just an ordinary one,' 'of no great value,'
                 or 'any old.' An example is truckoonh, 'just any old truck.' Con-
                 temptives should be distinguished from PEJORATIVES. Contemptives
                 are formed by adding a SUFFIX to a NOUN base.

CONTENT QUES- A question that asks for information other than a simple yes (enh) or
TION          no (gaawii(n)), such as who, what, where, when, why, how, and how
              many questions. Such questions in Nishnaabemwin have the ques-
              tion word at the beginning of the sentence, and the verb has CON-
              JUNCT ORDER INFLECTION. For example: Wenesh gaa-bkobiised,
              'Who fell into the water?' Compare YES/NO QUESTION.

CONVERSA-        The physical and social setting in which speech takes place, includ-
TIONAL           ing the particular time, the particular place, and the particular partic-
CONTEXT          ipants. Compare TEXTUAL CONTEXT.

COORDINATION     Putting two (or more) related things together, such as in the expres-
                 sion bkwezhgan miinwaa doodooshaaboo, 'bread and milk.'

DAUGHTER LAN- A language that is the descendent of an earlier (mother) language.
GUAGE         Two languages that descend from the same language are said to be
              SISTER LANGUAGES, for example, Ojibwe and Cree are daughter lan-
              guages of Proto-Algonquian, and sisters of each other.

DEFAULT          Constituting the basic, most commonly used form of a grammatical
                 element. For example, for many speakers of Nishnaabemwin, /doo-/
                 has become the default form of the THIRD PERSON PREFIX.

DEFECTIVE FOOT A METRICAL FOOT consisting of a single syllable, usually containing
               a LONG VOWEL. For example, the word emkwaan, 'spoon,' begins
               with a defective foot consisting of the syllable /em/.

DEGREE ADVERB An adverb that expresses the idea of "how much," or "to what
              extent." Examples: zaam, 'too much,' niibwa, 'a lot, much.'

DEICTIC          A word which relates an utterance to a particular physical context,
                 including references to the speaker, the addressee, people and
                 objects in the physical context, and the time and place of speaking
                 (or writing). Common deictic forms are PERSONAL PRONOUNS and
                 DEMONSTRATIVES.
1020   • DELAYED MODE



DELAYED MODE Referring to a command that is to be carried out at a later time, such
             as Baamaa waabang bi-zhaakan, 'Come over tomorrow.' Compare
             IMMEDIATE MODE.

DEMONSTRATIVE A PRONOUN such as maaba, 'this (anim.),' or giw, 'those (anim.),'
PRONOUN       that picks out referents on the basis of their closeness (proximity) to
              some reference point, often the speaker's location. Demonstrative
              pronouns specifying closet proximity to the speaker are said to be
              PROXIMAL (not to be confused with PROXIMATE), those further away,
              DISTAL, and those furthest away, REMOTE.

DENOMINAL         Referring to any morphological process that takes a noun as a base
                  and produces a word of a different part of speech, in Nishnaabem-
                  win, usually a verb. For example, a verb of being, such as niniiwi,
                  'be(come) a man.'

DENTAL            Referring to a CONSONANT articulated roughly in the area behind the
                  upper front teeth, for example /d/ and /t/ for some Nishnaabemwin
                  speakers.

DEONTIC           Referring to modals that express permission and obligation, as in
                  English you may leave now (permission) or you must leave now
                  (obligation). Compare EPISTEMIC.

DEPARTICIPIAL     Nouns formed from intransitive verbs by the application of initial
NOUNS             change, and the addition of a contemptive suffix, e.g., dekaashiinh,
                  'tourist,' from vai dkaashi, 'be carefree, have fun.' These nouns are
                  more noun-like than regular participles in lacking all verbal inflec-
                  tion. See PARTICIPLE.

DEPENDENT         A CLAUSE that cannot stand alone as a fully-formed sentence by
CLAUSE            itself. For example, in the complex sentence Miinwaa dash gaa
                  gegoo waa-zhichged iw wii-zaagdooded, 'There was nothing he
                  could do to crawl out,' the dependent clause is iw wii-zaagdooded,
                  'that he crawl out,' which would not ordinarily be used by itself.
                  Also called a SUBORDINATE CLAUSE.

DEPENDENT         Referring to a NOUN that requires a POSSESSOR, such as nkaad, 'my
NOUN              leg,' and ngwis, 'my son.' In Nishnaabemwin, most BODY PART
                  TERMS and terms for relations (KINSHIP TERMS) are dependent
                  nouns. Compare INDEPENDENT NOUN.
                                                                    DIALECT CHAINING • 1021



DERIVATION       1. The process of applying all applicable rules to the basic form
                 (base form) of a word in order to move from an abstract shape stored
                 in a person's memory to the actually pronounced form of a word. 2.
                 Referring to the process of creating new words (stems) in the lan-
                 guage.

DERIVE           To take a STEM and add AFFIXES which produce a new stem differing
                 significantly in either meaning, part of speech, or basic form. For
                 example, the SUFFIX /-magad/ can be added to VAI verbs to derive
                 corresponding VII verbs, as in kidoomgad, 'INsg says,' from VAI
                 kido, 'say, speak.'

DESCRIPTIVE      A Nishnaabemwin verb which describes a person or thing, for exam-
VERB             pie, biinzi, 'ANsg is clean,' and ggaan 'gaade, 'ANsg has long legs,'
                 are both descriptive verbs.

DESIDERATIVE     Expressing a desire. See VOLITIONAL.

DETRANSITIVIZE To make a TRANSITIVE VERB into an INTRANSITIVE by eliminating
               one of its SEMANTIC ROLES. Specific DETRANSITIVIZING processes
               have their own names, such as PASSIVE and ANTIPASSIVE.

DEVERBAL         Referring to something that has been changed from being a VERB
                 into something else. For example, bboon, 'be winter, be a year,' is a
                 verb, but bboon can also be used as a noun, in which case it can be
                 called a DEVERBAL NOUN, as opposed to say, mik, 'beaver,' which
                 has not been changed from a verb into a noun, and so is not dever-
                 bal.

DEVOICING        A phonological (sound) process whereby a normally VOICED sound
                 becomes voiceless. For example, the PHONEMES /b/, /d/, /g/, /z/, /zh/
                 and /j/ are all DEVOICED at the end of a word in Nishnaabemwin, and
                 are thus pronounced as [p], [t], [k], [s], [sh], and [ch], respectively.

DIALECT          A regional VARIETY of a language, often identified by name, such as
                 Chippewa or Odawa.

DIALECT CHAIN-   See CHAINING.
ING
1022 • DICTIONARY



DICTIONARY          An ordered listing of the words of a language, along with pronuncia-
                    tions, meanings, and various GRAMMATICAL FORMS. There is at
                    present (in the year 2000) no real dictionary in Nishnaabemwin, as
                    all existing wordlists are really glossaries, which define Nishnaabe-
                    mwin words in terms of their English translation correspondences.

DIMINUTIVE          Designating a noun referring to a small or immature member of a
                     group, formed by adding /-ens/ or some variant to a base noun. For
                    example, mikoons, 'beaver kit,' is the diminutive of mik, 'beaver';
                    jiimaanens, 'little boat,' is the diminutive ofjiimaan, 'boat.'

DIRECT SPEECH       Reported speech which quotes the very words of the speaker, with-
                    out adjustment, e.g., Mii dash gaa-naad aw mshkikiiwnini, [Gego
                    nendangen]. The doctor told her, ["Do not feel that way about it."]'
                    (AM30.21). Compare INDIRECT SPEECH.

DIRECTIONAL         Designating a small set of MORPHEMES that appear in both PREVERB
                    and ROOT form, and specify the direction of a verbal action in some
                    way. Some directional PREVERBS are hi-, 'towards speaker' (root
                    /biid/), ni-, 'away from speaker' (root /anim/), bbaa-, 'around' (root
                    /babaam/), and oo-, 'go and...'

DISJOINT            A requirement on the relationship between the fillers of the SEMAN-
REFERENCE           TIC ROLES of VERBS in Nishnaabemwin, which requires that they be
                    GRAMMATICALLY differentiable in crucial ways. FIRST and SECOND
                    PERSON fillers must be completely different; THIRD PERSON fillers
                    must differ in GENDER or OBVIATION. So, for example, one cannot
                    say the equivalent of 'I see us,' because the NOMINAL 'us' would
                    include reference to 'I.'

DISJUNCTION         Contrasting two or more things, as in, Bezhig na maage niizh?,
                    'One, or two?'

DISTAL              Designating a demonstrative pronoun that refers to objects at a sec-
                    ond degree of distance from the speaker. For example, in Nishnaabe-
                    mwin, the PROXIMAL INANIMATE DEMONSTRATIVE is maanda (or
                    ow), and the DISTAL is iw (also wi).

DISTINCTIVE         Those sounds in a language which are used crucially to distinguish
SOUNDS              words of different meaning. For example, in Nishnaabemwin, /b/
                    and /p/ are distinct sounds, as can be seen from the words naapi,
                    'ANsg laughs in such a way,' and naabi, 'ANsg looks (somewhere).'
                                                                             EMPHATIC « 1023



DISTRIBUTIVE   Number terms that indicate both quantity and distribution, such as
NUMBERS        bebezhig, 'one by one, one each,' or neniizh, 'two by two; two each.'

DITRANSITIVE   Designating a verb, such as miinaad, 'give Y to AN,' which has two
               objects, a SECONDARY OBJECT (in the case of miinaad, what is
               given) and a PRIMARY OBJECT (in the case of miinaad, the recipient).

DUBITATIVE     1. One of four MODES of Nishnaabemwin, endings on VERBS that
               indicate information either about the time of an action, or the
               speaker's certainty that a statement being made is true, or both. For
               example, in wiisnidig, 'ANsg must be eating,' the speaker is making
               an assertion, but allowing for the possibility that it isn't true, that is,
               is indicating some doubt about the reality of the assertion. This is
               dubitative. 2. Characterizing a particle that indicates doubt, such as
               gnimaa, 'maybe.'

DUBITATIVE     See PRETERIT DUBITATIVE.
PRETERIT

DUBITATIVE     A PRONOUN such as wegwen(h), 'someone or other, something or
PRONOUN        other,' which is used in contexts of doubt and/or uncertainty.

DUMMY          1 .Dummy subject. In English, all main verbs must have a GRAM-
               MATICAL SUBJECT, even when they logically do not have one, as in
               weather and date expressions. In such cases, English uses the pro-
               noun it, as in 'it's raining,' or 'it's Tuesday.' Nishnaabemwin uses
               IMPERSONAL VERBS to express many meanings similar to those in
               which English uses the dummy subject, it. In these cases Nishnaabe-
               mwin has a dummy INFLECTIONAL subject. 2. Any inherently mean-
               ingless element that occurs on the basis of structural requirements.

EASTERN        A sub-group of the ALGONQUIAN language family, which includes
ALGONQUIAN     Delaware, Micmac, Malecite-Passamaquoddy, Natick, and many
               other languages.

EMPHATIC       Designating a group of ADVERBIAL PARTICLES used to mark empha-
               sis of particular words or phrases. The most common emphatic parti-
               cles are gwa (also go), naa, sa, and dash.
1024   • ENCLITIC



ENCLITIC            A particle which attaches to a word preceding it, often reducing by
                    losing some of its segments. For example, in English, the word not is
                    often enclitic to do, producing don't. In Nishnaabemwin, the word
                    dash is often encliticized to the word that precedes it, for example,
                    miish (also spelled mii-sh), from mii dash.

ENCLITICIZE         To attach something to a preceding word as a CLITIC. See ENCLITIC.

ENDING              A SUFFIX, or more particularly, a grouping of all the suffixes on a
                    word taken together as a unit. See SUFFIX.

EPENTHESIS          A phonological process in which a vowel is added in order to sepa-
                    rate two vowels, or a consonant is added in order to separate two
                    vowels. For example, /y/ is sometimes added between a vowel-final
                    base and the conjunct suffix /-aan/, '1st person,' as in
                    boodweyaan(h), '(when) I make a fire.'

EPISTEMIC           Referring to modals that express possibilty or certainty, as in -
                    English it might be raining (possibility), or it must be raining (cer-
                    tainty). Compare DEONTIC.

EQUATION            Considering two things equal, as in naasaab aapiitnigdoon nanda
                    mkakoon, 'these boxes weigh the same.'

ERGATIVE            Designating any structural contrast which groups the subject of an
                    intransitive verb and the object of a transitive verb together (as abso-
                    lutives), in distinction to the subject of a transitive (as ergative).

EXCLUSIVE           A distinction made in FIRST PERSON PLURAL. First person plural
                    exclusive excludes the person being spoken to (the SECOND PER-
                    SON), as in nwiisnimi(n), 'we (but not you) are eating,' or
                    ndaansinaa(n), 'our (which doesn't include you) daughter.' Com-
                    pare INCLUSIVE.

EXCRESCENT          A nasal consonant that is inserted in certain well-defined phonologi-
NASAL               cal contexts, such as the [n] in nDebid, a common Nishnaabemwin
                    pronunciation of English David.

EXISTENTIAL         Any predicate or predication that asserts the existence of an entity at
                    a particular time or place, or generally, e.g., Yaa gwa Gzhe-mnidoo.
                    'There is a God.' (MC); Gye go games wii-yaanoon,
                    ggwejkandiwnan. 'Also there will be games and races.' (AM 17.5)
                                            FINAL SHORT VOWEL AND GLIDE DELETION •         1025



EXOCENTRIC       Designating compounds and other expressions that do not have
                 internal HEADS. For example, jiibaakwe-kik, 'cooking pot,' is inter-
                 nally headed, having kik, 'pot,' as its head; gchi-mookmaan, 'Amer-
                 ican,' is not internally headed, because mookmaan, 'knife,' is
                 inanimate and cannot serve as the head of an animate compound
                 noun.

EXPERIENCER      The SEMANTIC ROLE of the perceiver or undergoer, voluntary or
                 involuntary, of some stimulus, such as a sight, a sound, a smell, a
                 taste, or a thought. All verbs of perception have experiences as
                 actors, as in mnomaandan, 'smell IN and like its smell' (VTI).

EXPRESSION       A very general term that is usually used to group together some lan-
                 guage elements that share a property. For example, the term numeric
                 expression could be used to specify various kinds of constructions in
                 Nishnaabemwin that have NUMBERS in them, such as a PHRASE with
                 an independent number WORD, together with a PRENOUN plus NOUN
                 combination.

EXPRESSIVE       A PARTICLE such as oonh or otaayaa that is used to express an emo-
PARTICLE         tional reaction to a statement or situation.

EXTENDED (PER- The longer forms of PERSON PREFIXES, containing /d/ and a follow-
SON) PREFIXES  ing VOWEL, such as ndoo-, gdoo-, and doo-. See PERSON PREFIX.

FEMININE         Referring to any English word or expression that can have associ-
                 ated with it the PRONOUN she, that is, an expression that is grammat-
                 ically treated as female. This category has little relevance to
                 Nishnaabemwin grammar, since the GRAMMATICAL GENDER con-
                 trast is ANIMATE and INANIMATE.

FINAL            The last element in the basic structure of a word, usually defining its
                 PART OF SPEECH. For example, in minwenim, 'like AN,' the final is
                 /enim/. Finals may be CONCRETE or ABSTRACT.

FINAL SHORT    A PHONOLOGICAL RULE specifying that final SHORT VOWELS and
VOWEL AND      GLIDES (/w/ and /y/) are deleted at the end of a word. For example,
GLIDE DELETION the basic verb /wiisimV shows the deletion of its final short vowel in
               the form nwiisin, 'I am eating'; the noun meaning 'man' has a STEM
               shape /aniniw/, but its FINAL /w/ is deleted in the PROXIMATE SINGU-
               LAR form, nini.
1026   • FIRST PERSON



FIRST PERSON        Within the grammatical system of person, refers to the speaker. For
                    example, niin, 'I/me/my' is a first person pronoun, because it refers
                    to the speaker, and the verb form nwiisin, 'I am eating,' has a first
                    person subject. See PERSON.

FOCUS               With reference to syntactic constructions, referring to those that
                    function to give explicit emphasis to a particular constituent. See,
                    e.g., Mil FOCUS.

FOOT                see METRICAL FOOT.

FORCE               A SEMANTIC ROLE specifying a notionally INANIMATE (meaning not
                    an animal, human, manitou or other spirit being) entity which exerts
                    effects similar to AGENCY, but without willful intent. For example,
                    the VTA aakshkadegshkaagod, 'give AN a stomach ache,' has a force
                    exerting a kind of AGENCY, which makes someone sick. See AGENT,
                    SEMANTIC ROLE.

FORM                1. Any identifiable element in a language. For example, wiisnin,
                    gwiisin, and wiisniyaanh are all forms in Nishnaabemwin. 2. Pro-
                    nunciation or structural patterning as opposed to meaning or func-
                    tion.

FORMAL              1. More commonly in linguistics, concerning the form of a linguistic
                    element, as opposed to how it is used (its function) or its meaning. 2.
                    Designating a social act, such as speaking, that is regulated on the
                    basis of explicit convention rather than spontaneity. See NOTIONAL.

FORTIS              Characterizing CONSONANTS that are made with relatively greater
                    force. The VOICELESS consonants of Nishnaabemwin are sometimes
                    said to be fortis. Compare LENIS.

FOURTH PERSON A term often sometimes used to designate the OBVIATIVE, to distin-
              guish it from the PROXIMATE THIRD PERSON. See DEVIATION.

FRICATIVE           A CONSONANT sound made by channeling the flow of air through a
                    narrow passage and creating turbulence in the airstream. The frica-
                    tives of Nishnaabemwin are /z, s, 3, J7 (standardly spelled «z s zh
                    sh»). See STOP, AFFRICATE, NASAL, GLIDE.

FRONT               Characterizing a VOWEL produced with the tongue placed relatively
                    forward in the mouth. The front vowels of Nishnaabemwin are /i/,
                    /ii/, and Id. See also CENTRAL, BACK.
                                                                              GERUND •     1027



FUNCTIONAL        Having to do with how a grammatical form is used, that is, what
                  grammatical purpose it serves. Any given linguistic form has an
                  associated function, and different forms can have the same function.
                  For example, the SUFFIX /-wag/ found on many verbs, as in
                  ngamwag, 'ANpl are singing,' functions to indicate that the SUBJECT
                  of the verb is ANIMATE THIRD PERSON PLURAL, and that the verb is
                  the MAIN VERB in a sentence.

GEMINATE          Usually refers to a doubled consonant, such as the p 's in English top
                  priority. In Nishnaabemwin, two lenis consonants made adjacent by
                  SYNCOPE often sound like their fortis correspondent, e.g., the two g's
                  in gga- (from /gi/, second person prefix and /ga-/ future tense) sound
                  like [k] to some speakers, and this sequence is sometimes spelled
                  «ka».

GENDER            1. Referring to the grammatical system of NOUN CLASSES in Nish-
                  naabemwin, ANIMATE and INANIMATE. 2. Referring to
                  socially-defined differences between males and females in a society,
                  which always includes patterns of language use.

GENERAL           An ADVERB that specifies an amount, but without making reference
QUANTIFIER        to a specific number. Examples: kina, 'all,' and aanin(d), 'some.'

GENERALIZED    Verbs that carry special INFLECTION to indicate that they refer to
ACTIVITY VERBS general activity rather than to a specific individual or individuals.
               For example, Eshkam znagad wii-debnaming iw waa-boodweng. 'It
               is getting harder and harder to obtain firewood.' (AM 15.15) Here the
               reference is to the general situation, and there are special inflections
               to indicate the generality.

GENETIC        Classification of languages on the basis of common ancestry. Over
CLASSIFICATION time a language may come to be spoken by groups isolated from
               each other, and each group may show different innovations in their
               speech, ultimately resulting in different languages. Genetic classifi-
               cation seeks to trace the processes of innovation in individual lan-
               guages back to a common ancestor.

GERUND            In English, a verbal noun, that is an element functioning as a noun,
                  but formed from a verb by adding suffix /-ing/, as in Swimming is
                  good exercise. Nishnaabemwin makes similar constructions with
                  NOMINALIZER /-win/, as in bgizowin, 'swimming.' Also, Nishnaabe-
                  mwin PARTICIPLES are verbs used as nouns.
1028 • GLIDE



GLIDE          A type of CONSONANT sound created by gliding the tongue to an
               area quite close to that of a VOWEL. The glides of Nishnaabemwin
               are /y/ and./w/. The glide /w/ is closely related to the vowels /o, oo/;
               the glide /y/ is closely related to the vowels /i, ii/.

GLOSS          A brief translation of a word, phrase or sentence, representing the
               closest equivalent in another language. Glosses are commonly
               enclosed within single quotes, e.g., the gloss of kwe is 'woman.'

GLOTTAL        Referring to a sound made in the vicinity of the VOCAL CORDS. The
               Nishnaabemwin sound /?/ «h», GLOTTAL STOP, is made so.

GLOTTAL STOP   A distinct sound (PHONEME) of Nishnaabemwin, made by drawing
               the VOCAL CORDS tightly together for a moment, and temporarily
               stopping the flow of air. Glottal stop is spelled with the letter «h»
                in the standard orthography.

GLOTTIS        The opening between the VOCAL CORDS.

GOAL           In a TRANSITIVE PREDICATION, the MACROROLE associated with the
               recipient of an action. For example, in Mik ndayan wwaabmaan,
               'The beaver sees my dog,' the form ndayan, 'my dog,' is the goal of
               the transitive verb waabmaad.

GRAMMAR        l.The system of forms and rules that speakers of a language make
               unconscious use of in speaking their language. 2. A written account
               of the forms and rules of a language.

GRAMMATICAL    Knowledge of the grammar of a language (in the sense of 1. in the
COMPETENCE     preceding entry), including the patterns of PRONUNCIATION,
               word-formation, INFLECTION, SYNTAX, and some aspects of mean-
               ing. Such knowledge must be distinguished from COMMUNICATIVE
               COMPETENCE.

GRAMMATICAL    A system that ranks grammatical items in some way. In Algonquian
HIERARCHY      languages, a prominent grammatical hierarchy is the TOPICALITY
               HIERARCHY.
                                                                      HEADWORD •       1029



GRAMMATICAL   Any recognizable patterned behaviour in language. Languages are
PATTERN       not random collections of information, but instead show immense
              patterning in the ways that they work. For example, in the CONJUNCT
              ORDER of Nishnaabemwin verb inflection, there is a limited number
              of PERSON, NUMBER and DEVIATION categories, with each combina-
              tion indicated by a different combination of SUFFIXES occurring in
              Specific STRUCTURAL SLOTS.

GRAMMATICAL   Designating a set of syntactic roles that can be assigned to the ARGU-
RELATIONS     MENTS filling the SEMANTIC ROLES of VERBS (or any other predica-
              tor). The most common grammatical relations are those of subject,
              object, and indirect object. These relations are not as important in
              Nishnaabemwin as they are in English. In Nishnaabemwin, th
              SEMANTIC MACROROLES of ACTOR, GOAL, and S-ROLE are much
              more prominent, since these roles are explicitly marked on the VERB
              with INFLECTIONS.

GRAMMATI-     Properties of a REFERENT that are coded in the grammar of a lan-
CALLY         guage. For example, in English, the property of (mostly) sexual gen-
RELEVANT      der is coded in PRONOUNS such as he, she, and it; this property of
PROPERTIES    referents is not coded in Nishnaabemwin, but properties of gram-
              matical ANIMACY are. Languages vary as to which properties are
              central to their grammars.

HARD PALATE   The hard portion of the roof of the mouth, where PALATAL sounds
              are made.

HEAD          1. In a SYNTACTIC construction such as a PHRASE or CLAUSE, the
              central element around which the phrase or clause is organized. For
              example, in niizh kwewag, 'two women,' the NOUN kwewag is the
              head; in the clause Semaan gii-miinaawag kiwenziinyag, 'the old
              men were given tobacco,' the head is the VERB gii-miinaawag, 'they
              were given.' 2. The main component of a word.

HEADWORD      The form of a lexeme (word) that is used to list it in the dictionary.
              For example, the verb translated as 'give,' in English has many dif-
              ferent forms in Nishnaabemwin, including nmiinaa, nmiinig,
              nmiin'goo, etc., but the form it is listed under in the dictionary is
              miinaad, the CONJUNCT THIRD PERSON SINGULAR PROXIMATE acting
              on THIRD PERSON OBVIATIVE. See also CITATION FORM.
1030 • HEIGHT



HEIGHT          Characterizing the relative height of the tongue in the pronunciation
                of VOWELS. Vowels may be HIGH, MID, or LOW.

HIGH            Characterizing a VOWEL made with a relatively high tongue posi-
                tion. The high vowels of Nishnaabemwin are III and /ii/, and some-
                times /o/ and /oo/. High vowels often cause following ALVEOLAR
                 sounds to PALATALIZE.

HORTATIVE       A command including the speaker (FIRST PERSON), thus indicating
                the notion 'let's,' as in wiisnidaa, 'let's eat!'

HOST            The word that a CLITIC attaches to.

IDIOLECT        The speech of a particular individual, including personal habits of
                vocabulary, sentence patterning and style.

II VERB         An intransitive verb having an inanimate subject. In this work, usu-
                ally abbreviated VII.

IMMEDIATE       Referring to commands that are to be carried out immediately, such
MODE            as wiisnin!, 'eat!' Compare DELAYED MODE.

IMPERATIVE      One of three inflectional systems on VERBS for indicating the gram-
ORDER           matical properties (PERSON, NUMBER, GENDER, and DEVIATION) of
                ACTORS and GOALS. The imperative order system is used to give
                commands, for example, bi-wiisnin!, 'come and eat,' is an impera-
                tive form. See also ORDER; CONJUNCT ORDER; IMPERATIVE ORDER.

IMPERSONAL      A vii verb that does not usually have an overt SUBJECT, such as
VERB            shpaagnagaa, 'be high snow.' Many verbs describing geographical
                and weather conditions are impersonal.

INANIMATE         One of two grammatical GENDERS, or NOUN CLASSES, of Nishnaabe-
                  mwin, the other being ANIMATE. Membership in the inanimate
                ' grammatical class is largely based on meaning, in that non-living
                  things, such as objects of manufacture and natural 'non-living'
                  things are included in it.

INANIMATE       A subclass of verbs, having a single SEMANTIC ROLE (and thus being
INTRANSITIVE    intransitive), in which the role must be filled by an INANIMATE sub-
VERB            ject.
                                                                 INDEPENDENT ORDER • 1031



INCEPTIVE        Focusing on the beginning of an action, event, or state, or transition
                 into it.

INCHOATIVE       See INCEPTIVE.

INCLUSIVE        A distinction made in FIRST PERSON PLURAL. First person plural
                 inclusive includes the person being spoken to (the second person), as
                 in gwiisnimi(n), 'we (including you) are eating,' or gdaansinaa(n),
                 'our (including your) daughter.' Compare EXCLUSIVE.

INCORPORATION The process of putting one thing inside of another, typically in Nish-
              naabemwin, incorporating a NOUN representing a GOAL into a VERB,
              as in naadsabii, 'fetch one's net,' which has sab, 'net,' incorporated
              within the verb. Incorporation is often a form of BACKGROUNDING.

INDEFINITE       A construction in which an anonymous possessor is specified on a
POSSESSOR        noun. Used only with dependent nouns when the possessor is not
                 known or not important. For example, kaad, 'a leg,' as opposed to
                 nkaad, 'my leg' (where the possessor is niin, 'me') or gkaad, 'your
                 leg,' (where the possessor is giin, 'you'). See POSSESSION.

INDEFINITE       The PRONOUNS \vaya (wiya), 'someone, anyone,' and gegoo(n),
PRONOUN          'something, anything.'

INDEPENDENT      A noun that does not require a POSSESSOR, but may optionally have
NOUN             one. For example, jiimaan, 'boat,' can be used without specification
                 of a possessor, as in Jiimaan nwaabndaan, T see a boat,' or with a
                 specified possessor, as in Njiimaan nwaabndaan, 'I see my boat.'
                 Other than BODY PART TERMS and KINSHIP and marital relations in
                 Nishnaabemwin, most nouns are independent. Compare DEPENDENT
                 NOUN.

INDEPENDENT      One of three inflectional systems on VERBS for indicating the gram-
ORDER            matical properties (PERSON, NUMBER, GENDER, and DEVIATION) of
                 ACTORS and GOALS. The independent order system is used when the
                 verb is the main verb of the sentence, for example, Nongo nwiisin,
                 'I'm eating now' is independent. See ORDER; CONJUNCT ORDER;
                 IMPERATIVE ORDER.
1032 • INDEPENDENT



INDEPENDENT      The process of change whereby two daughter languages indepen-
PARALLEL         dently show similar innovations, on the basis of structural pressures
DEVELOPMENT      inherited from their mother language. Thus, two widely separated
                 daughter languages may show similar developments over time that
                 are not necessarily due to continued close contact between the lan-
                 guages.

INDEX            To mark in some way as to show the presence of a property. For
                 example, Nishnaabemwin NOUNS are INDEXED for PLURALITY, by
                 means of a PLURAL SUFFIX, as injiimaanan, 'boats.' This suffix also
                 indexes the GENDER of the noun, as INANIMATE.

INDICATIVE       See MOOD.
MOOD

INDIRECT         Reported speech or thought which does not represent the actual
SPEECH           words spoken or thought, but rather adjusts the quotation to some
                 reference point other than the original, for example, [Rogeran
                 zaaghigod] gii-nendam Maanii. 'Mary thought [that Roger loved
                 her]' (MC). Here, the actual thought would be Roger nzaaghig,
                 'Roger loves me,' but the quotation has been made indirect by shift-
                 ing it to third person, in which case Roger is made obviative.

INFLECTION       1. Any PREFIX or SUFFIX added to a word to indicate some grammat-
                 ical meaning, for example, zhiishiibag, 'ducks,' has an inflectional
                 suffix -ag, meaning ANIMATE PLURAL. 2. The system of PREFIXES
                 and SUFFIXES in a language which is used to signal grammatical
                 information.

INFLECTIONAL A passive that operates on a derivationally transitive verb, producing
PASSIVE      an inflectional intransitive that has a transitive THEME SIGN, e.g.,
                 nwaabmigoo, 'I am seen,' or waabamaa, 'ANsg is seen,' from VTA
                 stem /waabam/, 'see AN.' Compare LEXICAL PASSIVE.

INFLECTIONAL     The inventory and configuration of PREFIXES and SUFFIXES in a lan-
SYSTEM           guage used to signal grammatical information.

INHERENT         A noun that represents a substance or objects that are usually
PLURAL           referred to with plural reference, such as biiwekdamaagnan, '(wood)
                 shavings' (W); bootsan, 'boots' (from English boots, Od).
                                                                              IRREGULAR •      1033



INITIAL            1. The first structural slot in basic word structure. The initial may be
                   simple, as in bookgaade, 'break a leg,' where it is /bookw/, or com-
                   plex, as in bookgaadeshin, where it is /bookgaade/. Compare
                   MEDIAL and FINAL. 2. Designating the first element in an ordering.
                   For example, Ntaa-gshkigwaaso ndaanis, 'my daughter sews well,'
                   has verb-initial word order.

INITIAL CHANGE A MORPHOLOGICAL process applying to the first VOWEL in a word,
               changing it to a specified different vowel, for various grammatical
               purposes. For example, the vowel /ii/ changes to /aa/, so that when
               initial change applies to the preverb \vii-, it becomes \vaa-. Initial
               change effects the following changes in Nishnaabemwin: /a/, III »
               /e/; /o/» /(w)e/; /ii/ » /aa/, Id » /aye/; /oo/ » /waa/; /aa/ » /ayaa/. SYN-
               COPE then applies to the changed forms.

INTERROGATIVE Designating questions.

INTERROGATIVE A PRONOUN used in asking questions of who or what, such as
PRONOUN       wenesh.

INTRANSITIVE       Referring to a verb that has only a single SEMANTIC ROLE associated
                   with it, such as wiisni, 'ANsg is eating,' where the only role is that of
                   an eater. Compare transitive Wiiyaas nmiijin, 'I am eating meat,'
                   where there are two roles, that of an eater, in this case filled by 'I,'
                   and that of a thing eaten, in this case filled by wiiyaas, 'meat.' Com-
                   pare TRANSITIVE.

INVERSE-ONLY       Designating a small set of TRANSITIVE ANIMATE VERBS indicating
VTA                various effects on the body, which can only be used with INVERSE
                   INFLECTION, that is, cannot have FIRST or SECOND PERSON ACTORS.
                   An example: aakziishkaagod, 'make AN sick (of things ingested).'

IPA                The name of the PHONETIC ALPHABET used in this grammar, an
                   abbreviation of International Phonetic Alphabet.

IRREGULAR          Indicating an INFLECTIONAL or DERIVATIONAL form that is not
                   formed according to some usual or "default" pattern. For example,
                   for some speakers, the LOCATIVE form ofoodewin, 'town,' is irregu-
                   lar oodenaang. Standard locatives are formed by adding /-ing/ to a
                   noun, which would produce *oodewining.
1034 • ITERATIVE



ITERATIVE          1. Designating a SUFFIX /-i(n)/ that occurs on VERBS, along with
                   CHANGED CONJUNCT INFLECTION, to indicate activity that repeats
                   over time, as in gemwangi(n), 'whenever it rains.' 2. Any linguistic
                   form that indicates action repeated multiple times.

KINSHIP TERM       A word used to designate a kinship relationship (a relative of some
                   sort), such as ngwis, 'my son,' or nookmis, 'my grandmother.' In
                   Nishnaabemwin, almost all kinship terms are DEPENDENT NOUNS.

LABIAL             Of CONSONANT sounds, articulated at the lips, or involving the lips.
                   The labial sounds of Nishnaabemwin are /b/, /p/, /m/, and /w/.

LANGUAGE           A group of languages, genetically related by virtue of sharing a
FAMILY             common parent. The family to which Nishnaabemwin belongs is
                   called the ALGONQUIAN language family.

LARYNX             The voicebox, containing the VOCAL CORDS.

LENGTH             Referring to the relative duration of a VOWEL pronunciation, that is,
                   how long the vowel is pronounced relative to other kinds of vowels.
                   Short vowels are pronounced roughly half as long as long vowels.

LENE               A linguistic term for the more softly articulated consonant of a pair
                   of related consonants, associated with VOICING in Nishnaabemwin.
                   The PHONEMES /b/, /d/, /g/, /z/, /zh/ and /j/ all represent lenes, as
                   opposed to their FORTIS partners, /p/, /t/, /k/, /s/, /sh/ and /ch/, respec-
                   tively. See LENIS, FORTIS.

LENIS              Characterizing CONSONANTS that are made with relatively less force.
                   The VOICED consonants of Nishnaabemwin are sometimes said to be
                   lenis. Compare FORTIS.

LETTER             A written symbol used to represent a distinctive sound of a lan-
                   guage. Letters must be distinguished from sounds. For example the
                   letter «h» is used in Nishnaabemwin to represent a glottal stop, as
                   well as a glottal fricative in a few expressive terms, such as in
                   nahaaw, 'okay.'
                                                                           LEXICON • 1035



LEXEME          An established item of vocabulary in a language, such asjiimaan,
                'boat, canoe.' A lexeme can have a vast number of associated WORD
                FORMS in Nishnaabemwin. The form of the lexeme itself is deter-
                mined by removing all INFLECTIONAL elements and "undoing" the
                effects of any PHONOLOGICAL PROCESSES such as SYNCOPE, the
                deletion of final short-vowels and glides, or INITIAL CHANGE. Lex-
                emes are usually represented with a single main entry in a dictio-
                nary, but in a CITATION FORM that represents a common inflected
                form. See CITATION FORM, WORD FORM.

LEXICAL         1. Referring to the vocabulary of a language, especially with refer-
                ence to the mental 'dictionary' that speakers make use of in speak-
                ing. 2. Referring to any form in a language that must be memorized,
                either because its form or its meaning is not predictable from general
                principles. See LEXICALIZED.

LEXICAL CLASS   See PART OF SPEECH.

LEXICALIZED     Designating a specific inflectional form of a word that exists as an
                independent item of vocabulary in the language, with a meaning that
                is not determinable from the meanings of its component parts. For
                example, almost any noun can take a DIMINUTIVE suffix, such as
                jiimaanens, 'small boat,' fromjiimaan, 'boat.' There is a word in
                Nishnaabemwin, kidwin, 'word, utterance,' and some speakers have
                 suggested that a good word for 'morpheme' might be the diminutive
                 of this word, kidwinens. If such a proposal were accepted, then
                kidwinens would be a new word in Nishnaabemwin, and thus consti-
                tute a lexicalization of the diminutive of kidwin, since its meaning is
                not 'little word,' but, rather, 'morpheme.'

LEXICAL         A verb having a passive meaning, but with an intransitive deriva-
PASSIVE         tional suffix, e.g., mnopgozi, 'ANsg tastes good,' which has VAI final
                /-(i)zi/. Compare INFLECTIONAL PASSIVE.

LEXICON         The vocabulary of a language, taken collectively. Speakers of a lan-
                guage have mental lexicons (memorized vocabularies) which con-
                tain information about each of the words they know.
1036 "LINK VOWEL



LINK VOWEL     A vowel that is inserted between two MORPHEMES in order to facili-
               tate pronunciation and preserve as much as possible the basic forms
               of the morphemes in question. For example, VAI verbs that end in
               NASAL CONSONANTS show a link vowel between the verb STEM and
               SUFFIXES beginning with a nasal, as in ndgoshnami(n), 'we (excl.)
               are arriving.' Here the basic morphological structure is
               /ni+dagoshin+min/, and the /a/ that is inserted between the verb
               stem and the suffix has no function (i.e., no meaning) other than to
               make pronunciation easier.

LOANWORD       A word 'borrowed' from another language. For example, many
               Nishnaabemwin speakers use the English word phone when speak-
               ing Nishnaabemwin, making phone a loanword (from English) in
               Nishnaabemwin.

LOCAL          In the discussion of VERB INFLECTION, especially the functioning of
               THEME SUFFIXES, used to refer to predications that involve only
               FIRST and SECOND PERSONS as ACTORS and GOALS, in other words,
               in which the verbal predication is strictly 'local' to the conversa-
               tional context of speaker and addressee. For example, gwaabmin, 'I
               see you,' is local, but gwaabmig, 'ANsg sees you,' is not, because
               there is a third person involved in the verbal action. Compare
               NON-LOCAL.

LOCATIVE       1. Characterizing any grammatical element used to specify a loca-
               tion, for example, maanpii, 'here' can be described as a locative
               adverb. 2. Referring to a noun that is inflected with a locative SUF-
               FIX, such asjiimaaning, 'in the boat.' In this usage, the locative suf-
               fix does not always specify a location, since it is also used to identify
               the object of relative roots, as in Mhiingning izhnaagzi gday, 'your
               (sg.) dog looks like a wolf,' in which the word mhiingan, 'wolf,' has
               a locative suffix indicating that it is the object of the RELATIVE ROOT
               /izh/.

LONG VOWEL     Designating the class of VOWELS in Nishnaabemwin which is pro-
               nounced with relatively long duration, and which are not subject to
               SYNCOPE. The long vowels of Nishnaabemwin are /ii/, /e/, /oo/, and
               /aa/.

LOW            Characterizing a VOWEL made with a relatively low tongue position.
               The low vowels of Nishnaabemwin are /a/ and /aa/. Compare HIGH,
               MID.
                                                                   METRICALLY WEAK •       1037



MACROROLE        Designating any of three INFLECTIONAL roles associated with
                 VERBS, the ACTOR and GOAL of TRANSITIVE VERBS, and the S-ROLE
                 (also often called SUBJECT) of INTRANSITIVE VERBS. The AGENT and
                 EXPERIENCER semantic roles typically fill the actor macro-role of
                 transitive verbs, and the RECIPIENT fills the GOAL role. If there is no
                 recipient, the goal role is filled by the semantic PATIENT.

MAIN STRESS      Referring to the syllable receiving the greatest prominence of pro-
                 nunciation in a word.

MAJOR CLASS      A primary PART OF SPEECH, in Nishnaabemwin including NOUNS,
                 PRONOUNS, VERBS, and ADVERBS.

MANNER OF        Specifying the way in which a CONSONANT sound is made. Manners
ARTICULATION     of articulation in Nishnaabemwin include STOPS, FRICATIVES,
                 AFFRICATES, NASALS, and GLIDES.

MASCULINE        Referring to any English word or expression that can have associ-
                 ated with it the PRONOUN he, that is, an expression that is grammati-
                 cally treated as male. This category has very little relevance to
                 Nishnaabemwin grammar.

MASS NOUN        A noun, such as nbiish, 'water,' that is perceived as a mass, and not
                 as something that can be counted. Other mass nouns represent
                 abstractions, such as gaawendmowin, 'jealousy.' Mass nouns are
                 rarely used in the PLURAL.

MEDIAL           The middle morphological component found in some Nishnaabem-
                 win words, always having a very nounlike meaning. For example, in
                 baatiinoogaade, 'have lots of legs,' the medial is /-gaad-/, 'leg'.
                 Compare INITIAL, FINAL.

METRICAL FOOT A grouping of Nishnaabemwin SYLLABLES, ideally consisting of a
              WEAK syllable (containing a short vowel) and a STRONG syllable
              (containing either a short vowel or a long vowel). See also DEFEC-
              TIVE FOOT, STRESS, SYNCOPE.

METRICALLY       Within the system of STRESS, occupying a STRESSED (emphasized)
STRONG           position. See STRESS.

METRICALLY       Within the system of STRESS, occupying an UNSTRESSED position.
WEAK             See STRESS.
1038 • MID


MID            Characterizing a VOWEL made with the tongue neither lowered nor
               raised. The mid vowels of Nishnaabemwin are /e/, /o/ and /oo/.
               Compare LOW and HIGH.

MID CENTRAL    Characterizing the location of the tongue body in the production of
               some vowels. Mid central vowels have the tongue body neither low-
               ered nor raised, and neither fronted nor backed, i.e., roughly cen-
               trally located in the mouth.

Mil FOCUS      A construction that uses the particle mii as a device to give particular
               emphasis to a particular syntactic constituent, such as a noun phrase.
               For example, in mii gwa naa maampii gaa-ndaakwiiyaan, 'it's here
               that I shot from' (AM39.574), mii is used to focus on a particular
               location.

MINIMAL PAIR   Two words, of different meaning, that are pronounced the same
               except for one sound difference, which occurs at the same PHONO-
               LOGICAL position within the word. For example: bmose 'walk
               along,' and bmise 'fly along,' differ only by the presence of/o/ in the
               first and I'll in the second.

MODAL          The term modal is problematic for Nishnaabemwin, because it is the
               adjective form of both MODE and MOOD. See MOOD and MODE.

MODE           A system of endings on VERBS that indicate whether the action is
               viewed as completed relative to some point of reference, or the
               speaker's casting of a statement as true, conjectural, or based on tra-
               ditional knowledge.There are four modes in Nishnaabemwin, NEU-
               TRAL (or INDICATIVE), which shows no marking on the verb, and
               PRETERIT, DUBITATIVE, and PRETERIT DUBITATIVE. See each of
               these.

MODIFIER       An element which qualifies or specifies another in some way. For
               example, the NOUN PHRASE niizhkwewag, 'two women,' has the
               modifier niizh, 'two,' specifying the number of kwewag, 'women.'
                                                                   MORPHOPHONOLOGY •         1039



MOOD             Referring to the speaker's attitude towards a PREDICATION, as
                 expressed grammatically. In Nishnaabemwin, INDICATIVE MOOD
                 indicates a straightforward assertion of truth, as in Wiisni Zhaabdiis,
                 'John is eating.' MODAL MOOD adds some measure of possibility or
                 obligation, as in Daa-wiisni Zhaabdiis, 'John should/could/would
                 eat.' In Nishnaabemwin there is a single mood preverb, daa-, which
                 covers the range of meaning of most of the English modal auxiliary
                 verbs, such as should, could, would, might, and may.

MORPHEME         A fundamental, structurally identifiable component of a word. For
                 example, the word nwiisin, 'I am eating,' has two morphemes, /ni-/,
                 first person (independent order), and /wiisini/, 'eat' (VAI VERB). The
                 verb mnogaadewag, 'ANpl have nice legs,' has five morphemes,
                 /minw-/, 'good,' /-gaad-/, 'leg,' /-e/ VAI final 'have,' /-w/, third per-
                 son, and /-ag/, 'animate plural.' The study of morpheme patterns in a
                 language is called MORPHOLOGY.

MORPHOLOGI-   Refers to any word or portion of a word that is made up of more than
CALLY COMPLEX one identifiable element. For example, the word kidwin, 'word,
              utterance' is morphologically complex, because it can be said to
              consist of the elements kido, 'speak,' and -win, which makes an
              ABSTRACT NOUN. Most words in Nishnaabemwin are morphologi-
              cally complex.

MORPHOLOGY       The study of words and their component parts, called MORPHEMES.

MORPHOPHO-       An element used to identify a constituent phonological unit within a
NEME             morpheme, which is realized by more than one phoneme. In Nish-
                 naabemwin, there are two morphophonemes, /N/, realized as /n/ and
                 /zh/, and /S/, realized as /s/ and /sh/.

MORPHOPHONO-     A MORPHOPHONOLOGICAL RULE IS a PHONOLOGICAL RULE whose
LOGICAL RULE     operation is restricted to particular morphologically defined con-
                 texts, in other words, applies to a particular MORPHEME or class of
                 morphemes in the presence of other morphemes.

MORPHOPHO-       Relating to how MORPHEMES are 'spelled,' that is, how their constit-
NOLOGY           uent sounds are specified with respect to the PHONEMES of the lan-
                 guage.
1040 • MORPHOSYNTACTIC WORD



MORPHOSYN-        A WORD-FORM specified for its morphological and syntactic proper-
TACTIC WORD       ties. For example, the word-form gwaabmigoo represents both the
                  second person singular PASSIVE form, "you (sg) are seen,' and that of
                  a FIRST PERSON PLURAL acting on a SECOND PERSON SINGULAR, 'we
                  (excl) see you (sg),'

MUTUAL            The state obtaining between two forms of speech A and B, such that
INTELLIGIBILITY   A can understand B and B can understand A. The forms of speech,
                  for example, may be those of two different communities. If there is
                  mutual intelligibility between communities, the communities are
                  said to speak the same LANGUAGE. If there is not mutual intelligibil-
                  ity, they are said to speak different languages. This term is relative,
                  however, since speakers vary in how much they can understand of
                  another variety of speech.

/N/               A symbol used in the representation of those MORPHEMES that show
                  an alternation between /n/ and /zh/, for example, gmiinin, 'I give Y
                  to you,' versus miizhiyan, '(if) you give Y to me.' The basic stem
                  form of the word meaning 'give Y to AN' is written as /miiN/.


/rj/              A velar nasal, such as the last sound in English sing.

NASAL (CONSO-     A CONSONANT sound made by stopping the flow of air in the mouth,
NANT)             but lowering the VELUM (soft-palate) so that air is free to flow out
                  through the nose. The nasal consonants of Nishnaabemwin are /m/
                  and /n/.

NASAL ASSIMI-     The phonological process whereby a nasal changes its PLACE OF
LATION            ARTICULATION to be like that of a following consonant. For exam-
                  ple, the final /n/ ofdgoshin, 'ANsg arrives,' becomes VELAR before a
                  /g/, as in dgoshing, '(if) ANsg arrives.'

NASAL COMPLEX A term I use to refer to any CLUSTER of CONSONANTS containing a
              nasal element (/n/, /m/, or /rj/).

NASALIZED         Referring to ORAL sounds that are produced in some phonological
                  contexts with the SOFT PALATE (velum) lowered, so as to allow the
                  passage of air out through the nose. Long vowels in Nishnaabemwin
                  are sometimes nasalized, and are spelled with a following «nh», as
                  in boodoonh, 'tadpole.'
                                                                           NISHNAABEMWIN • 1041


NATURAL            In PHONOLOGY and MORPHOLOGY, characterizing a rule that is found
                   widely throughout the languages of the world, and can be explained
                   on the basis of sound general principles. For example, the rule of
                   devoicing in Nishnaabemwin, which changes the pronunciation of
                   /b/, /d/, and /g/ to [p], [t], and [k], respectively, is a very natural rule.
                   The rule which produces an alternation of /n/ and /zh/ in words such
                   as nmiinaa, 'I give it to her/him,' versus miizh, 'give it to her/him!'
                   is very unnatural. Many linguists would argue that this alternation is
                   so unnatural that it should not be considered a regular phonological
                   rule of Nishnaabemwin grammar.

NATURAL CLASS Constituting a group of sounds which share features and behave
              similarly in terms of their PHONOLOGICAL behaviour. For example,
              the sounds /b/, /d/, /g/, /z/, /zh/, and /j/ all constitute a natural class of
              VOICED STOPS in Nishnaabemwin, on the basis of their shared fea-
              tures and their behaviour in DEVOICING at the end of a word.

NEGATIVE           Making a negative assertion, as opposed to a POSITIVE one. For
                   example, wiisni sa, 'ANsg is eating,' is positive, but gaawii go
                   wiisnisii, 'ANsg is not eating,' is negative. Negative verbs are said to
                   have negativity POLARITY, and positive verbs, positive polarity. See
                   POLARITY, POSITIVE.

NEUTER             Referring to any English word or expression that can have associ-
                   ated with it the PRONOUN it, that is, an expression that is grammati-
                   cally treated as neither male nor female. This category has little
                   relevance to Nishnaabemwin grammar, since the GRAMMATICAL
                   GENDER contrast is ANIMATE and INANIMATE.

NIPISSING          A DIALECT of Anishinaabemowin (Ojibwe) spoken in the area of
ALGONQUIN          Maniwaki, Quebec, but historically spoken over a wider area.

NiSHNAABEG         PLURAL form of Nishnaabe, the Nishnaabemwin self-designation
                   for a member of the group of Ojibwe people. May also be used to
                   refer to any kind of North American aboriginal person.

NlSHNAABEM-        A term used to refer to the DIALECTS of Anishinaabemowin
WIN                (Ojibwe) spoken in southwestern Ontario, extending north to Mani-
                   toulin Island. Nishnaabemwin dialects come historically from
                   Odawa, Chippewa, Potawatomi, and perhaps other languages and
                   dialects.
1042 • NOMINAL



NOMINAL          A NOUN, PRONOUN, or PARTICIPLE functioning as an ARGUMENT of a
                 verb in a sentence. Example, bemaadzid, 'a person,' lit., 'one who is
                 living').

NON-HIGH         Used to distinguish the VOWELS III and /ii/ from /e/, the former being
VOWEL            articulated with the tongue placed relatively high in the mouth,
                 while the latter having the tongue placed relatively lower, and is thus
                 NON-HIGH. High vowels often cause PALATALIZATION of adjacent
                 consonants.

NON-LOCAL        In the discussion of VERB INFLECTION, used to refer to predications
                 that involve at least one THIRD PERSON as ACTOR or GOAL, in other
                 words, in which the verbal predication is not strictly 'local' to the
                 conversational context of speaker and addressee, but includes refer-
                 ence to someone or something outside of the conversational context
                 of speaker and addressee. Compare NON-LOCAL.

NON-PLURAL       The suffix /-n/ that occurs on TRANSITIVE INANIMATE (VTI) verbs
                 having SINGULAR ACTORS in the INDEPENDENT ORDER, such as
                 nwaabndaan, 'I see it,' (from /ni+waaband+am+n/), has been ana-
                 lyzed as having a meaning 'non-plural,' because it does not seem to
                 occur with plural actors, for example, nwaabndaanaan, 'we see
                 INsg,' (from /ni+waaband+am+naan/).

NOTIONAL         A grouping of objects on the basis of some shared feature of mean-
CLASS            ing, such as a grouping of the different kinds of berries, or of transi-
                 tive verb finals that have a meaning component of transport. Often
                 such notional classes show different alignments than structur-
                 ally-defined groupings do. See FORMAL.

NOUN             A word that identifies a person, place, or thing, has a P
                 (unless it is a MASS NOUN), a DIMINUTIVE, and a PEJORATIVE, and
                 may be POSSESSED, etc. Examples include zhiishiib, 'duckSjiimaan,
                 'boat,' and kidwin, 'word.'

NOUN CLASSES     1. The different classes, or groupings, of nouns on the basis of their
                 shared INFLECTIONAL behaviour, for example, how they form their
                 PLURALS and their DIMINUTIVES. There are 7 basic noun classes in
                 Nishnaabemwin. 2. The gender system classifying nouns into ani-
                 mates and inanimates.
                                                                           OJIBWE • 1043


NOUN PHRASE   A SYNTACTIC group consisting of a NOUN and any associated words,
              usually NUMBERS or DEMONSTRATIVE PRONOUNS in Nishnaabew-
              min.

NUCLEUS       The VOWEL portion of a SYLLABLE.

NUMBER        1. A number, one of the basic PARTS OF SPEECH of Nishnaabemwin.
              For example, bezhig, 'one,' niizh, 'two,' etc. 2. Referring to the mor-
              phological system having the categories SINGULAR and PLURAL, the
              latter of which is often marked on NOUNS and VERBS.

NUMBER ROOT   A root of a LEXEME that is a number. For example, the lexeme niizhi,
              'be two in number' (VAl), has a number root, /niizh/, 'two.'

NUMBER VERB   A VERB that specifies how many of something there is; for example,
              niizhwag ngwisag, 'my sons are two in number,' has number verb
              niizhi, 'be two in number.'

NUMBER PRE-   A PREVERB that specifies how many of something there is; for exam-
VERB          ple, niizhi-, 'be two.'

OBJECT        See PRIMARY OBJECT, SECONDARY OBJECT.

OBSTRUENT     The classes of CONSONANTS including STOPS, FRICATIVES, and
              AFFRICATES, taken as a group. Any member of this group.

DEVIATION     Referring to a system in Algonquian languages for keeping THIRD
              PERSONS distinct from each other. One third person in a sentence is
              made proximate, and other third persons are then obviative. Also
              called fourth person. Compare PROXIMATE, BACKGROUNDING.

OBVIATIVE     A THIRD PERSON in a sentence that is backgrounded relative to some
              other third person. For example, in Gii-baashkzwaan nini moozoon,
              'the man shot the moose,' moozoon, 'moose' is obviative, and is so
              indicated by means of an obviative SUFFIX. Compare PROXIMATE.

ODAWA         A DIALECT of Anishinaabemowin (Ojibwe) spoken along the eastern
              and northern shores of Lake Huron.

OJIBWE        A CENTRAL ALGONQUIAN LANGUAGE spoken in many REGIONAL
              dialects, including Algonquin, Mississauga, Chippewa, Saulteaux,
              Northern Ojibwe and Oji-Cree. Most dialects refer to the language
              as Anishinaabemowin.
1044 • OJI-CREE


OJI-CREE          A DIALECT of Anishinaabemowin (Ojibwe) spoken in northwestern
                  Ontario, called Anishininiimowin by its speakers.

ONOMATOPOEIA The process of naming a thing on the basis of the way it sounds, e.g.,
             gookookhoo, 'owl.' Birds are often so named in Nishnaabemwin.
             See also REDUPLICATION, ARBITRARY.

OPTATIVE          Any construction or form that is used to express wishes. Some
                  speakers of Nishnaabemwin use mbegish, as in Mbegish ndawaa
                  bbaaa-giiwsed, 'I wish he would go out and hunt.'

ORAL CAVITY       The interior region of the mouth, especially when distinguished
                  from the NASAL CAVITY.

ORDER             Used to refer to distinct INFLECTIONAL SYSTEMS for indicating par-
                  ticipants (ACTORS and GOALS) on verbs. There are three orders in
                  Nishnaabemwin, INDEPENDENT, CONJUNCT, and IMPERATIVE. Each
                  has its own way of indicating participants, for example, gwiisin,
                  'you (sg.) are eating,' is independent order, and indicates a SECOND
                  PERSON SUBJECT by means of a prefix /g-/; wiisniyan, '(if/when) you
                  (sg.) eat,' is conjunct, and indicates a second person subject by
                  means of a suffix, /-yan/; wiisnin, 'eat!' is imperative, and indicates
                  a second person subject by means of a suffix /-n/. Each way of indi-
                  cating the actor (in this case, second person singular) is thus differ-
                  ent for the different orders.

ORDINAL NUM-      A number EXPRESSION that represents a ranking in a series as
BER               opposed to an exact amount, such as e-ntam, 'first,' and
                  eko-niizhing, 'second.' Compare CARDINAL NUMBER.

ORTHOGRAPHY       A system for writing a language. See also STANDARD ORTHOGRA-
                  PHY.

OTTAWA            A DIALECT of Anishinaabemowin (Ojibwe) spoken in Michigan and
                  perhaps represented in Wisconsin.

PALATAL           Referring to a sound made in the area of the HARD PALATE of the
                  roof of the mouth, by raising the tongue. For example, /y/ is a palatal
                  glide in English and Nishnaabemwin.
                                                                              PATIENT • 1045



PALATALIZED      Referring to the pronunciation of consonants by which one of a pair
                 has a more PALATAL pronunciation than the other. For example, in
                 Nishnaabemwin, some morphemes show an alternation between /d/
                 and /j/, as in naadsabii, 'ANsg checks a net,' versuse naajmiijme,
                 'ANsg goes to get food.'

PARADIGM         A list of all the possible INFLECTIONAL forms of a word of a given
                 grammatical category.

PARTICIPLE       A VERB FUNCTIONING as a NOUN in a sentence, and which carries
                 special inflections to identify it as a nominal. For example,
                 bemaadzijig, 'people,' is a participial form of the verb bmaadzi, 'be
                 alive, live' (VAI). See also DEPARTICIPIAL NOUNS.

PARTICLE         Designating a small class of emphatic and expressive words that do
                 not readily fit into any other PART OF SPEECH category. Particles
                 include sa, go, dash, and oonh.

PARTITIVE        Referring to some part of a group or individual.

PART OF SPEECH Representing one of the basic classes of words in the language,
               defined on the basis of both morphological and syntactic behaviour.
               The parts of speech of Nishnaabemwin are nouns, verbs, adverbs,
               numbers, and particles. Also called WORD CLASS or LEXICAL CLASS.

PASSIVE VOICE    1. Designating a DERIVATIONAL TRANSITIVE VERB form which has
                 repressed the SEMANTIC ROLE of AGENT or EXPERIENCE^ shows
                 INTRANSITIVE INFLECTION of a TRANSITIVE VERB STEM, and has its
                 S-ROLE (SUBJECT) filled with something that is semantically the
                 PATIENT or RECIPIENT of action. Example: nwaabmigoo, 'I am seen.'
                 2. Designating a derivational intransitive verb that has a passive der-
                 ivational element and passive meaning, e.g., mnopgozi, 'AN tastes
                 good.' See INFLECTIONAL PASSIVE and LEXICAL PASSIVE.

PATIENT          The semantic role of the one affected by the action of an AGENT; the
                 object experienced by an EXPERIENCED Example: in baazhkzwaad,
                 'shoot AN,' the person or thing shot is the patient. Patients often fill
                 the GOAL MACROROLE of a TRANSITIVE VERB. See SEMANTIC ROLE.
1046   • PEJORATIVE



PEJORATIVE            A special form of a noun that indicates the speaker regards the per-
                      son or object being referred to with distaste, contempt, or displea-
                      sure. For example, gaazhgens, 'cat,' has a pejorative form
                      gaazhgenzhish, which might be translated in English as 'darned cat,'
                      or 'damned cat.' Compare CONTEMPTIVE.

PERSON                In grammar, indicating one of the three grammatical persons: FIRST
                      PERSON, referring to the speaker; SECOND PERSON, referring to the
                      addressee; and THIRD PERSON, referring to the topic of conversation.

PERSON PREFIX         A prefix appearing on a NOUN or VERB that indexes the PERSON of an
                      associated NOUN or PRONOUN, as either FIRST PERSON (speaker),
                      SECOND PERSON (addressee), or THIRD PERSON (spoken about). The
                      person prefixes of Nishnaabemwin each have several forms, for
                      example, first person may be indicated with «n», «nda-», «ndi-», or
                      «ndoo-», as in ngwis, 'my son,' and ndi-kid, 'I say.'

PERSONAL              A PRONOUN which identifies an individual on the basis of their role
PRONOUN               in the communicative act. The FIRST PERSON SINGULAR pronoun,
                      mm, for example, refers to the speaker.

PHONE                 Any discernible unit of pronunciation in a language. For example,
                      the phone [k] occurs at the end of most Nishnaabemwin speakers'
                      pronunciation of mik, 'beaver,' and gnebig, 'snake.' A phone may
                      represent a possible pronunciation of more than one PHONEME in a
                      language. Compare PHONEME.

PHONETIC              A writing system designed for representing speech independently of
ALPHABER              a particular language's spelling system (orthography). Phonetic
                      alphabets strive to have a particular symbol (usually a letter) for
                      each sound found in language.

PHONEME               A distinctive sound in a language. Each phoneme may be realized by
                      several pronunciations, called the ALLOPHONES of the phoneme.
                      Phonemes are represented in writing by putting them within slashes,
                      for example, /b/, /p/, /sh/, and /ii/.

PHONETIC              Concerned with fine details of pronunciation, typically involving
                      how a given distinctive sound (phoneme) is pronounced in a particu-
                      lar context.
                                                                            PLURAL « 1047



PHONOLOGICAL     Relating to the sound system of a language; having to do with the
                 behaviour of phonemes.

PHONOLOGICAL     The set of distinctive sounds in a language, usually organized in
INVENTORY        terms Of CONSONANTS and VOWELS.

PHONOLOGICAL     A rule of a language that specifies how phonemes are pronounced,
RULE             or which specify processes that apply to phonemes. For example,
                 one phonological rule of Nishnaabemwin specifies that final short
                 vowels and glides are deleted in nouns and verbs.

PHONOTACTICS     The patterns of phoneme sequences permitted in a language, usually
                 organized in terms of what consonants are allowed at the beginning
                 and ends of SYLLABLES, and what vowel sequences are allowed in
                 the syllable NUCLEUS.

PHRASE           A grouping of words to form a unit, organized around a HEAD word.
                 For example, the NOUN PHRASE niizh kwewag, 'two women,' con-
                 sists of a NUMBER and a head noun. Phrases are named for the cate-
