                 gory of their heads, such as here, where the whole phrase is called a
                 noun phrase because the head of the phrase is a noun.

PHRASE           Designating the structural relationships of hierarchy (which domi-
STRUCTURE        nates which) and precedence (which comes first) among the mem-
                 bers Of a PHRASE, CLAUSE, Or SENTENCE.

PLACE OF         Specifying where in the VOCAL TRACT a given CONSONANT sound is
ARTICULATION     made. For example, /b/ and /p/ are BILABIAL, /g/ and /k/, VELAR.

PLAIN CONJUNCT A verb form showing conjunct order inflection, but no initial change.
               For example, the first verb in Pit dash gii-bzigwiiyaan,
               gaa-zhi-gnabseyaang, '(but) when I stood up, we capsized,' is in
               plain conjunct and the second (with gaa-) is CHANGED CONJUNCT.
               Compare CHANGED CONJUNCT.

PLAINS           Used to designate the Algonquian languages spoken on the central
(ALGONQUIAN)     Plains of North America, including Arapaho, Blackfoot, and Chey-
                 enne.

PLURAL           Designating more than one of a thing. For example, zhiishiibag,
                 'ducks,' is the plural ofzhiishiib, 'duck' and nmadbiwag, 'they are
                 sitting,' is the third person plural form of the verb nmadbi.
1048 • POLARITY



POLARITY            Involving the contrast POSITIVE and NEGATIVE. Positive statements
                    are said to have positive polarity, and verbs inflected for negative are
                  1
                    said to have negative polarity. See NEGATIVE.

POSITIVE           Making a positive assertion, as opposed to a NEGATIVE one. For
                   example, wiisni sa, 'ANsg is eating,' is positive, but gaawii wiisnisii,
                   'ANsg is not eating,' is negative.

POSSESSED          1. A word that has had a possessive suffix -im attached to it, as in
THEME              wjiimaanim, 'ANsg's boat.' 2. The POSSESSIVE suffix -im.

POSSESSIVE         Designating a nominal construction in which the owner, controller,
                   or basis of relationship of a noun is specified by means of possessive
                   AFFIXES. For example, njiimaan(im), 'my boat,' is a possessive con-
                   struction, because the owner (or controller) ofjiimaan, 'boat,' is
                   specified by means of the prefix /ni-/, 'my.'

POSSESSOR          The one who owns or controls a thing. For example, in nikaad, 'my
                   leg,' niin, 'I,' am the possessor, and -kaad, 'leg' is the POSSESSUM.

POSSESSUM          The persons or things that are possessed in a POSSESSIVE construc-
                   tion. For example, in nzhiishiibminaanig, 'our (incl.) ducks,' the
                   possessum is zhiishiibag, 'ducks.' Compare POSSESSOR.

POST-CONSO-        A /w/ or /y/ that occurs directly after a consonant. For example, the
NANTAL GLIDE       /w/ in ndamwaa, 'I'm eating it (anim.), is post-consonantal, since it
                   follows an /m/. Some noun stems are commonly analyzed as having
                   final (post-consonantal) glides that are deleted by a phonological
                   rule of SHORT VOWEL AND GLIDE DELETION.

PRACTICAL          A writing system designed to be easily rendered with conventional
ORTHOGRAPHY        equipment, such as typewriters and computers.

PRAGMATIC          Referring to interpretations that are based on the social, cultural and
                   physical conditions and context in which language is used.

PREDICATE          Generally used in this work to refer to a VERB in a CLAUSE or SEN-
                   TENCE, especially when semantic aspects of the verb are at issue,
                   SUCh as its SEMANTIC ROLES.

PREFINAL           A divisible, meaningful portion of a final, usually having a relatively
                   concrete meaning, and distinguishable from the more abstract por-
                   tion of the final, which defines the lexical subclass of the word.
                                                                     PRETERIT MODE • 1049



PREFIX          A morpheme attached to the front of a stem. For example, /ni/ in
                nwaabmaa, 'I see ANsg,' is a prefix.

PREFIXAL-D      A PHONOLOGICAL (pronunciation) rule which inserts a /d/ between a
INSERTION       PERSON PREFIX and a STEM beginning with a VOWEL, e.g., as in
                ndankii, 'I am working,' from /ni+anokii/.

PRE-FORM        A general term for elements that can serve as pre-units (preverbs,
                prenouns, pre-adverbs) to more than one part of speech, e.g., dso-,
                'so many,' occurs with verbs, such as dso-bboon'gizi, 'ANsg is so
                many years old' (VAi), and dso-dbahaabaan, 'so many gallons' (Ni
                or AV).

PRE-MEDIAL      An element occurring before the explicitly nominal element of a
                medial, e.g., /-aa/ in /-aagonag-/, 'snow' (cf. goon, 'snow') and
                /-aakom-/, 'louse' (cf. /-ikom-/, possessed stem of/ikwa/, 'louse').

PRENOUN         An element which may be compounded to the front of a NOUN, to
                signal information such as size, colour, etc. For example, in
                gchi-Nishnaabe, 'elder,' the prenoun gchi-, 'great,' is added to the
                noun, Nishnaabe, 'Indian.'

PRETERIT MODE   1. With verbs, one of the four verbal modes; the preterit refers to a
                set of PARADIGMS used to express verbal predications that took place
                in the past and are no longer taking place, or in which the predica-
                tion precedes in time some reference predication that also took place
                in the past. Example: Ngoding dash go naa e-naabid shkweyaang
                aw ngashi ngii-waabmig aazhi go [gii-bkobiisewaambaa]. 'But at
                one time as my mother looked back, she saw [that I had indeed
                fallen into the water].' (AM5.4). 2. With nouns, indicates a form
                having a SUFFIX with /-ban/, usually indicating that the referent is
                deceased, e.g., nmishoomsiban, 'my late grandfather.'
1050 • PRETERIT


PRETERIT          One of four verbal MODES. The preterit dubitative is used to indicate
DUBITATIVE        an action, event, or state terminated in the past and for which the
MODE              speaker does not have firsthand knowledge. It is especially common
                  in narratives representing traditional knowledge, such as an aadsoo-
                  kaan (myth). Preterit dubitative mode inflectional forms often com-
                  bine PRETERIT inflections with DUBITATIVE, and this mode does
                  indeed represent the conjunction of these two modes. Example:
                  Nebozh giiwenh gii-bmosegban ddibew, 'Nenabush was, according
                  to tradition, walking along the shore.' Also called DUBITATIVE PRET-
                  ERIT. See MODE.

PREVERB           An element which may compounded to the front of a verb, to signal
                  information such as tense, direction, etc. For example, in
                  gii-ni-giiwe, 'ANsg went back home,' gii- and ni- are both preverbs.
                  Each preverb is set off with its own hyphen.

PRIMARY           Designating the object of the verb that receives inflectional indexing
OBJECT            by means of theme signs and other inflections. In Nishnaabemwin,
                  the primary object of DITRANSITIVES is the RECIPIENT or BENEFI-
                  CIARY, i.e., the typically human object, or what is commonly called
                  the indirect object in English. Compare SECONDARY OBJECT.

PRIMARY STRESS See MAIN STRESS.

PROCESS           Referring to a verb PREDICATION which shows change and/or devel-
                  opment. Nishnaabemwin verbs often show a systematic ambiguity
                  between STATIVE and PROCESS readings, e.g., booknike can mean
                  both 'break one's arm' (a PROCESS) and 'have a broken arm' (a
                  STATE). Compare STATE.

PROHIBITIVE       Designating a NEGATIVE IMPERATIVE form, such as gego
                  wiisnike(n), 'don't (you sg.) eat!'

PRONOUN           A basic part of speech, consisting of many small classes of words
                  that serve various grammatical functions associated with nouns and
                  nominals. Pronoun sets in Nishnaabemwin include PERSONAL PRO-
                  NOUNS, DEMONSTRATIVE PRONOUNS, INTERROGATIVE PRONOUNS,
                  DUBITATIVE PRONOUNS, and PAUSAL PRONOUNS, among others.

PRONUNCIATION The way in which a word is pronounced, to be distinguished from
              the way that it is spelled.

QUIAN
PROXIMAL         A category of DEMONSTRATIVES, referring to the closest degree of
                 proximity, e.g., maaba and maanda in Nishnaabemwin. Compare
                 DISTAL and REMOTE. Not to be confused with PROXIMATE.

PROXIMATE        Referring to an ANIMATE NOUN that is not marked OBVIATIVE. Prox-
                 imate refers to the category of a foregrounded THIRD PERSON, as
                 opposed to the backgrounded, which is OBVIATIVE.

PURPOSE          A CLAUSE that specifies the purpose for doing something. For exam-
CLAUSE           ple, the clause in square brackets in the following sentence serves to
                 identify a purpose: Aapji dash gii-mkadekewag naangodnong giw
                 dash shkinweg gye go shkniikweg [iw gegoo wii-gkendmowaad iw
                 waa-bwaadmowaad], 'Sometimes they fasted very much, those
                 young men and women, [in order to obtain that knowledge which
                 they were to get in a dream].' (AM23.5)

QUANTITY         Referring to the relative duration of a vowel pronunciation. SHORT
                 vowels are pronounced roughly half as long as LONG vowels.

QUANTIFIER       A word or expression which specifies the amount of some other
                 entity, e.g., niizh ninwag, 'two men,' has the quantifier niizh, 'two.'

REANALYSIS       The process of reinterpreting MORPHOLOGICAL structures over time.
                 For example, historically the word for 'ANsg's pipe' was
                 odoopwaaganan, which had the morphological structure
                 /od+opwaagan+an/. Many speakers have reanalyzed the /o/ of the
                 stem to be part of the prefix, and now treat the person prefix as
                 /doo-/ and the noun as /pwaagan/. The prefix /doo-/ is then used else-
                 where, even with stems that historically did not begin with /o/.

REASON CLAUSE A clause that expresses the reason for some action or event, as in Mii
              niinaa gaa-nji-ninaanh gbe-zhebaa wii-maajtaayin, 'That's why I
              told you all morning to get started.'
1052   • RECIPIENT



RECIPIENT            A SEMANTIC ROLE specifying the receiver of something transferred.
                     For example, in the sentence semaa ngii-miin 'goo, 'I was given
                     tobacco,' 7 (first person singular) is the recipient.

RECIPROCAL           Designating a situation in which the ACTOR and GOAL act upon each
                     other, as in waabmidwag, 'they see each other.' Reciprocals are
                     formed by adding VAI FINAL /-idi/ to a VTA VERB.

RECONSTRUC-          The linguistic process of determining the forms of a parent language
TION                 based on the traits of daughter languages. For example, one may
                     study the verb systems of two daughter languages, in order to recon-
                     struct the verb system of the parent language.

REDUCED              Characterizing VOWELS which are pronounced with relatively less
                     energy* with short duration and with less movement from the rest
                     position of the tongue. A fully reduced vowel is not pronounced at
                     all.

REDUCED              Pronouns, SUCh as INDEFINITE PRONOUNS and INTERROGATIVE PRO-
NOMINAL              NOUNS, which fail to distinguish all of the grammatical categories
PRONOUN              relevant to nouns, such as plural versus singular NUMBER.

REDUPLICATION A MORPHOLOGICAL process that copies a part of a word and then
              adds the copied part onto the word as a PREFIX (in Nishnaabemwin).
              For example, neniizh, 'two by two,' has a reduplicated first SYLLA-
              BLE, consisting of a copy of the /n/ of niizh, 'two,' together with the
              VOWEL Id.

REFERENT             A term used to indicate the people and objects in the "real" world
                     that are referred to by linguistic forms, especially NOUNS. A term
                     such as kwe, 'woman,' without any additional specification, has as
                     its referents all women; a more precise reference can be made by
                     using modifiers such as maaba kwe, 'this woman.'

REFLEXIVE            Designating a situation in which an ACTOR acts upon herself or him-
                     self. In Nishnaabemwin REFLEXIVE verbs have VAI FINAL /-idizo/, as
                     in waabmidzo, 'ANsg sees self.'

RELATIVE             A clause which identifies a referent. Example: waa-bi-zhaajig,
CLAUSE               'those who will come'; naagaanzid, 'the one leading.'
                                                                         SAULTEAUX • 1053


RELATIVE PAST    Time reference to something past relative to something already past.
TENSE            Example: Ngoding dash go naa e-naabid shkweyaang aw ngashi
                 ngii-waabmig [aazhi go gii-bkobiisewaambaanh], 'Once when my
                 mother looked back, she saw [that I had already fallen into the
                 water].' Here the falling into the water is prior to the looking back,
                 which is itself past tense.

RELATIVE         The PREVERB form of a RELATIVE ROOT. Relative preverbs in Nish-
PREVERB          naabemwin are zhi-, nji-, piichi-, ko-, dzhi-, and dso-. See RELATIVE
                 ROOT.

RELATIVE ROOT Specifying one of six ROOTS that function to relate a verb to some-
              thing else. The relative roots in Nishnaabemwin are /iN/, /ond/,
              /apiit/, /akw/, /daN/, and /daS(w)/. Relative roots and RELATIVE PRE-
              VERBS often cause INITIAL CHANGE in associated verbs.

RELATIVIZE       To make into a RELATIVE CLAUSE form.

REMOTE           Referring to a demonstrative pronoun that refers to objects at a third
                 degree of distance from the speaker. For example, in Odawa, the
                 PROXIMAL ANIMATE DEMONSTRATIVE is maabd, and the DISTAL is
                 aw (also wa); the remote is wedi. See PROXIMAL, DISTAL.

ROOT             A core component of a word, occupying the first positional slot
                 within a word's derivational structure. The term root is usually
                 restricted to morphologically simple elements, as opposed to initials,
                 which can be complex. Also called an INITIAL.

ROUNDED          Characterizing a VOWEL or GLIDE made with the lips rounded. The
                 rounded vowels of Nishnaabemwin are /o/ and /oo/. The glide /w/ is
                 also rounded. Some CONSONANTS also have lip-rounding associated
                 with them, notably /g/ and /k/ when they are followed by an /o/ or
                 /oo/.

/S/              A symbol used in the representation of those MORPHEMES that show
                 an alternation between /s/ and /sh/, for example, gdasin, 'I put
                 you...,' versus ashiyan, '(if) you put me...' The basic stem form of
                 the word meaning 'put AN (someplace)' is written as /aS/.

SAULTEAUX        A dialect of Anishinaabemowin (Ojibwe) spoken in Manitoba,
                 Saskatchewan, Alberta, and extreme western Ontario.
1054 • SCHWA



SCHWA            A minimal vowel, involving minimal movement of the tongue from
                 rest position. Example: the first sound in the English word about.

SECOND PERSON The grammatical PERSON of the addressee, that is, the one spoken to,
              corresponding to English 'you.' See PERSON.

SECOND           A loose term for the position of certain CLITIC elements, such as the
POSITION         YES/NO QUESTION PARTICLE na, or the EMPHATIC element dash.
                 Usually these elements come directly after the first word in their
                 clauses, which I call SECOND POSITION. Technically, though, they are
                 ENCLITICIZED to the first word in the clause, and so have no position
                 of their own.

SECONDARY        Designating the less (inflectionally) prominent object of a DITRANSI-
OBJECT           TIVE verb, typically filling the semantic role of PATIENT, i.e., repre-
                 senting the non-human object transferred or affected in some way.
                 Compare PRIMARY OBJECT.

SECONDARY        Characterizing a SYLLABLE that receives some STRESS (emphasis),
STRESS           but not as much as the syllable receiving main (PRIMARY) stress.

SEGMENT          Any individual sound, corresponding to a PHONEME, such as /b/, /ii/
                 or/h/.

SEMANTIC         Having to do with meaning.

SEMANTIC ROLE One of a small set of roles that are associated with verbs, such as
              AGENT, the one initiating an action, and PATIENT, the one undergo-
              ing whatever action is undertaken by the agent. For example, in
              nganwaabmaa, 'I look at ANsg,' the FIRST PERSON is in the role of
              AGENT, the one looking, and the THIRD PERSON SINGULAR is in the
              role of PATIENT, or receiver of the role.

SEMANTIC ROLE A chart that shows the SEMANTIC ROLES of a VERB, along with the
CHART         elements filling those roles, and how the SEMANTIC ROLES are real-
                 ized as MACROROLES.

SEMI-VOWEL       A GLIDE consonant, /w/ or /y/.

SENTENTIAL       A complement that is itself a clause. E.g., Maanii gii-dbaajma
COMPLEMENT       [Rogeran gii-ni-boontaad], 'Mary said that Roger quit.' Here the
                 complement of gii-dbaajma is the entire clause within brackets. See
                 COMPLEMENT.
                                                                              STATIVE • 1055



SEXUAL GENDER A system of GENDER (noun classification) based all or in part on sex-
              ual (MASCULINE and FEMININE) properties of REFERENTS.

SHORT VOWEL       One of the class of VOWELS in Nishnaabemwin which are pro-
                  nounced with relatively short duration and are subject to SYNCOPE
                  and other PHONOLOGICAL PROCESSES which delete vowels. The
                  short vowels of Nishnaabemwin are /a/, /i/, and /o/.

SIMPLIFICATION The phonological processes of CONSONANT adjustment that take
               place when consonants are juxtaposed due to the SYNCOPATION of a
               VOWEL between them. For example, the word giisoog, 'months,'
               shows a simplification of the /z/ and /s/ of the singular, giizis, that
               have been juxtaposed by the syncopation of the short vowel /i/
               between them.

SLASHES           The character /, used in writing to set off PHONEMES, e.g., Pol repre-
                  sents a phoneme as opposed to a PHONE or a letter. See also PHO-
                  NEME, PHONE.

SOCIOLECT         A form of language shared by members of a particular social group,
                  such as men or women, young or old, rich or poor.

SQUARE            The characters "]" and "]", used to set off PHONETIC elements
BRACKETS          (PHONES), as Opposed to PHONEMES or written LETTERS.

S-ROLE            Designating the single SEMANTIC MACROROLE associated with an
                  INTRANSITIVE VERB. This term is of my own devising. Often the sin-
                  gle role of an intransitive is called a SUBJECT.

STAGING           In reference to SUBORDINATE CLAUSES which provide background
                  information for a MAIN verb. For example, Debkadnig
                  gii-dgoshnoog, 'they arrived just at dark,' has debkadnig, 'when it
                  got/was dark,' as a staging expression.

STANDARD          A widely-accepted standardized way of writing a language. A stan-
ORTHOGRAPHY       dard is designed to allow a language to be written in a consistent
                  way by different writers, whose individual pronunciations may vary.

STATIVE           Referring to an ongoing (minimally changing) state of affairs. E.g.,
                  zhmaagnishiiwi, 'be a soldier,' is a STATIVE VERB, attributing a rela-
                  tively static (unchanging) quality to its SUBJECT. Compare PROCESS.
1056 • STEM



STEM             1. The basic core of word, consisting of the word minus any inflec-
                 tional affixes; 2. Any word to which an additional affix is added (see
                 BASE).

STEM-INITIAL     Referring to a sound (SEGMENT) that is the first in a stem. For exam-
                 ple /j/ is stem-initial mjiimaan, 'boat.'

STOP             A CONSONANT made by stopping the flow of air momentarily some-
                 where in the VOCAL TRACT. The stop consonants of Nishnaabemwin
                 are /b, p, d, t, g, k, h/.

STRESSED         Within the system of syllable prominence in a language, stressed
                 syllables are those that receive greater prominence, such as the sec-
                 ond syllable of the word photography and the first syllable of the
                 word photograph.

STRONG           With reference to SYLLABLES and VOWELS, designates those which
                 receive prominence in pronunciation. Also called STRESSED. See
                 STRESS, SYNCOPE.

STRUCTURE        Patterning based on the form or shape of things. For example, a verb
                 in Nishnaabemwin such as mnogaade, 'have nice legs,' has a struc-
                 ture consisting of three identifiable components, an INITIAL /minw/,
                 a MEDIAL /-gaad-/ and a FINAL /-e/. Each of these components repre-
                 sents a STRUCTURAL SLOT.

STRUCTURAL       An identifiable position within a pattern. For example, the word
SLOT             damnosiiwag, 'they (anim.) are not playing,' has several structural
                 positions, the first filled by the VERB damno, 'play,' the second by
                 the NEGATIVE SUFFIX, /-sii/, the third by the independent order third
                 person suffix /-w/, and the last by the ANIMATE PLURAL SUFFIX /-ag/.

STRUCTURAL-W Involving a spelling convention used by some writers of Nishnaabe-
             mwin, in which the third person prefix /o/, which is usually deleted
             by SYNCOPE, and thus not pronounced, is spelled with «w», as in
             wnik, 'ANsg's arm,' or wzaaghaan, 'ANsg loves ANobv'

SUB-CLASS        Designating one of the sub-categories of a basic PART OF SPEECH.
                 For example, verbs (a basic part of speech) in Nishnaabemwin are
                 sub-classified into VTA, VTI, VAI, and vn.
                                                                         SYNTAX • 1057



SUB-DIALECT    A recognizable sub-group of a DIALECT. For example, within the
               dialect complex of Nishnaabemwin, the speech of each community
               may be said to represent a distinct sub-dialect.

SUBORDINATE    See DEPENDENT CLAUSE.
CLAUSE

SUBORDINATOR   A PREVERB that serves to mark a verb as being subordinate, or
               dependent on, another verb. An example is a- (changed form e-).

SUBSTANTIVE    See CONTENT QUESTION. Compare YES/NO QUESTION.
QUESTION

SUBSTITUTE     A PRONOUN such as nahii, 'watchamacallit,' that can be used to sub-
PRONOUNS       stitute for a word that one is trying to remember.

SUFFIX         A MORPHEME attached to the end of a stem. For example, /igw/ in
               nwaabmig, 'ANsg sees me,' is a suffix.

SUPERLATIVE    Designating the most extreme degree of a qualitative descriptive
               expression. For example, in English the superlative form of an
               ADJECTIVE is often made by adding SUFFIX -est, as in biggest, oldest.

SYLLABLE       A unit of sound consisting of a VOWEL and associated CONSONANTS.
               In Nishnaabemwin, a word always has as many syllables as it does
               vowels. For example, the word jiimaan, 'boat,' has two syllables.

SYNCOPATED     Designating a vowel that has been deleted by SYNCOPE.

SYNCOPE        The rule associated with Nishnaabemwin STRESS that deletes
               UNSTRESSED (WEAK) vowels. For example, in waagosh, 'fox,' an /o/
               appears in the last SYLLABLE, but in waagshag, 'foxes,' this /o/ has
               been deleted (is not pronounced) by the operation of the rule of syn-
               cope. Syncope is one of the most important rules of Nishnaabemwin
               phonology.

SYNTACTIC      The grammatical rules of a language involving relationships among
STRUCTURE      words, phrases, clauses and sentences, and focusing especially upon
               the what elements make up a unit, what the main element (HEAD) of
               a unit is, and the order and grouping of elements within a unit.

SYNTAX         The study of how words are put together to form PHRASES, CLAUSES,
               and SENTENCES.
1058 • SYNTHETIC



SYNTHETIC          Characterizing an approach to language research and presentation
                   that proceeds by putting related items together and seeking to deter-
                   mine general principles at work in the overall system of language.
                   For example, a synthetic approach to verb inflection might involve
                   laying out paradigms which show all of the inflectional possibilities
                   of the language. The system can then be analyzed to determine its
                   component elements and the principles at work in their interaction
                   with each other. Compare ANALYTIC.

TA VERB            A transitive verb having an animate goal. In this work, usually
                   abbreviated VTA.

TEMPORAL           Having to do with time or the specification of time.

TEMPORAL           A noun, derived from a verb, that represents a time, a day, a month,
NOUN               or a season. For example, giizhig, 'day' Nl.

TENSE              Relating to the time of the action or state specified by a VERB. The
                   three tenses of Nishnaabemwin are PRESENT, PAST, and FUTURE.

TERM OF            Used to denote the form of a noun used in making REFERENCE, for
REFERENCE          example, when referring to one's grandfather, the term of reference
                   is nmishoomis. This is contrasted with a vocative form, used to
                   directly address someone, and which may be distinct from the term
                   of reference. See VOCATIVE.

TEXTUAL CON-       The location of a linguistic form, such as a NOMINAL, a CLAUSE, or a
TEXT               SENTENCE, within a linguistic context, that is, the context in which a
                   given word or sentence occurs relative to other words and sentences
                   in the discourse.

THEME              1. A SEMANTIC ROLE specifying the thing transferred in a verb of
                   transfer. For example, in the sentence semaa ngii-miin'goo, T was
                   given tobacco,' semaa, 'tobacco,' is the theme. 2. A THEME SUFFIX.

THEME SUFFIX       L A SUFFIX that occurs with TRANSITIVE VERBS, indicating either a
                   LOCAL GOAL, or a relative relationship when a THIRD PERSON is
                   involved in a PREDICATION. 2. The suffix /-im/ occurring on many
                   possessed nouns.

TI VERB            A transitive verb having an inanimate object. In this work, usually
                   abbreviated VTI.
                                                                  UNSPECIFIED ACTOR • 1059



TOPICALITY       A grammatical ranking of PERSON, GENDER and DEVIATION catego-
HIERARCHY        ries relevant to the choice of TRANSITIVE THEME SIGNS, PERSON PRE-
                 FIXES and SUFFIXES in Nishnaabemwin NOUN and, especially, VERB
                 INFLECTION. The topicality hierarchy specifies the ranking 2 > 1 > X
                 > 3 > 3' > 0, in which 2 outranks 1, and so on.

TRACHEA          The windpipe. Air passes from the lungs into the trachea and from
                 there into the oral and nasal cavities in the production of speech
                 sounds.

TRANSFER VERB A term used by the author to refer to transitive verbs which involve
              the transfer of something from a source to a RECIPIENT, e.g., miizh
              (or miinizh), 'give Y to AN,' and bi-niindaah, 'send Y t o AN.' Such
              verbs are always VTA, and the recipient always fills the MACROROLE
                 of GOAL.

TRANSITIVE       1. Referring to a verb that has more than one SEMANTIC ROLE associ-
                 ated with it, and in the prototypical case, there is transfer of action
                 from actor to goal, such as mshiimin ndamwaa , 'I am eating the
                 apple,' where there is a role of one eating, and of one eaten. Com-
                 pare to wiisni, 'ANsg is eating,' where the only role is that of an
                 eater. Compare INTRANSITIVE. 2. Referring to a verb that is used
                 with an object, such as Jiimaan ndadaawen, T sold a boat.'

TRUNCATION       A morphological process which derives a form by taking material
                 away from the BASE. In Nishnaabemwin, truncation is sometimes
                 used to form VOCATIVES, such as nmishoo, 'grandfather,' formed
                 from stem /mishoomis/.

UNIVERSAL        The word kina, 'all, every,' and associated phrases in Nishnaabem-
QUANTIFIER       win, which indicate that all member of some group fit a particular
                 description or requirement.

UNROUNDED        Characterizing VOWELS and GLIDES that lack ROUNDING of the lips
                 in their articulation.

UNSPECIFIED      Designating a GRAMMATICAL ROLE in certain verbs in which the
ACTOR            semantic role of actor is either not specified, as in PASSIVES, or very
                 general, as in general activity statements. For example, in passive
                 nwaabmigoo, T am seen (by some unspecified actor),' the actor is
                 unspecified— such an actor must exist, in order for the transitive
                 verb to be used, but the actor is not specified.
1060 • UNSTRESSED



UNSTRESSED          Within the system of SYLLABLE prominence in a language,
                    unstressed syllables are those that receive little or no prominence,
                    such as the third syllable of the word photography. In Nishnaabem-
                    win, METRICAL FEET ideally consist of a WEAK (UNSTRESSED) sylla-
                    ble followed by a STRONG (STRESSED) syllable.

VAI                 An INTRANSITIVE VERB with an ANIMATE SUBJECT (S-ROLE).

VAIO                An INTRANSITIVE VERB which can optionally be inflected for a
                    THIRD PERSON GOAL (either ANIMATE or INANIMATE).

VARIANT             Any distinguishable version of some linguistic element. For exam-
                    ple, a PHONEME such as /aa/ can be pronounced with several vari-
                    ants, or a VERB form may have different variants among different
                    speakers, for example ngii-googiimin, 'we (excl.) dove,' versus
                    ngii-googiimi.

VARIETY             Any identifiable form of speech, whether that of an individual, a
                    community, a social group, or a language.

VELAR               Of CONSONANTS, articulated in the region of the SOFT PALATE
                    (VELUM), the back of the mouth. The velar consonants of Nishnaa-
                    bemwin are /g/, /k/ and /rj/.

VELUM               The soft palate, that is, the soft portion at the back of the roof of the
                    mouth.

VERBAL POLAR-       See POLARITY.
ITY

VERB MEDIAL         A construction which has a VERB in the middle, such as English
                    clauses, e.g., I see you, where the verb is the middle element, flanked
                    by the SUBJECT and the OBJECT.

VERB OF ABUN-       A verb that specifies that something exists or is present, formed by
DANCE               adding the vn FINAL /-kaa/ to a NOUN STEM, e.g., miishkoonskaa,
                    'there is (a lot of) grass' VII.

VERB OF             Designating a Nishnaabemwin VTA VERB such as wiidbim, 'sit with
ACCOMPANI-          AN,' in which the ACTOR of the VERB specifies someone who
MENT                accompanies, assists, or associates with the ANIMATE GOAL in some
                    way. Sometimes called COMITATIVES.
                                                                       VOCAL TRACT • 1061



VERB OF ADDIC- A VAI verb having the final /-ishki/, almost always indicating a
TION           socially-dispreferred inclination or habitual behaviour. E.g.,
               gtimshki, 'be a lazy person,' in which /-ishki/ is added to gtimi, 'be
               lazy.'

VERB OF BEING     1. Referring to verbs formed by combining the FINAL element /-wi/,
                  'be,' (VAI) or /-wan/ (VII) with a NOUN INITIAL, as in gwiiwzenswi,
                  'be a boy,' or oodenaawan, 'be a town or village.' 2. In reference to
                  the verbs aawi (VAI) and aawan (VII), 'be an X.'

VERB OF IDEN-     A verb used to identify someone or something as being a particular
TITY              thing. The verbs of identity are aawi VAI and aawan VII.

VERB OF           Referring to animate intransitive verbs (VAI) formed with the final
MAKING            element /-ke/, 'make, gather, get,' such as kokbinaagnike, 'make
                  baskets,' or ziizbaakdoke, 'make (maple) sugar.' These verbs have a
                  DERIVATIONAL structure consisting of a noun INITIAL, to which is
                  added the VAI FINAL /-ke/. Their meanings vary between making,
                  gathering, hunting, and other socially constructive activities.

VERB OF           A verb that specifies a number, such as niizhwag, 'they are two (in
NUMBER            number).'

VERB OF           Referring to ANIMATE INTRANSITIVE VERBS (VAI) formed by com-
POSSESSION        bining the FINAL element /-i/, 'have,' with a noun INITIAL formed
                  from the THIRD PERSON SINGULAR POSSESSIVE, as in wzhoonyaami,
                  'ANsg has money' (with NOUN INITIAL wzhoonyaam, 'ANsg's
                  money') or wniijaansi, 'ANsg has (a) child(ren),' (with noun initial
                  wniijaanis, 'ANsg's child').

VII               An INTRANSITIVE VERB taking an INANIMATE SUBJECT (S-ROLE).

VOCAL CORDS       Also called vocal folds. Bands of muscle and tissue in the LARYNX
                  that can be drawn closely together and made to vibrate when air is
                  forced through them. Sounds made in this fashion are said to be
                  VOICED; sounds made with vocal cords apart, and thus not vibrating,
                  are said to be VOICELESS.

VOCAL TRACT       That part of human anatomy that is involved in the production of
                  speech, including the lungs, TRACHEA (windpipe), LARYNX (voice-
                  box), the oral cavity (and its parts) and the nasal cavity.
1062 • VOCATIVE


VOCATIVE          Referring to a form of a NOUN that is used in direct address. For
                  example, the vocative form of nmishoomis, 'my grandfather,' is
                  nmishoo, used when directly addressing one's grandfather. See also
                  TERM OF REFERENCE.

VOICE             Designating whether the casting of a TRANSITIVE VERBAL PREDICA-
                  TION is ACTIVE VOICE, that is, from the perspective of the SEMANTIC
                  AGENT or EXPERIENCER, or PASSIVE VOICE, that is, from the perspec-
                  tive Of the PATIENT Or RECIPIENT. See ACTIVE VOICE, PASSIVE VOICE.

VOICED            Referring to a sound which is produced with vibration of the VOCAL
                  CORDS. In Nishnaabemwin, all VOWELS are voiced, as are the CON-
                  SONANTS /b/, /d/, /g/, /z/, /zh/, /j/, /w/, /y/, /m/ and /n/. OBSTRUENTS
                  in Nishnaabemwin are represented in voiced and voiceless pairs,
                  e.g., voiced /b/ has voiceless partner /p/, etc. Compare VOICELESS.

VOICELESS         Referring to a sound which is produced with the VOCAL CORDS far
                  enough apart that they do not vibrate. In Nishnaabemwin, /p/, /t/, /k/,
                  /s/, /sh/, /ch/ and /h/ are all voiceless. OBSTRUENTS in Nishnaabem-
                  win are represented in voiced and voiceless pairs, e.g., voiced /b/ has
                  voiceless partner /p/, etc. Compare VOICED.

VOLUNTATIVE       Indicating a desire. Sometimes expressed in Nishnaabemwin with
                  the PREVERB wii-. Example: Aapji nii-damin gegoo. 'I really want to
                  play with something.'

VOWEL             One of the two basic classes of sounds in language, the other being
                  CONSONANTS. Vowels are generally produced by putting the VOCAL
                  CORDS together so that they vibrate (creating voicing), and putting
                  the tongue and lips into particular configurations. The vowels of
                  Nishnaabemwin are /a, i, e, o, ii, aa, oo/. Vowels may be SHORT or
                  LONG.

VOWEL             See BACKNESS.
BACKNESS

VOWEL HEIGHT      See HEIGHT.

VOWEL SYNCOPE The process of deleting (not pronouncing) UNSTRESSED vowels. See
                  SYNCOPE.

VTA               A TRANSITIVE VERB With an ANIMATE GOAL.
                                                                  YES/NO QUESTION •      1063



VTAI           See INVERSE ONLY VTA.

VTI            A TRANSITIVE VERB with an INANIMATE GOAL.

WEAK           In reference to syllables or vowels, designates those which are not
               stressed. See STRESS; UNSTRESSED.

WHEN-CLAUSE    A clause that specifies the time of an action or event. For example,
               Niibnini maa naa odi [gii-ndomndwaaji-wi-wzhibiihgewaad]. 'It
               was summer there [when they were called to go there to sign the
               treaty].' (AK10.20)

WORD-FINAL     Designating the last unit in a word. Usually in reference to sounds,
               e.g., /n/ is word final in the wordjiimaan, 'boat.'

WORD FORM      Any of the possible inflectional forms of a lexeme. For example,
               word forms associated with the LEXEME jiimaan, 'boat,' include the
               PLURAL jiimaanan, the LOCATlVEjiimaaning, and the various pos-
               sessed forms, such asjiimaanim, 'ANsg's boat.' See LEXEME, MOR-
               PHO-SYNTACTIC WORD.

WORDSTOCK      The vocabulary of a language. See LEXICON.

X              1. Designating an UNSPECIFIED ACTOR. Since TRANSITIVE VERBS in
               Nishnaabemwin theoretically require two roles, an ACTOR and a
               GOAL, in those predications corresponding to English passives, that
               is, those in which only the goal can be expressed, such as
               nwaabmigoo, 'I am seen,' the actor is considered unspecified, and
               any grammatical elements that make reference to the actor are said
               to be unspecified actor forms. 2. For intransitive verbs, used to iden-
               tify affixes associated with verbs naming generalized activity, such
               as niimhidim, 'there is a dance.'

YES/NO QUES-   A question that expects an answer of yes or no. In Nishnaabemwin
TION           such questions usually have na, e.g., Ndaa-ni-maajaa na go?, 'May
               I go?' Compare CONTENT QUESTION.
